units.la: CLARISSIMO & REVERENDO viro, omni eruditionis & virtutis genere praestantissimo, JOANNI DALLEO, APVD PARISIENSES fidelissimo Verbi Dei Ministro, S. P. D. I. M.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and reverend man, outstanding in every kind of learning and virtue, John Daillé, most faithful minister of the Word of God at Paris: greetings in the Lord.

units.la: ICET quicquid operum hactenus edidisti, Vir reverende, mihi plurimum placuerit, tum aque omnia, cum Latine, tum Gallicè scripta, aequali plausu ab eruditis, atque adeo à piis omnibus, excepta sint, fateri tamen non possum laborum tuorum primitias. Tractatum nempe de Patrum in decidendis de Religione Controversiis usu, me plurimum semper cepisse. Non solum enim opus istud mira rerum lectu & scitu jucundissimarum dignissimarumque varietate refertum est, verum etiam eloquentia orationisque nitor cum rebus ipsis certant, tantaque eruditione & facundia argumentum illud pertractasti, ut vix quicquam magis elaboratum erudito hoc saeculo prodiisse videatur. Cum ergo hoc tempore in hoc maxime incumbant praestantissima quaeque Gentis nostrae ingenia, ut in linguam nostram transfundant quicquid doctum, quicquid praeclarum habuit Antiquitas, existimavi me operae pretium facturum si in studio ab isto non multum alieno aliquid & ipse conarer, dumque nostratium auribus Latinorum Graecorumque Scripta accommodantur, vicissim & nostratium scriptum aliquod Latinitate donarem: sperans sic futurum, ut non solum ab exteris, & qui Gallicum nostrum sermonem
units.tr: Although I must admit that, of all the works you have so far published, reverend sir, I have been greatly pleased with every one, whether written in Latin or in French, and although all of them have been received with equal applause by the learned and indeed by all the godly, I cannot claim that your first fruits of labour are those works. I have always been most captivated by your treatise on the use of the Fathers in deciding the controversies of religion. This work is not only full of a remarkable variety of matters, most pleasant and most worthy to be read and known, but the elegance of its style and the polish of its language also vie with the subject matter itself. You have handled that subject with such learning and eloquence that scarcely anything more elaborate seems to have appeared in this learned age. Since at this time the most outstanding minds of our nation are especially devoted to this task, namely to render into our own tongue whatever is learned and admirable in antiquity, I judged that I would be doing a worthwhile service if I myself attempted something in a field not very far removed from this one. And while the writings of the Latins and Greeks are being fitted to the ears of our countrymen, I would in turn put into Latin some work of our own people, hoping that in this way I would win favour not only with foreigners and those who have not learned our French language, but also that I would refresh and restore a spirit almost cast down and prostrated by the most troublesome cares and by the most afflicted condition of the Church, over which God has set me.

units.la: non didicerunt, gratiam inirem. verum etiam animum molefliffimis curis & afflictissimo Ecclesiæ, cui Deus me præfecit, statu tantum non dejectum prostratumque hoc avocamenta reficerem & recrearem. Hujusmodi pratentamentum quoddam, in hoc ipso libro, cum superioribus annis, summus mihi amicus Claudius de Vineux, ὁ μαχαιρίτης, fidus Dei servus, Ecclesiæ Calniacensis Pastor, vidisset, à filio meo exercitationis gratia exaratum, hortari cum coram, tum per epistolas, quoad vixit, non destitit, ut quod non omnino infeliciter cœptum judicaret ad incudem revocarem & absolverem. Parvi ergo, eoque libentius quod non solum accepi hoc ipsum opus ab ornatissimo viro Tho. Smitho in Anglicum idioma translatum, verum etiam consilium hoc meum tecum communicatum non improbasti, futurumque non admisiti (quod & strenuè à te præstitum est) ut & interpretationem meam pro jure tuo recenseres & calligares & opus ipsum, tametsi per se jam numeris suis absolutum, variis è recondita tua eruditionis penu hausitis observationibus locupletares. Qua quidem de re est mihi quod gratulor, qui hoc meo consilio atque instituto factum videam, ne Ecclesia Dei utilissimis istis ad opus tuum additamentis careat. Quicquid autem in interpretanda tuo opere laboris impendit, id observantia in te mea publicum testimonium futurum tibi offero, utque ea fronte qua me ipsum soles, excipias rogo. Bene vale, vir mihi omnibus nominibus colende, & me, quod nulla meo merito sponte facis, porro amare perge. Augusta Veromanduorum Kal. Jan. 1654.
units.tr: Some years ago my dearest friend Claude de Vineux, ὁ μαχαιρίτης [the swordsman], faithful servant of God and minister of the Church of Calniacum, saw a sort of trial piece of this kind, which I had drawn up as an exercise for my son, in this very book. He urged me, both in person and by letters, for as long as he lived, not to give up, asking that I revise and complete what he judged had not been begun entirely unsuccessfully. So, I yielded, the more readily because I not only received this very work translated into the English language by the most distinguished man Thomas Smith, but also you did not disapprove of my plan, which I had shared with you, and you did not allow it to be that (as you have strenuously done) you would not both review and polish my translation as your right, and enrich the work itself, already complete in its own parts, with various observations drawn from the hidden store of your learning. For this I rejoice, since I see that this has been done by my plan and purpose, so that the Church of God may not lack those most useful additions to your work. Whatever labour I have spent in translating your work, I offer to you as a public testimony of my esteem, and I ask that you receive it with the same good grace with which you are wont to receive me. Farewell, sir, to be honoured by me in every respect, and continue to love me, which you do of your own accord though I have done nothing to deserve it. Augusta Veromanduorum, 1 January 1654.

units.la: ILLVSTRI FOEMINÆ ANNÆ MORNÆÆ ILLVSTRIVM VIRORVM PHILIPPI quidem MORNÆI filiæ, JACOBI verò DES NOVES TABARERII viduæ, JOANNES DALLÆUS S. P. D.
units.tr: To the illustrious lady Anne de Mornay, daughter of the illustrious Philippe de Mornay and widow of Jacques Des Noves Tabarerius: Jean Daillé sends his greetings.

units.la: PHILIPPUS DES NOVES, fani Herminiani Baro, tuus, Domina, dilectissimus filius, & spei dum vixit maximæ, & memoriæ, postquam vivere desiit, optimæ adolescens, cùm ante annos ferè quatuor in urbe versaretur, & in familiari quodam sermone ea apud me commemoraret quæ sibi quotidie homines aulici pro Romana Religione contra reformatam obiectarent, referebat eos in primis de antiquitate, verustissimorúmque Christianismi Doctorum consensu solitos fuisse gloriari, ita ut nihil frequentius, aut procacius quàm hæc nomina iactarent. Ac tametsi satis ipse per se intelligeret quàm futilis esset iliiusmodi obiectio, testabatur tamen gratissimum sibi fore, si in sui gratiam hoc argumentum paulò accuratius ac penitius explicarem. Feci quàm potui diligentissimè, & fusè quæ de eo mea esset sententia sum exsecutus. Quod cum ipsi placuisset, eóque spes facta esset posse & aliis esse usui, disputationem totam aliquanto post liteiis mandavi, & in hunc quem vides commentatium conjeci. Caeterum animus erat illi ipsi quicquid hujus est opusculi inferibere, in cujus gratiam id primùm meditatus eram, ut hoc, scilicet, qualicunque officio testarer, quanto juvandi ipsius in pietate profectus studio tenerer. Verùm cùm ille nobis, proh dolor! acerbissimo funere, florenti aetate, in celeberrima Sylvae-ducis obsidione ante biennium praereptus fuerit, neque jam nobis quicquam praeter mortales egregii adolescentis exuvias, praestantissimaeque virtutis memoriam, cum gravissimo ob tam immaturum factum dolore conjunctam superfit, nunc cogor consilium quod primum ceperam mutare. Neque enim placet hominem mortuum, & coelo, in meliorem vitam, receptum familiarter, velut adhuc apud nos versantem, compellare, tametsi non nescialm & olim fuisse, & nunc esse, qui aliter judicent, neque absurdum aut indecorum putent ad eos qui ex hac vita migraverint orationem convertere, & cum iis colloqui. Mihi verò cùm inane ac supervacaneum esse videtur absentem, & à nobis immensò spatio sejunctum, neque nostra audientem, affari, tum inhumanum ac propemodum impium, foeliciffimè procul à noftris certaminibus in Domino quiescentis pacem nostris sermonibus sollicitare. Videt jam ille in purissima luce constitutam veritatem, fruitur beata aeternitate, qua benignissimus servator ejus cum fidem, tum immotam in nominis sui timore perseverantiam coronavit. Satis igitur mihi erit eximiae virtutis, praestantissimi, ingenii, judicii acerrimi, suavissimae indolis, optimarúmque artium quibus ille instructus ac praeditus fuit, maximè verò singularis illius pietatis, quam tota vita excultam ad extremum usque spiritum constanter retinuit, jucundissimam memoriam usurpare, servare, summóque in pretio habere dum vivam. Libellum verò hunc tibi uni donari vel inscribi fas est; qui ei elaboratus ac destinatus fuerat, cujus tu quando sic Deo libuit, tametsi invitissima, ac praeter solennem naturae ordinem, praeterque que ardentissima & tua & nostra vota, hæres facta es. Ipsum opus fateor esse hujusmodi quod tibi, nisi me hæc, ut sic dicam, officii necessitas compulisset; nunquam oblaturus eram. Quam enim continet disputationem, ea omnis non modo à sexu studióque tuo, sed maximè etiam ab eo luxu aliena est in quo tu jam acerbissimo cum mœrore, versaris, carissimi conjugis morte nuper, cùm à filii funere vix respirares, afflicta atque oppressa. Sed cùm juris mihi antiquior quàm decori ratio sit, hunc libellum, tametsi alieno tempore, ad te mittere malui, quàm cum nonnulla cujusdam veluti furti conscientia, apud me detinere, qui tristissimè quidem à luctuosissimè, sed tamen justæ ac necessariæ hæreditatis jure tuus est. Accipe ergo, Domina, hanc supellectilis, quæ filii tui fuit, partem, quam per aliquod tempus apud me custoditam, nunc bona fide sub omnium oculis tibi repræsento, hoc uno forsan nomine non indignam quæ in seriniis tuis locum apud te habeat. Hoc enim unum à te nunc postulo. Nam præterquam quod eximia tua pietas, longè firmioribus nixa radicibus, nihil his disputationibus indiget, scio te tuäque eo loco esse, ut hæc sine tædio atque molestia legere jam non possis. Olim, si ita feret animus, tibi hæc nostra evoluere ac percurrere licebit, cum te deus Spiritus sui vi atque efficacia consolatus fuerit. Obnixissimè ab eo pero ut potentem manum tibi sublevandæ admoveat, ac in te, liberósque quotquot supersunt, omnigena gratiæ suæ dona largissimè effundat, eósque omnes salvos & incolumes tibi diutissimè felicissiméque confervet. Vale. Lutet. Parisi. 18. Kal. Septembr. 1631.
units.tr: PHILIPPUS DES NOVES, Baron of Fani Herminien, your dearest son, Madam, a young man of great promise while he lived and of the best memory now that he has ceased to live, was in the city about four years ago. In a familiar conversation he told me of the things that courtiers daily objected to him in defence of the Roman religion against the Reformed. He reported that they above all were accustomed to boast of antiquity and of the agreement of the most ancient doctors of Christianity, so that they hurled no names more often or more boldly than these. Although he himself understood well enough how flimsy such an objection was, he declared that it would be most welcome to him if, for his sake, I explained this subject somewhat more carefully and thoroughly. I did this as diligently as I could and set out at length my own opinion of it. When this pleased him, and there was hope that it might be useful to others as well, I committed the whole discussion to writing some time later and cast it into the little commentary you see. My intention, however, was to dedicate whatever this little work is to him, for whose sake I had first conceived it, so that I might bear witness, by this humble service, to how strongly I was moved by a desire to help his progress in piety. But since he was snatched from us, alas, by a most bitter death in the flower of his age, two years ago, during the famous siege of Bois-le-Duc, and nothing now remains to us except the remains of an excellent young man and the memory of his outstanding virtue, which is joined with a most grievous sorrow over so untimely a loss, I am now forced to change the plan I had first made. For it does not please me to address a man who is dead and received into heaven, into a better life, as though he were still living among us and speaking with us as a friend. Although I know that there have been, and still are, some who judge otherwise, and who think it neither absurd nor unseemly to turn one's speech to those who have departed this life and to converse with them, it seems to me empty and superfluous to address one who is absent and separated from us by an immense distance, and who cannot hear our words; and it seems inhuman, and almost impious, to disturb with our talk the peace of one who rests most happily in the Lord, far from our struggles. He now sees the truth set in the purest light, he enjoys blessed eternity, with which his most kind Saviour has crowned both his faith and his steadfast perseverance in the fear of his name. It will therefore be enough for me to keep and cherish, for as long as I live, and to hold in the highest regard, the most pleasant memory of his outstanding virtue, his excellent intellect, his very sharp judgement, his sweetest disposition, the fine arts with which he was furnished and endowed, and above all of that singular piety which he cultivated throughout his life and constantly preserved until his last breath. It is right, however, to offer and dedicate this little book to you alone. It was worked out and intended for him, and since God has been pleased to make you, though most unwilling, and contrary to the customary order of nature and to our most ardent wishes and yours, his heir. I confess that the work itself is of such a kind that I would never have offered it to you, had not the necessity of this duty, if I may so call it, compelled me. For the whole discussion it contains is not only far removed from your sex and your pursuits, but above all from that grief in which you now live, crushed and overwhelmed by the recent death of your dearest husband, and when you had scarcely begun to recover from the funeral of your son. But since the claim of right is older than the consideration of propriety, I preferred to send this little book to you, though at an unfitting time, rather than keep it with me under a certain sense of almost theft. It belongs to you by the right of an inheritance, most sorrowful and mournful indeed, but still just and necessary. Accept then, Madam, this part of the household goods that belonged to your son. I have kept it for some time, and now I present it to you in good faith before everyone's eyes, perhaps not unworthy, for this one reason alone, of a place among your own chests. For this is the only thing I now ask of you. Your outstanding piety, resting on far firmer roots, has no need of these discussions, and I know that you and your affairs are in such a state that you cannot now read these things without weariness and distress. Someday, if your mind is so inclined, you will be able to turn over and run through these pages of mine, once God has consoled you by the power and efficacy of his Spirit. I earnestly pray him to stretch out his mighty hand to lift you up, and to pour out the gifts of his grace in every kind most abundantly upon you and upon your children, whoever of them survive, and to keep all of you safe and sound for as long as possible and in the greatest happiness. Farewell. Paris, 18 days before the Kalends of September, 1631.

units.la: TOTIVS OPERIS SYNOPSIS & Argumentum.
units.tr: Synopsis and Argument of the Whole Work

units.la: PATRES non possunt sedere iudices in controversiis quae Romanam Ecclesiam inter & Protestantes hodie iactantur. I. Quia, si non impossibile, saltem difficillimum est, quid super illis senserint liquidò & definitè constituere. II. Quia cum eorum sententia (etiamsi certò de ea constaret) non sit infallibilis, nec extra erroris aleam omnem constituta, non tantum habet authoritatem ut in ea acquiescere possit animus, qui in iis quae ad religionem pertinent, nec potest, nec debet alia credere, quàm ea de quorum veritate sibi certò constat.
units.tr: The Fathers cannot sit as judges in the controversies that are today being raised between the Roman Church and the Protestants. I. Because, if not impossible, it is at least very difficult to determine clearly and definitely what they thought about those matters. II. Because, even if their opinion could be known for certain, it is not infallible, nor established beyond every chance of error, and so it does not carry such authority that a mind which, in matters pertaining to religion, neither can nor ought to believe anything except what it is certain is true, could rest in it.

units.la: Prior ratio probatur his argumentis.
units.tr: The first reason is proved by the following arguments.

units.la: I. Patrum, maximè primi, secundi & tertii saeculi, pauca scripta habemus.
units.tr: I. We have few writings of the Fathers, especially of the first, second and third centuries.

units.la: II. Quae habemus illius aetatis scripta de rebus alienissimis ab hodiernis controversiis agunt.
units.tr: II. The writings we do have from that age deal with matters very remote from today's controversies.

units.la: III. Scripta, quae Patrum nomen praeferunt, eorum revera non sunt omnia, sed pleraque, seu olim, seu postremis saeculis conficta.
units.tr: III. The writings that bear the name of the Fathers are not, in truth, all theirs; most of them were composed either in ancient times or in the later centuries.

units.la: IV. Genuina Patrum scripta multis in locis tempore, imperitia, fraude, vel pia, vel maligna, antiquis & posterioribus saeculis adulterata fuerunt.
units.tr: IV. The genuine writings of the Fathers were in many places corrupted, in both ancient and later centuries, through time, ignorance, and fraud, whether pious or malicious.

units.la: V. Difficile est Patrum scripta intelligere, tum propter linguas & idiomata quibus utuntur, tum propter rerum explicandarum variis plerumque Rhetorica figuris & ornamentis, Dialecticis, aculeis & argutiis, & huiusmodi artibus obscuratam & impeditam rationem, tum quod vocabula, ut plurimum, longè alio, quàm qui nunc in usu est, sensu usurpent.
units.tr: V. It is difficult to understand the writings of the Fathers, partly because of the languages and idioms they use, partly because their reasoning is obscured and hindered by the rhetorical figures and ornaments they use for explaining things, by dialectical barbs and subtleties, and by arts of this kind, and partly because they generally use words in a sense quite different from the one now in use.

units.la: VI. Quantumlibet diserte posita sententia in Patris alicujus scripto occurrat non possumus ideo statuere ipsum in ea fuisse, cùm saepe aliena à mente sua scripserint, seu aliorum sententias suppresso nomine referant (quod frequenter in Commentariis faciunt) faciant) seu in disputationibus cum adversariis; quo in scriptorum genere aliud dicere, aliud sentire sibi licere autumant, seu quid sentiant, dispensatione aliqua dissimulent, ut in homilius, quo ad captum quorundam auditorum suorum se accommodent.
units.tr: VI. However clearly a statement may be expressed in the writing of some Father, we cannot therefore conclude that he himself held it, since they have often written things far from their own mind, or report the opinions of others without naming them (as they frequently do in commentaries), or do so in disputations with opponents. In this kind of writing they think it permissible to say one thing and feel another. Or they conceal what they think by some dissimulation, as in homilies, where they adapt themselves to the understanding of some of their hearers.

units.la: VII. Posito conflare Patrem quempiam sententiam, ut suam referre, inquirendum nihilominus fuerit qua atate in ea fuerit, an nondum, vel jam maturis studiis. Nonnunquam enim iis accidit, ut senes ea revocaverint, qua juvenes censuerant.
units.tr: VII. Even granting that some Father put forward an opinion as his own, it must still be inquired at what age he held it, whether before or after mature study. For it sometimes happens that, when old, they retracted what they had held as young men.

units.la: VIII. Verum, posito quod Pater quispiam in aliqua sententia fuerit, disputiendum est quo modo, & quo fidei gradu in ea fuerit, num eam tanquam necessariam, vel probabilem tantum, habuerit, & rursus quo in gradu necessitatis & probabilitatis eam collocaverit, cum fidei articuli non sint ex aquo omnes vel necessarii, vel probabiles.
units.tr: VIII. But granting that some Father held a certain opinion, it must be discussed in what way, and with what degree of faith, he held it: whether he regarded it as necessary or only as probable, and again in what degree of necessity or probability he placed it, since the articles of faith are not all equally necessary or equally probable.

units.la: IX. Videndum deinde erit an sententiam illam tanquam suam ipsius privatam; (tum enim necessario de fide non esset) an tanquam a sui seculi Ecclesia receptam referat,
units.tr: IX. Next it must be considered whether he reports that opinion as his own private view (for then it would not necessarily be a matter of faith), or as received by the Church of his own age.

units.la: X. Tum distinguendum erit num illam universali, an vero particulari tantum Ecclesiae tribuat, cum qua sententia sunt in pleraque Ecclesia promiscue recepta, ea non semper ab omnibus & singulis ejus partibus retenta fuerint.
units.tr: X. Then it must be distinguished whether he attributes it to the universal Church or only to a particular Church, since opinions commonly received in most churches were not always retained by all and each of their parts.

units.la: XI. Denique, seu omnes in universum Christiani seu Pastores omnes tantum Ecclesiae nomine intelliguntur consilare non potest qua fuerit seculo aliquo integro totius Ecclesiae sententia, cum saepe accidat, ut eorum, qui sunt alicujus nominis, sententia non recipiantur, immo nonnunquam in dubium vocentur & repudientur a privatis & obscuris ejusdem Ecclesiae hominibus, qui cateroquin de doctrina & pietate cum reliquis contendere poterant, quorum proinde non minor ratio quam illorum habenda erat.
units.tr: XI. Finally, whether by the Church one understands all Christians in general or all ministers only, it cannot be determined what the view of the whole Church was in any entire century, since it often happens that the opinion of those of some reputation is not accepted, and is sometimes even called into doubt and rejected by private and obscure men of the same Church, who nevertheless could contend with the others concerning doctrine and piety, and whose view therefore deserves no less consideration than theirs.

units.la: Ratio II. Neque testimonia, neque documenta Patrum esse infallibilia, argumentis sequentibus confirmatur.
units.tr: Reason II. That neither the testimonies nor the documents of the Fathers are infallible is confirmed by the following arguments.

units.la: I. Sibi, suisq; nudis assertionibus simpliciter & absolute non esse fidem adhibendam ipsi Patres testantur.
units.tr: I. The Fathers themselves testify that their own statements and bare assertions are not to be trusted simply and absolutely.

units.la: II. Ea ratione scribunt, ut facile sit videre eos, dum scriberent, nihil minus quàm de nobis judicandis cogitasse.
units.tr: II. They wrote in such a way that it is easy to see that, while they were writing, they had thought of nothing less than judging us.

units.la: III. In variis capitibus hallucinati sunt, vel singuli seorsum, vel simul complures.
units.tr: III. They went astray in various matters, either each one separately or several together.

units.la: IV. Acriter alii ab aliis dissident; nec inter se etiam de quibusdam magni momenti consentiunt.
units.tr: IV. They disagree sharply with one another, and they do not even agree among themselves on some matters of great importance.

units.la: V. Denique, si quod res est fatemur, neutra pars eos pro judicibus agnoscit, sed eos libere & nulla religione interdum rejicit. Utrique multa ponunt quæ apud Patres nulla fuerunt, multaq; vicissim repudiant quæ illi recipiebant. Protestantes quidem, cùm illi contra, vel præter Scripturam docent: Romani vero cum suis sive Pontificibus, sive Conciliis adversantur. Cùm ergo utrique suum authoritatem aliis judicibus tribuant, licet divina per se essent Patrum authoritas; idonea tamen non est ad eorum dirimendas controversias, vel ad pacem inter eos conciliandam.
units.tr: V. Finally, if we confess the truth, neither side acknowledges them as judges; rather, each sometimes rejects them freely and without scruple. Each side sets forth many things which were not held among the Fathers, and in turn rejects many things which they accepted. The Protestants indeed do so because the Fathers teach things against or beyond Scripture; the Romanists oppose them with their own Popes or Councils. Since therefore each side ascribes authority to other judges, even if the authority of the Fathers were in itself divine, it is nevertheless not suitable for settling their controversies or for reconciling peace between them.

units.la: Ex quibus sequitur de nostris controversiis alias, quàm per ipsorum scripta, disceptandum esse mediis, & eam in religione methodum sequendam, quæ in aliis omnibus disciplinis observatur, ut de quibus inter nos convenit, ea ad controversia illustranda adhibeamus: utriusque partis accurate collatis conclusionibus cum uniuscujusque principiis, ab utraque, sive in ratione, sive in revelatione divina, confessis. Patres vero ipsos sedulo legendos, & sine ulla sive in hanc, sive in illam partem anticipata opinione, adeo ut in eorum monumentis, non nostras, sed ipsorum sententias quæramus, ductis argumentis ex iis quæ apud ipsos occurrunt, negative potius quàm affirmative, id est ut dubia habeamus ea capita quæ apud ipsos nulla exstare deprehenduntur, cum non fiat verisimile, adeo præstantes viros, articulos fidei principes & maximè necessarios, ignorasse; non tamen quæ apud eos habentur statim pro veris certisfi, omnia pariter admittamus. Cùm enim homines, licet sancti fuerint, fieri potest, ut nonnunquam hallucinati sint; sive ex simplici mentis errore, sive etiam, ex aliquo animi studio, atque affectu; à quo non fuisse eos plane immunes ex ipsorum, quæ supersunt, scriptis perspicuè apparet.
units.tr: From these things it follows that our controversies must be decided by other means than the writings of the Fathers, and that in religion we should follow the method observed in all other disciplines: that is, we should use, to illustrate the controversy, those points on which we agree, carefully comparing the conclusions of each party with the principles of each, admitted by both, whether in reason or in divine revelation. The Fathers themselves, however, are to be read diligently and without any preconceived opinion, either for this side or for that, so that in their works we seek not our opinions but theirs. Arguments should be drawn from what occurs among them, rather negatively than affirmatively; that is, we should regard as doubtful those points which are found to be nowhere present among them, since it is not likely that such eminent men, the principal and most necessary teachers of the articles of faith, were ignorant of them. Yet we should not at once accept as true everything that is held among them. For although men, even if holy, may sometimes be led astray, either by a simple error of mind or also by some zeal or passion of the spirit; and it is clear from the surviving writings of the Fathers that they were not wholly free from this.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: VIcQUID hodie Romanam Ecclesiam inter & Protestantes in Religione controversiarum est, id omne versatur in quibusdam capitibus quæ magni ad fidem momenti esse, omninóque ad salutem pertinere. Romana quidem Ecclesia contendit, Protestantes verò negant. Quæ enim Protestantes ipsi credunt, quibúsque Religionem contineri existimant, ea adeo perspicuæ & indubitatæ sunt veritatis ut ab adversariis, non minùs quàm ab ipsis agnoscantur & recipiantur; quippe quæ perspicuè in Scripturis doceantur, diserte à Veteribus Conciliis & Doctoribus probentur, & uno animo ferme ab omnibus, qui usquam fuerunt, Christianis, toto orbe, recipiantur. Hujusmodi sunt, exempli causa, hæc quæ sequuntur dogmata. Unum esse summum Deum, Creatorem cœli & terræ: hominem ad ejus imaginem creatum, excussoejus obedientiæ jugo, cum omnibus posteris, in summám & æternam calamitatem incidisse, peccatoq;, tanquam lethali lepra, contaminatum, reumque Dei iræ, & ejus maledictioni obnoxium. Creatorem ejus misertum, mira clementia filium suum Jesum Christum in mundum misisse. Hunc vero Dei Filium Deum esse cum Patre æternum. Hunc assumpta, in B. Virginis utero, carne nostra, in ipsa fecisse & pertulisse quæcumque erant ad salutem nostram necessaria, expiatis, maximè, in suo sanguine peccatis nostris: Istis confectis, in cœlum ascendisse, & ad dexteram Patris consedisse, indeq; aliquando venturum, ut genus humanum judicet, singulisq; secundum opera ipsorum reppendat: Illum ipsum, ut nobis impertiat salutem quam meritus est, nobis largiri Spiritum suum Sanctum à Patre & Filio procedentem, unumq; & eundem cum illis Deum, ita ut tres ista persone sint unus & solus Deus bene-
units.tr: Whatever controversies there are today in religion between the Roman Church and the Protestants, they all turn on certain chapters that are of great weight for faith and wholly pertain to salvation. The Roman Church maintains them, but the Protestants deny them. For the things the Protestants themselves believe, and think make up their religion, are so plainly and indubitably true that they are acknowledged and accepted by their adversaries no less than by themselves, since they are clearly taught in the Scriptures, expressly proved by the ancient Councils and Doctors, and received by almost all Christians everywhere in the world with one mind. Of this kind, for example, are the following doctrines: That there is one supreme God, Creator of heaven and earth; that man, created in his image, shook off the yoke of his obedience and fell with all his posterity into supreme and eternal calamity, and, polluted with sin as with a deadly leprosy, became liable to the wrath and curse of God. That their Creator, moved by pity and with wonderful clemency, sent into the world his Son Jesus Christ. That this Son of God is God, eternal with the Father. That he, having taken on our flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin, did and suffered in it all that was necessary for our salvation, above all making expiation for our sins in his own blood; and, this being accomplished, ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of the Father, and from there will at some time come to judge the human race and to repay each one according to his works; that he himself, in order to bestow on us the salvation he has merited, sends us his Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, and one and the same God with them, so that these three persons are one and only God, blessed forever.

units.la: dictus in secula: Spiritum illustrare mentes nostras, fidémque, qua justificamur in nobis creare: Adhæc Dominum Juos Apostolos, qui salutarem islam doctrinam prædicarent, per universum orbem misisse; Eos Ecclesias hic illic passim in orbe constituisse, in iisq; singulis Pastores ordinasse, eósque reverenter audiendos, & ab iis Baptismum, regenerationis nostræ Sacramentum & sanctam Eucharistiam, nostræ item cum Jesu Christo communionis Sacramentum recipere oportere. Denique id nostri esse officii, ut & Deum summa pietate colamus, & proximum sincera caritate diligamus: & sanctissimam illam disciplinam summo studio observemus, quam Deus in libris Testamenti Novi sanxit: cujus, sicut & Veteris, Scriptores suo veritatis Spiritu afflavit, ita ut nihil quod non sit verissimum in utrisque habeatur.
units.tr: That the Spirit enlightens our minds and creates in us the faith by which we are justified. Further, that the Lord sent his Apostles throughout the whole world to preach this saving doctrine; that they established Churches here and there across the world, and in each of them ordained ministers, whom we ought to hear with reverence, and from whom we ought to receive Baptism, the sacrament of our regeneration, and the holy Eucharist, the sacrament of our communion with Jesus Christ. Finally, that it is our duty both to worship God with the highest piety and to love our neighbour with sincere charity, and to observe with the utmost zeal that most holy discipline which God has enacted in the books of the New Testament; and that the writers of these books, as of the Old, were inspired by his Spirit of truth, so that nothing is held in either that is not most true.

units.la: His, & si quæ sunt alia ejusdem generis non multa, continetur universa Protestantium fides, eáque si, quemadmodum illis, sic & omnibus Christianis reliquis satis essent, nullum schisma foret: Sed præter hæc multa alia eorum adversarii addunt, quæ urgent & commendant tanquam necessaria, & quasi ea in dubium vocanti nulla ad salutem via pateat. Exempli gratia, statuunt Papam Romanum Ecclesiæ Christianæ, quæ in terris versatur, caput & summum Monarcham esse: ipsum, aut saltem Ecclesiam quæ ipsi subest, in rebus fidei errare nunquam posse; Sacramentum Eucharistiæ, quia non panis, ut videtur, sed ipse Christus revera est eo adorandum esse; Missam esse sacrificium quo realiter expiantur fidelium peccata: Imagines Dei & sanctorum in templis Christianorum habere, iisque cultum religiosum exhibere, & coram iis prostrumbere fas & jus esse: Animas sanctorum suo functorum & Angelos invocare licere, imo & maxime expedire: Animas nostras, antequam in cœlos recipiantur, per quendam ignem transituras, gravissimasque pœnas daturas, ut hac ratione pro peccatis suis satisfaciant: Nec posse, nec debere quenquam peccati sibi conscium ad S. Eucharistiam admitti, quin priuspeccata sua sacerdoti clam confessus fuerit: & in aurem insusurraveris: Eucharistiam non alium, quàm qui consecravit vit, teneri sub duabus speciebus fumere; & alia ejus farinæ multa, quæ negant Protestantes se salva conscientia posse admittere. Super his tota est controversia; Romanis quidem contendentibus ea ab omni ævo in Ecclesia Christi; tanquam ab ipso tradita & revelata, credira & admissa fuisse; Nostris contra nitentibus, & in alia omnia euntibus. Quoniam autem in Novo Testamento (quod Christianorum est antiquissimum & maximè authenticum instrumentum) de his altum est silentium; qui ea tuentur, ex scriptis Doctorum, qui quatuor aut quinque post Apostolos vixerunt seculis, quique ut plurimum Patres vocantur, probationes petunt. Consilium meum est, an istis controversiis dirimendis medium hoc sufficiat in hac disputatione expendere. Imprimis autem duo quædam statuimus & præstruimus, quæ nemo, ut reor, sanus facilè negaverit: Prius est, cùm hic agatur de superstructendis testimonio aut dictis Patrum quibusdam fidei capitibus, necessarium esse ut loci, qui ex iis petuntur, certi sint & perspicui, id est hujusmodi, ut nemo ambigere possit, vel de ipsorum authore, an ejus vere sint cujus esse feruntur; vel de eorum sensu, an is sit scilicet, qui esse dicitur. Nam cum testimonium vel sententia nullam habeat vim aliam, nisi eam quam petit ab authoritate testis, vel judicis, patet, quandiu de ea non constat, ad fidem faciendam non esse ista idonea. Eadem ratione, si scriptoris testimonium, aut judicis sententia, obscura sunt, aut ambigua; quis non videt neque his posse controversiam decidi? eum alia supersit ante explicanda quæstio, quis, scilicet, hujus vel illius sensus sit. Alterum verò quod pro fundamento hujus disputationis pono (nempè ut in his controversiis valeant scripta Patrum) hoc est, iis necessariò maximam authoritatem esse tribuendam, tantam videlicet, ut in rebus fidei in eorum sententiam concedere teneamur: Nisi enim hæc ipsis tribuatur authoritas, ut ut perspicua sit & diserta eorum de capitibus controversis sententia, patet tamen eam ad definiendam causam non fatis momenti habituram. Hic ergo duo nobis erunt excutienda. Primus; An quæ de controuersiis istis Sanctorum Patrum sententia fuerit hodie certò & perspicuè constare possit. Alterum. An eorum authoritas tanta sit, ut quilibet fidelis, cui certò & perspicuè constat, quæ fuerit Patrum de quolibet religionis capite sententia, in eam tanquam veram pedibus ire tenetur. Nam si hæc duo demonstrari possint; constabit sane Romanæ communionis homines veterum de religione testimonia ac sententias jure merito aduersariis objicere, & dum sic agunt, eam disputandi rationem usurpare, quæ vero congrua ac consentanea sit. Quod si contra vel de utroque vel certe de altero non constat; nemo, mea quidem sententia erit vel tantillo judicio præditus, qui non statim intelligat hanc disputandi rationem, qua Romana Ecclesia hactenus usa est, vanam esse atque inefficacem; adeoque istis alio confugiendum esse, firmioraque & aptiora argumenta conquirendo, si id quod cupiunt conficere velint; nempe vetera esse, quæ nunc protestantes vel negant, vel in dubium vocant.
units.tr: By these, and a few other things of the same kind, the whole faith of the Protestants is contained; and if this were enough for them, as it is for them, so also for all the other Christians, there would be no schism. But besides these, their adversaries add many other things, which they press and commend as necessary, as if without them no way to salvation lay open. For example, they hold that the Roman Pope is the head and supreme monarch of the Christian Church that dwells on earth; that he, or at least the Church subject to him, can never err in matters of faith; that the Eucharist is to be adored there, because it is not bread, as it seems, but Christ himself in truth; that the Mass is a sacrifice by which the sins of the faithful are really expiated; that it is right and lawful to have images of God and the saints in Christian churches, and to offer religious worship to them and to prostrate oneself before them; that it is lawful, and even most expedient, to invoke the souls of the departed saints and the angels; that our souls, before they are received into heaven, must pass through a certain fire and pay most grievous penalties, so that in this way they may make satisfaction for their sins; that no one conscious of sin may or should be admitted to the holy Eucharist unless he has first confessed his sins secretly to a priest and whispered them into his ear; that the Eucharist is not to be taken under both kinds by anyone other than the one who consecrated it; and many other things of this sort, which the Protestants say they cannot admit with a clear conscience. On these points the whole controversy turns: the Romanists contend that these things have been believed and admitted in the Church of Christ from every age, as handed down and revealed by Christ himself, while our side strives against this and goes in the opposite direction. But since in the New Testament (which is the oldest and most authentic record of the Christians) there is great silence on these matters, those who defend them seek their proofs from the writings of the Doctors who lived four or five centuries after the Apostles, and who are for the most part called Fathers. My aim is to weigh in this disputation whether this means is enough for settling these controversies. First, however, I lay down and set forth two things which, I think, no sane person will readily deny. The first is that, when we build up some chapters of faith on the testimony or sayings of the Fathers, it is necessary that the passages drawn from them be certain and clear, that is, of such a kind that no one can doubt either whether they truly are by the author to whom they are ascribed, or whether their meaning is what it is said to be. For since a testimony or opinion has no force other than that which it draws from the authority of the witness or judge, it is plain that, so long as it is not certain, such things are not fit to establish faith. By the same reasoning, if the testimony of a writer or the sentence of a judge is obscure or ambiguous, who does not see that the controversy cannot be settled by these either, since a further question must first be explained, namely what the meaning of this or that is? The second thing, which I lay down as the foundation of this disputation (namely, that the writings of the Fathers have weight in these controversies), is that the greatest authority must necessarily be granted to them, so great that we are bound to yield to their opinion in matters of faith. For unless this authority is granted to them, then however clear and express their opinion on the disputed chapters may be, it will plainly not have enough weight to decide the cause. Here, therefore, two questions must be examined by us. The first: whether the opinion of the holy Fathers on these controversies can today be known with certainty and clarity. The second: whether their authority is so great that every believer who knows with certainty and clarity what the opinion of the Fathers was on any chapter of religion is bound to go over to it as true. For if these two things can be shown, it will certainly be established that the men of the Roman communion rightly and deservedly object to their adversaries the testimonies and opinions of the ancients about religion, and that in doing so they use a method of disputation that is truly fitting and consistent. But if, on the contrary, neither of these two, or at least one of them, is not established, then no one of sound judgement, in my opinion, will fail to see at once that the method of disputation the Roman Church has so far used is vain and ineffective; and therefore they must turn elsewhere, seeking firmer and better-suited arguments, if they wish to achieve what they desire, namely to prove that the things Protestants now either deny or call in question are ancient.

LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: BOOK ONE.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Ratio 1. Aegrè constare posse quid circa nostras de religione controversias senserint Patres, cùm pauca extent ab iis scripta, tribus præ- sertim antiquissimis seculis.
units.tr: Reason 1. It can hardly be established what the Fathers thought about our controversies concerning religion, since few of their writings survive, especially from the three most ancient centuries.

units.la: I essest animus eam adhibere in hoc argumento methodum qua adversum S. Scripturam non paucos Ecclesiæ Romanæ Doctores nunc uti cernimus : nullo negotio conficere posse mus, ut quicquid senserunt Patres, id planè dubium & incertum esse videatur. Hi enim quoties ab adversario aliquis Veteris aut Novi Testamenti locus affertur, quærere solent, unde & quo modo sciat ejusmodi libro à Prophetis & Apostolis, quorum nomina & titulos præferunt, verè scriptos fuisse? Si ergo, qui Iustinum, Irenæum, Ambrosium, Augustinum & alios nobis objiciunt, eos hac itidem quæstione remoraremur ut docerent unde & qua ratione constet Patres horum, quæ iis tribuuntur, voluminum verè auctores fuisse ; facilè est videre, longè majus iis negotium exhiberi posse, quàm ipsi nobis facessunt dum divinorum titulorum probationem exigunt ; quorum scilicet veritas multò facilius, quàm cuiuslibet humani scripti demonstretur. Sed hanc nimium vafram ac versutam difputandi rationem mitto, & hoc unum dico non facile videri ex scriptis Patrum certò exculpere quid ii senserint de omnibus capitibus, quæ hodie Protestantes inter & Pontificios controvertuntur. Multa sunt quæ hanc cognitionem difficilem, ac impeditam reddunt. Nos priori disputationis parte horum quædam afferemus; quæ, singulari quadam observatione digna videntur.
units.tr: Had I wished to use in this subject the method that many doctors of the Roman Church now use against Holy Scripture, we could without any difficulty make it appear that whatever the Fathers thought is entirely doubtful and uncertain. For whenever an opponent cites some passage of the Old or New Testament, they are accustomed to ask how and by what means one knows that these books were truly written by the Prophets and Apostles whose names and titles they bear. If, then, we were to hold up to the same question those who object to us Justin, Irenaeus, Ambrose, Augustine and others, and ask them to show how and on what grounds it is established that the Fathers were truly the authors of the volumes ascribed to them, it is easy to see that a much greater task could be set before them than they set before us when they demand proof of the divine titles, whose truth is far more easily demonstrated than that of any human writing. But I set aside this overly crafty and subtle way of arguing, and say only this: it does not seem easy to extract with certainty from the writings of the Fathers what they thought on all the chapters that are now disputed between Protestants and Papists. Many things make this knowledge difficult and hindered. In the first part of this disputation we shall set out some of these, which seem worthy of particular observation.

units.la: Prima ergo hæc esto ratio; Quod pauca sint veterum Doctorum scripta, præsertim eorum qui primo, vel secundo, vel tertio sæculo floruerint, quorum tamen potius quàm inferiorum rationem haberi decebat. Cùm enim inter causas, propter quas Ecclesia Romana Patrum scripta allegat, hæc ferè ordinem ducat, ut, scilicet, ex Antiquitate, quam veræ fidei notam censer, doceat quàm vera sint ea quæ se credere profitetur, planum est antiquissimorum potissimam esse debere rationem. Sanè longè probabilius est Religionem Christianam in suis primordiis puram & sinceram fuisse, quàm iis temporibus quæ postea consecuta sunt: cùm ut plurimum res, prout à sua origine recedunt, sic etiam in dies in pejus ruant, & retrò sublapsæ ferantur, ut videre est in rebus publ. legibus, disciplinis, & linguis, quarum nativus decor minuitur, ex quo fastigium roboris sui, & veluti virium suarum florem, semel prætergressæ sunt. Neminem autem fidelem insiciatum puto vigorem istum & florem Christianismi maximè excelluisse superstitibus sanctis Domini Apostolis, cum sine summa eorum injuria dici nequeat, quenquam eorum, qui ipsis in regenda Ecclesia successerunt, vel voluisse, vel potuisse aliquid, quod illos fugerit, ad eam perficiendam adjicere. Sequitur ergo tempora, quæ ad ipsorum ætatem proximè accedunt, à suspicione corruptelarum, sive in doctrina, sive in moribus, sive in Christianorum disciplina remotissima esse debere, cùm credibile sit, corruptelas istas, si quæ acciderunt, sensim & paulatim irrepsisse, quod usu venire solet in rebus ejusmodi. Sed vero objiciat sæculum ipsum, quod proximè ætatem Apostolorum
units.tr: Let this, then, be my first argument: the writings of the ancient teachers are few, especially those of the men who flourished in the first, second, or third century, whose testimony ought nonetheless to have been weighed before that of later writers. For among the reasons the Roman Church gives for citing the writings of the Fathers, the chief is generally this: from antiquity, which it regards as the mark of true faith, it shows how true are the things it professes to believe. It is plain, then, that the claim of the most ancient writers ought to be the strongest. Indeed, it is far more probable that the Christian religion was pure and sincere in its beginnings than in the times that followed. As a rule, things decline for the worse the further they move from their origin and slide backwards day by day, as one may see in states, laws, disciplines and languages, whose native grace diminishes once they have passed the peak of their strength and, as it were, the flower of their powers. Now I think no believer will deny that the vigour and flower of Christianity were at their greatest while the holy Apostles of the Lord were still alive, since it cannot be said, without great injury to them, that any of those who succeeded them in governing the Church either wished or was able to add anything to perfect it that had escaped the Apostles. It follows that the times nearest to the Apostles' own age must be free from suspicion of corruption, whether in doctrine, morals, or Christian discipline, since it is credible that such corruptions, if any arose, crept in gradually and little by little, as usually happens in such matters. But suppose someone objects that the age itself, the one immediately following the age of the Apostles,

units.la: Apostolorum stolorum consecutum est, non debere ab ista suspicione immune esse, cum Hegesippus,apud Eusebium, * testetur Ecclesiam virginem intactam & incorruptam usque ad Trajani tempora permansisse ;sed è medio sublatis Apostolis, conspirationem erroris retecto capite in apertum sese producere incepisse, equidem non repugnabo , sed hoc tantum dicam, si statim post istorum Ecclesiæ sidesrum occasum, cum eorum lux & præsentia vix dum subducta esset,ausus est inimicus homo nonnihil zizanorum inter frumenta spargere,non esse dubitandum quin longè majora pejoráq; molitus fit seculis post secutis, cùm summorum istorum Doctorum cùm sanctitate rum simplicitate paulatim ex hominum memoria evanescente,curiositas, luxuriantiúmqueingeniorum variæ artes in eorum locum invaserunt. Vnde restat præterea colligendum, antiquissima ista Christianisimi secula, si ab omni prosus depravatione in doctrina non vacarunt, saltem longè incorruptiora fuisse quàm sequentia, ac proinde illa nulla non ratione his anteponenda, ut Christianorum temporum non alia ferè sit ratio quàm quatuor illorum seculorum quæ finxerunt Poetæ, inter quas sequens semper superiore deterius est. Quod enim nonnulli censent, ad veram veteris Ecclesiæ de religione sententiam pernoscendam eorum maximè evolvenda esse scripta qui à Magno Constantino usque ad Leonem Papam, immo usque ad Gregorium,vixerunt (idest à tertio seculo exeunte usque ad septimi initia) id sinquam, ipsum ostendit quidem quàm isti pauca agnoscant nobis superesse scripta trium illorum seculorum quæ Constantinum antecesserunt, haudquaquam verò probat trium posteriorum quàm trium superiorum potiorem apud nos esse debere auctoritatem. Quod si nobis horum non pauciora quàm illorum, testimonia ac documenta superessent, ne ipsos quidem negaturos puto, quin recentioribus antiquiora anteponenda essent. Sin aliter sentiunt,sibique fingunt Ecclesiam,quæ Constantini tempora subsecuta est,incorruptio-
units.tr: which followed the age of the Apostles, should not be free from this suspicion, since Hegesippus, in Eusebius, testifies that the Church remained a virgin, intact and uncorrupted until the times of Trajan, and that only after the Apostles were removed did the conspiracy of error, its head now uncovered, begin to come out into the open. I will not indeed contradict this, but I will say only this: if, immediately after the setting of those lights of the Church, when their light and presence had scarcely been withdrawn, that enemy of mankind dared to scatter some tares among the wheat, then there is no doubt that in the centuries that followed he devised far greater and worse things, when the simplicity and holiness of those highest teachers gradually faded from human memory and curiosity and the various arts of over-luxuriant minds invaded their place. Hence it remains to be further concluded that those most ancient ages of Christianity, if they were not wholly free from every corruption in doctrine, were at least far more uncorrupted than those that followed, and therefore should be preferred to them on every ground. So for the times of the Christians there is scarcely any other principle than that of the four ages which the poets invented, in which the later is always worse than the earlier. As for what some think, that to learn the true opinion of the ancient Church on religion one should above all study the writings of those who lived from Constantine the Great down to Pope Leo, or even down to Gregory (that is, from the end of the third century to the beginning of the seventh), this only shows how few writings from the three centuries before Constantine have survived to us, and by no means proves that the three later centuries should carry more authority with us than the three earlier. And if we had no fewer testimonies and documents from the earlier centuries than from the later, I do not think even these men would deny that the older should be placed before the more recent. units.la: Cassand. in Ferd. p. 394. ad Cassand. rem fuisse quàm illam quæ ipsum antecessit, ferent me si dicam, hoc ipso eos testari se causæ suæ diffidere, dum eam, à priorum temporum luce summotam, rejiciunt in secula, in quibus minùs virtûm, minúsque splendoris habuisse eam quàm in superioribus clarum est. Planè præter Cyprianimentem qui præclarè docet, pergendum esse ad fontem, cùm doctrinæ & traditionis Ecclesiasticæ canalis vitio interruptus, aut bibulus factus est. Sed quicquid isti senserint, certè ex eorum dictis mihi videtur Protestantium causa non minimum juvari, nam illi, dum sic agunt, facis hoc ipso fatentur, quæ à Protestantibus negantur Romanæ Ecclesiæ dogmata, ea nusquam in Scriptis trium vetustissimorum seculorum clarè tradita haberi, quæ si in iis extarent, eorum profectò probatio absurdè ac præposterè in tria subsequentia secula rejiceretur, quibus, multò minùs quàm antiquioribus, tribuere Romanorum adversarios satis superque notum est. Sed præter quam quod isti id nobis ultrò dant, res ipsa docet, ad dirimendas controversias nostras, paucula è tribus primis Christianismi seculis superesse scripta. Videntur enim plerique illorum temporum fideles satis habuisse fidem suam fulgore vitæ inculpatæ, & sanguine quem pro Christo constantissimè effundebant, in hominum cordibus inscribere; de libris verò scribendis parum laborasse: seu id placeret, quod eleganter docet Origenes, Christianismum vitæ innocentia, morúmque honestate potius quàm pigmentis oratoriis propagari & retineri debere; sive per continuas quibus afflictabantur calamitates, ipsis non liceret ad id animum appellere; seu quapiam alia de causa à scribendo deterrerentur, vel avocarentur. Utcunque sit, certum est, exceptis Apostolorum sacris voluminibus, perpaucos primis istis temporibus libris conscribendis operam dedisse: unde illa Eusebii initio historiæ solicitudo, quòd exigua, imò nulla lux aliunde affulgeret quam sequeretur, nullaque vestigia occurrerent, quæ premeret, cùm nullis superiorum trita esset ea via quam capessebat. Sed neque ea ipsa
units.tr: Cassander, against Ferdinand, p. 394. than the Church which preceded him, they will forgive me if I say that by this very thing they testify that they distrust their own cause, since they reject it, removed from the light of earlier times, into centuries in which, as is clear from the earlier record, it possessed less virtue and less splendour. Indeed, apart from Cyprian, who rightly teaches that one must go back to the source, when the channel of doctrine and ecclesiastical tradition has been broken or made muddy. But whatever they think, it seems to me that the cause of the Protestants is not a little helped by their words, for in so acting they confess that the Roman dogmas which the Protestants deny are nowhere clearly taught in the writings of the three most ancient centuries. If they were found there, their proof would absurdly and preposterously be pushed off onto the three following centuries, to which, far less than to the earlier ones, the Romans' adversaries are well aware they ascribe authority. But apart from the fact that they grant us this readily, the matter itself shows that, for settling our controversies, few writings survive from the first three centuries of Christianity. For most of the believers of those times seem to have been content to impress their faith on men's hearts by the brightness of a blameless life and the blood they shed so steadfastly for Christ, and to have taken little trouble over writing books. Whether this was by choice, as Origen aptly teaches, that Christianity should be spread and kept by the innocence of life and the honesty of manners rather than by the ornaments of rhetoric, or because the continual calamities with which they were afflicted did not allow them to turn their minds to it, or because they were deterred or diverted from writing for some other reason, is uncertain. Whatever the case, it is certain that, apart from the sacred volumes of the Apostles, very few men in those first times devoted themselves to writing books. Hence Eusebius, at the beginning of his history, shows his anxiety that there was little or no light from elsewhere to follow, and no traces to press upon, since no earlier writers had worn down the path he was taking. Pars major intercidit, vel temporis, quod omnia absumit, injuria, vel hominum in abolendis quæ ad palatum non sapiebant, audacium fraude, ut exempli causa Papiæ Episcopi Hierapolitani quinque libri, Quadrati Atheniensis, & Aristidis Apologiæ, Castoris Agrippæ opus contra Basilidis hæretici libros viginti quatuor, Hegesippi quinque libri; Melitonis Sardensis Episcopi, Dionysiii Corinthii, Apollinaris Hierapolitani opera, Pinyti item Cretensis epistola, Philippi, Musani, Modesti, Bardesanis, Pantæni, Rhodonis, Miltiadis, Apollonii, Serapionis, Bacchyli, Polycratis Episcopi Ephesini, Heraclii, Maximi, Hammonii, Tryphonis, Hippolyti, Iulii Africani, Dionysii Alexandrini & aliorum monumenta quorum nuda nobis nomina & tituli apud Eusebium & Hieronymum & aliós supersunt. Etsi autem fieri potuerit, ut bona veterum istorum monumentorum pars, sola, vel temporum injuria, vel hominum negligentia intercideri, non est tamen dubitandum quædam etiam eorum dolo ac fraude abolita esse, qui extare nolebant suæ à primo Christianismo diversitatis argumenta. Nisi enim aliquod hominum studium in istis supprimendis fuisset adhibitum, nulla apparet rario cur sanctissimorum atque antiquissimorum virorum labores potiùs intercidere passi sint Christiani, quàm alia non pauca storum multò deteriorum. Verbi gratia; cur quæso Tertulliani, gravi ob Montanismum invidia laborantis, opera plurima perennarunt, Apollonii viri inter Catholicos laudatissimi nihil ad nos pervenit? Ac illius quidem (quod mireris) liber de jejuniis, proprie adversus Catholicos scriptus (quos ille psychicos falso & contumeliosè vocat) mansit tamen, hujus contra Montanistas pro Catholicis disputatio periit. Quæ ista fuit tam præpostera Christianorum hominum, vel in hostem caritas, vel in civem negligentia, ut illum servatum vellent, hunc interire paterentur? Nulla rei tam incredibilis ratio occurrit probabilior, quàm quòd receptis postmodu m apud Christianos jejuniorum legibus, xerophagiarumque disciplinis,quas veteres in Montani partibus damnaverant, posteri Apollonium veterum defensorem perire non inviti passi sint;Tertullianum ob ejus cum suis conformitatem suum fuisse putantes, fovcrint. Sanè tanta est Tertullianeæ doctrinæ cum hodierna Romana conformitas, ut ejus pro Montano adversus Psychicos disputationem, non ignobiles apud Romanos Theologi a Perefius & b Turrianus pro Catholicis suis contra hæreticos institutam esse censuerint. Eandem causam Hegesippo, Papiæ & aliis perniciem vel attulisse, vel certè maturasse crediderim,nec,si servarentur,eorum simplicitas,& alienà à seculorum infequutorum moribus fidesac disciplina, recentiorum inventis fraudem facerent. Vtcunque sit, illud quidem constat pauca superesse ex illis seculis certa & indubitata. In hoc censu sunt Tractatus quidam Iustini Philosophi & Martyris, qui anno post Christum natum centesimo & quinquagesimo alteram suam Apologiam scribebat; Irenæi, qui Iustinum proximè secutus est, quinque libri, Clementis item presbyteri Alexandrini, qui exeunte secundo seculo vivebat, tres eximiæ & eruditæ lucubrationes. Varia quoque Tertulliani, qui sub idem tempus florebat, opera Epistolæ & disputationes Cypriani, qui Carthagine Episcopus fuit, ubi & martyrium fecit, A. D. 258. Scripta Lactantii & Arnobii ejus discipuli,& paucorum aliorum. Nam quantùm attinet ad Cypriani æqualem Originem, ex quo uno, si salvus perduraffer,plus lucis nobis accederet quàm ex reliquis aliis, & à quo forsàn potiùs quàm à cæteris omnibus haberemus in quo acquiesceremus, paucula sunt, & maximam partem, fœdè lacera, & miserè immutata quæ sub illius nomine feruntur. Magni enim & mirandi istius viri monumenta,neque temporum,neque hominum injuriam superare potuerunt. Atque haud scio annon horum invidia gravius eum afflixerit, quàm ipsa tot seculorum vetustas quæ ab ipsius morte ad nos fluxerunt. Hæc ferè sunt quæ à tri-
units.tr: Yet even what the Christians then published, though little, has not all come down to us. Most of it has perished, either through the injury of time, which consumes everything, or through the malice of men who were bent on destroying whatever did not suit their taste. Examples are the five books of Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis; the works of Quadratus of Athens and the Apology of Aristides; the work of Castor and Agrippa against the twenty-four books of the heretic Basilides; the five books of Hegesippus; the writings of Melito, Bishop of Sardis, of Dionysius of Corinth, and of Apollinaris of Hierapolis; likewise the letter of Pinytus of Crete; and the works of Philip, Musanus, Modestus, Bardesanes, Pantaenus, Rhodo, Miltiades, Apollonius, Serapion, Bacchylus, Polycrates, Bishop of Ephesus, Heraclitus, Maximus, Hammonius, Tryphon, Hippolytus, Julius Africanus, Dionysius of Alexandria, and others, whose bare names and titles survive only in Eusebius, Jerome and other writers. Although it may be that only a good part of these ancient monuments perished through the injury of time or the negligence of men, it is nonetheless not to be doubted that some of them were also destroyed by the deceit and fraud of those who did not want the proofs of their own departure from original Christianity to survive. For unless some human zeal had been applied to suppressing them, there appears no reason why the Christians should have allowed the labours of such holy and most ancient men to perish rather than many other, far inferior, writings. For example: why, I ask, did the many works of Tertullian, who laboured under the grave odium of Montanism, survive, while nothing of Apollonius, a man most praised among the Catholics, has come down to us? Indeed, the book of Apollonius on fasting, written expressly against the Catholics (whom he falsely and insultingly calls psychics), has remained, while his disputation against the Montanists on behalf of the Catholics has perished. What was this so perverse charity of Christians toward an enemy, or this negligence toward a fellow citizen, that they wished the one preserved and allowed the other to perish? No explanation of so incredible a thing seems more probable than this: that, once the laws of fasting and the disciplines of xerophagy had later been received among the Christians, which the ancients had condemned on the side of Montanus, the later men, thinking Tertullian to have been conformed to them, cherished him, and did not unwillingly allow Apollonius, the defender of the ancients, to perish. Indeed, so great is the conformity of Tertullian's doctrine with the present Roman doctrine, that not unimportant Roman theologians, Pererius and Turrianus, have judged that his disputation for Montanus against the psychics was instituted for their own Catholics against the heretics. I would believe that this same cause brought ruin, or at least hastened it, to Hegesippus, Papias and others; nor, if they had been preserved, would their simplicity, and their faith and discipline, foreign to the morals of later ages, have made any fraud upon the inventions of more recent men. However that may be, it is certain that few writings survive from those centuries that are certain and undoubted. In this number are certain tracts of Justin the Philosopher and Martyr, who was writing his second Apology in the hundred and fiftieth year after Christ's birth; the five books of Irenaeus, who followed Justin most closely; and the three outstanding and learned works of Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, who lived at the end of the second century. There are also the various works of Tertullian, who flourished at about the same time; the letters and disputations of Cyprian, who was Bishop of Carthage, where he also suffered martyrdom, in the year of our Lord 258; the writings of Lactantius, and of Arnobius his pupil, and of a few others. For as far as concerns Origen, Cyprian's contemporary, from whom alone, had he survived intact, more light would have come to us than from all the rest, and from whom perhaps we would rather than from all others have had something in which to rest, only a few things remain, and for the most part shamefully torn and wretchedly altered, which are carried under his name. For the monuments of that great and wonderful man could overcome neither the injury of times nor of men. And I know not whether the hatred of these things has not afflicted him more grievously than the very antiquity of so many centuries which has flowed down to us since his death. These are nearly the things which, from the three earlier centuries of Christianity, have come down to us as certain and undoubted.

units.la: è tribus prioribus Christianisimi seculis ad nos certa & indubitata pervenerunt. Caetera enim scripta quae iisdem temporibus tribuuntur partim ab ipsis etiam Pontificiis notha & fictitia esse agnoscuntur, partim ab ipsorum adversariis tam probabilibus, imo adeo firmis argumentis rejecta sunt, ut ea inter testimonia & authoritates quibus opus habemus ad lucem inferendam controversiis nostris, locum habere nullum possint.
units.tr: Other writings that are attributed to the same times are recognised, in part, even by the Papists themselves as spurious and fictitious; in part, they have been rejected by their adversaries on such probable, indeed such firm, arguments that they can have no place among the testimonies and authorities we need in order to bring light to our controversies.

units.la: Scripta quarti & quinti seculi fuerunt fateor, & longè majori numero quam superiora, & in eo etiam feliciora quod ad nos usque perennarunt; sed longè absunt à priorum authoritate, maximè apud Protestantes, qui admodum probabiliter censent Christianismum labem paulatim contraxisse, & singulis seculis de pristina & nativa sua puritate aliquid amisisse. Adde, quod metuendū videtur, ne tanta ista librorum, duobus illis seculis editorum multitudo, non minus negotii nobis facesset, quàm ante in mora fuit eorum exiguus numerus, & ne, qui antea inopia laborabamus, nunc copia obruamur. Aliquando enim vera hominum sententia, non minus verborum & voluminum copia, quam silentio ipso obruitur, dum mens nostra, his impedita, quae sit vera & communis sententia inter tot verborum ambages, his hoc modo, illis alio rem ipsam osserentibus capere satagit. Certum quippe est, in tanta & penè infinita ingeniorum & linguarum varietate, raro occurrere posse duos qui praesertim in rebus difficilibus atq; abitrusis, quales sunt quae ad religionem spectant, eandem rem eadem ratione, iisdem imaginibus, quantuscunque eorum sit in reipsa consensus, concipiant. Quantumvis autem haec varietas in solis rei circumstantiis versetur, non potest tamen res ipsa non ea videri affici.
units.tr: I admit that the writings of the fourth and fifth centuries are both more numerous than the earlier ones, and in this also more fortunate, in that they have survived to us; but they are far from the authority of the earlier ones, especially among Protestants, who quite reasonably hold that Christianity gradually contracted a taint and lost something of its original and native purity with each century. Add to this that it seems to be feared lest this so great multitude of books, published in those two centuries, should cause us no less trouble than their small number caused us in the past, and lest we who once laboured under poverty should now be overwhelmed by abundance. For sometimes the true opinion of men is buried no less by the abundance of words and volumes than by silence itself, while our mind, hindered by these, struggles to grasp what is the true and common opinion amid so many verbal windings, some presenting the matter one way, others another. For it is certain that, in so great and almost infinite a variety of minds and languages, it can rarely happen that two people conceive the same thing in the same way, with the same images, in matters especially difficult and abstruse, such as those that concern religion, however great their agreement in the thing itself may be. Yet however much this variety lies only in the circumstances of the thing, the thing itself cannot fail to appear affected by it.
