units.la: Ratio II. Quæ supersunt è tribus prioribus seculis s- cripta maximam partem agere de rebus alie- nissimis ab iis quæ hodie circa religionem in controversiam vocantur.
units.tr: Reason II. The writings that survive from the first three centuries deal for the most part with matters very remote from those which today are called into controversy concerning religion.

units.la: IAm ad hanc librorum,& vetustissimorum paucitatem, & recentiorum multitudinem,qua utràque non parum laboramus,accedit aliud non levius incommodum,quod scilicet difficile sit certò scire quæ utrorumque auctorum fuerit de hodiernis controversiis fides ; à quibus plane sunt aliena quæ veteres in suis illis operibus tractant. Hi enim pro suorum temporum ratione,vel Christianismum criminationibus quibus per calumniam gravabatur,purgant ; velinsulsa & impia Ethnicorum sacra exagitant; vel obduratam Iudæorum pervicaciam coarguunt ; vel portentosa hæreticorum sui temporis deliria confutant; vel fideles ad patientiam ;& crucem Christi fortiter perferendam hortantur ; vel quosdam denique Scripturæ locos interpretantur. Hæc omnia perparum ad controversias nostras faciunt, quas isti nunquam fere nisi casu atque obiter & aliud agentes attingunt, cùm nihil minùs quàm nos nostràque in animo haberent. Occurrunt quidem hinc inde quædam apud illos in quibus utrique sibi videntur sententiam suam clarè expressam videre ; sed ut plurimum fiuftra ; ac fere non aliter,quàm fiquis in campanarum sono animi sui cogitata & studia se observare putet. Iustinus & Tertullianus,Theophilus & Lactantius, Clemens & Arnobius fictitiorum numinum vanitatem accuratè ostendunt, Ethnicósque docent lovem,Martem, & Iunonem,&c. mortales fuisse;Deum verum unum esse, cœli & terræ creatorem. Irenæus Basilidis, Valentinianorum & reliquorum Gnosticorum Theologiæ omnium foedissimæ & insulsissimæ fabricorum portenta profligat. Tertullianus præter hos, quos & ipse confutat, Marcionem quoque, & Hermogenem, & Apellem, & Praxeam, & alios debellat qui duos Deos, aut duo principia constituebant, aut personas Patris & Filij confundebant. Cyprianus in excolendis tum disciplina tum virtutibus Ecclesiæ Christianæ fermè totus est. Arius, & Macedonius, & Eunomius, & Photinus, & Pelagius, & post illos Nestorius, & Eutyches quarto & quinto seculo negotium exhibuerunt. Horum contra Christi vel personam, vel naturas, & contra S. Spiritus vel numen vel efficaciam pridem, Dei beneficio, sepultæ blasphemiæ, piorum qui illis temporibus floruerunt ingenia & calamos exercuerunt. Nam circa ista maximè versantur qui nobis illius memoriæ supersunt etiamnum libri. Quid ista quæso ad transsubstantiationem & ad Eucharistiæ adorationem, vel Papæ Monarchiam, aut arcanæ confessionis necessitatem, aut imaginum cultum, aut alia capita de quibus nunc contenditur; de quibus Veterum nullus diserte & ex professo egerit; quæ etiam fortasse iis in mentem nunquam venerunt. Quanquam certè istorum super his capiribus, quæ tanti nunc fiunt, tam altum silentium non est omnino mutum, nec de nihilo, & forsan tantidem faciendum est, ac si de iis diserte egissent: at non eorum bono qui pro istis, tanquam pro aris & focis, pugnant. Verùm, ut ut sit, in certis & indubitatis Veterum voluminibus nulli occurrunt Tractatus qui eo consilio scripti fuerint ut pro dogmatibus istis, vel adversum ea disputaretur. Equidem fateor lubens, hominis sapientis fidem corpus constituere, cujus partes inter se cohærent, & aliæ ad alias referuntur, ita ut ex iis quæ conceptis verbis docet, colligere fit quæ mens ejus fuerit circa ea de quibus silet, credátne ea, an secus; cùm non fiat verisimile, ipsum ea admittere quibus euertuntur fidei capita quæ ponit, vel rejicere ea quæ ex ipsis necessariò consequuntur. Sed præter quam quod ista disputandi ratio supponit Veterum fidem totam apte inter se cohaerere; nullas eius partes vitium facere; omnes inter se esse exquisite coagmentatas & arcte connexas (quod non esse prorsus extra dubium suo loco docebimus) praeterea, inquam, requirit ingenium acutum & perspicax, quod actutum & clare singularum rerum consecutiones pervideat; & memoriam expromptam & amplam, ut possit ad amussim eorum omnium recordari quae veteres ponunt, & judicium acre, minimeque anticipatis opinionibus praepeditum, ut Veterum sententiam cum ea quae nunc obtinet, accurate possit conferre. Quae quidem omnia, si in quopiam occurrerent, hanc scriptorum veterum versandi rationem longe utilissimam & ad eorum mentem penitus introspiciendam accommodatissimam futuram fateor. Verum, proh dolor! rarissima sunt ista, nigroque simillima cygno. Adde quod si fides habeatur nonnullis doctoribus Pontificiis nihili est, nulliusque usus universa ista methodus, quae argumenta scilicet & ratiocinationes adhibet; haec enim cum, istis judicibus, instrumenta sint fallacia, non sunt idonea ad fidem faciendam, maxime in iis quae ad religionem spectant, in quibus nulla fides debetur nisi locis clatis & differtis. Itaque, si eorum sententia stetur, istorum, si sapiamus, fidei capitum nullum apud nos fidem obtinebit tanquam Patribus creditum & traditum, nisi ad ipsum in eorum voluminibus de verbo ad verbum legamus, id est, iisdem ad literam verbis quae in Decretis & Canonibus Concilij Tridentini habentur. Cum ergo, ex istorum sententia, testimonia, ut fidem mereantur, diserta esse necesse sit, cumque haec de quibus quaeritur inter nos plerDque nuiquam apud Patres diserte agitata inveniantur, is in Logicae praecepta neutiquam peccabit, qui ex istis omnibus colligit, aegerrime fieri posse (si modo ulla ratione poterit) ut pernoscamus quae genuina fuerit Veterum sententia super plerisque Ecclesiae Romanae dogmatis quae nunc a Protestantibus repudiantur.
units.tr: To this scarcity of very ancient books and abundance of recent ones, by which we both labour no little, there is added another no less serious inconvenience: namely, that it is difficult to know with certainty what the belief of each author was concerning today's controversies, from which the things the ancients treat in those works are wholly alien. For these, according to the circumstances of their times, either purge Christianity of the slanders with which calumny burdened it; or attack the foolish and impious rites of the Gentiles; or expose the obstinate stubbornness of the Jews; or confute the monstrous delusions of the heretics of their own time; or exhort the faithful to patience and to bear the cross of Christ bravely; or finally interpret certain passages of Scripture. All these things contribute very little to our controversies, which they almost never touch except by chance and incidentally, while attending to other matters, since they had no thought at all of us and our concerns. There do indeed occur here and there certain passages in them in which each side seems to itself to see its own opinion clearly expressed; but for the most part in vain, and almost no differently than if someone should think he observes the thoughts and pursuits of his own mind in the sound of bells. Justin and Tertullian, Theophilus and Lactantius, Clement and Arnobius accurately show the vanity of fictitious deities, and teach that the Gentiles' Jupiter, Mars, Juno, etc., were mortals, and that the true God is one, the creator of heaven and earth. Irenaeus overthrows the monstrous fabrications of Basilides, the Valentinians and the other Gnostics, the most foul and silly of all theologies. Tertullian, besides these whom he himself also refutes, also wars against Marcion, Hermogenes, Apelles, Praxeas, and others who posited two Gods or two principles, or confused the persons of Father and Son. Cyprian is almost entirely occupied with cultivating both the discipline and the virtues of the Christian Church. Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Photinus, Pelagius, and after them Nestorius and Eutyches gave trouble in the fourth and fifth centuries. Against these blasphemies concerning either the person or the natures of Christ, or the divinity or efficacy of the Holy Spirit, long since buried by God's favour, the talents and pens of the pious who flourished in those times were exercised. For it is chiefly about these things that the books which remain to us from that period are concerned. What, I ask, do these have to do with transubstantiation and the adoration of the Eucharist, or the monarchy of the Pope, or the necessity of secret confession, or the cult of images, or the other chapters about which there is now contention? Concerning these none of the ancients has spoken clearly and professedly, and perhaps they never even came into their minds. Yet certainly the silence of these men about those points which are now held in such esteem is not altogether mute, nor without meaning, and perhaps it is to be treated as if they had spoken about them clearly; but not to the advantage of those who fight for these things as for altars and hearths. However that may be, in the certain and indubitable volumes of the ancients no treatises occur that were written with the aim of disputing for those dogmas or against them. I freely confess that the faith of a wise man constitutes a body whose parts cohere with one another and refer to one another, so that from what he teaches in express words it is possible to gather what his mind was about those things on which he is silent, whether he believed them or not; since it is not probable that he admitted those things by which the articles of faith he sets forth are overturned, or rejected those things which necessarily follow from them. But apart from the fact that this method of arguing presupposes that the whole faith of the ancients coheres aptly together, that no part of it is faulty, and that all are exquisitely fitted together and closely linked (which we shall show in its place is not entirely beyond doubt), it further requires, I say, a keen and perceptive mind, which quickly and clearly sees through the consequences of each thing; and a ready and ample memory, so that it can recall exactly all that the ancients affirm; and a sharp judgment, least hindered by preconceived opinions, so that it can accurately compare the opinion of the ancients with that which now prevails. All of these, if they were found in anyone, would make this way of handling the writings of the ancients by far the most useful and best suited to looking deeply into their mind, I confess. But, alas! such qualities are very rare, and very like the black swan. Add that, if credit is given to some Papist teachers, this whole method, which employs arguments and reasonings, is worthless and of no use; for since these are, in the view of those judges, deceptive instruments, they are not fit to create faith, especially in matters that concern religion, in which no faith is owed except to clear and explicit passages. Therefore, if their opinion is followed, no article of faith of theirs will, if we have any sense, win credit among us as handed down and believed by the Fathers, unless we read it in their volumes word for word, that is, in the very words found in the Decrees and Canons of the Council of Trent. Since, then, according to their opinion, testimonies must be explicit in order to deserve credit, and since most of the things about which we dispute among ourselves are nowhere found discussed expressly among the Fathers, he will by no means err against the rules of logic who concludes from all these things that it is very difficult (if indeed it can be done by any means) for us to learn what was the genuine opinion of the ancients about most of the dogmas of the Church of Rome that are now rejected by the Protestants.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CAPVT III.

units.la: Ratio III. Quod Patrum vere certoque non sint quæcunque nunc eorum nomine circumferuntur, sed pleraque iis vel olim, vel his demum posterioris seculis affixa ac suppositæ.
units.tr: Argument III. That not everything now circulating under the names of the Fathers is truly and certainly theirs, but that most of it was either attached to them and falsely ascribed to them in earlier times, or in the later centuries.

units.la: Accedo iam ad longè maximi momenti rationes, cum superiores illæ duæ, licet non contemnendæ, leves tamen sint præ iis quæ sequuntur; plerorumque enim istorum, de quibus agimus, librorum confusio tanta est ut immane quantum difficile sit, vel eorum auctores, vel sensum certò cognoscere. Hoc primum ex eo nascitur, quod veteribus falsò adscripti & supposititi nullo numero inveniuntur libri. Simile quid in omni cùm Litterarum, tum Disciplinarum genere accidit, nec in vlla alia re, vel in Philosophicis, vel in Literis humanioribus, magis desudant Critici, quàm dum delectum inter ejusmodi fœtus nothos vel adulterinos, & genuinos legitimòsque adhibent. Sed nullibi fœdius & impudentius quàm adversus Scriptores Ecclesiasticos fraus grassata est. Omnes tam harum quàm illarum partium de eo queruntur, & ad fastidium vsque in lectoribus ex intricatissimis impostorum istorum commentis educendis laborant, etsi plerumque parum proficiant, propter vehementiora partium studia, dum libri, non tam ex suo merito, quàm ex legentium vsu ac commodo æstimantur, ac probantur. Qui adversatur, explodитur: qui favet, laudantur. Itaque, ut quod res est dicam, plerique non de suis opinionibus ex libris Patrum, sed de Patrum libris ex suis opinionibus judicium ferunt. Qui nobiscum sentit vel loquitur, is Cyprianus est & Chrysostomus; Si secus, scriptor est recens & imperitus; veterator est, qui lacinias suas præstantissimorum istorum virorum purpusa studuit contegere. Quod si nou alios quàm qui studiis ducuntur hæc caligo involueret, spes esset sepositis studiis, tenebras discuti & lucem affulgere posse; habiturà que in quo conquiescerent sedata saltem moderatàque ingenia. Verùm nondum incommodorum finis. Superest & aliud, idque omnium impeditissimum, & ad quod, si uspiam alibi, Delio (quod aiunt) natatore opus est. Caligo ista, scilicet, res ipsas obsidet; unde fit ut, vel propter erroris antiquitatem, vel ob veri & falsi inter se similitudinem, non nisi magno cum labore ac molimine ex ea liceat emergere; interdum verò ne omnino quidem liceat. Non enim comminiscendi fingendique artes novæ sunt; harum fraudum artifices ante quatuordecim secula extitere. Passim occurrunt Patrum voces de hæreticis conquerentium, quod ij, vt somniis suis authoritatem conciliarent, libros quibus ea in vulgus profeminabant, celeberrimi cujusque Ecclesiæ Doctoris, imo & Apostolorum ipsorum nominibus inscribere ausi essent. Hac ipsa de re Magno Basilio Cæsareæ Archiepiscopo tanto in pretio habitus Iconij Episcopus Amphilochius Commentarium scripserat; ex quo septimæ Synodi Patres locum confutant ab Iconoclastis ex inepto quodam opere laudatum quod Itinerarium Apostolorum dicebatur.
units.tr: I now turn to the reasons of by far the greatest weight, since the two earlier ones, though not to be despised, are slight compared with those that follow. The confusion among most of the books we are discussing is so great that it is extraordinarily hard to know with certainty either their authors or their meaning. This arises first from the fact that books falsely ascribed and spuriously attributed to the ancients are found in countless numbers. Something similar happens in every kind of literature and every field of learning. In no other matter, whether philosophical or humanistic, do critics sweat more than in distinguishing between such spurious or adulterated offspring and the genuine and legitimate ones. But nowhere has fraud been more shameless and widespread than against the ecclesiastical writers. Both parties complain about this, and they labour, to the point of weariness for their readers, to disentangle the most intricate inventions of these impostors. Yet they generally make little progress, because of the more violent zeal of the parties, while books are judged and approved not so much on their own merit as on the use and convenience of their readers. What opposes us is rejected; what favours us is praised. So, to speak plainly, most people judge the books of the Fathers according to their own opinions, not their own opinions according to the books of the Fathers. Whoever agrees with us or speaks as we do is a Cyprian or a Chrysostom; if otherwise, he is a recent and ignorant writer, or a cheat who has tried to hide his own rags under the purple of these most distinguished men. If this fog enveloped only those led by their own pursuits, there would be hope that, once those pursuits were set aside, the darkness could be dispelled and light could shine forth, and that calm and moderate minds would have something to rest upon. But the end of the troubles is not yet in sight. There is another difficulty, the most hindering of all, for which, if anywhere, one needs a Delian diver, as the saying goes. This fog, namely, besieges the very things themselves. Hence it happens that, either because of the antiquity of the error or because of the resemblance between true and false, one can emerge from it only with great labour and effort, and sometimes not at all. The arts of inventing and feigning are not new; the practitioners of these frauds existed fourteen centuries ago. Everywhere the Fathers complain of heretics who, in order to lend authority to their fancies, dared to inscribe the books in which they spread them among the people with the names of the most famous teachers of any church, or even of the Apostles themselves. On this very matter, Amphilochius, Bishop of Iconium, who was held in such high esteem by Basil the Great, Archbishop of Caesarea, had written a commentary. In it, the Fathers of the Seventh Synod refute a passage which the Iconoclasts had cited from a foolish work called the Itinerary of the Apostles.

units.la: Atque utinam eruditi istius antistitis extaret lucubratio; facile forsan ex ea foret multorum ridiculorum scriptorum, quæ celeberrimorum & vetustissimorum inter Christianos virorum nomen falsò ementiuntur reuincere vanitatem. Hieronymus varia scripta Apocrypha Apostolorum, & eorum qui proximè iis successere, veluti Petri, Clementis, Barnabæ, & aliorum nomina præferentia proscribit. Eodem loco habentur à septima Synodo Euangelium secundùm S. Thomam & Epistola ad Laodicenses. Si nebulones isti de nominibus Apostolorum sic luserunt; quo licentiæ non proruperunt in Patres? Enim verò fraus isthæc iis semper solennis fuit. Sic legimus Nestorianos Epistolam, quà hæresis eorum primus author
units.tr: And would that the learned bishop's work had survived; perhaps from it one could easily refute the vanity of many ridiculous writers who falsely bear the names of the most famous and most ancient men among Christians. Jerome rejects various apocryphal writings that bear the names of the Apostles and of those who came immediately after them, such as Peter, Clement, Barnabas and others. The Seventh Synod likewise holds the Gospel according to Saint Thomas and the Epistle to the Laodiceans in the same disrepute. If these rascals have played such games with the names of the Apostles, what licence did they not indulge in against the Fathers? Indeed, this kind of fraud was always customary among them. units.la: c Concil. 9. Act. 1. Tom. 2. p. 560. b. author & patrónus, Theodorus Mopsuestiæ Episcopus pugabatur, sub S. Cyrilli Alexandrini nomine promulgasse; sic altera ex parte Eutychianos, ut imperitæ plebi fucum facerent, quosdam Apollinaris libros doctoribus orthodoxis falsò adscriptos in vulgus sparsisse. De hoc argumento Leontius librum scripsit, quo demonstrat homines istos Gregorij Neocæsariensis, Iulij Episcopi Romani, & Athanasij Alexandrini nominibus imprimis ab usos fuisse: Imò librum, cui titulus est, ἡ κατὰ μέρος φύσις, id est fides sigillatim expositæ, quem Turrianus Iesuita, quem Gerardus Voßius, quem Gregorij Neocæsariensis postremæ editio pro genuino & legitimo ejus fœtu obtrudunt, ipsius non esse revera, sed hæretici Apollinaris dolcet. Et qui Bibliothecam Patrum ediderunt idem judicium fecerunt de duodecim anathematibus quæ vulgò eidem Gregorio tribuuntur. His vestigiis insistentes Monothelitæ homiliam à Menna Patriarcha Constantinopolitano ad Vigilium Episcopum Romanum misfam confinxerunt: Item, eiusdem Vigilij libros duos ad Iustinianum & Theodoram, in quibus diserte docebatur eorum hæresis, eàque tria scripta per fraudem quintæ Synodi Codici in Bibliotheca Patriarchatus Constantinopolitani asseruato inseruerunt. In sexta Synodo fraus in lucem protracta & convicta fuit. Aliàs quis illa in tam authentico exemplari legens in errorem adductus non fuisset? Pauca ejus rei exempla tantùm referro, ad specimen hæreticorum audaciæ in iis quæ in hoc genere tentarunt, imò & reipsa effecta dederunt. Hæc autem omnia sub finem seculi septimi, id est, ante nongentos annos acciderunt. Postea in disputationibus de imaginibus, & in controversiis Græcorum cum Latinis, & in plerisque contentionibus Ecclesiasticis, nihil frequentius hinc inde objici videas, quam falsa & supposititia esse quæ alij adversum alios in causæ suæ de fensionem afferunt; ut inde proclive sit colligere, quid hæretici huiusmodi artibus promoverint, quas, etsi in aliis argumentis, frequentes adhibuerunt. Itaque verisimillimum videtur multa nunc sub veterum doctorum nomine legi, ab ipsorum adversariis conficta, ip:ifque supposita, itaut non raro cum hæretico nobis res sit, dum auctorem orthodoxum legere nos putamus, & hostis sub amici persona latet; quo fit ut metuendum sit,ne interdum & nobis & à nobis tanquam veteris Ecclesiæ placita & pronunciata, ea objiciantur, quæ reipsa sunt hæreticorum somnia. Nec enim existimandi sunt adeo hebetes fuisse hærerici, ut statim aperirent venenum,quo ejusmodi pestifera scripta inficiebant: imò illud arte & latenter huc illuc affudisse, & veluti à longinquo hæreseŵn suarum fundamenta substruxisse, censendi sunt, ut fraus, sicut tectior & minùs obvia, sic & perniciosior foret. Sed quamvis hujusmodi dolis veteres libros hæretici plurimum confuderint, attamen, si ij soli his fraudibus grassari fuissent, non ita difficile esset nos ex iis expedire. Verum quod teterrimum est & ferme insanabile malum apud ipsam Ecclesiam, & quidem à veruftissimis usque temporibus fraus illa in vsu fuit. Tanti mali auctores sæpius fuisse existimo Bibliopolas & librarios, qui ante iuventum Typographiam libros manu exarabant. Iam suo tempore querebatur & quidem vehementer Hieronymus de eorum negligentia & audacia in corrumpendis libris. Scribunt (inquit) non quo i inveniunt,sed quod intelligunt,& dū alienos errore emendare nituntur,ostendunt suos.Dubium non est quin quâ licentiâ libros corruperunt, eadem & supposuerint, eóque magis quod hoc suo, eóque magno, illud verò nullo facie- bant compendio. Nec enim quicquam in rem suam faciebant, cum libros corrumpebant& vitiabant; sed cùm pro vilibus & obscuris nominibus grandia & illustria sufficiebant, longè luculentiùs & cariùs eos vendebant. Quoties in manus veniebat opus anonymum, vel nomen quidem præferens,sed ignobile, vel infame, tum illi ne fœdis & inuidiosis istis notis merx sua vilescerer, novum, priore inducto, nomen audacter apponebant, quod in Ecclesia earum esset & venerabile, ut eâ gratiâ merci pretium adderent. Exempli causa: Merito inuidia inter Christianos laborabat Nouatiani nomen; author enim fuerat schismatis aduersùm Ecclesiam Romanam. Tertullianus vero cùm propter ætatem, tum propter ingenium & eruditionem merito magni fiebat. Hoc animadvertens Librarius ad rem attentus vnius lucri gratia, meâ quidem sententiâ. mutare instituit, & librum de Trinitate Tertulliano inscripsit, qui tamen revera erat Nouatiani, quod ipsum ab Hieronymo accepimus. Eandem, vel certè similimam fuisse fortem libri de Pœnitentia qui hodie Tertulliano tribuitur pœne sentio. Sic libro de Operibus Christi cardinalibus, ab auctore suo (quod ipse profitetur) suppresso nomine ad Papam quendam missus (cuius & ipsius nomen in codicibus editis tacetur, manuscripti nonnulli Hadrianum praeferunt) Cypriano inscriptus est, à Librario commodis suis seruiente; adeo vt quemadmodum olim, sic & nunc sub isto nomine feratur; tametsi satis pateat non esse Cypriani; quod & multi tam harum quàm illarum partium viri docti ingenuè agnoscunt. Non erat nullius in Ecclesia nominis Ruffinus; longè tamen aberat à fama & existimatione Cypriani: hinc factum est vt, Ruffini in Symbolum Apostolorum opus, Cypriano tribuerint Librarij. Narrat Senator Cassiodorus, qui A. D. 514 suo nomine Consul signavit, quasdam in x i i i. Pauli Epistolas annotationes subtilissimas quidem & brevissimas,sed erroris tamen Pelagiani venenis infectas,suo tempore in cunctorum manibus ita celebres habitas fuisse,ut eas à S Gelasio Papa vrbis Roma doctissimi viri studio dicerent fuisse conscriptas; quod solent(inquit)facere qui res vitiosas cupiunt gloriosi nominis auctoritate defendere.Haec de veteribus.Sed & sui,id est, superioris seculi librarios multum hac in parte peccasse quèritur Sixtus Senensis. Nihil(inquit) praeter quaesitu arte sua quarentes novos quotidie librorum foenus emittunt.
units.tr: c Council 9, Act 1, vol. 2, p. 560 b. author and patron, Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia, was attacked; and so, on the other side, the Eutychians, in order to deceive the unlearned common people, spread abroad among the public some books of Apollinaris falsely ascribed to orthodox teachers. On this subject Leontius wrote a book in which he shows that these men used above all the names of Gregory of Neocaesarea, Julius, Bishop of Rome, and Athanasius of Alexandria. Indeed, the book entitled ἡ κατὰ μέρος φύσις, that is, the faith set forth part by part, which the Jesuit Turrianus, Gerardus Vossius, and the latest edition of Gregory of Neocaesarea put forward as the genuine and legitimate offspring of that author, is in fact not his at all, but the work of the heretic Apollinaris. Those who edited the Bibliotheca Patrum likewise reached the same judgement about the twelve anathemas commonly attributed to the same Gregory. Following these footsteps, the Monothelites forged a homily sent by Menas, Patriarch of Constantinople, to Vigilius, Bishop of Rome; likewise two books of the same Vigilius to Justinian and Theodora, in which their heresy was plainly taught. These three writings they fraudulently inserted into the Codex of the Fifth Synod preserved in the library of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The fraud was brought to light and exposed at the Sixth Synod. Otherwise, who reading in so authentic a copy would not have been led into error? I mention only a few examples of this kind, to show the audacity of the heretics in what they attempted in this line, and indeed actually accomplished. All these things happened at the end of the seventh century, that is, nine hundred years ago. Afterwards, in the disputes about images, in the controversies between Greeks and Latins, and in most ecclesiastical contests, you will see nothing more frequently objected on every side than that the things the other party brings forward in defence of its cause are false and spurious. Hence it is easy to infer what the heretics advanced by such arts, which they used frequently in other matters as well. Accordingly, it seems very probable that much that is now read under the names of the ancient teachers was invented by their own adversaries and falsely attributed to them, so that we often have to do with a heretic while we think we are reading an orthodox author, and the enemy lies hidden under the mask of a friend. As a result, we must fear that sometimes those things are objected to us, and by us to others, as the opinions and pronouncements of the ancient Church, which are in fact the dreams of heretics. For the heretics must not be thought so dull that they would at once reveal the poison with which they infected such pestilential writings; rather they must be judged to have poured it in here and there cunningly and secretly, and to have laid the foundations of their heresies from a distance, so that the fraud, being more covert and less obvious, was also more pernicious. But although the heretics greatly confused the ancient books by such tricks, yet if they alone had practised these frauds, it would not be so difficult for us to extricate ourselves from them. But the foul and almost incurable evil within the Church itself, and indeed from the most ancient times, is that this fraud was in use. I think the authors of so great an evil were very often the booksellers and scribes who copied books by hand before the invention of printing. Already in his own time Jerome complained, and vehemently, of their carelessness and audacity in corrupting books. They write, he says, not what they find, but what they understand, and while they strive to correct the errors of others, they display their own. There is no doubt that with the same licence with which they corrupted books they also ascribed false authorship, the more so because the one practice gave them a great and profitable shortcut, while the other gave them none. For they gained nothing for themselves by corrupting and spoiling books; but when they gave great and illustrious names to works of obscure and humble ones, they sold them far more brilliantly and dearly. Whenever an anonymous work came into their hands, or one bearing a name that was obscure or infamous, then, lest their wares lose value under those ugly and odious marks, they boldly put a new name in place of the former one, one that was honoured and revered in the Church, so that by this means they might add value to the merchandise. For example: the name of the Novatians was rightly hated among Christians, for their author had been the founder of a schism against the Church of Rome. Tertullian, on the other hand, was rightly held in high regard, both for his age and for his talent and learning. Noticing this, a bookseller attentive to his business, in my opinion for the sake of gain alone, began to change the title, and inscribed a book on the Trinity with Tertullian's name, although in fact it belonged to Novatian, as we learn from Jerome. I think the fate of the book On Repentance, which is today attributed to Tertullian, was the same or very similar. So too the book On the Cardinal Works of Christ, sent by its author (as he himself declares) to a certain Pope without his name (the name of the Pope is also omitted in the printed editions, though some manuscripts give Hadrian), was inscribed with the name of Cyprian by a bookseller serving his own interests. Thus it is carried under that name now, just as it was formerly, although it is quite clear that it is not Cyprian's, as many learned men of both parties frankly acknowledge. Ruffinus was not a man of no reputation in the Church; yet he was far from the fame and estimation of Cyprian. Hence it came about that the booksellers attributed Ruffinus's work on the Apostles' Creed to Cyprian. The senator Cassiodorus, who was consul under his own name in the year 514, relates that certain very subtle and very brief annotations on the thirteen Epistles of Paul, yet tainted with the poison of Pelagian error, were held in such esteem in his time among everyone that they were said by men of great learning in the city of Rome to have been written by Pope Gelasius; which, he says, is what people usually do who wish to defend faulty things by the authority of a glorious name. These things are said of the ancients. But Sixtus of Siena complains that the booksellers of his own time, that is, of the preceding century, also sinned greatly in this respect. Nothing, he says, but what is sought after, they bring out every day new interest on books, by their skill at contriving.

units.la: adulterinos,supposititios,pfeudepigraphos,& nothos,prapofitu absque vllo iudicio & pudore in frontispiciis operum,quo ipsa & cariùs & citius vedant falsis auctorum illustrium infcriptionibus.Hoc sanè artificio supposuerunt nobis inter multos spurios partus Quaftiones in Genefin Philonis Iudai,Quaftiones Inftini Philosophi & Martyris ad gentes, Quaestiones duì Athanafij ad Antiochum. Origenis Paraphrasim in Iob,eiufdemque in eundem Commentarios.Item Arnobij Rhetoris in Psalmos Commetaria,Eusebij Emefeni homilias in Evangelia, Ambrosij in Apocalypsim explanationes, Hieronymi in Proverbia lib.3.& in Lamentationes Hieremia libros tres,Eucherij in Genefeos & Regum historias libros octo,& cum his alia plurima sub nomine praesertim Veterum Patrū afcititia opera, quorum dogmata stilus ac tempora magis ab ipforū titulis & inscriptionibus distant quàm cælum à terra. Tum quorumdam vesaniam exaggerat qui sub diversis duorum aut trium auctorum titulis unum idemque opus exhibuerunt; ut qui easdem in Leviticum homiljas, modo Origenis, modo Cyrilli nomine excuderunt; qui eandem in Ecclefiaften Paraphrafin Gregorii modò Neocaefariensis, modò Nazianzeni titulo praenotarunt; eofdem in Proverbia Commentarios primo Bedæ, postea Hieronymo tribuerunt; easdem in Iob commentationes modò Philippi Presbyteri, modò Bedæ nomine vulgarunt; & eadem collectanea in Hexaemeron tum Bedæ, tum lunilii Afri appellatione censuerunt; & eafdem denique Psalmorum explanationes, prius Hugoni Carensi,posterius Alexandro Halensi inscripserunt. Atque haec hactenus quidem Sixtus; pleraque verissimè. Nec sola librariorum auaritia his fraudibus ansam praebuit. Inscitia etiam cùm ipsorum,tum illorum quos confulebant, foetibus his adulterinis plerumque obstetricara est. Si scripti dubii nomen ad aliquod vetus accederet ; fi stilum referret; fi argumentum conueniret, vel quaepiam alia ratio saltem probabilis priorum esse temporum suaderet, nomen antiqui alicuius auctoris illico præfigebant, & sub eo exscriptum ad sui temporis homines, & per eos ad posteros transmittebant. Nec soli librarii eiusmodi fraudum accusandi. Nunquam non extitere ingenia stultè ambitiosa quæ quoquomodo sensa sua in lucem edere gestierunt, & plurimum ad has sallacias contulerunt. Cùm se homines isti neque viribus, neque gratia satis instructos esse intelligerent, ut per se populo placerent, Veterum nomina sunt ementiti, cum mallent sibi sub alieno nomine plaudi, quam se sub vero & proprio exsibilari. Hi pro captu suo fœlicius infeliciusve Veterum stilum & ingenium expresserunt & effinxerunt, & sub eorum nomine sua opera in vulgus nullo pudore ediderunt. Cùm autem inter mortales mini. ma ferè sapientum & eruditorum copia sit, qui minùs cauti & perspicaces fuere, nullo discrimine subditittios istos fœtus exceperunt & fouerunt, iisque Bibliothecas omnes referserunt. Fuere alij quos ad easdem artes non ambitio, sed quædam alia prava & incondita studia impulere. Sic fuere qui cùm vehementi vel hominum quorundam, vel etiam sententiarum studio tenerentur, de ijs scribere in animum induxerunt sub nomine virorum clarorum, ut pondus & efficaciam suis scriptis adderent.
units.tr: Spurious, supposititious, pseudepigraphal and bastard works are put out, without any judgement or shame, on the title pages of books, so that they may sell both more dearly and more quickly under the false inscriptions of illustrious authors. Indeed by this trick they have foisted on us, among many spurious offspring, the Questions on Genesis of Philo the Jew, the Questions of Justin the philosopher and martyr to the Gentiles, and the Questions of the so-called Athanasius to Antiochus. They have also given us Origen's Paraphrase on Job and his Commentaries on the same book, the Commentaries of Arnobius the rhetorician on the Psalms, the homilies of Eusebius of Emesa on the Gospels, Ambrose's explanations of the Apocalypse, Jerome's three books on Proverbs and on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, Eucherius's eight books on Genesis and the histories of the Kings, and with these very many other works foisted on the names especially of the ancient Fathers, whose doctrines, style and times differ from their titles and inscriptions as far as heaven from earth. Then he exaggerates the madness of those who have put out one and the same work under the titles of two or three different authors. Some printed the same homilies on Leviticus sometimes under the name of Origen and sometimes under that of Cyril; some prefixed the same paraphrase on Ecclesiastes to Gregory's name at one time and to that of Gregory of Neocaesarea or Gregory Nazianzen at another; some attributed the same commentaries on Proverbs first to Bede and later to Jerome; some published the same commentaries on Job under the name of Philip the Presbyter at one time and of Bede at another; some ascribed the same collections on the Hexaemeron both to Bede and to Junilius Africanus; and some finally inscribed the same explanations of the Psalms, first to Hugh of Saint-Cher and later to Alexander of Hales. So far Sixtus, and mostly very truly. Nor was the greed of booksellers the only source of these frauds. Ignorance, both of the authors themselves and of those whom they consulted, has mostly acted as midwife to these adulterine offspring. If the name of a doubtful writing came near some ancient one, if the style agreed, if the subject matched, or some other at least probable reason suggested an earlier date, they at once prefixed the name of some ancient author, and copied the work under his name and handed it on to the men of their own time, and through them to posterity. Nor are booksellers alone to be accused of such frauds. There have never been lacking foolishly ambitious minds, eager to bring their opinions into the light by whatever means, and they contributed greatly to these deceits. When these men realised that they were not sufficiently equipped, either in ability or in favour, to please the public by their own efforts, they falsely used the names of the Ancients, preferring to be applauded under another's name rather than hissed under their own real one. According to their capacity, more or less successfully, they expressed and imitated the style and genius of the Ancients, and under their names they published their own works to the public without any shame. But since among mortals there are very few wise and learned men, those who were less cautious and less perceptive received these spurious offspring without distinction, cherished them, and opened all libraries to them. There were others whom not ambition but some other perverse and ill-considered zeal drove to the same arts. Thus there were those who, held by a vehement attachment either to certain men or even to certain opinions, resolved to write about them under the names of famous men, so that they might give weight and efficacy to their writings.

units.la: Ista propemodum videtur fuisse mens Presbyteri illius, qui Pauli & Theclæ in lucem edidit; qui de eo conuictus apud S. Ioannem, confessus est quod esset libri auctor, seque id amore Pauli fecisse. Talis item fuit Ruf fini Presbyteri Aquileiensis audacia, quem iure optimo passim & quidem acriter reprehendit Hieronymus, Ille, ut Origenis honori consuleret, sub nomine sancti, infigque martyris Pamphili, Apologiam pro eo scripsit, licet revera eam, partim ex primo & secundo libro Eusebii de eodem argumento desumpsisset, partim suo marte fabricatus fuisset. Eiusmodi libido ipsum incessit cum Sexti cuiusdam Philosophi Pythagorei librum sub Sancti Sixti martyris nomine edidit, ut gratior esset & acceptior. Quid amplius? Nonne eodem tempore, ipsoque
units.tr: This seems to have been almost the mind of that presbyter who published the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and who, when he was convicted of it before St John, confessed that he was the author of the book and that he had done so out of love for Paul. Such too was the audacity of Rufinus, the presbyter of Aquileia, whom Jerome rightly and indeed sharply reproved everywhere. In order to do honour to Origen, Rufinus wrote an Apology for him under the name of the saint and martyr Pamphilus, although in fact he had partly drawn it from the first and second books of Eusebius on the same subject, and partly fabricated it with his own hand. The same lust seized him when he published the book of a certain Sextus, a Pythagorean philosopher, under the name of St Sixtus the martyr, so that it might be more pleasing and more acceptable. What more? Did not the very same thing happen at the same time, in the lifetime of Jerome,

Queritur enim suo nomine ab Andrea quodam Græco monacho scriptos fuisse sermones; inter diversa mala (inquit) aliquos etiam sermones scripsit, atque eos ex nostro nomine titulavit. Ipse eos rescindi & omnino aboleri jubet, ut quod (inquit) imperitus litterarum, & Scriptura divina nescius nostro, sicut diximus, nomine prænotavit quorundam animos non possit inficere. Quis ad tantam audaciam non obstupescat? Quis hæc fieri vel potuisse crederet, nisi Hieronymus & Gregorius facta esse ipsi testarentur, deque illata sibi injuria quererentur? Iisdem studiisducebantur (licet minus iniquis) antiquissimi illi Christiani, qui Sibyllina vaticinia de Christo, ejusque regno primi in vulgus sparserunt, ut facilius fidem ab Ethnicis impetrarent; quod & ipsis probro vertere non neglexit Celsus apud Originem. Sed quod longè maximi momenti est, ipsi etiam Patres, seu propriæ sententiæ studio tenerentur, seu affectibus nimis indulgerent suis, has artes interdum adhibuerunt. Exemplum habemus insigne & quod Latinis ante ducentos annos Græci objecerunt. Contendentibus inter se Pontificibus Romanis & Synodis Africanis; illis quidem totius orbis Christiani ad suam sedem appellationes sibi vindicantibus, his contra nitentibus; Zozimus & Bonifacius Episcopi Romani obtrusere Africanis quosdam Canones, quasi Concilii Nicæni, quibus eas ad se pertinere confirmarent, Commoni Afri (hæc autem incunte quinto seculo acta sunt) illico Constantinopolini, Alexandriam, & Antiochiam mittere; in optima, incorruptissima, adeoque authentica Concilii Nicæni exemplaria inquirere, nec labori nec diligentiæ parcere; Canones verò isti, Nicæni, scilicet, nusquam comparere. Enimverò quamuis Canones & acta Nicæna, quæ nunc tervVitur, ex illo tempore per multas manus transfiuerint, iis tamen nihil eiusmodi continetur, ne quidem in editionibus quas homines dignitatis Pontificiæ studiosissimi procurarunt; qualis illa Latina est, quam collegit & edidit Dionysius exiguus, circa annum Domini 525. neque in vllis aliis, seu veteribus, seu recentibus. Nam quod attinet ad illud Concilij Nicæni exemplar quod nescio quis Fr. Ioannes in Synodo Florentina solum illibatum evasisse à corruptelis Arianorum, propterea que sub clauì diligenter clausum & sigillo munitum Romæ asservatum contendit, lex quo Canones illi desumpti sunt; nè oportet revera arctissimè observatum & obsignatum fuisse: cuius in re tanti momenti ne tribus quidem Pontificibus Romanis, Zozimo, Bonifacio & Celestino copia facta est: maximè tum laborantibus in afferenda apud Patres Africanos fide sua; ut vehementer minum sit, qui Fratri Ioanni, homini mille anni post nato, id in mentem venerit, cùm illi ipsi qui illud penes se, scilicet, habebant, ne verbulum quidem de eo unquam fecerint; quod argumento inuicto, est, exquisiti istius voluminis sigilla nunquam aperta aut reserata alibi fuisse nisi in fraterculi istius cerebro; in quo uno fabricatum & reconditum, natum & mortuum simul esse apparet: maxima quippe pars eorum qui subsecuti sunt fiuolum istud commentum neglexere, neque eo quisquam in hisce controversiis nunc utitur. Sed si verum amamus, ne id quidem quod ipsi excusandis istis pontificibus comminiscuntur hilo est Fr. Ioannis mendacio prabilius. Isti scilicet, caussantur suos illos Pontifices Nicænam & Sardicensem Synodos (in qui postremâ habenturCanones ab ijs citati) pro una eademque habu'isse. Cui enim fidem facient pro uno & eodem Concilio consendos duos coetus Ecclesiasticos, totis viginti duobus annis inter se dissitos, à diversis imperatoribus convocatos, ob causas admodum diversas? Illum quidem ad Illustrationem fidei, hunc vero ad restituendos duos Episcopos, adhaec in locis remotissimis, alterum Nicaeae, Sardicae alterum habitos, quorum denique Canones plurimum inter se discrepant, argumento, numero, authoritate? Cum Nicaenos quidem semper ab omni Ecclesia receptos, Sardicenses vero in Oriente ne notos quidem fuisse constet? Id confirmare qui queant, qui tam acriter invehuntur in Graecos, quod in multo majori cum rationis specie sextae Synodo tribuant C I I. Canones Constantinopoli decennio post in coetu cui plerique sextae Synodi Patres intererant conditos? Qui in vetere Ecclesia receptum istud fuit, cum in antiquorum istorum Canonum collectione Graeca Sardicenses plane omissi sint, & in illa Latina, quam Dionysius exiguus ab hinc mille & centum annis centexuit Romae, non cum Nicaenis, aut proxime post illos, quasi unum corpus cum iis constituentes, sed longe infra illos, & post omnium quae hactenus habita fuerant Conciliorum Canones reiecti sint? Unde quoque accidit ut, si ea fuit Veterum istorum Pontificum sententia, dum eos allegant prosus de ea tacent? Negabant constanter Africani Episcopi istos sibi a Romanis objectos canones in suis codicibus habere. Cur ad haec non respondebant Romani, eos extare in illa altera quam recentiores nunc memorant canonum Nicaenorum parte, inter eos qui Sardicae conditi sunt? Nonne id in promptu erat, si Nicaenam & Sardicensem Synodos pro una eademque habuere; Maximè cum bonos istos Africanae Synodi Patres, ut se ex his ambagibus expedirent, demittendo Constantinopolim & Alexandriam senserunt deliberare? Et tamen de ea re ne γρῦ quidem. Si Canones Sardicensis pro Concilii Nicaeni parte habiti sunt, mirandum est tot Africanos Praesules, tam doctos adeoque pios, Aurelium, Alypium, sanctumque ipsum Augustinum, clarissimum Africae, totiusque Ecclesiae iubar, id prorsus latuisse.
units.tr: { } Illegible marginal references in the margins were not reliably read. a certain very eloquent man, resenting that Jerome had put Hebrew volumes into Latin, and as if he had been led in youth to that purpose by the Hebrews, forged a letter in Jerome's name, in which he seemed to repent of it, and secretly, without his knowledge, spread it abroad at Rome and in Africa among the people. Gregory the Pope, surnamed the Great, testifies that something similar happened to himself. For he complains that sermons had been written in his name by a certain Greek monk, Andrew: among his various faults (he says) he also wrote some sermons and titled them with our name. He orders that they be cut up and utterly abolished, so that what (he says) a man unlearned in letters and ignorant of divine Scripture has marked with our name, as we have said, may not be able to infect the minds of some. Who would not be astonished at such audacity? Who would believe that these things could have been done, unless Jerome and Gregory had themselves testified that they had been done and complained of the wrong inflicted on them? Under the same zeal (though less malicious) were led those most ancient Christians who first spread the Sibylline prophecies about Christ and his kingdom among the people, so that they might more easily win belief from the heathen; Celsus, in Origen, did not fail to turn this to their disgrace. But what is of far greater importance, the Fathers themselves, whether they were held by zeal for their own opinion or indulged their own feelings too much, sometimes resorted to these arts. We have a notable example, which the Greeks objected to the Latins about two hundred years ago. When the Roman Pontiffs and the African synods were contending with each other, the former claiming for their see appeals from the whole Christian world, and the latter resisting, Zosimus and Boniface, bishops of Rome, thrust upon the Africans certain canons, as if of the Council of Nicaea, by which they might confirm that such appeals belonged to Rome. The Africans (and this happened at the beginning of the fifth century) at once sent to Constantinople, Alexandria and Antioch to seek out the best, most uncorrupted and therefore authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea, sparing neither labour nor diligence. But those canons, the Nicene ones, appeared nowhere. Indeed, although the canons and acts of Nicaea which are now in circulation have passed through many hands since that time, nothing of that kind is contained in them, not even in the editions which men most zealous for papal dignity have produced, such as that Latin one which Dionysius Exiguus collected and published about the year of the Lord 525, nor in any others, ancient or recent. As for that copy of the Council of Nicaea which a certain Fr. John claimed at the Synod of Florence had alone escaped the corruptions of the Arians, and which therefore he said had been carefully kept under lock and sealed at Rome, from which those canons were taken: it must surely have been observed and sealed most strictly. Yet of a matter so important not even three Roman Pontiffs, Zosimus, Boniface and Celestine, were granted access, although they were labouring most of all to establish their faith before the African Fathers. So it is very ridiculous that this should have occurred to Brother John, a man born a thousand years later, when those very people who had it in their own keeping never said a single word about it. This is an unanswerable argument that the seals of that exquisite volume were never opened or unlocked anywhere except in the brain of that little brother, in which alone it appears to have been fabricated and hidden, born and dead at the same time. For the greater part of those who came after neglected that trifling invention, and no one now uses it in these controversies. But if we love the truth, what they devise to excuse these Pontiffs is no more credible than Fr. John's lie. They plead, forsooth, that those popes held the Nicene and Sardican synods (in which the canons cited by them are finally found) to be one and the same. For who will make us believe that two ecclesiastical assemblies, separated from each other by a full twenty-two years, convened by different emperors for very different causes (the one for the illustration of the faith, the other for restoring two bishops), and held in most remote places, the one at Nicaea and the other at Sardica, whose canons differ greatly among themselves in subject, number and authority, were one and the same? When it is established that the Nicene canons were always received by the whole Church, but that the Sardican were not even known in the East? Who can confirm this, when they inveigh so bitterly against the Greeks because, with far greater show of reason, the Greeks assign to the Sixth Synod 102 canons made at Constantinople ten years later, in an assembly which most of the Fathers of the Sixth Synod attended? How could that view have been received in the ancient Church, when in the Greek collection of those ancient canons the Sardican are omitted altogether, and in that Latin collection which Dionysius Exiguus compiled at Rome a thousand and a hundred years ago they were rejected, not placed with the Nicene canons or immediately after them as forming one body with them, but far below them, and after the canons of all the councils held hitherto? Whence it also follows that, if this was the opinion of those ancient Pontiffs, while they cite the canons they say nothing at all about it. The African bishops steadfastly denied that they had in their codices those canons objected to them by the Romans. Why did the Romans not reply that they were to be found in that other part of the Nicene canons which recent writers now cite, namely among those drawn up at Sardica? Would this not have been at hand if they had held the Nicene and Sardican synods to be one and the same, especially since they saw that the good Fathers of the African synod, to extricate themselves from these ambiguities, were deliberating about sending to Constantinople and Alexandria? And yet not a whisper [γρῦ] about this matter. If the Sardican canons were regarded as part of the Council of Nicaea, it is astonishing that so many African prelates, so learned and so pious, Aurelius, Alypius, and St Augustine himself, the most famous ornament of Africa and of the whole Church, should have been entirely ignorant of it.

units.la: Codex Canon. Eccles. Vni-vers. Dionys. epig. p. 99. latuisse. Sed portentum plane est, eorum non miserios tres Pontifices Romanos,eorumque Legatos, nec dignatos vno aut altero verbo, quod perfacile fuit, eos ex tam crassa, tamque suis rebus noxia ignorantia liberare. Stet erg.o immotum, Zozimum & Bonifacium Pontifices, non alia habuisse Canonum Nicænorum exemplaria quàm nostra, neque censuisse Sardicæ decreta Concilii Nicæni partem facere; sed scienter & prudenter Synodo Nicenæ Canones Sardicenses supposuisse. Illi nimirum ex quadam vulgari sententia, & superioribus seculis recepta, & ab horum temporum moribus minimè alienà, existimarunt ad bona & sancta promovenda consilia fas interdum esse astu rem gerere, & fraudes illas quas pias dicunt adhibere. Cum ergo apud se constituissent, Sedis suæ supra omnes alias primatum magni esse momenti, & ad rem Christianam plurimum conferre, non est quod miretur,si adjura illius confirmanda, paululum de via deflexerunt, & Sardicam pro Nicæa subiecerunt,rati futurum vt,si voti compotes fierent, rei ipsius vtilitas, & secutura ex ea commodo, facilè farcirent quicquid in re ipsa peccatum esset. Neque tum accepta ab Africanis Patribus repulsa obstitit quominus aliquot post annis Leo Papa,ad Theodosium Imperatorem scribens, eadem arte ipsum adoriretur, & Sardicensem pro vero Canone Nicæno supponeret. Vnde fit ut Valentinianus & Galla Placidia, ad eundem Theodosium scribentes, extra dubium ponant Veteres, & Nicænos Canones,de fide & Præsulibus Ecclesiæ judicandi jus Pontifici Romano concessisse. Authore, scilicet, Leone, à quo Sardicense decretum, pro Canone Nicæno acceperant. Atque ita porro perrectum est in fraude ista pia, vt maximæ Christianorum parti persuasum sit Nicæni Concilij decreto Romanum Primatum fuisse constitutum, ita ut in hac controversia maxima illius Synodi auctoritas pro hac sententia passim obtrudatur.Ignoscè, benigne Lector,quod tam diu,& forsan vltra quam pro-
units.tr: Codex Canon. Eccles. Vniv. Dionys. epig. p. 99. latuisse. But it is a plain portent that the three Roman Pontiffs and their legates did not think it worth one word or another, which would have been very easy, to free those Fathers from such a gross and self-harming ignorance. Let it therefore stand firm that the Popes Zosimus and Boniface had no other copies of the Nicene Canons than ours, and did not judge the decrees of Sardica to be part of the Council of Nicaea; rather, they knowingly and prudently passed off the Sardican canons as Nicene. For they had held the common opinion, received in earlier centuries and not far removed from the customs of our own times, that it is sometimes right to act by stratagem for the promotion of good and holy aims, and to employ those deceits which they call pious. Having therefore settled in their own minds that the primacy of their See above all others was of great importance and contributed much to the Christian cause, it is no wonder that, in order to confirm that primacy, they strayed a little from the path and substituted Sardica for Nicaea, reckoning that if they succeeded, the usefulness of the thing itself and the advantage to follow from it would easily make up for whatever was wrong in the matter. Nor did the rejection received from the African Fathers prevent Pope Leo, some years later, writing to the Emperor Theodosius, from attacking him by the same device and passing off the Sardican canon as the true Nicene canon. Hence Valentinian and Galla Placidia, writing to the same Theodosius, place beyond doubt that the ancients and the Nicene canons granted to the Roman Pontiff the right of judging concerning faith and the bishops of the Church. Leo was the author, of course, from whom they had received the Sardican decree as the Nicene canon. And so this pious fraud was carried on until the greater part of Christians came to be persuaded that the primacy of Rome had been established by a decree of the Council of Nicaea, so that in this controversy the great authority of that Synod is everywhere thrust forward in support of this opinion. Pardon me, kind reader, that I have dwelt so long, and perhaps longer than my plan allowed, on this argument; for it seemed to me of the greatest importance in this controversy.
