units.la: polito meo conveniebat, ut remoratus sim in hoc argumento, id enim mihi magni omnino momenti esse visum est in hac controversia. Quid enim (inquiunt Protestantes) expectandum nobis est à reliquis Episcopis & Doctoribus, quandoquidem Papæ duo, quos omnium Christianorum Pontifices & Coryphæos volunt, falsa suppositi-unt? Et quidem in ipsis quinti seculi initiis, quibus fides & doctrinæ sinceritas plurimum viguisse putantur; Qui iis temporibus talia ausi sunt, qu'd non secerunt in sequentibus; Quibus scriptoribus pepercerunt qui sacro Nicæni Concilii illustrissimi, post verbum Dei, in Christianismo monumenti nomine abuti non sunt veriti? Qui in adeo angusti coetus luce, in ore doctissimorum sanctissimorumque totius Africæ Episcopo-rum, Immo sub magni ipsius Augustini oculis, talia commiserunt & usurpare non dubitarunt, quid alias sibi non permiserunt? Quid non inceptum & susceptum est in longis densisque tenebris quæ per totum post secula secula in totam terram incubuerunt, Mihi quidem certè nunc non est propositum eos, vel accusare propterea, vel excusare. Hoc unum volo, non esse adeo proclive quàm prima fronte videatur, veras Patrum sententias ex iis scriptis intelligere quæ sub eorum nomine hodie circumferuntur, quandoquidem, qui tanto tempore ante nos ea apud se habuerunt sic se in iis gesserunt. Non ablimilis postea fuit Hadriani I. Romani quoque Pontificis versutia, qui ut suam de Sabbati jejunio traditionem Egilæ Episcopo & cæteris Hispanis commendaret, non dubitavit Ambrosii auctoritate abuti. Iubet enim Egilam B. Augustini opusculal legere, vbi (inquit) egregium praedicatorem atque doctorem suum S. Ambrosium meminit pro jejunio Sabbati Sanctam Catholicam Apostolicam nostrum Romanam nimis lan iasse Ecclesiam. Hoc vero longe salsissimum est. Extat enim Augustini ad Casulanum epistola, ad quam respicit hoc loco Hadrianus; unde discere licet Ambrosium, neque Romanam, quod Sabbato jejunaret, neque suam Mediolanensem, quod Sabbato non jejunaret. Laudasse Ecclesiam, sed utrumque ritum nullo plane discrimine habuisse, observandumque divo simodo censuisse, pro more Ecclesiæ in qua versamur. Quando hic sum, (inquit, id est, Medi lani) non jejuno Sabbato; quando Romæ sum, jejuno Sabbato; & ad quamcunque Ecclesiam veneritis, eius morem servate, si patiscandalum non vultis, aut facere.
units.tr: For what (say the Protestants) are we to expect from the other bishops and teachers, since the two Popes whom they wish to be the pontiffs and leaders of all Christians have falsified things? And indeed, in the very beginnings of the fifth century, when faith and purity of doctrine are thought to have flourished most, who dared such things at that time that they did not do in later ages? Whom did they spare among writers, those who were not afraid to abuse the sacred monument of the most illustrious Council of Nicaea, which after the Word of God is the monument of Christianity? In the very light of so narrow an assembly, in the presence of the most learned and holiest bishops of all Africa, nay, under the very eyes of the great Augustine himself, they committed such acts and did not hesitate to use them; what did they not permit themselves elsewhere? What was not begun and undertaken in the long and thick darkness which for centuries afterwards brooded over the whole earth? For my part, I certainly have no intention now either to accuse them for this or to excuse them. This one thing I wish: it is not nearly as easy as it seems at first sight to understand the true opinions of the Fathers from those writings which now circulate under their names, since those who had them in their hands for so long a time before us conducted themselves in this way with regard to them. Not unlike this was the trickery of Hadrian I, also Pope of Rome, who, in order to commend his tradition about fasting on the Sabbath to Bishop Egila and the other Spaniards, did not hesitate to abuse the authority of Ambrose. For he bids Egila read the little work of blessed Augustine, where (he says) he recalls that his distinguished preacher and teacher, St Ambrose, greatly praised our holy, Catholic, Apostolic Church of Rome for fasting on the Sabbath. But this is by far the most absurd thing. For there exists Augustine's letter to Casulanus, to which Hadrian refers at this point; from it one may learn that Ambrose praised neither the Roman Church for fasting on the Sabbath nor his own Milanese Church for not fasting on it, but that he regarded both customs as having no difference at all, and judged that each should be observed in accordance with the custom of the Church in which one lives. When I am here (he says, that is, at Milan) I do not fast on the Sabbath; when I am at Rome I fast on the Sabbath; and to whatever Church you come, observe its custom, if you do not wish to give or take scandal.

units.la: Non plura apud Augustinum Ambrosius. Hoccine quæsio illud est quod somniat Hadrianus, pro jejunio Sabbati Ecclesiam Romanam nimis laudare? Ipse vero Ambrosium si probat, cur non sequitur? Cur Egilam, non Romæ, sed in Hispania consistentem, Sabbato jejunare jubet? Vides quam ingeniosus fuerit Hadrianus, qui quem ritum se ferre, eiusque se pro loci ac temporis ratione accommodare ait Ambrosius, eum sic laudatum fingit, quasi necessariò ac ubique retinendum censuisset. Augustinus ipse Ambrosii quidem prudentiam atque caritatem probat ac sequitur, non obscurè tamen significat, se putasse cærorum Christianorum, qui Sabbato prandebant, probabiliorem quam Romanorum qui jejunabant, morem fuisse. Sic etiam videmus paribus animorum suorum studiis obscuros peccasse Concilii V. Patres, apud quos Acta & totius Synodi silentio probato fuit suppositicia Theodoreti de morte Cyrilli Epistola, tam evidenter falsa, ut, qui Conciliorum generalium editioni Romæ præfuerunt, eam falsitatis arguerint & convicerint. Eiusdem fuit allata in Concilio VII. tóraque inserta, sub nomine Athanasii, de miraculo ab imagine Christi patrata in urbe Beryto, narratio, adeo quidem inepta & indigna lepore & nitore magni illius ingenii, ut sensu communi carere oporteat qui eam illi tribuant. Unde factum videmus, ut neque exemplo, neque auctoritate Concilii deterreri potuerint vel Nannius, vel Bellarminus, vel Possevinus, quominus eam Athanasii esse negaret, alterius esse confiterentur. Eodem loco pono donationis Constantini decantatissimum instrumentum, quod tam diu authenticum, validissimumque habitum fuit, adeo ut in decreto infertum, & ab Episcopo Eugubino, adversus Laurentij Vallæ objectiones, pertinacissime defensum fuerit. At qui jam donationem ipsam ratam volunt & tuentur instrumentum istud tanquam futile & suppositicium repudiant. Non sunt meliores illi Antiochenæ vetustissimæ & Apostolicæ (si licet credere) Synodi canones, quos ex lesuitæ Turriani vanissimi fabulatoris mendacissimis scriniis depromptos Baronius fusè memoravit, & inverecundissimus Baronii expilator Binius in Ecclesiasticos Conciliorum Tomos (in quibus nullum hactenus locum invenerant) audacissimè pessimoque exemplo referre non dubitavit. In hoc quoque censu collocanda sunt Sylvestri P. R. acta, fabulis & mendaciis referta, quorum partem aliquam detegit ac coarguit Baronius. Quod verò ipse hariolatur hæc falsa addita fuisse aliena manu, seque sperat spuria à veris posse secernere, cause Papalis studio de more abreptus nos ludit. Nam & illa quæ de Eusebio auctore in præfatione habentur, quæque ipse adjitia esse vult, jam ante octingentos annos in his Actis plane, ut hodie, extitisse satis docet Rathramni Corbeiensis auctoritas, qui duo quædam loca ex his Actis, libro quarto adversus oppositia Græcorum nondum edito, describens utrumque diserte citat, ex Eusebio Historiographo Cæsariensi Episcopo in libello vitæ Sylvestri, vel, quem de gestis Sylvestri Papæ compositum. Unde apparet Acta illa plane eadem olim, Caroli Calui temporibus fuisse, quæ nunc sunt; id est, falsa & fictitia; quorum cum fidem in his & aliis quibusdam labare ipse confiteatur Baronius, non video cur, vel qua ratione, eam in cæteris quæ his Actis superstruit prestare possit. Non dubito quin sint ejusdem farinæ Acta illa Synodi Romanæ 280. Epiphanii Synodi, quæ A.D. 324. ab eodem Sylvestro habita fuisse fingitur, & secunda dicitur; & Sinvessanæ quoque illius Synodi, trecentorum scilicet Episcoporum, quæ A.D.
units.tr: Ambrose says no more than this in Augustine. Is this the thing which Hadrian dreams of, that he praised the Roman Church greatly for fasting on the Sabbath? But if he approves of Ambrose, why does he not follow him? Why does he order Egila, who stays not at Rome but in Spain, to fast on the Sabbath? You see how ingenious Hadrian was, who feigns that Ambrose, who said that he kept one custom and adapted himself to each place and time, had so praised that custom as if he had judged it to be necessarily and everywhere retained. Augustine himself indeed approves and follows Ambrose's prudence and charity, yet he does not obscurely hint that he thought the custom of the eastern Christians, who dined on the Sabbath, more probable than that of the Romans, who fasted. So too we see the Fathers of the Fifth Council, who, through a like zeal of their minds, sinned in this respect, and in whose Acts the spurious letter of Theodoret on the death of Cyril was approved by the silence of the whole Synod, although it is so evidently false that those who oversaw the Roman edition of the general Councils convicted and proved it to be a forgery. Of the same kind was the narrative, produced at the Seventh Council and inserted there entire under the name of Athanasius, concerning a miracle wrought by an image of Christ in the city of Berytus; it is so silly and so unworthy of the wit and polish of that great genius that anyone who attributes it to him must lack common sense. Hence we see that neither the example nor the authority of the Council could deter Nannius, Bellarmine or Possevinus from denying that it was Athanasius's and from confessing that it belonged to another. In the same place I put the most celebrated instrument, the Donation of Constantine, which was held authentic and most valid for so long that it was inserted in a decree and defended most stubbornly by the Bishop of Gubbio against the objections of Lorenzo Valla. But now those who want the donation itself upheld and defended reject that instrument as trifling and spurious. The canons of the Antiochene Synod, most ancient and (if we may believe it) Apostolic, are no better; Baronius at length related them, drawn from the most mendacious papers of the Jesuit Turrianus, a most empty-headed fabricator, and the most shameless plunderer of Baronius, Binius, dared most boldly and with a very bad example to bring them into the Ecclesiastical Tomes of the Councils, where they had found no place until then. Among this class also must be placed the Acts of Pope Sylvester, filled with fables and lies, some part of which Baronius has uncovered and refuted. But when he himself guesses that these false additions were made by another hand, and hopes that he can separate the spurious from the true, he mocks us, carried away by the zeal of the Papal cause. For the authority of Rathramnus of Corbie amply shows that both those things which are found in the preface about Eusebius as author, and which he himself wants to be additions, already existed in these very Acts, as they are today, eight hundred years ago; for in his fourth book against the objections of the Greeks, not yet published, he quotes two passages from these Acts expressly, ascribing them to Eusebius the historian, bishop of Caesarea, in the little book of the life of Sylvester, or what he composed on the deeds of Pope Sylvester. Whence it appears that those Acts were then, in the times of Charles the Bald, entirely the same as they are now, that is, false and fictitious. And since Baronius himself confesses that their credibility wavers in these and some other matters, I do not see why, or on what ground, they could be trusted in the other things which he builds upon these Acts. I have no doubt that the Acts of the Roman Synod of 280 bishops, of the Synod of Epiphanius, which is feigned to have been held by the same Sylvester in A.D. 324 and is called the second, and likewise those of the Synod of Sinuessa, namely of three hundred bishops, which is recorded as having been celebrated in A.D. 303 concerning the cause of Marcellinus, bishop of the city, are of the same stuff, and Baronius himself wavers over them.

units.la: A. D 303. de Marcellini urbici Episcopi causa celebrata memoriatur, in quibus ipse Baronius fluctuat. Praeter universale omnium veteris ad annum usque fexcentefimum memoriae scripto rum silentium, qui de his gravissimis fiilicet frequentissimis ac nobilissimis Synodis plane nullum verbum fecerunt, non pauca sunt in ipsis earum Actis, quae utramque falsam ac commentitiam esse arguunt; de quibus vide si libet Ioannem Rainoldum, & Robertum Cocum Anglos fusius in suis quemque incubrationibus disputantes. Sunt & ejus generis alia innumerabilia, Martyrum passiones, & Episcoporum aut Sanctorum qui in primis Christianismi seculis flo ruerunt vitas praeferentia, certis verisque, tum Ecclesiasticae historiae scriptoribus, tum aliis istorum temporum indubitatis auctoribus ignota; adhaec eorum, quae ex authenticis habentur, fidei in multis saepe adversantia; postremo veritas temporum rationi repugnantia, & vel falsos, vel alienos Consules mentientia. Quo loco non possum non denotare scelieratam recentiorum in istis diligentiam, ex quibus, quaecunque extant certa falsitatis argumenta, ipsi delere & immutare non dubitant, ne quis eorum ex iis fidem vel revincere, vel suspectam habere in posterum queat. Verbi gratia; In Martyrologio Romano ad d.21. Octob. antehac ita legebatur. In Colonia Agrippinensi natale sanctarum undecim millium Virginum, quae pro virginitatis constantia martyrio vitam consummaverunt. Sed quod illa tam multarum Virginum multitudo narrationis absurditatem & falsitatem aigueret, emendatores earum numerum deleverunt, & totum locum ita refinxerunt, ut legere est in Baroniana editione; Apud Coloniam Agrippinam natalis Sanctarum Virgulae & Sociarum ejus, quae pro Christiana religione & Virginitatis constantia ab Hunnis interfectae, martyrio vitam consummaverunt, & plurima earum corpora Colonia condita fuerunt. Ejusdem est commatis, quod sequitur exemplum. Catharina in Legendis & Breviariis, & Martyrologiis omnibus Cofli Regis filia fuisse dicebatur. Iam quod ex veris, certisque constaret nullum Maxentii tempore, quo Catharina passa esse fingitur, Costum Regem in rerum natura extitisse; omnis haec inaufpicata Cofli mentio, quae narrationis vanitatem ofteudebat, in Pii P.R.V. Breviario prudenter (quis neget;) expuncta est. Sed & pro Maxentio,qui istic abipfo quoque Pio ex omnium retro Catharinae actorum fide relictus haeserat, pari postea actu Maximino à Clemente VIII. & Vrbano VIII.P.R.in Breviario à Baronio in Martyrologio Romano substitutus; nec scilicet eo indicio insulsa quidem, sed tamen bona fabula fe ipsam proderet; quod ex veteri historia eertum fit Alexandriae, ubi res geita fuisse narratur, non Maxentium, sed Maximinum per ea tempora imperafse. Magnus in hoc genere artifex fuit, homo quisquiliarum & fabularum auidissimus Turrianus, cui semper praesto sunt, caeteris, praeter ipsum mortalibus inuisi & inaudati, codices, & quibus suorum apocryphorum lectionem,quoties ea absurda est, pro sua libidine refingat. Ita quorum Praefectorum litterae PfeudoEuaristus mittere fe ad Afros Episcopos dicit, eos Turrianus in Prophetas transmutat; In exemplaribus (inquit) vetustissimis,vno Vaticana Bibliotheca, altero Florentina S. Marci non Praefectorum,sed Prophetarum scriptum est. Nimirum illae Praefectorum litterae, scriptorem alium esse ab Evarifto arguebant, cuius temporibus nulli Praefecti erant, qui litteras in decretorum Papalium gratiam in Provinciis scriberent. Sed turriani impofturam prodit fons ex quo totum hunc suum locum Pfeudo Euaristus deriuauit. Innocentius,scilicet,apud quem Praefectorum,non Prophetarum litera constanter legitur, Epistola XII. ex qua impudentiffimus juxta ac infulfiffimus plagiarius omnia illa verba descripserat. Idem quod in hoc Turrianus,alii in aliis fecerunt. Ita Baronius & Bellarminus, quae ex omnium codicum consensu Clementis prima est ad Jacobum Epistola, cam ad Symeonem est voluntj volunt; quòd Iacobi nomen, qui necessario reperitur, antequam ea epistola scriberetur mortuus, opus esse convinceret à maleferiato impostore jampridem suppositum. Ita Baronius ut Sinuessanæ Synodi acta ab apertissimo mendacio purget, quo narrant Diocletianum in bello Persico de Marcellino ab Episcopis condemnato audiuisse, pro his verbis, dum esset in bello Persarum, rescribi legique vult cum reversus esset è bello Persarum; quod intelligat ex veris Persicum Diocletiani bellum, imo & triumphum multo ante octavum Maximiania consulatum (quo Marcellinus damnatus esse fingitur ) gestum fuisse. Idem consimili audacia ac fraude in Actis Philippi Augustalis Egypti Praefecti, corrigi jubet quod istic in omnibus exemplaribus legitur, Philippum illum fuisse factum Alexandriæ Episcopum, quòd nempe crassum manifestúmque mendacium Actuum illorum falsitatem evidenter argueret. Sic quos Acta paffionis Stephani Papæ manuscripta exhibebant Valeriano 3. & Gallienum 2. Consules, idem Baronius Valeria A.D.260.§.1. num 4. & Gallienum 2. edit; quòd scriptus ille Consulatus rebus gestis non congruit. Acta Sebastiani & sociorum falsa revincuntur quòd quem Urbis Praefectum tabulæ publicæ Iunium maximum edunt, hæ Fabianum mentiantur. Baronius ut impostura argumentum debeat Fabium in tabulis pro Iunio, nullo libro auctore, pro sua libidine scribi jubet. Quin & huic suæ methodo ita confisus videtur, ut putaverit scripta vera ex falsis, genuina ex nothis fieri, postquam iis semel detraxit, quæ inerant falsitatis argumenta. Certè, de Epistola Fabiani P.R.Kal. Iulii Maximin. Aug. & Africano Coss. ad omnes comministros data, quodam loco sic loquitur; Tam (inquit) in titulo quàm etiam in Consulibus depravata adeo est ut spuria penitus censeatur, nisi nonnulla in ea posita corrigantur. Itaque putavit istis correctis nō futuram amplius spuriam; quod mirum profecto est hominis judicium; quasi verò ulla correctione fieri possit, ut verum ac genuinum fiat quod falsum & spurium est. Ita fieri fateor ut nemo posthac deprehendere facile possit, an id quod correctum est, revera falsum sit; ut non nisi falsum, nulla arte effici poterit. Vt enim Fabiani Epistola fuerit, quae revera non fuit, nullae Baronij spongiae, nulli unquam pumices praestabunt. Tantum efficient ut ea detractis falsitatis suae argumentis facilius in posterum homines sallat; quo, ut liquet, omnes istorum artes contendunt ac collimant. Iis vero & Binius, Baronium de more secutus, non raro utitur. Cum enim quae Cornelii Pontificis Rom. nomine fertur Epistola 1. eam notham esse & ab aliquo Ioano confictam clamet fabula de corporibus Petri & Pauli ex catacumbis rogatu Lucinae levatis, Binius ut epistolam hoc stigmate liberet, comminiscitur id iam eam mendose irrepsisse; cum tamen constans omnium codicum consensus doceat fabulam istam non ab alio infultam, sed ab ipso auctore ita primum scriptam ut nunc ibi legitur. Idem alibi eadem inverecundia singit Epistolae Eusebii P. R. tertiae aliunde assumptum esse quod illic in omnibus exemplaribus narratur de Christi cruce nuper d.s. Id. Maji, suis temporibus repetit; quod, hoc, scilicet, commentum liquido 'extendat Epistolam, non Eusebii, sed impostoris alicujus esse. Idem cum sallus Felicium & Maximiani Consulatus primam Iulii P. R. epistolam in cujus omnibus exemplaribus adscriptus est, notham & suppositam iam esse arguerret, impudenter scribit Feliciano & Tiliano Coff. datam esse. Idem, Baronii audaciam secutus, cortigi vult finem secundae epistolae Ioannis P. R. & pro his verbis, quae omnia exemplaria pariter exhibent. Data 5. Id. Iun. Maximo & Olybrio coff. reficribi. Data Olybrio coff. quia scilicet, & commentitius Maximi cum Olybrio consulatus, & dies 5. Id. Iun. (ante quem mortuus est Ioannes) epistolam spuriam & Ioanni impudenter affictam, atque suppositam esse docent; quam Baronius & Binius exeo animi studio veram esse cupiunt. Sed & has, & alias item plurimas epistolas falsas esse, etiam aliunde constat, quæ Clemente, Anacleto, Euaristo, Alexandro, Sixto, Telesphoro, Hygino, Pio, Aniceto, & aliis usque ad S. Icium, id est, usque ad annum Christi cccLxxxv. antiquissimis Episcopis Romanis tribuuntur, ut ut sub venerandis istis titulis jam ab octingentis annis legantur. Illæ epistolæ, fatentur, non paucas controversias, maximè verò eam quæ de Monarchia Papali est, decidunt quidem secundùm Romanos, sed hoc ipsum argumentum est, quæ meas & quod consilium fuerit Mercatoris illius qui primus eas venales habuit. Pleræque certè à doctis viris Henrico Kaltheisen, Nicolao Cusano, Iurreremara. Cardinale utroque, Erasmo, Ioanne Dediodone, Claudio Espenseo, Cafsandro, Simone Vigorio, Baronio & aliis spuriæ habentur. Et reuera satis superque patet earum falsitas, tum ex stili barbarie, tam ex erroribus quibus scatent passim, cùm in Chronologia, tum in Historia, tum quod centones sint male consuti ex variis hinc inde corrasis scriptorum, quæ etiamnum hodie extant, locis, tum deni que ex omnium auctorum qui primis octo seculis floruerunt altissimo de iis silentio. Iam sex, septemve prioris seculi ...
units.tr: In the year 303 A.D. a council is recorded as having been held on the case of Marcellinus, bishop of Rome, and Baronius himself wavers over it. Apart from the complete silence of all the ancient writers down to the year 600, who said nothing at all about these very serious, very numerous and very famous synods, there are not a few things in their own Acts which prove that both are false and invented. On these see, if you like, John Rainolds and Robert Cook, the Englishmen, who argue at length on the subject in their own separate treatises. There are also countless other stories of this kind: the sufferings of martyrs and the lives of bishops or saints who flourished in the first ages of Christianity, which are unknown to the certain and true writers of ecclesiastical history, and to the other undoubted authors of those times; moreover, they often contradict what is held on the authority of genuine sources, and finally, they conflict with the truth of chronology and name consuls who are either false or belong to other years. Here I cannot but point out the wicked diligence of more recent writers in dealing with these matters. Wherever there are sure proofs of falsehood, they do not hesitate to delete and alter them, so that no one may afterwards be able either to refute these tales by means of them or to regard them with suspicion. For example, in the Roman Martyrology under 21 October it used to be read: At Cologne, the birthday of the holy eleven thousand virgins, who completed their life by martyrdom for the constancy of their virginity. But because so great a multitude of virgins betrayed the absurdity and falsehood of the story, its correctors removed the number and so recast the whole passage that it can be read thus in the Baronian edition: At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of St Virgula and her companions, who, slain by the Huns for the Christian religion and the constancy of their virginity, completed their life by martyrdom, and very many of their bodies were buried at Cologne. The following example is of the same sort. In the legends, breviaries and all the martyrologies, Catherine was said to be the daughter of King Costus. Since it is established by certain and true evidence that no King Costus existed at the time of Maxentius, when Catherine is supposed to have suffered, all this ill-omened mention of Costus, which exposed the vanity of the story, was prudently (who would deny it?) struck out in the Breviary of Pius V. But also, in place of Maxentius, who had remained there even in the Breviary of Pius himself, since on the testimony of all the earlier acts of Catherine he had been left in, a similar step was afterwards taken: Maximinus was substituted by Clement VIII and Urban VIII in the Breviary, and by Baronius in the Roman Martyrology. Not that the tale, foolish but still pleasing, would thereby betray itself, since it is certain from ancient history that in Alexandria, where the event is said to have happened, it was not Maxentius but Maximinus who ruled at that time. Turrianus was a great craftsman in this kind of thing, a man most greedy for trifles and fables, who always had at hand manuscripts, unknown and unpraised by all other mortals, with which he could remould, as he pleased, any reading of his apocryphal works whenever it was absurd. Thus, where Pseudo-Evaristus says that he sent letters of the Prefects to the African bishops, Turrianus changes them into Prophets: In the most ancient copies (he says), one in the Vatican Library, the other in the Florentine library of St Mark, it is written not of the Prefects but of the Prophets. Surely those letters of the Prefects showed that the author was someone other than Evaristus, in whose time there were no prefects who wrote letters in the provinces in support of papal decrees. But the source from which Pseudo-Evaristus drew this whole passage betrays Turrianus's imposture. That is, Innocent, in whose work the phrase letter of the Prefects, not of the Prophets, is consistently read in Epistle XII, from which that most shameless and most foolish plagiarist copied all those words. What Turrianus did here, others have done elsewhere. Thus Baronius and Bellarmine, since the first Epistle of Clement to James, which all manuscripts agree is addressed to James, they want to read as addressed to Simon, in order to avoid the conclusion that the name of James, which is necessarily found there, shows the work to have been written after James had died, and so put forward by a wicked impostor long after the event. Thus Baronius, to clear the Acts of the Synod of Sinuessa of the most obvious lie, in which they tell that Diocletian, while on the Persian war, heard of Marcellinus being condemned by the bishops, wishes the words while he was in the Persian war to be rewritten and read as when he had returned from the Persian war, because he understands that, according to true history, Diocletian's Persian war, and indeed his triumph, took place long before the eighth consulship of Maximian (in which Marcellinus is supposed to have been condemned). Baronius, with similar boldness and deceit, in the Acts of Philip, Prefect of Egypt, orders the correction of what is read in all the copies there, namely that Philip was made bishop of Alexandria, because of course this crude and manifest lie clearly proves the falsity of those Acts. So too, where the manuscript Acts of the Passion of Pope Stephen give the consuls Valerian for the third time and Gallienus for the second, the same Baronius prints Valeria, A.D. 260, §1, no. 4, and Gallienus for the second time, because the consulship as written does not agree with the events recorded. The Acts of Sebastian and his companions are refuted because the public records name Junius Maximus as Prefect of the City, while these Acts give Fabianus. Baronius, so that the forgery may have a basis, orders Fabius to be written in the records in place of Junius, without any author, as he pleases. Indeed he seems to have trusted so much in this method that he thought writings that were true could be made out of false ones, and genuine ones out of spurious ones, once he had removed from them the signs of falsehood. Certainly, of the Epistle of Pope Fabian, dated the Kalends of July in the consulship of Maximinus Augustus and Africanus, sent to all his fellow ministers, he speaks in one place thus: Such is the state of the title and of the consuls in it, that it must be judged wholly spurious unless some points in it are corrected. So he thought that once these had been corrected it would no longer be spurious; a marvellous judgement indeed for such a man! As if any correction could make true and genuine what is false and spurious. I admit that it may come about that no one can easily detect afterwards whether what has been corrected is truly false; yet it can never be made anything but false by any art. For however much the Epistle of Fabian may have been what it really was not, no sponges of Baronius, no pumice-stones of anyone, will ever make it otherwise. They will only succeed in removing its signs of falsehood, so that it will more easily deceive men in the future; and this, as is plain, is the aim and purpose of all their arts. Binius, following Baronius as is his custom, uses such methods often. When the first letter attributed to Pope Cornelius, which cries out that the story about the bodies of Peter and Paul being raised from the catacombs at the request of Lucina is a spurious fable invented by someone called John, Binius, to free the letter from this brand, contrives to say that it has crept in here with a mistake; yet the constant agreement of all the manuscripts shows that the fable was not added by another, but was first written by the author himself exactly as it now reads there. Elsewhere he feigns with the same shamelessness that what is narrated in all the copies of the Epistle of Eusebius, Pope, about the Cross of Christ, recently shown on the day before the Ides of May, was borrowed from elsewhere and repeated in his own times, which clearly shows that this fiction proves the letter to be the work not of Eusebius but of some impostor. Again, when Binius was arguing that the first Epistle of Pope Julius, in all the copies of which the consuls Felicianus and Tilianus are named, is already known to be spurious and forged, he shamelessly writes that it was given in the consulship of Felicianus and Tilianus. Again, following Baronius's boldness, he wishes the end of the second Epistle of Pope John to be corrected, and for the words, which all copies equally give, Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Maximus and Olybrius, he prescribes the reading Given in the consulship of Olybrius. Clearly, because both the consulship of Maximus with Olybrius is a fiction and the date, the fifth day before the Ides of June (before which John died), show that the letter is spurious and impudently fathered on John, and forged; yet Baronius and Binius are eager to have it accepted as genuine. But it is also established from other sources that these and many other letters are false, which are attributed to the most ancient Roman bishops, Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, and others down to St Siricius, that is, down to the year of Christ 385, and are read under those venerable titles for eight hundred years now. These letters, it is admitted, decide not a few controversies, and above all that concerning the papal monarchy, indeed in favour of the Romans; but this very point is itself a proof of what their purpose was, and of the design of that merchant who first had them for sale. Most of them are certainly regarded as spurious by learned men: Henry Kalteisen, Nicholas of Cusa, Juan de Torquemada (both cardinals), Erasmus, John Dedieu, Claude d'Espence, Cassander, Simon Vigor, Baronius and others. And indeed their falsity is plain enough, and more than enough, both from the barbarity of their style and from the errors with which they are everywhere full, both in chronology and in history, and because they are badly stitched patchworks taken here and there from the passages of writers that still survive today, and finally from the total silence about them of all the authors who flourished in the first eight centuries. Now six or seven of the earlier century ...

units.la: {y} ... excluderet. Cui jam constare potest, qui sint, quàlesque tam multi libri quos quotidie ex iisdem illis Officin's prodire videmus, in quibus olim ejusmodi ludibria impune fabricabantur? Exempli causa. Quis nobis illa Flavii Lucii Dextri, & Maximi fragmenta præstabit, quæ cum hactenus tam multis seculis ignota fuissent, Hispani nuper Barcinone emiserunt ? Mitæus quidem Antuerpiensis Decanus testatur ista eruditis videri ejusdem farinæ cum Berofo Annij Viterbiensis, hoc est, cum putido crassi impostoris figmento. Aspera passim operi mendacia arguunt novitium esse foetum, non alio, ut videtur, sive ab Hispanis editum, quàm ut aniles de suo Iacobo fabellos, antiqui nominis auctoritate commendarent. Sed utcunque stent vel cadant multei istius Dextri fortunæ, illud quidem admodum probabile est, tempore auctam potius quàm imminutam istam, quæ jam olim in mundo viguit, impostorum quidvis mentiendi fingendique seu libidinem, seu industriam. Cùm ergo præter hæreticorum techuas Librariorùmque cùm avaritiam, tum imperitiam, ambitio etiam & prava hominum studia à mille jam & quadringentis annis assiduè fermè, etsi non unum ob finem, in id incubuerint, haud mirum est si novissimis his temporibus supposita Veteribus scripta occurrunt tanta numero, ut, si in acervuum cogerentur, ad quattam, vel minimum ad quintam veterum monumentorum partem accessura non injuria dici queant.
units.tr: {y} ... excluded. For who can now be sure what sort of books they are, and how many, that we see pouring out every day from those same workshops, in which such mockeries were once fabricated with impunity? For example, who will furnish us with those fragments of Flavius Lucius Dexter and Maximus, which, though unknown for so many centuries, the Spaniards recently published at Barcelona? Mitaeus, dean of Antwerp, testifies that learned men judge them to be of the same stamp as the Berosus of Annius of Viterbo, that is, a stinking fabrication of a gross impostor. Its rough lies everywhere show it to be a novel brood, put out by the Spaniards, as it seems, for no other purpose than to lend the old wives' tales about their James the authority of an ancient name. But however the fortunes of that Dexter stand or fall, it is quite probable that the lust or the industry of impostors for lying and inventing, which flourished in the world long ago, has grown rather than diminished over time. Since, therefore, apart from the trickery of heretics and the greed and ignorance of booksellers, ambition too and perverse human zeal have been busy at this for almost fourteen hundred years, not for one end indeed, it is no wonder if in these latest times writings falsely ascribed to the ancients turn up in such numbers that, if they were heaped together, they could not unfairly be said to amount to a quarter, or at least a fifth, of the monuments of the ancients.

units.la: Sed ne quis iniquam esse putet nostram de fupetiorum fculorum in fingendis, adulterandisque libris sufpicionem, tametsi jam multa dixerimus quæ eam abundè purgant, tamen ut omnis tollatur dubitandi ratio, non erit fortasse inutile de istorum temporum hominibus & ingenio quædam hic observare. Illud imprimis constat per septem illa secula, quæ ab An. D. 800. ad 1500. decurrerunt, rem litterariam, & sacram & profanam, vix alios in Occidente tractasse quam Monachos & Clericos. Illius vero ordinis hominibus plerisque vulgo persuasum fuisse, si quid ad religionis commodum conferre videretur, id impune fingere ac spargere licere, satis, ut ego quidem reor, probant tam innumerabiles istis temporibus exortæ ac disseminatæ de Ecclesiarum originibus, de sanctorum prodigiis de Angelorum vel mortuorum hominum visionibus, deque aliis id genus ad religionem utilibus rebus fabulæ. Ita Hilduinus Abbas, sub Ludovico pio, paulo post noni seculi initia Dionysium, qui Parisiensis Episcopus fuit, Pauli discipulum, domo Atheniensem fuisse, præter veterum fidem, primus finxit, & posteris persuasit, edito, quod etiam hodie superest, de hoc argumento Areopagiticon opere, fabellis & imposturis bene instructo; cujus vanitatem viri eruditissimi, Iacobus Sirmondus & Petrus Launoyus, Romanorum partium Theologi, ita nuper demonstrarunt, ut nemo credarus repugnare possit. Ad hoc postea exemplum Abbas quidam Lemovicensis, circa A. D. 1024. cum toto suorum Monachorum grege, Martialem quoque suum Apostolorum choro inferre, & falsa antiquitate exornare ausus est, & licet repugnantibus qui sanioris erant judicii, tandem obtinuit ut Martialis Apostolis coævus, & Gallicarum Apostolus, vulgo habeatur, quod fusè apud Roscquetum docet Ioannes Cordesius Lemovicensis Canonicus, ex Iordani, veteris ejusdem civitatis Episcopi, literis. Multis ante hunc annis, pro more seculi synchronisimum Apostolorum vbiq; affectantis (inquit Launoyus Fulco Bernensis Archiepiscopus Sixtum suum Adam Petri discipulum asservit, Remorū Episcopum constituit, & ex auctoritate Petri, & totius Gallicanæ regionis Primatem. Paribus studiis impulsi Arelatenses Trophimum, Paulum Narbonenses, Gratianum Turonenses, Catalaunenses Memmium, Vienrenses Crescentem ab Apostolis ad se missos commenti sunt; ac breviter paucissimæ fuerunt vel in nostra Gallia, vel in vicina Hispania, ac Britannia paulò vetustiores. cel̃ b· Iocesque Ecclesiæ, quibus Apostolicam originem non affixerint supe-rio·um seculo-um Monachi: unde sabulorum & quidem pro auctorum captu, plerumq; ie infullissimarum non una ilias exocta est. Singula persequi & immensum, neque nunc nostri iusticeti est; Francisci Bolqueti de Ecclesiastica nostræ gentis historia optime meriti testimonium hic recitare satis est, qui præfatus incertam longa antiquitate & posterorum commentis esse Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ originem, cùm commentorum auctores persequens; Primos (inquit) si verum est minus hu-jus modi Zelotas Monachos in Gallia habuimus. Illi simplices ac fervidæ ideoque minus cauti, ac sepe in onsultæ religionis perculsi, ad illiciendas hominum mentes, & angustior sa ctorum nomine ad eorum cultum revocandas, illustres eorum titulos primùm sibi dein credulæ plebi persuasos provocauerunt. Ex horum officina Martialis Lemovicensis Apostolatus, Pri sini Bnuricensis discipulatus, Dionisij Parisiensis Areopagitica, Pauli Narbonensis proconsularis dignitas, amborum Apostoli Pauli magisterium & in aliis Ecclesiis similia pro tiere. Hæc de nostris Bosquetus ita primo scripserat; atque ita excusa ex codice sibi lecto describit Vsserius, qui po tea mu-tavit, Dominæ, ut suspicor, Romæ irato satis di-si vericus. De suis Britannicis eadem Rever. Vsserius, & ret sitatur ipse discerte, & laboriosissimo Antiquitatum opere satis fatetur, in quo tam prodigiosis mendaciis, fabellisque conspurcatæ à Monachorum gente cernuntur Ecclesiarum Britannicarum origines, ut planè patientem in multis desiderent lectorem. Hispanienses notum est quanta sibi contentione vindicarint Iacobum Apostolum præter omnem veri speciem, ut ipse Baronius, quantumvis aliòqui fabulatorum hujusmodi avidus, aliquandiu dubitarit. Sed quid bonis istis Hispanis faciat, qui primas omnium serum ac disciplinarum origines suæ patriæ tanto studio atque ardore vindicant, ut etiam Muhammedem prima imposturæ suæ tirocinia apud suos majores posuisse velint; suaque venena in Hispania prius
units.tr: But lest anyone think our suspicion of the later ages, in inventing and corrupting books, unfair, then although we have already said much that thoroughly clears them of it, yet, so that every ground for doubt may be removed, it will perhaps not be useless to note here some things about the men of those times and their talents. It is above all established that through those seven centuries which ran from AD 800 to 1500, literature, both sacred and profane, was handled in the West scarcely by anyone but monks and clergy. And it was commonly persuaded among men of that order, as I at least think, that if anything seemed to serve the advantage of religion, it was lawful to invent and spread it with impunity. The countless fables about the origins of churches, the miracles of saints, the visions of angels or dead men, and other things of this kind useful to religion, which arose and spread in those times, sufficiently prove this. Thus Hilduin, abbot under Louis the Pious, shortly after the beginning of the ninth century, was the first, contrary to the faith of the ancients, to invent that Dionysius, bishop of Paris and disciple of Paul, was an Athenian by birth, and he persuaded posterity of it by publishing the Areopagitica on this subject, which survives even today, richly furnished with fables and impostures. The vanity of this work the most learned men, James Sirmond and Peter Launoy, theologians of the Roman party, have recently demonstrated so thoroughly that no one can credibly resist them. Following this example, a certain abbot of Limoges, about AD 1024, together with his whole flock of monks, dared to bring his Martial into the company of the Apostles and to adorn him with false antiquity; and although those of saner judgment resisted, he at last prevailed, so that Martial, a contemporary of the Apostles and apostle of the Gauls, is commonly held to be so. John Cordesius, canon of Limoges, teaches this at length in Bosquetus, from the writings of Jordan, bishop of that same ancient city. Many years before this, (says Launoy) following the custom of an age that everywhere aimed at synchronism with the Apostles, Fulco, archbishop of Bourges, asserted that his Sixtus, a disciple of Peter, was Adam's ... and made him bishop of Reims and, by the authority of Peter, primate of all Gaul. Driven by like zeal, the people of Arles invented Trophimus, those of Narbonne Paul, those of Tours Gratian, those of Châlons Memmius, those of Vienne Crescens, all sent to them by the Apostles; and in short there were very few churches, either in our Gaul or in neighbouring Spain and Britain, somewhat older, to which the monks of the later centuries did not attach an apostolic origin. Hence not one of these fables, and indeed of the most absurd of them, according to the capacity of their authors, was produced. To pursue each one would be endless and is not our business now; it is enough to cite the testimony of Francis Bosquet, who deserved well of the ecclesiastical history of our nation. After saying that the origin of the Gallican Church is uncertain because of long antiquity and the inventions of posterity, he traces the authors of the inventions, saying: first (he says) if it is true, we had fewer monks of this zealous sort in Gaul. They, being simple and fervent, and therefore less cautious, and often ill-advised in their zeal for religion, to win over men's minds and to recall them to the cult of the saints, first devised illustrious titles for them, and then put them forward to credulous common people as persuaded fact. From this workshop came the apostolate of Martial of Limoges, the discipleship of Priscus of Bourges, the Areopagitica of Dionysius of Paris, the proconsular dignity of Paul of Narbonne, the teaching of the Apostle Paul for both, and similar things in other churches. Bosquet had first written this about our countrymen, and Ussher describes it so from a copy he read; who afterwards changed it, I suspect, because the Roman lord was angry enough. About his own British churches, the same Reverend Ussher both retracts it himself and openly admits in his very laborious work on antiquities, in which the origins of the British churches are seen to be defiled by the monks' race with such prodigious lies and fables that they plainly require a patient reader in many places. It is well known with how much effort the Spaniards claimed the Apostle James, beyond all semblance of truth, so that Baronius himself, however otherwise eager for fabulists of this kind, hesitated for a while. But what does it matter to those good Spaniards, who claim for their own country the first origins of all things and of the disciplines with such zeal and ardour, that they even want Muhammad to have placed the first apprenticeship of his imposture among his own ancestors, and to have spread his poisons in Spain first

units.la: priùs quàm in Arabia sparsisse ? Jam in exornandis varia fictorum prodigiorum narratione Sanctorum vitis quantùm sibi superiorum seculorum scriptores indulserint, & res ipsa loquitur, & nonnullorum, licèt eorundem temporum,tamen verecundiorum, querelæ testantur; cujusmodi hæc est Letaldi Monachi ( qui Iuliani Cenomanensis vitam A. D. 1020. descripsit) à Ioanne Launoyo Parisiensi Theologo non semel commemorata ; Sunt (inquit) nonnulli qui, dum attollere sanctorum facta appetunt,in lucem veritatis offendunt, quasi Sanctorum gloria mendacio erigi valeat, qui, si mendacij sectatores suissent, ad sanctitatis culmen nequaquam ascendere potuissent, Petrus Damiani Cardinalis, qui ad annum 1060. floruit, eundem hominum sui temporis morbum tangit, qui se in vita Mauri Cæsenatis narranda veritati confulturum præfatus,quod temerarius sit narrator,quidam laudum præconiis alios extollere nititur,ipse mergi in falsitatis barathrū non veretur, hæc continuo addit, Nonnulli enim se Deo deferre existimant,si ad deferenda(fortasse legendum efferenda) laudis ejus insignia falsitatis argumenta componant, qui nimirum si egregii prædicatoris verba diligenter attenderent, talia non sentirent. Tum recitatis Pauli ex 1.Cor.15. vers. 14.15. verbis : Secundum hac ergo (inquit) Apostolica verba falsa testis Deo merito dicitur qui indiscrete eum cupiens laudare mentitur,& adversus Deũ proculdubio perhibet testimonium , quisquis in ejus laude perversa molitur arte commentum. Item alibi : Nonnullos esse ait, quise Deo deferre existimant,si in extollendis sanctorum virtutibus mendacio fingant,quique ignorantes Deum nostro non egere mendacio, relicta veritate , qua ipse est , falsitatis siputant se placere posse commento. Ex istorum genere, vel aliquanto etiam deteriori erat Gausbertus ille sub Hildegario Lemovicensi Episcopo Chorepiscopus, qui scripturam de S. Fronto (sive Frontone) Petracoricensi novam lucri causa edidit ; quod à Solemniacense quodam Abbate in Lemovicensi Concilio A. D. 1031. observatum ac traditum
units.tr: before they were spread in Arabia? How far the writers of the earlier centuries have indulged themselves in embellishing the lives of the saints with a varied narration of fictitious prodigies, both the thing itself speaks, and the complaints of some men, though of those same times yet more modest, bear witness. Of this kind is the complaint of Letaldus, a monk (who described the life of Julian of Le Mans in AD 1020), often cited by John Launoy, Parisian theologian: There are some (he says) who, while they desire to raise up the deeds of the saints, run into the light of truth, as if the glory of the saints could be exalted by a lie, when, if they had been followers of falsehood, they could never have ascended to the height of holiness. Peter Damian, cardinal, who flourished about 1060, touches on the same disease of the men of his time, who, when he has promised at the start of the life of Maurus of Cesena to consult the truth, since the narrator is rash, some strive to exalt others with praises, not fearing to plunge themselves into the abyss of falsehood. He immediately adds: For some think they bring honour to God, if they compose proofs of falsehood to set forth (perhaps read "to extol") the signs of his praise; who, if they had attentively heeded the words of that distinguished preacher, would not feel such things. Then, having quoted the words of Paul from 1 Cor. 15. verses 14, 15: According to these apostolic words, therefore, he is rightly called a false witness of God who, desiring to praise him indiscreetly, lies, and undoubtedly bears witness against God, whoever devises a fiction by a perverse art in his praise. Likewise elsewhere he says that there are some who think they bring honour to God if in extolling the virtues of the saints they invent by lying, and who, not knowing that God has no need of our lie, leaving the truth, which he himself is, think they can please him by a fiction of falsehood. Of this kind, or even of a somewhat worse sort, was that Gausbert, chorepiscopus under Hildegar, bishop of Limoges, who published a new writing about St Fronto (or Front) of Périgueux for the sake of gain; which was observed and reported by a certain abbot of Solignac at the Council of Limoges in AD 1031, as the same Launoy relates. But the vanity of those who falsify the lives of the saints in writing is so clear and manifest that we have very grave men, even of the communion of the Roman see, confessing it.

units.la: E fuisse refert idem Launoyus. Sed haec eorum qui sanctorum vitas literis mendarunt vanitas ita clara manifesta que est, ut viros etiam de Papae Vrbici communione gravissimos de ea confitentes habeamus. Melchior Canus, Canariarum Episcopus, insignis Theologus, quique unus ex Tridentinis Patribus fuit: Dolenter hoc (inquit) dico potius quam cotumeliose, multo a Laertio severius vitas Philosophorum scriptas, quam a Christianis vitas Sanctorum longe incorruptius et integrius Suetonium res Caesarum expositsse, quam exposuerint Catholici, non dico res Imperatorum, sed Martyrum, Virginum et Confessorum. Illi enim in probis aut Philosophis aut Principibus nec vitia nec suspiciones vitiorum tacent, in improbis vero etiam colores virtutum producunt. Nostri autem plerique vel affectibus inseruiunt, vel de inductrix quoque ita multa confinguunt, ut eorum me nimirum non solum pudeat, sed etiam taedeat. Hos enim intelligo Ecclesiae Christi, cum nihil utilitatis attulisse, tum incommodationis plurimum.
units.tr: Launoy himself reports this as well. But the emptiness of those who have falsified the lives of the saints in writing is so clear and manifest that even men of the highest standing in the communion of the Pope of Rome have confessed it. Melchior Canus, Bishop of the Canaries, an outstanding theologian and one of the Fathers at Trent, says: I say this with grief rather than with abuse: the lives of the philosophers were written far more harshly by Laertius than the lives of the saints have been written by Christians, and Suetonius set out the affairs of the Caesars far more faithfully and honestly than Catholics have set out the affairs, I do not say of emperors, but of martyrs, virgins and confessors. For Suetonius, in the case of upright men, whether philosophers or princes, conceals neither their vices nor the suspicions of their vices, while in the case of wicked men he even brings forward a show of virtues. Our writers, however, for the most part either serve their own passions, or else deliberately invent so many things that I am not only ashamed of them but actually weary of them. For I mean these men, who have brought the Church of Christ no benefit, but very great harm.

units.la: Item, Iustissima est Ludovici querela, de historicis quibusdam in Ecclesia consictis. Prudenter sane ac graviter eos arguit qui pietatis loco duxerint mendacia pro religione fingere. Tum, Qui falsis atque mendacibus scriptis mentes mortalium concitare ad divorum cultum voluere, hi nihil mihi aliud videntur egisse, quam ut veris propter falsa adimiatur fides, &c. Quasi vero sancti Dei homines nostris mendaciis egeant, qui tam multa vera pro Christo gesserunt. Denique Ecclesia (inquit) Christi vehementer incommodant qui res divinas praeclare gestas non se putant egregie expositurus, nisi eas fictis, et revelationibus et miraculis adornarint. Haec Canus. Patirius quoque Massonus, mendaciis fabulisque anilibus, sola disturnitate temporis, labsu fidem apud posteros nactis, non modo profana, sed etiam sacra infecta esse confitetur. Nec enim (inquit) permisfentur vitis Sanctorum pauciores fabulae, quia alibi, quia pars earum multis post seculis ab imperitis scripta est, ex quotidianis vulgi sermonibus, saepe delirantis, semperque aliquid adjicientis de suo. Quin eadem fuerit crudissimi Sirmondi sententia dubitare nos non finit ejus.
units.tr: Likewise, Ludovicus's complaint about certain historians who have been made up within the Church is most just. He rightly and gravely rebukes those who have thought it a form of piety to invent lies on behalf of religion. Then: Those who wished to stir the minds of mortals to the worship of the saints by false and lying writings seem to me to have done nothing else than to take away belief in true things on account of false ones, etc. As if the holy men of God had need of our lies, they who have performed so many true deeds for Christ. Finally: Those, he says, do great harm to the Church of Christ who do not think that divine deeds, nobly performed, can be set forth well unless they have adorned them with made-up revelations and miracles. So Canus. Papirius Massonus also confesses that the lives of the saints, tainted by lies and old wives' fables, have gained credit among posterity only through the lapse of time, and that not only profane but also sacred matters have been corrupted. For (he says) the fables in the lives of the saints are not fewer because they were written elsewhere, or because part of them was written many centuries later by unskilled people, from the everyday talk of the common folk, which is often raving and always adding something of its own. Indeed, the view of the most learned Sirmond was the same, and his words leave us in no doubt about it.

units.la: Del cit. Theol.lib.11. c. 6. de duobus Dionysiis Lucubratio Ioannes vero de Lau noy, vir & doctissimus & φιλαληθίςατος, Parisiensis Theologus, iam non semel à nobis nominatus, non modo eadem sentit, sed etiam ultra progressus, nihilque veritus τῆ φιλομύθῳ, quos apud suos plurimos esse novit, odio ac invidiam, horridam illam ac squalentem à Caroli magni temporibus enatam, ac longè lateque fructicantem fabularum ac figmentorum, sylvam, immissō acutissimæ ac sagacissimæ disquisitionis, criticesque, ut sic dicam, ferro, ita nuper concidit ac demessuit, ut ni mens læva à pulcherrimo incœpto mortales deterreat spes sit cætera, si ejus exemplum ac fortitudinem, invictumque veri studium imitaremur purgari tandem posse. Tanto autem licentius in hoc genere veri sati sunt qui post octavum seculum vixerunt, quod superiorum temporum Patres nonnulli, præsertim verò Severus in opera de Martini vita, Gregorius Romanus in Dialogis, Beda in historiis, & alibi passim, suo exemplo præjuissent, veris multa fabulæ propiora admiscentes; ut ex inspectis eorum libris patet In his quidem duobus, Gregorio inquam & Beda, judicij severitatem & curam Canus ipse diserte desiderávit; Equidem, (inquit) hi storiolas illas (ab istis narratas intelligit) probarem mo gis, si earum auctores juxta præfinitam normam severitati judicij curam in eligendo majorem adjuxiffent. Ulinus Legenda (ut vulgo vocant) aurea liber, magnæ proximorum retrò seculorum deliciæ, satis oftendit quàm immanis fuerit istorum hominum quidvis pro libidine in hoc genere fingendi audacia, ut ipsi nunc de Romana communione Theologi scribere non dubitent, hujus operis auctori os quidem fuisse ferreum, cor vero plumbeum, & animum parum sincerum ac prudentem; item vires eruditos ad ejus nomen expallescere, id genus operis execrari & aversis in sinistram palmis abominari. In visionibus quæ & ad hoc genus pertinent, non fuisse veraciores, unum, sed illustre, exemplum probabit. Provinciarum Remensis & Rotomagensis Episcopi, Cari- E 2 fiaci A. D. 858. congregati Ludovico Germaniæ Regi, tum in Attiniaco palatio consistentes, epistolam mense Novembri scripserunt, in qua hæc narratio habetur. S. Eucherius (inquiunt) Aurelianensium Episcopus in oratione positus ad alterū seculum est raptus, & inter cæteras quæ Domino sibi ostendente conspexit, vidit illum (Carolum Principem, Pippini Regis patrem, quem vulgo Martellum vocant) in inferno inferiori torqueri. Cui interroganti ab Angelo ejus ductore responsum est, quia Sanctorum indicatione, qui in futuro iudicio cum Domino indicabunt, quorumque res abstulit & divisit, ante illud iudicium, animā & corpore sempiternis poenis est deputatus, & recipit simul cum suis peccatis poenas propter peccata omnium, qui res suas & facultates in honore & amore Domini ad Sanctorum loca in luminaribus divini cultus & alimoniis servorum Christi ac pauperum, pro animarum suarum redemptione tradiderāt. Qui in se reversus (Eucherius, scilicet) S. Bonifacium & Fulradum Abbatem monasterij S. Dionysij, & summum Capellanum Regis Pippini ad se vocavit, eisque talia dicens insignum dedit, ut ad sepulcrum illius irent, & si corpus ejus non reperissent, ea quae dicebat vera esse concederent. Ipsi autem pergentes ad prædictum monasterium ubi corpus ipsius Caroli humatum fuerat, sepulcrum ejus illius aperientes, visus est subito exisse draco, & totum illud sepulcrum interius inventum est denigratum, ac si fuisset exustum. Nos autem illos vidimus, qui usque ad nostram aetatem duraverunt, qui huic rei interfuerunt, & nobis viva voce veraciter sunt testati, qua audierunt atque viderunt. Tum nonnullis interjectis. Hanc etiam relationem & in Scriptura habemus, & quidam nostrum etiam viva voce Dominum Ludovicum Imperatorem patrem vestrum referre audivimus. Hæc Veteres illi duarum Provinciarum Episcopi, quorum pars erant Hincmarus Remensis & Wenilo Rotomagensis, nobilissimi illius ævi antistites. Eadem narrant tum Flodoardus Remensis, qui A. D. 966. Chronicon ut ipse testatur scptuagenarius absoluit, tum scriptor vitæ Eucherij * vetustissimus & ex Surio Eucherij æqualis, & auctor vitæ Rigoberti Remensis Episcopi. Et hanc ramen tot tantisque illorum temporum auctoribus firmatam relationem meriam esse fabulam, non tantum ipse tei apparatus, ille ex imo monumento crepens draco, illa tumuli, velut exusti, nigricans species, omnia ad mendacij pompam ac speciem adornata suadent, sed etiam alia non pauca evincunt; Quale illud est in primis quod isti, præter Scripturæ auctoritatem, hominem, etiam corpore, apud inferos ante ultimum Iudicium cruciari fingunt. Tum & quæ narrantur pugnant cum historiæ veritate. Nam qui hic corpore & anima in æternum damnatus dicitur Carolus, is princeps fuit & religione & cæteris bonis artibus florentissimus, à Gregorio III. P. R. ob pietatem laudatus, unicum illis temporibus rei Christianæ columen, cujus in victa manu cæsæ sunt uno & altero prælio Maurorum innumerabiles copiæ, depulsumque à totius Europæ cervicibus Mahumedismi jugum. Sed & qui testis inducitur Ludovicus, adeo nescivit quod isti calumniantur, ut aliud diserte affirmet. Nam in Epistola ad Hilduinum, summo quod decuit, cum honore de Carolo proavo suo loquens ait, eum decursō mortalitatis tempore,quod carius potuit habere depositum,corpus scilicet proprium in manus Domini præsentandam spiritui animam fideliter Dionysio commendasse. Quid? quod & Bonifacius, unus, ut isti volunt ex revelationis testibus, quo loco ipsam illam Caroli in bona Ecclesiastica licentiam exagitat, & pœnas quibus eam Deus ultus est exaggerat, nihil de iis monstris memorat, quæ quo erat ingenio, omissurus profecto tali loco non fuit, si quid ejusmodi vel vidisset, vel audivisset unquam. Tantum ait Carolum longa torsione & verenda morte consumptum esse. Haiste Bonifacius,longa torsione & verenda morte consumptü, sed placidè & optata morte compositum fuisse, his verbis. Post multiplices alias & insignes victorias, quas ob prolixitatis fastidium silentio supprimo, diuisit regnum duobus filiis suis, ac deinde bellicosissimus at victoriosissimus princeps IN PACE quievit. Et manuscriptus Bibliothecæ Alexandri Petavij Codex, Carolus (inquit) Princeps Parisiis basilicam S.Dionysij Martyris multis muneribus ditavit. Veniens Carriacum (leg. Carisiacum) Villam palatij super Ifiram fluvium validà febri correptus obyt. Obtinuit principatum annis 27. Denique Fredegarius Scholasticus,in Chronico quod Childebrandi Pippini Regis patrui iussu, adeóque proximis post Caroli obitum temporibus scripsit, narrat cum cùm in villa Verinbrea (al. Vermeria) super Iffara fluvio agrotare cœpisset,ditata multis muneribus Parisiensis S. Dionysij basilica, venientem Carisiaco,villa palatij super Issaram fluvium,valida febre correptum obiisse IN PACE, cunctis in gyro regni acquisitis cùm regissset utraque regna annos 25. Hæc profectò mors non verenda, quod ait Bonifacius, sed felix & optanda potiùs fuit. Sed fac Carolum longa illa torsione (cujus nulla in istis historicis apparent vestigia) consumptum, quod vult Bonifacius,fuisse, ne sic quidem à temeritate purgari poterit malignum ejus iudicium, qui in divinorum iudiciorum abyssum parum reverenter irrumpens, maximi Principis letalem mortem sic interpretatur ac si ei ob violata Ecclesiarum bona inflictus fuerit;quasi nō quotidie longa torsione consumi videamus etiam pios & sanctos viros,quorum non modo à sacrilegio, sed & à cæteris gravioribus criminibus vita omnis immunis fuerat. Deo suorum iudiciorum plerumque humanis sensibus imperscrutabilem rationem committi decet. Itaque illa Bonifacij, de morte Caroli, verba morbum animi iltis solennem produnt; quo ut mortales à suis tangendis bonis deterreant, quidvis solent in eos comminisci; quos sua vel leviter libasse suspicantur. Quid ergo sic affectus in Carolum fuit, dubitandum randum non est quin si cum resciuisset corpore & animâ obviolatas Ecclesiæ opes æternaliter diminutum, id in primis hoc loco commemoraturus fuerit. At ille nihil hujusmodi hic narrat. Ergo, neque eum quicquam ejusmodi sciuisse (quod mentitur superior Epist. oportuit relatio clarum certumque est. Sed & ipse Eucherius, qui præcipuus totius relationis auctor fuisse fingitur, quo tempore Carolus in æde Dionysii sepulcus est; jam prídem ipse mortuus erat, aut neque in cestasin rapi, neque ea quæ viderat Bonifacio & Fulrado narrare, neque ut Principis sepulcrum explorarent jubere potuerit. Constat enim ex Eucherij vita ipsum annis vel 14. (quod ponit Molanus) vel certè decem (quod vult Baronius ) ante mortuum esse quam Carolus vivere desierit; cuius mortem A. D. 741. contigisse certa fides est. Denique & illud quoque falsum esse liquidò deprehenditur, quod disserte habet eadem relatio, Fulradum Abbatem summum Capellanum Regis Pippini ab Eucherio ad se vocatum fuisse. Cum enim constet Pippinum regis nomen, decimo demum post Caroli Patris obitum anno Domini 751. sumpsisse, fieri non potest ut ante illud tempus Fulradus summus Pippini Regis Capellanus fuerit, ut Eucherium, si quid cum illo Regis Capellano gesserit, planè necesse sit post A. D. 751. vixisse, quod immane est, & ab omnium veterum scriptorum rationibus alienum mendacium. His rationibus (quas ex iis pkrafque collegimus) victi non modò Pithœus & Sirmondus , sed & ipse Annalium parens Baronius , totam hanc Episcoporum de Caroli damnatione narrationem fabulosam esse & confitentur & probant. Sed ut noris quam sit istorum genus, salsissima ista relatio tota etiam hodie legitur in Decreti Gregoriani novis annotationibus ; ac ne nostra quidem memoria defuit Theologus qui optimam fabulam sibi de manibus eripi doleret, ac penè indignaretur; & tametsi nihil haberet quod ad clarissimas Baronij Sirmondisque rationes reponeret, negaret tamen ea conuellenda, quæ ex Patrum scriptis maximè ex Synodorum Actis, habentur, quasi mendacium usquam fit ferendum. Sed istum quidem plorare, suaque crepundia deflere sinamus. Nos quod sacra rerum ipsarum veritas jubet, quod Pithoeus, quod Baronius, quod Sirmondus, viri amplissimi atque celeberrimi consentiunt, constituamus, bonos illos Remensis ac Rotomagensis provinciarum Episcopos hanc fabellam, aut (quod verisimillimum est) finxisse ipsos, aut certè ab aliis ejusdem seculi ac genij hominibus confictam temerè excepisse, exceptamque ad illustrissimi & gloriosissimi Principis infamiam inhumanè sparsisse, & uni ex ipsius nepotibus Ludovico sanè parum verecundè narrasse: Ita omne illis judicium, omnem modestiam ac pudorem, omnem denique humanitatem eripuerat acerrimum quoddam opum (ut vocant) Ecclesiasticarum studium, ad quas ab omni Principum injuria tuendas & confictum & avidè disseminatum fuisse apparet Tartareum istud commentum. Extant in illorum seculorum libris aliæ sexcentæ ejusdem furfuris impostura: Tu ab una, disce omnes; quas sigillatim recensero neque hujus loci, neque nostri instituti est. Illud quidem non videtur omittendum, Monachorum Benedictini instituti (qui diu in Occidentali Ecclesia viguerunt, ac penè regnarunt) jampridem in hoc rerum genere subleistam esse fidem. Ex eorum enim officina multa supposititia jam olim prodierunt, è quorum numero impiis esse videtur Sancti Medardi Suessionensis Monasterij privilegium Gregorio P. R. I. affictum, è quo nunc Baronius & Bellarminus sui in Reges Pontificis potestatem astruere non dubitant. Id vero quam sit falsum, & à Gregorio alienum, ut cæteros taceam, luculentissimè demonstravit Blondellus noster in opere de Spuriis veterum Paparum Decretalibus. Sed inter Benedictinos jam ante multa secula exaisit de sui auctoris corpore controversia, quæ quo ipsi sint ingenio abundè patefecit.
units.tr: Above cited, Theol. book 11, ch. 6, on the two Dionysii: Lucubratio. John of Launoy, a man both most learned and most truth-loving [φιλαληθέστατος], a Paris theologian whom I have already named more than once, not only holds the same view but goes further. Fearing nothing from those [τῇ φιλομύθῳ] who, he knows, have very many supporters, he has, with the sharp and keen blade of a most acute and discerning criticism, as I may call it, cut down and mown that horrid and squalid forest of fables and fictions, which sprang up in the time of Charlemagne and spreads its branches far and wide. If an evil mind did not frighten mortals away from so noble an undertaking, there would be hope that the rest could at last be cleansed, if we imitated his example, his courage and his unconquered zeal for the truth. Those who lived after the eighth century have been all the more free in this kind of falsehood because some Fathers of earlier times, especially Severus in his work on the life of Martin, Gregory the Roman in the Dialogues, Bede in his histories, and many others elsewhere, had gone before them by example, mixing many fables with the true accounts. This is clear from an inspection of their books. In these two, I mean Gregory and Bede, Canus himself expressly wished for severity of judgment and care. "Indeed," he says, "I would approve those little stories (he means those told by them) more, if their authors had applied greater care in selecting them, according to a fixed standard of strict judgment." Ulinus's book Legenda aurea (as it is commonly called), the great delight of the last few centuries, shows well enough how monstrous was the audacity of those men in inventing whatever they pleased in this field. So much so that Theologians of the Roman communion now do not hesitate to write that the author of this work had an iron face, a leaden heart, and a mind little sincere and prudent; likewise that learned men turn pale at his name, execrate that kind of work, and abominate it with palms turned to the left. Among the visions which also belong to this class, one, but a famous one, will show that they were not more truthful. The bishops of the provinces of Reims and Rouen, gathered at Quierzy in the year 858 and staying at the palace of Attigny with Ludwig, King of Germany, wrote a letter in November, in which this account is found. "Saint Eucherius," they say, "bishop of Orléans, while at prayer, was caught up for a second age, and among the other things that he saw, the Lord showing them to him, he saw that man (Charles the Prince, father of King Pippin, whom they commonly call Martel) being tormented in the lower hell. When he asked his angelic guide the reason, he was answered that, by the designation of the saints who will sit in judgment with the Lord at the future judgment, and whose goods he took away and divided, he was condemned before that judgment to eternal punishments in soul and body, and bears together with his sins the punishments for the sins of all those who, for the honour and love of the Lord, had given up their goods and possessions to the places of the saints, for the lights of divine worship and the sustenance of Christ's servants and the poor, for the redemption of their souls. Coming to himself, Eucherius summoned to him Saint Boniface and Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis and chief chaplain of King Pippin, and speaking to them of these things gave them a sign, that they should go to his tomb, and if they did not find his body, they should concede that the things he said were true. And they, going to the aforesaid monastery where the body of Charles had been buried, opening his tomb, suddenly a dragon seemed to come out, and the whole inside of that tomb was found blackened, as if it had been burnt. We have seen those who were present at this matter and lasted until our own age, and they have told us truthfully by word of mouth what they heard and saw." Then, after some words were inserted: "We also have this account in Scripture, and some of us have heard our father, the Lord Emperor Ludwig, relate it by word of mouth." These are the words of those ancient bishops of the two provinces, of whom one part were Hincmar of Reims and Wenilo of Rouen, the most noble prelates of that age. The same account is given by Flodoard of Reims, who finished his Chronicle, as he himself attests, at the age of seventy in the year 966; by the writer of the life of Eucherius, very ancient and a contemporary of Surius's Eucherius; and by the author of the life of Rigobert, bishop of Reims. Yet that account, backed by so many and such great authorities of that time, is a pure fable. Not only does the very apparatus suggest that all of it was adorned for the display of a lie: that dragon bursting from the deepest tomb, that dark appearance of the mound as if burnt. Many other things also prove it. Among these is, above all, that they pretend, against the authority of Scripture, that a man is tormented in body also in hell before the last judgment. Then, what is narrated also conflicts with historical truth. For Charles, who is said to be damned in body and soul, was a prince most flourishing in religion and other good arts, praised for piety by Pope Gregory III, the only pillar of the Christian cause in that age, by whose conquering hand countless troops of the Moors were slaughtered in one and another battle, and the yoke of Mohammedanism was thrown from the necks of the whole of Europe. And Ludwig, who is brought in as a witness, knew so little of what these men allege that he expressly affirms something else. For in his letter to Hilduin, speaking of his great-grandfather Charles with all the honour due, he says that, having run through the time of mortality, he had committed to Dionysius, as a deposit most dear to him, his own body to be presented into the hands of the Lord, and his soul faithfully to the spirit. What of this, that Boniface, who, as they wish, is one of the witnesses of the revelation, in the very place where he rebukes that licence of Charles against the ecclesiastical goods, and magnifies the punishments with which God avenged it, says nothing of those monsters; which, given his talent, he would certainly have not omitted in such a place, if he had ever seen or heard anything of that kind. He says only that Charles was consumed by a long torment and a dreadful death. But Boniface, in these words, shows that he was consumed by a long torment and a dreadful death, yet that he was laid to rest peacefully and in a welcome death: "After many other remarkable victories, which I pass over in silence to avoid tedious length, he divided the kingdom between his two sons, and then that most warlike yet most victorious prince rested IN PEACE." And the manuscript codex of the library of Alexander Petavius: "Prince Charles (he says) enriched the basilica of Saint Denis the Martyr in Paris with many gifts. Coming to Quierzy (read Carisiacum), a villa of the palace on the river Oise, he died seized by a strong fever. He held the principate for 27 years." Finally Fredegar the Scholastic, in the Chronicle which he wrote by the order of Childebrand, uncle of King Pippin, and therefore in the times immediately after Charles's death, relates that, when he had fallen ill in the villa of Verinbrea (other reading Vermeria) on the river Issara, after the basilica of Saint Denis in Paris had been enriched with many gifts, coming to Carisiacum, a villa of the palace on the river Issara, seized by a strong fever, he died IN PEACE, all the lands of the realm having been acquired, when he had ruled both kingdoms for 25 years. This death was surely not dreadful, as Boniface says, but happy and to be desired. But grant that Charles was consumed by that long torment (of which no trace appears in these historians), which Boniface wishes, even so the malicious judgment of the man will not be cleared of rashness, for he, rushing irreverently into the abyss of divine judgments, interprets the deadly death of a very great prince as if it had been inflicted on him for violating the goods of the Churches; as if we did not daily see pious and holy men consumed by a long torment, whose whole life was free not only from sacrilege but also from other, more grievous crimes. It is fitting that God's judgments, for the most part, be committed to an unsearchable reason beyond human sense. Therefore those words of Boniface about the death of Charles betray that disease of the mind which is customary for them; by it they are wont to invent whatever they please against mortals, to deter them from touching their goods, and against those whom they suspect of having lightly tasted of them. What, then, was the state of mind towards Charles? There is no doubt that, had he known that, in body and soul, the wealth of the Church had been diminished for ever by his violation, he would above all have recorded it in this place. But he says nothing of the kind here. Therefore it is clear and certain that he knew nothing of the sort (which the above-mentioned letter falsely claims). But also Eucherius himself, who is pretended to be the chief author of the whole account, at the time when Charles was buried in the church of Denis, had long been dead, or else he could neither have been caught up into ecstasy, nor have related to Boniface and Fulrad what he had seen, nor have ordered them to explore the Prince's tomb. For it is established from the life of Eucherius that he died either 14 years (as Molanus puts it), or certainly ten years (as Baronius wishes) before Charles ceased to live; and the death of Charles is certainly known to have occurred in the year 741. Finally, it is also clearly shown to be false what the same account states expressly, that Fulrad, abbot and chief chaplain of King Pippin, was summoned to him by Eucherius. For since it is established that Pippin took the title of king only in the year of the Lord 751, ten years after the death of his father Charles, it cannot be that Fulrad was chief chaplain of King Pippin before that time; so that, if Eucherius had had any dealings with that royal chaplain, he must of necessity have lived after the year 751, which is a monstrous lie and alien to the reasoning of all the ancient writers. Convinced by these arguments (which we have largely gathered from them), not only Pithou and Sirmond, but Baronius himself, the father of the Annals, both acknowledge and prove that the whole narrative of the bishops about the condemnation of Charles is fabulous. But that you may know what sort of people these are, that most salted account is still read today, entire, in the new annotations to the Gregorian Decretum; and in our own memory there was not lacking a theologian who grieved that a very good fable had been snatched from his hands, and nearly took it indignantly; and although he had nothing to set against the most clear arguments of Baronius and Sirmond, yet he denied that those things should be overturned which are found in the writings of the Fathers, chiefly in the Acts of the Synods, as if a lie were anywhere to be borne. But let us allow him to lament and bewail his rattles. We, as the sacred truth of the matter itself requires, and as Pithou, Baronius and Sirmond, men most distinguished and most celebrated, agree, shall establish that those good bishops of the provinces of Reims and Rouen either themselves invented this little fable, or (what is most likely) rashly received it, invented by others of the same age and character, and, having received it, inhumanely spread it to the infamy of that most illustrious and most glorious prince, and rather shamelessly related it to Ludwig, one of his grandsons. So completely had a certain most fierce zeal for (as they call it) ecclesiastical goods robbed them of all judgment, all modesty and shame, and finally all humanity; for that infernal invention appears to have been both devised and eagerly spread to defend those goods against every injury from princes. Six hundred other impostures of the same chaff exist in the books of those centuries; from one, learn all of them. I am not going to list them one by one, and this is neither the place nor the purpose of my undertaking. This point, however, does not seem to be passed over: that among the Benedictine monks (who long flourished in the Western Church and nearly reigned), faith in this kind of thing was long ago undermined. For many spurious works have long since come out of their workshop, among which the privilege of the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons, supposedly granted by Pope Gregory I, seems to be impious; from it Baronius and Bellarmine now do not hesitate to build up the power of the Pontiff over kings. How false this is, and how alien to Gregory, to pass over the others, Blondel, our countryman, has demonstrated most brilliantly in his work on the spurious Decretals of the ancient Popes. But among the Benedictines, many centuries ago, a controversy arose about the body of their own founder, which has sufficiently revealed what sort of minds they themselves have.

units.la: A.D. 593 §.8 Pont. R. Ponti. in ep. 40. 647.ad p. 665. fecit. Benedicti enim corpus ex Cassinensi Monasterio in Floriacensi ad Ligerim olim translatum, ibidemque adhuc quiescere, contendunt Galli plerique illius ordinis fratres. Itali contra pugnant id in Cassinensi Monasterio & fuisse semper, & nunc etiam seruari. NoftriPauli Diaconi, & Adrevaldi, antiquissimorum monachorum, traditione se tuentur; Itali Leonis Hostiensis testimoniis nituntur. Magnis utrimque contentionibus agitur. Multa Paparum & Principum rescripta ac diplomata afferuntur. At nostri quidem quae ab Italis in rem suam eduntur Benedicti VIII. Alexandri II. Vrbani II. & Zachariae Pontificum Romanorum bullae, eas falsas confictasque & absurdis scatere dejerant, ipsumque Leonem Historiensem qui a 1112. floruit mendaciter esse loquutum affirmant, & Cassinenses Monachos mendacij falsitatis & impostura insimulant. Itali in nostros si milia spargunt, eosque viciissim fraudis & Sophisticēs accusant. Fieri potest ut utrique mentiti fuerint, ut neutri non possit. Sed & nuper, in te pene nihili, apparuit quàm sit promptum ad fingendum istorum ingenium.
units.tr: A.D. 593 §.8 Pont. R. Ponti. in ep. 40. 647. ad p. 665. fecit. The body of Benedict was once moved from the monastery of Monte Cassino to Fleury on the Loire, and most of the French brothers of that order contend that it still rests there. The Italians argue against this, maintaining that it has always been at Monte Cassino and is kept there even now. Our side relies on the tradition of Paul the Deacon and Adrevald, very ancient monks; the Italians lean on the testimony of Leo of Ostia. The dispute is waged with great heat on both sides. Many papal and royal letters and charters are cited.
