Our writers declare that the bulls of the Roman pontiffs Benedict VIII, Alexander II, Urban II and Zachary, which the Italians put forward in their own cause, are false and forged and full of absurdities, and they affirm that Leo of Ostia, who flourished after 1112, spoke falsely, and they accuse the monks of Monte Cassino of lying, fraud and imposture. The Italians, in turn, spread slanders against our side and accuse them of trickery and sophistry. It may be that both have lied; it is certain that neither is free from lying. But recently, in a matter of almost no importance, it has become clear how ready these men are to invent.

units.la: Vt enim suo ordini afferrent opusculum de Christi imitatione, quod vulgò sub nomine Thomae à Kempis circumfertur, sparserunt esse Romae apud suos aliquot manuscriptos optimae fidei codices, in quibus id opus Ioanni Gerson Vercellensi sui ordinis Abbati inscriberetur. Eruditissimus Gabriel Naudaeus A. D. 1641. cum esset Romae, secum communicatos illos libros repetit sodalis Naudaeus cujusdam Benedicti scelere corruptos fuisse ac vitiatos, & rei totius historiam, quod digna hominum memoria atque animaduersione videretur, litteris simpliciter mandatam ad clariss. viros Puteanos Fratres huc misit, quae cum, post annos aliquot, à Ioanne Frontone S. Genouefae Canonico Benedictinorum adversario esset publici juris facta; Benedictini tanto impetu Naudaeum invaserunt, tamque foedis ac procacibus calumniis asperserunt, ut is coactus sit jure apud Praetorem cum F cum iis experiri, toramque iniquitatis & fraudis eorum scenam aperire. Prostant typis excusæ multiplices ejus defensiones, in quarum una allatis xx. argumentis sive exemplis insignibus farè demonstrat hoc Benedictinorum proprium esse quarto modo (sic enim ille loquitur) ut falsis, adulteratis, ac interpolatis documentis in omnibus suis negotiis utantur ac nitantur. Ita Naudæusiâ quo non abluditquod alter vir doctissimus, Theologus Parisiensis, Ioannes de Launoy, quasdam Pippini litteras è Sandionysiano Benedictinorum Monachorum armario sibi objectas refutans. Tabularium (inquit) unde prodierunt plurimarum chartarum & privilegiorum officina quondam fuit, ut constat legentibus Antiquitates S. Dionysij quas Iacobus Dubletius in lucem emisit. Sed non soli Benedictini illa fingendi prurigine laborarunt. Rhenanus quidem certè Benedictinum fuisse non dicit, magnum illum, etiam gratis mentiendi artificem, de quo lepidam hanc historiolam narrat. Quidam (inquit) superioribus annis, quem adhuc audio superesse. Beatum anachoretam Helveticum ut vulgus praedicat, Suetonium fuisse vocatum affinxit, illius vitam describens, & socium habuisse cui nomen esset Achita. Adij hominem quæsituru undenam id assereret. Putabam enim hæc illum absque auctore non dicere. Sed audi impudentiam. Propterea (inquit) addidi Suetonium fuisse vocatum, quod legerem è Surdia prodiisse, & quia Æneæ Virgiliano fidus Achates semper adhæsit, ideo sodalem illius hoc nomine donau, alioqui anonymum futurum. Et tamen hæc historia, si ita vocare libet, non solum pictura est in templis ac scripta, sed etiam typis excusa. Hactenus Rhenanus. Qui etiam gratis tam facile mentiti sunt, quid eos fecisse putandum est, ubi spes fuit aliquam fore mendacij mercedem? Iesuitarum, quibus nulli sunt inter recentiores monachos nobiliores, non esse sanctiorem aut religiosiorem in his fidem multa testantur, ut eorum proprium de æquivocationis usu dogma, item illa publicè ab iis in Collegio Lovaniensi propositæ ac defensa thesis. Non esse peccatum, saltem lethale. detrahentis auctoritatem magnam, tibi noxiam, falso crimine elidere; & illud longè etiam horribilius dogma, Licere clerico, vel religioso, calumniatorem graviacrimina de se, vel de sua religione spargere minătem, occidere, quando alius defendendi modus non suppetit. Nam si isti, quos homines suæ religioni adversari vident, iis vel famam, vel etiam vitam ipsam eripere sibi fas esse putant; quanto magis literas & chartas (res inanimes & mutas) fidei & Ecclesiæ, vel noxias abolere & immutare, uel faventes procudere & extrudere liberum esse existimabunt. Sed Iesuitarum de his sensum ipsa praxis clarè docet; cujus exempla & multa & insignia videre est in concertatione quæ illis est cum iis Theologis qui vulgo Jansenistæ dicuntur. Hi quidem nihil illis frequentiùs objectant quàm desperatam quandam quidvis pro re sua mentiendi fingendique licentiam ac (ut cætera mittam) ista quæ vulgò nota sunt, passim exprobrant. Iesuitas contra Arnaldi de frequenti communione volumen epistolam falso cujusdam Atrebatensis Officiarii nomine edidisse; Bullam Vrbani VIII. contra Jansenii Augustinum falsò sparsisse; anonymo Protestanti Ministro velut ad Sorbonicum Doctorem scriptam epistolam prodigiosis mendaciis scatentem affinxisse, ac publicasse; item Inquisitionis Romanæ decretum pro authentica Innocentis X. in Catechismum de gratia censura A. D. 1650. inverecundè disseminasse, & suam Jansenianæ doctrinæ expositionem Theologis Portus Regalis (id est Jansenistis ipsis) nullo pudore affictam & suppositam sub Manifesti no mine vulgasse. Quo fit ut Jansenistæ meritò metuendum dicant, ne quod nunc illorum proprium est Iesuitarum nomen; id in posterum in analogiam eorum commune evadat quicunque fabulas fingunt vel saljas historias narrant. Huc accedit quod hujus generis fabulis etiam qui non credunt favent tamen. Narrat Mariana notissimus Iesuita Germanicum quendam centurionem, obs violata missæ sacra, subito dirupù effusisque visceribus Iudæ instar periisse. Sed parum licet tibi comperta, ait interesse publicè ut credantur. Et alibi quas nostri scriptores memorant alternas Bonifacii P. R. 8. & Philippi Regis epistolas, quod eæ ad Papæ dignitatem parum faciant,interesse ait ad exemplum ut falsæ esse videantur. Interest scilicet humani generis, ut vel quæ falsa fictæque sunt, pro veris, vel quæ vera certaque sunt, pro dubiis ac falsis habeantur. Multa idem in Hilpanicis historiis ejusdem generis inspersit, à veteribus quidem tradita, sed incredibilia & ab omni veri specie abhorrentia; quod ne ipsi fraudi apud Lectorem esset non plane stultum, quasi ea qui facundè tradit vera quoque esse crediderit, hanc suspicionem occupandam ratus, non alicubi diserte monet, se multo plura transcribere quàm credere.
units.tr: For when they wished to claim for their order a little work on the imitation of Christ, which is commonly circulated under the name of Thomas à Kempis, they spread the report that several manuscript codices of the highest reliability existed at Rome among their own people, in which the work was ascribed to John Gerson of Vercelli, an abbot of their order. The most learned Gabriel Naudé, when he was at Rome in 1641, reports that those books had been handed to him, and that they had been corrupted and falsified through the crime of a certain Benedictine monk. He simply committed the whole history of the affair, since it seemed worthy of men's memory and attention, to writing and sent it to the most distinguished Puteani brothers at home. After some years, when it had been published by John Fronto, a canon of St Genevieve and an opponent of the Benedictines, the Benedictines attacked Naudé with such violence and smeared him with such foul and insolent calumnies that he was forced to bring a lawsuit against them before the magistrate and to lay bare the whole stage of their iniquity and fraud. Many defences of his are in print, and in one of them, by setting out twenty arguments or notable examples, he almost proves that this is a peculiar habit of the Benedictines (for so he puts it), that they use and rely upon false, adulterated and interpolated documents in all their affairs. Nor is Naudé alone in this. Another very learned man, the Parisian theologian John de Launoy, when refuting certain letters of Pepin which had been thrown at him from the Benedictine monks' archive of Saint-Denis, says: The archive from which so many charters and privileges have come was once a workshop of them, as is evident to readers of the Antiquities of St Denis which James Doublet brought to light. But it was not only the Benedictines who suffered from this itch for invention. Rhenanus certainly does not call him a Benedictine, that great master of lying even when it brought him no gain, about whom he tells this charming little story. Some man (he says) in recent years, who I hear is still alive, invented a story, as the common people proclaim, that the blessed Helvetian anchorite was called Suetonius, describing his life, and that he had a companion named Achita. I went to the man to ask where he got this claim from, for I thought he would not say such things without an authority. But listen to his impudence. For this reason (he says) I added that he was called Suetonius, because I read that he had come out of Suetonius, and because the faithful Achates always clung to Virgil's Aeneas, so I gave his companion that name, otherwise he would have been nameless. And yet this story, if one may call it that, is not only painted and written in churches but has also been printed. So far Rhenanus. If men who lied so easily even without gain behaved in this way, what must we suppose they did when there was some hope of reward for their lie? The Jesuits, among whom there are no more notable monks than among the recent ones, are said by many to be no more holy or scrupulous in this matter: witness their own doctrine on the use of equivocation, and also that thesis publicly proposed and defended by them in the College of Louvain, that it is not a sin, at least not a mortal one, to overthrow by a false charge the great authority of an accuser who is harmful to you; and that other, far more horrible doctrine, that it is lawful for a cleric or a religious, when no other means of defence is open, to kill a calumniator who threatens to spread grave charges about him or about his religion. For if these men, whom they see as opposed to their religion, are held to be justified in taking from them either their reputation or even their very life, how much more will they judge it lawful to abolish or alter letters and papers (lifeless and dumb things) that are harmful to the faith and the Church, or to forge and thrust forward those that are favourable? The Jesuits' own practice clearly teaches what they think on these matters, and many striking examples of it may be seen in the dispute they have with those theologians who are commonly called Jansenists. These men, indeed, object nothing more often to the Jesuits than a certain desperate licence to lie and invent anything in the service of their cause, and (to pass over the rest) they everywhere reproach them with those things that are commonly known. They charge the Jesuits, on the contrary, with publishing Arnauld's volume on frequent communion under the name of a certain official of Arras; with spreading abroad, falsely, the bull of Urban VIII against Jansen's Augustinus; with fabricating and publishing, as though written to a Sorbonne doctor, a letter full of monstrous lies, under the name of an anonymous Protestant minister; and also with shamelessly disseminating, in 1650, the decree of the Roman Inquisition, falsely presented as an authentic censure of Innocent X against the Catechism on grace; and with publishing, under the title of a Manifesto, their own exposition of Jansenist doctrine, shamelessly invented and fabricated and attributed to the theologians of Port-Royal (that is, to the Jansenists themselves). Hence the Jansenists say, not without reason, that there is to be feared lest the name of Jesuits, which is now peculiarly theirs, should in future, by analogy, become common to all who invent fables or tell lying stories. To this must be added that those who do not believe such fables nevertheless favour them. Mariana, a very well-known Jesuit, tells of a certain German centurion who, having violated the sacred mass, burst open and died with his bowels spilled, like Judas. But, he says, although you have found little to vouch for it, it is in the public interest that it be believed. And elsewhere, of the alternating letters of Boniface VIII and King Philip, which our writers mention, because they do little to the credit of the papal dignity, he says it is in the public interest, as an example, that they should seem false. It is clearly in the interest of the human race that what is false and invented should be held true, and what is true and certain should be held doubtful and false. The same writer has scattered many things of this kind through his Spanish histories, handed down by the ancients but incredible and far removed from any appearance of truth; and so that he should not be thought to deceive the reader, as if he who relates them so eloquently also believed them to be true, he judged it necessary to forestall this suspicion, and at one point he plainly warns that he transcribes much more than he believes.

units.la: Quod autem talia non credit, ratio, ut opinor, hæc fuit, quod non putauit esse cordati hominis ea credere, anilesque (ut loquitur) fabulas pro veris habere. Et hic tamen publicè interesse censet, ut hæc credantur; credi que ipse à lectoribus cupit; qui, ni fallor, ea credi optavit, quæcunque credi publicè interest. Vnde videtur consequens esse, ut lectores suos stultos esse cupiverit, ut ea scilicet quæ ipse tradit quidem, non tamen credit, illi pro veris certisque habeant. Hic vero insigni quodam Romanæ fallaciæ exemplo fraudandum lectorem non puto; quo imprimis docemur, quanta sit iitorum & in corrumpenda rerum gestarum memoria, & in fingendis pro libidine suæ causæ documentis tum audacia, tum vafrities. Meminisse adhuc possumus quotquot paulo provectioris ætatis sumus, quanto cum animi sui dolore Paulus P. R. V. Venetos quos paulo ante proscripserat, ac sacris interdixerat, in communionem suam nulla neque præstita, neque pacta ab iis satisfactione, quadam rerum ipsarum necessitate compulsus, simpliciter, redintegrarit. Sed ne inglorium hoc fœdus & sibi, & sedi suæ probro, vel etiam detrimento sit, ex quo scilicet patet fulmina Vaticana im-
units.tr: As for why he does not believe such things, the reason, I suppose, was that he did not think it befitted a sensible man to believe them or to hold as true the fables of old women (as he puts it). Yet he nevertheless judges that it is in the public interest that these things should be believed, and he himself wishes to be believed by his readers; and, unless I am mistaken, he desired them to believe whatever it is in the public interest to believe. Hence it seems to follow that he wished his readers to be fools, so that they would hold as true and certain the things which he himself sets down but does not believe. But I do not think the reader should be cheated here by an outstanding example of Roman deceit; it teaches us above all how great both the audacity and the cunning of these men are, in corrupting the memory of past events and in inventing documents at will for their own cause. We who are of any age at all can still remember with what grief of spirit Pope Paul V, compelled by a certain necessity of affairs, simply took back into his communion the Venetians whom he had lately proscribed and forbidden the sacraments, without any satisfaction having been offered or terms agreed by them. But lest this inglorious treaty become a reproach, or even a loss, to himself and to his see, since it plainly shows that the Vatican thunderbolts were despised to some extent, let us now hear by what arts he took early thought for both the reality and the reputation of his own cause, already then contriving in secret and in corners those means by which the truth of any past event could, without any trouble, be cast out by his own people and utterly overturned.

units.la: pune aliquan Jo contemni; nunc audi quibus artibus & rei,& famæ suæ maturè prospexerit, jam tum clam & in angulis ea molitus, quibus olim omnis rei gestæ veritas nullo negotio à suis disjici, ac plane subuerti possit. Primo ergo ad Cardinalem Ioüsam (cujus ex Regis Henrici I V. mandato atque auctoritate præcipuæ erant in omni hujus reconciliationis negotio partes) Breve quoddam (ut vocant) nomine suo datum ordinavit; quo facultatem scilicet illi concedit Venetos ab excommunicatione, & censuris absoluendi. Tum Paulum quemdam Catellum, Apostolicum Protonotarium in loûsæ comitatu Venetias summisit, qui iştic clanculum cum paucis sceleris conscîis quam potuit versutissime tria quædam instrumenta; proximè ad verum effectus rerum, temporum, ac personatum circumstantiis, confecit. In primo præter verum, contra omnem hominum præsentium fidem narrat Venetos à Ioüsa interdicto, & censuris rite exsolutos, addita lege, ut pœnitentiam pro Confessarii arbitrio imponendam luerent; eamque Ducem, & Consiliarios,& Sapientes Venetos humiliter accepisse. In altero fingit Clericos aliquot, qui in publico carcere iamdudum Senatus auctoritate, captiui attinebantur, eodem tempore liberates Claudio nescio cui Montano Papæ ministro à Marco Ottobono Reipublicæ Secretario simpliciter absque ulla protestatione, conditione, vel juris reservatione in manum fuisse traditos. In tertio denique instrumento mentitur se ex sacris Senatus tabulis * descripsisse quoddam de revocandis monachis Senatusconsultum, qui ex ditione Veneta ob interdictum profugerant. Quatuor autem hæc scripta Romani homines neque tunc, neque annis proximis Iucem aspicere passi sunt, quod ea intelligerent recenti adhuc rerum memoria facile posse coargui. Sed ita consecta clam apud se in tenebriseo animo, ut apparet, sed uant,ut olim, cum sublatis paulatim omnibus rerum illarum testibus, ac monumentis opportunum erit, reperi-
units.tr: ...unpunished in some way, the thunderbolts of the Vatican are despised. Now hear by what arts he provided for both his affairs and his reputation. Even then he had secretly and in corners contrived the means by which, as in the past, the whole truth of an event could without difficulty be cast aside by his own people and utterly overturned. First, then, he had a certain document, called a brief, issued in his name to Cardinal Joyeuse (whose part, by the command and authority of King Henry IV, was chief in the whole business of this reconciliation). It granted him, namely, the power to absolve the Venetians from excommunication and censures. Then he sent one Paolo Catelli, apostolic protonotary, into Venice in Joyeuse's train. There, secretly and with a few accomplices in the crime, Catelli drew up as cunningly as he could three documents, closely fitted to the true circumstances of the events, times and persons. In the first, contrary to the truth and to the faith of everyone present, he relates that the Venetians were duly freed by Joyeuse from the interdict and censures, with the added condition that they should undergo the penance imposed at the confessor's discretion, and that the Venetian Doge, Counsellors and Wise Men had humbly accepted this. In the second he invents that several clerics, who had long been held captive in the public prison by authority of the Senate, were at the same time released and simply handed over without any protest, condition, or reservation of rights into the hands of a certain Claudio Montano, minister of the Pope, by Marco Ottobono, Secretary of the Republic. Finally, in the third document he falsely claims to have copied from the Senate's records * a decree concerning the recall of monks who had fled from Venetian territory because of the interdict. The Romans would not allow these four writings to see the light, neither then nor in the years that followed, because they understood that they could easily be refuted from the still-fresh memory of events. But they kept them hidden in their own store, in darkness of mind, as it seems, so that when all the witnesses and records of those matters have gradually been removed, it will be opportune for them to find

units.la: * Reg. ... dd. tè ex suis ctyptis prodeant, & fidem apud homines nacta posteris persuadeant Venetum negotium Paulo ex voto & ex dignitate Romana cessisse, scriptorumque, qui secus tradunt, narrationem vel planè labefactent, vel certè suspectam reddant. Hæc ego ex manuscripto hominis Veneti, civis optimi, atque integerrimi commentarii habuit; qui ipsis illis temporibus, cum de hac historum fraude certior esset factus, rem dignam observatione sua putavit, & pro sua in patriam caritate argumento satis multa in suam illam dissertationem conjecit, quibus hæ historum impostura siquando ex angulis emergere, & caput attollere audeant, facile patefieri, ac refelli possint. Atque hæc quidem hactenus; ex quibus velut ex quodam specimine satis jam constare arbitror, plerosque vulgo mortales, præsertim Clericos & Monachos Latinos ab octavo ad nos usque seculo sensisse fas esse quædam confingere, mutare, & interpolare, si quando id ad suæ religionis emolumentum conferre videretur.Itaque cum quidquid habemus venerum librorum non ab aliis, quàm ab iltis habeamus: ego non tam mirandum puto, quod plurima nunc veterum nomine circumferantur, partim falsa & supposititia, partim viciata & corrupta quàm quod aliqua, licèt pauca, vera & sincera ad nos pervenire potuerint.
units.tr: * Reg. ... dd. and bring them out of their crypts, and persuade posterity, having gained credit with men, that the Venetian affair turned out to Paul's wish and to the dignity of Rome, and either utterly weaken or at least render suspect the account of the writers who report otherwise. I have these things from a manuscript commentary of a Venetian, an excellent and most upright citizen, who, when he had been informed of this fraud in history at that very time, thought the matter worth his notice, and out of his love for his country he inserted into that dissertation of his many things sufficient to prove the case, by which, if this historical imposture should ever dare to emerge from its corners and raise its head, it could easily be exposed and refuted. And so far, so much; from these things, as from a kind of specimen, I think it is now sufficiently established that most mortals, especially Latin clerics and monks from the eighth century down to our own time, have thought it lawful to invent, alter and interpolate certain things whenever this seemed to serve the advantage of their religion. Therefore, since whatever true books we possess we have only through those same men, I do not think it so remarkable that many writings now circulate under the names of the ancients, partly false and spurious, partly corrupted and falsified, as that some, though few, true and sincere ones have been able to reach us.

units.la: Equidem scio viros doctos penè innumerabilia ejusmodi scripta observasse, & in editionibus quas adornarunt ut plurimum in postrema volumina rejecisse, & de hoc argumento libros totos compositise, quales sunt Apparatus Antonij Possevini, Catalogus Bellarmini, Medulla Patrum Sculteti, Criticus Sacer Riveti, Censura Roberti Coci, & alij ejusmodi, ab utriusque religionis hominibus editi. Sed quis fidem faciet nullum ab iis omissum. Adde quod novus hinc accrescat labor, superiore haud multa levior, in tot scriptis recentibus evolvendis. Sed nec sine examine admittenda sunt omnium judicia, cùm enim ad ea ferenda, partium, quibus enutriti fuerant, plerique atruletiunt anticipatas opiniones, quis pro iis fide jubebit? quis eos affirmabit nihil partium suarum studio & gratiæ dedisse? Hujus suspicionis adeo evidens ratio est ut neminem, vel tantillum in his controversiis versatum, esse putem, qui ejus à me probationem sir quæsiturus. Quam vera iustaque sir nostra hæc suspicio sit, ut alia taceam,docet ipse judiciorum conflictus, dum hi passim tanquam genuina admittunt, quæ illi tanquam adulterina exautorant & repudiant. Neque de his illi modo dissentiunt qui aliam atque aliam religionem sequuntur. Earumdem etiam partium Theologi sæpe de istis inter se certant. Pontificii Theologi quos supra retulimus maximam partem Decretalium antiquissimis Romæ Episcopis affictarum explodunt. Turrianus pro iis omnibus tanquam pro aris & focis pugnat, & de hoc argumento ingens volumen condidit. Baronius Recognitionum libros Clementi Romano tributos tanquam cænosum qurgitem protentosis mendaciis & insanis delirijs refertum improbat & procul rejiciendum non dubitat. Bellarminus contrà; libros istos, vel Clementis Romani, vel alterius æquè docti ac antiqui esse dicit. Sunt qui fragmenta Hilarij quæ Nicolaus Faber edidit pro genuinis & legitimis habeant; nou desint qui repudient. Erasmus, Sixtus Senensis, Melchior Canus, Baronius librum de nativitate B. Virginis Mariæ falso tribui Hieronymo existimant. Christophorus à Castro Iesuita Hispanus, aliter sentit. Cardinalis Cajetanus, Lautentius Valla, Erasmus, & nonnulli alii libros Dionysii Areopagitæ pro dubiis & incertis habent. Baronius & alii fermè omnes de iis dubitari non sinunt. Iesuita Turrianus, Bovius & alij Constitutiones Apostolorum pro indubitatis obtrudunt. Baronius, Possevinus, Petavius eas in medio relinquunt. Super hoc argumento fexcenta occurrunt in Scriptoribus Pontificiis ejusmodi judiciorum divortia. Si quis aveat exempla colligere legenti passim erunt obuia, maximè apud Cardinalem Petronium qu', non minùs ab aliis in hac Critice , quàm in disputa'di methodo sæpissime diuortium facit. Inter istas pugnantes sententias constitutus quo se vertet? Quem cursum tenebit sub ducibus tam parum inter se consentientibus? Verum enimuero fac istos nullis stu'diis duƈtos, nullis præconceptis opinionibus præpediros in id opus incubuisse, quis fide iudebit tanto oneri pares, idoneisque facultatibus instructos fuisse? An tu cuiusuis esse putas Antiquitatem uniuersam veluti in catinum fusorium excoquendam coniicere, spurcitiamque & scoriam omnem, & recrementa, quæ non solum ei adhærent, sed quæ unà permixta in unum veluti cum ea corpus coaluere, detergere ac repurgare? Hoc verò opus magnum, ut liquet, virum requirit, qui sit imprimis accerrimo ingenio acplanè defæcato, naso sagacissimo, oculis perspicacissimis, auribus purissimis, qui omnem & Ecclesiæ & seculi cum veterem, tum recentem historiam ad unguem calleat, qui linguas eruditorum omnes, atque disciplinas accuratissimè didicerit, qui & scriptores omnes veteres, medios, recentes, diuturno ac in defesso studio pervolutarit, qui singuiorum os ac vultum, venam, ut sic dicam, ac pulsum familiariter norit, inuentionem, dispositionem, elocutionem diligenter obseruarit (singula enim secula, singulæ nationes, singuli scriptores , habent proprios characteres & aliquid singulare) ut ex his omnibus certum de iis iudicium ferre queat. Vix secusum integrum huiusmodi hominí condendo fatis fit. Qui verò nostris temporibus in hoc argumento versati sunt nemo non videt eos ad id operis plerosque accessisse vel ab omnibus his, vel certè à plerisque partibus inparatos. Sed esto; Præstà sit vir aliquis harum rerum peritissimis, qui se ad opus tantum ab omni parte paratus accingat. Ille fateor) fraudem facile odorabitur, si incidat in crassum & plumbeum impostorem, qui scriptoris,quem simulare, ac commentiri instituit, typum, formam, colorem & pondus inepte, ac pingui Minerua expresserit; Exempli gratia, si Hieronymo aut Chrysostomo balbutiem aut sermonis infantiam adscripserit; si stilum barbarismis, incondita Latinitate, aut putido Hellenifmo respersserit; si in loquendi formulis, siue in rebus ipsis, siue etiam in allegatis authoribus ea quæ non nisi longo post tempore in usu fuerunt, adhibuerit: si ab eo, quod fingit, sæculo aliena argumenta usurpauerit; si auctores secum pugnantes induxerit, sententiásque non suas iis tribuerit; qualia fuere pleraque Scripta, quæ nostri Critici & Censores hactenus proscripsere. Sin res sit cum elaborato vafri & ingeniosi artificis opere, qui linguam, qui res gestas, qui arcana, mores, cognationes, inimicitias eius familiæ in quam irrepere satagit, ad unguem didicerit, qui omnia cum arte adhibuerit; pro certo affirmare ausim nostrum Aristarchum in huiusmodi fraude detegenda haud minus sudaturum, quàm in conuincendis Martini Guerræi imposturis in Gallia olim laboratum fuisse accepimus. Cur autem fiat verisimile, inter tot veteratores qui variis de causis, tanto studio in confingendis & supponendis libris operam posuerunt, non extitisse tot seculis aliquos, & eos quidem non paucos qui tanta arte stilum & ingenium transformarint, & personam alienam induerint, ut sucus nemini patere queat? Cum præsertim ea nomina usurpare potuerint, quæ cum ex authoribus ipsis sola in hominum memoria supersint, nec vestigium nec indicium ullum præbere possint vel stili, vel sententiarum quarum in hoc examine usus esse possit. Qua quidem in re cum qui Dionysio Areopagitæ opera sua supposuit prudentissimum fuisse iudico. Cum enim Auctoris illius scriptum nullum certum & indubitatum superfit, quocum furtum illud conferri queat fallacia vix reuinci potest; quod ipsum longè difficilius futurum erat, si auctor genus orationis medestius humiliùsque secutus esset. At cum Hieronymi, Cyprianí, Augustini, & similium plurima genuina & indubitata scripta habeamus, si qui eorum nomina mentiti sint, & sola collatione stili, nullo negotio, fraus retegitur. Gothicis quippe se-miserisque ingeniis in adumbrandis magnorum virorum lepore & elegantia non felicius ceßit quàm asino (quod aiunt) ad Lyram. Postremo neque illud hoc loco omisserim, quod quicquid illud est subsidii, quod ad dijudicanda inscripta antiquitati monumenta conferre nobis possit recentiorum scriptorum industria, id magna ex parte Inquisitorum & Censorum Latinorum vi, atque insidiis intetvertitur. Hi enim Protestantium primo labores, qui non pauci de hoc argumento diligentissimè disputarunt, ex ipso auctorum nomine damnatos, studiosissimè exuruntur, & quaecunque peste possunt ex hominum manibus, ac sinu excutiunt; Tum ne suis quidem parcunt; & si quid in eorum lucubrationibus offendant, quod suae de Patrum scriptis falso ut plurimum praeiudicatae opinioni adversetur, id statim expungunt, ac ne in lucem exeat, sedulo cavent; cuius rei illustre imprimis exemplum à Ioanne Rainoldo iampridem ebservatum referre non pigebit. Antonius Contius nobilis apud nos in Schola Bituricensi Antecessor Annotationes in ius Canonicum scripserat. Cum ex a. d. 1570. Antuerpiae Plantiniani typis excuderentur, tota operis Praefatio ideo praetermissa est, quod in ea Contius multis, iisque claris rationibus demonstraret falsas esse omnes episcoporum, qui Romae ante Sylvestrum sederunt, decretales (ut loquuntur) epistolas. Si rogas, unde id constet; ipsum opus capite licet tuncatum, & suam iniuriam, & alienum sceleus loquitur. Accidit ninirum, ut Censor praefati nis à se expunctae immemor per incogitantiam (neque enim omnia corruptores & mendaces meminerunt) annotationem quandam intactam dimiserit, in quâ nos Contius rem totam docet, diserte ibi scribens multas se in praefatione rationes adduxisse, quibus omnes Pontificum, qui Silvestrum praecesserunt, decretales; tales falsus esse manifestè ostendit. Hæc scilicet Latino Censori inuisa veritas misero scriptori operis sui capite, magna lectoris fraude, luenda fuit. Rainoldus per amicum à Plantino quæsivit, cur Contiana præfatio non fit edita? an superfit? liceret-ne ipsam videre? Plantinus pro suo candore respondit, censorem non permisisse, ut ederetur; neque se meminisse, quid eâ factum fuerit. Neque in his stetit Censoris impudentia. Satis ei non fuit præclarum viri doctissimi de epistolarum falsitate testimonium mendaci spongia delere; nisi eidem insuper diuersam de earum ueritate sententiam immani pefirdia affingeret. Hanc enim in ipso illo Contii opere annotationem scribi, excudique curauit, qua auctorem ea ipsa refellentem inducit, quæ se multis rationibus manifestè demonstrasse ipse in alia operis parte sancte testatus erat; Scio quosdam (inquit in illa fictitia annotatione (istorum Pontificium à Petro proximè sequentium decretales falsi insimulare. Sed majorem ab hiis probationem requirerem, cum & in omnibus quotquot extant canonum corporibus ab Isidoro ex libro Damasi urbis Romæ episcopi collectis ... reperiantur Atque ita Contium Confor Romanus adulterauit; perfidiane, an amentia majori, incertum. Erasmi Annotationibus in Actus Apostolorum locus erat de iis libris, qui Dionysii Areopagitæ nomine circumferuntur, luculentissimus; in quo eos negabat esse Dionysii; idque & uirorum doctorum testimonio, & rationibus non pauciis firmabat, & præter alia non pauca, hæc etiam habebat; Mihi (inquiebat) non videtur priscis illis temporibus tantum fuisse Christianis caremoniarum, quantum illi describunt. Deinde mirum sit tàm priscus auctor fuit, & tam multa scripsit, à nemine veterum seu Gracorum, seu Latinorum fuisse citatum; non ab Origene, non à Chrysostomo, nec ab Hieronymo quidem, qui nihil intentatum reliquit. Quin & Gregorius ipse, vir probæ fidei, citas hujus litteras, non indicat eum fuisse Dionysium Areopagitam. Porro cùm in Ecclesiastica historia multa fiat mentio de libris Dionysij Corinthiorū Episcopi, non est probabile taci-
units.tr: Indeed, I know that learned men have noted almost countless writings of this kind, have for the most part relegated them to the last volumes of the editions they prepared, and have composed whole books on this subject, such as the Apparatus of Antonio Possevino, the Catalogue of Bellarmine, the Medulla Patrum of Sculteti, the Criticus Sacer of Rivet, the Censura of Robert Cocus, and others of this kind, published by men of both religions. But who will vouch that none of these has been omitted by them? Moreover, a new labour arises from this, not much lighter than the former one, in unrolling so many recent writings. Nor can the judgments of all be admitted without examination. For when most men pass judgment, they bring to it anticipated opinions, bred into them by the parties to which they belonged, and who will stand surety for them? Who will affirm that they have given nothing to the zeal and favour of their own party? The reason for this suspicion is so evident that I think no one, even one who has taken only a small part in these controversies, would seek proof of it from me. How true and just our suspicion is, to say nothing of other things, the very conflict of judgments shows, since these men everywhere admit as genuine what those reject as spurious and cast out. Nor do they disagree on these matters only with those who follow one religion or another. Theologians of the same party often dispute about them among themselves. The Papist theologians whom we cited above mostly reject the Decretals ascribed to the most ancient bishops of Rome. Turrianus fights for all of them as for altars and hearths, and has written a huge volume on this subject. Baronius disapproves of the Recognitions attributed to Clement of Rome, calling them a muddy whirlpool, crammed with monstrous lies and insane delusions, and does not hesitate to reject them far away. Bellarmine, on the contrary, says that these books are either by Clement of Rome or by another equally learned and ancient author. There are those who hold the fragments of Hilary that Nicolas Faber edited to be genuine and legitimate; there are not lacking those who reject them. Erasmus, Sixtus of Siena, Melchior Canus and Baronius think that the book on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary is wrongly attributed to Jerome. Christopher de Castro, a Spanish Jesuit, thinks otherwise. Cardinal Cajetan, Lorenzo Valla, Erasmus, and some others regard the books of Dionysius the Areopagite as doubtful and uncertain. Baronius and almost all the others do not allow any doubt about them. The Jesuit Turrianus, Bovius and others force the Constitutions of the Apostles upon us as indubitable. Baronius, Possevinus and Petavius leave them undecided. On this subject countless such divergences of judgment occur among Papist writers. If anyone wishes to collect examples, they will be met everywhere to the reader, especially in Cardinal Petronius, who, no less in this criticism than in his method of disputation, very often departs from the others. Placed between these conflicting opinions, where will he turn? What course will he hold under leaders who agree so little among themselves? But indeed, suppose these men, led by no zeal, hindered by no preconceived opinions, had applied themselves to this work: who will believe that they were equal to so great a burden and furnished with suitable abilities? Do you think anyone can cast the whole of antiquity into a smelting pot, as into a crucible, and scour and purge away all the filth, dross and refuse that not only cling to it but have been so mixed together with it that they have fused into one body? Truly, this great work, as is clear, requires a man who is first of all of the keenest and most thoroughly refined intellect, with the sharpest nose, the most penetrating eyes, the purest ears, who knows to a nicety the whole history both of the Church and of the world, both ancient and recent; who has learned thoroughly all the languages and disciplines of the learned; who has thumbed through all the writers, ancient, medieval and recent, in long and unwearied study; who knows intimately the face and countenance, the vein and, so to speak, the pulse of each; who has carefully observed invention, arrangement and style (for each age, each nation, each writer has its own characteristics and something peculiar to itself), so that he may be able to pass a sure judgment on them from all these things. Scarcely does a man of this sort suffice to be made entire. But those who in our times have been engaged in this subject, no one fails to see, mostly came to the task unprepared in all or at least most of these respects. But grant it; let some man most skilled in these matters set about the work fully prepared in every respect. He, I admit, will easily smell out a fraud if he falls upon a coarse and leaden impostor, who has clumsily and crudely shaped the type, form, colour and weight of the writer whom he sets out to imitate and counterfeit; for instance, if he has ascribed stammering or childishness of speech to Jerome or Chrysostom; if he has sprinkled his style with barbarisms, uncouth Latinity or stinking Hellenism; if he has used in turns of phrase, whether in the matters themselves or even in the authors he cites, things that were not in use until a long time after the age he feigns; if he has borrowed arguments foreign to the century he imitates; if he has introduced authors who contradict themselves, and attributed to them opinions not their own. Most of the writings which our critics and censors have hitherto condemned are of this sort. But if the matter concerns a work wrought by a shrewd and ingenious craftsman, who has learned to a nicety the language, the deeds, the secrets, the customs, the kinships and enmities of the family into which he strives to creep, and who has applied all these things with art, I dare affirm for certain that our Aristarchus would sweat no less in detecting such a fraud than we have heard that effort was made in Gaul in refuting the impostures of Martin Guerre. But why should it be thought likely that among so many old hands, who for various reasons have devoted such zeal to fabricating and foisting books, there has not arisen in so many centuries some, and indeed not a few, who transformed their style and talent with such art and assumed another's persona, so that no trace of the fraud could lie open to anyone? Especially since they could have used those names which, as far as the authors themselves are concerned, survive only in human memory and yet offer no trace or sign of style or opinions by which the matter could be examined. In this respect, the man who foisted his works on Dionysius the Areopagite, I judge, was most prudent. For since no certain and indubitable writing of that author survives, with which that deceit could be compared, the fraud can hardly be refuted; and this would have been far more difficult still had the author followed a more modest and humble manner of speaking. But since we have many genuine and indubitable writings of Jerome, Cyprian, Augustine and the like, if anyone had counterfeited their names, the fraud would be detected with no trouble, by comparison of style alone. For among Gothic and dull wits, in shadowing forth the charm and elegance of great men, things went no more happily than with the ass (as they say) at the lyre. Lastly, I should not omit here that whatever help the industry of recent writers can offer us for judging monuments of antiquity that bear a false inscription is for the most part thwarted by the force and snares of the Latin Inquisitors and Censors. For these men, the first labours of the Protestants, which were not few and discussed the subject with great diligence, they most eagerly burn because of the author's name alone, and by whatever plague they can, they shake them out of men's hands and bosoms. Nor do they spare even their own; and if they find in their publications anything that runs counter to their own opinion, which, as is mostly the case, was prejudged falsely about the writings of the Fathers, they at once strike it out and take careful pains that it not come to light. I will not be sorry to relate an illustrious example of this, long ago observed by John Rainolds. Antonius Contius, a man of note among us, a teacher in the school at Bourges, had written Annotations on the Canon Law. When these were printed at Antwerp in the Plantin press in 1570, the entire Preface of the work was omitted for this reason, that in it Contius demonstrated by many and clear arguments that all the so-called decretal epistles of the bishops who sat at Rome before Sylvester are false. If you ask how that is known: the work itself, though mutilated in its chapter, speaks both of its own wrong and of another's crime. It happened, of course, that the censor, forgetful through inattention of the preface he had struck out (for corrupters and liars do not remember everything), left untouched a certain annotation, in which Contius teaches the whole matter, plainly writing there that in the preface he had brought forward many reasons by which he had clearly shown that the decretals of all the Popes who preceded Sylvester were spurious in such a way. This truth, hateful to the Latin censor, had to be paid for, to the great deceit of the reader, by the wretched writer through the loss of the chapter of his own work. Rainolds asked through a friend of Plantin why the preface of Contius had not been published: was it still extant? Might he see it? Plantin, true to his candour, replied that the censor had not permitted it to be published, and that he did not remember what had been done with it. Nor did the censor's impudence stop there. It was not enough for him to wipe out with a lying sponge the illustrious testimony of that most learned man concerning the falsity of the letters; unless he further ascribed to him, with monstrous shamelessness, an opinion about their truth contrary to his own. For he took care that an annotation be written and printed in that very work of Contius, in which he introduces an author refuting those very points which Contius had solemnly declared, in another part of the work, to have been clearly demonstrated by him with many arguments. "I know," it says in that fictitious annotation, "that certain men accuse the decretals of those popes who came next after Peter of being false. But I would require a greater proof from them, since in all the bodies of canons that exist, collected by Isidore from the book of Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, they are found..." And so the Roman censor corrupted Contius; whether from treachery or from greater folly, it is uncertain. In Erasmus's Annotations on the Acts of the Apostles there was a most conspicuous passage about those books which circulate under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, in which he denied that they were by Dionysius; and he confirmed this both by the testimony of learned men and by not a few arguments, and among many other things he also had this: "It does not seem to me," he said, "that the Christians of those early times had as many ceremonies as those books describe. Again, it is strange that so ancient an author, who wrote so much, should have been cited by none of the ancients, whether Greek or Latin; not by Origen, not by Chrysostom, nor even by Jerome, who left nothing untried. Indeed Gregory himself, a man of sound faith, cites his letters but does not indicate that he was Dionysius the Areopagite. Furthermore, since in Ecclesiastical History much mention is made of the books of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, it is not probable that Eusebius would have kept silent about so great a disciple of Paul, if he had left so many volumes."

units.la: {y} Apud Contii in d. II. c. Cle. ; Annot. in Act. c.17.34. in quibus & Dionys. sine. turum fuisse Eusebium de tanto Pauli discipulo,fi tantu voluminum reliquisset. Hieronymus in Catalogo f.riptorum illustrium unum,aut alterum Dionysium recenset,hujus libros nõ recenset. Laurentius * indicat fuisse [sua aetatu doct:ssimos viros,qui judicarint eos libros esse Apollinarii. Tameisi eius nominis duos commemorat Hieronymus,alterum Hieropolitanũ Episcopum,qui floruit sub M Antonino secundo,alterum Lao-dicenum in Syria Episcopum, neutri tamen hujusmodi quam tribuit operum. Neque enim opinor,hac Apollinaris heretico tribuenda. Ante complures annos,ut mirmimi,vir incôparabilis Gulielmus Grocinus,ut Theologus sumus,ita in nulla disciplina non exquisitè doctus & exercitatus, auspicaturus Londini in ede D. Paulo sacra enarrationem cœlestis Hierarchia,meditata prafatione multũ asseuerauit hoc opus esse Dionysii Areopagita,vehementer destomachans in eorũ impudentiam,qui dissentirent. At idem priusquam operis dimidiũ conseccisset,ubi gustum attentius cepisset,ingenuè coram auditoria fassum est sibi verso calculo nõ videri id opus esse Dionysij Areopagita. Demiror autem cur, &c. Hæc quidem Erafmus jampridem & doête, & sapienter & facunde, ut solet, scripsit; sed frustra tamen (plerisque quidem certe lectoribus) scripsit. Hunc enim locum, ex quo sapere & veriora intelligere poterant, eorum optima fide expunxerunt librorum novi de Hispania non censores, sed rectores, & cadnifices censura in Tomum V I. Erafmi; Annotat. in Actus Apost. cap.17. ad verb: illa, In quibus & Dionysius,p.312. à medio post illud, & εἰς, dele usque ad illud pag. seq sui initium, Demiror autem cur, exclus. Lata semel hac sententia nullus in omnibus provinciis, in quibus isti Bibliomastiges longè, latéque imperitant, reperitur Erasmi codex, in quo non sit erasa illa de pseudo Dionysii libris observatio. Cum vero illi in cæteros ejusdem generis scriptores, quorum de dubiis veterum libris diversa est à sua sententia, pari immanitate grassentur, eorumque judicia vel mutent, ut Contii, vel deleant, ut Erasmi; vides quam exiguum nobis super.
units.tr: Cf. Contius on d. II, c. Cle.; Annotations on Acts 17:34. In these passages Eusebius would certainly have mentioned Dionysius, so great a disciple of Paul, if he had left so many volumes. Jerome, in his Catalogue of Illustrious Writers, lists one or another Dionysius but does not list these books. Laurentius indicates that in his own day there were very learned men who judged these books to be by Apollinaris. Yet Jerome mentions two men of that name, one the bishop of Hierapolis, who flourished under Marcus Antoninus the Second, and the other the bishop of Laodicea in Syria, but neither is credited with works of this kind. Nor, I think, should these be attributed to the heretic Apollinaris. Some years ago, as I remember, the incomparable William Grocyn, a theologian and a man thoroughly learned and practised in every branch of learning, was about to begin in London, in St Paul's cathedral, a lecture on the Celestial Hierarchy. After a carefully prepared preface he strongly affirmed that this work was by Dionysius the Areopagite, and was vehemently indignant at the impudence of those who disagreed. But the same man, before he had got through half the work, having tasted it more attentively, frankly confessed before his audience that, on turning the pages, it did not seem to him to be the work of Dionysius the Areopagite. I wonder, however, why, etc. Erasmus wrote these things long ago, learnedly, wisely and eloquently, as is his way; yet he wrote in vain, at least for most readers. For this passage, by which they might have grown wiser and understood the truer view, was in good faith struck out by the men who were not censors but rulers and executioners of censorship of the new books of Spain, in volume VI of Erasmus. The passage is in his Annotations on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 17, at the words "In quibus & Dionysius", p. 312: from the middle, after the words "and [εἰς]", delete everything up to the words at the start of the next page, "I wonder, however, why", the sentence being excluded. Once this judgment was made, there is no copy of Erasmus in any of the provinces where those Bible-scourges rule far and wide in which that observation about the books of the pseudo-Dionysius has not been erased. And since they rage with equal savagery against the other writers of the same kind whose view on the disputed books of the ancients differs from theirs, either altering their judgments, as with Contius, or deleting them, as with Erasmus, you see how little is left to us

units.la: * Vide notam ad Apocalypsin. superesse in recentiorum labore ac diligentia adversus antiquitatis adulteratores praesidium.
units.tr: * See the note on the Apocalypse. The protection against the corruptors of antiquity remains in the labour and diligence of more recent scholars.

units.la: Iam ad veteres ipsos veniamus; ex quorum cum luce, tum industria fateor nobis suggeri quae in hac investigatione viam complanent, & longè maximi usus esse queant. Veteres enim ipsi nonnunquam de aliis Ecclesiae Scriptoribus agunt, qui sive suo tempore, sive superiore vixerunt. Inter Latinos Hieronymus Authorum Ecclesiasticorum, qui ab Apostolis ad sua usque tempora ad cognitionem suam venerant, Catalogum praetexuit, quem Gennadius continuavit. Addo his temporibus editam, cum nulla alia conferendam, Photii Patriarchae Bibliothecam in qua vir ille magnus sentiam suam de Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Graeciae maxima parte nobis exponit. Istius autem subsidij duplex potest esse usus. Alter ad libri approbationem, si ejus mentionem faciant; alter ad rejectionem, fide cofileant. Prior ex authorum qui librum qui in dubium vocatur probant, authoritate & conditione pendet, nam, ut supra monuimus & veterum nonnulli his artibus usi sunt. Alii quod a consiliis suis & propositio non essent alienae, eas ab aliis adhiberi non invitari passi sunt, alij fraudes non olfecerunt, alii notas retegere, vel non potuerunt, vel quacunque ratione ducerentur, noluerunt. De iis qui ejusmodi commenta ediderunt nihil repetam, qui vero alienatis fraudibus ac impostura fuerunt eorum exempla obvia sunt. Iustinus, Theophilus, & alii ex carminibus Sibyllinis, quam is proculdubio supposititiis, argumenta, tanquam ex oraculis, petunt. Quoties Clemens Alexandrinus, veterum, judice Hieronymo, eruditissimus, allegat li bros Apocryphos sub Apostolorum & discipulorum nomine, quibus falsò tribuebantur? Nonne Barnabae & Hermae offlicta citat? Nonne denique, quod & supra dixi tum est a nobis, in Concilio septimo quaedam sub nomine Athanasij, & alia non melioris commatis suppositia in medium prolata fuere? Patres autem non sciunt. per iis facultatis fuisse instructos, quibus omnes ejusmodi fraudes possent retegere, quis in dubium uocabit, qui quanta ad hanc operam omnino necessaria ejus defuerint non ignorabit? Hieronymus ipse Latinorum omnium, maximè in hoc eruditionis genere, doctissimus, quædam non raro in medio reliquit, ueluti cùm de libro quodam Minutii fœlicis contra Mathematicos agens, subjungit, Sitamen inscriptio non mentitur auctorem. Et alibi, quæcunque fuerit facti ratio, Pauli ad Senecam & Senecæ ad Paulum epistolas agnoscit atque probat, quæ tamen Baronio & Bellarmino suspectæ reduntur, & supposititiciæ, quales re ipsa sunt, censentur. Sed & ii ipsi qui scripta notha infamare potuerunt, id neglexerunt, uel ne authores ipsos in se prouocarent, uel ne iis libris authoritatem omnem abrogarent, quibus tamen utilia nonnulla, nihil uerò falsi, uel noxij, contineri arbitrarentur. Unde fit ut præstare existimarent libros istos quorumdam manibus teri, quàm sibi odium & invidiam, si eos aliqua animi religione infamarent, gratis quærere, cùm in illo nihil periculi esset, in hoc uerò labor & molestia. Sic, mea quidem sententia, ut hoc exemplum afferam, nunquam Hieronymus in retegendis Ruffini commentis & suppositionibus operam posuisset, ejusque malevolentiam in se prouocasset, ni alia de causa ab ipso alienatus fuisset, nec, ut irem censeo, Patres Africani de suppositiciis Nicænæ Synodi canonibus tam acriter cum Zozimo disputassent, ni sua multum interfuisset. Nec enim, quandiu aliter fieri potest, grauis & sapientis viri est cum quoquam amicitiam dissoluere; nec aduersus abusus, ni magni, & periculi certissimi pleni sint, solent leui negotio viri cordati insurgere. Palàm autem est incommodo, quæ fraudes istas consequuta sunt, primo quoque tempore non apparuisse, licèt cum tempore & sensim bonos genuinosque libros penè oppressérint. His animaduertis, facilè, mea quidem sententia. patet de titulo libri, ejusque natalibus, non fatis constare, quamvis sub eodem nomine apud unum aut alterum Veterum citatus occurrat. Sic exempli gratia & Iustinus ipse, & Clemens † Alexanallatos scimus libros sex de Sacramentis, & deinceps ab omnibus fere Theologis, tum veruftioribus, ut Lanfra co & Guitmundo, tum recentioribus eodem quoque loco ac numero habitos. Atqui res ipsa negat eos esse Ambrosij, ut est à Roberto Coco & aliis fusè sollideqi demonstratum ; vix repugnante Arnaldo Magistro Sorbonico. Concilium Lateranense, sub Martino I. P. R. tria quædam loca Athanasij nomine citat, ex sermone in illa verba. Quicunque dixerit Verbum, &c. Neque tamen dubitarunt Petronius Cardinalis, & Coiffetellus Madaurae Episcopus negare sermonem esse Athanasij. Homiliae in Matthaeum Latinae, quarum Opus impersectum vulgo dicitur, ante annos 792. ab Hincmaro Chrysostomi nomine laudatae, ex omnium consensu habentur, & quidem vere ac merito, pro hominis haeretici, & Chrysostomo multo recentioris operae . Symbolum ad Damasum, quod incipit Credimus in Deum Patrem, Hieronymi nomine citauit,& Carolus magnus ante annos 858. & Remigius Lugdunensis Episcopus ante annos fere 800. Atqui id Symbolum neque Hieronymi est,neque hominis catholici; neque simplicis & priuati cuiuspiam haeretici, sed ipsius haeresiarchae Pelagij ut utrarumque partium erudite ex Augustino pari consensu obseruarunt. Eiusdem quoque Pelagij (ut hoc obiter dicam) certò esse docti deprehenderunt, & epistolam ad Demetriadem Virginem, quae incipit, Si summo ingenio, & Commentarios in omnes Pauli Epistolas, quod utrumque onus, à multis retro seculis ad nostram memoriam, inter Hieronymi opera, magno errore, legitur. Librum Quaestionum Veteris & Noui Testamenti, ante annos 828. Augustino tribuit Synodus Parisiensis l sub Ludovico Pio : Atqui id opus, & ab Augustino alienum esse consentiuntur omnes eruditi, & alicuius haeretici esse pronunciat Bellarminus. Hincmarus, n & Hypognosticon, & de Praedestinatione & Gratia libros, velut Augustini genuinos citabat a. D. 859. Iam vero constat neutrum esse Augustini, vel Bellarmino teste libros de vita contemplativa Prospero asserunt Partes Aquisgranenses , a. d. 816. & Theodulfus Aureliamensis, a. 809. quos tamen non Prosperi, sed Iuliani Pomerij esse veiis certisq; rationibus demonstravit Sirmondus Prudentius Tricassinus, circa a. d. 860. librum Mythologiarum seu virgiliana continentia (quem Fulgentij Placiadis esse etiam pueri nunc sciunt non minis æquivoco deceptus Fulgentio Ruspensi, celeberrimo, sed in longè diversa eruditione Episcopo tri- buit. Parili errore Rathramnus Corbeniensis, & eorumdem temporum Menachus, Gennadi Constantinopoli tani Episcopi esse putavit librum de Ecclesiasticis dogmatibus, cuius certissimus auctor est Gennadius Massilienfis Presbyter. Multa eius generis afferre possem, sed haec, ut videtur, satis sunt ad id quod instituera mus probandum; ut nemo nunc miretur, quod Ignatii Epistolas, tametsi ex maiori, ut videtur, parte Eusebij testimonio firmatas, è Protestantibus non pauci veluti pusrias explodant. Quod vero pertinet ad alteram rationem, qua liber ex silentio Veterum in dubium vocatur, fateor neque ex ea plane certò atque indubitò argumentari licere, cùm fieri posset ut Patrum uni aut multis ignotus fueiit superiorum scriptorum aliquis, vel, etiamsi notus, tamen, vel errore vel consilio, omissus fuerir. Sed tamen si & qui de alicuius Vetustioris scrip-to tacuit vir graui & eruditus fuit causasque habuit cur de eo non taceret, & scriptum ipsum illustre esse,vel ob auctoris nomen, vel ob argumentum debuit, admodum probabile est nullum eius tempore extitisse quod uir talis huiusmodi locis tacuit. Itaque huiusmodi probatione merito usus est Hypatius Ephesius a. d. 532. ad euertendum Dionysij Pseudo Areopagitæ fidem, cùm quædam eius testimonia ab hæreticis quibuscum disputabat objiceremtur (quo loco obiter observandum primum hunc videri ex omni Antiquitate locum quo facta repetitur istorum Dionysiacorum, quæ nunc orbem sua fama impleuerunt, mentio.) Illa (inquit Hypatiusu): estis
units.tr: Now let us come to the ancients themselves. I confess that from their light, and from their diligence, there are suggestions that smooth the way in this investigation and can be of very great use. For the ancients themselves sometimes write about other writers of the Church, who lived either in their own time or earlier. Among the Latins, Jerome prefaced his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Authors, who had come to his knowledge from the Apostles down to his own time, and Gennadius continued it. I add to these the Bibliotheca of Photius the Patriarch, published in these times, which can be compared with no other, in which that great man sets out for us his judgment on the greater part of the ecclesiastical writers of Greece. The use of this aid can be twofold: one to approve a book, if they mention it; the other to reject it, if they are silent about it. The first depends on the authority and standing of the authors who approve a book that is called in doubt, for, as we noted above, some of the ancients too used these arts. Others, because the matter was not foreign to their own purposes, allowed these things to be used by others and did not object; others did not smell the frauds; others could not, or would not, for whatever reason, expose the marks. I shall say nothing of those who published such fabrications; but examples of those who were deceived by forged works are plentiful. Justin, Theophilus and others draw arguments, as if from oracles, from the Sibylline verses, which are without doubt spurious. How often does Clement of Alexandria, in the judgment of Jerome the most learned of the ancients, cite apocryphal books under the names of the Apostles and their disciples, to which they were falsely attributed? Does he not cite the writings of Barnabas and Hermas? Finally, as I have said above, were not some things under the name of Athanasius, and other spurious items of no better stamp, brought forward in the Seventh Council? Now, since the Fathers were not instructed in those skills by which they could expose all such frauds, who will doubt it, and who will not know how much of what was entirely necessary for this work was lacking to them? Jerome himself, the most learned of all the Latins, especially in this kind of scholarship, not rarely left certain things undecided, as when, discussing a book of Minucius Felix against the mathematicians, he adds: Although the title does not lie about the author. And elsewhere, whatever the reason for the matter, he acknowledges and approves the epistles of Paul to Seneca and of Seneca to Paul, which nonetheless are regarded with suspicion by Baronius and Bellarmine, and are judged spurious, as they really are. But even those who were able to brand spurious writings with infamy neglected to do so, either lest they provoke the authors themselves against them, or lest they strip those books of all authority, books which they judged to contain some useful things and nothing false or harmful. Hence it came about that they thought it better that such books should be worn in the hands of certain readers than that they should, by branding them with some religious scruple, gain for themselves hatred and envy for nothing, since in the one case there was no danger, but in the other labour and trouble. So, in my opinion, to bring forward one example: Jerome would never have taken pains to expose the fabrications and forgeries of Rufinus, and provoked his ill will against himself, had he not been estranged from him for some other reason; nor, I think, would the African Fathers have disputed so bitterly with Zosimus about the spurious canons of the Nicene Synod, had their own interests not been deeply involved. For it is not the mark of a serious and wise man to break off a friendship with anyone, as long as it can be done otherwise; nor do wise men usually rise up against abuses with little effort unless they are great and full of most certain danger. It is clear, however, that the frauds which followed did not appear at the first opportunity, although over time and gradually they nearly overwhelmed good and genuine books. With these points noted, in my opinion it is easily seen that there is not enough certainty about the title of the book and its origin, although under the same name it occurs as cited by one or another of the ancients. So, for example, we know that Justin himself, and Clement of Alexandria, and the six books On the Sacraments, and afterwards were held almost by all theologians, both older ones such as Lanfranc and Guitmund, and more recent ones, in the same place and rank. Yet the thing itself denies that they are by Ambrose, as has been fully and solidly demonstrated by Robert Cocus and others, scarcely opposed by Arnold, the Sorbonne master. The Lateran Council under Martin I, Roman Pontiff, cites three passages of Athanasius under his name, from a sermon on the words Whoever shall say the Word, etc. Nevertheless Cardinal Petronius and Coiffetellus, bishop of Madaura, did not hesitate to deny that the sermon is by Athanasius. The Latin homilies on Matthew, which are commonly called the Opus imperfectum, were cited under the name of Chrysostom by Hincmar more than 792 years ago; they are held by universal agreement, and indeed truly and rightly, to be the work of a heretic, and of a man much later than Chrysostom. The creed to Damasus, which begins We believe in God the Father, Charlemagne, more than 858 years ago, and Remigius, bishop of Lyons, nearly 800 years ago, cited under the name of Jerome. Yet that creed is neither Jerome's nor that of any Catholic, nor that of some simple and private heretic, but of the heresiarch Pelagius himself, as learned men on both sides have observed with equal agreement from Augustine. It has also been discovered by learned men, with certainty, that the same Pelagius (to mention this in passing) wrote the letter to the virgin Demetrias, which begins If with supreme talent, and the commentaries on all the Epistles of Paul; both of these burdens, for many centuries down to our own memory, have been read among the works of Jerome through a great error. The Synod of Paris under Louis the Pious, more than 828 years ago, ascribed to Augustine the book of Questions on the Old and New Testament; yet all learned men agree that this work is alien to Augustine, and Bellarmine declares that it is by some heretic. Hincmar also cited the Hypognosticon, and the books on Predestination and Grace, as genuine works of Augustine, in the year 859. Now it is certain that neither is Augustine's; and as Bellarmine bears witness, the Aachen fathers, in the year 816, and Theodulf of Orléans, in the year 809, assert that the books On the Contemplative Life are by Prosper; yet Sirmond, Prudentius of Troyes, around the year 860, demonstrated by clear and certain arguments that they are not Prosper's but Julian Pomerius's. The book of Mythologies, or containing Virgilian matters (which even boys now know to be by Fulgentius Planciades), was attributed by a no less misleading confusion to Fulgentius of Ruspe, a very celebrated bishop, but of quite different learning. By a similar error Rathramnus of Corbie, and Menachus of the same times, thought that the book On Ecclesiastical Dogmas was by Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, whose most certain author is Gennadius the presbyter of Marseilles. I could bring forward many things of this kind, but these, it seems, are enough to prove what we are undertaking; so that no one now should be surprised that Ignatius's Epistles, although confirmed for the most part by the testimony of Eusebius, are by no few Protestants cast out as spurious. But as to the second ground, by which a book is called in doubt from the silence of the ancients, I confess that one cannot argue from it plainly, certainly and without doubt, since it could happen that some earlier writer was unknown to one or many of the Fathers, or, even if known, was omitted through error or design. Yet if a man who was serious and learned kept silent about some older writing, and had reasons why he should not keep silent about it, and the writing itself ought to have been famous, either on account of its author's name or its subject, it is most probable that no writing of that kind existed in his time, since such a man would not have kept silent about it. Therefore Hypatius of Ephesus, in the year 532, rightly used this kind of proof to overturn the credit of the pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, when some of his testimonies were thrown at him by the heretics with whom he was disputing. (In this place it should be observed in passing that this seems to be the first place in all antiquity where mention is made of those Dionysian writings which now fill the world with their fame.) Those writings (says Hypatius) which you call

units.la: monia quæ vos Dionysii Areopagitæ dicitis unde potest is os sen de re vera esse sicut suspicamini? Si enim eius erant, non potuissent latere B.Cyrillum. Quid autem de B.Cyrillo dicēdum est, do & B.Athanasius, si pro certo scisset eius suisse, ante omnia in Nicæno Concilio de consubstantiali Trinitate eadem testimonia protulisset aduersus Arij diuersa substantia blasphemias. Si autem nullus ex antiquis recordatus est ea, unde nunc potestis ostendere quod illius sint nescit.Hactenus Hypatius. Quo exemplo nominis valide argumentamur, supposititias esse eas epistolas quæ iam ab Eusebij seculo Ignatij nomine circumferuntur.Si enim eius erant non potuissent (inquam) latere B Irenæum, qui earum disertissima de Patris rerum omnium Creatoris Deitate, Christique Filij veritate testimonia aduersus hæreticos protulisset, qualiter Clementis epistolam ad Corinthios, & Polycarpi ad Philippenses laudauit a. Ille erò nusquam istas Ignatii epistolas recordatus est, tametsi tacito eius nomine, quoddam dictum alicubi referat, quod in iis hodie legitur nempe ex Irenæo ab impostore qui eas finxit ad rem suam usurpatum, ὡς εἴπέτις τῷ ῥυτίφων (inquit, Irenæus) b ut dixit quidam de nostris. Non ait ut scripsit, vel ut in epistola aliqua dixit sed simpliciter ut dixit. Neque ex Epistolæ, si verè erant, Clementem Alexandrinum qui ipsis etiam Apocryphis libris multum utitur, latuissent, vel Tertullianum qui nusquam eas memorauerunt. Sed hæc disputandi ratio prætestquam quod admodum est probabilis, & illud etiam habet præcipui, quod prioti longè est tutior, cùm multo minus periculosum fit scriptum aliquod genuinum repudiare, quam supposititium admittere. Leuius enim est veritate aliqua carere, quàm mendacio, quod ei opponitur, fidem adhibere. Quemadmodum enim minùs peccat, qui bonum aliquod omittit, quàm qui malum, quod ei opponitur, committit. Sic eius qui, quod res est, credere abnuit, qui m eius qui falsum, quod rei veritati opponitur, temere admittit, leuior error est. Ea est veterum librorum consusio, eaque rationum, quibus veri à falsis, genuini à suppositiis discerni possint, infirmitas, adeo ut sæpenumero leuioris sit negotij quid respondum, quàm quid recipiendum sit constituere. Iudicet nunc Lector cùm Scripta ista tot seculis volutata sint, & per tot manus vel nullius, vel certè dubiæ fidei transierint, veritate ipsa languidè & quasi perfunctoriè aduersus fraudes istas obsistente, annon, inter tot librorum, qui sub nomine Patrum feruntur millia, qui sint veri & legitimi, qui vero nothi & supposititij difficillimum sit certò statuere. Quod si in genere tantæ molis est Patrum libros alios ab aliis secernere, quanto maioris negotij erit singulorum super controversiis nostris sententias indagare & constituere? Non enim cujus Patris sint parum referre putandum est. Nam sive authoritatem, sive doctrinam, sive usum spectes, non minus est discrimen inter Veteres illos, quàm inter recentes scriptores. Adde ætatem & unius etiam seculi discrimen magni omnino momenti, apud Protestantes præsertim censeri annoíque & canitiem pretium Scriptis addere. Neque sanè id immeritò fit, cùm vel mediocriter in ipsorum lectione versato notum sit, cum tempore maximas mutationes, non minùs in doctrinam & disciplinam Veterum, quàm in cætera alia sensim inuectas fuisse. Fixum ergo & immorum maneat, cuique qui apud se decreverit quæ fuerit, super capitibus hodie controversis, Veteris Ecclesiæ sententia certò explorare necessarium pariter ac difficile esse, omnium istorum Scriptorum & nomen & ævum ad unguem tenere, & in comperto habere.
units.tr: "Those writings which you call the works of Dionysius the Areopagite: how can it be known that they are really his, as you suppose? For if they were his, they could not have remained hidden from St Cyril. And what must be said of St Cyril, and of St Athanasius too? If he had known for certain that they were his, he would above all have brought forward those same testimonies at the Council of Nicaea, on the consubstantiality of the Trinity, against the blasphemies of Arius about a different substance. But if none of the ancients remembered them, how can you now show that they are his? It is unknown." Thus far Hypatius. By this example of the name we argue forcefully that those letters which have been circulated under the name of Ignatius since the age of Eusebius are spurious. For if they were his, they could not (I say) have remained hidden from St Irenaeus, who, in his most eloquent passages on the Deity of the Father, the Creator of all things, and the truth of Christ the Son, brought forward testimonies against the heretics; and who praised the letter of Clement to the Corinthians and that of Polycarp to the Philippians. Yet he never mentions those letters of Ignatius. Although he cites somewhere, without naming him, a saying which is today read in them, he took it from Irenaeus, and the impostor who forged them used it for his own purposes: as a certain one of ours said [ὡς εἶπέ τις τῶν ἡμετέρων] (says Irenaeus). He does not say "as he wrote" or "as he said in some letter," but simply "as he said." Nor, if they were genuine, would they have escaped Clement of Alexandria, who makes much use even of the Apocryphal books, or Tertullian, who never mention them. But this method of argument, besides being quite probable, has this particular advantage: it is much safer than the other, since it is far less dangerous to reject some genuine writing than to admit a spurious one. For it is a lesser evil to lack some truth than to give credence to the lie opposed to it. Just as he who omits some good sins less than he who commits the evil opposed to it, so the error of one who refuses to believe what is the case is lighter than that of one who rashly admits what is false and opposed to the truth. Such is the confusion of the old books, and such the weakness of the criteria by which the true may be distinguished from the false, the genuine from the spurious, that very often it is a lighter task to decide what should be rejected than what should be accepted. Let the reader now judge: since these writings have been tossed about for so many centuries and have passed through so many hands, of no one or at least of doubtful trustworthiness, while truth itself has resisted these frauds only feebly and, as it were, carelessly, is it not very difficult to determine with certainty, among the many thousands of books that go under the name of the Fathers, which are true and legitimate and which are spurious and counterfeit? But if in general it is such a great undertaking to separate some books of the Fathers from others, how much greater a task will it be to investigate and establish the opinions of each on our controversies? For it should not be thought of little importance whose each work is. Whether you look to authority, to doctrine, or to usage, there is no less difference among those ancients than among recent writers. Add their age: even the difference of a single century is of great importance, especially among the Protestants, who are accustomed to attach value to writings for their age and grey hair. Nor is this done without reason, since anyone moderately versed in reading them knows that over time very great changes crept gradually into the doctrine and discipline of the ancients, no less than into other things. Let it therefore remain fixed and settled for everyone who has decided for himself what the view of the ancient Church was on the chapters controverted today: to ascertain this with certainty is necessary and equally difficult, and it requires having the name and age of all these writers at one's fingertips and fully known.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Ratio iv. Prioribus & posterioribus seculis, temporè, Imperitia, fraudibus, cum piis, tum malignis genuina S. Patrum scripta varie in locis immutata & adulterata fuisse.
units.tr: Reason 4. That in earlier and later centuries the genuine writings of the Holy Fathers were variously altered and corrupted in places, through the passage of time, through ignorance, and through frauds, both pious and malicious.

units.la: VErumenimvero esto indefessis, multoque cum judicio institutis studiis genuina Patrum monumenta à supposititiis secreta & distincta habeas. Ecce tibi qui superiore exantlato surgit labor longè molestior, cujusque eventus multo magis in merito situs est. Semel enim constitutis genuinis scriptis; superest necessario ut, quæ sunt ab authore ipso, ab aliunde affutis & infartis seccernas, ut, quod tempore perierit, vel dolo malo sublatum fuerit, restituas, vel, quod hic vel ille de suo addiderit, expungas. Alias nunquam certò assequeris quæ vera & genuina fuerit auctorum ipsorum sententia, propter varias depravationes quæ in illos multifariam diversitque temporibus invaserunt. Scribarum errores mitto, qui non quod inveniunt, sed quod intelligunt scribunt (ut est apud Hieronymum.) Illos item qui de ipsa librorum exscriptione orti sunt. Neque enim fieri potest, ut libri, millies intra decem aut duodecim secula in varios codices traducti & transcripti, à librariis parum inter se seu in doctrina, seu in scriptionis characterè, convenientibus, semper & ubique servarint eundem succum, eundemque habitum ipsamque illam formam retinuerint, quam olim præscribebant, cum adhuc recentes ab auctoris officina prodirent. Quid tinea, qui blattæ, quid caries, sexcentæque hujusmodi temporis injuriæ in iis corruperint, prudens mitto. Bonas literas tot seculis sepultas, & veluti in tumulo iacentes, vermibus erośas, situ & pulvere absumptas, in primigenium statum restituere humanæ opes non fuit. Hæc omnis generis librorum sors fuit. Inde quæ penè omnes Scriptores obsidet lectionum varietas tanta nata est ex qua quidem pugnare animus non est, licèt in rem præsentem faciat,& magno præiverint exemplo, inter adversarios Doctores, nonnulli, dum tantillum in Sacris paginis lectionum varietatem, licèt nullius, vel saltem minimi momenti, ipsi S. Scripturæ in calumniam vertunt,cjusque qua ipsa per se erga unumquemque mortalium pollet, infirmatum eunt, authoritatem. At si propositum nobis esset istorum vestigiis insistere, &, quæ ipsi de Sacra Scriptura dicunt & colligunt, ea ad Patrum scripta applicare, id longè potiori jure facere possemus, cùm nullomodo fiat verisimile, non plures ejusmodi depravationes Veterum Scripta passa fuisse, quam volumina Divina, cùm hæc longè majori studio, quàm ulla alia in Ecclesia asservata, apud omnes nationes memoriæ mandata, in omnes linguas transfusa, ab omnibus sectis, orthodoxis & hæreticis, Catholicis & Schismaticis, Græcis & Latinis, Sarmatis & Æthiopibus recepta fuerint, aliis aliorum oculos & manus accuratè observantibus,ita ut ne minima quidem, quæ ullius esset momenti,depravatio acciderit potuerit, quin, ut ita dicam, universus insurgeret orbis, & de illata injuria apud omnes ubique quererretur. At Patrum libri, maximam partem, negligenter habiti,& scitanter transscripti lectiquefuere,idque à paucis, & raro, adeo ut vix noti fuerint, nisi suæ linæ hominibus, quo factum ut in ejusmodi depravationes pronior lapsus, eorûque animadversio difficilior fuerit. Stilus item & obscuritas quorumdam peculiaris facit ut quælibet immutationes majoris sint momenti. Exempli gratia, in manus sumatur Tertullianus, voculam si addideris, vel sustuleris, vel levissimè immutaveris, punctum vel virgulam alieno loco si posueris, sensum adeo interturbaueris, ut quid sibi velit nulla ratione queas exculpere. At in scriptis facilè fluentibus, apertis.
units.tr: Indeed, grant that you have pursued your studies with unwearied diligence and with much judgment, so that you have separated the genuine monuments of the Fathers from the spurious. Behold, after that toil, a far more troublesome labour rises up before you, and its outcome depends much more on the merits of the case. For once the genuine writings are established, it remains necessary to separate what comes from the author himself from what has been added and inserted from elsewhere, so that you may restore what has been lost in time or removed by evil design, or strike out what this or that man has added of his own. Otherwise you will never be certain what the true and genuine opinion of the authors themselves was, on account of the various corruptions that have crept into them in many ways and at different times. I pass over the errors of scribes, who write not what they find but what they understand (as Jerome has it). I likewise pass over those errors that arose from the very copying of the books. For it cannot happen that books, transferred and transcribed a thousand times within ten or twelve centuries into various codices by copyists who agreed poorly with one another, whether in doctrine or in the form of their handwriting, should always and everywhere have kept the same flavour, the same appearance, and that very form which they had when first issued from the author's workshop. What moth, what bookworm, what decay, and the countless other injuries of time have done to them I prudently pass over. Human resources have not been able to restore to their original state good literature buried for so many centuries, lying as in a tomb, eaten away by worms, and consumed by mould and dust. This has been the fate of books of every kind. Hence has arisen that great variety of readings which besets almost all writers.
