I have no wish to quarrel over it, although it would serve my purpose, and some of our opponents among the teachers have set a great example here: while they turn to calumny the slight variety of readings in the sacred pages, though it is of no importance or at least of the smallest importance, they weaken the authority of Holy Scripture itself, which by its own nature carries weight with every mortal. But if it were our purpose to follow in their footsteps, and to apply to the writings of the Fathers what they say and infer about Holy Scripture, we could do so with far better right. For it is in no way likely that the writings of the ancients suffered not more such corruptions than the divine volumes, which have been guarded in the Church with far greater care than any other, committed to memory among all nations, translated into all languages, and received by all sects, orthodox and heretical, Catholic and schismatic, Greeks and Latins, Sarmatians and Ethiopians, while others watched their eyes and hands closely, so that not even the smallest corruption of any importance could have occurred without the whole world, so to speak, rising up and complaining everywhere of the injury done. But the books of the Fathers, for the most part, were held in little regard, copied and read carelessly, and that by few and rarely, so that they were hardly known except to men of their own circle. The result is that a lapse into such corruptions is more likely, and their detection more difficult. Moreover, the style and obscurity of certain writers make any alteration of greater consequence. For example, take up Tertullian: if you add or remove a single little word, or alter it even very slightly, or place a point or a comma in the wrong place, you will so disturb the sense that you can in no way work out what he means. But in writings that flow easily and are plain and clear, such as those of Holy Scripture for the most part, such changes are harmless, since the sense cannot be so obscured that it cannot be grasped with slight effort. But these quibbles and wrangling, which call everything into doubt like the Pyrrhonists and Academics, befit such men rather than Christians, who should support their faith frankly and sincerely.

units.la: & perspicuis, cujusmodi sunt passim S.Scripturæ,Ista manus sunt noxia,cùm adeo obscurari sensus nequeant,quin leui, negotio percipi possit. Sed argutias & vitiligatio– nes istos, tanquam Pyrrhoniis & Academicis, omnia in dubium vocantibus, potiùs quàm Christianis,quo fidem suam fulciant ingenuè & candidè quærentibus convenientes omitto. Agam tantùm de mutationibus quas facere instituerunt qui scienter & de industria Veterum Patrum sententiam, vel silentio obruere, vel adulterarè, vel ampliare studuerunt. Ex duùm sunt genera. Quædam enim ab animo non malo profecta sunt; Aliæ vero ad fraudem & fucum faciendum comparatæ. Aliæ rursus iam olim procusæ; Aliæ vero postremis hisce Patrum nostrorum, aut nostris demum temporibus fabricatæ sunt. Fuere denique qui ad auctores ipsos aliquid de suo & quod non habebant attexuerunt. Alii auctores truncaverunt & quod ad palatum non faciebat sustulerunt. Nec mirum videri debet rudes & incautos veteres has artes dedignatos non fuisse, cùm aliquando non magna ipsis esset religio totos libros auctoribus non veris propter bonum finem supponere. Quod quidem inceptum, quàm istud, magis insolens & audax mihi videtur. Cùm non dubium sit monetam improbam cudere, gravius esse crimen, quàm probam tantillum circumcidere, vel adulterare. Mortalium animis hæc semper insedit opinio. Ad auctoritatem conciliandum veritati, & rebus bonis (vel fakem quæ ejusmodi videantur) expedire,ut quicquid obesse aut remoari possit, de via amoucatur; & quæ in rem conferre possunt apponere, vel saltem non tollere, quæcunque aliàs hæc vel illa sint, periculo vacare. Inde nobis tot antiquæ suppositiones profluxere. Hinc nobis natæ tot miraculorum & visionum adeo stupendæ narrationes, multis confingere amantibus Dæmonum contra se pugnantium portenta (ut est apud Hieronymum) & alia ejusmodi commenta, à cautioribus etiam animaduersa, nec minus rus tamen tolerata,& non nunquam commendata, quod ad pupi'li seu filem seu religionem confirmandam vel amplificandam conducere existimarentur. Sed quod magis mirum videatur , etiamnum hodie eorum ipsorum nonnulli qui fe ab istis veifutiis maximopere abhorrere profitentur , sibi tamen temperare nequeunt quin, fi quos edant veteium libros, in iis quicquid à sententia , quam veram censent , vel minimum diferepat, statim deleant vel interpolent,ne perifta ( inquiunt ) imperiti in fraudem inducantur, adeo altè mentibus hominum ea insidet opinio. Equidem iuiéne an iniuria id faciant nunc non disputo. Hoc tantùm obiter moneo,& has artes non fine probro & dedecore veritati tribui, vel ut iis ad fe tuendam indigeat, nec fatis armorum ei fit, vel ad fui defensionem , vel ad reportandam de hoftibus victoriam, sed ea ab adversariis mutuari & emendicare opus habeat, & praeterea periculi plenas esse.Vbi enim fraus semel patuit, sæpissimè tota, in cuius gratiam contexta est, causa in meritam suspicionem venit, ita ut fi artibus istis apud imperitorum quosdam rem Christianam promouerint, eosque vel ad fidem converterint , vel in ea confirmauerint, vetendum fit tamen ne nafutiores ab eadem auertant, tandemque & rudes ipsos eorum exemplo ab ea auocent,& in eius fastidium adducant. Verùm quicquid fit de fallacia ista, deqi incommodis quæ eam consequuntur , fatis mihi est ad hoc quod ago, eam in hoc ipso, quod præ manibus habeo,argumento, iam olim usurpatam fuisse. Quod ut probem eius exempla quædam in medium afferam. Hæretici quidem huius fraudis semper suspecti fuerunt Omitto ea quæ antiquissimi in scripturis ipsis pro viribus adulterauerunt. Eorum fi specimen videre animus fit, idque notatu dignissimum, adeundi sunt Tertullianus & Epiphanius , apud quos videre est quàm miseré Marcion Lucæ Euangelium & quascunque admittebat Pauli Epistolas truncaret & depravaret. Quæ subsecuta sunt secula in hisce rebus religiosiora non fuerunt Patres id ex Ruffini in expositione Symboli, & in Tractatu de hoc argumento, quaerimoniis, contradicente & repugnante quidem Hieronymo, † sed quantum ad hypothesin, Origenem videlicet, at minimè omnium quantum ad thesin ipsam. Nec aliena ab his legere est apud Cyrillum & veterum *alios multos, imò & inter recentiores apud eos ipsos qui Romæ Concilia generalia praefuerunt in Ant. Conc. lo subjecerunt. Queruntur illi Præfatione quam primo volumini † præfixerunt, temporis iniu ia & hæreticorum fraudibus factum fuisse, ne Conciliorum illorum acta integra habeamus, neve quæ, exiis superfuit pura atque sincera sint. Quocirca vicem nostram vehementer dolent; quod tanto & tam pretioso thesauro spoliati & orbati simus. Quod certè testimonium instar est mille aliorum, cùm, meo iudicio, homo hominum plurimum referret alia omnia proloqui. Quid enim? si Roma quam fidei magistram & sequestram volunt, Concilia, quæ pro Ecclesiæ Canone habet, ulla ratione perire passa est, quid reliquis factum est? Quid in iis vel hæretici, vel schismatici non potuerunt? Si verè omnia illa monumenta istorum fraude depravata fuerunt, quomodo quæ de controversiis nostris fuerit veterum sententia ex iis hauriemus? Neque negaverim mihi non parum mirum videri, & quod tanti Conciliorum Acta faciant, & quod tam acriter in hæreticos propter eorum partem aliquem suppressam & abolitam invehantur. Si enim tanto usui nobis esse possunt monumenta ista; cur hinobis Concilii Tridentini acta invident, quo nullum ab octingentis retro annis maioris momenti apud Christianos habitum est, sive Latinos ipsos, sive etiam Latinorum adversarios Protestantes spectemus? Si crimini vertunt haereticis quod huiusmodi κεμάλια interverterint; nonne ab eodem sibi probro metuere ipso par est criminis quod reprehendunt, reos? Sed proculdubio latet aliquid quod discrimen ponit inter ista; & quod facit ut apud illos non eadem horum sit quæ illorum est ratio. Et mirati subit quare eam non edant. Rerum enim imperiti, dum alia non occurrit, sibi fingunt (forsan abs re) id arte fieri à Romanis, & tam arctè poltremi Concilii Acta ab iis clausa teneri, quod censeant eorum promulgationem obfuturam, aut saltem nihil profuturam dignitati Romanæ, hariolentur contra, Acta illa quæ ab hæreticis è medio sublata volunt, quæque tam sollicitè defidegant, multa continuisse, quibus illa miris modis juvari, magisque ac magis confirmari potuisset. Vrcunque sit, equidem istorum ingenuitatem non possum non laudare, ut ut enim malè rationibus suis consulere videantur, ultro quæ extant hodie Acta Conciliorum, ea confitentur neque integra, neque incorrupta esse. Sed deinceps inquiramus annon & Ecclesiæ homines ad veterum Scriptorum depravationem aliquid ipsi quoque contulerint. Refert Epiphanius in bonis & emendatis S.Lucæ exemplaribus legi Christum fleuisse eoque testimonium ut apud Irenæum. Sed Catholicos timore quodam inductos vocem sustulisse, ne ea hæretici abuterentur. Verane hæc narratio an falsa sit fides penes auctorem esto. Hoc unum inde, quidem, ut mihi videtur, evidentissimè colligo. Nullam veteribus Catholicis religionem futuram fuisse vocem aliquam, si eam sententiæ suæ repugnare, aut hæreticum corruptelis obnoxiam esse censerent ex Patrum scriptis expungere. Cùm enim Epiphanio auctore, ne ipsi quidem Filij Dei Euangelio parcerent, an maiore religione scripta humana habita fuisse probabile est? Ruffinus certè in pretio & fratris loco, ante exortam cum eo simultatem, habitus ab Hieronymo & ab Augustino etiam, qui ægerrime se cum eo discordiam ferre testatur, & à Gennadio cum magno elogio Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Catalogo insertus, tanta licentia in scriptis Origenis Eusebii & aliorum, quæ de Græcis Latina fecit, versatus est, ut nulla in eius interpretationibus pagina occurrat, in qua non ali-
units.tr: and clear, such as are found everywhere in Holy Scripture. Such tampering is harmful, since the meaning cannot be so obscured that it cannot be grasped with little effort. But I leave aside the subtleties and quibbling, which suit the Pyrrhonists and Academics, who call everything into doubt, rather than Christians who seek, frankly and sincerely, to strengthen their faith. I shall deal only with the alterations deliberately and purposely made by those who have sought either to bury the opinion of the ancient Fathers in silence, or to corrupt it, or to expand it. There are two kinds. Some have arisen from a not evil mind; others have been devised for fraud and deception. Some were forged long ago; others were fabricated in the most recent times of our Fathers, or in our own age. Finally, there were those who added to the authors themselves something of their own that they did not have. Others truncated the authors and removed whatever did not suit their taste. Nor should it seem strange that the crude and unwary ancients did not disdain these arts, since at times they had no great scruple about attributing whole books to authors who did not truly write them, for a good end. Yet this undertaking seems to me more insolent and bold than that one. For there is no doubt that to coin false money is a graver crime than to clip or adulterate a genuine coin, even slightly. This opinion has always settled in the minds of mortals: that to win authority for the truth, and for good things (or for things that seem to be such), it is expedient to remove from the way whatever could hinder or delay, to add whatever can contribute to the matter, or at least not to remove it, and that whatever else these or those things may be, they are safe from danger. From this so many ancient forgeries have flowed for us. Hence have arisen so many accounts of miracles and marvellous visions, invented by many who love to fabricate the monstrous portents of demons fighting against one another (as in Jerome) and other such inventions, which the more cautious have noticed, yet nonetheless tolerated and at times even commended, because they were thought to conduce to confirming or amplifying the piety or religion of the people. But what seems more surprising is that even today some of those who profess to abhor these frauds utterly cannot restrain themselves: if they publish any ancient books, whatever in them differs even slightly from the opinion they hold to be true, they straightaway delete or interpolate, lest (they say) the unskilled be led into deception. So deeply does that opinion sit in men's minds. Whether they do this rightly or wrongly I do not now discuss. This only I note in passing: these arts are not attributed to the truth without disgrace and shame, as if it needed them for its protection, as if it had not enough weapons for its own defence or for winning victory over its enemies, but had to borrow and beg these from its adversaries. Moreover, they are full of danger. For once a fraud has come to light, very often the whole cause in whose favour it was contrived falls under just suspicion. So even if by these arts they advance the Christian cause among some of the unlearned, and convert them to the faith or confirm them in it, it must still be feared lest they turn the more astute away from it and, finally, by their example, call even the simple away from it and bring them to loathe it. But whatever may be said about that deceit and the inconveniences that follow it, it is enough for my purpose that this very deceit was used long ago in the very argument I have before me. To prove this I will bring forward some examples. Heretics indeed have always been suspected of this fraud. I pass over those things which the most ancient of them corrupted in the Scriptures themselves, as far as they could. If one wishes to see a specimen of this, and one most worthy of note, one must consult Tertullian and Epiphanius, where one may see how wretchedly Marcion mutilated and corrupted the Gospel of Luke and whatever Epistles of Paul he admitted. The ages that followed were not more scrupulous in these matters. That the Fathers were not appears from Rufinus, in his exposition of the Creed and in his treatise on this subject, where complaints are made, Jerome contradicting and opposing, indeed, † but only as to the hypothesis, namely Origen, and not at all as to the thesis itself. Nor are things foreign to these to be read in Cyril and many other ancients, and even among more recent writers, among those very men who presided over the general Councils at Rome and who placed them in the collection of the Councils. They complain in the preface they prefixed to the first volume that, through the injury of time and the frauds of heretics, it has come about that we do not have the acts of those Councils entire, nor are those which have survived pure and sincere. Wherefore they grieve greatly on our behalf, that we have been despoiled and bereft of so great and precious a treasure. This certainly is a testimony worth a thousand others, since, in my judgement, it would have been much better for the man to say everything else. For what? If Rome, which they want to be the teacher and guardian of the faith, and which holds the Councils as the rule of the Church, has allowed them to perish in any way, what has happened to the rest? What could heretics or schismatics not have done with them? If truly all those monuments were corrupted by fraud, how shall we draw from them what the opinion of the ancients was on our controversies? Nor would I deny that it seems to me not a little strange both that they make so much of the Acts of the Councils and that they inveigh so bitterly against heretics for having suppressed and abolished some part of them. For if these monuments can be of such great use to us, why do they grudge us the Acts of the Council of Trent, than which nothing of greater importance has been held among Christians for eight hundred years past, whether we look at the Latins themselves or at the Protestant adversaries of the Latins? If they charge heretics with the crime of having altered such documents, ought they not rather fear the same reproach and be held guilty of the very crime they rebuke? But doubtless something lies hidden that makes a distinction between these cases and makes their reasoning not the same as the other side's. And one is struck with wonder why they do not publish it. For the unskilled, while no other explanation occurs to them, imagine (perhaps without reason) that this is done by art on the part of the Romanists, and that the Acts of the last Council are kept so tightly closed by them because they think their publication would harm, or at least do no good to, Roman dignity. They conjecture on the contrary that those Acts, which the heretics want removed from the midst and which they so anxiously guard, contained much by which that dignity could have been wondrously aided and more and more confirmed. However that may be, I for my part cannot but praise the candour of these men: although they seem ill-advised in their own interests, they freely confess that the Acts of the Councils which exist today are neither complete nor uncorrupted. But let us next inquire whether the men of the Church also contributed something themselves to the corruption of the ancient writers. Epiphanius reports that in the good and emended copies of St Luke it was read that Christ wept, and that this testimony is found as in Irenaeus; but that the Catholics, moved by a certain fear, removed that voice, lest the heretics should abuse it. Whether this story is true or false, let its author answer for it. This one thing, indeed, I gather from it most evidently, as it seems to me: there would have been no religious scruple among the ancient Catholics about deleting from the writings of the Fathers any word which they thought opposed their opinion or liable to be corrupted by heretics. For if, on Epiphanius's authority, they did not spare even the Gospel of the Son of God, can it be probable that human writings were held in greater reverence? Rufinus certainly was held in esteem and as a brother by Jerome, and by Augustine too, who testifies that he bore the discord with him most unwillingly, before the enmity arose between them. He was inserted by Gennadius with great praise into his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers. Yet he was so free in handling the writings of Origen, Eusebius and others, which he turned from Greek into Latin, that no page is found in his translations in which he has not cut something out, or added something, or interpolated something.

units.la: I quid truncarit, vel addiderit, vel inter polauerit. Hieronymus licet inimicitias cum eo exerceret, tamen in hoc cum illo sensisse comperitur †, ipseque passim agnoscit se Origenem vertisse in Latinum, sed ita ut noxia quaeque truncauerit, utilia vero ranium reseruauerit, & mala in bonorum interpretatione subtraxerit; quod, siquid intelligo, significat, si quid cum sententia, quae tum temporis apud Christianos obtinebat, pugnaret, rudibusque offensioni esse posset, id ab ipso expunctum & amputatum fuisse in versione quam adornauit; eandemque interpretandi methodum sequutos fuisse Hilarium & Eusebium
units.tr: If he had cut anything out, added something, or interpolated it. Although Jerome carried on enmity with him, he is nonetheless found to have agreed with him on this point. Jerome himself repeatedly admits that he translated Origen into Latin, but in such a way that he cut out whatever was harmful and kept back whatever was useful, and removed what was bad in translating what was good. As far as I understand it, this means that if anything conflicted with the opinion then prevailing among Christians, and could give offence to the unlearned, he expunged and removed it from the version he prepared. He says that Hilary and Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, followed the same method of translating.

units.la: Episcopum Vercellensem docer. Alibi, P. Cocmio in libro Eusebii de locis Hebraicis, profitetur se omisisse quae digna memoria non sunt visa, & pleraque mutasse. Vt videas autem illud ei in more positum fuisse, confer, si placet, Cronicon eius Latinum cum iis quae superstunt ex Graeco Eusebii; ex eo facile videbis quantum sibi veteres in scriptis alienis permisserint ac indulserint. His tanto exemplo praeeuntibus magistris quis dubitet quin eorum discipuli, e suis, sive vel sionibus, seu etiam exemplaribus, quacunque vel cum sententiis, vel cum moribus suo tempore in Ecclesia receptis non conuenirent, cum cura expunxerint? Imo etiam, si ubi deerant quae opportuno loco iis pondus & authoritatem conciliarent, quin quae ex usu esse iudicarent, addiderint. Vnde alias nobis nata essent in Veteribus scriptoribus tot loca hiulca, tot molestae lacunae, tot inepiissimè adfuta, quae passim inter legendum occurrunt? Vnde viles illae, ferosaque ac tactu ipso horridae lacuniae, quas in media ipsorum purpura offendimus? Profecto non aliud clamat illa pulsus spiritusque inaequalitas, quam in eodem homine, minimo spatio, legendo experimur? Molestum esse, tædunq; plenissimum omnia exempla congerere, cum recentiorum qui in edendis Patribus operam posuerunt, nullus sit qui ea non animaduerterit, & qui de iis non queratur. Vnde in Patrum libris marginales illae iliæ notæ Hic videtur aliquis assuisse suas nugas †, & alias eiusmodi. Et Ludouici Viuis ad Augustini de Ciuitate Dei lib. xxi. * Annotatio Decem aut duodecim versus, qui capite XX I V. habentur & quibus diserte Purgatorium docetur in antiquis libris, Brugensi & Coloniensi, non legi, vt neque in exemplaribus Friburgi excusis; Immo & carere iis exemplar Parisiense, vt testantur qui editioni 1531. praefuerunt. Holsteinius, qui nunc Romæ degit, Præfatione in Athanasij opera, testatur se, in Bibliothecæ Regiæ Manuscriptis, multa Patrum monumenta hoc modo fœdata inuenisse. Neque (inquit) solius Athanasij ea fortuna, vt ineptissimorum interpolatorum manus subiret, cum Chrysostomi, Procli, aliorumque homiliis similibus sequiorum seculorum ineptiis fœdatas in iisdem Regiis codicibus inuenerim.
units.tr: Elsewhere, in his preface to Eusebius's book on the Hebrew places, P. Cocmius professes that he omitted what did not seem worth remembering and changed a great deal. So that you may see that this was a common practice with him, compare, if you please, his Latin Chronicle with what survives of Eusebius in Greek. From this you will easily see how much the ancients allowed themselves and took liberties with the writings of others. With such examples set before them by their masters, who could doubt that their disciples, in their own translations or even in their copies, carefully removed whatever did not agree with the opinions or customs then accepted in the Church? Indeed they even added whatever they judged useful, where something was lacking that might lend weight and authority at the right place. Otherwise, whence would we have so many gaps in the ancient writers, so many troublesome lacunae, so clumsily patched, which we meet everywhere as we read? Whence those vile, savage gaps, so rough to the touch, that we stumble upon in the very purple of their writings? Surely that unevenness of pulse and breath, which we experience in the same man within a very short space of reading, cries out nothing other than this? It is tedious and wearisome to heap up all the examples, since none of the more recent men who have laboured in editing the Fathers has failed to notice them, and none has failed to complain of them. Hence in the books of the Fathers those marginal notes, Here someone seems to have stitched in his own trifles, and others of that kind. And Ludovicus Vives, in his note on book 21 of Augustine's City of God: Ten or twelve verses, which are found in chapter 24, and in which Purgatory is expressly taught in the old books, the Bruges and Cologne ones, are not read, nor are they in the printed copies at Freiburg; indeed the Paris copy also lacks them, as those who oversaw the 1531 edition testify. Holstenius, who now lives at Rome, testifies in his preface to the works of Athanasius that he found many monuments of the Fathers defiled in this way in the manuscripts of the Royal Library. Nor (he says) was Athanasius alone in having the fate of falling into the hands of the most inept interpolators, since I found the homilies of Chrysostom, Proclus and others of the same kind, defiled by the follies of later ages, in the same royal codices.

units.la: Sed omittere non possum has depravationes in monumentis sacratissimis, & maximè publicis, cuiusmodi fuere Ecclesiæ Liturgiæ & similia, locum habuisse. Hanc autem observationem, quo maioris fit momenti Andreæ Masij verbis referre animus est: fuit enim vir ille, non solùm singulari & recondita eruditione, sed etiam candore & probitate supra exquisitam doctrinam longè magis mirabili, ideòque moderatis omnibus quibuscunque partibus addicti sint, gratus & acceptus, propter excellentes istas dotes. Is igitur cùm animaduerteret breuiorem esse apud Syros quàm apud Græcos S. Basilij Liturgiam, hanc eius rei affert rationem. Quippe ut (inquit) fuit perpetuo hominum in religione sensus, vt intra præscriptas à Patribus cærimonias, quantumuis sanctissimas, se contineri pauci potuerint; Vnde pro temporis tractu ad illas pro vario Antistitu pietatis affectu alia atque alia addita: Multa etiam mutata videre est, & quod est longè minus malum, non paucas etiam superstitiones esse enatas. Qua in re mihi videtur fuisse Syri tanto Græcis, Latinisque teperantiores, quanto minus in tranquillo, ne dicam luxuriosò, apud illos Christianas res statu est versata. Atque hæc quidem eruditissimus Masius. Sic etiam Cassander, qui innocentissimè
units.tr: But I cannot omit that such corruptions took place in the most sacred monuments, and especially the public ones, such as the Church's liturgies and the like. I intend to give this observation in the words of Andreas Masius, so that it may carry greater weight. For that man was remarkable not only for his singular and recondite learning but also, far more admirably than his exquisite learning, for his candour and integrity; and therefore he was welcome and acceptable to all moderate men of whatever party, on account of these excellent gifts. When he noticed that the liturgy of St Basil is shorter among the Syrians than among the Greeks, he gave this reason for it. Indeed (he says), as there has been a perpetual sense among men in religion, few have been able to keep themselves within the ceremonies prescribed by the Fathers, however holy; whence, as time passed, different things were added to them according to the varying zeal of the bishops. Many changes may also be seen, and, what is far less bad, not a few superstitions have sprung up. In this matter the Syrians seem to me to have been so much more temperate than the Greeks and Latins, as Christian affairs among them have been less settled in tranquillity, not to say luxury. Thus far the most learned Masius. So also Cassander, who most innocently

units.la: {*} Ibid. ex Mafio, in Ludovici Vivis ad Augustini de Civitate Dei lib. xxi. in Antiquitate versatus elt agnoscit, & ex aliis auctoribus probat, Veteribus Liturgiis multa paulatim addita fuisse. Eandem rationem secutos Canonum Ecclesiasticorum collectores observat eruditissimus Sirmondus; quos ait in Conciliorum canonibus ea saepe recitare, & immutare, qua vel obsoleta & inutilia indicant, vel ab sui ipsius morbus aliena. Canon erat Concilii Carthaginensis quarti; Clericus ne comam nutriat, nec barbam radat. Hic canon in Decretalibus sic mutilatus recitatur; Siquis ex clericis, comam relaxaverit, anathema sit. Cur Quia nimirum (inquit Sirmondus) postquam contra canonem radi a clericis barba capit, canonem, qui vetaret, extare non placuit. Canon erat (eodem quoque Sirmondo ex manuscriptis libris auctore) Araufcanae I. Synodi negans chrisma semel in baptismo acceptum repeti postea necesse esse; non ut praeiudicans quicquam (inquit) sed ut necessaria habeatur repetita chrismatio. Gratianus canonem sic effingit, ac si plane contra affirmaret chrismatis repetitionem esse necessariam; non praeiudicantes cuiquam hoc dicimus (inquit) sed ut necessaria habeatur chrismatio. Sic quoque in secunda nouissimae Conciliorum editionis tomo legitur, addito in fine participio repetita. Unde tanta mutatio? Nempe Gratianus canonem adempta clausula negatione ad temporum suorum consuetudinem (inquit Sirmondus) iure ac more suo accommodavit. Gratiani videlicet saeculo, ut & nostro, chrismatum non putant Latini, nisi quem Episcopus etiam post acceptum à presbytero in baptismate chrisma denuo chrismauerit. Araufcanorum Patrum aevo semel in baptismo acceptum chrisma satis erat; quod utriusque chrismationis, & presbyteralis & Episcopalis eadem esset ratio; quae nunc ita inter se differunt, ut haec sola verum sacramentum, illa mera sacramenti (id est baptismi) caerimonia censeatur. Canon erat Tiullanus xxxv i. Renovantes, quae à CL Patribus in hac à Deo conferenda & regia urbe, &c. conflituta sunt, DECERNIMUS, ut thronus CPol aequalia priuilegia cum antiquaRoma throno obtineat,& in Ecclesiasticis ut illæ rebus, magnificat, ut qui sit secundus post illum. Et hunc quoque Solertissimus Gratianus ad sui sæculi gustum ita temperavitRenovantes(inquit)Sanƈti C P. TIMVS, ut CP Sedes similia privilegia, quæ superior Roma habet accipiat; NON TAMEN in Ecclesiasticis rebus magnificetur, ut illæ; Sed hæc secunda post illam existens priusquam Alexandrina sedes numeretur. Gregorianos Censores pesfidiæ puduit. Hi enim non hæc (quæ & omnes veteras Gratiani libri habent, & ipsa sententiæ per voculam adversatiuam sed connexæ ratio necessario flagitat) sed alia plane contraria ediderunt hoc modosimilia, &c. privilegia accipiat; NEC NON in Ecclesiasticis, &c. Sed liquet Gratianum IVRE illo suo (quod ei tribuit Sirmondus) hic quoque usum esse; jure scilicet quidvis pro re Romana mentiendi, fingendique : quo& alibi usus est non semel: ut cum canonem Synodi Carthag. IV simpliciter vetantem ne mulier,quamvis docta, aliquos 9. & 100. baptizare præsumat: ipse ne suos pulsaret, qui mulieri, etiam indoctæ, baptizandi jus in necessitate concedunt, adhibita exceptione ita callidè diluit; Mulier, quamvis docta & sancta, viros in conventu docere, vel aliquos baptizare non præsumat, NISI necessitate cogente. Ita enim scripsisse Gratianum, non autem quomodo ediderunt Gregoriani censores, & omnes libri veteres tum manu scripti, tum typis excusi docent, & firmat Lombardus canonem in hunc quoque modum adulteratum referens. Eandem artem alibi in molliendo Milevitanorum Patrum canone adhibet, dum quod illi olim simpliciter & absolutè decreverant excommunicandos quicumque trans mare appellassent, ipse cum exceptione sic recitat; Ad transmarino autem, qui putaverit appellandum nullo intra Africam in communione suspiciatur, NISI forte Romanam sedem appellaverit. Plura alia sunt exempla. Ego libri. unum addam, quo Gratianus ex suo illo IVRE more que ad Decretales suorum Pontificum epistolas, sane 1.3 nequiter ac flagitiosè, detorsit quæ Augustinus de divinis Apostolorum litteris scripserat. Verba Augustini erant;In Canonicis autem Scripturis Ecclesiarum Catholicarum quamplurimum auctoritatem sequatur(vir scilicet divinarum Scripturarum studiosus) inter quas sane illa sunt quæ Apostolicas sedes habere, & epistolas accipere meruerunt.
units.tr: {*} Ibid., from Masius, on Ludovicus Vives's note to book 21 of Augustine's City of God. Cassander, who was well versed in antiquity, acknowledges this and proves from other authors that many things were gradually added to the ancient liturgies. The most learned Sirmond observes that the collectors of ecclesiastical canons followed the same method; he says that they often recite and alter in the canons of councils those things which show either that they are obsolete and useless, or that they are foreign to their own customs. The canon of the Fourth Council of Carthage was: A cleric shall not grow his hair, nor shave his beard. In the Decretals this canon is cited so mutilated: If any of the clerics lets his hair grow long, let him be anathema. Why? Clearly (says Sirmond) because, after shaving the beard came into practice among clerics against the canon, it was not thought fit that the canon forbidding it should remain. The canon of the First Council of Orange (Sirmond again being the authority from manuscript books) denied that chrism once received in baptism need afterwards be repeated: not as prejudging anything (he says), but so that repeated chrismation may be held necessary. Gratian shapes the canon as if it plainly affirmed that the repetition of chrism is necessary: We say this not prejudicing anyone (he says), but so that chrismation may be held necessary. So too it is read in the second volume of the latest edition of the Councils, with the participle repeated added at the end. Whence such a change? Namely, Gratian, by removing the negative clause (says Sirmond), adapted the canon to the custom of his own times, by his own right and manner. For in Gratian's age, as in ours, the Latins do not regard a chrismation as valid unless the bishop has anointed again with chrism after it was received from a presbyter in baptism. In the age of the Fathers of Orange, chrism received once in baptism was enough, since the reason for either chrismation, presbyteral or episcopal, was the same; whereas now they differ from each other in such a way that the one is counted the true sacrament and the other a mere ceremony of the sacrament (that is, of baptism). The canon of the Trullan council, number 36, reads: Renewing what was established by the 150 Fathers in this city, to be given by God and royal, etc., we DECREE that the throne of Constantinople shall obtain privileges equal to those of the throne of old Rome, and in ecclesiastical matters be magnified as that one is, being second after it. Gratian, most skilful of men, tempered this too to the taste of his own age: Renewing (he says) ... that the See of Constantinople should receive similar privileges to those which the higher Rome has; YET in ecclesiastical affairs it shall not be magnified as those are; but this, being second after that, shall be counted before the Alexandrian see. The Gregorian censors were ashamed of the treachery. For they did not publish these words, which all the old books of Gratian have, and which the very sense of the passage, joined by the adversative little word but, necessarily requires; they published quite different words in this form: similar ... let it receive privileges; AND LIKEWISE in ecclesiastical matters, etc. But it is clear that Gratian here too used that right of his (which Sirmond attributes to him), namely the right to lie and invent whatever suits the Roman cause. He used it elsewhere more than once, as when the canon of the Fourth Council of Carthage simply forbids that a woman, however learned, presume to baptize anyone: lest he strike his own people, who grant to a woman, even an unlearned one, the right to baptize in necessity, he so cleverly softened it with an exception: A woman, however learned and holy, shall not presume to teach men in assembly, or to baptize anyone, UNLESS compelled by necessity. That Gratian wrote thus, and not as the Gregorian censors published, is shown by all the old books, both manuscript and printed, and Lombard confirms it, citing the canon in this altered form too. He uses the same art elsewhere in softening the canon of the Fathers of Milevis: where they had once decreed simply and absolutely that whoever appealed overseas should be excommunicated, he recites it thus with an exception: But whoever thinks he should appeal overseas, let no one in Africa regard him as in communion, UNLESS perhaps he has appealed to the Roman see. There are many other examples. I will add just one, in which Gratian, by his own right and after his manner, most wickedly and shamefully twisted to the Decretal letters of his Popes what Augustine had written about the divine letters of the Apostles. Augustine's words were: In the canonical Scriptures let him follow very much the authority of the catholic Churches (a man, of course, devoted to the divine Scriptures), among which are certainly those which have deserved to hold Apostolic sees and to receive epistles.

units.la: Ex his Latinus canonum Rhapsodus ad præsentem Ecclesiæ usum mirabiliter transformatis ista, quæ sequuntur effecit, nobisque pro vere Augustinianis in suis divini scilicet juris tabulis propinavit; In Canonicis Scripturis Ecclesiarum Catholicarum quamplurimum diminutarum Scripturarum solertissimus indagator auctoritatem sequatur, inter quas sane illa sint quas Apostolica sedes habere, & ab ea alij meruerunt accipere epistolas. Ex quibus colligit, quod & præfert ipse titulus, Decretales epistolas inter Scripturas Canonicas connumerari. Immanem hominis audaciam de Patrum corio tam proterve ludentis digne notavit, ac castigavit Alphonsus à Castro. Sed quid facias? Id erat & isti & cæteris juris ac moris, ut ad eam, quam suo tempore Romæ cernebant rerum faciem, omnia nova, vetera, Apostolica, Ecclesiastica, per fas nefasque traherent.
units.tr: From these passages the Latin compiler of canons, by remarkably reshaping them for the present use of the Church, produced the following, and offered it to us as if it were truly Augustine's own words in his tablets of divine law: In the canonical Scriptures of the Catholic Churches, let the most diligent investigator of much-diminished Scriptures follow the authority of those which the apostolic see has merited to have, and to receive epistles from it, among which are surely those. From this he concludes, as the title itself also announces, that the Decretal Epistles are to be counted among the canonical Scriptures. Alphonsus à Castro rightly noted and rebuked the monstrous audacity of a man who played so shamelessly with the skins of the Fathers. But what can one do? It was the custom and practice both of him and of others to drag everything, new, old, apostolic, ecclesiastical, by right and by wrong, into the face of things as they saw it in Rome in their own time.

units.la: Hac ratione, prout est immutatus orbis, secum etiam quæ sibi supererant ex Antiquitate reliquiæ, eas immutari voluit, ratus, scilicet, æquum esse ut libri isti nonnihil tempori cederent; quorum nempe auctores, si tum ipsi superfuissent, non dubitabat ad præsentium hominum gustum atque ingenium & linguam & calamum temperaturos fuisse. Ad venustatem & gratiam iis conciliandam, eadem arte curati sunt quà solent molliculi & sciculi senes. His barba picta, & si quid hirsutum horreret attonsum, cutis læuigata, os fucatum, vox infracta, vestis color paulo auferior ad suavitatem dilutus; ita ut vehementer metuendum sit, ne sæpenumero dum in personatis istis scriptoribus veræ antiquitatis sermonem genuinum, vjuidumque colorem inquirimus, oleum & operam o eram perdamus. His doctoribus didcit Eusebius in Chronico Telesphorum Quadragesimæ iciunium, Pium vero, (utrumque Episcopum Romanum) diem Dominicum cum instituisse; quæ sanè ne per somnium quidem bono Eusebio in mentem venerunt unquam, ut patet ex eius Manuscriptis quibusdam in quibus de his capitibus bus, licet recentioribus longè acceptissimis, alterum est silentium, Sed ut ad temporis seriem redeamus, credvit licentia ista prout scula in peius rucbant, & dum ab Auctoribus ipsorum ætate recedebatur fallacias istas reuincere difficilius in dies evadebat: maximè cùm clarissima Ecclesiæ lumina ab his artibus aliquando non abstinerent, & suo exemplo singulis ad eiusmodi audenda animum adderent. Nam, amabo te, nonne stupendum est Leonis Papæ Legatos, iam anno 451. coram toto Concilio Chalcedonensi, apud sexcentos selectissimos Episcopos, totius Ecclesiæ decorem, sextum canonem Concilij Nicæni recitasse cum hisce, in quibus rei summa vertitur, verbis, Ecclesiam Romanam semper Primatum habuisse, quæ non magis quàm à Friså Zosimo obtuli canones, in illo codicum Græcorum inuenta sunt, ut neque hodie habentur, velin codicibus Græcis, vel in Latinis, vel in editione Dionysij exigui, qui annis quinquaginta post vixit. Cùm mecum reputo tam sancti Pontificis legatos eiusmodi lacinia tam venerabilem canonem fœdare non dubitasse; pene in eam adducor sententiam, ut ex Antiquitate nihil sani, nihil incorrupti superesse exiltimem, præter ea quæ nullius fuere momenti, vel quæ sine summa infamia & omnibus reclamantibus contaminari & alterari non potuere. Nec sine certissima Dei Providentia accidisse reor, ut facti istius memoria ad nos usque permaneret, ut docceremus quàm cautè, quàm prudenter in his versandum sit; quamquè non temere, tanquam Nicænum, aut Constantinopolitanum, vel tanquam Cypriani aut Hieronymi accipiendum sit, quicquid nobis hodie istis nominibus, obtruditur. Septuaginta quatuor annis post Concilium Chalcedonetife, proxime nominatus Dionysius exiguus Romæ instituit Canones colligere, ciusque codex ex antiquissimorum Manuscriptorum fide, non ira pridem cum privilegio Regis Parisiis excusus est. Quisquis cum cura cum euoluer plurima depravata fuisse animaduertet quorum hic exempla aliquot subjiciam, ut pateat quàm antiquus sit technarum istarum inter Christianos usus. Cùm postremus Concilij Laodicensis Canon, qui est 163. codicis Græcis Ecclesiæ uniuersæ, in Ecclesia libros ullos alios legi præter quàm Canonicos prohibeat eosdem omnes ordine recenset. Inseruit quidem in codice suo Dionysius exiguus principium canonis quo prohibetur ne, præter Veteris & Noui Testamenti volumina, ulli alii libri legantur; Sed eorumdem librorum Cathalogum prorsus omisit, verirus, reor, ne Ecclesiam Romanam offenderet, in qua multis ante annis Innocentius Pontifex in Veteris Testamenti canonem retulerat Maccabæos, Sapientiam, Ecclesiasticum, Tobiam, Iudith, quorum apud Parres Laodicenos nulla est mention, cum viginti duorum tantum Veteris Testamenti librorum meminerint, & è Nouo dè Apocalypsi tacuerint. Si cui refciffionis istius probabilior occurrat ratio, per me eam edat licet: mihi quidem ea visu est verisimillima. Verum quicquid sit, quo consilio Dionysius exiguus canonem illum truncarit diuinare non tenemur, qualecunque enim fuerit, satis est inde apparere iam tum nulli fuisse apud Christianos religi ni Canonum ipsorum Textum decurtare, quoties ita opus erat Quod, si magno nostro bono, Canon ille in variis aliis Antiquitatis monumentis, velut in Græcorum collectione, imò & in Antiquis Galliæ Conciliis integer & incorruptus non perstitisset, prorsus nunc nescíremus quæ super Sacrosanct. Scripturarum Canone (nobili nostro seculo controversia) Partium Laodicenorum fuerit sententia. Fateor Latinos habere quod regerant, nec Græcos id impunè ferrè. Aiunt enim Latini Græcos è sua Codicis canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ interpretatione expunxisse libros Maccabæorum è Catalogo Scripturarum qui habetur Canone 24. collectionis ipsorum præter fidem omnium exemplarium Latinorum, tam typis excusorum, quàm manuscriptorum, referente Cardinale Perronio. Etsi non desint qui * testentur in collectione Crisconij Episcopi Africani manuscripta in hoc canone nullam Maccabæorum fieri mentionem. Exhibet nobis deinceps Codex Græcus septem canones Concilij Constantinopolitani I. qui extant etiam apud Balsamonem & Zonaram & in editione Græcolatina Conciliorum generalium Romæ excusorum. Horum tres postremi in Dionysij Codice Latino desiderantur, licet propter argumentum quod complectuntur non leuis sint momenti; instituitur enim in iis ordo observandus, cùm in judiciis de Episcopis qui accusantur, tum in admittendis iis, qui ab hæretici ad Ecclesiæ communionem transeunt. Difficile est statuere quid collectorem ad Concilium hoc truncandum impulerit. Hoc tamen scio in canone VI. (quem ille inter alios omisit, quique de judicandis iis Episcopis agit qui in crimen vocantur) de appellationibus sedis Romanæ nullam fieri mentionem, neque item de causis ullis referuatus, in quibus soli Papæ de Episcopis judicium ferre liceat. Ius & arbitrium omnes eiusmodi causas cognoscendi & componendi in Synodos prouinciales & Dioecesanas plane & fine ulla exceptione confertur. Siue autem additamentum illud ad Concilium Constantinopolitanum assuerint Græci (quod minimè sit verisimile) siue Dionysius, vel Ecclesia Romana id reiciderint, inde saltem patet scripta Ecclesiastica truncandi, vel infartis additamentis corrumpendi audaciam, non nunc primùm in usu esse cœpisse. In Codice Græco post Canones Constantinopolitanos sequuntur octo Canones Vniuersalis Concilij Ephesini, qui referunt item à Bal-
units.tr: In this way, just as the world has been changed, they wished that the remains of antiquity left to them should also be changed, judging, of course, that it was fair for those books to yield somewhat to the times; for their authors, had they themselves still been alive then, would not have hesitated to adapt their style, their wit, their language and their pen to the taste of the men of the present. To win them charm and grace, they were treated by the same art that is used on the mincing and dainty old men: a painted beard, and if anything bristly were shuddering, it was shaved off; smooth skin, a made-up face, a broken voice, a garment colour a little more fair and diluted for pleasantness. So that it is greatly to be feared that, while we often seek the genuine speech and the living colour of true antiquity in those masked writers, we lose our oil and our labour in vain. From these authors Eusebius learned in his Chronicle that Telesphorus instituted the Lenten fast, and that Pius (both bishops of Rome) instituted the Lord's day; yet these things never came into the mind of the good Eusebius, not even in a dream, as is clear from certain of his manuscripts, in which there is silence about these chapters, though the more recent manuscripts, which are by far the most accepted, contain them. But to return to the sequence of time: this licence, as the ages slid for the worse, grew, and as men moved away from the age of the authors themselves, it became ever more difficult day by day to refute these deceits. This was especially so since the brightest lights of the Church did not at times abstain from these arts, and by their example encouraged individuals to dare such things. For, I ask you, is it not astonishing that the legates of Pope Leo, already in the year 451, in the presence of the whole Council of Chalcedon, before six hundred most select bishops, the glory of the whole Church, recited the sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea with these words, in which the substance of the matter turns: that the Roman Church had always had the primacy; which canons, offered no less than by Pope Zosimus, were not found in that Greek codex, nor are they held today either in the Greek codices, or in the Latin, or in the edition of Dionysius Exiguus, who lived fifty years later. When I consider with myself that the legates of so holy a Pontiff did not hesitate to defile so venerable a canon with such a patch, I am almost led to this opinion, that I think nothing sound and nothing uncorrupted survives from antiquity, except those things which were of no importance, or which could not be contaminated and altered without great disgrace and the protest of everyone. Nor do I think it happened without the most certain providence of God, that the memory of that deed remained with us even to the present, so that we might be taught how cautiously and how prudently one must deal with these matters; and that whatever is now thrust upon us under those names is not to be accepted rashly, as if it were Nicene or Constantinopolitan, or as if it were of Cyprian or Jerome. Seventy-four years after the Council of Chalcedon, the aforementioned Dionysius Exiguus began in Rome to collect canons, and his codex, drawn from the faith of the most ancient manuscripts, was not long ago printed at Paris with the king's privilege. Whoever studies it carefully will notice that very many things were corrupted, of which I shall add some examples here, so that it may be clear how ancient is the use of these tricks among Christians. Whereas the final canon of the Council of Laodicea, which is number 163 in the Greek codex of the whole Church, forbids anything to be read in the Church except the canonical books, Dionysius Exiguus in his codex did insert the opening of the canon by which it is forbidden that any books be read besides the volumes of the Old and New Testaments; but he completely omitted the catalogue of those same books, presumably, I think, so as not to offend the Roman Church, in which many years before Pope Innocent had listed among the canon of the Old Testament the Maccabees, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Tobit, Judith, of which there is no mention among the Fathers of Laodicea, who mention only twenty-two books of the Old Testament, and from the New are silent about the Apocalypse. If anyone can find a more probable reason for this excision, let him publish it by my leave: to me indeed this seems most likely. But whatever the case, we are not bound to guess what purpose led Dionysius Exiguus to truncate that canon; for whatever it was, it is enough to see from this that even then it was not a matter of religious scruple among Christians to cut short the text of the canons themselves, whenever the need so required. And if, to our great good, that canon had not remained entire and uncorrupted in various other monuments of antiquity, such as the Greek collection, and indeed in the ancient councils of Gaul, we would now know nothing whatever of the opinion of the Fathers of Laodicea on the canon of Holy Scripture, a controversy of our own noble age. I admit that the Latins have something to throw back, and that the Greeks do not bear it with impunity. For the Latins say that the Greeks, in their Latin version of the canons of the African Church, erased the books of the Maccabees from the catalogue of Scriptures which is contained in canon 24 of their collection, contrary to the testimony of all Latin copies, both printed and manuscript, as Cardinal Perron reports. Yet there are not lacking those who attest that in the collection of Cresconius, the African bishop, in manuscript, no mention of the Maccabees is made in this canon. Next the Greek codex presents us with seven canons of the First Council of Constantinople, which are also found in Balsamon and Zonaras, and in the Greek-Latin edition of the general councils printed at Rome. The last three of these are missing from the Latin codex of Dionysius, although on account of the subject they deal with they are of no slight importance; for in them an order to be observed is laid down, both in the judgments about bishops who are accused, and in the admission of those who pass from heresy into communion with the Church. It is difficult to determine what moved the collector to truncate this council. This much, however, I know: in canon VI (which he omitted among others, and which deals with the judging of those bishops who are called to account for a crime) there is no mention of appeals to the Roman see, nor likewise of any reserved causes in which the Pope alone may pass judgment on bishops. The right and power of hearing and settling all such cases is conferred plainly and without any exception upon provincial and diocesan synods. Whether, however, the Greeks added that addition to the Council of Constantinople (which is very unlikely), or Dionysius or the Roman Church rejected it, at least it is plain from this that the audacity of truncating ecclesiastical writings, or of corrupting them by inserted additions, did not first begin to be practised now. In the Greek codex, after the canons of Constantinople, there follow eight canons of the Universal Council of Ephesus, which likewise are cited by Balsamon and Zonaras, and are also printed with the Acts of the same Council of Ephesus in the first volume of the Roman edition.

units.la: K famone & Zonara, & excusi quoque habent ir cum Actis eiusdem Concilij Ephesini, primo Tomo editionis Romanæ. Sed apud Lionysium exiguum nusquam occurrunt, nec facilè dixerim cur eos ille omiserit, nisi forsan grauis & molestus ei fuit Canon octauus, in quo scilicet decernitur ut Episcopi Cypri i suas ipsi ordinationes faciant, non adhibito Patriocheno Anthiocheno, & ut idem in aliis Diœcesibus & provincis obseruetur, adeo ut nulli Episcopo in prouinciam quam ipse, vel ancecessores in potestate non habuerint, liceat invadere,
units.tr: ...famon and Zonaras, and printed also with the Acts of the same Council of Ephesus, in the first volume of the Roman edition. But they are nowhere to be found in Dionysius Exiguus, and I could not easily say why he omitted them, unless perhaps the eighth canon was a grave and troublesome thing for him, namely the one which decrees that the bishops of Cyprus are to make their own ordinations without the intervention of the Patriarch of Antioch, and that the same is to be observed in other dioceses and provinces, so that no bishop may be permitted to invade a province over which he himself or his predecessors had no power,

units.la: ne Canones Patrum violentur, ac ne sub pratextu administrationis rerum sacrarum (inquiunt fantissimi illi Patres) faslus potentia mundana in Ecclesiam irrepat, imprudentesj, libertatem quam nobis sanguine suo Dominus nostrer Iesus Christus dedit, paulatim amittamus. An haec constitutio & haec verba metu Latinis iniecerint, ac effecerint quominus reciperent Canones Ephesinos in suum Codicem, haud equidem scio, attamen nusquam in eo comparent, & ante ut ter ccc l. anni ex quo Anastasius Papae Bibliothecarius non inueniri in veteribus exemplaribus Latinis testatus est Graecoque, quasi eos supposuissent criminatus est. Ipsi viderint. Siue Graeci eos confinxerint, siue eos Latini expunxerint, hoc constat iam ab octingentis annis fraudem esse factam. Sed in eo quod sequitur exemplo vix ullus erit de fraudis auctore dubitandi locus. Codex Graecus, num. 106. pro Canone 28. Oecumenici Concilij Chalcedonensis nobis exhibet Decretum Patrum iistorum quo, perinde ac in primo Concilio Constantinopolitano, definiunt, ut quandoquidem Constantinopolis Senatus & Imperii sedes est, æquisque cum vetere Roma honoris prerogatiuis prædi- cta est, in negotiis Ecclesiasticis exaltetur ut illa, cum sit cunda effet post eam, & ut eius sit ordinare Metropolitanos trium Diœcesum Ponti, Asiæ & Traciæ, Balsamon, Zonaras, atque adeo Canonistæ Græci omnes eundem Canonem iisdem verbis referunt. Historiqi
units.tr: that the canons of the Fathers may not be violated, and lest, under the pretext of administering sacred things (as those most holy Fathers say), worldly pride and power creep into the Church, and we, without noticing, gradually lose the liberty which our Lord Jesus Christ gave us with his blood. Whether this constitution and these words frightened the Latins and so brought it about that they did not admit the Canons of Ephesus into their Code, I do not know for certain. Yet they appear nowhere in it. For about three hundred and fifty years, since Anastasius, librarian of the Pope, testified that they were not found in the old Latin manuscripts, and accused the Greeks of having forged them as if they had inserted them, the question has been in dispute. Let them see to it. Whether the Greeks invented them or the Latins expunged them, it is established that a fraud has been committed, and that for eight hundred years now. But in the example that follows there will scarcely be any room for doubt about the author of the fraud. The Greek codex, no. 106, gives us, in place of Canon 28 of the Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, a decree of those Fathers by which, just as at the First Council of Constantinople, they define that since Constantinople is the seat of the Senate and of the Empire, and is endowed with the same prerogatives of honour as old Rome, it should be exalted in ecclesiastical affairs as Rome is, being second after it, and that it belongs to it to ordain the metropolitans of the three dioceses of Pontus, Asia and Thrace. Balsamon, Zonaras, and indeed all the Greek canonists, cite the same canon in the same words. The historians

units.la: Ecclesiastici plerique, cùm Græci tum Latini, id constitutum fuisse Chalcedone ceftantur, remque totam, prout gesta est, in ipsis Concilij Actis legere est. Attamen apud Dionysium exiguum nullam canonis iltius vestigium extat, quasi de eo Chalcedone ne verbum quidem unquam factum fuerit. Pontificem Leonem, & successorem eius nonnullos, Canonem iltum repudiasse nescij non sumus, Sed qui nobis spondet se regulas Ecclesiasticas ordine digesturum ac de Græco in Latinum sermonem conuersas editurum, iltam adeo insigem quo iure, aut quo modo potuit omittere? Si alia periissent monumenta, unquámne nobis in mentem venisset aliquid simile Chalcedone vel tantatum fuisse? Vnde & qua ratione de dcxxx. iltorum Patrum, qui illuc super isto, summi inter huius temporis controuersias momenti capite, conuerunt sententia, nobis constitisset? Fluxere undecim secula ex quo omissio illa facta est. Quis in tot aliis, siue Conciliorum, siue Scriptorum priuatorum monumentis Græcos vel Latinos similibus artibus non lusisse idonè caucbit? Ex his quæ ad cognitionem nostram venerunt quis non colligat alias multas & magno numero nos fugisse; Inter Veterum libros imprudens versaris, quasi quæ fuerit eorum genuinasententia ex iis habituras. At ecce iam incunte sexto seculo, si quid vel in sacratissimis monumentis minus cum receptis illis temporibus opinionibus conuenire visum est, nulla religione sublatum est. Quantumuis nullo alio argumento id factitatum fuisse nobis constaret, nonne hoc uno satis doceremur nobis hic viam quasi prætentandam, magnaque cautione opus esse? Sequitur notandà maximè insignis epistolæ Adriani I. ad Imperatorem Constantinum, tempore Concilij Nicæni secundi, depravatio. Nam in editione Anastasij, quæ ab hinc septingentis & quinquaginta annis facta est, Adrianus de sedis suæ Primatus magnificè disserit, Græcosque quod Tarasium Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum Occumenicum Episcopum dixissent pellime excipit. Horum tamen omnium neuerbum quidem habetur, neque in editione Graeca Concilii septimi, neque in vulgata Latina. Causatur Roma truncatam à Graecis epistolam, contendunt Graeci variis affutis à Latinis vitiatam & corruptam. Vtri fidem mereantur non est magnum negotium pernoscere. Sed in quam partem propendeas nunc non refert, satis est quod hinc sole meridiano clarius patet, iamdudum inter Christianos, Scriptores uc teres truncare, velvariis additamentis pro temporum ratione adulterare ac interpolare, in more positum fuisse. Idem quoque manifestum fit ex ea quae in eodem Concilio sequitur Epistola Adriani ad Tarasium; planè enim alia in codice Graeco est, alia in Latino Anastasii, id quae in rebus cjusdem cum superioribus momenti. Sic Act. V. in editione Graeca & Veteri Latina tina Tarasius dicitur Episcopus Oecumenicus. Apud Anastasium titulus iste nullus est. Eadem Actione Patres. Iconoclastas criminantur quod in Bibliotheca Constantinopolitana librum quendam rescissis pluribus foliis corrupissent, & in urbe Photia triginta volumina concremassent, alibi Annorata quaedam ex nescio quo libro deleuissent, eaque omnia prae studio quo ferebantur adversus imagines quae in libris illis porpugnabantur. Sed qua ratione ab iis quae Athanasio supposuisse supra monuimus ipsi se purgare possint equidem non video, ut nec à praua verborum quorumdam. Eusebij expositione. Eum enim ut in invidiam adducerent, fingunt d'xiffe formam carnalem tefu Christi mutatam fuisse in Deitatis naturam cum tantum dixerit, mutatam fuisse à Deo Patre. Sed tale quae in ea inhabitabat. Vnde apparet quantum iis fidei debeamus, cum hinc inde mirabilia quaedam & inaudita allegent, & cum quaecunque ad Adversariis obiiciuntur cum fastidio rejiciunt, maximè cum repudiant quod ipsis ex Epiphanio obiectum fuerat. Id illi tanquam suppositicium respuunt, quis (inquiunt) fi Epipha-nius aliu imaginum fabricationem à Christo alienam exstimassèt, eam in numero haeresewn posuit. Annon eadem ratione probari posset Epiphanium cum Iconoclastis sensisse quamquidem eorum opinionem haeresibus non accensuit? In dubio pariter relinquo quod tam secure Teodoti Ancyrani & aliorum locos explodunt. Ex illo tempore nihil frequentius occurrit in libris cùm Graecorum tum Latinorum quàm eiusmodi criminationes, sibi inuicem expobrantium corrupta & adulterata esse causae instrumenta. Sic in Synodo Florentina Marcus Episcopus Ephesinus, de processione Spiritus Sancti disputans, ad objectos locos, alterum ex Epiphanij Anchorato, alterum ex Basilio contra Eunomium respondet, ad illum quidem, iam à longo tempore Epiphanij Tractatum esse corruptum ad hunc uero aliquem Latinorum sententia studiosum, eum ad ipsorum sensum accommodasse, sanctè affirmans Constantinopoli nonnisi quatuor exemplaria libri istius exstare in quibus uerba à Latinis prolata haberentur esse autem in eadem urbe supra mille inquibus desiderarentur. Regerunt Latini Orientalium, non Occidentalium esse libros adulterare, quod ut probent locum supra à nobis ex Cyrillo allatum profererunt, quo tamen de haereticis quibusdam, Nestorianis videlicet, qui Athanasii ad Epistolam epistolam corruperant, non uero de omnibus Orientalibus, multò minus de Ecclesia Graeca agit. Instant Graeci in Latinos & ex Zosimi capite superiore relata historia argumentum petunt, & sic alii aliis inuicem uapulant grauissime, in accusando utrique quàm in purgando longè, ut cuius intuenti uidere licet, foeliciores ac probabiliores. Hoc item refero cuiusdam Gregorij Monachi Graeci (unionis Florentiae institutae defensoris acerrimi) ad locum ex Ioannis Damasceni libro responfionem. Ferebatur is scripsisse Patrem solum esse causam, in Trinitate uidelicet. Reponit ille haec verba in veteribus exemplaribus non inveniri; argumento manifesto ca à Græcís, quo Scriptorum istum in partes suas traherent, affuta fuisse. Petauius, proximè, sic soluit obiectionem quæ petitur ex 68. canone Apostolorum adversus ieiunium Sabbathi quod in Ecclesia Romana observatur. Tanquam spurium (inquit) & alienum canon ille reiicitur & ab ottosis Græculis verba sunt intertexta. Sed si cui cordi sit quâ dubia & incerta sint postremæ huius Antiquitatis scripta considerare, legat Synodum octauam, quam Occidentales volunt Occidentales; codices Latinos cum Græcis conferat, & expendat maximè Analtasij, Papæ Bibliothecarij, præsationem. Is postquam accerrimè in Græcorūm ambitionem inuectus est, postquam quos hi habent terrij Concilij Canones eos veluti supposititios rejecit, ut paucis rem expediat, nihil circuitione usus, omnia Concilia, nullo nisi primo excepto, Græcos depravasse affirmat. Quibus jam scriptis aquiescemus, quandoquidem pestis illa adeo altè insedit, penitusque ipsa Concilia, hoc est monumentorum Ecclesiæ Vetererum cor ipsum occupauit? Symbolum ipsum, tot conciliis Oecumenicis consecratum, ejusmodi depravationibus subduci non potuit. Nam ut nihil dicam de hisce leuis momenti verbis, de cœlis, secundum Scripturas, Deum de Deo, quæ in quibusdam Symbolis haberi, in aliis verò desiderari obseruauit, in Synodo Florentina, Cardinalis Iulianus, fluxere iam integra secula ex quo inter Orientales & Occidentales de voce Filiosque in capite de processione Spiritus Sancti contenditur: Illi quærentibus ad his additam; his mussantibus ab illis sublatam; quæ quidem alteratio, licèt videatur in speciem leuis, magni tamen est momenti, adeo ut ex ea pendeat quæstionis summi momenti decisio: hæc enim est quæ hactenus inter utrosque schisma fecit; videlicet num Spiritus Sanctus non minus procedat à Filio quàm à Patre. Indicio certissimo factum studio partium (quiqui sint criminis huius rei) ut manus tam sacro monumento injicerentur. Sed quicquid aentatum est olim in hisce rebus
units.tr: Most ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin, declare that this was decreed at Chalcedon, and the whole affair, as it was done, can be read in the Acts of the Council itself. Yet in Dionysius Exiguus there is no trace of that canon at all, as if nothing had ever been said about it at Chalcedon. We are not unaware that Pope Leo and some of his successors rejected that canon. But he who promises us that he will arrange the ecclesiastical rules in order and publish them translated from Greek into Latin, by what right, or in what way, could he have omitted so remarkable a one? If other monuments had perished, would it ever have come into our minds that anything of the kind had happened at Chalcedon, or even been proposed there? Whence, and by what means, would we have learned the opinion of the six hundred and thirty Fathers who gathered there and gave their judgment on that chapter, which is of the highest importance among the controversies of this time? Eleven centuries have passed since that omission was made. Who can safely guarantee that in so many other monuments, whether of Councils or of private writers, Greeks or Latins did not play similar tricks? From what has come to our knowledge, who would not conclude that many others, in great number, have escaped us? You move imprudently among the books of the Ancients, as if you could draw from them what their genuine opinion was. But see: already at the beginning of the sixth century, if anything even in the most sacred monuments seemed less in agreement with the opinions then accepted, it was removed without any scruple. Even if we had no other proof that this was practised, would we not be taught sufficiently by this one alone that we must here tread, as it were, carefully, and that great caution is needed? Next follows the corruption of the letter of Hadrian I to the Emperor Constantine, written at the time of the Second Council of Nicaea, which deserves especial notice. For in the edition of Anastasius, made about seven hundred and fifty years ago, Hadrian discourses magnificently on the primacy of his see, and rebukes the Greeks severely because they had called Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, "Ecumenical Bishop." Yet none of this is found at all, neither in the Greek edition of the Seventh Council nor in the Latin Vulgate. The Greeks charge that the letter was cut short at Rome; the Greeks in turn contend that the Latins corrupted and falsified it with various additions. Which side deserves trust is no great task to learn. But in which direction you lean now does not matter. It is enough that it is clearer than the midday sun that for a long time among Christians it has been the custom to cut short the ancient writers, or to adulterate and interpolate them with various additions as the times required. The same is made plain by the letter of Hadrian to Tarasius which follows in the same Council, for the one in the Greek codex is quite different from the one in Anastasius' Latin, and in matters of the same weight as those above. Thus in Act V, in the Greek edition and the old Latin version, Tarasius is called "Ecumenical Bishop"; in Anastasius that title does not occur. In the same Action the Fathers accuse the Iconoclasts of having corrupted a certain book in the Constantinopolitan library by tearing out several leaves, of having burnt thirty volumes in the city of Photius, and elsewhere of having erased certain annotations from some book; all of which, they say, was done out of zeal against the images that were defended in those books. But by what reasoning they can clear themselves of the charge of having forged things in Athanasius, which we noted above, I do not see, nor of their perverse exposition of certain words of Eusebius. To bring him into odium they pretend that he said the carnal form of Jesus Christ was changed into the nature of the Deity, whereas he said only that it was changed by God the Father, and into such a form as dwelt in it. From this it appears how much faith we owe them, when they allege on all sides certain wonderful and unheard-of things, and when they reject with disdain whatever their adversaries object to them, especially when they repudiate what had been objected to them from Epiphanius. That they spurn as spurious, saying: "For if Epiphanius had thought the making of images alien to Christ, he would have counted it among the heresies." Could it not by the same reasoning be proved that Epiphanius agreed with the Iconoclasts, since he did not count their opinion among the heresies? I likewise leave in doubt what they so confidently explode from the passages of Theodotus of Ancyra and others. From that time nothing occurs more often in books, both Greek and Latin, than such accusations, each side reproaching the other that its writings have been corrupted and adulterated, to serve its cause. Thus in the Council of Florence, Mark, Bishop of Ephesus, disputing about the procession of the Holy Spirit, answers the passages objected to him, one from Epiphanius' Ancoratus, the other from Basil against Eunomius. To the former he replies that the treatise of Epiphanius has been corrupted for a long time; to the latter, that some partisan of the Latin opinion has accommodated it to their sense. He solemnly asserts that at Constantinople there are only four copies of that book in which the words cited by the Latins are found, while in the same city there are more than a thousand in which they are lacking. The Latins retort that it is the Orientals, not the Occidentals, who adulterate books, and to prove it they produce the passage from Cyril quoted above by us. That passage, however, deals with certain heretics, namely the Nestorians, who had corrupted the letter of Athanasius, and not with all Orientals, much less with the Greek Church. The Greeks press the Latins, and from the story related in the preceding chapter of Zosimus they seek an argument; and so each lashes the other most severely in turn, and in accusing both are far less successful than in clearing themselves, as anyone looking on can see, and their cases seem more fortunate and plausible. I cite likewise the reply of a certain Gregory, a Greek monk and most fierce defender of the union established at Florence, to a passage from the book of John Damascene. He is said to have written that "the Father alone is the cause," namely in the Trinity. He replies that "these words are not found in the old copies," a plain sign that they were added by the Greeks to draw the writer to their side. Petavius recently answered in the same way the objection drawn from the 68th canon of the Apostles against the Sabbath fast observed in the Roman Church: "That canon," he says, "is rejected as spurious and alien, and the words were woven in by some Greek triflers." But if anyone cares to consider how doubtful and uncertain the writings of this latest antiquity are, let him read the Eighth Synod, which the Occidentals wish to be recognised; let him compare the Latin codices with the Greek, and weigh especially the preface of Anastasius, librarian of the Pope. After he has most bitterly inveighed against the ambition of the Greeks, and rejected as supposititious the canons of the Third Council which they hold, he states briefly, without any circumlocution, that all the Councils, except the first alone, were corrupted by the Greeks. Shall we now acquiesce in these writings, since that plague has so deeply settled in and has taken hold of the very heart of the monuments of the ancient Church? The Creed itself, consecrated by so many Ecumenical Councils, could not be exempt from such corruptions. To say nothing of those words of slight weight, "from the heavens," "according to the Scriptures," "God from God," which, as Cardinal Julian observed at the Council of Florence, are found in some Creeds and lacking in others: for whole centuries have passed since the dispute began between Orientals and Occidentals over the word "and the Son" in the article on the procession of the Holy Spirit. The one side asked why it had been added, the other murmured why it had been removed. This alteration, though it may seem slight in appearance, is of great importance, so much so that the decision of a question of the highest moment depends upon it, for it is this that has hitherto made a schism between the two: namely whether the Holy Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father. It is a most certain indication that, whoever was guilty of this, the hands were laid on so sacred a monument out of party zeal. But whatever was done of old in these matters

units.la: pene iocus & ludus cen ebitur, ficum iis comparetur qu-æ facta sunt nouissimis hisce temporibus, quibus adeo studiis incanduere miseri mortales, ut, ratione & pu dore proculcatis, nnlli neque Scripto neque Auctori pepercerint, quin passim obvia quæque scedarint. Eorum certè qui eò audaciæ proruperunt nunquam satis damnare potest mala fides; quapropter nonnihi summacum ratione mihi quæ sequuntur visus est scrpsisse Erasmus præfatione in Hieronymi Opera ad Guilielmum VV aramum Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem. Extat ( inquit ille) eximiis vereq; Sacrosanctiis auctoribus quos nobis vel erudita dedit Gratia, vel huius æmula prodidit Itali avel olim sluuiis florentissima produxit Gallia, vel ingeniosa peperit Africa, vel laboru patiens edidit Hispania rara quadā eruditione suipiciendos, eloquentia claros, vita sanctimonia venerandos, quaso te quàm pauci super sunt, casu seruati magis quàm nostro beneficio; atque hi rursus ipsi quàm sædè mutilè quàm contaminati, quàm prodigiosis mendis undique scatentes, ut non magni referat sic superesse. Equidem ut non aspernor simplicem vulgi pietatem, ita non possum non mirari tā præposterum multitudinis iudicium. Calceos, Sanctorum & sudariola muco sordentia exosculamur, & eorundem libros sanctissimas & efficacissimas Diuorum reliquias, neglestos incerepatimur: Tuniculam aut indusiolum Dini aureis gemmatisq, theca reponimus, & libros ab illis elaboratos in quibus id quod illorum fuit optimum nobis adhuc viuit spirat, cimicibus tineis ac blattis impunè radendos relinquimus. Neque verò difficile sit hucusce rei causam coniecturis assequi. Postea quæ Principum mores planè iam in barbariam, quandam tyrannidem degenerarsent, tum Episcopi profanam ditionem magis cæpissent ápletii, quàm ab Apostolis traditum docendi munus mox universa docēdi provincia in istos quosdam est relegata qui charitatis & religionis cognomen scu peculiare sibi vindicant: Iam negligi cœpta bona litterafastidita Græcanici sermo au peritia, multoq; magis Hebraici, spretum aloquentia studium, quin & ipsa lingua Latina sic conspurcata est subinde. nova barbarie, vt iâ nihil minùs esset quàm Latina, nec historia nec Antiquitatis ulla cura, tantùm ad Sophisticas quasdā argutias contracta res literaria, & eruditionis summa penes Summularios quosdā collectores ac excerptores esse cœpit, hoc nimirum impudentiores quo minus eruditos. Proinde Veteres illos Scriptores facile vel antiquari passi sunt, vel quod vero propius est, ipsi abolendos curarunt, ut quos iâ frustra legerent nimirum his rebus destitui, sine quibus illi non queunt intelligi. Et tamen ex illis utcunque decerpta quædam suis Commentariis admiscuerunt, qua gratia magis etiam in rem ipsorum erat illos interire, ne quando vel plagii convincerentur, vel infscitia. Scilicet tanti erat antiquari Clementem, Irenæum, Polycarpum, Origenem, ut horum vice Occam, Durandum, Capreolum, Lyranum, Burgensem & his etiâ indoctiores legeret orbis. Sub horum igitur diutina tyrannide tanta fuit bonarum literarum ac bonorum auctorum ποικιλία, ut è doctorum ordine pelleretur qui vel paululum litteraturæ melioris attigisset. His rebus factum est ut tot orbis lumina quorum titulos dutaxat, nec id sine lachrymis, legitimus funditus interierint, & si quos contigit suis superesse fatis, hi sic modis omnibus depravati sunt, adeo truncati cotemeratiq, ut felices videri possint qui perierunt. Haec de omnibus in genere Patribus protocutus, accedit demum ad ipsum id cuius opera præfababatur Hieronymum. Atque id profecto cum mihi vehementer indignū videtur in omnibus eruditis, tum longè indignissimum in Hieronimo............. At nunc haud scio an quisquam omnium tractatus sit indignius. Bana pars vigiliarum eius interciditi. Quod superest non depravatum erat, sed prorsus extinctum & obliteratum: idq, partim illiteratorum vitio scribarū, qui solent ex emendatis inemendata describere, ex mendosis mendosiora reddere praetermittere quod non legunt, corrumpere quod non intelligunt, velut Hebrea Græcaq vocabula, qua frequenter intermisceti Hieronimus: sed multo sceleratius a sacrilegis haud scio quibus studio detruncatapermulta, addita nonnulla, mutata pleraque depravata, sordidata cofusa pene omnia, ut vix ulla sit periodus quam eruditus possit inoffensè legere. Imo quod est pestilentissimum vitiandi genus, perinde quasi parum esset tot insulsissimas nugas juxta infantes atque ineruditas in homines eloquentissimi pariter ac doctissimi nomen ac titulu contulisse, medius illus commentarius passim admisceuerunt suis manias, ne quis repurgare posset. Nam librum falso inscriptum permulta sunt quae corrupta sunt, caeterum fragmenta passim intermixta, veluti frumento confusum lolium, quo tandem cribro repurget aliquis? Atque hac omnia sic esse facta docebimus mox in operum ipsius Catalogo, tum secundi Tomi duabus praefationibus ac censuris. Commovit itaque me partim tam insignis Ecclesiae Doctoris non ferenda contumelia, in cujus immortalia monumenta sic impie debacchati sunt isti plusquam apri Calydonij, partim publica studiosorum utilitas quos videbat tam eximiis epulis hisce rebus submoveri, &c.
units.tr: almost a joke and a game will be made of it. It may be compared with what has been done in these most recent times, when wretched mortals have been so inflamed with zeal that, with reason and modesty trampled underfoot, they have spared no writing and no author, but have everywhere defiled whatever came to hand. No bad faith can condemn enough those who have broken out into such audacity. For this reason I think Erasmus wrote the following, not without reason, in his preface to the works of Jerome, addressed to William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury: Extat ( he says) those excellent and truly most holy authors whom either learned Grace gave us, or Italy, a rival of this grace, produced, or Gaul, most flourishing in former times, brought forth, or ingenious Africa bore, or Spain, patient of labour, put forth, men of rare learning, worthy of being looked up to, famous for eloquence, venerable for the sanctity of their lives: I ask you, how few are left, preserved by chance more than by our benefit; and these again, how foully, how mutilated, how defiled, how teeming everywhere with monstrous errors, so that it matters little whether they survive at all. Indeed, while I do not scorn the simple piety of the common people, I cannot but wonder at so perverse a judgement of the multitude. We kiss the shoes of the saints and their handkerchiefs grimy with sweat, and we hold their books, the most holy and most efficacious relics of the godly, in neglect. We place a little tunic or undershirt of God in golden and jewelled cases, but the books they laboured over, in which what was best in them still lives and breathes for us, we leave to be gnawed away with impunity by bedbugs, moths and book-lice. Nor is it difficult to work out the cause of this by conjecture. Afterwards, when the manners of princes had wholly degenerated into a kind of barbarous tyranny, and bishops had begun to seek secular dominion more than the duty of teaching handed down by the Apostles, the whole province of teaching was soon handed over to certain men who claim for themselves the name of charity and religion.
