Then good letters began to be neglected and despised; knowledge of Greek, and much more of Hebrew, was scorned; the study of eloquence was spurned; and even the Latin tongue was thereafter so defiled by a new barbarism that it was no longer Latin at all. There was no concern for history or for any antiquity; literary study shrank to certain sophistical subtleties, and learning came to reside with certain summulists, collectors and excerptors, who were the more shameless the less learned they were. Accordingly, those ancient writers were either allowed to become obsolete with ease or, what is nearer the truth, were themselves taken care to be abolished, since men who read them in vain were, of course, lacking in those things without which they cannot be understood. And yet they picked out some things from them, however they could, and mixed them into their own commentaries; for it was even more in their interest that those authors perish, lest at some time they be convicted of plagiarism or ignorance. Clearly it was so important to be made obsolete, Clement, Irenaeus, Polycarp, Origen, that in their place the world read Occam, Durand, Capreolus, Lyra, Burgensis, and people even less learned than these. Under this long tyranny there was such a variety of bad letters and bad authors that anyone who had touched even a little of better literature was driven from the rank of the learned. From these causes it came about that so many lights of the world, whose titles alone we know, and that not without tears, have perished utterly, and if any have been allowed to survive their fates, these have been so depraved in every way, so mutilated and so tampered with, that those who perished may seem fortunate. Having spoken thus of the Fathers in general, he at last comes to Jerome himself, whose works he was prefacing. And indeed, while this seems to me a most unworthy fate for all learned writers, it seems by far the most unworthy for Jerome. ............ But now I do not know whether any of all the treatises is more unworthily treated. A large part of his Vigils has been cut away. What remains was not merely depraved but utterly destroyed and obliterated; and this partly through the fault of unlettered scribes, who are accustomed to copy the emended as unemended, to make the mendacious more mendacious, to omit what they do not read, to corrupt what they do not understand, such as the Hebrew and Greek words which Jerome often mixes in. But much more wickedly by I know not what sacrilegious men, very many things have been mangled by design, some things added, many changed, depraved, befouled and confused almost everything, so that there is hardly a sentence which a learned reader could read without stumbling. Indeed, what is the most pestilential kind of corruption: as if it were not enough to have attributed so many silly trifles, fit for infants and the unlearned, to a man of the name and title of the most eloquent and most learned, a certain middle commentary has everywhere mixed in its own errors, so that no one could purge them. For many things are corrupted in the book falsely inscribed, and besides, fragments are scattered throughout, like darnel mixed with wheat; through what sieve could anyone purge it? And that all these things have been done in this way I shall show shortly in the catalogue of the works themselves, and then in the two prefaces and censures to the second volume. I have been moved, partly by the intolerable insult to so remarkable a Doctor of the Church, against whose immortal monuments those men, more than Calydonian boars, have raged so impiously, and partly by the public usefulness to students, whom I see being kept away from such choice feasts by these matters, etc.

units.la: Hactenus Erasmus. Hunc autem locum licet paulo prolixiorem huc totum transcribere placuit, cum quod ingenue & luculenter, non solum malum ipsum, verum etiam mali fontes & causas aperuisse mihi videatur, tum etiam quod fuftra sit qui hic harioletur non rei indignitate permotum, sed partium studio ductum in has querelas erupisse Erasmum. Ante natas quippe controversias quae discessionem in religione fecerunt, & ista scripsit vir ille magnus & Hieronymi opera, ex quibus ea desumpsi, excusa sunt anno scilicet 1516. Basileae, apud I. Frobenium. Sed Erasmi quaerelae recentiores non deterruerunt quin simili audacia in veterum monumenta grassarentur. Ioannem quidem Gagnejum Parisiensem Theologum cum Alcimi Avititi poemata, A. D 1536. Lugduni ederet, & alia pro arbitrio immutasse ac depravasse, & quingentis prope versibus praeter librorum tum manuscriptorum tum etiam a. 1507. & 1509. Coloniae editorum fidem inaudito atque incredibili facinore interpolasse observavit erudititissimus Sirmundus. Ita plurimorum de Sanctorum veterum vitis scriptorum lucubrationes in sua illa tricubitali farragine Surius Carthusianus pro sui ingenii captu varie ac multipliciter in-
units.tr: Thus far Erasmus. I have chosen to transcribe this whole passage here, though it is somewhat long, both because it seems to me to have candidly and clearly revealed not only the evil itself but also the sources and causes of the evil, and because it is pointless for anyone to babble that Erasmus broke out into these complaints moved not by the unworthiness of the matter but driven by partisan zeal. For before the controversies arose which made the division in religion, that great man wrote these things, and the works of Jerome from which I have taken them were printed in the year 1516 at Basel, by J. Froben. But Erasmus's later complaints did not deter others from attacking the monuments of the ancients with similar audacity. The most learned Sirmond has observed that John Gagney, a Parisian theologian, when he published the poems of Alcimus Avitus at Lyons in 1536, altered and depraved other things at will, and with an unheard-of and incredible crime interpolated nearly five hundred verses, against the testimony of the manuscripts and of the editions published at Cologne in 1507 and 1509. Thus the labours of very many writers of the lives of the ancient saints were variously and in many ways in-

units.la: L terpelauit ; qusfacinus optimus monachus adeo non erubuit, vt de pierisque ipse monuerit, se eorum stilum mutasse.Ita in vita Martinæ Virginis , Concordij, Gernouefuæ, Rigoberti, Iuliani & Bafilissæ, Guilielmi Bituricensis, Boniti Aruerni, Speufippi & Eleufippi, Sulpitij Bituricensis, Launomari, Pontiani, Sebastiani, Præjecti, Popponis, Margaritæ, Constantii monentur lectores, stilum in gratiam lectoris à Surio mutatum esse. Sed & in aliis sexcentis, quos recensere longum est, idem quoque se ausum esse profitetur. Clarissimus Bofquetus hanc eius fraudem in Saturnini actis notauit, in quibus quod auctor scripserat sensim & gradatim in omnem terrā sonus Euangelii exiuit, TARDOQVE pro cessu in regionibus nostris Apostolorum pradicatio coruscauit, id more corrupit pariqueprocessu pro tardo edidit, ne videlicet hinc disceremus Dei religionem serius trans Alpes susceptam (vt ait Sulpitius Seuerus) Sic frustra quaras in editionibus Operis imperfecti in Matthæum, quas Mahufius quidam francifcanus procurauit, varia quaestiones hinc inde à multis scriptoribus ex illo de Scriptura, de notis Ecclesiæ de Eucharistia afferuntur. Illa omnia, dum se fingit opus id à sæcibus Arianorum repurgare, mundumque saq tersum dare velle, sæde substulit Monachus, nec venerandum Chrysostomi nomen, quo (licet vt supra monuimus, falsò s inscribitur obstitit quominus sic truncaretur. Nec vnus hanc Latinorum hominum audaciam, vidit & denot auit Erasmus. Laurentius Brochellus, diu postea, Pi æsatione in Decreta Eccl. siæ Gallicanæ, id ipsum, licet non ita fusè, persequitur.
units.tr: terpolated by Surius the Carthusian in his three-cubit-long heap, according to the measure of his own talent. This wicked monk was so far from blushing at this deed that he himself admitted, concerning many of them, that he had changed their style. Thus in the lives of Martina the Virgin, Concordius, Gernoefa, Rigobert, Julian and Basilissa, William of Bourges, Bonitus of Auvergne, Speusippus and Eleusippus, Sulpicius of Bourges, Launomarus, Pontianus, Sebastian, Prejectus, Poppo, Margaret, and Constantius, readers are warned that the style has been changed by Surius for the reader's sake. But he also professes that he dared the same in six hundred others, which it would be long to list. The most distinguished Bosquet noted this fraud of his in the Acts of Saturninus, in which, where the author had written that "gradually and by degrees the sound of the Gospel went out into all the earth, and the preaching of the Apostles shone forth more slowly in our regions as it progressed," Surius corrupted the phrase in the same manner and published "with equal progress" instead of "slow", lest we should learn from this that the religion of God was received beyond the Alps later (as Sulpicius Severus says). So in vain would you seek, in the editions of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew which a certain Franciscan, Mahusius, prepared, the various questions that many writers cite from it, concerning Scripture, the marks of the Church, and the Eucharist. The monk, pretending that he was cleansing that work from the errors of the Arians and wishing to give the world a thoroughly cleaned text, foully removed all those passages, and the venerable name of Chrysostom, under which the work was (though, as we have noted above, falsely) inscribed, did not prevent it from being so mangled. Nor did only one of the Latin men see and denounce this audacity; Erasmus did too. Laurentius Brochellus, long afterwards, in his preface to the Gallican Decrees of the Church, pursues the same point, though not at such length.

units.la: Taceo inquit innumeros auctores sacros profanos, veteres, recentiores, ab istis tam improbi quam infelicis ingenij hominibus miserabiliter decurtatos, vel ipsis Regibus parcere non assuetis, nedum S. Ludouico, cuius Prag matica, vivocant Sanctionis articulos nonnullos, maximè ad rei Gallicæ statum pertinentes, abs Bibliotheca illa SS. Patrum, constitutionibus Regiis & statutis Epis. Episcoporum quorundam Synodalibus, Regina urbium Lutetice nuper impressis expunxerunt. Vasiterum væ, ut cumvidente exclamen nebulonibus, qui tales Musarum castitati & integritati venerandæ non solum insidias struunt, sed & Musas ipsas impudenter & nequiter subdolo religionis zelo nullius frontis homines deuirginant, fucumque istum, pietatis nomen ementitum, inter pias fraudes numerant. Sed hic aduersus illos non scribimus. Satis est, quod luce clarius est confirmasse istos additis & rescissis plurimis innumera fidei veterum monumenta immutasse & deprauasse. Isti sunt qui in hac x 11. Cypriani ad populum Carthaginensem Epistolæ periodo. Audiant quasi patienter consilium nostrum, expectent regressionem nostram, ut cum ad vos per Dei misericordiam venerimus, convocati coepiscopi plures secundum Domini disciplinam, & Confessorum præsentiam, & vestram quoque sententiam, beatorum martyrum literas & desiderunt examinare possimus, ex editionibus Gryphianis Lugdunensis 1528. & 1537. & Pamelij voces has, secundum vestram quoque sententiam quæ in aliis, puta Manutij & Morellij in Parisiis 1564. habentur, per scelus expunxerunt; quia ex iis discimus, quod nos nescire sua referre censuerunt, plebem fidelem, scilicet, in suæ Ecclesiæ negotiis partes suas, iusq; suffragij aliquomodo habuisse. Illi ipsi sunt qui, in epistola quadragesima, de petra petrum fecerunt, & qui corruptorum priscorum vestigiis insistentes eiusdem Tractatum de unitate Ecclesiæ fœdè adulterarunt, in medias eius periodos variis de suo insertis, contra optimorum manuscriptorum fidem cuiusmodi hæc sunt Super illum unum (Petrum) ædificat Ecclesiam suam & illi pascendas mandat oues suas. Item Primatus Petro datur ut vna Ecclesia Christi, & Cathedra una monstretur. Denique; Cathedra Petri super quam fundata est Ecclesia Cathedram constituit quæ verba dicit ...
units.tr: "I say nothing," he continues, "of the countless sacred and profane authors, ancient and more recent, whom these men, as wicked as they are unlearned, have miserably mutilated. They do not spare even kings, much less St Louis, whose Pragmatic Sanction (as they call the articles of the Sanction) and several of its provisions, bearing chiefly on the state of French affairs, along with royal constitutions and the synodal statutes of certain bishops, they have expunged from that Library of the Holy Fathers recently printed in the city of Paris. Woe to them! As I would cry out with the poet against those scoundrels who not only lay snares for the venerable chastity and integrity of the Muses, but also shamelessly and wickedly deflower the Muses themselves under a crafty pretence of religious zeal. Men of no shame, they count this mask, which falsely bears the name of piety, among pious frauds." But I am not writing against those men here. It is enough that they have confirmed, clearer than the light, that by adding and cutting out very many things they have altered and corrupted the innumerable monuments of the faith of the ancients. These are the men who, in this passage of the eleventh epistle of Cyprian to the people of Carthage, "Let them listen to our counsel as it were patiently, and let them wait for our return, so that when, by the mercy of God, we have come to you, having summoned several fellow bishops according to the discipline of the Lord, and the presence of the Confessors, and your own opinion too, we may be able to examine the letters of the blessed martyrs, which they desire," have wickedly removed, following the Gryphian editions of Lyon of 1528 and 1537, and Pamelius, the words "and your own opinion too," which are found in other editions, for instance that of Manutius and Morel at Paris in 1564. They removed them because from these words we learn what they thought we should not know: that the faithful people had, in some measure, their own part and a right of suffrage in the affairs of their Church. These are the same men who, in the fortieth epistle, made petrum out of petra, and who, following the footsteps of earlier corrupters, foully adulterated Cyprian's treatise on the unity of the Church, inserting into the midst of its sentences various additions of their own, against the faith of the best manuscripts; such as these: "Upon that one (Peter) he builds his Church, and commands him to feed his sheep." Likewise: "Primacy is given to Peter, so that one Church of Christ and one Chair may be shown." Finally: "The Chair of Peter, upon which the Church is founded, he sets up as the chair, which words he speaks..."

units.la: verba dicit ... Gryph. 1537. p. 144. & Mar. 1564. p. 13. Cypr. Pam. ibid. Primatus Petro datur ut una Ecclesia Christi & Cathedra una monstretur & pastore suum ... Gryph. Morell. ut supra. Cypr. Pam. p. 13. col. 1. Quia Cathedram Petri super quam fundata est Ecclesia ... Cypr. & Morell. adiuvat in qua mente.
units.tr: "...which words he speaks..." Gryph. 1537, p. 144, and Mar. 1564, p. 13; Cypr. Pam. ibid. "Primacy is given to Peter, so that one Church of Christ and one Chair may be shown, and his sheep..." Gryph., Morell., as above. Cypr., Pam., p. 13, col. 1. "Because the Chair of Peter, upon which the Church is founded..." Cypr. and Morell. support it, in which sense...

units.la: Quorum quidem additamentorum nemo est qui scopum, & quamente assuta fuerint, non videat. Illi ipsi sunt qui quàm molestè ferant non suppressam Fitmiliani Cæsariæ Cappadocum Episcopi, magni, suo tempore, nominis, epistolam non obscurè ferunt. Cum enim ex ea pateat quanta libertate veterum seculorum Episcopi cum Papa ageret, eam de inductia Manutius in Cypriani editione Romana omiserat. Verum Morellius eam in sua editione restituit, Cyprianique, ad quem scripta est, epistolis inseruit, magno argumento quibus studiis isti trahantur, & quot ciusmodi factus clam praefocarint. Hæc est Officina ex qua miser ille Ambrosius tam foedè interpolatus, prodiit, & cuius fortem graviter lamentatus est Nicolaus Faber . Boni illi artifices qui eum ediderunt, nimis,( ut inquit ille ) in alieno opere ingeniosi, mutarunt, miscuerunt, transpofuerunt quicquid libuit, ut hoc maxime quod ipse notat. Libros de interpellatione Iobi & Davidis in aliis editionibus coniunctos diuiserunt, quod ut facerent exemplo paulum laudabilii inseruerunt & interpolarent nonnulla, quod & fecerunt in prima Apologia Dauid; sed longe peius in altera, ex cuius capite octauo quinque aut sex lineas, quæ in omnibus veteribus editionibus legunter, expunxerunt. Tribuerunt item Scriptoni illi Tractatus quosdam, qui eius non sunt, quales sunt liber de arbore prohibita. Item alius in postremum caput Proverbiorum. Et tamen ex ista Ambrosii editione expressa est ea quæ Parisiis anno 603. prodiit. Neque vero hanc, quam Faber denotauit, primam fuisse putes Rε manutium Censorum in Ambrosium iniuriam. Aliam i. m ante grauissimus, ac sanctissimus scriptor ab eiusdem farinæ correctoribus passus erat, eiusdem generis contumeliam, quam ego hoc loco Francisci Iunii, testis αὐτο' ατή fide ac verbis exsequar. Ante annos (inquit) viginti septem cum Lugduni agerem (egi autem a 1548. & sequente correctione quodam typographico usus sum familiari, cui Ludovico Sario, variofmit numen. Habitabat ille non procul a Mercuriali vico, in aedibus coniunctis trium columbarum signo. Cum ad salutandum hominem venissem, casu vel potius singulari Dei providentia accidit, ut versantem cum offenderem in recognoscendis D. Ambrosii operibus, quae tu Frelonius excudebat. Variis autem sermonibus ultro citroque habitis, cum me avocaret to esse ab opere nolle offenderem, ille redorsus lectionem unius pagina, Vides me inquit hanc formam Ambrosianae editionis nostrae quam sit elegans, accurata, et in speciem omnibus anteponanda aliis, quae adhuc in lucem prodiuerunt? Postea continuentiopus et probanti elegantiam eius dixit: Ego vero si quod exemplum Ambrosiani operis mihi emendum esset, quodvis exemplum aliud potius, quam hoc quod vides, compararem. Scilicet atus sum huius dicti causam. Tum ille de forulis sub mensa sua latentibus aliquot paginas promens (erant autem paginae, ut loquuntur Graeci xiχωμμένα, sive cancellatae, aliae ex parte, et aliae univers.) Haec est (inquit prima) forma paginarum, quas his paucis diebus ad exemplum veteris, et certi exemplaris optima fides impressimus. Franciscani autem duo pro auctoritate has omnes paginas dispunxerunt, ut vides, et illas subsitui in locum priorum curaverunt praeter omnem nostrorum librorum fidem, quae res sumptum et molestiam Frelonio creavit gravissimam; Nam pretium chartae, operarumque amisit universum, tempori iacturam passus est, et typographicas illas priores plagulas communi novis ad libidinem istorum oportuit magno malo nostro et admiratione mea. Hactenus lunius de Latii sex Francisci sodalitio censoribus. Horum enim aut similium recentiorum, an aliorum vetustiorum male corruptus fuerit Isidori in Originibus de sacrificio locus, recisa ejus ultima parte, haud facile dixerim; Mutilatum quidem ac decurtatum locum ex Rathrammo (sive Bertramo) constat, qui eum cum ante annos pene octingentos descripserat, ita exhibuit; Cujus panis et calicus sacramentum Graeci Eucharistiam dicunt, quod Latine bona gratia interpretatur. Et quid melius corpore et sanguine Christi? Panis vero et vinum ideo corporis et sanguinis: Domini comparantur, quia sicut visibilis huius panis vinique fustantia exteriorem nutrit & inebriat hominem, ita verbum Dei quiest panis vivus participatione sui fidelium recreat mentes. Atque hæc quidem apud Rathramnum Ifidorus; sed ista ultima frustra in vulgatis ejus codicibus quærras, † in quibus locus in hæc verba definit; Et quid melius corpore & sanguine Christi? Nimirum Latinos, qui post Isidori secula, primo Paschasij Ratberti novitates, tum & ipsam transsubstantiationem, admiserunt, movit quod Isidorus panem & vinum nominat, & quod utrumq; corpori & sanguini comparari dixit, non in ipsius corpore & sanguinis Dominici substantiam sua aiuissa conuectu. Quæ fortasse ratio eosdem, vel certè ejusdem generis artifices, compulit hæc in alio Isidori opere ita scribere atque edere. Porro ex hinc sexta succedit confirmatio sacramenti, vt ablatio quæ Domino offertur, sanctificata per Spiritum Sactum corpori Christi & sanguini confirmetur, vel nullo vel inepto sensu; Quid enim quæso est confirmari corpori Christi vel quod in Patrum Bibliotheca habetur corpus Christi. Cassander, qui nunc ipsum locum recitans legit conformetur, & res ipsa atque sensus docent, scribum ab Isidoro fuisse corpori Christi & sanguini conformetur. Sed id verbum Latinis sequiorum temporum dilutius visum est quàm ut suæ μυστηριώσεως mysterium repræsentaret. Itaque audacter mutarunt, Isidorique nullum hic esse quàm sibi adversantem sensum maluerunt. Iam in homines non absimilis ingenij incidit ille quoque fœdissimè truncatus & mutilatus Anastasij, vel potius Damasi, aut alterius, Anastasio longè vetustioris, de vitis Pontificum liber. Nam primo ab iis Auctoris ad Hieronymum Præfatio sublata est, quod hodierno Cuius Romanæ stilo non multum conveniat. Deinde ex vita S.Petri periodum quam hic inferam, prout in omnibus manuscriptis exemplaribus extat, expunxerunt. Hic B. Clementem Episcopum consecravit, eius Cathedram, vel Ecclesiam omnem disponendam commisit, dicens. Sicut mihi gubernandi tradita est à Domino meo Iesu Christo potestas,ligandi,foluendiq;ita & ego tibi committo,vt ordines. dispositores diuerfarû causarum per quos actus Ecclesiasticus profligetur,& tu minime in curis seculi deditus reperiaris;sed solummodo ad orationē & pradicationem populi vacare stude Post hanc dispositionē martyrio coronatur.His verbis testamentum concipiebat Petrus, sed quod eo cauerat suppressum est, haereditibus enim onus & officia imponebat immensum quantum ab ipsorum proposito & mor bus alienā. Alibi, apud eundnem scriptorem, ubi in omnibus manuscriptis codicibus Papa vrbis, id est, Romae legitur ; falsarij isti, Papam orbis substituerunt: sic enim nunc Romæ loquuntur. Voces illæ, Episcopus vrbis Romæ,pridem obloleuerunt. Illiipsi sunt qui apud Fulbertum Episcopum Carnotensem, quo loco insignia Augustini verba profert, Figura est ergo praecipiens pastioni Domini esse communicandū, has voces inseruerunt,figura ergo est,dicet haereticus astuie haeretico tribuentes sententiam quæ reuera Augustini est, qualiter etiam à Fulberto allegabatur. Iidem sunt qui apud Gregorium ma- gnum sacerdotum exercitus in sacerdotum exitus [ per quos apostasias & defectiones volunt intelligi ] transformarunt.Legunt enim Epist.38. lib. 4.Omnia &c. quae pradicta sunt siunt, Rex superbia prope est,& quod dici nefas est,Sacerdotum ei praeparatur exitus;cum Manuscripti codices [iimo exercitus. Iidem alium Gregorij insignem locum pari fraude corruperunt, qui in libris manu scriptis sic habe̅t. Peruenit quoque ad nos quosdam scandalizatos fuisse, quod presbyteros chrismate tangere infronte,eos qui baptizati sunt,& prohibuimus.Et nos quidem secundū veterem vsum Ecclesiae nostrae fecimus.Sed si omnino hac de re aliqui cōtristrantur vbi, Episcopi desunt, vt presbyteri etiam in frontibus baptizatos chrismate tangere debeant,concedimus.Recentiores haec quę hodierno Romanorum, de chrismatis in fronte ministro, dogmati aduersari videbant [soli enim nunc Episcopo baptizatorum frontes chrismate licet) audacter in editionibus mutarunt, & pro eo qu ɔd-scri pserit Gregorius,chrismate tangere in fronte eos qui baptizati sunt; item, in frontibus baptizatos chrismate tangere, impudenter scripserunt, eos qui baptizandi sunt, & baptizandos chrismate tangere. Bella minus ipse monuit corruptum esse lo- cum, & veram quam exhibuimus libro um lectionem, tum ex altero, ex ipsius Gregorij loco, qui extat eodem libro, epist.9. tum ex Gratiano & Thoma confirmat; qui hunc (inquit) locum ita citant, ut esse debet, non ut modo legitur in codicibus impressis. Illi ipsi sunt qui hanc Augustini locum commutarunt, quod suæ transmi trationis dogmati adversaretur; corpus Domini (inquit ille) in quo resurrexit, uno loco esse oportet; veritas autem ejus ubique diffusa est. Sic enim scripsisse Augustinum & res ipsa clamat, & apertissimè testantur tuo Cartonensis a, Algerus b, Lombardus c, Gratianus d, Thomas e, Bonaventura f, Scotus g, Durandus h, Biel i & alii vererès, qui hæc verba sic plané secutì. Recentiores Latini pro illis verbis, uno loco esse oportet, hæc, pessima & inverecunda s. audè, substituerunt, uno loco esse potest, ut videre est in omnibus Augustini editionibus quæ ex eorum officinis prodierunt. Ab eadem mana & causa est quod sequitur. Augustinus in Ioannem, tractatu 26. extremo, scripserat; A per hoc qui non manet in Christo, & in quo non manet Christus, proculdubio nec miducat carnem ejus, nec bibit ejus sanguinem, etiamsi tanta rei sacramentum ad judicium sibi manducet & bibat. Qui novissimam Augustini editionem Parisiis an. d. 1635. procurarunt, fatentur se locum ita scriptum in codicibus manuscriptis sex repertisse; atque ita lectum fuisse etiam Thomæ Aquinatis tempore, ex ejus Catena (quod & editores isti annotarunt) patet; quod & ipsum ex Prospero quoque clarissimè confirmatur, qui sententiam 319. quam ex hoc loco eruit, ita expressit: Nam qui discordat à Christo, nec carnem ejus manducat, nec sanguinem bibit, etiamsi tanta rei sacramentum ad quæ udicium sua praesumptionis quotidie indifferenter accipiat quae ita laudata sunt iam ante aliquot secula, & ab suone Carnotensi, & à Gratiano, & ab ipso Lombardo. At nuperas omnes editiones verba Augustini ridiculè sic interpolata exhibent. Ac per hoc qui non manet in Christo & in quo non manet Christus proculdubio nec manducat spiritualiter carnem eius, nec bibit eius sanguinem, licèt carnaliter & visibiliter premat dentibus sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi, sed magis tanta rei sacramentum ad iudicium sibi manducat & bibit, quia immundus praesumptit ad Christi accedere sacramenta, quae aliquis non indignè sumit, nisi qui mundus est, de quibus dicitur, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Hactenus Latini corruptores; quorum nemo non videt quo spectet crassa ista planeqi incepta Augustinianae orationi attexta lacinia; nempe ut persuadeant Christi carnem, quam Augustinus simpliciter negauerat ab indigne communicantibus sumi, ab iis carnaliter & visibiliter sumi, tametsi eadem spiritualiter ab ipsis non sumatur: Iidem in tractatu de rectitudine catholica consuerfationis (qui non Augustini, sed Eligii Noviomensis a.D.663. donati, verè est) Sirmond. Conc. ita de fideli aegrotante legant, Oleum benedictum fideliter ab Ecclesia petat, unde corpus suum VNGATVR. At scrip-tum fuisse olim, unde corpus suum ungat clarè restatur Valdensis, dum locum ita citat; & sane id ipsum poscit Latini sermonis ratio (dicendum enim erat unde corpus eius ungatur, non autem corpus suum) ac firmat denique Sermo de Tempore apud Augustinum 215. hinc excerptus, in quo ungat legitur, non autem ungatur. Corruptores ungatur subiiciuerunt, ne haec Eligiana unctio à sua extrema videretur aliena; quam nemo agrotus sibi ipsi ministrat, ut notum est. Illi ipsi sunt qui Aimoino, vel eius certe Continuatori, supposuerunt quae sequuntur In qua Synodo(quam octavam universalem illuc convenientes appellarunt) de imaginibus adorandis secundum quod Orthodoxi Doctores antea differierant statuerunt cum profusis con- Hieronymi Dronaeri. tra scripsisset,aliter quàm orthodoxi definierát sla'uerunt,ut apparet tum ex manuscriptis codicibus, tum ex antiquioribus editionibus, tum ex Baronio ipso,qui hoc postremo modo hunc locum laudat, Annalium Tomo decimo ad annum Christi oc&tingentefimum sexagesimum nonum. Illi sunt qui ex Oecumenio locum sequentem Oi ✓ ✓ etotum expunxerunt. † Qui enim Legi patrocinabātur venerationem etiam Angelorum inducebant,quia Lex per ipsos data est,māsit autem consuetudo illa in Phrygia,adeo ut Synodus Laodicena lege prohibuerit ad Angelos accedere,eosque precari,unde est quod apud eos sunt multa templa Michaelis Archangeli, vel sumi ducis exercitus. Quem locum David Hoeschelius in notis suis ad librum Origenis contra Celsum pag.483. testatur se vidisse & legisse in manuscriptis Oecumenii codicibus, qui tamen nullus est in hactenus excusis. Sed quod istos impulit causæ Kemanæ studium Oecumenio sua hæc cripere, idem eos ista aliena Theodoreto commodare & affingere subegit.
units.tr: Nor can anyone who looks closely at these additions fail to see their purpose and the hand that stitched them in. These are the very people who are not pleased, and do not hide their displeasure, that the letter of Firmilian, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man of great name in his day, was not suppressed. Since it plainly shows how freely the bishops of earlier ages dealt with the Pope, Manutius had left it out of the Roman edition of Cyprian. Morel, however, restored it in his edition and inserted it among the letters of Cyprian, to whom it is addressed. This is a strong proof of the zeal with which these men are driven, and of how many such documents they have secretly suppressed. This is the workshop from which that wretched Ambrose came forth, so foully interpolated, and over whose fate Nicolas Faber lamented gravely. Those clever craftsmen who published him, as he says, being too clever with another man's work, changed, mixed up and transposed whatever they pleased, as he especially notes. They separated the books on the interpellation of Job and of David, which were joined together in other editions; to do this they inserted, with somewhat more plausibility, and altered some passages, which they also did in the first Apology of David. But they did far worse in the second, from whose eighth chapter they struck out five or six lines that are read in all the old editions. They likewise attributed to that same writer some treatises that are not his, such as the book On the Forbidden Tree, and another on the last chapter of Proverbs. Yet from this edition of Ambrose was copied the one that appeared at Paris in 1603. Nor should you think that the edition Faber pointed out was the first wrong done to Ambrose by these censors. Another most grave and holy writer suffered the same kind of insult at the hands of correctors of the same stamp, and I shall set it out here in the words and on the faith of Francis Junius, an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης] himself. "Some twenty-seven years ago," he says, "when I was at Lyons (I was there from 1548 on, and I made use of a certain printer, a familiar of mine, Ludovicus Sarius, a man of varied temper), he lived not far from the Mercurial street, in a house joined to the sign of the three doves. When I came to greet the man, it happened by chance, or rather by the singular providence of God, that I found him busy in revising the works of St Ambrose, which Frellonius was printing. As we talked back and forth, and I saw that he did not want to be called away from the work, he, turning back a page, said: 'You see, this form of our Ambrose edition, how elegant it is, how accurate, and in appearance to be preferred to all the other editions that have so far come out?' Then, continuing the work and praising its elegance, he said: 'Indeed, if I had to buy a copy of the Ambrose work, I would rather buy any other copy than the one you see.' I was surprised at the reason for this remark. Then he, drawing out some pages from the little drawers hidden under his table (they were pages, as the Greeks say, ruled [κεχωσμένα], some partly, some wholly), said: 'This is the first form of the pages which we have printed in these last few days, faithfully following the old and certain exemplar. But two Franciscans, with an authority of their own, have struck out all these pages, as you see, and have had those others substituted in their place, against all faith in our books. This has caused Frellonius very great expense and trouble, for he has lost the whole price of the paper and the labour, has suffered a loss of time, and those first printed sheets had to be discarded in favour of new ones at the whim of those men, to our great harm and to my astonishment.'" So far Junius, about the censors of the Franciscan brotherhood of Lyons. Whether the passage on sacrifice in Isidore's Origins was corrupted in the same way by these or similar more recent men, or by others of older date, I can hardly say, once its last part had been cut away. It is certain that the passage was mutilated and cut short, as Rathramnus (or Bertram) shows, who copied it nearly eight hundred years ago and gave it in this form: "Of this bread and cup the Greeks call the sacrament the Eucharist, which in Latin means good grace. And what is better than the body and blood of Christ? Bread and wine are compared to the body and blood of the Lord because, just as the visible substance of this bread and wine nourishes and refreshes the outer man, so the word of God, which is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful by their participation in it." So much for Isidore as Rathramnus gives him; but you will look in vain for this last part in the common manuscripts of his work, where the passage ends with the words: "And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?" Certainly the Latins who came after Isidore's age, when first the novelties of Paschasius Radbertus and then transubstantiation itself were admitted, were moved by the fact that Isidore calls it "bread and wine," and that he said both are compared to the body and blood, and did not in his own words lead the thought to the substance of the Lord's body and blood. Perhaps this reason also led the same men, or at least men of the same stamp, to write and publish in another work of Isidore as follows: "Next after this comes the sixth confirmation of the sacrament, that the offering which is offered to the Lord, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, be confirmed [confirmetur] to the body of Christ and blood," which makes no sense or a foolish one. For what, I ask, is it to be "confirmed to the body of Christ," or what does the phrase in the Library of the Fathers, "the body of Christ," mean? Cassander, who now quotes the passage itself, reads conformetur, and the matter itself and the sense show that the scribe of Isidore wrote: "be conformed to the body of Christ and blood." But that word seemed too weak to later Latins to represent the mystery [μυστηριώσεως] of their sacrament. So they boldly changed it, and preferred that Isidore should have no meaning here but one opposed to themselves. Next, that wretched Anastasius, or rather Damasus, or another writer much older than Anastasius, falls into a similar kind of mutilation: the book on the lives of the Popes was also most foully truncated and mutilated by men of not dissimilar ability. For first they removed from it the Preface of the author to Jerome, because it did not agree well with the style of today's Roman court. Then they struck out of the life of St Peter a sentence which I shall insert here, as it stands in all the manuscript copies: "Here he consecrated Blessed Clement as Bishop, committed to him his chair, or the whole Church to be ordered, saying: 'As the power of binding and loosing has been given to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I also commit it to you, that you may appoint ministers for the different causes through whom the ecclesiastical business is carried on, and that you yourself, far from being given over to the cares of the world, may be found devoted only to prayer and to the preaching of the people.' After this arrangement he was crowned with martyrdom." Peter drew up his testament in these words, but what he had provided for was suppressed, for it imposed on the heirs an immense burden and duties far removed from their purpose and manners. Elsewhere, in the same writer, where all the manuscript codices read "Pope of the city," that is, of Rome, these forgers have put "Pope of the world," for that is how they now speak in Rome. Those words, "Bishop of the city of Rome," have long since perished. These are the same men who, in Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres, where he cites the famous words of Augustine, "Therefore it is a figure that orders the body of the Lord to be communicated," inserted the words, "therefore it is a figure," saying that the heretic cunningly attributes to a heretic the sentence which is really Augustine's, as Fulbert also cited it. They are the same men who, in Gregory the Great, turned "the armies of priests" into "the exits of priests" [per quos apostasias et defectiones volunt intelligi, through whom they wish apostasies and defections to be understood]. For they read in Epistle 38, book 4: "All the things that have been foretold are coming to pass; the king of pride is near, and, what is wrong even to say, an exit of priests is being prepared for him," whereas the manuscript codices [nay, "the armies"] have it otherwise. The same men corrupted another notable passage of Gregory by the same trickery, which in the manuscript books reads as follows: "It has also come to our ears that some have been scandalized because we forbade presbyters to touch with chrism on the forehead those who have been baptized. And we indeed have done this according to the ancient custom of our Church. But if some are troubled about this matter, where bishops are lacking, we allow that presbyters too should touch with chrism on the forehead those who are baptized." The more recent men, seeing that these words were at odds with the present Roman doctrine about the minister of chrism on the forehead (for now the forehead of the baptized is anointed with chrism only by the Bishop), boldly changed them in their editions, and for what Gregory wrote, "to touch with chrism on the forehead those who have been baptized," and likewise "to touch the baptized on the forehead with chrism," they shamelessly wrote, "those who are to be baptized, and to touch those to be baptized with chrism." Gregory himself warned that the passage was corrupted, and confirms the true reading which we have given, both from another passage of Gregory himself, which is found in the same book, epistle 9, and from Gratian and Thomas; "they cite this passage (he says) as it ought to be, not as it is now read in the printed codices." The same men changed this passage of Augustine, because it opposed their dogma of transmigration: "The body of the Lord," he says, "in which he rose again, must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere." For that Augustine wrote thus both the matter itself cries out, and the following most clearly bear witness: the Cartusian, Algerus, Lombard, Gratian, Thomas, Bonaventure, Scotus, Durandus, Biel, and other older writers, who plainly followed these words in this form. The more recent Latins, in place of those words, "must be in one place," put this most wicked and shameless phrase, "can be in one place," as can be seen in all the editions of Augustine that have come out of their workshops. From the same hand and cause comes what follows. Augustine, at the end of his Tractate 26 on John, had written: "Therefore he who does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, undoubtedly neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment." Those who prepared the latest edition of Augustine at Paris in 1635 confess that they found the passage so written in six manuscript codices; and that it was read so even in the time of Thomas Aquinas is clear from his Catena (which those editors also noted). This is also most clearly confirmed by Prosper, who, in his sentence 319, which he draws from this passage, expressed it thus: "For he who disagrees with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he indifferently receives the sacrament of so great a thing daily to the judgment of his own presumption." These passages were cited so many centuries ago, both by the Cartusian, and by Gratian, and by Lombard himself. But all the recent editions present the words of Augustine in this ridiculously interpolated form: "And therefore he who does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, undoubtedly neither eats his flesh spiritually nor drinks his blood," although he carnally and visibly bites the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ with his teeth; but rather he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment, because, being unclean, he presumes to approach the sacraments of Christ, which anyone does not take worthily unless he is clean, of whom it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." So far the Latin corruptors. No one fails to see to what end these crude additions, sewn plainly onto the fabric of Augustine's words, are directed: namely to persuade that the flesh of Christ, which Augustine simply denied is taken by those who communicate unworthily, is taken by them carnally and visibly, even though it is not taken by them spiritually. The same men, in the treatise On the Right Catholic Way of Life (which is not Augustine's but truly that of Eligius of Noyon, dated 663, given by Sirmond in the Councils), read thus about the sick believer: "Let him fervently ask for blessed oil from the Church, whereby his own body is anointed." But that it was once written "whereby he anoints his own body" is clearly attested by Valdensis, who cites the passage thus; and indeed the very reason of the Latin idiom demands it (for it had to be said whereby his body is anointed, not his own body); and finally the Sermon for the Season, drawn from Augustine's 215, confirms it, in which anoints is read, not is anointed. The corruptors added is anointed, lest this anointing of Eligius should seem alien to its extreme form, which, as is well known, no sick man administers to himself. These are the same men who attributed to Aimoin, or at least to his Continuator, the following words: "In which Synod (which those who gathered there called the eighth universal) they decided about the adoration of images differently from what the orthodox doctors had earlier stated." When Hieronymus Dronaeus had written the passage with a profusion of words, "they decided otherwise than the orthodox had defined," as appears both from the manuscript codices and from the older editions, and from Baronius himself, who cites this passage in the last of these forms in the tenth tome of his Annals, at the year of Christ 869. These are the men who, from Oecumenius, cut out entirely the following passage: "For those who defended the Law also introduced veneration of the angels, because the Law was given through them; and that custom remained in Phrygia, so much so that the Synod of Laodicea forbade by law to approach the angels and to pray to them. Hence it is that among them there are many temples of Michael the Archangel, or of the leader of the army." David Hoeschelius, in his notes on Origen's book against Celsus, p. 483, testifies that he saw and read this passage in the manuscript codices of Oecumenius, which however is not in any of the editions published so far. But the same zeal for the Roman cause that impelled them to snatch these things from Oecumenius also drove them to foist these alien passages on Theodoret and to fabricate them.

units.la: τὸ τοῦ ἀγίου πνεύματος ἐν ᾧ κα ἀλλ' ἐκ τοῦ ψυχῆ ἀρχὴ πρὸς τὸ ἐρωτήσεω. Hunc ipsum ignem purgatorium credimus in quo anima purgantur, sicut aurum in conflatorio. Hæc enim tanquam Theodoreti verba & Latini Græcis iam pridem objectantur ex Nilo pater, & Bellarminus & Gagnæus velut ex Scholiis Theodoreti in 1 Cor.3. nunc quoque in disputatione de Purgatorio afferunt. Quæ & olim Græci Theodoreti sui esse negarunt, & nos hodie frustra siue in illius Patris in Pauli Commentariis,siue in aliis operibus quærimus, quæ nusquam istic reperiuntur, ne in nouissima quidem Theodoreti editione.
units.tr: Hunc ipsum ignem purgatorium credimus, in quo animae purgantur, sicut aurum in conflatorio. These words are cited from Nilus, as if they were the words of Theodoret, and the Latins have long thrown them at the Greeks. Bellarmine and Gagnaeus still bring them forward in their disputation about Purgatory, as if they came from Theodoret's scholia on 1 Corinthians 3. The Greeks themselves long ago denied that these words were Theodoret's, and we today search in vain for them in that Father's Commentaries on Paul or in his other works. They are nowhere to be found there, not even in the most recent edition of Theodoret.

units.la: Similia alterius Larinorum de sui Papæ primatu dogmatis studium I homam Aquinatem olim subegit falsa quædam testimonia & Chalcedonensibus Patribus, & Cyrillo Alexandrino affingere. Namadversus Græcos pseudos putans hæc velut Calcedonensis Concilij decreta affert; Si quis Episcopus prædicatur infamis, liberam habeat sen-.
units.tr: A similar zeal for the dogma of the Pope's primacy once led the other Thomas, Thomas Aquinas, to attribute certain false testimonies to the Chalcedonian Fathers and to Cyril of Alexandria. Thinking them spurious, he cites them against the Greeks as decrees of the Council of Chalcedon: "If any bishop is publicly declared infamous, let him have a free right of appeal

units.la: d Parisienfi a. 1642 in sol. Græc. Lat. 4. Tom. In opusculo s. sr.srer Græc. ad Vibanum. R.4. [f]ententiam appellandi ad beatissimum Episcopum antiquae Romae, quia habemus Petrum petram refugij; & ipsi soli libera potestate, loco Dei sitius discernendi, secundum clausulam Domino sibi datus. Item; Omnia ab eo definita tanquam a Vicario Apostolici throni: Denique, legitur (inquit) in Chalcedonensi Concilio, quod TOTA Synodus clamavit Leoni Papae, Leo [sanctissimus, Apostolicus, & Icumenicus (acumenicum ni fallor intelligit) Patriarcha multos vixit annos. Cyrillum vero idem Thomas haec quae ipse refert, in Thesauro scripsisse ait? Sicut Christus accepit a Patre super omnem principatum & potestatem, ut ei cuncta curventur, plenissimam potestatem; sic & Petro & eius successoribus plenissime committit. Item; Nulli alii, quam Petro Christus quod suum est plenum, sed ipsi soli dedit. Tum & illud; Apostoli in Evangeliis & epistolis affirmarunt in omni doctrina Petrum esse loco Dei & eius Ecclesiam. Et, Illi (Petro) omnes iure, divino caput inclinant, & primates mundi tanquam ipsi Domino Iesu obediunt. Denique; Nos ut membra manere debemus in capite nostro Pontifice Romano, & Apostolico throno, a quo nostrum est quaerere quid credere & quid tenere debemus; quoniam solius Pontificis est arguere, corrigere, increpare, ratum facere, disponere, soluere, & ligare. Haec Thomas sane perquam impudenter; quorum nihil in veris vel Chalcedonensis Synodi actis, vel Cyrilli operibus hodie usquam legitur aut apud Graecos aut apud ipsos etiam Latinos. Quin & nunc quoque in tanta litterarum luce in similem tamen audaciam nonnunquam tamen multo quam olim parcius erumpunt.
units.tr: to the most blessed bishop of ancient Rome, because we have Peter, the rock of refuge; and let him alone, with free power, in the place of God, judge, according to the clause given to him by the Lord." Likewise: "All things are decided by him as by the Vicar of the Apostolic throne." Finally, he says, it is read in the Council of Chalcedon that the whole Synod cried out to Pope Leo: "Leo, most holy, Apostolic and Ecumenical Patriarch (I think he means Oecumenical), has lived many years." And Thomas says that Cyril wrote in his Thesaurus the following words, which he himself reports: "Just as Christ received from the Father the fullest power over every principality and authority, so that all things should bow to him, so he most fully commits the same to Peter and his successors." Again: "Christ gave what is his in full to no one but Peter, and to him alone." Then also: "The Apostles affirmed in the Gospels and Epistles that in all teaching Peter is in the place of God and of his Church." And: "All bow the head to him (Peter) by divine right, and the princes of the world obey him as they would the Lord Jesus himself." Lastly: "We ought to remain as members in our head, the Roman Pontiff and the Apostolic throne, from whom we must seek what we ought to believe and hold; for it belongs to the Pontiff alone to argue, correct, rebuke, ratify, arrange, loose and bind." Thomas says these things quite shamelessly. None of them is read anywhere today in the true acts of the Chalcedonian Synod or in the works of Cyril, either among the Greeks or even among the Latins themselves. Indeed, even now, in so much light of learning, such audacity sometimes breaks out, though far more sparingly than before.

units.la: Ita Bellarminus ut genuinum Athanasij opus esse probet id quod eius nomine circumfertur Symbolum, Augustin quaedam de suo verba affingere non dubitauit; Augustinus (inquit nominatim Athanasium Episcopum Alexandrinum citans, in Psalm 120. integrum articulum huius symboli adducit. Iterum alibi; Sanctus (inquit) Augustinus tractatu in Psalm. 20, sic loquitur explicans illu l, Per diem Sol non oret; De hoc Sole Pater Athanasius Alexandrinus ita pulchrè locutus est. Non factus,nec creatus,nec genitus. Quis Bella. mino hæc,non semel, sed bis affirmanti non crederet? At certum est tamen ista, quæ velut Augustini citat ac describit nusquam apud eum in tota Pfalm. 120. enarratione legi, nusquam illic extare Athanafii nomen quem iste nominatim ibi citari scribit. Vnum causæ studium hominem transversum egit, & quæ Augustino nunquam in mentem venerant, ea velut ab ipso diserte scripta fingere compulit. Eadem quoque Augustino Pofseuinus impudenter tribuere non est veritus. Simili de causa vitiatum est Prosperi Chronicon ad a. Arcadij & Honorii Imperatorum xxiii. quo loco auctor scripserat.Prædestinatorum harefis quæ ab Augustino accepiße dicitur initium bis temporibus serpere exorsa. Vtflerius ita scriptum fuisse testatur in duobus Anglicanis optimæ notæ manufcirptis libris, altero bibliothecæ Re- giæ, altero Benedictini, apud Canrabrigienfes, collegij Sic quoque habere & codices duos Gallicanos æque manuscriptos, alterum S. Victoris Parifienfis; alterum qui Antonij Oifelij olim fuit, diserte tradidit Iacobus Sirmondus. Editores nè hinc pateret Augustinum ipsum fuisse illa Prædeftinatianifmi calumnia appetitum, & qui Maffilienfibus Prædeftinatiani sunt, eos reuera fuisse sinceros Augustini discipulos, locum mutarunt & pro iis quæ exhibuimus ex manuscriptis libris, ista quæ in codicibus excusis vulgò habentur ediderunt. Prædestinatorum harefis quæ ab Augustini libris malè intellectis accipisse dicitur initium his temporibus serpere exorsa. Inde etiam est quod quandam Fausti famosissimi Pelagianorum signiferi epistolam, illius sectæ venenis refertam, velut à IX Episcopis in Concilio ætscio quo Archrensi approbatam,eorumq; nominibus & subscriptionibus munitam ediderint†, quam Sirmondus & apud Hincmarum & in veterib.optimis quibusq; libris solum Fausti auctoris nomen præferre restatur, *tamen, quod meritò mireris, iste quoque, partium studio victus, in Conciliorum Gallicanorum editione eam ab his ipsis Episcopis subscriptam
units.tr: So Bellarmine, in order to prove that the creed circulated under the name of Athanasius is a genuine work of Athanasius, did not hesitate to attribute to Augustine words of his own. He says: Augustine, citing by name Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in Psalm 120, brings forward the whole article of this creed. And again elsewhere: Saint Augustine, in his tractate on Psalm 20, speaks thus, explaining that passage, "The sun shall not burn by day": "Concerning this Sun, Father Athanasius of Alexandria spoke so beautifully: unmade, uncreated, unbegotten." Who would not believe Bellarmine, who affirms this not once but twice? Yet it is certain that these things, which he cites and describes as Augustine's, are nowhere to be read in Augustine's whole exposition of Psalm 120, and that the name of Athanasius, which he writes is cited by name there, does not appear there at all. A single zeal for a cause drove this man into perversity, and compelled him to invent, as if Augustine had expressly written them, things that had never come into Augustine's mind. Posevinus too did not hesitate shamelessly to ascribe the same things to Augustine. For a similar reason, Prosper's Chronicle, under the twenty-third year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, has been corrupted. In that passage the author had written: The heresy of the predestinarians, which is said to have received its beginning from Augustine, has begun to creep in these times. Usher testifies that it was written thus in two English manuscripts of the highest quality, one in the Royal Library and the other in the Benedictine college at Cambridge. James Sirmond openly reported that two Gallican manuscripts likewise have the same reading, one from St. Victor at Paris, and the other which once belonged to Antoine Oisel. But so that it might not appear from this that Augustine himself was assailed by that calumny of predestinarianism, and so that it might not appear that the Massilians who are called predestinarians were in fact sincere disciples of Augustine, the editors changed the passage. Instead of what we have shown from the manuscript books, they published what is commonly found in the printed codices: The heresy of the predestinarians, which is said to have received its beginning from a misunderstanding of Augustine's books, has begun to creep in these times. From the same source comes their publication, as if approved by nine bishops at some Council of Arles, of a letter of Faustus, the most notorious standard-bearer of the Pelagians, full of the poisons of that sect and furnished with their names and signatures. Sirmond testifies that in Hincmar, and in all the best old books, the letter bears only the name of its author, Faustus. Yet it is remarkable that this man too, overcome by partisan zeal, did not hesitate in his edition of the Gallican Councils to present it as subscribed by those very bishops.

units.la: repræsentare non dubitarit. Fausti me nomen monet ne indicatam præteream insignem Margarini de la Bigne impostutam, qui Fausti huius non uno à veteribus stigmate notati librum de gratia & libero arbitrio in altera Bibliothecæ Patrum editione lectori velut opus insigne propinat. Quin & hominem aperte Semipelagianum non satis habens de infami hæreticorum turba eripuisse, cœlitum sanctorum choris inseruit modo Beatum †, † modo Divum * appellitans. Ac licet in recentissima Bibliothecæ editione expunctis Margarini elogiis Fausti longe aliis pro suo merito ornatus fuerit †; tamen nec † nunc quidem apud lesuitas desunt, qui pro eius nomine ac fama pugnent. * Sed, ut institutam orationem persequar, quis credat, ne Breviaria quidem & Missalia ipsa ab hac istorum audacia intacta mansisse? Notarunt viri docti & probitate insignes, in collecta quæ in festo Cathedræ S. Petri legitur, hæc antea fuisse verba. Deus qui B. Petro Apostolo tuo collata claviibus regni cœlestis animas ligandi Pontificium tradidisti, Sed in posterioribus Breviariorum & Missalium editionibus induetam vocem animas, * nec Papæ potestas ad spiritualia tantum, minime verò ad temporalia pertinere censeretur: Et in Euangelio fr. tertiæ quæ tertiam Quadragesimæ Dominicam minime sequitur exciderunt. Dixit Iesus Discipulis suis, cum in veteribus exemplaribus legatur. Respiciens te fratrem tuum, vasiè subductis vocibus, Simoni Petro, ne videretur Dominus Petrum, idest Pontificem Romanum, tribunali Ecclesiæ, ad quod ipsum amandat, subjecisse, Et si Tridentini Patres Thomæ Passij Valentini Canonici sententiam concessissent, expuncti fuissent è Pontificali loci omnes qui in ordinatione Ministrorum Ecclesiæ populi suffragii, consensusque eius mentionem faciunt, & hic maximè quo ordinatione Presbyteri Episcopus dicit. Neque fuit frustra à Patribus instituta, ut de electio ne illorum qui ad regimen altaris adhibendi sunt, consulatur. Græcís, quo Scriptorum istum in partes suas traherent, assuta fuisse. Petauius, proximè, sic soluit objectionem quæ petitur ex 68. canone Apostolorum adversus ieiunium Sabbathi quod in Ecclesia Romana observatur. Tanquam spurius (inquit) & alienus canon ille reycitur & ab otiosis Graculis verba sunt intertexta. Sed si cui cordi sit quà dubia & incerta sint postremæ hujus Antiquitatis scripta considerare, legat Synodum octauam, quam Oecumenicam volunt Occidentales; codices Latinos cum Græcis conferat, & expendat maximè Analtafij, Papæ Bibliothecarij, præfationem. Is postquam accerrimè in Græcorùm ambitionem inuectus est, postquam quos hi hibent tertij Concilij Canones eos veluti supposititios rejecit, ut paucis rem expediat, nihil circuitione usus, omnia Concilia, nullo nisi primo excepto, Græcos depravasse affirmat. Quibus jam scriptis aquiescemus, quandoquidem pestis illa adeo altè insedit, penetrũsque ipsa Concilia, hoc est m onumentorum Ecclesiæ Veterum cor ipsum occupauit? Symbolum ipsum, tot concilijs Oecumenicis confeceratum, ejusmodi depravationibus subduci non potuit. Nam ut nihil dicam de hisce levis momenti verbis, de cœlo, secundum Scripturas, Deum , quæ in quibusdam Symbolis haberi, in aliis verò desiderari obseruauit, in Synodo Florentina, Cardinalis Iulianus, fluxere iam integra secula ex quo inter Orientales & Occidentales de voce Filiosque in capite de processione Spiritus Sancti contenditur: Illi querentibus ad his additam; his mussantibus ab illis sublatam; quæ quidem alteratio, licèt videatur in speciem levis, magni tamen est momenti, adeo ut ex ea pendeat quæstionis summi momenti decisio: hæc enim est quæ haćtenus inter utrosque schisma fecit; videlicet num Spiritus Sanctus non minus procedat à Filio quàm à Patre. Indicio certissimo factum studio partium (quiqui sint criminis hujus rei) ut manus tam sacro monumento injicerentur. Sed quicquid aentatum est olim in hisce rebus
units.tr: The name of Faustus reminds me not to pass over the notable imposture of Margarin de la Bigne, who in the second edition of his Bibliotheca Patrum offers the reader, as an outstanding work, the book of this Faustus On Grace and Free Will, a man marked with a stigma by the ancients, and not one only. Not content to have rescued a man openly Semipelagian from the infamous crowd of heretics, he enrolled him among the choirs of the heavenly saints, sometimes calling him Blessed, sometimes Divine. And although in the most recent edition of the Bibliotheca the eulogies of Margarin were removed, and Faustus was adorned with very different titles according to his merit, yet even now there are not lacking among the Jesuits those who fight for his name and reputation. But, to pursue the line of argument I began, who would believe that even the Breviaries and Missals themselves have been left untouched by this audacity of theirs? Learned men, distinguished for integrity, have observed that in the collect read on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, the words used to be: O God, who gave to your Apostle Blessed Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the power of binding souls. But in later editions of the Breviaries and Missals the word souls has been inserted, lest the power of the Pope be thought to extend only to spiritual matters and not at all to temporal ones. And in the Gospel of the third Sunday, which does not follow the third Sunday of Lent, the words have been dropped: Jesus said to his disciples, though they are read in the old copies. Turning to Simon Peter, and turning to your brother, with a veiled voice, lest the Lord seem to have subjected Peter, that is the Roman Pontiff, to the tribunal of the Church, to which he sends him. And if the Fathers of Trent had agreed with the opinion of Thomas Passi, the canon of Valence, all those passages would have been removed from the Pontifical which mention the consent and agreement of the people in the ordination of the ministers of the Church, and especially this one, in which the bishop says at the ordination of a priest: Nor was it without reason that the Fathers ordained that the election of those who are to be admitted to the service of the altar should be consulted. These were stitched on to the Greek writers so that they might draw that writer to their own side. Petavius, recently, answered the objection drawn from the sixty-eighth canon of the Apostles against the Sabbath fast observed in the Roman Church thus: "That canon is rejected as spurious and foreign, and its words were woven in by idle Graculi." But if anyone cares to consider how doubtful and uncertain the writings of this latest antiquity are, let him read the eighth Synod, which the Westerners call Ecumenical, compare the Latin codices with the Greek, and weigh especially the preface of Anastasius, librarian of the Pope. After he has most sharply inveighed against the ambition of the Greeks, and after he has rejected as supposititious the canons of the Third Council which they hold, he states plainly and without circumlocution that all the Councils, except the first, have been corrupted by the Greeks. Shall we now be satisfied with these writings, since that plague has so deeply taken root that it has penetrated even the Councils, that is, has occupied the very heart of the monuments of the ancient Church? The Creed itself, consecrated by so many Ecumenical Councils, could not be withdrawn from such corruptions. For, to say nothing of those words of small weight, from heaven and according to the Scriptures, which some Creeds have and others lack, which Cardinal Julian observed in the Synod of Florence, centuries have already passed since the dispute began between the Easterners and the Westerners over the word and the Son in the article on the procession of the Holy Spirit. The one party complains that it was added, the other that it was removed. This alteration, though it may seem slight in appearance, is of great importance, so much so that the decision of a question of the highest importance depends on it. For this is what has so far made a schism between the two sides: namely, whether the Holy Spirit proceeds no less from the Son than from the Father. It is a most certain sign that, whoever is guilty of this crime, zeal for a party led men to lay hands on so sacred a monument. But whatever was formerly done in these matters

units.la: pene jocus & ludus cenſebitur, fi cum iis comparetur qu'ſſ faͤta sunt nouissimis hisce temporibus, quibus adeo studiis incanduere miseri mortales, ut, ratione & pu dore proculcatis, nnlli neque Scripto neque Auctori pepercerint, quin passim obvia quæque sœdarint. Eorum certè qui eò audaciæ proruperunt nunquam satis damnare poͤtest mala fides; quapropter nonnihi summacum ratione mihi quæ sequuntur visus est scrpsisse Erasmus præfatione in Hieronymi Opera ad Guilielmum V V aramum Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem. Extat ( inquit ille) eximiis verē Sacroſanctis auctoribus quos nobis vel erudita dedit Gratia, vel huius amula prodidit Itali avel olim studiis floretiſsima produxit Gallia, vel ingenioſa peperit Africa, vel laboru pattens edidit Hispania rara quadam eruditione suſpiciendos, eloquentia claros, vita sanctimonia venerandos, quaso te quam pauci ſuperſunt, caſu seruati magis quam nostro beneficio; atque hi rurſtu ipsi quam fæde mutili quam contaminati, quam prodigiosis mendis undique scatentes, ut non magni referat sic ſuperesse. Equidem ut non aspernor simplicem vulgi pietatem, ita non possum non mirari tã praposterum multitudinis iudicium. Calceos, Sanctorum & sudariola muco sordentia exosculamur, & eorumdem libros sanctissimas & efficacissimas Divorum reliquias negleCtos iacere patimur. Tuniculam aut induſiolum Diui aureis gemmatisq; thecis reponimus, & libros ab illis elaboratos in quibus id quod illorum fuit optimum nobis adhuc viuit spiratq;, cimicibus tineis ac blattis impuné rade ndos relinquimus. Neque verò difficile fit hucusce rei cauſam conieCturis assequi. Postea quæ Principum mores plane iam in barbariam, quondam tyrannidem degenerarssent, tum Episcopi profanam ditionem magis cæpissent aplecti, quam ab Apostolis traditum docendi munus mox universa docendi provincia in istos quosdam est relegata qui charitatis & religionis cognomen seupeculiare sibi vindicant: Iam negligi cæpta bona littera sastidita Græcanici serme nu peritia, multoq; magis Hebraici, spretum aloquentia studium, quin & ipsa lingua Latina sic confusurcata est suibinde.
units.tr: would be counted almost a joke and a game if it were compared with what has been done in these most recent times, when miserable mortals have been so inflamed by partisan zeal that, with reason and decency trampled underfoot, they have spared no one, neither writing nor author, but have defiled whatever came to hand. Bad faith can never condemn sufficiently those who broke out into such audacity. Wherefore I think it worth quoting what Erasmus wrote, with good reason, in his preface to the works of Jerome, addressed to William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury: There exist (he says) truly most holy authors, whom either learned Grace gave us, or Italy, rival of this land, brought forth, or Gaul, once most flourishing in studies, produced, or ingenious Africa bore, or Spain, enduring its labours, published, to be esteemed for a rare kind of learning, distinguished for eloquence, venerable for the sanctity of their lives. I ask you, how few survive, saved more by chance than by our care; and these again, how foully mutilated, how contaminated, how teeming on every side with monstrous errors, so that it matters little whether they survive at all. Indeed, as I do not scorn the simple piety of the common people, so I cannot but wonder at the so perverse judgement of the multitude. We kiss the shoes of the saints and their sweat-stained handkerchiefs, and we allow their books, the most holy and efficacious relics of the divines, to lie neglected. We put their little tunic or shirt in golden and jewelled caskets, and we leave the books they laboured over, in which what was best in them still lives and breathes, to be gnawed with impunity by bedbugs, moths and book-lice. Nor is it difficult to grasp the cause of this by conjecture. Afterwards, when the morals of princes had sunk altogether into barbarism, and had degenerated from tyranny, then bishops began to embrace profane dominion more than the office of teaching handed down by the Apostles; soon the whole province of teaching was relegated to certain men who claim the name of charity and religion as their own peculiar property. Now good letters began to be neglected, Greek learning was despised almost wholly, and much more Hebrew; the study of eloquence was scorned, and even the Latin language was so often confused.

units.la: noua barbarie,vt iā nihil minus esset quàm Latina,nec historia nec Antiquitatis ulla cura,tantum ad Sophisticas quasdā argutias contracta res literaria , & eruditionis summa penes Summularios quosdā collectores ac excerptores esse cœpit,hoc nimirum impudentiores quo minus eruditos.Proinde Veteres illos Scriptores facilè vel antiquari passi sunt , vel quod vero propius est,ipsi abolendos curarunt,ut quos iā frustra legerent nimirum his rebus destituti, sine quibus illi non queunt intelligi. Et tamen ex illis utcunque decerpta quaedam suis Commentariis admiscuerunt,qua gratia magis etiam in rem istorum erat illos interire,ne quando vel plagii conuincerentur, vel inscitia.Scilicet tanti erat antiquari Clementem,Irenaeū, Polycarpum,Origenem,vt horum vice Occam,Durandum, Capreolum.Lyranum Burgensem & his etiā indoctiores legeret orbis.Sub horum igitur diuturna tyrannide tanta fuit bonarū literarum ac bonorum auctorum πανολσθρία, vt è doctorum ordine pelleretur qui vel paululū litteratura melioris attigisset. His rebus factum est ut tot orbis lumina quorum titulos dūtaxat,necid sine lachrymis,legitimus funditus interiernt, & si quos contigit suis superesse satis,hi sic modis omnibus depraunati sunt,adeo truncati cōtemeratiū,ut fœlices videri possint qui perierunt.Hæc de omnibus in genere Patribus protocutus,accedit demum ad ipsum id cuius opera præsababatur Hieronymum.Atque id profecto cùm mihi vehementer indignū videtur in omnibus eruditis,tum longè indignissimū in Hieronimo.............. At nunc haud scio an quisquiam omnium tractatus sit indigniùs.Bana pars vigiliarum eius intercidit. Quod superest non depraunatum erat sed prorsus extinctum & obliteratum:idq; partim illiteratorum vitio scribarū, qui solent ex emendatis inemendata describere , ex mendosis mendosiora reddere praetermittere quod non legunt,corrūpere quod non intelligunt ,velut Hebrea Graecaq; vocabula, quae frequenter intermiscet Hieronimus: sed multo scleratius & sacrilegis haud scio quibus studio detruncata permulta,addita nonnulla,mutata pleraque depravata,sordidata cōfusa pene omnia,vt vix ulla sit periodus quam eruditus possit inoffense legere.Imo quod est pestilentissimum vitiandi genus,perinde quasi parum esset tot infulsissimas nugas juxta infantes atque ineruditas in hominis eloquentissimi pariter ac doctissimi nomen ac titulū contulisse,mediis illius commentariis passim admiscuerunt suas nanias,ne quis repurgare posset. Nam librum falso inscriptum permulta sunt qua coargunt, caeterum fragmenta passim intermixta, veluti frumento confusum lolium, quo tandem cribro repurget aliquis? Atque hac omnia sic esse facta docebimus mox in operum ipsius Catalogo, tum secundi Tomi duobus prafationibus ac censuris. Commovit itaque me partim tam insignis Ecclesia Doctoris non ferenda cotumelia, in cujus immortalia monumenta sic impie debacchati sunt isti plusquam apri Calydonij, partim publica studiosorum utilitas quos videbā à tam eximiis epulis hisce rebus submoveri, &c.
units.tr: by a new barbarism, so that nothing was less than Latin; neither history nor any care for antiquity remained, and literary study was reduced to certain sophistical subtleties, and the highest learning came to rest with certain summulists, collectors and excerptors, all the more shameless the less learned they were. Accordingly, those ancient writers were either allowed to fall into oblivion, or, what is nearer the truth, they themselves took care to have them abolished, since those men, lacking the very things without which those authors cannot be understood, would read them in vain. And yet they mixed certain things picked out of them, in whatever way, into their own commentaries; and it was all the more in their interest that those authors perish, lest they should at some time be convicted of plagiarism or ignorance. Clearly it was so important to have Clement, Irenaeus, Polycarp and Origen made obsolete, that in their place the whole world should read Occam, Durandus, Capreolus, Lyranus of Burgos, and others even less learned than these. Under the long tyranny of these men, then, there was such a general destruction of good letters and good authors that anyone who had touched even a little of better literature was driven from the ranks of the learned. For these reasons it came about that so many lights of the world, whose titles alone, and not without tears, have come down to us, perished utterly; and if any of the others happened to survive in sufficient number, they were so depraved in every way, so mutilated and carelessly corrupted, that those who perished might seem fortunate. Having spoken thus of the Fathers in general, he comes at last to Jerome himself, the very author whose work he was introducing. And truly, when this seems to me most unworthy in all learned men, it seems far most unworthy in Jerome. And yet now I do not know whether anyone's writings have been treated more unworthily. A large part of his Vigils has perished. What remains was not merely depraved but utterly destroyed and obliterated; and this partly through the fault of unlettered scribes, who are accustomed to copy the emended as unemended, to make the faulty worse, to omit what they do not read, to corrupt what they do not understand, as with the Hebrew and Greek words which Jerome often interposes. But much more wickedly, by I know not what sacrilegious zeal, very many passages have been cut short, some added, most changed, depraved, befouled, and almost everything confused, so that there is scarcely a sentence which a learned reader could read without stumbling. Indeed, which is the most pestilential kind of corruption, as if it were not enough to have ascribed so many utterly silly trifles, childish and unlearned, to the name and title of a most eloquent and most learned man, they have also everywhere mixed their own nonsense into the middle of his commentaries, so that no one can purge it out. For there are many things which prove the book falsely inscribed, and the fragments are everywhere intermixed, like darnel confused with wheat; what sieve could anyone use to purge them out? And that all these things have been done in this way I shall show shortly, in the Catalogue of the works themselves, and then in the two prefaces and censures of the second volume. Thus I was moved partly by the insufferable insult offered to so notable a Doctor of the Church, against whose immortal monuments those men raged so impiously, more than the Calydonian boars; partly by the public usefulness of the students, whom I saw being kept back from such excellent feasts by these things, etc.

units.la: Hactenus Erasmus. Hunc autem locum licet paulò prolixiorem huc totum transcribere placuit, cum quod ingenuè & luculenter, non solùm malum ipsum, verùm etiam mali fontes & causas aperui sse mihi videatur, tum etiam quòd frustra sit qui hic harioletur non rei indignitate permotum, sed partium studio ductum in has querelas erupisse Erasmum. Ante naras quippe controversias quae discessionem in religione fecerunt, & ista scripsit vir ille magnus & Hieronymi opera, ex quibus ea desumpsi, excusa sunt anno scilicet 1516. Basileae, apud I. Frobenium. Sed Erasmi quaerelae recentiores non deterruerunt quin simili audacia in veterum monumenta grassarentur. Ioannem quidem Gagnejum Parisiensem Theologum cum Alcimi Avititi poemata, A. D 1536. Lugduni ederet, & alia pro arbitrio immutasse ac depravasse, & quingentis prope versibus praeter librorum tum manuscriptorum tum etiam a. 1507. & 1509. Coloniae editorum fidem inaudito atque incredibili facinore interpolasse observavit eruditissimus Sirmundus. Ita pluri-morum de Sanctorum veterum vitis scriptorum lucubrationes in sua illa tricubitali farragine Surius Carthusianus pro sui ingenij captu varie ac multipliciter interpelauit: qu ... Episcoporum quorundam Synodalibus, Regina vrbium Lutetice nuper impressis expunxerunt. Væ, iterum væ, ut cumvidente exclamen nebulonibus, qui tales Musarum cæsitati & integritati venerandæ non solum insidias struunt, sed & Musas ipsas impudenter & æquiter subdolo religionis zelo nullius frontis homines deuirginant, fucumque islum, pietatis nomen ementitum, inter pias fraudes numerant. Sed hic aduersus illos non scribimus. Satis est, quod luce clarius est confirmasse istos additis & rescissis plurimis innumera fidei veterum monumenta immutasse & depravasse. Isti sunt qui in hac X I I. Cypriani ad populum Carthaginensem Epistolæ periodo. Audiant quæso patienter consilium nostrum expectent regressionem nostram, ut cum ad vos per Dei misericordiam venerimus, conuocati coepiscopi plures secundum Domini disciplinam, & Confessorum præsentiam, & vestram quoque sententiam, beatorum martyrum literas & desi se undum veteria examinare possimus, ex editionibus Gryphianis Lugd. 1528. & 1537. & Pamelij voces has, secundum vestram quoque sententiam quæ in aliis, puta Manutij & Morellij Parisiis 1564. habentur, per seclus expunxerunt; quia ex nos nescire sua referre censuerunt, plebem fidelem, scilicet, in suæ Ecclesiæ negotiis partes suas, iusque suffragij aliquomodo habuisse. Illi ipsi sunt, qui, in epistola quadragesima, de petra petrum fecerunt, & qui corruptorum priscorum vestigiis insistentes eiusdem Tractatum de unitate Ecclesiæ fœdè adulterarunt, in medias eius periodos variis de suo insartis, contra optimorum manuscriptorum fidem cuiusmodi hæc sunt Super illum unum (Petrum) ædificat Ecclesiam suam, & illi pascendas mandat oues suas. Item Primatus Petro datur ut vna Ecclesia Christi, & Cathedra una monstretur. Denique; Cathedra Petri super quam fundata est Ecclesia
units.tr: So far Erasmus. I have decided to transcribe this whole passage here, though it is somewhat lengthy, both because it seems to me to have laid open not only the evil itself but also the sources and causes of the evil, frankly and clearly, and because it is in vain that anyone should carp at it by claiming that Erasmus broke out into these complaints not moved by the unworthiness of the matter but driven by partisan zeal. For those works of Jerome, from which I have taken these passages, were written by that great man before the controversies arose that made the division in religion, and they were published in the year 1516 at Basel by J. Froben. But Erasmus's later complaints did not deter others from rushing into the monuments of the ancients with similar audacity. Gagnaeus, a Parisian theologian, when he published the poems of Avitus Alcimus at Lyons in 1536, altered and corrupted them at will, and, as the most learned Sirmond observed, interpolated nearly five hundred verses, with an unheard-of and incredible crime, against the testimony of the manuscripts and of the editions printed at Cologne in 1507 and 1509. In the same way Surius the Carthusian, in his three-cubit-thick heap of the lives of the saints, variously and in many ways tampered with the writings of many authors according to the measure of his own talent. ... Certain bishops' Synodals, recently printed in the Queen of cities, Lutetia, they expunged. Woe, again woe, so that I may cry out with the Lord watching over these scoundrels, who not only lay snares for the venerable chastity and integrity of the Muses, but also shamelessly and unjustly deflower the Muses themselves, men of no shame, under the deceitful zeal of religion, and count that disguise, which has falsely borrowed the name of piety, among holy frauds. But I am not writing against those men here. It is enough that it has been shown, clearer than the light, that by additions and deletions very many of them have changed and depraved innumerable monuments of the faith of the ancients. They are the men who, in this twelfth period of Cyprian's Epistle to the people of Carthage, Let them, I beg, hear our counsel patiently, and wait for our return, so that when we come to you through God's mercy, with many fellow bishops gathered according to the discipline of the Lord, and in the presence of the Confessors, and also your opinion, we may examine the letters of the blessed martyrs and ... from the Gryphius editions of Lyons of 1528 and 1537, and Pamelius, have expunged the words and your opinion too, which are found in other editions, for example those of Manutius and Morellius at Paris in 1564; because they judged that the common people, namely the faithful, had no share in the affairs of their own Church and no kind of right of suffrage. These are the same men who, in the fortieth epistle, made petra into petrum, and who, following the footsteps of earlier corrupters, foully adulterated the same treatise of Cyprian on the unity of the Church, inserting into the middle of its periods various things of their own, against the faith of the best manuscripts; such things as these: On that one (Peter) he builds his Church, and to him he entrusts his sheep to be fed. Likewise: Primacy is given to Peter, so that one Church of Christ and one chair may be shown. And finally: The chair of Peter, upon which the Church is founded.
