Pāp. 1/s. zol. 1 Cathedram Petri super quā s. data est Ecclesia, dicuntur ā Cypr. & Morell. edit. ibi se quæ supra.
units.tr: The words [are] in the edition of Gryphius, 1517, p. 144, and in others at p. 19: "Primacy is given to Peter, so that there may be one Church of Christ and one Chair is shown, and [he feeds] his sheep and flocks," as those who... Matth. 16; Ioan. 21. These words, and especially "one Church is shown," were not in the Gryphius edition, nor in Morellius, as above. The words "the Chair of Peter upon which the Church is founded" are attributed to Cyprian, and [appear] in Morellius' edition in the same place as above.

units.la: Quoium quidem additamentorum nemo est qui scopum, & qua mente assuta fuerint, non videat. Illi ipsi sunt ⁊ qui quàm molestè ferant non suppressam Firmiliani Cæsariæ Cappadocum Episcopi, magni, suo tem-pore, nominis, epistolam non obscuiè ferunt. Cum enim ex ea pateat quanta libertate veterum seculorum Episcopi cum Papa agerent, eam de industria Manutius in Cypriani editione Romana omiserat. Verum Morellius eam in sua editione restituit, Cyprianiqueadquem scripta est, epistolis inseruit, magno argumento quibus studiis isti trahantur, & quot ciusmodi factus clam præfocarint. Hæc est Officina ex qua miser ille Ambrosius
units.tr: No one who considers these additions can fail to see their purpose and the spirit in which they were inserted. These are the same men who are not at all pleased that the letter of Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man of great reputation in his day, has not been suppressed. For since it is plain from that letter how much freedom the bishops of earlier ages took in dealing with the Pope, Manutius had deliberately left it out of the Roman edition of Cyprian. Morellius, however, restored it in his own edition and inserted it among the letters of Cyprian, to whom it was addressed. This is a strong proof of the zeal with which these men pursue their ends, and of how many such passages they have secretly suppressed. This is the workshop from which that unhappy edition of Ambrose

units.la: tam fœdè interpolatis, prodiit, & cuius fortem grauiter lamentatus est Nicolaus Faber . Boni illi artifices qui eum ediderunt, nimis,( ut inquit ille ) in alieno opere ingeniosi, mutaverunt, miscuerunt, transposuerunt quicquid libuit, ut hoc maximè quod ipse notat. Libros de interpellatione Iobi & Davidis in aliis editionibus coniunctos diuiserunt, quod ut facerent exemplo parum laudabili inseruerunt & interpolarunt nonnulla, quod & fecerunt in prima Apologia Dauid; sed longè peius in altera, ex cuius capite octauo quinque aut sex lineas quæ in omnibus veteribus editionibus leguntur, expunxerunt. Tribuerunt item Scriptoni illi Tractatus quosdam, qui eius non sunt, quales sunt libri de arbore prohibita. Item alius in postremum caput Proverbiorum. Et tamen ex ista Ambrosij editione expressa est ea quæ Parisiis anno 603. prodiit. Neque vero hanc, quam Faber denotauit, primam fuisse putes Recmanorum Censorum in Ambrosium iniuriam. Aliam ium ante grauissimus, ac sanctissimus scriptor ab eiusdem farinæ correctoribus passus erat, ciusdem generis contumeliam, quam ego hoc loco Francisci Iunii, testis αὐτὸ ταῦτ' fide ac verbis exsequar. Ante annos (inquit) viginti septem cum Lugduni agerem (egi autem a 1598. sequente correctione quoddam typographico usus sum simili ariter, cui Ludouico Sa-nario) vario fuit nomen. Habitabat ille non procul à Mercuriali vico, in ædibus coniunctis trium columbarum signo. Cum ad salutandum hominem venissem, casu vel potius singulari Dei providentia accidit, ut versantem cum offenderem in recognoscendis D. Ambrosii operibus, quae tunc Frelonius excudebat. Variis autem sermonibus ultro citroque habitis, cum me anocamèto esse ab opere nolle offenderem, ille redorsus lectionem unius pagina, Vides ne, inquit, hanc formam Ambrosiana editionis nostrae quam sit elegans, accurata, & in speciem omnibus anteponanda aliis, quae adhuc in lucem prodiérunt? Postea contuenti opus & probanti elegantiam eius dixit: Ego vero si quod exemplum Ambrosiani operis mihi emendum esset, quodvis exemplum aliud potius, quam hoc quod vides, compararem. S. i. citatus sum huius dicti causam. Tum ille de foruli sub mensa sua latentibus aliquot paginas promens (erant autem paginae, ut loquuntur Graeci κεχωσμένοι, sive cancellatae, aliae ex parte, & aliae universe.) Haec est (inquit prima) forma paginarum, quas his paucis diebus ad exemplum veteris, & certi exemplaris optima fides impressimus. Franciscani autem duo pro auctoritate has omnes paginas dispunxerunt, ut vides, & illas subfituit in locum priorum curaverunt praeter omnem nostrorum librorum fidem, quae res sumptum & molestiam Frelonio creavit gravissimam; Nam pretium chartae, operarumque amisit universum, tempora iacturam passus est, & typographicas illas priores plagulas communtari novis ad libidinem ipsorum oportuit magno malo nostro & admiratione mea. Haftenus Iunius de Latinis ex Franciscì sodalitio censoribus. Horum enim aut similium recentiorum, an aliorum veteriorum mane corruptus fuerit Isidori in Originibus de sacrificio locus, recisa eius ultima parte, haud facile dixerim; Mutilatum quid mac decurtatum locum ex Rabbamo (siue Bertramo) constat, qui eum cum ante annos pene oltingentos descripsisset, ita exhibuit; Cuius panis & calicis sanctum Graeci Eucharistiam dicunt, quod Latinè bona gratia interpretatur. Et quid melius corpore & sanguine Christi? Panis vero & vinum ideo corpori & sanguini.
units.tr: so badly interpolated came forth, and whose fate Nicolaus Faber lamented bitterly. Those clever craftsmen who published him, being, as he says, too ingenious with another man's work, changed, mixed up and transposed whatever they pleased, as he especially notes. They separated the books on the Interpellation of Job and David, which in other editions had been joined together; to do this, they inserted and interpolated some passages, with a rather unworthy example, which they also did in the first Apology of David; but far worse in the second, from whose eighth chapter they struck out five or six lines that are read in all the older editions. They likewise ascribed to that writer certain treatises that are not his, such as the book on the forbidden tree, and another on the last chapter of Proverbs. And yet the edition of Paris of 1603 was copied from this edition of Ambrose. Nor should you think that the one Faber pointed out was the first insult to Ambrose by the censors of Reims. A far more serious and holy writer had suffered an earlier one, of the same kind, at the hands of correctors of the same stamp, which I shall here set out in the words and on the testimony of Francis Junius. "Some twenty-seven years ago (he says), when I was at Lyons (I was there from 1598), it so happened, by a singular providence of God rather than by chance, that I was lodging with a certain Ludovicus Sanarius, a printer who [had] a shop near the Mercury quarter, in a house joined to the sign of the three doves. When I came to greet the man, I found him busy revising the works of St Ambrose, which Frelonius was then printing. After various talk back and forth, when I found that he did not wish me to be detained from the work, he turned back a page and read it through: 'Do you see,' he said, 'how elegant, accurate and superior in appearance this form of our Ambrose edition is to all others that have yet come to light?' Afterwards, when I looked at the work and approved its elegance, he said: 'If I had to buy a copy of Ambrose, I would rather buy any other copy than this one that you see.' I asked the reason for this remark. Then he drew out from under his table some pages that had been hidden there (the pages were, as the Greeks say, [κεχωσμένοι], that is, cancelled, some in part and some entirely). 'This (he said first) is the form of the pages which we printed a few days ago, with the best faith, after the model of an old and certain copy. But two Franciscans, by their authority, have struck out all these pages, as you see, and have had those others substituted in their place, contrary to all faith in our books; and this has caused Frelonius very heavy expense and trouble. For he has lost the entire price of the paper and the workmen's wages, and has suffered the loss of time, and those earlier printed sheets had to be exchanged for new ones at their pleasure, to our great harm and to my astonishment.'" So far Junius, concerning the Latin censors of the Franciscan brotherhood. As to whether the passage in Isidore's Origins on sacrifice was corrupted by these or similar recent censors, or by others of older date, with its final part cut off, I could hardly say. It is clear that a mutilated and shortened passage is found in Rabanus (or Bertram), who, when he had transcribed it nearly eight hundred years ago, presented it thus: "The Greeks call the holy thing of this bread and cup the Eucharist, which in Latin means good grace. And what is better than the body and blood of Christ? Bread and wine are indeed compared to the body and blood of the Lord

units.la: Domini comparantur,quia sicut visibilis huius panis vinique fustantia exteriorem nutrit & inebriat hominem,ita verbum Dei quiest panis vivus participatione sui fidelium recreat mentes. Atque hæc quidem apud Rathramnum Ifidorus; sed ista ultima frustra in vulgatis ejus codicibus quæras, †in quibus locus in hæc verba definit; Et quid meius corpore & sanguine Christi? Nimirum Latinos,qui post Isidori secula , primo Paschasij Ratberti novitates, cum & ipsam transsubstantiationem , admiserunt , movit quod Isidorus panem & vinum nominat,& quod utrumq; corpori & sanguini comparari dixit,non in ipsius corpore & sanguinis Dominici substantiam sua aımissa conuectu. Quæ fortasse ratio eosdem, vel certè ejusdem generis artifices, compulit hæc in alio Isidori opere ita scribere atque edere. Porro ex hinc sexta succedit confirmatio sacramenti; vt ablatio quæ Domino offertur,sanctificata per Spiritum Sanctum corpori Christi & sanguini confirmetur, vel nullo vel inepto sensu; Quid enim quæso est confirmari corpori Christi vel quod in Patrum Bibliotheca habetur corpus Christi. Cassander, qui nunc ipsum locum recitans legit conformetur, & res ipsa atque sensus docent, scribendum ab Isidoro fuisse corpori Christi & sanguini conformetur. Sed id verbum Latinis sequiorum temporum dilutius visum est quàm ut suæ μετασχώσεως mysterium repræsentaret. Itaque audacter mutarunt, Isidoriqué nullum hic esse quàm sibi adversantem sensum maluerunt. Iam in homines non absimilis ingenij incidit ille quoque fœdissimè truncatus & mutilatus Anastasij, vel potiùs Damasi, aut alterius, Anastasio longè vetustioris, de vitis Pontificum liber. Nam primo ab iis Auctoris ad Hieronymum Præfatio sublata est, quod hodierno Cuiusque Romanæ stilo non multum conveniat. Deinde ex vita S.Petri periodum quam hic inseram, prout in omnibus manuscriptis exemplaribus extat, expunxerunt. Hic B. Clementem Episcopum consecravit,eiq; Cathedram, vel Ecclesiam omnem disponendam commisit, dicens. Sicut
units.tr: for this reason: just as the visible substance of this bread and wine nourishes and refreshes the outward man, so the Word of God, which is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful by their participation in it. So Isidore is quoted by Rabanus; but you will look in vain for these last words in the common manuscripts of his work, where the passage ends with these words: And what is better than the body and blood of Christ? Doubtless the Latins who came after the age of Isidore, first with the novelties of Paschasius Radbertus, and then when they admitted transubstantiation itself, were moved by the fact that Isidore calls it bread and wine, and says that both are compared to the body and blood of Christ, not that their substance is changed by a transfer into the substance of the body and blood of the Lord. This perhaps moved the same men, or at least men of the same kind, to write and publish in another work of Isidore as follows: Next follows the sixth confirmation of the sacrament: that the offering which is made to the Lord, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, may be confirmed to the body of Christ and to the blood, a sense that is either none or absurd. For what, I ask, is it to be confirmed to the body of Christ, or what does the Patristic library have as the body of Christ? Cassander, who now quotes the passage itself, reads conformetur, and the thing itself and the sense show that Isidore must have written may be conformed to the body of Christ and to the blood. But the Latins of later times thought that word too weak to represent the mystery of its transubstantiation [μετασχώσεως]. So they boldly changed it, and preferred to find in Isidore no sense here but one opposed to them. Now there fell upon men of no less unlike temper that other book, the life of the Popes, so foully truncated and mutilated, which bears the name of Anastasius, or rather of Damasus, or of some other writer far older than Anastasius. For first the author's preface to Jerome was removed, as it does not greatly suit the present style of the Roman [Church]. Then they struck out from the life of St Peter a sentence, which I shall insert here as it stands in all the manuscript copies: "Here he consecrated Blessed Clement as bishop, and committed to him the chair, or the whole Church to be ordered, saying: 'As

units.la: mihi gubernandi tradita est à Domino meo Iesu Christo potestas, ligandi, soluendi, ita & ego tibi committo, vt ordines. dispositores diuersarū causarum per quos actus Ecclesiasticus prosligetur, & tu minimè in curis seculi deditus reperiaris sed solummodo ad orationē & prædicationem populi vacare stude Post hanc dispositionē martyrio coronatur. His verbis testamentum concipiebat Petrus, sed quod eo cauerat suppressum est, hæredibus enim onus & officia imponebat immensum quantum ab ipsorum proposito & mor bus alienā. Alibi, apud eundnem scriptorem, ubi in omnibus manuscriptis codicibus Papa urbis, id est, Romæ legitur ; falsarij isti, Papam orbis substituerunt: sic enim nunc Romæ loquuntur. Voces illæ, Episcopus urbis Romæ, pridem obloleuerunt. Illiipsi sunt qui apud Fulbertum Episcopum Carnotensem, quo loco insignia Augustini verba profert, Figura est ergo præcipiens passioni Domini esse communicandi, has voces inseruerunt, figura ergo est, dicet hæreticus astuè hæretico tribuentes sententiam quæ reuera Augustini est, qualiter etiam à Fulberto allegabatur. Iidem sunt qui apud Gregorium magnum sacerdotum exercitus in sacerdotum exitus [ per quos apostasias & defectiones volunt intelligi. ] transformarunt. Legunt enim Epist. 38. lib. 4. Omnia &c. quæ prædicta sunt fiunt, Rex superbia prope est, & quod dici nefas est, Sacerdotum ei præparatur exitus; cum Manuscripti codices [imo & ipse Bellarminus † ] legant Sacerdotum ei præparatur exercitus. Iidem alium Gregorij insignem locum pari fraude corruperunt, qui in libris manu scriptis sie habet. Peruenit quoque ad nos quosdam scandalizatos fuisse, quod presbyteros chrismate tangere in fronte, eos qui baptizati sunt, prohibuimus. Et nos quidem secundū veterem vsum Ecclesiæ nostræ fecimus. Sed si omnino hac de re aliqui cōtristrantur vbi, Episcopi desunt, vt presbyteri etiam in frontibus baptizatos chrismate tangere debeant, concedimus. Recēntiores hæc quę hodierno Romanorum, de chrismatis in fronte ministro, dogmati aduersari videbant [ soli enim quæ Epis-
units.tr: the power of binding and loosing has been given to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I too commit to you that you appoint orders of officials for the various causes, through whom the ecclesiastical business may be carried on; and that you, not being given over to the cares of the world, be found devoted only to prayer and the preaching of the people.' After this arrangement he was crowned with martyrdom." Peter wrote his will in these words, but what he had provided in it was suppressed, for it imposed on his heirs an immense burden and duties far removed from their purpose and manners. Elsewhere, in the same writer, where all the manuscript codices read Pope of the city, that is, of Rome, those forgers have substituted Pope of the world; for that is how they now speak in Rome. The words "Bishop of the city of Rome" have long since dropped out of use. These same men, in the work of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, where he cites the famous words of Augustine, Therefore it is a figure which commands that the Lord's passion be shared, inserted these words: Therefore it is a figure, the heretic will say, craftily ascribing to the heretic a sentiment which is really Augustine's, as Fulbert was quoting it. They are also the men who, in Gregory the Great, changed an army of priests into an end of priests [by which they wish apostasies and defections to be understood]. For they read in Epistle 38 of book 4: All the things foretold are coming to pass; the king of pride is near, and, what is impious to say, the end of the priests is prepared for him; whereas the manuscript codices [and Bellarmine himself] read the army of priests is prepared for him. The same men corrupted another notable passage of Gregory by the same fraud, which in the manuscript books reads thus: It has also come to us that some have been scandalised because we forbade presbyters to touch with chrism on the forehead those who have been baptised. We have done this according to the old custom of our Church. But if in this matter some are troubled, where there are no bishops, we allow that presbyters too should touch the baptised on the forehead with chrism. More recent men, who saw that these words were opposed to the present doctrine of the Romanists concerning the minister of chrism on the forehead [for only bishops, they hold, may anoint the forehead of the baptised], boldly changed them in the editions, and in place of what Gregory wrote, "to touch with chrism on the forehead those who have been baptised," and "to touch the baptised on the forehead with chrism,"

units.la: Matth. 16. Ioan. 21. Concil. p. 664. [marginal references, partly illegible] copo baptizatorum frontes chrismare licet) audacter in editionibus mutarunt, & pro eo quod scripsit Gregorius, chrismate tangere in fronte eo: qui baptizati sunt; item, in frontibus baptizatos chrismate tangere, impudenter scripserunt, eos qui baptizandi sunt, & baptizandos chrismate tangere. Bellarminus ipse monuit corruptum esse locum, & veram quam exhibuimus lectionem, tum ex altero, ex ipsius Gregorii loco, qui extat eodem libro, epist.9. tum ex Gratiano & Thoma confirmat; qui hunc (inquit) locum ita citant, ut esse debet, non ut modo legitur in codicibus impressis. Illi ipsi sunt qui hunc Augustini locum commutarunt, quod suae transfusionis dogmati adversaretur; corpus Domini (inquit ille) in quo resurrexit, uno loco esse oportet; veritas autem ejus ubique diffusa est. Sic enim scriptum: Augustinum & res ipsa clamat, & apertissime testantur Iuo Cartonensis, Alger rus, Lombardus, Gratianus, Thomas, Bonaventura, Scotus, Durandus, Biel & alii veteres, qui haec verba sic plane recitant. Recentiores Latini pro illis verbis, uno loco esse oportet, haec, pessima & inverecunda fraude, substituerunt, uno loco esse potest, ut videre est in omnibus Augustini editionibus quae ex eorum officinis prodierunt. Ab eadem manu & causa est quod sequitur. Augustinus in Ioannem, tractatu 26. extremo, scripserat; A per hoc qui non manet in Christo, & in quo non manet Christus, procul dubio nec manducat carnem ejus, nec bibit ejus sanguinem, etiamsi tantae rei sacramentum ad iudicium sibi manducet & bibat. Quinovissimam Augustini editionem Parisiis anno 1635. procuraverunt, fatentur se locum ita scriptum in codicibus manuscriptis sex reperiri; atque ita lectum fuisse etiam Thomae Aquinatis tempore, ex ejus Catena (quod & editores isti annotarunt) patet; quod & ipsum ex Prospero quoque clarissime confirmatur, qui sententiam 319. quam ex hoc loco eruit, ita expressit: Nam qui discordat a Christo, nec carnem ejus manducat, nec sanguinem bibit, etiamsi tantae rei sacramentum ad quae {·}edicium sua praesumptionis quotidie indifferenter accipiat quae ita laudata sunt iam ante aliquot secula, & ab suone Carnotensi, & à Gratiano, & ab ipso Lombardo. At nuperas omnes editiones verba Augustini ridiculè sic interpolata exhibent. Ac per hoc qui non manet in Christo & in quo non manet Christus praesuldubio nec manducat [spiritualiter carnem eius, nec bibit eius sanguinem, licèt carnaliter & visibiliter premat dentibus sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi, sed magis tanta rei sacramentum ad iudicium sibi manducat & bibit, quia immundus praesumpsit ad Christi accedere sacramenta, quae aliquis non indignè sumit, nisi qui mundus est, de quibus dicitur, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Hactenus Latini corruptores; quorum nemo non videt quo spectet crassa ista planeq; inepta Augustinianæ orationi attexta lacinia; nempe ut persuadeant Christi carnem, quam Augustinus simpliciter negauerat ab indignè communicantibus sumi, ab iis carnaliter & visibiliter sumi, tamen si eadem spiritualiter ab ipsis non sumatur: Idem in tractatu de rectitudine catholicae conuersationis (qui non Augustini, sed Eligii Nouiomensis a.d.663. donati, verè est Oleum benedictum fideliter ab Ecclesia petat, unde corpus suum VNGATVR. At scriptum fuisse olim, unde corpus suum ungat clarè restatur Valdensis, dum locum ita citat; & sane id ipsum posci t Latini sermonis ratio (dicendum enim erat unde corpus eius ungatur, non autem corpus suum) ac firmat denique Sermo de Tempore apud Augustinum 215. hinc excerptus, in quo ungat legitur, non autem ungatur. Corruptores ungatur subticuerunt, ne haec Eligiana unctio à sua extrema videretur aliena; quam nemo agrotus sibi ipsi ministrat, ut notum est. Illi ipsi sunt qui Aimoino, vel eius certè Continuatori, supposuerunt quae sequuntur In qua Synodo (quam octavam universalem illuc convenientes appellarunt) de imaginibus adorandis secundum quod Orthodoxi Doctores antea definierant statuerunt cum prorsus contra scripsisset,aliter quàm orthodoxi definierãt sla'nerunt,ut apparet tum ex manuscriptis codicibus, tum ex antiquioribus editionibus, tum ex Baronio ipso,qui hoc postremo modo hunc locum laudat, Annalium Tomo decimo ad annum Christi oȼingentefimum sexagesimum nonum. Illi sunt qui ex Oecumenio locum sequentem † Qui enim Legi patrocinabātur ve- data ess,mãsit autem consuetudo illa in Phrygia,adeo ut Synodus Laodicena lege prohibuerit ad Angelos accedere,eosque precari,unde est quod apud eos sunt multa templa Michaelis Archangeli, vel sumi ducis exercitus. Quem locum David Hoeschelius in notis suis ad librum Origenis contra Celsum pag.483. testatur se vidisse & legisse in manuscriptis Oecumenii codicibus, qui tamen nullus est in hastenus excusis. Sed quod istos impulit causæ Romanæ studium Oecumenio sua hæc cripere, idem eos ista aliena Theodoreto commodare & affingere subegit. τᾶτο τὸ ἀπὸ ποσ δοματῶ ἐ] καθαρπόιλον ἐν ᾧ καθαῦ-ζο τοι αὶ ψυχαὶ ὡς χρυσὸς ἐν τὰ χανδ-ποἱω. Hunc ipsum ignem purgatorium credimus in quo animæ purgantur sicut aurum in conflatorio. Hæc enim tanquam Theodoreti verba & Latini Græcis iam pridem objectantur ut ex Nilo patet, & Bellarminus & Gagnæius velut ex Scholiis Theodoreti in 1 Cor.3. nunc quoque in disputatione de Purgatorio afferunt. Quæ & olim Græci Theodoreti sui esse negarunt, & nos hodie frustra siue in illius Patris in Paulum Commentariis,siue in aliis operibus quærimus, quæ nusquam istic reperiuntur, ne in nouissima quidem Theodoreti editione. Similia alterius Latinorum de sui Papæ primatu dogmatis studium Lhomam Aquinatem olim subegit falsa quædam testimonia & Chalcedonensibus Patribus, & Cyrillo Alexandrino affingere. Namadversus Græcos psiputans hæc seluti Calcedonensis Concilij decreta affert; Si quis Episcopus prædicatur infamis,liberam habeat sen. sententiam appellandi ad beatissimum Episcopum antiqua Romaniquia habemus Petrum petram refugij ; & ipsi soli libera potestate loco Dei sitius discernendi secundum clausa Domino sibi datas. Item ; Omnia ab eo definita tanquam à Vicario Apostolici throni: Denique , legitur ( inquit ) in Chalcedonensi Concilio quod TOTA Synodus clamauit Leoni Papae, Leo sanctissimus, Apostolicus, & Icumenicus (acumenicum ni fallor intelligit) Patriarcha multos viuat annos. Cyrillum vero idem Thomas haec quae ipse refert, in Thesauro scripsisse ait?Sicut Christus accepit à Patre super omnem principatum & potestatem, vt eicuncta curvenitur, plenissimam potestatem ; sic & Petro & eius successoribus plenissime committit. Item;Nulli alii, quam Petro Christus quod suum est plenum, sed ipsi soli dedit. Tum & illud;Apostoli in Evangelijs & epistolis affirmarunt in omni doctrina Petrum esse loco Dei & eius Ecclesiam. Et, Illi (Petro) omnes iure, diuino caput inclinant, & primates mundi tanquam ipsi Domino Iesu obediunt. Denique;Nos vt membra manere debemus in capite nostro Pontifice Romano, & Apostolico throno, à quo nostrum est quaerere quid credere & quid tenere debemus; quoniam solius Pontificis est arguere, corrigere, increpare, ratum facere, disponere, soluere, & ligare. Haec Thomas sane perquam impudenter ; quorum nihil in veris vel Chalcedonensis Synodi actis, vel Cyrilli operibus hodie vsquam legitur aut apud Graecos aut apud ipsos etiam Latinos. Quin & nunc quoque in tanta litterarum luce in similem tamen audaciam nonnunquam tamen multo quam olim parcius erumpunt.
units.tr: Matthew 16; John 21; Council, p. 664. [marginal references, partly illegible] to the bishop it is lawful to anoint the foreheads of the baptized) they boldly altered in the editions. In place of what Gregory wrote, "to touch with chrism on the forehead those who have been baptized," and likewise "to touch the baptized on the forehead with chrism," they shamelessly printed "those who are to be baptized, and to touch those to be baptized with chrism." Bellarmine himself admitted that the passage is corrupted, and he confirms the true reading that we have given, both from another passage of Gregory himself in the same book, Epistle 9, and from Gratian and Thomas. "Those who cite this passage," he says, "cite it as it ought to be, not as it is now read in the printed copies." These are the very men who changed this passage of Augustine, because it opposed their doctrine of transubstantiation. "The body of the Lord," he says, "in which he rose again, must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere." For that is how it was written. The matter itself cries out that this is Augustine's text, and the following writers most plainly attest it, quoting these words exactly as they stand: Ivo of Chartres, Alger, Lombard, Gratian, Thomas, Bonaventure, Scotus, Durandus, Biel, and other older authors. The recent Latin editors, by a wicked and shameless fraud, substituted for the words "must be in one place" the words "can be in one place," as may be seen in all the editions of Augustine that have come from their presses. From the same hand and the same motive comes what follows. At the end of Tractate 26 on John, Augustine had written: "Therefore whoever does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, without doubt neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment." The most recent edition of Augustine, prepared at Paris in 1635, admits that the passage is found written thus in six manuscripts; and that it was read thus even in the time of Thomas Aquinas is clear from his Catena (as those editors also noted). This is also most clearly confirmed by Prosper, who, in sentence 319, which he draws from this passage, expressed it thus: "For whoever disagrees with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he receives the sacrament of so great a thing to the judgment of his own presumption every day without distinction." These words were quoted long ago, some centuries since, by Ivo of Chartres, by Gratian, and by Lombard himself. But all the recent editions display Augustine's words in a ridiculously interpolated form: "And therefore whoever does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, without doubt does not eat [his flesh spiritually, nor drink his blood," although he presses with his teeth, carnally and visibly, the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ; but rather he eats and drinks "the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment," because, being unclean, he has presumed to approach the sacraments of Christ, which no one takes worthily unless he is clean, of whom it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Thus far the Latin corrupters; and none of them fails to see to what end this crude and plainly inept patch has been stitched onto Augustine's discourse: namely, to persuade that the flesh of Christ, which Augustine had simply denied is taken by those who communicate unworthily, is taken by them "carnally and visibly," even if it is not taken by them spiritually. Likewise, in the tractate On the Rectitude of Catholic Life (which is not Augustine's but truly that of Eligius of Noyon, dated 663), there is the phrase: "Let him faithfully seek the blessed oil from the Church, from which his body is anointed." But that it was formerly written "from which his body anoints (himself)" is clearly attested by the Waldensian, who cites the passage in this way; and indeed the very rule of Latin usage demands this (for it would have to be said "from which his body be anointed," not "his own body"), and the sermon De Tempore among the works of Augustine (number 215), taken from this passage, confirms it, since in it the reading is "anoints," not "be anointed." The corrupters kept silent about "be anointed," lest this unction of Eligius should seem alien to extreme unction, which, as is well known, no sick man administers to himself. These are the same men who attributed to Aimoin, or certainly to his continuator, the following words: "In which Synod (which those assembling there called the eighth universal council) they decreed concerning the adoration of images according to what the orthodox doctors had defined before," whereas the author had written exactly the opposite, "they decreed otherwise than the orthodox had defined." This appears both from the manuscript codices, from the older editions, and from Baronius himself, who cites this passage in this later form in the tenth volume of his Annals, at the year of Christ 869. These are also the men who, from Oecumenius, put forward the following passage: "For those who defended the Law... that custom remained in Phrygia, so much so that the Synod of Laodicea forbade by law to approach the angels and to pray to them; whence it is that among them there are many temples of Michael the Archangel, or of the leader of the army." David Hoeschel, in his notes on Origen's book against Celsus, page 483, testifies that he saw and read this passage in manuscript copies of Oecumenius, though it is not in any of the printed editions so far. But the same zeal for the Roman cause which drove them to snatch these words from Oecumenius also compelled them to ascribe and attach these other passages to Theodoret. [τοῦτο τὸ ἀπὸ πυρὸς καθαρτήριον ἐν ᾧ καθαίρονται αἱ ψυχαὶ ὡς χρυσὸς ἐν τῷ χωνευτηρίῳ.] "We believe that this very fire is a purgatory in which souls are purified as gold in the furnace." For these words are objected to the Greeks, long since, as if they were Theodoret's words, and as Latins, as is clear from Nilus; and Bellarmine and Gagnaeus, citing them as if from the Scholia of Theodoret on 1 Corinthians 3, still bring them forward today in their disputation on Purgatory. The Greeks of old denied that these were Theodoret's, and we today seek them in vain in that Father's Commentaries on Paul, or in his other works, where they are nowhere to be found, not even in the most recent edition of Theodoret. A similar zeal for the primacy of his own Pope once drove another of the Latins, Thomas Aquinas, to ascribe certain false testimonies to the Fathers of Chalcedon and to Cyril of Alexandria. For against the Greeks, in his Contra Errores Graecorum, he brings forward the following as decrees of the Council of Chalcedon: "If any bishop is accused of infamy, let him have free right of appeal to the most blessed bishop of ancient Rome, since we have Peter, the rock of refuge; and to him alone, in place of God, is given the free power of judging, according to the keys given to him by the Lord." Likewise: "All things defined by him as by the Vicar of the Apostolic throne." Finally, he says, "it is read in the Council of Chalcedon that the whole Synod cried out to Pope Leo: 'Leo most holy, Apostolic and Ecumenical (I think he means oecumenicus) Patriarch, may you live many years.'" And the same Thomas says that Cyril wrote in his Thesaurus as follows: "As Christ received from the Father all principality and power, so that every knee should bow, the fullest power; so also he most fully committed it to Peter and his successors." Likewise: "Christ gave what is his, in full, to no one but Peter, and to him alone." And also this: "The Apostles affirmed in the Gospels and the Epistles that in all teaching Peter is in the place of God, and his Church." And: "To him (Peter) all men bow the head by divine right, and the princes of the world obey him as they would the Lord Jesus himself." Finally: "We ought to remain as members in our head, the Pope of Rome and the Apostolic throne, from whom we must seek what we ought to believe and hold; for it belongs to the Pontiff alone to argue, correct, rebuke, ratify, dispose, loose, and bind." These things Thomas indeed asserts most shamelessly; yet none of them is read today anywhere in the true acts of the Council of Chalcedon or in the works of Cyril, either among the Greeks or among the Latins themselves. Indeed, even now, in such a light of learning, similar audacity sometimes breaks out, though much more sparingly than of old.

Fausti me nomen monet ne indictam præteream insignem Margarini de la Biblioth. gne impofturam, qui Fausti huius non uno à veteribus stigmate notati librum de gratia & libero arbitrio in altera Bibliothecæ Patrum editione lectori velut opus infigne propinat. Quin & hominem aperte Semipelagianum non fatis habens de infami hæreticorum tuba eripuiffe, cœlitum sanctorum choris inseruit modo Beatum †, † modo Divum * appellitans. Notarunt viri do ctrina & probitate insignes, in collecta quæ in festo Cathedræ S. Petri legitur, hæc antea fuisse verba. Deus qui B. Petro Apostolo tuo collatis claues regni cœlestis animas ligandi Pontificium tradidisti; Sed in posterioribus Breviariorum & Miffalium editionibus induffam vocem animas. * ne Papæ potestas ad spiritualia tantum, minime verò ad temporalia pertinere censeretur: Et in Euangelio fidei tertiæ quæ tertiam Quadragesimæ Do-miniçam sequitur excuderunt. Neque fuit frufra a Patribus institutum, vt de electio ne illorum qui ad regimen altarũ adhibendi sunt, consulatur M 3 etiam populus, quia de vita & conversatione praefetandi, quod nonnunquam ignoretur a pluribus sciturà paneis, & necesse est ut facilius ei quòs obedientiam exibebat, ordinato cui assensum praebuerit ordinando. Volebat bonus ille Canonicus haereticis omnia quae inde petunt argumenta erepta, ac proinde ut loci isti omnes de Pontificali expungerentur, ne ullum eorum in posterum vestigium superesset. Constat ex Hincmaro die S. Leonis dictam olim in Ecclesia Latina fuisse hanc orationem. Annue nobis Domine, ne, ut anima famuli tui Leonis hac prosit oblatio, quam immolando totius mundi tribuisti telaxari delicta. Constat ex Innocentio III. eandem in antiquis Missalibus plane ita conceptam fuisse. Respondet enim quaerenti, quare haec verba mutata fuerint, quae antiquiores codices continebant, pro quibus in modernis Sacramentariis ista haberi dicit quae& in nostris hodie leguntur: Annue nobis quaesumus Domine ut intercessione B. Leonis haec nobis prosit oblatio. Nempe deleta est ea oratio nis forma quae docebat Veteres etiam pro sanctis & quicte fruentibus animabus precari solitos; non adeo putasse quod apud Latinos postremorum temporum obtinuit, pro iis dunctaxat animabus esse precandum quae in fictitio purgatorij ignis carcere cruciarentur. In Martyrologia, quorum praecipuam inter publica Ecclesiae monumenta fidem atque integritatem est: decebat, eodem quoque modo nouitas atque aulacia grassata est. Ipse Areopagiticae Dionysio fabulae vindex ac defensor Milletus, scribit nulla ad nos nisi adjectione nouorum Sanctorum, aut Graecorum imitatione corrupta Martyrologia peruenisse. Bedae quidem Martyrologio [quod vetustissimum putatur] multa à Floro, multa ab aliis subinde addita vel detracta notat Launoyus, neque ea facile ab ipsis Bedae verbis discerni posse. Quod vero Eusebij dicitur, quam non fit Eusebij, ex eo, vt idem obseruauit, parer quod Hieronymum, Augustinum, Leodegarium, dedicatione Corbeiensis Ecclesiae memorat; quam vero fidem mereatur ex eo quod crucis Domi-
units.tr: Thus Bellarmine, to prove that the Creed circulating under Athanasius's name is a genuine work of his, did not hesitate to put some words of his own into Augustine's mouth. Naming Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, explicitly, Augustine (he says) in Psalm 120 quotes the whole article of this creed. Elsewhere again: "Holy Augustine (he says), in his tractate on Psalm 20, speaks thus, explaining that 'The sun shall not burn by day'; ... Father Athanasius of Alexandria did not hesitate to represent ..." I am reminded of the name of Faustus, lest I pass over the notable imposture of Margarin de la Bibliothèque, who in the second edition of the Bibliotheca Patrum offers the reader the book *On Grace and Free Will* by this Faustus, which has been branded by more than one of the ancients, as if it were an outstanding work. Not content to have rescued a man who was openly a Semipelagian from the infamous trumpet of the heretics, he has also admitted him to the choirs of the heavenly saints, calling him now *Blessed* †, now *Divine* *. And although in the most recent edition of the Bibliotheca, with Margarin's eulogies struck out, Faustus has been adorned with very different titles in line with his real merit †, yet even now there are no lack of Jesuits who fight for his name and reputation †. * But, to continue the line of argument I began, who would believe that even the Breviaries and Missals themselves have remained untouched by this audacity of theirs? Men distinguished for learning and integrity have noted that in the collect read on the feast of the Chair of St Peter the earlier words were: "O God, who gave to Blessed Peter your Apostle the keys of the heavenly kingdom and the power of binding souls"; but in the later editions of the Breviaries and Missals the word *souls* has been removed, so that the power of the Pope might be thought to extend only to spiritual matters and not at all to temporal ones. And in the Gospel for the third Sunday after the Quadragesima they have altered the text, where the old copies read "Jesus said to his disciples", to "Jesus, looking upon his disciples, said to Simon Peter, If your brother sins against you", and have omitted the words *to Simon Peter*, so that it would not seem that the Lord had sent Peter, that is the Roman Pontiff, to the tribunal of the Church, to which he refers him. And if the Fathers of Trent had agreed with the opinion of Thomas Pasquius of Valence, the Canon, all those passages in the Pontifical which mention the consent and agreement of the people in the ordination of ministers of the Church would have been struck out, and especially this one, where the bishop says at the ordination of a presbyter: "It was not without reason that the Fathers instituted that the people also should be consulted about the choice of those who are to be admitted to the ministry of the altar, because it is known to few what sort of life and conduct a man has who is to be placed in authority, and it is necessary that those over whom he is set should more readily render him obedience, once he has been ordained, to whom they have given their assent before his ordination." That good Canon wished all the arguments the heretics draw from these passages to be removed, and so all these places to be expunged from the Pontifical, so that not a trace of them should remain in future. It is established from Hincmar that the following prayer was once used in the Latin Church on the feast of St Leo: "Grant to us, O Lord, that through the intercession of your servant Leo this offering, which you have bestowed on the whole world to be offered, may bring the forgiveness of sins." It is established from Innocent III that the same prayer was plainly worded thus in the ancient Missals. For when asked why these words were changed, which the older codices contained, and in place of which the modern Sacramentaries have what we read today in ours, he replies: "Grant to us, we beseech you, O Lord, that through the intercession of Blessed Leo this offering may profit us." Clearly that form of prayer was deleted which taught that the ancients were accustomed to pray also for the saints and for souls enjoying rest; they did not think, as obtained among the Latins in later times, that prayer should be made only for those souls which are tormented in the imaginary prison of purgatorial fire. In the Martyrologies, whose chief trustworthiness and integrity lies among the public monuments of the Church, the same novelty and boldness have likewise run riot. Milletus, the champion and defender of the Areopagite Dionysius' fable itself, writes that the Martyrologies have come down to us only corrupted by the addition of new saints, or by imitation of the Greeks. Launoy notes that many things were added or removed from Bede's Martyrology (which is thought to be the most ancient) by Florus and others at various times, and that these cannot easily be distinguished from Bede's own words. As for the Martyrology that is said to be Eusebius's, how far it is not Eusebius's, he observed from this, that it mentions the dedication of the church of Corbie by Jerome, Augustine and Leodegarius; and what credit it deserves from the fact that it says the finding of the Lord's cross

Ianuarij: Cenomannis depositio S. Iuliani, primi eiusdem urbis Episcopi.
units.tr: happened 133 years after Christ's passion. As for more recent ones, it would be long and useless. I shall report only a few things noted by the same Launoy from the Roman Martyrology (which is the standard for all of them). On 28 May the Roman Martyrology, published at Padua about 1500 and at Venice in 1549, had: "St Caraunus, martyr, who at the city of Chartres won his martyrdom by beheading." Likewise on the Nones of August: "The deposition of Blessed Memmius, first bishop of the same place, who, among very many miracles, becoming illustrious by raising the dead, and whose tomb is made famous by most celebrated miracles." Likewise on 27 January: "At Le Mans, the deposition of St Julian, first bishop of the same city."

units.la: Sed postquam Monachis placuit & harum & multarum aliarum ciuitatum primos Episcopos homines fuisse Apostolicorum temporum, mutata est ad eorum gustum, vetus haec lectio. Petrus enim, primum, Galesinius Mediolanensis, tum etiam Baronius Cardinalis, in sua utrque Martyrologij Romani recognitione, primo quidem loco ita ediderunt. Carnoti in Gallia S. Caraunī Martyris, qui SVB DOMITIANO IMPERATORE capite amputato martyrium sumpsit. Secundo vero ita subsituerunt. Catalaunii in Gallia S. Memij CIVISROMANI QVIAS. PETRO illius ciuitatis Episcopus consecratus post sibi comissum ad Euangelij veritatem perduxit. Tertio denique haec recripserunt: Apud Cenomannos depositio S. Iuliani primi eiusdem urbis Episcopi QVEM S. PETRI SILLVC AD PRAEDICANDVM EVANGELIVM MISIT. Ita miserum Martyrologium posterorum impostura coegit testari Caraunum & Memmium & Iulianum Apostolorum, quod haetenus nescieuerat, temporibus vixisse, passoique esse. Idem Martyrologium Patauij à Bellino editum ad Kal. Octob. haec habet: Tornaco S Piatonis Presbyteri & Martyris, qui cum B.D I ONYSIO Episcopo, eiusque, sociis, ab urbe Roma Galliam praedicationis causa expetiit, ac postea in persecutione Maximiani consummato Martyrio migrauit ad Dominum. Hic vides. Dionysium Epi{s}copum (id est Parisiensem) cum eo homine venisse in Galliam, qui sub Maximiano (id est post A D.289 ) passus est, adeoque ; Areopagitam Pauli Discipulum esse non potest. Nostri Romani, ne haec impotuna vox suauia iuorum Areopagitarum somnia turbaret, totum locum pro sua libidine, sic ut est apud Baronium effinxerunt. Tornaci S. Piatonis Presbyteri & martyris, quicum B. Quintino eiusdem sociis ab urbe Roma in Galliam profectus, dicationis causa perrexit, ac postea in persecutione Maximiani consummato martyrio migrauit ad Dominum. In eadem veteri Patauina editione, ad d. 9. Non. Octob. ita scriptum habebatur. Natale B. Dionysy Episcopi & Martyris, qui post clarissimam confessionem fidei, post grauissima tormentorum genera gloriose martyrio coronatus est, ut testatur Aristides Atheniensis. Ad d. vero 7. Id. Octob. haec eadem in editio exhibebat; Natale SS. Martyrum, Dionysii Episcopi, Rustici presbyteri, & Eleutherij Diaconi, qui B. Episcopus a P. R. in Gallias praedicandi gratia directus, prefatam urbem deuenit, ubi per aliquot annos commissum sibi opus fideliter prosequens, tandem a Praefecto Fescennino unacum sociis gladio animaduersus martyrium compleuit. Istud Dionysiorum Episcoporum & Martyrum par, duobus diebus diuersis passorum, nostris Romanis disiplicuit, qui viderent, scilicet, eo nos doceri priorem quidem, d. 9. Non Octob. passum, Atheniensem fuisse; posteriorem vero, d. 7. Id. Octob passum, Parisiensem liquido esse, alium adeo ab Atheniensi. Itaque, ut tuta securaque; esset sua de Pationensi Areopagita fabula, effecerunt, ut prior ille Dionysius, d. 9. Non, iam passus, iterum, non quidem in gladium sed in spongiam incumbebat, ac de medio tollebatur. Alter solus, ad d. 7. Id Octob. superesset; quo loco, post Galesium, expuncta alterius ad 9. Non mentione, haec quoque habet Baronius Natalis SS Martyrum Dionysij AREOPAGITAE Epif. opi, &c. Ex quibus Dionysius AB APOSTOLO PAVLO BAPTIZATVS, PRIMVS ATHENIENSIVM EPISCOPVS EST ORDINA;
units.tr: But after it pleased the monks that the first bishops of these and many other cities were men of the Apostolic age, this old reading was changed to suit their taste. For Peter Galesinius of Milan first, and then also Cardinal Baronius, in their respective revisions of the Roman Martyrology, printed in the first place as follows: "At Chartres in Gaul, St Caraunus, martyr, who UNDER THE EMPEROR DOMITIAN won his martyrdom by beheading." In the second place they substituted: "At Châlons in Gaul, St Memmius, A ROMAN CITIZEN, who, consecrated bishop of that city by ST PETER, afterwards led to the truth of the Gospel those committed to him." Lastly they wrote this: "At Le Mans, the deposition of St Julian, first bishop of the same city, WHOM ST PETER SENT THERE TO PREACH THE GOSPEL." Thus the wretched Martyrology, by the imposture of later men, was forced to attest that Caraunus, Memmius and Julian lived in the time of the Apostles and suffered, which it had not known until then. The same Martyrology, as edited by Bellinus at Padua, has this at 1 October: "At Tournai, St Piatus, priest and martyr, who, with Blessed Dionysius the bishop and his companions, set out from the city of Rome into Gaul for the sake of preaching, and afterwards, in the persecution of Maximian, having completed his martyrdom, departed to the Lord." You see here that Dionysius the bishop (that is, of Paris) came into Gaul with a man who suffered under Maximian (that is, after A.D. 289), and so cannot be the Areopagite, the disciple of Paul. Our Romans, lest this troublesome word should disturb the sweet dreams of the Areopagite's admirers, invented the whole passage at their own pleasure, just as it stands in Baronius: "At Tournai, St Piatus, priest and martyr, who set out from the city of Rome into Gaul with Blessed Quintinus his companion, went on for the sake of preaching, and afterwards, in the persecution of Maximian, having completed his martyrdom, departed to the Lord." In the same old Padua edition, under 7 October, this was written: "The birthday of Blessed Dionysius, bishop and martyr, who, after a most famous confession of the faith, after the most grievous kinds of torment, was gloriously crowned with martyrdom, as Aristides of Athens attests." Under 9 October the same edition gave this: "The birthday of the holy martyrs Dionysius the bishop, Rusticus the priest, and Eleutherius the deacon, who, sent by the Holy See into Gaul for the sake of preaching, came to the aforesaid city, where for some years, faithfully carrying on the work entrusted to him, at last, by the prefect Fescennius, with his companions, was put to the sword and completed his martyrdom." This pair of bishops and martyrs of the same name, who suffered on two different days, displeased our Romans, who saw, of course, that we were being taught that the former, who suffered on 9 October, was the Athenian, and that the latter, who suffered on 7 October, was clearly the Parisian, and so quite different from the Athenian. Therefore, so that their fable of the Parisian Areopagite might be safe and secure, they arranged that the former Dionysius, already martyred on 9 October, should fall a second time, not on the sword but on a sponge, and be removed from the scene. Only the other remained, under 7 October; in that place, after Galesinius, with mention of the other on 9 October struck out, Baronius also has this: "The birthday of the holy martyrs, Dionysius the AREOPAGITE, bishop, etc. Of these, Dionysius, BAPTIZED BY THE APOSTLE PAUL, was ordained FIRST BISHOP OF THE ATHENIANS."

units.tr: Dionysius, baptized by the Apostle Paul,

units.la: I nunc,& nega istos viros esse.Sed Galesinius vetitus,credo,ne martyres haberet iratos,quod ex Ecclesiæ Diptychis unius de suis soldalibus nomen evasisset, numerum eorum ingeniose suppleuit, aliunde adscitis & in suam Martyrologij editionem præter vetustiorum librorum, cum scriptorum tum excusorum fidem infulcis aliorum martyrum nominibus ; ut ad d. 7. Kal. Iun. Vienne (inquit) S. Zachariæ Episcopi & Martyris, qui sub Traiano passus est. Item ad d.6.Id.Decemb.Treuirij S. Eucharij, discipuli B. Petri Apostoli,& primi eiusdem ciuitatis Episcopi Item ad d.18.Kal.Oct.Treuirij S.Materni Episcopi, discipuli B.Petri Apostoli,qui Tungrenses,Colonienses & Treuirenses aliosq; finitimos populos ad Christi fidem perduxit. Hæc adfabulas suas firmandas inuenta, & Galesinius Martyrologio Romano primus adjecit, & Baronius retinuit, quæ φιλαλνδίςατ Launoyus negat in veteribus libris,quoscunquè inspexit, extare. Sed & Galesinius suis Diuis nouam sanè, neque in hoc unquam orbe antea visam vel auditam comitem addidit, Synoridem Antiochenam , scilicet, Martyrem,quam ad d. 24. Ianu. ita consignauit ; ibidem ( id est Antiochiæ Sanctæ Synodi Martyris. Magnus Annalium parens in prima Martyrologii sui editione Galesinium bona fide secutus est,& hanc ad eius verba annotationem scripsit; De ea ( inquit, id est Synoride) Scribit S.Ioannes Chrysostomus homilia quarta de Lazaro. De alia iuniori,&c. Locus autem Chrysostomi in quo se suam Synoridem reperi sse putauit ita habebat apud Latinum interpretem. Verum non existimauimus esse statutum B Babylæ & Synorides Sanctorum Martyrum qui Babylæ secuti sunt recte facta præterire. Hinc etiam plane ioculari pro singulari sua in Græcis eruditione decepti Galesinius & Baronius Synoridis nomen esse putarunt mulieris alicuius proprium , quam, quia Babylæ coniungitur, & martyribus eum secutis , Antiochiæ &
units.tr: Go on now, and deny that these men existed! But Galesinius, fearing, I suppose, that the martyrs would be angry because the name of one of his own comrades had dropped out of the Church's diptychs, cleverly made up the number. He drew in names from elsewhere and inserted into his own edition of the Martyrology, alongside the testimony of older books, both manuscript and printed, the names of other martyrs. For example, at 7 Kalends of June he writes: Vienne (he says) S. Zachariæ Episcopi & Martyris, qui sub Traiano passus est. Likewise at 6 Ides of December: Treuirij S. Eucharij, discipuli B. Petri Apostoli, & primi eiusdem ciuitatis Episcopi. Likewise at 18 Kalends of October: Treuirij S. Materni Episcopi, discipuli B. Petri Apostoli, qui Tungrenses, Colonienses & Treuirenses aliosq; finitimos populos ad Christi fidem perduxit. These fables, invented to lend support to their own tales, Galesinius was the first to add to the Roman Martyrology, and Baronius retained them. Launoy, the lover of trifles, denies that they are found in any of the old books he has examined. But Galesinius also gave his saints a new companion, certainly one never before seen or heard of in this world: Synoris of Antioch, a martyr, whom he recorded under 24 January in these words: ibidem (that is, at Antioch) Sanctæ Synodi Martyris. Magnus, the parent of the Annals, following Galesinius in good faith in the first edition of his Martyrology, wrote this note on his words: De ea (he says, that is, concerning Synoris) Scribit S. Ioannes Chrysostomus homilia quarta de Lazaro. De alia iuniori, &c. The passage of Chrysostom in which he thought he had found his Synoris read as follows in the Latin translator: Verum non existimauimus esse statutum B. Babylæ & Synorides Sanctorum Martyrum qui Babylæ secuti sunt recte facta præterire. Hence Galesinius and Baronius, deceived by a foolish misreading (in their singular learning in Greek, that is, quite a joke), supposed that Synoris was the proper name of some woman, whom, because she is joined with Babylas, and with the martyrs who followed him, they decreed had suffered at Antioch and had been celebrated after the passion down to Chrysostom's time.

units.la: N passam esse, & post passionem ad Chrysostomi tempora celebratam decreverunt. Græca auctoris immanem istorum hallucinationem vel pueris produnt, quæ sic ha-bent,Αλλ' ὑχ ἀσθαλὴς ἴ) Ϲ‌ρομίσαμψ τὼ μαρτυρ ... Ἰ... τὰ χαπροθώματα. Sensum s sse,quem Fiomo Ducæus lesuita erudissimus in sua editione expressi, omnes qui Græcè sciunt vident; Verum existimavimus esse tutum B. Babylæ, & ξωοεἰδος, bigæ Sanctorum Martyrum, qui post illum occurrerunt, benefacta præterir. Hæc Martygum Synoris,sive biga, luventium & Maximum sig ificar, quos d. Ian.25. laudaverat, cum d. præcedente hoc est Ian.24.) Babylam laudasset, ut ex ea ipsa oratione apparet, quam in illos dixit. Sic enim eam orditur: O' μακαριος Βαβυ-λας ... λας ἀπαλω ὑμῶς ὁ ἴταξε μετα παιδων τεων σωτηρα. Synoris militū(i.e.par siue biga)in acie exercitum Christi ostendit.Heri quadrita Martyrum, hodie Synoris biga Martyrum. Illa ergo Chrysostomea Synoris,nō Virgo Antiochena,quod delirantes hatiolantur noui Mar-tyrologi,sed par duorum Martyrum est,luventius & Maximus,qui pro Christo una passi sunt.Rem fusè explicat Ducæus Notis ad posteriorem hunc locum,quem, si quis volat,consulat. Audio Baronium ipsum à Nicolao Fabio, & aliis amicis de fœdo & puerilli errore admonitum, & Galesinianum textum, & suam in eum Annotationem sustulisse (à posterioribus quidem Martyrologij editionibus absunt) & Synoridem siam retro, in nihilum, unde malis avibus venerat, egisse. Verisimile est simili errore Gais idum, vetetum Britanniæ historicum,& alios eum secutos, cum non intelligerent quid sit amphibalum (quod nomen significat birrum utrimque vilolum) in his Gildæ ve bis, sub sanctia Abbatis amphibalo,id pro viri proprio nomine accepisse, & apud Gildam ea psuisse quæ in aliquibus codicibus leguntur, sub sanctis Abbate. Amphibalo; ut suspicari quem posse ait reuerendiss. Vf serius; quod si verum est, ita ex cuculla vel birro factus fuerit Abbas, quod non est difficilius quam ex biga fieri virginem Martyrem Synoridem.
units.tr: The Greek of the author reveals their monstrous blunder even to boys. It reads: [Ἀλλ' οὐχ ἀσφαλὲς ἡγησάμεθα τὸν μακάριον Βαβύλαν καὶ συνωρίδα τῶν μαρτύρων ... τὰ κατορθώματα]. Everyone who knows Greek sees the sense, which the most learned Jesuit Fronto Ducaeus expressed in his edition: Verum existimavimus esse tutum B. Babylæ, & συνωρίδος, biga Sanctorum Martyrum, qui post illum occurrerunt, benefacta præterire. This Synoris, or pair (biga), of martyrs means Juventius and Maximus, whom he had praised on 25 January, the day after he had praised Babylas on 24 January, as appears from the very oration he delivered about them. For he begins it thus: "O blessed Babylas..." And further: "The pair (synoris) of soldiers shows the army of Christ in battle. Yesterday a quadriga of martyrs, today a biga of martyrs." So the Synoris of Chrysostom is not a virgin of Antioch, as the new Martyrology's dreamers prattle, but a pair of two martyrs, Juventius and Maximus, who suffered together for Christ. Ducaeus explains the matter at length in his notes on this latter passage, which anyone who wishes may consult. I hear that Baronius himself, admonished of his foul and childish error by Nicolas Fabri and other friends, both removed the Galesian text and his own note on it (they are absent from the later editions of the Martyrology), and sent Synoris back to nothing, whence she had come with ill omens. It is likely that Geoffrey of Monmouth, the old British historian, and others following him, through a similar error, not knowing what amphibalum means (the word signifies a double-sided cloak), took it in the words of Gildas, sub sanctis Abbatis amphibalo, as the proper name of a man, and that they read in Gildas what is found in some manuscripts, sub sanctis Abbate Amphibalo, as the most reverend Ussher suspects. If this is true, an abbot was made out of a hooded cloak or a cloak, which is no more difficult than making a virgin martyr Synoris out of a biga.

units.la: Sed satis non fuit his modis quædam ex quibus de veteris Ecclesiæ sententia nobis constare poterat monumenta depravare, in libros totos sæuitum est, & in iis magno numero abolendis allaboratum. Quod ut pernoscamus, sciendum est prioribus seculis Imperatores Christianos in scriptis, quæ rectæ fidei aduersari censebantur, exterminandis gnauiter incubuisse, ut patet ex libris Arianorum, Nestorianorum & aliorum eiusmodi, quos certum est seueris Principum istorum Edictis non solum prohibitos, sed etiam profligatos & abolitos suisse. Quinimo Ecclesia ipsa, sicubi in libris superiorum aliquid animadverteret, quod cum receptis suo tempore sententiis non conveniret, eorum scripta, licet pridem in Catholicorum communione obdormiissent, infamia notabat. Sic in Synodo quinta Oecumenica, cum Theodoro, Theodoreto, & Iba, illo Mopsuestensi, isto Cyrenensi, hoc Edesseno, Episcopis, licet longè ante in Ecclesiæ pace defunctis, actum est, ut & cum Origene, etsi tre centis annis ante mortuo. Non defuit hic Pontifex Romanus sibi, vestigiis istorum institit, ni etiam dicendus sit eos cum tempore superasse. Visit, secuit, imo & penitus ipsa monumenta oppressit, si quid in Veterum scriptis occurrit à sententia sua alienum. Nec duorum, triumue, quatuor, aut quinque seculorum, vel etiam plurium ætati parcitum est. Exempli causa; Num vetus Ecclesia in templis suis Christi & sanctorum imagines habuerit coluerit ve, hodie disputatur. Certatum est etiam super hac controuersia diu & acriter in Græcia. Cùm in Concilio VII. Nicææ habito superiores euasifsent qui cum affirmantibus sentiebant, prohibuerunt ne quis adversarum partium libros apud se haberet, iusse runtq; ut ad Patriarchan Constantinopolitanum comportarentur omnes, ut scilicet, iis fieret secundum Papæ Adriani Legatorum postulata, & flammis mandarentur quæcunque scripta su ssent aduersus venerabiles imagi Nec dubium est quin eadem clade perierint, quæ cunque è libris veterum repugnare viderentur. Cuiusmodi fuere Eusebii ad Constantiam, & Epiphanij ad Ioannem Hierosolymitanum epistolæ, & aliæ quæ ea calamitate absumptæ, ut probabile est, nunc desiderantur. Epistola enim Epiphanij quam habemus est ex interpretatione Hieronymi & in Occidente conseruata, ubi studium imaginum longè remissius fuit quàm inter Orientales, apud quos Archetypos Græcum periit. Hos imitatus Adrianus II in suo Concilio decernit in Acta Concilij, quod Photius aduersum Ecclesiam Romanam cogerat, cum iis omnibus quæ cum Photius, tum qui à partibus eius stabant, contra sedem Romanam scripse- rant ignibus tradantur; quod & in Synodo VIII. quam Latini Occumenicam volunt, denuo imperauit. Fieri non potest quin iis ignibus conflagrarint plurima mo numenta quæ usui esse potuissent in illustranda veteru m sententia, seu super imaginibus, de quibus in Synodo VII. actum erat, seu super auctoritate Pontificis Romani, de qua maximè certabatur in controuersia Photij, cuius ea de causa, etiamnum Romæ sub clavi cohibentur scripta nonnulla, quæ proculdubio edita habe- remus, si tam in rem Romanam fuissent, quàm probabile est ab ea esse aliena. Inter hodiernas controversias nulla fere est ea nobilior quæ de panis Eu. haristici transsubstantiatione agitatur. De hac nono etiam seculo diuersæ fuerant doctorum virorum sententiæ. Nam cùm Paschasius Rarbertus Adbas Corbeiensis a. 818. librum edidisset quod transsubstantiationem aperte ponere videtur, Theologi aliquot horum & proximorum temporum eruditissimi, inde orta rei accuratius expendendæ occasione, contra nouum illud dogma. scripserunt. In primis Amalarius Archidiaconus Tre- uirenuirensis, Rabanus Abbas primò Fuldensis & Moguntiacus demum Archiepiscopus, & apud nos Heriboldus Episcopus Antisiodorensis, Ioannes Scotus, siue Erigen.,& Rathramnus, siue (ut vulgo nunc dicitur) Bertramus. Cùm Berengarius, qui undecimo postea seculo Ratberti opinionem vehementer confutabat, Ioannis Erigenæ de hoc argumento opus afferret, magniq; faceret, Synodus Vercellensis à Leone Papa IX. de hac causa habita est; atque in ea Ioannis illius Scoti de Eucharistia liber lectus est ac damnatus, (inquit Lanfrancus tum vetus tradit, Berengarium Romam à Nicolao P. R. euocatum, Ioannem Scotum igni combussisse, id est Scoti librum; ipse enim in Britannia ante annos 167. hoc est A. D. 883. in summa eruditionis atque pietatis opinione mortuus erat, ut tradit Guilielmus Malmesburiensis. Vecunque fit Vercellensi illo, Romanoq; fulmine ita aflatum concidit Ioannis opusculum, ut plane penitusq; interiit; quod tamen si superesset, luculentissimum testimonium prohiberet de novitate transsubstantiationis. Eadem ut videtur causa & Rabani ad Egilonem Epistolæ, & Heriboldi Antisiodorensis disputationi perniciem attulit, quos duo de hoc argumento contra Ratberti opinionem tractatus extitisse certam fidem facit vetustissimum manuscriptum opusculum, quod in Bibliotheca Thuanæa seruatur. Et manuscripti opuscul testimonium firmant Thomas Valdensis de utroque viro verba, dum Vicleff de Eucharistia sententiam refellens, scribit eum consonare Heribaldo & Rabano Moguntinensi ponentibus (inquit) venerabile sacramentum altaris ob noxium esse ieiesuni, vel (ut eorum sententiam in disputatione titulo inuidiose expresserat) corpus Domini in sacramento esse cibum digerendum in humanam carnem. Sed quia Ratberti dogma postea praualuit, eo factum, ut iis qui essent, tamen veterum, sc. ipta quae receptae opinioni repugnarent, ea paulatim obliterarentur; neque alia manerent quàm quæ cum præsentis sæculi fide congruerent. Itaque Ratberti quidem liber vivit ac floret, Ioannis verò Scoti, Ereboldi Antisiodorensis, Rabani ipsius, viri alioqui clarissimi, sed in has causa improbati, contraria Ratberto opuscula perierunt. Vnius Rathramni fœlicius fatum fuit, cuius de tam multis Ratberti adversariis opus hostium manus effugit, & ad nos incolume peruenit; sed à nostræ memoriæ hominibus pessimè, ut mox dicemus, exceptum Eo tandem deventum est, ut Leo x. in Concilio Lateranensi, quod anno 1518 finem habuit, decreverit ne ullus librum aliquem, seu aliam quamcunque scripturam, primere seu imprimi facere præsumeret, nisi prius in urbe per sacri Palatij Magistrum, in aliis verò Diœcesibus, per Episcopum vel alium ab Episcopo ad id deputandum, & Inquisitiorem hæretica pravitatis diligenter examinetur; sub pœna et qui secus præsumpserit, ultra librorum impressorum amissionem, & illorum publicam combustionem, solutionis centum ducatorum fabricæ Principis Apostolorum de Vrbe, sine spe remissionis (cuius quidem multæ nullum in ullis Veteris Ecclesiæ canonibus exemplum occurrit) ac suspensionis anni continui exercitij impressionis, & sententiæ ex communicationis quæ innodatus existat. Quo decreto generali non minus Patrum opera quàm alia comprehenduntur, ut apparet ex eo quòd cum Episcopus Melfitanus, lecto decreto, respondit, sibi placere de novis operibus, non autem de antiquis, reliqui omnes Patres simpliciter placere dixerunt, nec ulla decreto addita fuit limitatio. Idipsum distertis conceptisque verbis confirmauit Concilium Tridentinum, præsertim qui libros recognoscerent & recenserent, & de eo ad Concilium referrent, ut facilius possent varia & peregrina doctrina, tanquam Zizania à Christi. Siana veritatis tritico separarent, id est, ut expungi & induci usu sacrorum queat quicquid Ecclesiæ Romanæ palato non sapit. Sed cùm ipsis Patribus per otium non licuisset in tam sanctum opus incumbere, qui ad id delecti fuerant, iusi sunt quicquid præstirissent Pontifici Romano exhibere. † Hinc profluxere Pij iv. primùm, deinde Sixti v. & Clementis viii. jussu editæ regulæ, & Indices libro-rum & Auctorum quos abolendos aut repurgandos censuerunt; tam accuratè & sollicitè librorum impressioni consuluerunt, ut in locis,in quibus ex istorum præcepto viuitur, nullo modo metuendum sit, ne vel minimum quid in lucem exeat, quod vel Ecclesiæ Romanæ noxium sit, vel adversariis ejus commodum. Has autem omnes regulas, quas, quod prolixæ sint, molestum esset hic inserere,ad finem Concilij Tridentini,ad quod plerumque subtexi solent, videre est. Deinceps strenuè operi manus admoræ & procusi sunt Indices expurgatorij (quos vocant Belgicus, Madritianus, Sandoualianus, & alij, quibus egregij isti Censores veluti totidem machæris libros omne genus confodiunt, laniant, concerpunt, exscindunt, periodos, capita, tractatus totos pro sua libidine mutant, vel effingunt, idque sæpe in operibus Scriptorum qui, maximam partem, nati, educati & mortui in eorum communione sunt. Si ab hinc octingentis, aut nongentis annis eadem fuit Christianorum diligentia ac praxis, operam ludit qui altiùs ascendit, ut pernoscat quæ fuerit Veterum Christianorum sententia super controuersiis nostris, quæcunque enim fuerit, vix fieri potuit ut eiusmodi Censorum manus effugerit. Quod si nihil simile vel institutum vel usu receptum in Ecclesia fuit, quare, qui nos Antiquitatis adeo studiosos fingimus, huiusmodi novitates usurpamus? Scio profiteri Censores istos,se nonnisi in recentiores, cultros & novaculas stringere; sed quis non videt fucum fieri, & hoc obtendine Poetici Iouis ipsis objiciatur sœuitia, qui ne patris quidem sui genitalibus pepercit? Quæ adeò sollicitè recentiorum scriptis expunguntur, longè magis noxia sunt, cum iu Veterum libris (ut plerumque fit) occurrunt. Quæ,malum,est hæc, seu moriositas,seu inconstantia, ea, ubi magis nocenec relinquere, ubi verò minùs nocent, tollere? Inquisitio Adorari folium Dei est quæ tamen ipsissima sunt verba Athanasij†.Idem Patet dicit* esse quosdam libros,) præter eos quos recensuerat scilicet) qui in Canonem recepti non sunt,sed ad id à Patribus constituti ut legantur iis qui accedunt ad Arianos,& qui volunt instituì in verbo pietatis, quo in ordine ponit Sapientiam, Ecclesiasticum, ludith, Esther, Tobiam,& alios quosdam. Et tamen iidem Expurgatores, ex Indice operum Athanasii,verba quibus libros istos non esse Canonicos significatur delent. † Ex Indice Augustini hæc verba expungunt. quæ tamen diserte & totidem syllabis habentur apud Augustinum ipsum, contra Adimant. cap. 12. Ex eodem hæc quoque inducì jubent. Augustinus putat Eucharistiam negotiorum esse fantibus,licet in ea sententia fuerit Augustinus paßimque in operibus ejus, cùm iisdem verbis, tum aliis, ut infra videbimus, occurrat. Ex eodem similiter dicent Templa Angelis non sunt construenda, & tamen diserta sunt Augustini verba; Nonne si templum alicui sancto Angelo excellentissimo de lignis & lapidibus faceremus anathematizaremur à veritate & ab Ecclesia? Censores Belgæ & Hispani eadem methodo utuntur in multis aliis locis quos hic referre necesse non est. Si vero eiusmodi gnomas ex indiciis expungis, quare eas è textu ipso non euellis? Aut si in hoc relinquis quare in illis deles? Quid sibi vult in hominibus adeo sapientibus consilium tam insolens? Sed quis non videt quomodo se res habent? Gnomæ illæ, quæ istis dant adeo graues poenas, non minùs ipsis inuisæ sunt apud Veteres, quam apud recentes Scriptores,& cùm id tutò licet, non minùs ex illis quàm ex his eas expungunt: Sed palam non audent, ne maior ex eo oriatur offensio, quàm ea est cui mederi student. Si enim adeò inuerecundè Antiquitatem haberint, reuerentiam qua omnes eam prosequuntur penitus euerterent. Cum autem ab eorum rebus id multis de causis fit
units.tr: But it was not enough to corrupt, in these ways, some of the records from which the opinion of the ancient Church could be known: they raged against whole books and laboured to destroy great numbers of them. To see this, we must know that in earlier centuries Christian emperors vigorously set about exterminating writings thought to oppose the true faith, as is clear from the books of the Arians, the Nestorians and others of that kind, which were certainly not only forbidden but also destroyed and abolished by the severe edicts of those princes. Indeed the Church itself, wherever it noticed in the books of earlier writers anything that did not agree with the opinions received in its own time, branded their writings with infamy, even though they had long since fallen asleep in the communion of the Catholics. Thus in the Fifth Ecumenical Council, Theodore, Theodoret and Ibas (the first of Mopsuestia, the second of Cyrrhus, the third of Edessa), bishops who had died long before in the peace of the Church, were condemned, and Origen too, though he had died three hundred years earlier. The Roman Pontiff has not been lacking to himself; he has followed in their footsteps, unless indeed it must be said that they have been outdone by time. He visits, cuts and even utterly suppresses the monuments themselves, if anything in the writings of the Ancients is alien to his opinion. Nor has the age of two, three, four or five centuries, or even of more, been spared. For example, whether the ancient Church had images of Christ and the saints in its temples, and whether it worshipped them, is disputed today. This controversy was also long and bitterly fought in Greece. When, at the Seventh Council of Nicaea, those who agreed with the affirmers had gained the upper hand, they forbade anyone of the opposing party to keep books in his possession, and ordered that all of them be brought to the Patriarch of Constantinople, so that they might be dealt with as the legates of Pope Adrian demanded, and that whatever writings had been published against the venerable images be committed to the flames. There is no doubt that whatever seemed to oppose the ancient books perished in the same disaster. Of this kind were the letters of Eusebius to Constantia and of Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, and others which, as is probable, were consumed in that calamity and are now lost. For the letter of Epiphanius that we have is in Jerome's translation and was preserved in the West, where zeal for images was much milder than among the Easterners, among whom the Greek original perished. Imitating these men, Adrian II in his council decreed, in the Acts of the council that Photius had gathered against the Roman Church, that all the writings which Photius, and those who stood on his side, had written against the Roman See should be handed over to the flames; and in the Eighth Synod, which the Latins wish to be ecumenical, he ordered the same thing again. It cannot be but that very many monuments which could have been useful in illustrating the opinion of the ancients were burnt in those fires, whether concerning images, which had been debated at the Seventh Synod, or concerning the authority of the Roman Pontiff, which was the chief point of contention in the controversy with Photius. For this reason some writings are still kept under lock and key at Rome, which we would undoubtedly have published if they were as favourable to the Roman cause as it is probable they are alien to it. Among today's controversies there is scarcely any more notable than the one about the transubstantiation of the bread of the Eucharist. Concerning this, the opinions of learned men were also divided in the ninth century. For when Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, published in 818 a book which seems plainly to posit transubstantiation, several very learned theologians of that time and the next, prompted by this occasion to weigh the matter more carefully, wrote against that new doctrine. Foremost among them were Amalarius, archdeacon of Trier, Rabanus, first abbot of Fulda and then archbishop of Mainz, and among us Heribold, bishop of Auxerre, John Scotus, or Eriugena, and Ratramnus, or (as he is commonly called now) Bertram. When Berengar, who in the eleventh century vigorously refuted Radbert's opinion, brought forward and greatly valued John Eriugena's work on this subject, a synod was held at Vercelli on this cause under Pope Leo IX; and in it that book of John Scotus on the Eucharist was read and condemned (as Lanfranc says, handing on the old tradition that Berengar, summoned to Rome by Pope Nicholas, burnt John Scotus in the fire, that is, Scotus's book; for Scotus himself had died in Britain 167 years earlier, that is in AD 883, held in the highest esteem for learning and piety, as William of Malmesbury relates). By whatever that Vercelli or Roman thunderbolt was struck, the little work of John was so utterly destroyed that it perished completely; yet had it survived, it would have given the clearest testimony against the novelty of transubstantiation. For the same reason, it seems, the letter of Rabanus to Egilo and the treatise of Heribold of Auxerre also met their ruin; a very old manuscript pamphlet, preserved in the Thuanaean library, makes it certain that these two men wrote treatises on this subject against Radbert's opinion. And the words of Thomas Waldensis about both men confirm the testimony of the manuscript pamphlet, when, refuting Wyclif's opinion on the Eucharist, he writes that Wyclif agrees with Heribold and with Rabanus of Mainz, who hold that the venerable sacrament of the altar is harmful to eat when fasting, or (as in his disputation he had invidiously put their opinion in the title) that the body of the Lord in the sacrament is food to be digested into human flesh. But because Radbert's dogma later prevailed, it came about that those writings which, though they were by the ancients, opposed the accepted opinion were gradually obliterated, and only those remained which agreed with the faith of the present age. Thus Radbert's book lives and flourishes, while the works of John Scotus, Heribold of Auxerre, and Rabanus himself, a most distinguished man otherwise but condemned in this cause, opposed to Radbert, have perished. Only the fate of Ratramnus was happier: of so many opponents of Radbert, his work escaped the hands of enemies and came down to us unharmed; but it was very badly treated by men of our own memory, as we shall say shortly. At length it came to this, that Leo X, in the Lateran Council which ended in 1518, decreed that no one should presume to print, or cause to be printed, any book or other writing unless it had first been carefully examined in the city by the Master of the Sacred Palace, and in other dioceses by the bishop or by someone the bishop appoints for this, and by the Inquisitor of heretical depravity; under penalty, for whoever acts otherwise, besides the loss of the printed books and their public burning, of a payment of one hundred ducats to the fabric of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, without hope of remission (of which penalty no example is found in any canon of the ancient Church), and of suspension from the practice of printing for a whole year, and of the sentence of excommunication under which he stands bound. By this general decree the works of the Fathers are included no less than others, as appears from the fact that when the Bishop of Melfi, on hearing the decree read, replied that he approved of the new works, but not of the old, all the rest simply said they approved, and no limitation was added to the decree. The Council of Trent confirmed the same thing in plain and express words, especially that those who should revise and review the books and report on them to the Council should do so so that they could more easily separate the various and foreign doctrines, like tares, from the wheat of Christ's truth; that is, so that whatever does not suit the palate of the Roman Church may be expunged, and whatever it likes may be introduced into the use of the sacred rites. But since the Fathers chosen for this holy work had no leisure to apply themselves to it, they were ordered to present to the Roman Pontiff whatever they had done. † Hence came the rules issued by order first of Pius IV, then of Sixtus V and Clement VIII, and the Indexes of books and authors which they judged to be abolished or purged; and they have looked after the printing of books so carefully and anxiously that in places where men live under their precepts there is no need to fear that even the smallest thing harmful to the Roman Church, or advantageous to its adversaries, should come to light. These rules, which are too lengthy to insert here, may be seen at the end of the Council of Trent, to which they are usually appended. Then the expurgatory Indexes (which they call the Belgian, the Madrid, the Sandoval, and others) were vigorously set to work and printed, by which those excellent censors, as with so many swords, hack, tear, rend and cut out books of every kind, change or invent periods, chapters and whole treatises at their pleasure, and this often in the works of writers who, for the most part, were born, educated and died in the communion of those very men. If for eight or nine hundred years before, Christians had the same diligence and practice, the man who goes further back is wasting his effort if he wishes to learn what the ancient Christians thought on our controversies; for whatever it was, it could hardly have escaped the hands of such censors. But if nothing similar was either instituted or customary in the Church, why do we, who pretend to be so devoted to antiquity, use such novelties? I know that those censors profess that they sharpen their knives and razors only against recent writers; but who does not see that this is a pretence, and that by this pretext they might be charged with the cruelty of the Poetic Jove, who did not spare even his own father's genitals? Those things which are so carefully expunged from recent writings are far more harmful when they occur in the books of the ancients, as they usually do. What, for heaven's sake, is this, whether fastidiousness or inconstancy, to leave alone where they do more harm, and to remove where they do less harm? They delete To adore the leaf of God is [Adorari folium Dei est], although these are the very words of Athanasius.
