The same Athanasius says that there are certain books (besides those he had listed) which are not received into the canon, but were appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who come over from the Arians, and who wish to be instructed in the word of piety; in which class he places Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Esther, Tobit and certain others. And yet the same expurgators, from the Index of Athanasius's works, delete the words by which those books are declared not to be canonical. † From the Index of Augustine they delete these words, which nevertheless are found expressly, and in exactly the same syllables, in Augustine himself, Against Adimantus, chapter 12. From the same Index they also order this to be introduced: Augustine thinks the Eucharist is a matter of business for the hungry, although Augustine was of that opinion, and it occurs throughout his works, both in these very words and in others, as we shall see below. From the same Index they will similarly say: Temples are not to be built for angels; and yet the words of Augustine are express: Should we not be anathematized by the truth and by the Church, if we made a temple of wood and stone to some most excellent holy angel? The Belgian and Spanish censors use the same method in many other places, which it is not necessary to mention here. But if you expunge such maxims from the indexes, why do you not tear them out of the text itself? Or if you leave them in the text, why do you delete them from the indexes? What does such an unusual policy mean in men so wise? But who does not see how the matter stands? Those maxims, which bring such heavy penalties on these men, are no less hateful to the Ancients than to recent writers; and since they can do it safely, they expunge them from the one no less than from the other; but they do not dare to do it openly, lest a greater offence arise from it than the one they are trying to remedy. For if they treated antiquity so shamelessly, they would utterly overturn the reverence with which all men follow it. But since this happens in their affairs for many reasons, and is very far from their own interest,

units.la: vehementer alienum plane ipsorum magnopere interest,reuerentiam illam, saltem in speciem sartam & tectam tueri. Sed dum tam acriter castigant miserellos illos qui in Veterum opera indices construxerunt, vna fidelia (ut est in Prouerbio) duos parietes dealbant. Inuisas quidem sententias conuellunt, dum hos recentiores tam acerbè excipiunt, reuerentiam vero erga veteres rebus suis necessariam testantur, dum Patribus, veris sententiarum auctoribus, parcunt. Quanquam ne illud quidem simpliciter verum est, quod Patribus parcant, quorum plurima monumenta non una ratione aboleuerunt, vt ex iis exemplis patet quæ vel memorauimus, vel mox affetemus. Quæso enim nonne Patres erant illi trecenti Francofordiensis Synodi Antistites, quorum Binius Canones in Conciliorum editione suppressit ob damnatam secundo Cenone Nicænam de cultu imaginum definitionem; Nonne Patres erant Synodi Pariensis, sub Ludouico pio, Episcopi, quorum isti librum modis omnibus infamare atque abolere conantur, quemque Hispanici Censores diserte inter prohibitos nominant; Ludouici(inquiunt) Imperatoris nomine liber sictus contra sacras imagines. Ille vero adeo non est sictus, vt( quod mox dicemus) etiam à Iesuita celeberrimo Sirmondo pro vero & genuino Episcoporum à Ludouico Lutetiæ a. d. 824. congregatorum fœtu agnoscatur. idem eos quoque Caroli libros pro veris, & octauo seculo scriptis habet, quos Tridentini Bibliomastiges in interdictorum, atque delendorum operum ordinem retulerunt. Quid de Synodo Remensi dicam, cuius Acta ante sexcentos quinquaginta annos ab eo homine edita qui postea Romæ Pontifex sedit, isti nunc boni posteri desputant & ex omnibus libris delent? Certè & inter veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores clarnit ille Ioannes Erigena, siue Scotus, (id est, vt hodie loquimur, Hibernus) cuius de Eucharistia liber fere ducentis post auctoris mortem annis exstitit, vt iam diximus. Neque causa:
units.tr: It is plainly not in their interest to preserve that reverence, at least in outward appearance, intact and covered. But while they attack so fiercely those poor fellows who compiled indexes of the works of the Fathers, they are, as the proverb says, whitewashing two walls with one bucket of lime. They do tear out the hated opinions, by treating these more recent writers so harshly, and they testify to the reverence for the ancients that their cause requires, by sparing the Fathers, the true authors of those opinions. Yet even this is not simply true, that they spare the Fathers, whose many monuments they have destroyed for more than one reason, as the examples we have mentioned, or shall soon mention, make clear. For were not those three hundred bishops of the Synod of Frankfurt Fathers, whose canons Binius suppressed in his edition of the Councils, because of the definition about the worship of images that the Nicene Council had condemned at the Second Council of Nicaea? Were not the bishops of the Synod of Paris under Louis the Pious Fathers, whose book these men try by every means to discredit and abolish, and which the Spanish censors expressly list among the prohibited books, calling it "a book falsely put out in the name of the Emperor Louis against sacred images"? Yet it is so far from being "falsely put out" that, as we shall say presently, it is acknowledged as a true and genuine product of the bishops gathered at Paris by Louis in the year 824 by the famous Jesuit Sirmond himself. The same Sirmond also holds those books of Charles to be genuine and written in the eighth century, which the Tridentine book-burners have placed in the list of forbidden and destroyable works. What shall I say of the Synod of Reims, whose acts were published six hundred and fifty years ago by the man who afterwards sat as Pope at Rome, and which those good descendants now dispute and delete from all their books? Certainly among the ancient Doctors of the Church that famous John Erigena, or Scotus (that is, as we would say today, the Irishman), also shines; his book on the Eucharist existed nearly two hundred years after the author's death, as we have already said. Nor can a reason be given why Rathramnus of Corbie should not also be counted among the Fathers, whose treatment of the same subject, disputed, we shall presently show how badly these men have received.

units.la: Neque vero de recentiorum numero fuit Huldaricus Augustanus huius nominis Episcopus prior, † Rathramni (vt videtur) aequalis, cuius epistolam ad Nicolaum. P. R.I. pro Sacerdotum coniugio nono saeculo scriptam simpliciter exungunt & Tridentinorum & Hispanorum indices † Est quoque inter veteres censendus nobilissimus scriptor Sigebertus Gemblacensis, quem ante annos quingentos, & quod excurrit undecimo saeculo praecipiti, ineunte duodecimo floruisse constat, Atqui ne huius quidem operibus parcitum est, Turpes mitto notas quibus eius chronicon, laudatissimum opus, deformarunt censores Hispani †. Sed & hi, & ante hos ipsi quoque Tridentini insignem Sigeberti de Papali in Principes tyrannide suo primum tempore ab Hildebrando vsurpata disputationem in suos vtrique indices, veluti exitio deuotum opus, retulerunt, his verbis, Sigeberti hber contra Papam Gregorium, & contra epistolam Pas- chalis Papae. Circa eadem tempora scriptus est liber de vnitate Ecclesiae conseruanda pro Henrico IV. Augustoaduersus Hildebrandum Apologeticus; siue eum Venerico Vercellensi, siue Valramo Naumburgensi, siue denique Conrando Trajectensi Episcopo tribuamus. Atqui & in hunc ipsum dicta est ab Hispanis tristis haec sententia; Pracidatur tota Apologia Henrici IV. Neque mitius iudicarunt de sacris ipsius Augusti literis Expungantur (inquiunt) nomen epistolae Henrici IV. Imperatoris. Eo minus mirandum, quod in Honorium Aug. Istodunensem, ² in Dantem ᵇ in Petrarcham, in Theodoricum à Niem, ᶜ c ibid.in Fal. in ᵈ Ockamum, ᵉ & alios sequentium temporum Scriptores, tametsi pro nostro saeculo veteres grassari aui sint. Neque ij disputationem quandam inter clericum & militem de ciuili & Ecclesiastica potestate ab incerto quidem auctore, sed tamen ante A. D. 1580. scriptam omiserunt Sed Romani nostri ne iis quidem nunc abstinent, quae publico suae ipsorum Ecclesiae usu consecrata erant. Nam Hispanicus; Index ex quodam libro, cuius hic erat titulus Ordo baptizandi cum modo visitandi iuxta ritum S. Romanae Ecclesiae, tria haec quae sequuntur loca deleri iubet. 1. Credis non proprie meritis, sed passionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi virtute & merito a d gloriam peruenire? 2. Credis quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus pro nostra salute mortuus esset? & quod ex propriis meritis, vel alio modo nullus possit saluari, nisi in merito passionis ipsius? 3. Non erit desperandum vel dubitandum de salute illius qui supra positas petitiones corde crediderit, & ore confessus fuerit. Haec Hispanici Censores, quae à suo de operum humanorum apud Deum meritis dogmate aliena, & contrariae Protestantium sententiae plane penitusque consona esse censebant, expungi praecipiunt ex libro illo Venetiis A.D.1575. apud Ioannem Guarisecum & Socios, excuso. Et infelicem librum iam antea, nisi corrigetur, proscripserat Index Romanus. Atqui haec quae isti delent etiam apud eorum maiores, etiam Romae in communi usu antehac fuisse, & ille ipse liber docet, & locupletissimus testis est Hosius Cardinalis, qui se Sacerdotale Romanum vidisse narrat, in quo ipsa illa quae nunc isti delent (ea enim describit) totidem verbis haberentur & confirmant denique Anselmi Cantuariensis ad fratrem morituum exhortatio, & aliorum formulae in quibus plane similia leguntur. Atque hae quidem sunt artes quibus isti extinguere atque abolere conati sunt quicquid Romanorum doctrinae aduersatur, si quis tamen veterum huius generis liber, rata aliqua genii sui foelicitate, superatis omnibus & temporum & hominum injuriis, ad nos usque manserit; ne sic quidem eo in his de religione disputationibus uti fruiqi; licebit. In hunc enim Romanorum partium Theologi facta veluti coniuratione plerumque insurgunt, hunc vel de medio, si licet, tollunt; si non licer, calumniantur, infamant, nullum non lapidem movent ut Scriptor fiat intestabilis; fine hoc quidem assequi possunt, testimonium certè ipsum, aut expungunt aut variis fraudibus interuertunt, ac, neufui esse possit, efficiunt. Ita Bellarminus (ut exemplis al'q.ior rem illuftrem) Marci Eremitæ Opuscula, quod multa continere videret de fide,deque iustitia apud Deum nostra, ab hodiernis Romæ placitis aliena, infamauit, scribens fe suspicari cogi vel ab hareticis nostri temporis confiĉta,aut valde depravata esse, id est, à Papæ Romani communione alienis,Exrat Gelasij P.R.de duabus Christi naturis contra Eutychem liber, in quo insignis habetur contra transfubftantiationem locus. Cùm librum vererem esse non possent negare Romani Theologi, eo confugerunt, ut alterius esse quam Gelasii Romani contenderent; quod, viri docti, & fui Pontificis, maximam est auctoritatem intelligerent. Primò ergo & Baronius, & Bellarminus, & Petronius, & alij, conquisitis undique sophismatis ac strophis, pugnant non esse Gelasij urbici Episcopi, tum miserum opusculum à vera ac genuina parentis fui familia abactum in alienum ignobilius nomen tranfcribunt; aliique Gennadii, alij Gelasij nescio cuius Cæsarienfis, alii denique alterius Gelasij Cyziceni fœtum effe affirmant; ut incerti auctoris testimonium nullius fit apud homines fidei. Nequicquam; quod hunc ipfiffimum libellum Gelasio Papæ jampridem asseruerint auctores duo omni exceptione maiores, Fulgentius Ruspensis*, & Ioannes P.R.II. † A.D.794. celeberrima 300. Episcoporum Synodus Francofordiæ habita est; in qua constans est omnium pene historicorum veterum fides, damnatam esse Nicænam alteram pro imaginum venerarione ac cultu Synodum. Quid hic Romanarum partium magistri? Illi vero negant quicquam huiusmodi in hac Synodo fuisse decretum; etiam aiunt in ea confirmatam fuisse Nicænam, adeoque & venerationem imaginum. Quin & eo impudentiæ progressi sunt, ut in
units.tr: Nor indeed was Huldaric, the earlier bishop of Augsburg of that name, one of the more recent writers; he was a contemporary (as it seems) of Rathramnus. Their censors simply strike out his letter to Nicholas I, written in the ninth century in defence of the marriage of priests, both in the Tridentine and in the Spanish indexes. † The most noble writer Sigebert of Gembloux must also be reckoned among the ancients; it is established that he flourished five hundred years ago, and, to go beyond that, at the very beginning of the twelfth century, just as the eleventh century was ending. Yet not even his works have been spared. I pass over the shameful marks with which the Spanish censors have disfigured his chronicle, a most praised work. † But these men, and before them the Tridentine men themselves as well, have placed in each of their indexes Sigebert's notable disputation on the papal tyranny over princes, first usurped by Hildebrand in his own time, as a work devoted to destruction, in these words: "Sigebert's book against Pope Gregory, and against the letter of Pope Paschal." About the same time was written the book "On preserving the unity of the Church," an apologetic work for the Emperor Henry IV against Hildebrand; whether we attribute it to Venerius of Vercelli, or to Walram of Naumburg, or finally to Conrad, bishop of Utrecht. Yet against this very book the Spaniards pronounced that grim sentence: "Let the whole Apology of Henry IV be cut away." Nor have they judged more gently the sacred letters of the same Emperor: "Let the name of the letter of the Emperor Henry IV be expunged," they say. All the less is it to be wondered at that they have acted in the same way against Honorius Augustodunensis, Dante, Petrarch, Theodoric of Niem, Ockham, and other writers of later times, although these are, for our century, almost ancient. Nor have they passed over a certain disputation between a cleric and a soldier on civil and ecclesiastical power, by an anonymous author, yet written before the year 1580. But our Romanists do not now even abstain from those things that had been consecrated by the public use of their own Church. For the Spanish Index, from a certain book whose title was "The order of baptizing together with the manner of visiting, according to the rite of the Holy Roman Church," orders these three passages that follow to be deleted: (1) "Do you believe that you come to glory not by your own merits, but by the power and merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ?" (2) "Do you believe that our Lord Jesus Christ died for our salvation, and that no one can be saved by his own merits, or in any other way, except in the merit of his passion?" (3) "There is no need to despair or doubt of the salvation of one who with his heart believes the petitions set out above and confesses them with his mouth." These the Spanish censors, judging them alien to the doctrine of human merits before God, which is theirs, and wholly and entirely consonant with the opposed opinion of the Protestants, order to be expunged from that book, printed at Venice in the year 1575 by John Guarisco and partners. And the Roman Index had already condemned this unhappy book, "unless it be corrected." Yet that these things, which those men now delete, were also in common use earlier among their own forebears, even at Rome, both the book itself teaches, and Cardinal Hosius, a most abundant witness, who says he saw a "Roman Sacerdotal," in which those very things that they now delete (for he describes them) were found word for word; and finally the exhortation of Anselm of Canterbury to a dying brother, and other formularies in which wholly similar things are read. These, indeed, are the arts by which they have tried to extinguish and abolish whatever is opposed to the doctrine of the Romanists. If any book of this kind from the ancients, by some happy good fortune of its own genius, has survived to our time, overcoming all the injuries of times and men, not even so will it be permitted to enjoy or use it in these disputations about religion. For the Romanist theologians, as if by a conspiracy, usually rise up against such a book; they remove it from the world, if that is allowed, and if not, they slander it and defame it, and they move every stone to make its author infamous. Though they cannot achieve this, they at least either expunge the testimony itself or distort it by various frauds, and bring it about, so that it may not be of use. Thus Bellarmine (to illustrate the matter with a single example), seeing that the works of Mark the Hermit contained much about faith and about our justice before God, alien to the present decrees of Rome, defamed them, writing that he suspected they had been "either forged by heretics of our time or greatly corrupted," that is, by men alien to the communion of the Roman Pope. The book of Gelasius, Roman Pope, on the two natures of Christ against Eutyches, in which a notable passage against transubstantiation is found, exists. Since the Roman theologians could not deny that the book was ancient, they took refuge in contending that it was by another author than Gelasius of Rome, which, learned men, and as men who understand the great authority of their own Pontiff, they would have to recognise. First, therefore, Baronius, Bellarmine, Petronius and others, gathering sophisms and tricks from every side, fight that it is not by Gelasius, bishop of Rome, and then they transcribe the wretched little work, cast out from the true and genuine family of its parent, under a foreign and less noble name. Others affirm that it is the offspring of a Gennadius, others of some Gelasius of Caesarea, I know not which, and others finally of another Gelasius of Cyzicus; so that the testimony of an author of uncertain identity should carry no faith with men. In vain: for two authors of the highest standing, beyond all exception, Fulgentius of Ruspe and John, have long since asserted this very little book to be by Pope Gelasius.

units.la: publicis atque authenticis Conciliorum Tomis, ubi ad hanc ventem est, hunc ei titulum præscripserint Tum Synodi ea quidem exhibent, quæ aduersus Elipandum acta sunt, Canones vero, quorum secundus est in Nicænam Synodum difertissimus, planè plenitusque omiserunt; id molientes, scilicet ut ij paulatim aboleantur. I hunc, & nega frontem perfe de rebus. Sed frustra & hi quoque fuerunt. Repertus est enim vir Romanæ communionis, & quidem leguita, eruditissimus Sirmondus, qui totam istorum sophisticen discussit, & omnes Synodi Francofordiensis Canones, & in his secundum, optima fide publicavit, & Nicænam pro imaginibus Synodum damnatam esse docuit. Extant item Caroli Magni libri, de imaginibus, quatuor, circa eadem tempora aduersus Nicænæ Synodi decreta scripti; parentum verò nostrorum memoria, A. D. 1549. à Ioanne Tilio Briocensi primùm, deinde Meldensi Episcopo editi; qui suorum inuidiam & odia veritas, interpolato suo nomine se pro Ioanne Eliam pro Tilio Phityram dixit, teste Paulo Petavio Parisiensi Senatore, quod Ioannes Baptistes alter Elias dictus fuerit; φιλύρα vero tilia arbor à nostris vocata sit, Tillet Hos libros statim inuaserunt Romani Theologi; & Sustius quidem assentiente Suarezo putida haereticorum fraude sub Caroli nomine excusos esse ait, non absque contumelia tam sanctii principis. Bellarminus opus esse dicit hominis barbari, imperiti, leuis, ac pene stulti. Alij miserum scriptorem aliis conuitiis perfunduntur. Sed quam sint immanes istorum sycophantiae, & res ipsa loquitur, Sirmondus satis eo fatetur quod scribit libros Caroli pro legitimis nunc omnes fere agnoscere, neque id inficiari posse nisi qui Hadriani Papæ ad eosdem libros responsionem seu confutationi quæ in omnium manibus versatur fidem detractam velit. A. D. 824. Kal. Nou. Ludouici Pij iussu habitus est Lutetiæ -oporum in Palatio conuentus, in quo dicta sunt multa hodierno Romanorum de imaginibus dogmati aduersantia. Extat de Actis illius Conuentus Liber, nomine Synodi Parisiensis, ex Pithoeano, manu, in membranis, scripto, eoq; vetustissimo ac optimæ fidei codice, qui etiam hodie in Bibliotheca Thuanæa seruatur, descriptus, & in Germania publicatus. Sed huic tamen libro Romani nostri, tametsi Episcoporum sit & Veterum & Catholicorum, & ab optimo ac Christianissimo Principe Ludovico probatus, locum in sua Conciliorum editione nullum esse passi sunt, ne hæc extarent suæ à veterum in Gallia Christianorum fide diuersitatis argumenta
units.tr: in the public and authentic volumes of the Councils, where the title has been prefixed to this one. They do print the proceedings against Elipandus, but they have completely and entirely omitted the canons, of which the second is the most explicit statement against the Nicene Synod. They did this, of course, so that these would gradually be abolished. Go on, then, and deny the facts with a straight face! But these men too have failed. For the very learned Sirmond, a man of the Roman communion and a Jesuit, has come forward. He has dismantled all their sophistry, published all the canons of the Synod of Frankfurt, the second among them in good faith, and taught that the Nicene Synod was condemned for the sake of images. There are also four books of Charlemagne on images, written about the same time against the decrees of the Nicene Synod. In the memory of our parents, in 1549, they were first published by John Tillet, bishop of Saint-Brieuc, and then by the bishop of Meaux. To avoid the hatred and odium that his own people would feel, he disguised his name, calling himself John Elias instead of Tillet, and Phityra instead of Tilia, as Paul Petau, a senator of Paris, testifies, because John the Baptist was called another Elijah; but the philyra [φιλύρα] is the tree our people call the lime tree (tilia). Roman theologians immediately attacked these books. Sanctius, with Suarez agreeing, says they were published under Charles's name through the foul fraud of heretics, to the insult of so holy a prince. Bellarmine says the work is that of a barbarous, unskilled, shallow, almost stupid man. Others heap other insults on the wretched writer. But how monstrous the slanders of these men are, the matter itself shows. Sirmond himself admits enough when he writes that nearly everyone now acknowledges Charles's books as genuine, and that this cannot be denied except by someone who wishes to take away the credibility of Pope Hadrian's reply to the same books, which is in everyone's hands. In the year 824, on the first of November, by the command of Louis the Pious, an assembly of bishops was held at Paris in the palace, in which many things were said that conflict with the present Roman doctrine on images. There exists a book of the acts of that assembly, called the Synod of Paris, copied from the Pithou manuscript, a handwritten parchment codex, very old and of the best authority, which is still preserved today in the Thuanus library, and it was published in Germany. But although this book is the work of bishops, both ancient and Catholic, and was approved by the best and most Christian prince Louis, our Romanists have not allowed it any place in their edition of the Councils, lest these should stand as proofs of the difference between their faith and the faith of the early Christians in Gaul.

units.la: Quin & locum qui huic debebantur, apud eos occupat verbosa ac sophistica Bellarmini in ipsum opus disputatio; in qua omnibus modis pugnat ut liber nullius sit fidei. Suspicatur vel totum esse confictum ab haereticis recentioribus, vel depravatum & auctum ad inuidiam Romanæ Ecclesiæ conciliandam, denique sive sit verus, sive conflictus sive partim sincerus, partim adulterinus, luce certè dignum esse negat, indignumq; pronuntiat in quo legendo tempus teratur, cuius scilicet dictio barbara sit, sententia insulsa, ordo perversus, crebra eorundem repetitio. His isti flosculis exornant etiam vetustissimos libros, quicunq; à Romanis placitis discedunt. Sirmondus librum quidem verum confitetur, & ab Episcopis Galliæ Ludovici iussu atque auctoritate confectum. Sed neque ipse totum suæ Conciliorum Gallicanorum collectioni inserere ausus, duas tantum Ludovici epistolas edidit Ceteris (ut ait) quæ in huius conuentus Actis continentur praetermissis, quod Gallorum eius seculi ab imaginum adoratione abhorrentium mharefim redolerent. Ita vir, alias satis candidus, antiquissimam maiorum nostrorum de imaginibus sententiam haereseos damnare, & quæ illi ea de re scripserant æterna oblivione sepelire maluit, quam suorum odia atque inuidiam provocare. Iam post Ludovici Pij tempora ad Carolum eius filium Rathramnus Corbeiensis, vulgò Bertramnus,
units.tr: Moreover, the place that was due to this book is taken among them by Bellarmine's verbose and sophistical disputation against the work itself. In it he fights by every means to show that the book is of no authority. He suspects that it is either entirely fabricated by recent heretics, or corrupted and enlarged to make the Roman Church odious; finally, whether it is genuine, or fabricated, or partly sincere and partly spurious, he denies that it is worth publishing, and declares it unworthy of anyone's time to read, since its language is barbarous, its meaning dull, its order confused, and its repetitions frequent. With these flowers they also adorn the most ancient books of any writers who depart from Roman opinions. Sirmond indeed confesses that the book is genuine and was produced by the bishops of Gaul by the command and authority of Louis. But he himself did not dare to insert the whole of it into his collection of the Gallican Councils; he published only two letters of Louis, leaving out the rest of what is contained in the acts of this assembly, because (as he says) they would smell of the heresy of the Gauls of that age, who abhorred the adoration of images. So this man, otherwise quite candid, preferred to condemn as heresy the most ancient opinion of our forefathers about images, and to bury what they had written on the subject in eternal oblivion, rather than provoke the hatred and odium of his own people. Now, after the time of Louis the Pious, Ratramnus of Corbie, commonly called Bertram, wrote to Charles his son,

units.la: Tom. 6. Concil. p. 306. C. 1. tramus, insigne de Christi corpore volumen testibus Trithemio & Sigeberto scripsit quod ad nos (vt nuper diximus) mansit, & auorum nostrorum memoria a. 1532. Coloniæ,& alibi postea, è manuscriptis codicibus optima fide publicatum est, vt vel ex iis antiquitatis notis appareat, quæ toto opere cernuntur. At Romanarum partium homines, ne suæ transsubstantiationis nouitatem inde possemus ediscere, librum, primò vexare, ac infamare, sum abolete; postremo vitiare & interpolare totis viribus agressi sunt. Sixtus Senensis scribere non dubitauit, pernitiosu esse Oecolampadij volumen aduersus sacramentum corporis Christi ab impiu suorum temporum hereticu, (sic enim ille nostros pro sua modestia appellat) invulgatum sub titulo Bertrami Presbyteri de corpore & sanguine Domini ad Carolum M. Tridentinæ verò Synodi deputati, intacto auctore, opus ipsum in secunda Indicis sust classe reposueruut, in quam, non auctores, sed libri sunt relati, qui propter doctrinam quam continent nō sanam aut suspectam reiiciuntur, etiasi auctores à quibus prodiere ab Ecclesia nunquam desciuerunt. Ergo nunc isti librum, non Oecolampadij, ut Sixtus sané temere & impudenter, sed Bertrami esse putarunt, quem tametsi scirent ac confiterentur nunquam ab Ecclesia desciuisse, eius tamen opusculum simpliciter & absolutè prohibuerunt quo scilicet doctrinam continet non sanam (id est à Papali fide alienam) iudicarent. Eadem sere est Molani, Aubetti Mirʒ †, & Gilberti Manguini * sententia. Ideo Index Hispanicus Tridentinos secutus. Totum (inquit (liber Bertrami Presbyteri penitus auferatur, ex orthodoxographo rum volumine. Censores verò Belgici cum eo agunt mitiùs dicam an inhumaniùs, dum si ipsum planè non iugulant, saltem membris mutilant, quasi alterum Deiphobum apud Poetam, Lacerum crudeliter ora, Ora, manusq́, ambas populatas, tempora raptisAuribus, & truncas inhonesto vulnere nares.
units.tr: Tom. 6 of the Councils, p. 306, C. 1. ...ramnus, a remarkable volume on the body of Christ, which, as the witnesses Trithemius and Sigebert state, has come down to us (as we said recently), and was published in good faith in Cologne in the year 1532 from manuscript codices, and later elsewhere, so that the marks of antiquity that appear throughout the whole work are evident even from them. But the men of the Roman party, lest from it we should learn the novelty of their transubstantiation, first attacked the book, defamed it, and then with all their strength set out to corrupt and interpolate it. Sixtus of Siena did not hesitate to write that the volume of Oecolampadius against the sacrament of the body of Christ is pernicious, put out by an impious heretic of our times (for thus he calls our people, with his usual moderation), published under the title of Bertram, presbyter, on the body and blood of the Lord, to Charles the Great. The deputies of the Council of Trent, however, left the author untouched, and placed the work itself in the second class of the Index, into which are placed not authors but books, which are rejected because of the doctrine they contain, which is not sound or is suspect, even though the authors from whom they came never departed from the Church. So now these men have thought that the book is not Oecolampadius's, as Sixtus rashly and shamelessly said, but Bertram's; and although they knew and admitted that he never departed from the Church, they nevertheless forbade his little work simply and absolutely, evidently judging that it contains doctrine that is not sound (that is, foreign to the Papal faith). The opinion of Molanus, Aubertus Miraeus, and Gilbert Mangin is nearly the same. Therefore the Spanish Index, following the Tridentines, says: Let the book of the presbyter Bertram be removed entirely from the volume of orthodox writers. The Belgian censors deal with it more gently, or I should say more harshly, since, if they do not outright cut its throat, they at least maim its limbs, like the other Deiphobus in the poet: They cruelly tore his face, his mouth, and both his hands, his ears, and cut off his nose with a shameful wound.

units.la: Prolixioresenim ex eo locos duos vno calami ductu expunt, adeo vt exigui Tractatus, qualis iste est, non minimam partem constituant, cum singuli viginti octo aut triginta versiculis constent. Cur autem Censores Belgici quem librum scirent a Tridentinis suis exserte prohibitum, exitioque deuotum, cum ipsi tolerandum, dummodo emendatum, iudicarint, operæ pretium est audire. Quanquam (inquiunt) librum istum magni non existimemus momenti, itaque non magnopere laboraturi simus, si vel nusquam fit, vel intercidat, attamen cum iam saepe recusus fit & lectus à plurimis, & per interdictum nomen omnibus innotuerit: hæreticis conflet de eius prohibitione per varios catalogos; fuerit Catholicus Presbyter, ac Monachus Corbeiensis cœnobii, Carolo non tam Magno, quum Calvo carus, ac venerabilis; iuuet historiam eius ætatis; in Catholicis veteribus aliós plurimos feramus errores & extenuemus, excuseamus, excogitato COMMENTO persæpe negemus, & commodum iusensum AFFINGAMVS, dum opponuntur in disputationibus, aut confutationibus cum aduersariis; non videmus cur non eandem æquitatem, & diligentiæ recognitionem mereatur Bertramus; nec hereticis agganniant nos antiquitatem pro ipsis facientem exurere, & prohibere? itaque mirum non esse pauca pro ipsis videri facere nobis Catholicis tam irreuerenter antiquitatem vel in speciem à nobis dissentientiæ exsibilare æquer. dere. Quin & illud metuimus, ne liber iste non solum ab hareticis, verum immorigeris quoque Catholicis ob interdictum: avidius legatur, odiosius allegetur, & plus vetitus, quam permissus noceat. Hactenus Belgæ Censores, quorum ego candorem exosculor; primo quod non dissimulant se vno hæreticorum quos vocant, & Catholicorum immorigerorum metu, non aliqua in antiquitatem reuerentia deterreri à perdendo Bertramo. Tu idem de cæteris dictum puta; siquid à sui Papæ dictatis abludunt. Sed & illud quanti est, quod sé Belgæ isti in veterum negotio veterat res esse ipsi simpliciter, ac optima quidem fide proficentur; dum edunt ingeneque, quæ suæ, quæ suorum sint in iis eludendis artes, quæ quin Patrum sint dubitari non potest? illa se scilicet extenuare, excusare,alio inflectere vel excogitato COMMENTO, vel AFFICTO sensu commodo. Equidem in omnibus ubi bici Papæ copiis non putoullos esse melioris fidei sophistas, quam bonos istos Belgas. Atqu;hinc,si lippus non es, videre potes,quæ sit universi Romanorum generis de Patribus istis, quas ad rauim clamitant, sententia quæ quantaque in eas humilitas, ac docilitas. Cæterum quin vere commentum sit quod ipsi mox Belgæ in artis suæ veteratoriæ experimentum, de Bertrami in suo libello mente, atque consilio excogitant; nemo dubitabit, qui rem ipsam paulo attentius consideraverit, neque se sciens volens istorum offuciis, ac præstigiis deludi siuerit. Sed duo tamen quod iam diximus, loca quæ suis scilicet artibus emolliri posse desperarunt, fortiter sane amputarunt; Alexandrum æmulati, qui quem manu non satis expediebat nodum, eum ferro exsecuit. Horum locorum alterum, quo lector de Censorum audacia certius iudicare queat, hic totum placuit describere. Considerandum quo quc(verba sunt Bertrami de sanċta Eucharistia agentis) quòdinpane illo,non solum corpus Christi,verum etiam corpus in eum credentis populi figuretur: unde multis frumenti granis conficitur, quia corpus populi credentis multus per verbum Christi fidelibus augmentatur (al.coagmentatur) qua de re sicut mysterio panis ille Christi corpus accipitur,sic etiam in mysterio membra populi credentis in Christum intimantur. Etsicut non corporaliter,sed spiritualiter panis ille credentiū corpus dicitur: sic quoque Christi corpus non corporaliter, sed spiritualiter necesse est intelligatur.Sic & in vino,squi sanguis Christi dicitur, aqua misceri iubetur,nec unum sine altero permittitur offerri,quia nec populus sine Christo nec Christus sine populo, sicut nec caput sine corpore,vel corpus sine capite valet existere. Aqua denique in sacramento populi gestat imaginem Igitur si vinum illud sanctificatum per ministrorum officium in Christi sanguinem corporaliter conuertitur, aqua quoque,quæ
units.tr: For they strike out two rather long passages from it, with a single stroke of the pen, so that a little treatise such as this one loses no small part, since each of the passages consists of twenty-eight or thirty short verses. It is worth hearing why the Belgian censors, knowing this book was expressly forbidden and doomed by their Tridentine masters, nevertheless judged it tolerable if only it were corrected. "Although," they say, "we do not think this book of great importance, and we would not labour greatly if it vanished or perished entirely; yet since it has been reprinted so often and read by so many, and its forbidden name has become known to everyone through various catalogues among the heretics; since it was written by a Catholic presbyter and monk of the monastery of Corbie, dear and venerable to Charles, not so much the Great as the Bald; since it helps the history of that age; since we bear with and minimise many other errors of the ancient Catholic writers, excuse them, and often deny them with a contrived commentary, and adapt a convenient sense when they are opposed in disputations or refutations against adversaries; we do not see why Bertram should not deserve the same fairness and careful revision. Nor should we allow the heretics to triumph over us by burning and forbidding an antiquity that favours them. Therefore it is no wonder that some things seem to favour them, when we Catholics so irreverently hiss at antiquity, or at least at what appears to dissent from us. Indeed we fear also that this book, because of the prohibition, may be read more eagerly by heretics and by unruly Catholics, cited more hatefully, and do more harm because it is forbidden than if it were permitted." So far the Belgian censors, whose candour I embrace; first, because they do not hide that they are deterred from destroying Bertram not by any reverence for antiquity, but by fear of the heretics, as they call them, and of unruly Catholics. Take the same to be said of the others, if they depart in any way from the dictates of their Pope. But this too is significant: those Belgians, in matters of antiquity, openly confess that they are themselves skilled cheats, and they do so in good faith and simply. They show plainly what tricks they use to elude the Fathers, and there can be no doubt that these are the Fathers' own tricks: namely to extenuate, excuse, and bend the text elsewhere, either by a contrived commentary or by an adapted sense that suits them. Indeed, I think that among all the papal forces there are no better-intentioned sophists than these good Belgians. And from this, if you are not blind, you can see what is the opinion of the whole Roman race about those Fathers whom they proclaim so loudly, and how great is their humility and docility toward them. But that it is truly a commentary which the Belgians themselves next devise, as a trial of their deceitful art, concerning Bertram's meaning and purpose in his little book, no one will doubt who considers the matter a little more carefully and does not knowingly and willingly allow himself to be deceived by their trickery and juggling. Yet they have boldly cut out two passages, which they despaired of softening by their usual arts, imitating Alexander, who, when he could not untie the knot by hand, cut it with the sword. So that the reader may judge more surely of the censors' boldness, I have chosen to describe here the one of these passages in full. We must consider (these are Bertram's words, treating of the holy Eucharist) that in that bread not only the body of Christ is figured, but also the body of the people believing in him. Hence it is made of many grains of wheat, because the body of the believing people is increased by the word of Christ to the faithful (another reading: is joined together). Just as by the mystery of the bread the body of Christ is received, so also in the mystery the members of the people believing in Christ are signified. And just as that bread is called the body of the believers not bodily but spiritually, so also the body of Christ must be understood not bodily but spiritually. Likewise in the wine, which is called the blood of Christ, water is commanded to be mixed, and it is not permitted that one be offered without the other, because the people cannot exist without Christ, nor Christ without the people, just as the head cannot exist without the body, or the body without the head. Finally, the water in the sacrament bears the image of the people. Therefore if that wine, sanctified by the ministry of the ministers, is converted bodily into the blood of Christ, the water also, which is mixed in the same way with the blood of the believing people, must be converted bodily into the blood of the people.

units.la: {b} Bertran. Presbyt. decorpore & sanguine. D.p.1140. pariter admixta est, in sanguinem populi credentū necesse est corporaliter convertatur. Vbi namque una sanctificatio est, una consequenter operatio, & vbi par ratio, par quoque consequitur mysterium. At videmus in aquam secundum corpus nihil esse conuersum, consequenter ergo & in vino nihil corporaliter ostensum. Accipitur spiritualiter quicquid in aqua de populi corpore significatur; Accipiatur ergo necesse est spiritualiter, quicquid in vino de Christi sanguine intimatur. Item quae a se differunt idem non sunt. Corpus Christi, quod mortuum est & resurrexit, & immortale factum iam non moritur, & mors illi ultra non dominabitur; aeternum est iam, non passibile: hoc autem quod in Ecclesia celebratur temporale est, non aeternum, corruptibile est, non incorruptibile, in via est, non in Patria. Differunt igitur a se, quapropter non sunt idem. Quod si non sunt idem, quomodo verum corpus Christi dicitur & verum sanguis? Si enim corpus Christi est, & hoc dicitur vere, quia corpus Christi in veritate corpus Christi est, & si in veritate corpus Christi incorruptibile & impassibile est, ac per hoc aeternum omnia. Hoc igitur corpus Christi quod agitur in Ecclesia, necesse est ut a fine paginae incorruptibile sit & aeternum: sed negari non potest corrumpi quoque quodam quod per partes commutatum dispartitur ad sumendum, & de pane illo, & cum tibus commolitum in corpus trajicitur. Haec tenus Bertramus. Alter eius locus hoc etiam prolixior est, & in eandem aliud sententiam: sed eum breuitatis causa omitto. Cum viderent egregij Censores neutri loco posse unquam cum Transsubstantiatione conuenire, utrumque expunxerunt, ne si quibus imperitis occurrerent, existimarent iam Caroli Calui tempore non defuisse sacramentarios. A. D. 99. Ind. 4. d. 15. Kal. Iul. habita est Remis Synodus in qua depositus fuit Arnulphus Remensis Archiepiscopus. In ea multa liberè dicta sunt contra Papae Romani tyrannidem, imprimis ab Arnulpho Aurelianensi Episcopo, viro grauissimo, & quod etiam ipsius inimici fatentur, honestis pollente moribus; quale illud est; Sed o lugenda Roma! quae nostris maioribus clara Patrum lumina prabuisti, nostris temporibus miserrimas tenetenebras futuro seculo famosas offudistí! Sed & illud mox de Papa Romano : Quid hunc reuerendi Patres,in sublimi folio residentem, veste purpurea & auro radiantem , quid hunc in quam esse censetis ? Nimirum si caritate destituitur, solaq; scientia inflatur & extollitur , Antichristus est in templo Dei sedere,& se ostendere tanquam sit Deus: Si autem nec caritate fundatur,nec scientia erigitur,in templo Dei tanquam statua tanquam idolum est,à quo responsa petere,marmora consulere est Hæc & alia eiusdem generis non pauca in illa Synodo passim obvia non tulerunt delicatæ Romanorum auriculæ.Itaque Acta Synodi , tametsi vetustissima , & ipsis illis temporibus scripta , & quidem à Gerberto(viro adeo Romæ probato, ut etiam Papa Romanus, assumpto Sylvestri II. nomine, A. D. 999. factus fuerit) nuspiam apud istos comparent, ne in immensa quidem illa Biniana farragine , in qua tam multa sunt vel falsa & commentitia, vel vana & ridicula. Quin & nuper Chefnæus , cùm in Francicorum Scriptorum collectione hujus Synodi historiam collocaret , sedulo cauit ne quid istic esset quod Romanos offendere posset. Nam & hæc quæ proximè descripsimus, & alia eiusdem generis omnia,pessimo exemplo, expunxit, & miseræ Synodi historiam multis resectis capitibus, optima sui parte mutilatam, edidit. Quid ab istis verum sincerumq; expectamus, qui ne Paparum quidem suorum . ut ut veterum,lucubrationibus parcunt , si quid in iis occurrat quod suis dogmatis adversetur ? Quin & ea etiam ex libris expungunt quæ pudendam superiorum temporum ignorantiam & supinitatem arguunt , ne quam ista suæ Ecclesiæ labem afferant; ut ex vetustissimis juris Pontificij Glossis hanc in nouis editionibus eraserunt quæ absurdissimam ac plane anilem de Stramineo Papa Cyriaco fabulam pro re certa affert. Datur certum exemplum de Cyriaco Papa , de quo legitur quod cum Vrsula & undecim millibus virginum martyriʒatus est. Scribitur enim de ipso quod sibi quondam revelatum est quod esset cum illis vir- P 2 ginibus palmam martyrij recepturus. Tunc congregatis Cæsar & Cardinalibus omnibus inuitis, & præcipuè Cardinalibus, coram ipsis renuntiauit dignitati & officio. Sed iste Cyriacus in Catalogo Romanorum Pontificum non denominatur, quia creditum fuit per Cardinales quòd, non propter devotionem, sed propter oblectamenta virginum Papatum dimississet. Hanc glossam quæ in antiquioribus editionibus habetur frustra in Gregoriana quæsitis.
units.tr: {b} Bertram the Presbyter, On the Body and Blood, D.p. 1140. Likewise mixed in with it, it must be changed bodily into the blood of the believing people. For where there is one consecration, there is consequently one operation, and where the reason is the same, the sacrament that follows is also the same. But we see that in the water nothing has been changed into the body. Consequently, then, nothing is shown to be bodily changed in the wine either. Whatever is signified in the water concerning the body of the people is taken spiritually; therefore whatever is signified in the wine concerning the blood of Christ must necessarily be taken spiritually. Likewise, things that differ from one another are not the same. The body of Christ, which died and rose again, and having been made immortal dies no more, and over which death shall no longer have dominion, is now eternal and not subject to suffering. But what is celebrated in the Church is temporal, not eternal; it is corruptible, not incorruptible; it is on the way, not in the homeland. Therefore they differ from each other, and for that reason they are not the same. But if they are not the same, how is it said to be the true body of Christ and the true blood? For if it is the body of Christ, and this is said truly, because the body of Christ is in truth the body of Christ, and if the body of Christ in truth is incorruptible and impassible, and for this reason eternal in every respect, then the body of Christ that is handled in the Church must necessarily be incorruptible and eternal from the end of the page onward. But it cannot be denied that something is corrupted, which, changed piece by piece, is divided for eating, and is turned into the body from that bread, ground together with grains. Thus far Bertram. His other passage is even longer and expresses the same opinion, but I omit it for the sake of brevity. When the distinguished censors saw that neither passage could ever agree with Transubstantiation, they struck out both, lest, if they came across them, some unlearned readers should think that sacramentarians had already existed in the time of Charles the Bald. In A.D. 991, in the fourth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, a synod was held at Rheims, at which Arnulf, Archbishop of Rheims, was deposed. In it many things were said freely against the tyranny of the Roman Pope, above all by Arnulf, Bishop of Orléans, a most serious man who, as even his enemies admit, excelled in upright morals; such as this: But O Rome, to be lamented! You who offered our forefathers the bright lights of the Fathers, have in our times spread the most wretched darkness, infamous for the age to come! And soon after, concerning the Roman Pope: What do you, reverend Fathers, think this man is, who sits on his lofty throne, glittering in purple robes and gold? Surely if he is destitute of charity, and is puffed up and exalted by knowledge alone, he is Antichrist, sitting in the temple of God and showing himself as if he were God. But if he is founded neither on charity nor raised up by knowledge, he is in the temple of God as a statue, as an idol, from which to seek answers is to consult marble. These and not a few other things of the same kind, which are found everywhere in that synod, the delicate ears of the Romans could not bear. Therefore the Acts of the Synod, although very ancient and written in those very times, and indeed by Gerbert (a man so approved at Rome that the Roman Pope himself, taking the name Sylvester II, was made in A.D. 999), appear nowhere among these men, not even in that immense Binian heap, in which so many things are either false and fabricated or vain and ridiculous. Indeed, recently Chesne, when he placed the history of this synod in his collection of the French writers, took careful care that nothing there should offend the Romans. For he expunged both these passages just described and all others of the same kind, by a very bad example, and published the history of the wretched synod, mutilated in its best part by many chapters cut out. What true and sincere things can we expect from men who do not spare even the writings of their own Popes, however ancient, if anything in them runs counter to their dogmas? Indeed they also erase from books those things which expose the shameful ignorance and sloth of earlier times, lest these bring some stain upon their Church. Thus from the most ancient glosses of Papal law they have, in the new editions, erased the most absurd and plainly old-wives' tale which presents as certain fact the fable of Pope Cyriacus of straw. There is a certain example of Pope Cyriacus, of whom it is read that he was martyred with Ursula and eleven thousand virgins. For it is written of him that it was once revealed to him that he would receive the palm of martyrdom with those virgins. Then, with the Emperor and all the Cardinals gathered, and especially the Cardinals, unwilling, he renounced his dignity and office before them. But this Cyriacus is not named in the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs, because it was believed by the Cardinals that he had given up the Papacy not out of devotion but for the pleasures of virgins. This gloss, which is found in the older editions, is sought in vain in the Gregorian.

units.la: Sed neque hanc istorum postremo fraudem omiserim qua quòties neque de scriptore, quin pius & Catholicus fuerit, neque de libro, quin verum eius opus fuerit, dubitare licet; calumniantur objectas voces operi ab hæreticis fuisse assutas. Hoc Bellarminus fecit in Epiphanij ad Iuvenem Hierosolymitanum Epistola; in qua sanctissimus ille vir pronuntiat hominis in Christi Ecclesia imaginem pendere nefas esse, idque; si fiat, cōtra auctoritatem Scripturarum fieri: Alanus quidem Copus notham & Epiphanio suppositam fuisse totam Epistolam dixerat; Marianus verò Victorius & Vasquez veram efse simpliciter concedentes, verba eius stropharum & glossarum suarum subtilitate declinare ac eludere conantur. Bellarminus cum illud quidem improbum & impudens, hoc verò arduum & penè impossibile esse iudicaret, aliter sibi consuluit, concedere enim & epistolam veræ esse Epiphanij, & verba ex ea objecta Iconoclastarum dogmati fauere, comminiscitur illam epistolæ partem, in qua leguntur, non Epiphanij sed alicuius esse hæretici, qui hanc suam laciniam Epiphaniano opusculo assuerit. Itaque, si Bellarminum audimus, delenda est hæc tota particula de Epiphanij operibus, vt inoffenso deinceps pede in iis decurrere possit lector ad vaguem catholicum.
units.tr: But I would not omit this last trick of theirs, by which, whenever it is possible to doubt neither the writer, that he was a pious and Catholic man, nor the book, that it is a true work of his, they falsely claim that the words objected to them were stitched into the work by heretics. Bellarmine did this in Epiphanius's Letter to the Young Man of Jerusalem, in which that most holy man declares that it is wicked for an image of a man to hang in the Church of Christ, and if this is done, it is done against the authority of the Scriptures. Alanus Copus had indeed said that the whole letter was spurious and attributed falsely to Epiphanius; but Marianus Victorius and Vasquez, simply granting that it is genuine, try to evade and elude its words by the subtlety of their quibbles and glosses. Bellarmine, judging that the former was shameless and impudent, and the latter difficult and almost impossible, provided for himself in another way: he concedes that the letter is genuinely Epiphanius's, and that the words cited from it favour the dogma of the Iconoclasts, but he invents that that part of the letter in which these words are read is not Epiphanius's but belongs to some heretic who stitched this patch of his into Epiphanius's little work. So, if we listen to Bellarmine, this whole passage about the works of Epiphanius must be deleted, so that the reader can thereafter run through them with an unhindered foot to the vague Catholic.

units.la: Par fuit Latini Latinij, in plurima Chrysostomi contra confessionem auricularem loca temeritas, atque inuercundia, qui in libello de confessione, à Baronio sum-mopere laudato, opuscula in quibus ilta leguntur, vel Chry-
units.tr: Latinus Latinius showed a similar rashness and shamelessness against the many passages of Chrysostom about auricular confession. In his little book on confession, highly praised by Baronius, he denies that the opuscula in which those passages are read are by Chry-

units.la: {a} Epiph. ad Iuvenem
units.tr: {a} Epiphanius, To the Young Man.

units.la: Chyrosoftomi esse praefacte negat,vel certe à Nauatia nis nescio quibus, vel olim, vel nuper, insertis suis, contra confessionis vocalis necessitatem, sententiis, corrupta atque interpolata esse contendit. Iraq; te huic quidem viro, & aliis, si quos habet consentientes, nulla erit religio, quaecunque apud Chrysostomum huius generis occurrunt, ea omnia simul semelque; ex libris & ex hominum memoria cuadere ac delere.
units.tr: sostom, or else he contends that they are corrupted and interpolated, either by certain Novatians, whoever they were, long ago or recently, inserted into them against the necessity of vocal confession. Hence to this man, and to others, if they have any who agree with him, there will be no scruple about wiping out and deleting all such passages found in Chrysostom, all at once, from the books and from human memory.

units.la: Eandem strophiam Bellarminus adhibet ad eludendam & Ignatij, & Canonum Apostolicorum de Sabbati à ieiunio immunitate legem; Posset fieri [inquit] ut tam in canone Apostolico, quia in epistola Ignatii solum prohiberetur ieiunium dici Dominica, sed postea à Graecis posterioribus insertum fuerit nomen Sabbati; quod sic ab omni veri specie abhorret, ut etiam ab ipso Binio * refellatur. Sed nusquam desperata hac exceptione vel frequentius, vel inverecundius vtuntur, quam in quaestione de suo Honorio; in qua eos vrit magna vis veterum monumentorum Romanum illum praesulem haereseos summo consensu damnatium Primo exstant duae Honorij ipsius epistolae Monotheletarum venenis conperse. Tum vrget sextae Synodi disertum & quidem non uno in loco repetitum anathema; tum & Leonis P.R. II. & Bedae, & aliorum, quos memorare longum est, testimonium; ut in tota Ecclesiae Christianae historia vix quicquam occurrat certius, clarius, c nstantius traditum. Quid hic Latini nostri; Bellarminus de more suum illud vsurpat fortasse ab haereticis confictas Concilio generali insertas Honorij epistolas*; Synodum Pighius † quidem simpliciter repudiauerat, & ter exsecrandum Concilium noncupauerat; Bellarminus vero affirmat Honorii nomen inter eos, qui damnantur à VI. Synodo, sine dubio insertum esse ab aemulis Romanae Ecclesiae, similiter quicquid aliud ibi dicitur contra Honorium*. Baronius ᵇ pro innata temeritate, ingenii que leuitate etiam vltra progressus sua nobis figmenta, veluti totidem historias venditat, & acta Synodi à P 3.
units.tr: Bellarmine uses the same trick to evade both the law of Ignatius and of the Apostolic Canons about exemption from fasting on the Sabbath: It could happen [he says] that in the Apostolic canon, since in the epistle of Ignatius only fasting on the Lord's Day was forbidden, the name of Sabbath was later inserted by later Greeks. This is so far removed from any appearance of truth that it is refuted even by Binius himself *. But nowhere do they use this desperate exception more often or more shamelessly than in the question about their Honorius, in which the great weight of ancient records presses them, which condemned that prelate of Rome as a heretic with the highest consensus. First, there exist two letters of Honorius himself, steeped in the poisons of the Monothelites. Then the explicit anathema of the Sixth Synod, repeated not in one place only, presses them; then the testimony of Pope Leo II and of Bede, and of others whom it would be long to recall, so that in the whole history of the Christian Church hardly anything more certain, clearer, or more consistently handed down can be found. What does our Latinus do here? Bellarmine, as is his custom, uses that old formula: perhaps the letters of Honorius were fabricated by heretics and inserted into a general council. Pighius indeed had simply rejected the Synod and called it a council to be cursed thrice †; but Bellarmine affirms that the name of Honorius among those who are condemned by the Sixth Synod was undoubtedly inserted by the rivals of the Roman Church, and likewise whatever else is said there against Honorius. Baronius †, through his innate rashness and levity of wit, has gone even further and peddles his own fictions to us as if they were so many histories, and the Acts of the Synod

units.la: Theodoro CPo. Præsule vitiata Honorii nomine pro suo ubique substituto refert; rei gestæ tempus, locum causas, occasiones, ac si præsens adfuisset, primus post A.D. 681. quo habita est Synodus, nullo sequentium temporum auctore, ipse sæculo 16o. natus confidentissime narrat; quod ei solenne est, ut suas coniecturas, suas suspiciones, sua denique vel vota, vel somnia in Annales diligentissime referat. Binius Baronii dictata bona fide de more ructat c. Iam Leonis II. epistolam Belarminus d quidem ab haeretici corruptam; Baronius e non corruptam, sed plane fictam fuisse, eorumque meram esse impostu ram contendit. Bedam postremo Bellarminus f nil dubitat eadem secum de Honorio sensisse; sed in eius libro sciolum aliquem nomen Honorii addidisse sibi ipse videtur merito vaticinari. Non exagito istorum vanitatem, atque inverecundiam; qui tabulas publicas, Graecorum pariter ac Latinorum communes, à nouem sexculis summo (quod constat) consensu inter se hactenus conspirantes, falsi insimulare nullo de veteribus auctore, nullo teste, nulla (si unum Papæ studium demus) ratione audent; quod & Ioannes Rainoldus g nostep olim & nuper ex ipsis adversariis Franciscus Combefis h iusta, ac erudita disputatione fuse demonstrarunt. Mihi nunc ad praesens institutum satis est, quod veterum libros ipsi qui nos eo provocant, mendosissimos esse prositentur.
units.tr: Under Theodore, Patriarch of Constantinople, Baronius reports that the name of Honorius has been corrupted and replaced everywhere by a substitute of his own choosing. He narrates the time, place, causes and occasions of the event as confidently as if he had been present, though he was the first to do so after AD 681, when the Synod was held, with no author of any later period to support him, and he himself was born in the sixteenth century. This is his habit: he records in his Annals, with great diligence, his own conjectures, suspicions, and even his wishes or dreams. Binius, in good faith, as is his custom, repeats Baronius's dictates. Bellarmine holds that the letter of Leo II was corrupted by heretics, whereas Baronius contends that it was not corrupted but plainly fabricated, and is pure imposture. Finally, Bellarmine has no doubt that Bede thought the same about Honorius, but he himself seems to foresee that some smatterer added the name of Honorius to Bede's book. I do not pursue the vanity and shamelessness of these men, who dare to accuse of forgery the public records, common to both Greeks and Latins, which have agreed with highest consensus for nine centuries, with no ancient author, no witness, and no reason (if we grant them their one aim, the Pope's advantage). John Rainolds among our own people, long ago, and recently Francis Combefis, who is one of their own adversaries, have demonstrated this at length in a just and learned dispute. For my present purpose it is enough that those who appeal to the ancient books themselves confess that these books are full of errors.

units.la: Huc quoque pertinet quod Baronius in Graecis eius epistolæ, quæ Ignatij nomine circumfertur, codicibus additum & infulum, vel à Nouatoribus (ut vocat) vel à recentioribus Graecis, Pauli inter Apostolos conjugatos nomen, contendit, nulla ratione, mero causæ studio cum ne unus quidem exiet sincerus eius epistolæ codex, in quo non legatur Pauli nomen. Quod enim incredibile putat, ut id ab Ignatio, præter evidentissimam veritatis lucem, scriptum fuerit, frustra est; quod verus, scilicet, eius epistolæ auctor sit, non Ignatius, ut ipse falso arbitratur ac sumit, sed aliquis de Græcorum gente impostor, cui mirandum non est eiusmodi erratum excidisse; maximè cùm apud non neminem ex vetustissimis Patribus aliquid huiusmodi legisset. Sed hæc temeritas Baronio familiaris est, ut, in rebus etiam non magni momenti, quæ sibi in Patrum libris displicent, illa audaciter affirmet esse aliena manu eorum verbis assuta, ut cùm ad Epiphanium ea ab aliquo fuisse addita hariolatur quæ is de Origenis lapsu tradidit Hæresi LXIV. & cùm alibi ab Irenæo scripta esse negat quæ in omnibus eius exemplaribus de Christi ætate, lib. 11. adversus hæreses cap. 39. habentur suis quibusdam coniecturis planè inanibus, adversus constantem omnium codicum fidem siustra pugnans, ut est à Petavio demonstratum. Sed hæc quidem hactenus; ex quibus constat, quàm facile sibi isti homines persuadeant vitiata ac mendosa esse veterum scriptorum monumenta, quoties ea vel cum Romana fide, vel cum priuatis suis opinionibus pugnant. Vnde porro quiuis non hebes intelligit eos in veterum codicibus, quos soli & omnes olim habuerant, & plerosque etiam nunc habent, & hæc ipsa quę adulterata esse disputant, libenter si id tuto licuisset, mutaturos fuisse, propue suo libitu emendaturos, & vero plurima alia eiusdem generis, quæ inuertere & ad rem suam effingere commodè in tenebris licuit, haut dubie mutasse.
units.tr: Here also belongs what Baronius urges about the Greek codices of the letter that circulates under the name of Ignatius: that the name of Paul, added among the apostles who were married, was inserted either by the Novatians (as he calls them) or by more recent Greeks. He argues this without any reason, from sheer partisanship, since not even one genuine codex of that letter exists in which the name of Paul is not read. For he thinks it incredible that Ignatius should have written this, against the most evident light of truth, but he is wrong: the true author of that letter is not Ignatius, as he falsely supposes and assumes, but some impostor of the Greek race, and it is no wonder that such an error slipped in, especially since he had read something of this kind in some of the most ancient Fathers. But this rashness is familiar to Baronius: even in matters of no great importance, whatever displeases him in the books of the Fathers, he boldly declares to be foreign to them, the words being stitched in by another hand. Thus he guesses that those things which Epiphanius reports about the fall of Origen in Heresy 64 were added to him by someone, and where he denies that Irenaeus wrote what is found in all his copies about the age of Christ, book 2 against heresies, chapter 39, he fights against the constant witness of all the codices with his own quite empty conjectures, as Petavius has demonstrated. But so much for this. From these things it is clear how easily such men persuade themselves that the monuments of the ancient writers are corrupted and full of error, whenever they clash with Roman faith or with their own private opinions. Moreover, anyone who is not dull can see that they would gladly have changed, and would have corrected at their pleasure, the ancient codices which alone and entirely they once possessed, and most of which they still possess, and these very passages which they argue are adulterated, if they could have done so safely; and undoubtedly they have changed very many other passages of the same kind, which they could easily twist and fashion to their own purpose in the darkness.

units.la: Quisquis es qui salutis tuæ doctrinam in veterum libris inuestigare tua referre in animum induxisti, ex huiusmodi strophis fallaciisq; quas velint nolint in lucem protrahimus, disce quot & quantis curis Veterum circa sacra sententiam, ubi vel tantillum à sua recedebat, oculis nostris subducere statuerint. Attende item quàm ipsis facile fuerit & nunc etiam sit, hac in re animo suo morem gerere, & apud te statuè magnis conatibus pares successus non defuisse: quibus si addas, quęcunque, vel tempus, vel hæreticorum nequitia, vel veterum Christianorum incauta & pia fraus, vel recentiorum.
units.tr: Whoever you are who have resolved to search out the doctrine of your salvation in the books of the ancients and to bring your mind to it, learn from such tricks and deceptions, which we bring into the light whether they will or not, what and how great were the cares with which those who handled sacred matters among the ancients took pains to remove from our eyes whatever departed even slightly from their own views. Consider also how easily it was, and still is, for them in this matter to indulge their own minds, and how, as you yourself settle the matter, success has not been lacking to those who undertook such great efforts. If to these you add whatever it may be, whether time, or the wickedness of heretics, or the rash and pious fraud of the early Christians, or of more recent writers,

units.la: ac dirimendis hisce controversiis idoneos esse libros obscurè scriptos. Ego verò haud scio annon de plerisque veteris Ecclesiæ scriptoribus merito id usurpari possit quod Hieronymus de quorundam in S. Scripturam Commentariis dixit. Plerisque nimium differtis accidere, ut maior sit intelligentia difficultas in eorum explanationibus quàm in iis quæ explanare conantur, id est, commentarios ipsos esse textu S.Scripturæ intellectu difficiliores. Nam ad veterum libros probè intelligendos imprimis necessaria est linguarum quibus plerique scripti sunt, Græcæ scilicet ac Latinæ, accurata cognitio. Qui enim Syriacè, vel Arabicè, vel Æthiopice, vel alia lingua vernacula scripserunt, ii quidem, ad pernoscendam veteris Ecclesiæ de religione sententiam, fortasse non minus essent utiles quàm quiuis alij; Sed eorum tamen nulla, quod sciam, extant publica monumenta, nisi in Græcum aut Latinum sermonem translata, qualia sunt Ephremi opera (si modo qui ostentantur genuini sunt eius fœtus) & Mosis Barcephæ de Paradiso liber quem Masius Latinum fecit, & forsan pauca alia. Scio plerosque interpretibus, siue Latinis siue vernaculis fidem habere, imò & eo ventum esse, ut nonnulli non dubitarint de Patribus Græcis, nulla (quantum quidem ex eorum scriptis apparet) Græcæ linguæ solida cognitione instructi, iudicare; quod magnæ fuisse temeritatis nemo, credo, inficiabitur. Res ipsa per se satis docet ac penitus introspiciendam scriptoris mentem, maximè in rebus magni momenti, quantum conducat eius linguam, phrases, vocabula, connexionisq; ipsorum inter se rationem ad unguem callere, cùm quælibet lingua habeat nescio quam vim significandi singularem, & quasi innatam, quam nemo quantumvis eruditus, disertus ac fidus sic assequitur ut interpretando non deterat ac diluat. Sed quod utile est in omnibus aliis argumentis, in hoc necessarium euasit, adeo exigua seu eruditione, seu fide instructi, ad hoc opus se accinxere plerique siue veteres siue recentiores Patrum interpretes. Q
units.tr: and books obscurely written, suited to settling these controversies. For my part I do not know whether what Jerome said of the commentaries of certain men on Holy Scripture may rightly be applied to most of the writers of the early Church: It happens to very many who write at length that the difficulty of understanding is greater in their explanations than in the things they try to explain; that is, the commentaries themselves are harder to understand than the text of Holy Scripture. For to understand the books of the ancients properly, an accurate knowledge of the languages in which most of them were written, namely Greek and Latin, is above all necessary. Those who wrote in Syriac, or Arabic, or Ethiopic, or some other vernacular language, might perhaps have been no less useful than any others for learning the opinion of the early Church about religion; yet, as far as I know, none of their public monuments survive, except those translated into Greek or Latin, such as the works of Ephrem (if those that are displayed as his genuine offspring really are his) and the book of Moses Barcephas on Paradise, which Masius made into Latin, and perhaps a few others. I know that most people give credit to interpreters, whether Latin or vernacular, and things have gone so far that some have not hesitated to judge the Greek Fathers without any solid knowledge of the Greek language, so far as one can see from their writings; and no one, I think, will deny that this was great rashness. The thing itself sufficiently shows that to look thoroughly into a writer's mind, especially in matters of great moment, it is very much to the point to know his language, idioms, words, and the connection between them perfectly, since every language has a certain peculiar and, as it were, innate power of signifying, which no one, however learned, eloquent and faithful, so grasps that he does not fail or dilute it in translating. But what is useful in all other arguments has become necessary in this one: so poorly equipped, either in learning or in faithfulness, have most interpreters of the Fathers, whether ancient or recent, set themselves to this work.

units.la: De Ruffini fide supra iam dixi. Quàm sit autem periculosum eius interpretationi credere, vel hoc exemplo discere. Ille in Ecclesiastica Eusebij historia Martyres Lugdunenses ita apud Pagmos loqui facit, ad pugnandum Thyestaeorum crudarum crimen; Multum erratis ô viri, putantes humanis viscetibus vesci eos, qui ne mutorum quidem animalium carnibus utuntur Pamelius ardentissimus Latinarum traditionum admirator, haec verba arripuit & ex iis conficit iam aetate B.Irenaei usitatum suisse in Galliis apud Christianos à carnibus abstinere, hodierno scilicet Romanorum ritu. Atqui de carnibus nihil apud Eusebium historiae auctorem legitur; longe aliae, haec scilicet leguntur; πῶς ἂν ποιήσαι φάγοιεν οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα μὴ ἐκ ἀλόγων ζώων αἵματα φαγεῖν ἔξεστι; Quomodo hi infantes comederent, quibus ne mutorum quidem animalium sanguinem gustare licet? Nempe ex Apostolico decreto (quod diutissimè in Ecclesia obseruatum est, etiam ultra decimum seculum) Christiani tum ab esu sanguinis & suffocati abstinebant. Hieronymus Ruffino vir fuit (fateor) haud paulo doctior; interpres nescio an multo fidelior ac religiosior. Anastasius (qui ante 800. annos vixit) qualiter se gesserit in Synodi VII. interpretatione ne non ita pridem monui. Is tamen Praefatione ad VIII. Synodum extra omnem dubitationis aleam ponit, nihil in sua editione non verum, non certum; falsum contra & suppositicium quicquid apud Graecos vel superat vel defit. Si reliqui interpretes ea essent fide, quam ille sibi arrogat, facilè Graecis codicibus carere possemus, & aequo animo fere pinguem illam Latinitatem quam ille in sua versione usus est. Sed neque fidem in his quae de se praedicat ab omnibus impetrauit, neque si is esset qui vult haberi, hoc est, si ipsi archetypo praestaret; eodem quoque loco ac numero caeteri interpretes censeri possent, maximè recentiores. Primò diversus ipsarum linguarum genius, etiam ubi abest partium studium, efficit tamen, ut apud interpretem nonnulla interdum occurrant ambiguè dicta, quae planè ac sine ulla ambiguitate auctor scripserat; cuius generis insigne ac memorabile imprimis dabo exemplum. Athanasii interpres quemdam, eius ex libro de Synodis Arimini & Seleuciae,locum sic tradit;Duo Dionysiij ante eos Septuaginta fuere qui Samosatensem fuslulerunt, quorum alter Romae alter Alexandriae Praesul erat. Baronius aliqua horum verborum ambiguitate deceptus, scribit testari Athanasium a duobus Dionysiis Romano & Alexandrino sublatum fuisse Paulum Samosatenum Non exagito pudendum, in tanto Annalista, ac plane puerilem errorem, in quem eum partim Papae studium, partium linguae Graecae ignorantia impulit. Vnum hoc dico, si Athanasium Graece legisset, clare animadversurum eum fuisse, non a duobus Dionysiis, sed a septuaginta illis Episcopis sublatum memorari ab Athanasio Paulum. Sic enim Graeca citra ullam ambiguitatem habent Διονύσιοι δύο ... Quod vero idem Annalista in alia parte operis, quae Eusebius de Christiana quadam nobili, & Alexandrina muliere scripserat Maximinum illam φυγὴν ζημιώσαι, ea perinde accipit ac si dixisset auctor eam fugam ex urbe Alexandria, & ex Aegypto elapsam esse; hoc inquam non interpretis, sed ipsius Baronii peccatum est, temere & pueriliter studentis quae de illa muliere a veris historicis traduntur ea ad Catharinam suam fictitiam accommodare, quam (& hoc quoque absurde & insciter) Hecatorinam † ab Hecate dictam olim fuisse hariolatur. Descriptus enim ab ipso Eusebii interpretes diserte habet eam mulierem, non quod ipse vult fuga lapsam, sed, quod tradit Eusebius, suga multatam,& omnibus facultatibus spoliatam, a Maximino scilicet tyranno. Sed praeter ipsam linguarum diversitatem, ex Interpretum animo plerumque etiam oriuntur magnae versionum a suis fontibus discrepantiae. Cum enim plerique interpretes partium suarum studio ducantur, parum, ut mihi quidem videtur, prudentis effec,eorum omnium fidem sequi. Si cui animus est periculum facere quantùm tribuendum sit eiusmodi versionibus, conferat, si tanti est, Præfationem Græcam Origenis in libros contra Celsum, cum interpretatione cuiusdam Christophori Persona, percutrat totum opus, & nisi Prototstantibus iudibrium debere velit, caveat ne ox adeo locupletis interpretis fide iis objiciat, ex quinto libro, hunc locum pro invocatione sanctorum Vota & preces omnes, & gratiarum insuper actiones ad Deum sunt per Angelum transmittenda qui per Pontificem & viuens verbum & Deum Angelus præfectus est. Videtur velle Christum Angelorum quempiam constituisse qui preces nostras excipiat,& per quem vota nostra ad Deum deferantur.
units.tr: I have already said above what to think of the good faith of Rufinus. How dangerous it is to trust his translation, you may learn from this one example. In the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius he makes the Lyonnese martyrs speak thus before Pagmos, to refute the charge of Thyestean cruelty: You are very wrong, sirs, in thinking that those people eat human flesh, who do not even use the flesh of dumb animals. Pamelius, a most ardent admirer of Latin traditions, seized on these words and from them concluded that already in the time of Irenaeus it was customary in Gaul for Christians to abstain from meat, in the present-day Roman manner. But nothing about flesh is read in Eusebius, the author of the history; quite different words are read there: [Pōs an poiēsai phagoien hoi ta toiauta mē ek alogōn zōōn haimata phagein exesti;] How would these infants eat, to whom it is not lawful to taste even the blood of dumb animals? Indeed, by the Apostolic decree (which was observed in the Church for a very long time, even beyond the tenth century), Christians then abstained from eating blood and from what was strangled. Jerome was (I admit) a man by no means less learned than Rufinus; whether he was a more faithful and conscientious interpreter, I do not know. I warned not long ago how Anastasius (who lived about 800 years ago) conducted himself in translating the Seventh Synod. Yet in his preface to the Eighth Synod he lays it down beyond all possibility of doubt that nothing in his edition is untrue or uncertain, and that whatever among the Greeks either exceeds or is lacking is false and spurious. If the other interpreters had the same trustworthiness that he claims for himself, we could easily do without the Greek codices, and gladly put up with that rather fat Latinity which he used in his version. But he has not obtained belief in what he says about himself from everyone, nor, even if he were what he wishes to be considered, that is, if he equalled the archetype itself, could he be rated in the same place and number as the other interpreters, especially the more recent ones. First, the differing genius of the languages themselves, even where partisan zeal is absent, nevertheless brings it about that some words sometimes occur in the translator's version as ambiguous, which the author had written plainly and without any ambiguity. I will give an especially notable example of this kind. A certain interpreter of Athanasius renders a passage from his book on the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia thus: There were two Dionysii before those Seventy who removed Samosatenus, one of whom was Bishop at Rome, the other at Alexandria. Baronius, deceived by some ambiguity in these words, writes that Athanasius bears witness that Paul of Samosata was removed by two Dionysii, the Roman and the Alexandrian. I do not rebuke, in so great an annalist, this shameful and quite childish error, into which he was driven partly by the Pope's cause and partly by ignorance of the Greek language. I say only this: if he had read Athanasius in Greek, he would have clearly noticed that Athanasius mentions Paul as removed not by two Dionysii, but by those seventy bishops. For the Greek has, without any ambiguity, Dionysioi duo [Διονύσιοι δύο] ... Again, that the same annalist, in another part of his work, takes the flight which Eusebius wrote that Maximinus punished in a certain noble Christian woman of Alexandria as if the author had said that she had escaped from the city of Alexandria and from Egypt: this fault is not the interpreter's but Baronius's own, who rashly and childishly strives to fit what true historians hand down about that woman to his fictitious Catharina, whom (and this too absurdly and ignorantly) he guesses was once called Hecatorina † from Hecate. For the interpreter copied from Eusebius himself expressly says that the woman was not, as he wishes, fled and escaped, but, as Eusebius relates, punished by exile and stripped of all her property, namely by the tyrant Maximinus. But beyond the very diversity of the languages, great discrepancies between versions and their sources often also arise from the mind of the interpreters. For since most interpreters are led by zeal for their own party, it seems to me not very prudent to follow all of them. If anyone wishes to test how much weight should be given to translations of this kind, let him compare, if it is worth the trouble, the Greek preface of Origen to the books against Celsus with the version of a certain Christophorus Persona, and let him read through the whole work; and unless he wishes to make the Protestants a laughing-stock, let him take care not to throw at them, on the authority of so wealthy an interpreter, this passage from the fifth book, in favour of the invocation of saints: All vows and prayers, and moreover thanksgivings, are to be transmitted to God through the Angel, who is set over the Pontiff and the living Word and God. He seems to want Christ to have appointed some Angel who would receive our prayers and through whom our vows would be carried to God.

units.la: At nihil tale Origenes. Sed prorsus contra, Omnem precationem, omne votum, omnem orationem & gratiarum actionem mitti oportere ad Deum qui est super omnia, persum Sacerdotem, qui est verbum viuens, & Deus supra omnes Angelos. Nec dissimilis est ratio Histo. iæ Ecclesiasticæ Ioannis Christophorsoni efendit enim variis in locis præter Auctorum quos interpretatus mentem, vehemens in interprete partium studium. Exempli gratia ? Ille Clementem Alexandrinum quodam apud Eusebium loco hæc loquentum inducit, Episcopus adolescentulum, &c. ad extremum Baptismi sacramento illuminauit: postea sigillo Domini, id est, sacramento Confirmationis, tanquam persecta, tutaque eius animi custodia obsignauit. Eleganter sanè,& planè ad rem Romanam. Quis neget?
