Nam nemo est qui hæc scripta legens non putet & Eusebij & Clementis, imo & ipsius Ioannis Apostoli, ad quem pertinet tota hæc narratio, temporibus iam in usu fuisse,& chrismatis Latini sacramentum, & ipsam quoque Confirmationis nomenclaturam Sed tu isti, si sapis, cave credas Hæc enim ipsius sunt, Eusebij non sunt, non sunt Clementis; cuius Græca ita habent. Οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τὸν παιδαγωγὸν ... φυλακῆς. φυλακτήριον ἐπισήμας τῶν σφραγῖδα τῆ Κυρίῳ. Sigillum Domini adolescenti adhibitum fuisse dicit à Presbytero qui ipsum baptizauit; Sigillum Domini esse sacramentum Latinae Confirmationis non dicit: Imo id Dominicum sigillum, non Latinum ch:ifma, sed illum ipsum fuisse baptismum quo rinctus fuerat adolescens perspicuè significat, ut viden' qui G.æcè sciunt Neque aliter ceperat Russinus; Tum vero (inquit) Presbyter adolescentem suscepit, &c. ad ultimum etiam Baptismi gratiam tradit. Post hæc iam veluti confidens gratia qua fuerat communitus † paulo indulgè tius iuvenem habere cæpit. Alud eundem Christophorsonum Ecclesia Smyrnensis de Paganis verba faciens, Illud quidem miseri(inquit)penitus ignorabunt, nimirum nos non aliquando in animum posse inducere, ut Christum deseramus, qui pro salute omnium, qui in toto mundo salui sint futu-ri, crucis tormenta perpessus sit, vel alium quempiam aliquando colamus ut Deum. Illum enim qui vere Dei Filius est adoramus. Martyres autem ut discipulos & imitatores Domini propter incredibilem eorum benevolentiam, quam in proprium Regem & Magistrum declaraverunt merito amplexamur. Hæc Christophorfonus; eo ipso quod negat quemquam à Christianis ut Deum coli, innuens coli aliquos religiosè, tametsi non ut Deum, quod est, ut liquet hodiernum Latinorum dogma. At veteres illi Smyrnenses simpliciter negant fieri posse ut alium præter Christum colant, Martyres vero à se amari profitentur. Ἀγωνίης (Pagani) ἐπι τὸν ἀρχηγὸν πονεῖ κατελπιτίν δυνάσθαι, &c. ἐπὶ ἐπεχειρῆσαι τιμᾶν σιγὴ τῶν μὴ ὁρᾶν, τῶν ἐπὶ Θεοῦ φρονιμῶς. Τοὺς δὲ μάρτυρας ὡς μαθητὰς τῆς Κυρίου ἡμῶν μιμητὰς ἀγαπῶμεν ἀξίως, &c. Idem alibi Irenæum de Paschali jejunio reddens; Quidam namque unum diem se jejunare oportere existimant, alii duos, non pauci plures, multi quadraginta. Planè quasi iam cum aliqui essent Christiani qui nunc solennem Latinis Quadragesimam observarent. Græca nihil huiusmodi tinniunt, sed significant fuisse, qui diem suum esurialem horis quadraginta diurnis noctur nisque metirentur; ex-
units.tr: But Origen says nothing of the kind. On the contrary, he says: Every prayer, every vow, every petition and thanksgiving ought to be sent to God who is above all, through the High Priest himself, who is the living Word and God above all angels. Johannes Christophorsonus's Ecclesiastical History follows much the same method: beyond the authors he translates, he defends his own views in many places, with a vehement partisanship in his interpreting. For example? He introduces Clement of Alexandria, speaking in a passage quoted by Eusebius, thus: The bishop, a young lad, etc., at last enlightened him by the sacrament of baptism; afterwards with the seal of the Lord, that is, the sacrament of Confirmation, as a perfect and secure guard of his soul, he sealed him. Very neatly indeed, and quite to the Roman purpose! Who would deny it? For no one who reads these writings fails to think that already in the times of Eusebius and Clement, and of John the Apostle himself, to whom this whole narrative belongs, both the sacrament of Latin chrism and the very name of Confirmation were in use. But you, if you are wise, take care not to believe it. For these are his own words, not Eusebius's, and not Clement's; the Greek of Clement reads thus: [Οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τὸν παιδαγωγὸν ... φυλακῆς. φυλακτήριον ἐπισήμας τῶν σφραγῖδα τῆ Κυρίῳ.] The seal of the Lord was applied to the youth, he says, by the presbyter who baptized him; he does not say that the seal of the Lord is the sacrament of Latin Confirmation. Indeed, it plainly signifies that the Lord's seal was not the Latin chrism but that very baptism with which the youth had been washed, as those who know Greek well can see. Nor did Rufinus understand it otherwise: Then indeed (he says) the presbyter received the youth, etc., and at last he also handed on the grace of baptism. After this, as if now confident in the grace with which he had been endowed, he began to treat the young man rather more indulgently. Speaking elsewhere of the pagans, the Church of Smyrna says the same Christophorsonus: Those wretches will utterly fail to understand that we could never bring ourselves to abandon Christ, who suffered the torments of the cross for the salvation of all who are to be saved throughout the whole world, or ever to worship anyone else as God. For we adore him who is truly the Son of God. But the martyrs, as disciples and imitators of the Lord, we rightly embrace for their incredible goodwill, which they have shown toward their own King and Master. Thus Christophorsonus; and by the very fact that he denies that Christians worship anyone as God, he implies that some are worshipped religiously, though not as God, which is, as is clear, the present dogma of the Latins. But those ancient Smyrnaeans simply deny that it is possible for them to worship anyone besides Christ, and they profess that the martyrs are loved by them. [Ἀγωνίης (Pagani) ἐπι τὸν ἀρχηγὸν πονεῖ κατελπιτίν δυνάσθαι, &c. ἐπὶ ἐπεχειρῆσαι τιμᾶν σιγὴ τῶν μὴ ὁρᾶν, τῶν ἐπὶ Θεοῦ φρονιμῶς. Τοὺς δὲ μάρτυρας ὡς μαθητὰς τῆς Κυρίου ἡμῶν μιμητὰς ἀγαπῶμεν ἀξίως, &c.] The same author, rendering Irenaeus elsewhere on the Paschal fast, says: For some think that one day ought to be fasted, others two, not a few more, many forty. Quite as though there were already some Christians who then observed the solemn Lent that the Latins now observe. The Greek says nothing of the kind, but signifies that there were those who measured their fasting day by forty hours of day and night.

units.la: Ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἁπάντων τὰ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ... cerum neminem memorant,cuius Pafcale illud ieiunium quadraginta dictum fuerit ; momorant quorum fuerit plurium quam duorum. Οἱ μὲν ϑ̄ οἱονταγ μίαν ἡμέ-ραν ἐλθ̄ αὐτὰς ἡς ευεν, οἱ ϑ̄ ἀνο ἡ πλείονας οἱ ϑ̄ πεσαρακοντα ἡμέρας ἡμεραις ἡ νυκτερας συμμιτρούσῃ τῶν ἡμέραν αὐτῶν Elt & hoc Criftophorfoni. Sozomenus de Liberio Episcopo Romano scribit, quod eum Constantius Au- gustus ἐδιάζετο ὁμολογῶν μὴ εἶ) τῶν πατέρα τὸν υἱὸν ὁμοούσιον; id est quod eum compulerit confiteri non esse Filium Patriconsubstantialem; & pauci interjectis, quod eum Basilius, & Eustathius & Eleutius principes Arianorum Episcopi ὀ-φ̄ σπλάζοντ ςῡνμίτω suo cuidam de fide male fano libello ; quæ verba significant eos effecisse , ut Liberius huic suo libello consentiret. Christophoꝛsonus in interpretatione Sozomeni sua , ut hanc à sue Pontifice labem amoliretur, verba sui auctoris pessima fide sic reddidit Constantius compellere (inquit) T E N T A V I T eum fateri Filium non esse Patri conjubstantialem: Sic quoque mox de Episcopis Arianis; C O N A N T V R (inquit)ut liberius huic(suo de fide libello)consentiat, Simile caussæ Romanę studium Ioannem quemdam Portefium transvertsum quoque egit, dum quæ Eusebius de ædificato & exornato à Constantino templo Hierosolymitano scribit ita interpretatus est;Sed huc accessit aurearum imaginum, argentearumq; vis infinita. Vnde Bellarminus, cæcus cæcum ducens sequens, concludit in sua de imaginibus sacris disputatione, Eusebium in libris de vita Constantini dicere in templis & Constantino extructis in Palestina fuisse maximam copiam imaginum aureorum & argenteorum Bellarminus Portefium tam incredibilis mendacij auctorem laudare debuerat. Eusebius, quem falsò & impudenter testem laudat nihil habet de imaginibus. Æ.l.m denariis aureis argenteisque lapillisque siue gemmis pretiosis exornatam fuisse dicit:Imaginem ullam in e i fuisse nullus dicit Ἐξόσμει ἀ αὐτὸν ( inquit ) ἀδιλήτοις ϰ̣̣ν̣ιεσι, πλείσων ϰαι ϰαὶ ἀργύρω ἢ λίθων ποντεᾶ ὀν διαλλατἈλλαττῆσαις ὕλαις Ἀναθήμασιν non sunt imagines, sed donaria. Lucas de Iudaico Hierosolymorum templo, in quo, ex Mosis disciplina, nulla fuisse imagines certum atque confessum est, λίθοις (inquit) καλοῖς ἢ ἀναθήμασιν κεκοσμημένοι, id est, ut habet vetus interpres Latinus bonis lapidibus, &, non imaginibus, sed donis ornatum erat. Belarminus idem inter cetera, quae pro auriculari confessione, adducit, haec ex Gregorij Nysseni Epistola ad Letoium describit; Recte habuerit si hodierno die, non solum eos qui ex regeneratione per lavacri gratiam transformati sunt adducamus, sed eos etiam qui per poenitentiam & CONFESSIONEM à mortuis operibus ad viventem viam ascendunt ad viventem spem tanquam manu deducamus. Haec Latine apud Bellarminum. Graeca auctoris nihil habent de consessione cuius vocabulum interpres delo malo pro ἐξομολογήσεως conuersione substituit Ἀλλὰ ἢ εἰς ἀξίαν τῆς μετανοίας τῶν ἢ ἐπιστροφῆς καὶ τῆς πίστεως ἐπιστρεφόντων... Sed eos etiam qui per poenitentiam & controversiae a mortuis operibus ad viventem viam ascendunt. Vt habet ipsa Nysseni editio nouissima Parisiensis. Peior etiam fuit cuiusdam Theologiae Doctoris (cui seu verum seu fictum Domini de S. Iuliano nomen praescribitur) in opere lingua vulgari edito. Is enim haec Augustini laudans, Colimus ergo martyres eo cultu dilectionis & societatis, quo & in hac vita colantur sancti homines Dei, quorum cor ad talem pro Evangelica veritate passionem paratum esse censemus; haec inquam Francice interpretata sic exhibet: Nous honorons donc les Martyrs de ce culte de DEVOTION & de societé, avec laquel on a accoustumé d'honorer les hommes de Dieu ceux qui menent une sainte vie, lors que l'on croit que leur coeur est disposé de souffrir la mort pour la verité de l'Evangile. In hac versione leuius videri potest quod haec Augustini, & in hac vita, plane penitus omisit, quae tamen ut quiuis videt, singulare hoc loco vim habent. Illud vero quis ferat, quod pro dilectione, quam Martyribus exhiberi ait Augustinus, hic noster interpres devotionem diis istis contentionibus cui constabit de Patrum mente, qui ipsos non convenerit, neque ex eorum quasi orem rem omnem habuerit? Hoc ergo tanquam fatis manifestum statuo, ad pernoscendum quid Patres senserint eorum linguam, non perfunctorie, sed accuratè esse intelligendam; cum unaquaeque lingua habeat quaedam loquendi genera& idiomata eruditis, quales fuere Patrum plerique, familiaria quae qui eam superficie tenus attigerit, ejusque arcana minimè penetraverit,nunquam planè penitùsque intelliget. Vin' tu scire quàm necessaria fit huius rei cognitio, quàm periculosa ignoratio? Sume in manus Theodoretum ubi de Eucharistia agens inquit,O'vdi ... Protestantes omnes nec non (ante Cardinalem Perronium) eorum omnes aduersarij hoc mī̄lo interpretati sunt. Neque enim Symbola mystica post sanctificationem recedunt à sua natura,manent enim in priore substantia & figura & forma. Quid potest difertius dici contra Transubstantiationem? Cardinalis verò Perronius,ex eodem,ni fallor,Linguae Graecae penu ex quo habuit μιαρεύ, idem esse quod nobis fumare est, mirificam nuper obtrufit, planéque novam ac inauditam hujus loci interpretationem, quasi vellet Theodoretus ligna Eucharistica manere in figura & forma prioris fuftantiæ, quod tacitè & indirectè transubstantiationi patrocinatur. retur. Certum quidem est hanc expositionem non folùm auctoris scopo, verùm etiam recepto Graecorum stilo repugnare; sed ni Graecam linguam ad unguem
units.tr: "Concerning all the brethren, the things in the Church..." Truly, they name no one by whom that Paschal fast was called forty days; they name those who were more than two. Some kept one day, others two, others more, others forty days, measuring their day by forty daytime hours and nights [Οἱ μὲν ... ἡμέραν ... οἱ δὲ δύο ... οἱ δὲ τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας]. This is also in Christophorsonus. Sozomen writes of Liberius, Bishop of Rome, that the Emperor Constantius tried to force him to confess that the Son is not consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father; that is, that he compelled him to confess that the Son is not consubstantial with the Father. A little later he says that Basil, Eustathius and Eleusius, the leading Arian bishops, persuaded him to consent to a certain badly composed little book of faith [ὁμολογῶν ... σπλάζοντ ... μίτω]; these words mean that they brought it about that Liberius consented to this little book of his. Christophorsonus, in his translation of Sozomen, wanting to clear this stain from his Pontiff, rendered his author's words with bad faith: Constantius, he says, tried to compel him to confess that the Son is not consubstantial with the Father; and so likewise a little later of the Arian bishops, they strive that Liberius consent to this (book of faith of his). A similar zeal for the Roman cause led a certain John Portesius to distort another passage too, when he translated what Eusebius writes about the Jerusalem temple built and adorned by Constantine in this way: But to this was added an infinite force of golden and silver images. Hence Bellarmine, a blind man leading the blind, concludes in his disputation on sacred images that Eusebius, in the books on the life of Constantine, says that in the temples built by Constantine in Palestine there was a very great quantity of golden and silver images. Bellarmine ought to have praised Portesius as the author of such an incredible lie. Eusebius, whom he falsely and shamelessly cites as a witness, says nothing about images. He says the temple was adorned with golden and silver coins and precious stones or gems; no one says that any image was in it. "It was adorned," he says, "with offerings of many kinds, of gold and silver and various precious materials" [Ἐξόσμει ... Ἀναθήμασιν]; these are not images but gifts. Lucas, on the Jewish temple at Jerusalem, in which, by the discipline of Moses, it is certain and admitted that there were no images, says it was adorned "with good stones or offerings" [λίθοις καλοῖς ἢ ἀναθήμασιν κεκοσμημένοι], that is, as the old Latin translator has it, with good stones, and it was adorned not with images but with gifts. Bellarmine too, among the other things he adduces for auricular confession, quotes from Gregory of Nyssa's letter to Letoius the following: It would be right if on this day we led by the hand not only those who have been changed by regeneration through the grace of the laver, but also those who, through repentance and confession, ascend from dead works to the living way, to the living hope. That is the Latin in Bellarmine. The Greek of the author has nothing about confession; the translator substituted this word, a bad choice, for the Greek word meaning acknowledgment [ἐξομολογήσεως]. The Greek reads: "But those too who, by the worth of repentance, of conversion and of faith, turn back..." [Ἀλλὰ ... ἐπιστροφῆς καὶ τῆς πίστεως ἐπιστρεφόντων], and so on: but also those who through repentance and [fitting] ... ascend from dead works to the living way. So it stands in the most recent Paris edition of Nyssen itself. Worse still was the work of a certain Doctor of Theology (whose name, real or invented, is given as Lord de St. Julien), in a book published in the vernacular. For quoting these words of Augustine, We honour the martyrs therefore with that cult of love and fellowship with which holy men of God are honoured in this life, whose heart we believe to be ready for such suffering for the truth of the Gospel, and rendering them into French, he gives: Nous honorons donc les Martyrs de ce culte de DEVOTION & de societé... In this translation the omission of and in this life from Augustine may seem a lesser matter, though as anyone can see these words have a special force in this place. But who could bear that for love (dilectione), which Augustine says is shown to the martyrs, our translator put devotion (devotionem)? With what certainty could anyone know the mind of the Fathers, when he has not agreed with them and has not had a full grasp of their thought? I therefore lay it down as clear enough that, to learn what the Fathers thought, their language must be understood not superficially but accurately; since every language has certain modes of speech and idioms familiar to learned men, as most of the Fathers were, and whoever has touched it only on the surface and has not penetrated its secrets will never understand it fully and completely. Do you want to know how necessary knowledge of this is, and how dangerous ignorance? Take up Theodoret, who, speaking of the Eucharist, says... All Protestants, and also (before Cardinal Perron) all their opponents, have interpreted this passage in one way. For the mystical symbols do not depart from their nature after consecration; they remain in their former substance, figure and form. What could be said more plainly against transubstantiation? But Cardinal Perron, from the same, I think, storehouse of Greek from which he got miarein, which for us means "to smoke," lately thrust upon us a wonderful and quite new and unheard-of interpretation of this passage, as if Theodoret meant that the Eucharistic elements remain in the figure and form of the former substance, which tacitly and indirectly favours transubstantiation. It is certain that this explanation contradicts not only the author's purpose but also the accepted style of the Greeks; but unless one knows the Greek language to the fingertips...

units.la: R gnem quandam emendationem inscriptionis epistolæ Constantini Imperatoris ad Militiadem Episcopum Romanum, in Historia Ecclesiastica Eusebij ? Legit enim Constantinus Augustus Miltiadi Episcopo Romano longum tempus, aut, prolixam occasionem, præter fidem exemplarium omnium, cùm manu scriptorum, tum typis editorum, quæ legunt, Constantinus Augustus Miltiadi Episcopo Romanorum & Marco, veritus, ut mihi quidem videtur, ne Imperator contra decorum peccasse putaret, si Marcum illum, cum Pontifice Romano, hullum secundum ferre solito, componeret atque æquiparet. Nullus esset si is si cætera hujus generis persequi vellem; Hac enim ille techna plurima Patrum loca vel eludit vel declinat, quæ alioqui videbantur in rem Protestantium disertissima. Atque hinc satis, ut mihi quidem videtur, patet quam sit ab probè capiendam veterum mentem necessaria Græcæ Latinæque linguæ cognitio. Ex quo porro illud, quod nos initio constituimus, evidenter consequitur, nempe, haud facile esse eorum scripta intelligere. Quis enim nescit quàm non leui negotio parabilis sit duarum linguarum omnibus numeris absoluta scientia? quotq; non solum laboribus, sed & ingenij facultatibus ad eam consequendam opus sit? memoria tenaci, ingenio perspicaci, studio indefesso, acri comprehensione, diuturna & tedria lectione, & aliis id genus, quæ nonnisi raro reperiuntur. Sed hoc ipsum quod efsuimus abundè etiam ex perpetuis eorum inter se contentionibus rixisque constat qui de Patrum arbitrio o compromiserunt, non enim minus pro eorum ctibunali de capitibus multis, de quibus nunquam inter ipsos convenit, digladiantur. Pontificiorum nonnulli in obscuritatis, quam, adversus Protestantes, Scripturæ impingunt, argumentum, afferunt sententiarum; inter ipsos Protestantes, super nonnullis capitibus, pugnas; Lutheranorum cum Calvinistis de Eucharistia, horum item cum illis & Arminianis, de libero arbitrio & Prædesti-
units.tr: Another correction of the inscription of Emperor Constantine's letter to Miltiades, Bishop of Rome, in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History? For he reads Constantinus Augustus Miltiadi Episcopo Romano longum tempus, or prolixam occasionem, against the reading of all the copies, both manuscript and printed, which read "Constantine Augustus to Miltiades, Bishop of the Romans, and to Marcus." He was concerned, as it seems to me, lest the Emperor be thought to have offended against propriety if he had placed that Marcus, who was accustomed to yield second place to no one, on a level with the Roman Pontiff and made them equals. I could go on at length if I wished to pursue other passages of this kind, for by this trick he either evades or sidesteps many passages of the Fathers which otherwise seemed most clearly to favour the Protestant cause. From this it is, as it seems to me, sufficiently plain how necessary a knowledge of Greek and Latin is for rightly grasping the mind of the ancients. It follows clearly from this what we laid down at the start, namely that their writings are not easy to understand. For who does not know how far from a trifling task it is to acquire a knowledge of two languages complete in every respect, and how much effort, and also how many gifts of intellect, are needed to attain it: a tenacious memory, a sharp mind, tireless zeal, keen comprehension, long and attentive reading, and other qualities of that kind, which are seldom found together? But this very point we have made is abundantly clear from the constant quarrels and disputes among those who have made the judgment of the Fathers their standard. Before their tribunal they fight no less over many chapters on which they have never agreed among themselves. Some Papists bring forward, as evidence of the obscurity which they charge against Scripture over against the Protestants, the variety of opinions. Among the Protestants themselves there are battles over some chapters: the Lutherans with the Calvinists over the Eucharist, and these in turn with those and with the Arminians over free will and predestination.

units.la: Eusebii lib. 10. Hist. Eccles. c. 5. p. 114. Zozomenus, Socrates, Pompeius, Card. Baronius. Kepl. p. 309. Vulgo lenditur. Sozomen. Magnus. Eusebius, Patrum loca... destinatione, altercationes. Si cuiusvis est haec ratio pretij quis non videt eam hic etiam valere, & probare quod contendimus? Profitentur enim tum Graeci, tum Latini se e Patrum authoritate pendere, & se iis iudicibus velle causam suam dicere, necdum tamen inter eos convenit. Suave est exercitatissimos utrimque pugiles in hac palaestra apud Synodum Florentinam certantes spectare pluresque horas, ac totos interdum dies in enucleandis pauculis vel Ephesinae Synodi, † vel Epiphanij, * vel Basilij † voculis consumentes, remque eo tandem molestissima disputatione deduci, ut quantumvis utrique de suarum expositionum perspicuitate glorientur, Patrum sensus multo fiat postremo obscuriot quam ante fuit, offusis in res ipsas, per tam longas altercationes, tenebris. Satis quidem probabiliter alij aliorum argumenta confutant, sed mirum quam parum solide sua ipsi adstruant. Latini sane, quorum ut causa melior ita & disputatio foelicior fuisse creditur, in loco quodam Basilij triumphant, & quasi victa causa, cantato epinicio, Graecis indignis modis insultant, verbisque eos mordacibus lacesserunt. Ipsi tamen adeo jejuna Dialectica usi sunt ad persuadendam quam afferebant explicationem ut etiamnum hodie in postrema Operum Basilij, quam Fronto recensuit, editione, interpretatio Latina explicationem Latinorum rejecerit, Graecosque, licet Schifmaticos, hoc loco secuta sit. Cum Protestantium nonnulli hoc pugnae genus super quibusdam controversiis capitibus cum iis iniissent, animadvertere quilibet potest, quanta sit locorum utriusque allatorum obscuritas. Si eadem fuit Tertulliani, quae est hodie Ecclesiae Romanae, de Eucharistia sententia, quicquamne fingi potest obscurius hoc loco e quarto libro contra Marcionem? Christus acceptum panem & distributum discipulis, corpus illum [suum] fecit, hoc est corpus meum dicendo, id est figura corporis mei. Si Augustino credita transubstantiatio quid sibi volunt haec eius verba. Non enim Dominus dubitavit dicere hoc est corpus meum,cùm signum dare corporis sui.Si loci isti & alij penè innumerabiles id volunt quod contendit Cardinalis Perronius, fuerùntne unquàm obscuriora, vel Sphyngis Thebanæ ænigmata, vel Sibyllæ oracula ? Quod si ad alteram partem te converteris, non pauciora fortasse hic quoque offendes,quæ Protestantium sensum nullo modo admittere posse videntur, qualia sunt quæ disertis verbis, vel aiunt panis naturam immutati & per omnipotentiam Dei verbi carnem fieri, vel negant Eucharistiam panem esse aut vinum. Sunt in singuliis controversiis similes loci, quorum alij Romanæ Ecclesiæ, alij Protestantium judicio in explicabiles videntur. Si Cardinalis Perronius & alij præstanti ingenio viri, tam harum quam illarum partium , sibi plana & aperta omnia videri confirmant,satendum est id confidentius, nec sine jactantia dici , longéque ipsos plus in fronte promittere quàm in recessu habeant, aut sanè reliquos homines præ istis acie cùm ingenij tum oculorum esse admodum hebere, cùm nihil nisi tenebras videant, ubi isti meram lucem sibi obversari testantur. Enim vero si obscuritas magna non est , unde fit ut ipsi tam sæpe adeo se torqueant, quare tot verbis, nullàque arte non adhibita in iis elucidandis laborant? Vnde fit ut cùm lectoribus se posse satisfacere desperant, in ipsos quos allegant auctores, aut in eorum scriptis invehuntur eorùmque fidem labefactent? Quod genus hoc judicij est, quod longe fusiore elucidatione opus habet quam res ipsa? quod lites, quas decidere debuit , ferit ? quod utrique parti æqualiter favere videtur ? De sensu horum Domini verborum contenditur. Hoc est corpus meum. Adduccuntur Tertullianus & Augustinus qui ea exponant. Fidem tam , lector , nonne æquè , immò magis perspicua sunt hæc ipsa Scripturæ verba , quam utriusque Scriptoris loca, qua quidem ratione explicantur ? Nullum hic judicem recuso ; te , lector,quisquis es , appello ; tantum ne te legere& expendere pigeat quæ in utramque lo-
units.tr: If this kind of argument has any weight, who does not see that it holds here too and proves what we contend? For both the Greeks and the Latins profess that they depend on the authority of the Fathers and wish to plead their cause before those judges, yet they have not agreed among themselves. It is pleasant to watch the most practised fighters on both sides contending in this arena at the Council of Florence, spending several hours, and sometimes whole days, in unravelling a few little words of the Council of Ephesus, or of Epiphanius, or of Basil. The matter is at last brought by such most tiresome disputation to the point where, however much each side boasts of the clarity of its own explanations, the meaning of the Fathers has become far more obscure at the end than it was before, the shadows having been cast over the matters themselves by such long altercations. Fairly plausibly, each side refutes the other's arguments, but it is remarkable how little solidly they establish their own. The Latins, whose cause is believed to be as good as their disputation was fortunate, triumph over a passage of Basil. As if the cause were won, they chant a song of victory and insult the Greeks in unworthy fashion, assailing them with biting words. Yet they used such thin dialectic to persuade people of the explanation they offered that even today, in the latest edition of Basil's works, which Fronton revised, the Latin translation has rejected the Latin explanation and followed the Greeks, though they are schismatics, at this point. When some Protestants entered this kind of combat over certain controverted chapters, anyone can see how great the obscurity is of the passages cited on both sides. If Tertullian's view of the Eucharist was the same as that of the present Roman Church, can anything more obscure be imagined than this passage from the fourth book against Marcion? Christ, having taken the bread and distributed it to the disciples, made that body [his own], saying "this is my body," that is, "a figure of my body." If Augustine believed in transubstantiation, what do these words of his mean? For the Lord did not hesitate to say "this is my body," when he was giving a sign of his body. If these passages, and almost countless others, mean what Cardinal Perron contends, were the riddles of the Theban Sphinx or the oracles of the Sibyl ever more obscure? But if you turn to the other side, you will perhaps find no fewer passages here which in no way seem able to bear the Protestant sense, such as those which in plain words either say that the nature of the bread is changed and, by the omnipotence of God, becomes the flesh of the Word, or deny that the Eucharist is bread or wine. In individual controversies there are similar passages, some of which seem inexplicable to the Roman Church, others to the judgment of the Protestants. If Cardinal Perron and other men of outstanding talent on both sides affirm that everything seems plain and open to them, this must be said more boldly, and not without boasting; they promise far more on their brow than they keep in reserve. Otherwise the rest of mankind must be very dull, both in intellect and in eyesight, compared with these men, since they see nothing but darkness where these men declare pure light is shining. Indeed, if the obscurity is not great, why do they so often twist themselves into knots, and why do they labour with so many words and every art to clear these passages up? How does it come about that, when they despair of satisfying their readers, they rail against the very authors they cite, or attack their writings and undermine their credibility? What kind of judgment is this, which needs a far longer explanation than the matter itself, which strikes at the disputes it ought to settle, and which seems to favour each side equally? The sense of these words of the Lord is contested: This is my body. Tertullian and Augustine are brought forward to explain them. Reader, are not these very words of Scripture, as to clarity, equally or even more clear than the passages of either writer by which they are explained? I reject no judge here; I appeal to you, reader, whoever you are. Only do not be reluctant to read and weigh what is said today on each side

units.la: cum hodie dicuntur, & quam longis ambagimus ad verum eorum sensum deducamur, Ac nisi doctissimi quibuscunque, in explicandis Patrum Scriptis aqua haereret, non est credibile Censores Belgicos, viros Lectissimos, suo exemplo praeire nobis voluisse, ut adeo turpibus effugiis eorum authoritate, dum opponuntur in disputationibus, aut conflictibus cumadversatiis, pressi, elabiconotaremur. ex cogitato videlicet, commento aut sensu commodo iis affecto. Sed de his hactenus satis, opinor, ut quilibet sui compos, per se agnoscat, non facile esse quid senserint Patres ex scriptis eorum pernoscere. Verum ne quis scrupulus resteret, expendamus breviter praecipuas quasdam istius obscuritatis causas. Sane cum Patres viri sapientes fuerint, ideo censendi sunt scripsisse, ut intelligerentur. Itaque cum plerique ingenio & doctrina excelluerint, mirum videri queat cur finem, quem sibi propositum habuerant, non sint assecuti. Sed in memoriam hic redeat quod supra monuimus, eos cum nondum natis nostris controversiis scripserint, non potuisse in animo habere de iis agere. Sapientes quippe quam minimum possunt dubia in religione movent. Adde quod non decerant illi, suis saeculis, variae & quidem nobiles controversiae, in quibus enodandis occuparentur, ut nihil opus esset ipsis ad nostras animum appellere. Super iis de quibus agunt perspicue quidem quid suae essent sententiae expositurunt. Inter obscuros Scriptores fere eminet Tertullianus: Attamen cum adversus Marcionem disputat, ita perspicue quid sentiat aperit, ut nullum dubio locum relinquat. Si ergo hisce temporibus vixissent, aut si superstitibus illis hodiernae controversiae agitatae fuissent, nullus dubito quin clare ac perspicue fuerint de iis actum. Nam, ut cuiuis notum est ex usu communi, sermones certo consilio, & ex destinato non habiti, nunquam sunt aperti & definiti, sed pendentes & ambiguita utad varios fines, imo saepe contra sensus & studia eorum quibus exciderunt referri possint. Sic ante ortam, quæ tam graviter veterem Ecclesiam afflixit, Arii pestem, pauca habentur, apud Patres, de æternitate Divinæ Iesu Christi naturæ, aut, si aliquid occurrit, appareret id obiter, non rotundé, & ab aliud agentibus, nec ex destinato dictum, unde fit ut quæ de hoc argumento habent, non minoribus sint tenebris obsita, nec solutu faciliora, quàm quæ apud eos ad nostras controuersias alludunt, quando pertinere videntur. Explica, sodes, hæc verba ex Iustino contra Tryphonem. Deum qui Mosi apparuit & Patriarchæ Filium fuisse, non Patrem, eo quod Pater nunquam locum mutet, nec ascendat nec descendat. Item, A nemine unquam visum Patrem, sed Filium quidem, & Angelum ejus, qui sit etiam Deus, per voluntatem Patris. Vix enim hæc sic resolvi possunt, quin diversitas naturæ in Patre & in Filio ponatur, quod Arianum est. Expende etiam quæ de hoc argumento habet Tertullianus. Patrem ex semet ipso proferendo Filium fecisse, & Patrem esse totam substantiam filium verò derivationem totius & portionem, & passim alia multa in præstanti illo, adversus Praxeam, opere obuia, quæ ad bonum sensum revocare non levis est operæ. Sic Dionysius Alexandrinus Filium opus, aut figmentum, Patris vocat, quæ sunt ipsamet verba apud Athar. quæ in Ario anathemate percussa sunt. Immò ipsi LXXX Patres, qui Paulum Samosatenum Episcopum Antiochenum damnarunt, dicunt Filium non esse ejusdem essentiæ cum Patre, qua ratione ὁμοούσιον negant, quod postea in Concilio Nicæno constitutum fuit. Hæc ipsa observatio leui negotio probare posset, & in aliis Ecclesiæ cum Macedonio, Pelagio, Nestorio, Eutychete & Monothelitis controuersiis Patres, videlicet, obscurissimè de hisce rebus locutos antequam in quæstionem vocarentur, cùm nempe de iis certo consilio non agerent. Iam olim illa scripta sunt Hieronymo. Antequam in Alexandria quasi daemonium meridianum Arius nasceretur, innocenter quædam minus cautè locuti sunt Ecclesiastici & quæ non possunt per versorum hominum calumniam declinare. Inter recentiores doctissimi hoc ipsum animadverterunt. Sic Cardinalis Peronius, Lic Petauinus, magno apud suos in pretio le suita, in Epiphanium icubens, ut Lucianum Martyrem Arianismi & Samosarenianismi suspicione liberarer, ait plerisque Veterum Patrum in ... negotio Trinitatis, tamen a lijs fidei Christianæ capitibus invenisse, ut ante errorum atq; hæreseon, quibus ea sigillatim oppugnabantur, originem nondum satu illustrata & patefactarum rei veritate quadam scriptis suis asperserint quæ cum orthodoxæ fidei regulæ minimè consentiant.
units.tr: and how far we are led by long detours to their true sense. Unless the most learned men everywhere were stuck fast in explaining the writings of the Fathers, it is not credible that the Belgian Censors, most distinguished men, would have wished to set us an example, so that we should be pressed by their authority when we are opposed in disputations or conflicts with adversaries, and should slip away with such shameful evasions as "by a contrived idea, an invention, or a sense convenient to them." But enough of this, I think, so that anyone of sound mind may recognise for himself that it is not easy to learn from their writings what the Fathers thought. Yet lest any doubt remain, let us briefly weigh some principal causes of this obscurity. Since the Fathers were wise men, they must be considered to have written so as to be understood. And since most of them excelled in talent and learning, it may seem strange that they did not attain the goal they had set themselves. But let there return to mind what we noted above: since they wrote before our controversies had arisen, they could not have intended to treat them. Wise men indeed raise doubtful questions in religion as little as they can. Add that in their own ages there were no varied and indeed notable controversies occupying them, so that there was no need for them to turn their minds to ours. On the matters they did treat, they set out clearly what their opinions were. Among obscure writers Tertullian almost stands out; yet when he disputes against Marcion, he reveals so clearly what he thinks that he leaves no room for doubt. If therefore they had lived in these times, or if today's controversies had been stirred while they were still alive, I have no doubt that they would have dealt with them clearly and plainly. For, as everyone knows from common usage, discourses not delivered with a fixed purpose and from a settled plan are never open and definite, but hang loose and ambiguous, so that they can be referred to various ends, and indeed often against the meaning and aims of those who uttered them. So before the plague of Arius arose, which so grievously afflicted the ancient Church, few things are found among the Fathers about the eternity of the divine nature of Jesus Christ. If something does occur, it appears incidentally, not fully, and is said by men busy with something else, not from a set purpose. Hence what they have on this subject is no less shrouded in shadows, and no easier to resolve, than what they say that alludes to our controversies when they seem to bear on them. Please explain these words of Justin against Trypho: God, who appeared to Moses and was the Son of the Patriarch, not the Father, because the Father never changes place, neither ascending nor descending. Likewise, the Father was never seen by anyone, but the Son indeed, and his Angel, who is also God, by the will of the Father. For these things can hardly be resolved in such a way that a difference of nature between the Father and the Son is not asserted, which is Arian. Weigh also what Tertullian has on this subject: that the Father, by bringing forth the Son out of himself, made him; that the Father is the whole substance, but the Son a derivation of the whole and a portion; and passim many other things in that excellent work against Praxeas, met everywhere, which it is no slight labour to bring back to a sound sense. So Dionysius of Alexandria calls the Son a work or a fabrication of the Father, which are his very words in Athanasius, which were struck down in the anathema against Arius. Indeed, the seventy-odd Fathers who condemned Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch, say that the Son is not of the same essence as the Father, by which reasoning they deny the homoousion, which was afterwards established at the Council of Nicaea. This very observation could easily prove that in the other controversies of the Church, with Macedonius, Pelagius, Nestorius, Eutyches and the Monothelites, the Fathers spoke very obscurely about these matters before they were called into question, since they did not deal with them on purpose. Long ago Jerome wrote these words: Before Arius was born in Alexandria like a noonday demon, some churchmen spoke somewhat carelessly and innocently in ways that cannot be defended against the calumny of perverse men. Among more recent scholars the most learned have noticed this very point. So Cardinal Perron, and Petavius, the Jesuit of great repute among his people, writing against Epiphanius so that he might free Lucian the Martyr from suspicion of Arianism and Samosatenism, says that most of the ancient Fathers, in the matter of the Trinity and in other chapters of the Christian faith, scattered in their writings things that do not agree with the rule of orthodox faith, before the origin of the errors and heresies by which those doctrines were attacked one by one had been brought to light, and before the truth of the matter had been clearly set forth.

units.la: Cùm ergo sic versati sint in aliis argumentis, quid mirum si in iis quæ nunc internos cōtroverterentur eadem ratione se gesserint? Si cùm longè ante motas has controversias vixerint, de iis obscurè, ambiguè, & confusè locuti sint? Equidem in ea sum sententia, longè magis mirum fore si aliter se res haberet, & vehemens apud me suppositionis indicium futurum, si in scripto veterum cuiquam tribuero, controuersiæ nostræ æquè perspicuè ac discrètè, ac sic hodie, excuterentur. Amabo te, confer Antiquissimorum de Divinitate & æternitate Filij Dei dicta cum iis quæ de Eucharistiæ natura aliquando apud ipsos occurrunt, enim vero patebit hæc, ab ea, quæ nunc obtinet super posteriore capite, sententia, non esse alienissima, quàm illa sunt à doctrina olim in Concilio Niceno statuta & recepta. Filium esse Patri consubstantialem Niceæ definitum fuit. Id Antiochiæ negatum. Affirmént ergo, vel negent Patres Eucharistiam esse corpus Christi realiter, sententiæ tuæ non adversabuntur vehementius, quàm Antiocheni Patres in speciem contradixerunt Nicænis. Adde jam quòd quemadmodum Ariani jure non potuerunt in sententiam suam trahere, neque tanquam copias causæ decretorias, voces istas quæ Patribus antiquissimis obiter tantùm, in alia argumenta, nullo consilio vt de hoc agerent, innocenter excidérunt allegare, sic æquius si verum amamus, neque à me, neque à re afferri, tanquam sententias secundùm nos in controversiis recens natis promuntiatas, ea quæ Patribus scripta sunt in alia argumenta, multis ante has exicitatis contentiones, seculis, de quibus ut nihil iis unquam in mentem venit, sic etiam varie admodum & obscurè locuti sunt, imò & quandocunque contradictoriè speciem. Et quemadmodum fideles qui post vetustissimos illos Patres vixerunt, illorum sententias ad veritatem quam profitebantur revocare conati sunt; qua ratione Athanasius erga Dionysium Alexandrinum & Patres Antiochenos se gessit; sic nostræ sunt partes nullum lapidem non movere, ut quàm commodissimè fieri possit, exponamus quicquid in eorum & similium scriptis videtur cum orthodoxa fide de Eucharistia & aliis capitibus pugnare, nec supra modum percelli, si aliquando loci qui in fobis plane videantur inexplicabiles in iis occurrant. Fieri enim potest ut reipsa ejusmodi sint, quandoquidem fieri item potuit ut de persona & naturis Filij Dei ea dixerint quæ supra retulimus, ut notum iis qui in eorum libris versati sunt. Fieri item potest ut eorum dicta, licèt reipsa explicabilia, nobis tamen videantur insolubilia, quia nobis ea subsidia desunt quæ ad lucem iis inferendam necessaria sunt; si, verbi gratia, vel scopum auctoris, vel quæ apud illum antecedunt, aut consequuntur, & alia nescimus, quæ omnino sunt ad quosvis scriptores intelligendos necessaria. Eadem enim est verborum quæ pictarum tabularum ratio, quas in idoneo lumine constitui decet, appareant quod sunt in mente auctoris, quaque pro varietate luminis, varie etiam apparere constat. Exempli gratia, si Dionysij Alexandrini vocula, qua Christum Patris opus, ποίημα, vocat, & alia nonnulla cruda quæ subjicit) qualia quotidie inter disputandum locorum fragmenta antecedentibus, & consequentibus mutila nobis objiciuntur (solitaria è corpore suo, & ex auctoris oratione avulsa, nobis obtruderentur, quis vel peritissimus sibi fingere posset non esse merum Arianismum? quis non pronuntiaret nodum esse insolubilem? Et tamen Athanasius locis supra notatis aliter
units.tr: Since they were so engaged in other subjects, what wonder is it if they behaved in the same way on those matters that are now being disputed among us? What if, although they lived long before these controversies were stirred up, they spoke of them obscurely, ambiguously and confusedly? Indeed, I hold the view that it would be far more surprising if things were otherwise, and I would take it as strong evidence of forgery if any writing of the ancients were found to treat our controversies as clearly and distinctly as they are handled today. Pray, compare what the most ancient writers say about the divinity and eternity of the Son of God with what they sometimes say about the nature of the Eucharist. It will then be plain that the opinion now prevailing on the latter point is not so far removed from the doctrine once laid down and received at the Council of Nicaea. It was defined at Nicaea that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; at Antioch this was denied. So if the Fathers affirmed or denied that the Eucharist is really the body of Christ, they would not oppose your view more vehemently than the Antiochene Fathers, in appearance, opposed the Nicenes. Add to this that, just as the Arians could not rightly draw those words of the most ancient Fathers, uttered only in passing while they were writing on other subjects and without any intention of treating this matter, into their own cause as decisive proofs, so, if we love the truth, it is fairer that neither I nor anyone else should adduce what the Fathers wrote on other subjects, many centuries before these contentions were stirred up, as though they had pronounced opinions in line with ours on controversies that had not yet arisen. About those matters they never thought at all, and so they spoke in varied and very obscure ways, and sometimes even in apparent self-contradiction. And just as the faithful who lived after those most ancient Fathers tried to recall their opinions to the truth they professed, as Athanasius did with Dionysius of Alexandria and the Antiochene Fathers, so it is our task to leave no stone unturned, so that we may explain, as conveniently as possible, whatever in their writings and in those of others seems to clash with the orthodox faith concerning the Eucharist and other heads of doctrine. Nor should we be greatly dismayed if passages that appear wholly inexplicable to us sometimes occur in them. For it may be that they really are of this kind, since it is likewise possible that they said of the person and natures of the Son of God the things we have cited above, as is known to those who have read their books. It is also possible that their sayings, though really explicable, nevertheless seem insoluble to us, because we lack those aids that are needed to throw light on them: for example, if we do not know the author's aim, or what goes before and after in his work, or other things which are altogether necessary for understanding any writer. For the case of words is the same as that of painted pictures, which ought to be set in a suitable light so that they may appear as they are in the mind of the artist; and it is well known that they appear differently according to the variation of the light. For instance, if the little word by which Dionysius of Alexandria calls Christ the work of the Father, ποίημα [creature], and some other harsh statements he adds, were thrust upon us as isolated fragments, torn from their context and cut off from their antecedents and consequents, as such fragments are thrown at us every day in disputation, who, however skilled, could imagine that it is not sheer Arianism? Who would not pronounce the knot insoluble? And yet Athanasius, in the passages noted above,

units.la: Athan. ep. ad Dionys. et Synod. Arim. ut supra. aliter docet,& ex luce tum è loco ipso petita,tum aliunde illata,ostendit voces illas, duriores licèt bonum sensum habere. Quod ut capiamus plenius ad alias obscuritatis Patrum causas pergendum est. Inter illas principem constituo, quod interdum student animi sui sensa penitus occultare, aut saltem ostendere non nuda & aperta in clara luce; sed objecto, ut sic dicam, velo, & quidem aliquando satis denso; ita ut nonnisi Lynceis oculiis sit pervium. Habebant nempe meditationes nescio quas, quas inutile imò & noxium infirmis & plebeis ingeniis aperire existimabant. Jurene, an injuria, sic senserint hoc loco non disputo.Mihi nunc satis quod ita senserint; ut inter alios ex Clemente Alexandrino patet. Is Strom.1.initio, de consilio suo agens haec habet. Nonnulla consulto praetermitto: timeas scribere quae etiam cavi dicere, non utique invidens, neque enim fas, sed iis metuens qui in ea inciderent,ne in aliam forte partem accipientes laberentur, & puero gladium, ut proverbio fertur, praebere invenimus. Caeterum subjungit se quaedam aenigmatice significaturum, adeo ut in quibusdam insistat, alia tantum dicat, ita ut occultans aperiat, & tacens offendat. Sed quod maximi est momenti hac ipsa methodo usi sunt circa quaedam capita quae hodie in controversiam vocantur; circa scilicet, sacramenta Ecclesiae. Cum enim ea mysteria nonnisi clam & seorsum apud suos celebrarent, neque ad ea contemplanda vel Ethnicos, vel Catechumenos, imo (ut quidam volunt) neque ullos alios quàm qui mysteriorum erant participes admitterent; Sic etiam in Tractationibus suis, maximè in homiliis quas ad populum habituri erant, nunquam nisi obscurè de iis agebant, ut de Eucharistia annotarunt Cardinalis Petronius, Casaubonus, Petavius & alii de Baptismo, de Confirmatione & aliis Christianorum sacris caerimoniis. Aspice, quaeso, quàm diligenter Theodoretus & Epiphanius sibi caveant ne Eucharistiae materiam nomine proprio indicent, ut semper eam designent vocibus generalibus, ab iis tantùm
units.tr: Athan. ep. ad Dionys. et Synod. Arim. ut supra. teaches otherwise, and from the light both drawn from the passage itself and brought in from elsewhere he shows that those words, though harsher, bear a good sense. To grasp this more fully, we must go on to the other causes of the obscurity of the Fathers. Among these I set first this: they sometimes took pains to conceal the feelings of their minds completely, or at least not to show them naked and open in the clear light, but, as I may put it, with a veil thrown over the object, and indeed at times a fairly thick one, so that it could be seen through only by lynx-eyes. For they had, I know not what, meditations which they judged useless and even harmful to be opened to weak and common minds. Whether they were right or wrong to think so here, I do not discuss; it is enough for me now that they did think so, as appears among others from Clement of Alexandria. In the beginning of the first book of the Stromata, speaking of his own design, he has these words: I deliberately pass over some things: you should fear to write what I have taken care not to say; not indeed grudging, for that is not lawful, but fearing for those who might fall into them, lest perhaps, receiving them in the wrong sense, they should slip; and we find that we are giving a sword to a boy, as the proverb goes. He adds that he will indicate some things enigmatically, so that he dwells on some things, and says only other things, so that by concealing he reveals, and by keeping silent he offends. But what is of the greatest importance is that they used this very method concerning certain heads of doctrine which are today brought into controversy; namely, the sacraments of the Church. For since they celebrated those mysteries only secretly and apart among their own people, and admitted to the contemplation of them neither pagans nor catechumens, nor indeed (as some hold) anyone except those who were participants in the mysteries, so also in their treatises, and especially in the homilies they were to deliver to the people, they never spoke of these things except obscurely. This has been observed of the Eucharist by Cardinal Petronius, Casaubon, Petavius and others, and of baptism, of confirmation and of the other sacred ceremonies of Christians. Behold, I beg you, how carefully Theodoret and Epiphanius guard themselves lest they name the matter of the Eucharist by its proper name, so that they always designate it by general terms, intelligible only to those who had at some time been partakers of it.

units.la: S qui ejus aliquando participes fuerant intelligendis. Finem quem sibi proponebant nunc non excutio; videntur mentes Catechumenorum ad reverentiam & vehementis desiderium Sacramentorum excitare voluisse. Verebantur, scilicet, ne rei ipsius conspectus, sermóque de materia & ratione Sacramentorum simplex & apertus hoc vel illud studium imminuerent. Cum ergo, tum in hoc argumento, tum in aliis ipsis propositum fuerit mentem suam caligine quadam veluti involvere, non debet mirum videri, si quæ scripserunt, sæpe sint obscura, &(quod obscuritatem consequitur) si aliquando secum ipsi pugnare videantur. Quin potius magis mirum existimandum esset, si viri ingenio doctrináque insignes, quales plerique fuere, de his ipsis argumentis, quæ occultari & celari debere censebant perspicuè tamen & diserte sententias suas inscriptis suis exposuissent. Sed est aliquid amplius; quandoque enim accidit, ut etiam ubi obscuritati non student, obscuri tamen sint. Sunt quibus obscuritatem conciliavit earum artium ignorantia quæ linguam fingunt, & bene loqui docent. Alii ita nati erant, ut eos neque ars, neque studium emendare potuerit. Epiphanium, absque injuria, in priori ordine collocari posse puto. Fuit quidem vir ille Sanctus, sed Grammaticæ ac Rhetoricæ admodum rudis, ut satis apparet ex ejus operibus, in quibus non solùm orationis nitorem, sed etiam seriem & syntaxin, periodorumque structuram, orationis omnis Lucem unicam, plerumque desideres; quæ quidem vitia variis multisque in locis necessario obscuritatem pariunt, quod & queruntur ejus interpretes. Studere quidem alii eleganter loqui, sed votis successus defuit, seu quod seriùs in id incubuerint, seu quod ingenio idoneo caruerint, ut non omnis fert omnia tellus, nec ullo labore ullàve industria fieri potest, ut quælibet materia cujuslibet formæ capax sit. His accenseri potest Victorinus ille, de quo satis lepidè Hieronymus. Victorino Martyri (inquit) in libris suis, licet defit eruditio, tamen non deest eruditionis voluntas. Hujus quoque census Ruffinus fuit cujus Latinitatem, elocutionis genus, acyrologias, & alia vitia, tam severè castigat magnus ille Antiquitatis Censor Hieronymus. Et is tamen Ruffinus plurima scriptitavit, quin & suos admiratores habuit. Fit enim nescio quo fato, ut doctissimi quique pauca scribant, neque alios ferè quam indoctos insanabile illud scribendi cacoethes teneat. Ejusmodi vitia in suorum Graecorum nonnullis scriptoribus notat in Bibliotheca sua Photius. Sed sanè longè majus in Patribus ab eruditione quàm ab imperitia obscuritatis periculum. Ex iis enim qui in literis & disciplinis humanioribus versati erant, quique ab incunte aetate in eloquentia & sapientia Graecorum erant instituti, semper cum colorem servavere, quo semel imbuti fuerant, adeo ut nonnunquam & eam ostentare gestiant, quo fit ut in Philosophiam Christianam verba & instituta aliena & res peregrinas invehant, quae quidem varietas non exiguae voluptati est eruditis, sed orationem tamen necessariò obscurat & involvit. Quid stromatibus (haec est enim inscriptio) & aliis Clementis presbyteri Alexandrini operibus variegatum & ornatum magis; textus est enim totus ille Scriptor allusionibus ad historias, sententias Apophtegmata & adagia literarum tum sacrarum tum profanarum. Hic vividis earum coloribus illustratus assurgit, alibi umbris obscuratus quodammodo delitescit. Itaque non est quod sperent qui literarum humaniorum cultu carent, se cum fructu & intelligentia in ejus scriptis versari posse. Quid dicam de Tertulliano qui praeter vehementis & acris ingenii naturalem, quae in eo passim apparet, asperitatem, & Știii Carthaginensis, cum reliquis Africanis, ipsi communem indolem, orationis suae splendorem tanta eruditione, tam multis vocibus, aut novis aut è Jurisprudentia translatis, tot subtiliter & acutè dictis obscuravit, ut lectores ad nutum attentissimè sagaces (ut non nemo dixit) sibi poscat, nullâq; nimia sit ad eum probè intelligendum vel doctrina vel attentio. Nostratem Hilarium, rerum & elocutionis m ajestate sublimem, cothurnúmq; illum Gallicum, quem in eo, & in aliis cisalpinis scriptoribus, observat Hieronymus prudens mitto, ut & Asiaticorum dicendi genus copiosum, Atheniensiúmq; , & eorum qui se ad mores illorum finxerant, argutias. His observationibus vix sufficeret volumen integrum. Hoc unum in genere dicam. Scribendi, Scripturasq; explicandi ratio, quæ ab initio simplex aperta & succincta apud Christianos fuerat, brevi immutata est, & subtilitatis ornamentorúmq;, humanorum sordes contraxit, ut apud Epiphanium testatur Methodius. Doctores, non jam quod optimum est, gravitatisq; plenum sludent, sed id duntaxat quod placet, & quod jecundo favore fertur respiciunt, uti sophiste facere consueverunt qui orationum suarum mercedem accipientes, doctrinæ & eruditionis suæ laudibus, tanquam vilí quódam pretio redimuntur. Ac priscis quidem temporibus, summa erat in explicando brevitas: cum in id illi potissimum incumberent, non ut oblectarent sed ut prodessent auditoribus. Idipsum graviter & eloquenter suo more queritur Gregorius Nazianzenus. Fuit quondam tempus cum res nostra florerent, ac præclare se haberent, cum nimirum superflua hæc & verborum lepore atque arte fucata tractandaTheologiæ ratio ad Divinas causas ne aditum quidem habebat : verum idem erat calculis ludere inversionis celeritate aspectum fallentibus , aut omnigenis & lascivis corporis flexibus spectatores ludificari, quod novi quidpiam & curiosi de Deo vel dicere vel audire. Simplex contra ingenua[?] oratio atque doctrina pietas exsistimabatur. At postquam Sexti & Pyrrhones , & contradicendi libidine incitata lingua, velut gravis quidam ac malignus morbus in Ecclesias nostras infauliter obrepsit, quod, Ad̃orum liber de Atheniensibus narrat, ad nihil aliud vacanus quàm ad novi aliquid dicendum vel audiendum, ô quis Hieremias confusionem nostram caliginemq; deplorabit, qui solus Lamentationes calamitatibus exaquare novit? Enimuero non diffimulat Hieronymus, in Epistola ad Pammachium scripta sua lectorem eruditum poscere, artiumq; Dialectica & Rhetorica non imperitum. Idémq; Judicium faciendum est de scriptis Origenis, Methodii, Eusebii, Appollinaris, Tertulliani, Cypriani, Minutii, Victorini, Lactantii, Hilarii & aliorum, quos eodem dicendi genere usos fuisse contendit. Quanquam vero sapientem neminem inficiaturum putem, quin Metaphoras & figuras (sive in dictione, sive maximè in rebus ipsis sint) & alia Rhetorica ornamenta, Dialecticae argutias, omniáq; ejusmodi liberalium disciplinarum artificia plurimum umbrarum & obscuritatis in Orationem invehant; Lubet tamen ad argumenti hujus majorem elucidationem probationes quasdam & exempla hic subtexere. Hieronymus hoc satis docet, cùm Commentariorum quorundam ex eo arcessit obscuritatem quod nimium esset diserti. Sixtus Senensis annotat Patres multa saepe dicere per hyperbolen, affectuum impetu & orationis cursu raptos, quae non sunt eo rigore accipienda quo primùm ad aures auditorum perveniunt. Et proximè Petavius; multa sunt, inquit, à sanctissimis Patribus, praesertim à Chrysostomo in homiliis aspersa, quae fi ad exacta veritatis regulam accommodare volueris boni sensus inania videbuntur. Utrique eos saepe sic excusamus, ut causa femur sub tot foliis & floribus, quibus quasi fertis & corollis scripta sua exornant, latere aliquando alium longè sensum quàm qui prima fronte apparet. Quis Chrysostomi, Hilarii, Ambrosii non observavit hyperbolas? Sed ut oculis ipsis subjiciam quantum tenebrarum ejusmodi ornamenta vero Scriptorum sensui offundant, unum exemplum huc ex Hieronymo referam. Is cùm ad Eustochium nobilem virginem scriberet,narratse,quod secularium literarum libros studiosiùs legeret, protractum fuisse ad tribunal Domini, ibique acriter cæsum, acerbas ejus peccati pœnas dedisse. Nec vero, inquit,sopor ille fuerat, aut vana somnia quibus sæpe deludimur. Testis est tribunal illud ante quod iacui, testis iudicium triste quod humi. Ita mihi tribunal illud ante quod iacui, testis iudicium triste quod timui. Ita mihi nunquam contingat in talem incidere questionem ; liventes fateor habuisse me scapulas, plagas sen-sisse post somnum, & tanto de hinc studio divina legisse quanto non ante mortalia legeram. Quis hæc legens non credat totam hanc narrationem esse veram? Quis non omnia ad literam, & prout verba sonant interpretetur? Atqui, ex iis quæ idem alibi dicit, certum est hæc nihil fuisse aliud quam somnium, & confictam more Rhetoribus familiari narrationem, ad vehementius deterrendos lectores à nimio librorum Ethnicorum studio. Cum enim Ruffinus ad eum lapidem impegisset, secureque objecisset ipsum, ne juratum quidem, abstinere à Gentilium literarum libris lectitandis; Hieronymus, post varia in sui defensionem adversus criminationem istam allata, Hac, inquit, diceremsi quippiam vigilans promisissem; nunc autem novum imprudentiæ genus objicit mihi somnium meum; eúmqʒ ad Prophetas amandat dicentes, Somniis non esse credendum, quia(inquit) nec adulterii somnium ducit me ad Tartarum, nec corona Martyrii in cælum levat, & uno verbo injuria à se exigi sponsionem somnii. Quis scit annon Malchi vita, quam ille tanta arte, totque adhibitis ornamentis pingit, ejusdemque modi cùm ejus tum aliorum scripta sint pariter ingenii lusus & industriæ specimina? Nec sanè dissimulat ipse de vita Pauli Eremitæ hoc factum fuisse judicium à quibusdam malevolis suis & vehementer probabile est epistolam 47. comptam in primis ac disertam, ejusdem esse ingenii, argumento ad faciendū eloquentiæ periculum, declamatorio more, suscepto ac consisto. Nec abnuit Episcopus Amerinus in
units.tr: ...those who had at some time been partakers of them, in order to understand them. I do not now examine the aim they had in view. It seems they wished to arouse the minds of catechumens to reverence for and an eager desire for the sacraments. For they feared, of course, that the sight of the thing itself, and a plain and open discourse about the matter and nature of the sacraments, would weaken that zeal. Therefore, since in this subject, as in others, they purposed to wrap their meaning in a kind of fog, it ought not to seem surprising if what they wrote is often obscure and, as a consequence of obscurity, sometimes seems to contradict itself. Indeed it would rather be more surprising if men distinguished by talent and learning, as most of them were, had set out their opinions plainly and clearly in their writings on these very subjects which they thought should be hidden and concealed. But there is something more. For it sometimes happens that even where they do not aim at obscurity, they are nonetheless obscure. For some were made obscure by ignorance of those arts which shape language and teach good speaking. Others were so born that neither art nor study could correct them. I think Epiphanius may, without injustice, be placed in the former group. He was indeed a holy man, but very unskilled in grammar and rhetoric, as is sufficiently plain from his works, in which you will often miss not only elegance of style but also sequence and syntax, and the structure of periods, the one light of all speech. These faults, in many places, necessarily produce obscurity, as his interpreters also complain. Others have striven to speak elegantly, but their wishes lacked success, either because they took up the task too late, or because they lacked suitable talent, for not every land bears every thing, nor by any labour or industry can it be brought about that any matter is capable of every form. To this group may be reckoned that Victorinus, of whom Jerome speaks rather wittily: To Victorinus the martyr (he says), in his books, although learning is lacking, the will to learn is not lacking. Ruffinus also belongs to this class; his Latin, his style of expression, his misuse of words, and other faults, the great censor of antiquity Jerome chastises so severely. And yet this Ruffinus wrote a great deal, and even had his admirers. For by some strange fate it happens that the most learned men write little, while that incurable itch for writing seizes almost none but the unlearned. Photius, in his Bibliotheca, notes faults of this kind in some of their Greek writers. But the danger of obscurity among the Fathers arose far more from learning than from ignorance. For those who were versed in the liberal arts and literature, and who had been trained from early youth in the eloquence and wisdom of the Greeks, always kept the colour with which they had once been steeped, so that sometimes they even eagerly display it. Hence they bring foreign words and institutions and strange matters into Christian philosophy, which variety is indeed a great pleasure to the learned, but nonetheless necessarily darkens and clouds the discourse. What is more variegated and adorned than the Stromata (for that is its title) and the other works of Clement, presbyter of Alexandria? For that whole writer is woven with allusions to histories, sayings, anecdotes, and proverbs, both sacred and profane. Here he rises up illuminated by their vivid colours, elsewhere he is in some way hidden, shaded by shadows. Therefore those who lack a cultivated acquaintance with literature should not hope that they can work through his writings with profit and understanding. What shall I say of Tertullian, who, besides the natural harshness of a vehement and sharp mind which appears everywhere in him, and the roughness common to him and the rest of the Africans, obscured the splendour of his style by so much learning, by so many words, either new or taken from jurisprudence, and by so many subtle and sharply turned sayings, that he demands readers most keenly attentive at a nod (as someone has said), and no learning or attention is excessive for understanding him properly? I pass over our Hilary, sublime in the majesty of his matter and expression, and that Gallic buskin which Jerome, wisely, observes in him and in other transalpine writers; likewise the copious style of the Asian orators, and the subtleties of the Athenians and of those who had moulded themselves on their manners. A whole volume would scarcely suffice for these observations. I will say this one thing in general. The manner of writing and of explaining the Scriptures, which among Christians had at first been simple, open and concise, was soon changed, and contracted the filth of human subtlety and ornament, as Methodius bears witness in Epiphanius. Teachers no longer strive for what is best and full of seriousness, but look only to what pleases and is carried along by a favour that is easy to win, as sophists are accustomed to do, who, receiving payment for their speeches, are bought, as it were at a cheap price, with praises of their learning and erudition. And in earlier times, indeed, brevity in explaining was supreme, since they chiefly applied themselves to this, not to delight but to profit their hearers. Gregory Nazianzen complains of the same thing, gravely and eloquently in his own manner. There was once a time when our affairs flourished and stood in good order, when, of course, this superfluous manner of treating theology, with the charm of words and artifice, did not even have access to the divine causes; but it was the same as playing with dice that deceive the eye by the speed of their turning, or amusing spectators with all sorts of wanton bodily contortions, since men thought that to say or hear something new and curious about God was everything. On the other hand, plain speech and sound doctrine and piety were thought of little account. But after the Sextii and Pyrrhonists, and a tongue stirred up by lust for contradiction, crept in unhappily among our churches like a grave and malignant disease, which, as the book of Adorus tells of the Athenians, is busy with nothing else than saying or hearing something new, oh, who will lament our confusion and our darkness, Jeremiah, who alone knows how to match lamentations to calamities? Indeed Jerome does not conceal that in his Epistle to Pammachius he requires of his reader one who is learned and not inexperienced in the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. And the same judgement must be made of the writings of Origen, Methodius, Eusebius, Apollinaris, Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Victorinus, Lactantius, Hilary and others, whom he contends used the same manner of speaking. Yet although I think no wise man would deny that metaphors and figures (whether in words or, more especially, in the things themselves), other rhetorical ornaments, the subtleties of dialectic, and all such devices of the liberal arts bring much shadow and obscurity into discourse, it is nonetheless pleasing, for the greater clarification of this matter, to set down here some proofs and examples. Jerome sufficiently teaches this when he says that the obscurity of certain commentaries arises from the fact that they are too eloquent. Sixtus of Siena notes that the Fathers often say many things by hyperbole, carried away by the force of their feelings and the course of their speech, which are not to be taken with the rigour with which they first reach the ears of the hearers. And more recently Petavius: Many things, he says, scattered by the most holy Fathers, especially by Chrysostom in his homilies, if you wish to fit them to the exact rule of truth, will seem empty of sound sense. We often excuse both of them in such a way that, under so many leaves and flowers with which they adorn their writings, as with garlands and wreaths, another meaning, far different from that which appears at first sight, sometimes lies hidden. Who has not observed the hyperboles of Chrysostom, Hilary and Ambrose? But to set before the eyes themselves how much darkness such ornaments pour over the true sense of the writers, I will cite here one example from Jerome. When he was writing to the noble virgin Eustochium, he related that, because he read the books of secular literature too eagerly, he had been dragged before the tribunal of the Lord, and there sharply scourged, and had paid the bitter penalties of his sin. Nor indeed, he says, was that a slumber, or vain dreams by which we are often deceived. The tribunal before which I lay prostrate is my witness, the grim judgement which I feared on the ground is my witness. So may it never happen to me to fall into such a question again; I confess I had bruised shoulders, I felt the blows after sleep, and from then on I read the divine books with as much zeal as I had never before read worldly ones. Who, reading these words, would not believe that this whole narrative is true? Who would not interpret it all literally, and just as the words sound? And yet, from what he says elsewhere, it is certain that this was nothing but a dream, and a narrative invented in the manner familiar to rhetoricians, to deter readers more vehemently from excessive study of the pagan books. For when Ruffinus struck him on this stone, and confidently objected to him that he had not even sworn to abstain from reading the books of the Gentile literature, Jerome, after various defences of himself against that accusation, says: I would have said these things if I had promised something while awake; but now my dream brings against me a new kind of folly; and he sends him off to the Prophets, saying: Dreams are not to be believed, since (he says) a dream of adultery does not lead me down to Tartarus, nor does the crown of martyrdom raise me to heaven, and in one word, that an injury was demanded from him by a pledge given in a dream. Who knows whether the life of Malchus, which he paints with such art and with so many ornaments, and his other writings of the same kind, are not equally sports of wit and specimens of diligence? Nor does he himself deny that this judgement was passed on his Life of Paul the Hermit by some of his ill-wishers; and it is very probable that Epistle 47, which is elegant and eloquent in the first place, is of the same character, undertaken and carried through in a declamatory manner, as an exercise to test eloquence. Nor does the Bishop of Amerina deny...

units.la: Hieron. Apol. advers. Ruff. T. 2. p. 310. in Epistolæ præfixa periocha. Satis jam vides, lector, quantis veterum libro tenebris Rhetoricæ humanæ schemata & artes involverint; dum enim frequentius & liberius pigmentis istis oratoriis indulgent,factum est, magno nostro malo,ut res ipsæ,genuinique ipsorum sensus nos fugerent. Quis idoneè cavebat non fuisse adhibitas easdem artes in Eucharistiæ negotio, ut Divinorum mysteriorum tum dignitatem, tum reverentiam auctum irent? Item de Præsulum dignitate, ut iis populorum observantiam obedientiámq; conciliarent?Ac denique de cæteris religionis capitibus quæ hodie in controversiam vocantur? An est probabile ipsos pigmentis, coloribus, umbris & luminibus suis pepercisse in iis argumentis quibus ista tanto poterant esse usui? Huc etiam refero quod non raro apud eos occurrit,(scilicet, ut negent vel affirment quædam quasi simpliciter & absolutè, quæ tamen reipsa neque negant, neque affirmant nisi comparatè cum aliis rebus tantùm. Quis Hieronymum non putet Marcionitarum & Encratitarum cœstro percitum fuisse, dum in nuptias tàm impotenter invehitur in libris contra Jovinianum, & alibi sæpe, usque adeo ut in hæc etiam verba proruperit? Si corruptio ad omnem coitum pertinet, incorruptio autem proprie castitatis est, præmia pudicitiæ nuptiæ possidere non possunt. Et infra. Existimo quod qui uxorem habet, quandiu revertitur ad id ipsum, ne tentet cum Satana, in carne feminet, & non in Spiritu. Qui autem in carne seminat (non ego sed Apostolus loquitur) metit corruptionem. Hæc verba, prout sonant, sumpta, nuptias, conjugiiqué omnem usum damnant. Quasi eo contaminarentur conjuges, spéque beatæ immortalitatis exciderent. Sed in Epistola ad Pammachium docet, † locos istos, aliósque ejusdem generis comparatè non absolutè accipiendos, sed hoc unum velle, tantam esse virginum fœlicitatem & puritatem, ut ad eos collati conjuges nullius esse loci aut dignitatis videantur. Quæ quidem clavis magni est
units.tr: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, vol. 2, p. 310, in the prefatory summary to the Epistle. You can now see, reader, how greatly the rhetorical figures and arts of human eloquence have clouded the books of the ancients. Because they indulged so often and so freely in these oratorical colours, it has come about, to our great loss, that the things themselves and their genuine meaning have escaped us. Who could be sure that the same arts were not used in the matter of the Eucharist, to increase both the dignity and the reverence of the divine mysteries? Likewise concerning the dignity of bishops, so that they might win the observance and obedience of the people? And finally concerning the other heads of religion which are now called into controversy? Is it likely that they spared their colours, hues, shadows and lights in those arguments by which these things could be of such great use? To this I also refer what often occurs among them: they deny or affirm certain things as if simply and absolutely, when in reality they neither deny nor affirm them except in comparison with other things. Who would not think that Jerome was stirred by the frenzy of the Marcionites and Encratites, when in his books against Jovinian, and often elsewhere, he inveighs so intemperately against marriage that he bursts out in these words: If corruption pertains to all coition, but incorruption belongs properly to chastity, marriage cannot possess the rewards of purity. And below: I think that he who has a wife, as long as he returns to that same act, lest he tempt with Satan, sows in the flesh and not in the Spirit. But he who sows in the flesh (it is not I but the Apostle who speaks) reaps corruption. Taken as they sound, these words condemn marriage and every use of wedlock, as if spouses were thereby defiled and fell from the hope of blessed immortality. But in his letter to Pammachius he teaches that these passages, and others of the same kind, are to be taken comparatively and not absolutely, and that he means only this: the happiness and purity of virgins is so great that married people, set beside them, seem to have no place or worth at all. This key is of great

units.la: usus in referendis Patrum sensibus, eaque solertissimè usi sunt VII. Synodi Patres * in solvendis quibusdam locis quos iconoclastæ objiciebant, hunc maximè ex Chrysostomo. Per scripturas fruimur præsentia sanctorum, habentes imagines, non corporum ipsorum, sed animarum, quæ enim dixerunt sunt eorum imagines animarum. Hunc item ex Amphilochio. Cure nobis non est coloribus depingere in tabulis facies carnales sanctorum (nam istis non indigemus) sed per virtutem imitari eorum vivendi rationem. Tertium denique ex Alterio. Christum ne pingas in fragulis, sed potius suppedita pauperibus istorum sumptuum expensas, sufficit enim ipsi quod semel se demisit, cum carnem nostram assumpsit. Quis ista audiens non sibi persuadet ex Iconomachorum genere fuisse tres istos Patres? Profecto vix videtur quicquam dici potuisse in hanc sententiam desertius. Volunt tamen Nicænæ Synodi Patres † illos loqui tantùm comparatè, & hoc tantum significatum velle, Imagines, scilicet, Jesu Christi & Sanctorum intueri, longè minoris esse ad pietatem usus quàm, vel ea quæ scripserunt legere, vel vitam eorum imitari, vel beneficentia pauperes prosequi.
units.tr: use in interpreting the sayings of the Fathers, and the Fathers of the Seventh Synod used it most skilfully in resolving certain passages which the iconoclasts objected, chiefly this one from Chrysostom: Through the Scriptures we enjoy the presence of the saints, having images, not of their bodies, but of their souls; for what they have said are images of their souls. Likewise this one from Amphilochius: We are not concerned to paint the fleshly faces of the saints on tablets with colours (for we have no need of these), but to imitate their manner of life through virtue. Third and last, this one from Asterius: Do not paint Christ on cloths, but rather give to the poor the expense of such luxuries; for it is enough for him that he once humbled himself when he took on our flesh. Who, hearing these words, would not persuade himself that these three Fathers belonged to the company of the image-breakers? Indeed, scarcely anything could have been said more meagrely in this sense. Yet the Fathers of the Nicene Synod wish these men to be speaking only comparatively, and to mean only this: that looking at images of Jesus Christ and the saints is of far less use for piety than either reading what they wrote, or imitating their life, or showing kindness to the poor.

units.la: Gregorius P.R.I. ad Augustini quæstionem de consanguinitatis gradibus intra quos matrimonium contrahere licet. Hæc, Beda teste, olim responderat. Necesse est ut jam tertia vel quarta generatio fidelium licenter sibi jungi debeat, nam secunda, quam duximus, a se omnino debet abstinere. Quis hæc legens non putet hanc fuisse ejus mentem, ut quæ personæ in tertio gradu & ultra consanguineæ sunt, eas fas sit, apud Christianos, connubio jungi? At cùm sequentibus post Gregorium seculis, placuisset ad septimum usque consanguinitatis gradum, conjugii prohibitionem extendere; illaque Gregoriana indulgentia displicere cœpisset, repertus est qui eam non generaliter omnibus fidelibus, sed, specialiter uni Anglorum genti recens ad Christum conversæ concessam esse interpretaretur, suamque hanc glosam, quo facilius admitteretur, ipsi GreGregorio affingeret, scripta ejus nomine ad Felicem Messanæ Episcopum epistola, quâ ipsum priorem illam à se Augustino datam legem hoc interpretamento mollientem ac diluentem inducit. Quod autem (inquit) scripsit Augustino Anglorum gentis Episcopo, alumno, videlicet, ut recordaris, tuo, de consanguinitatis conjunctione, ipsi & Anglorum genti quæ nuper ad fidem venerat, ne à bono quod ceperat, metuendo auferiora recederet specialiter & non generaliter, cæteris me scripsisse cognoscas. Baronius epistolam in qua hæc continentur pro vera ac genuina habet. Nos Blondello nostro assentimur, qui spuriam esse, & ex male confutis variorum auctorum, etiam Gregorio recentiorum, centonibus contextam claris & invictis argumentis demonstravit. Vetus tamen est, neque heri aut nudius tertius confecta. Ergo & Baronius, & quisquis eam veluti verò Gregorianam admittit, necessariò fateri debet supra allata Gregorii verba hoc, quem epistola exhibet, sensus scripta esse. Nos, qui epistolam fictitiam esse putamus, concedimus impostorem, qui eam olim produdit, exiitimasse ita inflecti posse Gregorii legem; cæterósque (id est, universos penè Papalis communionis homines qui epistolam veram censent) idem quoque sentire. Scio istas & hujus Pseudo-Gregorii & Nicænorum Patrum solutiones non carere suis difficultatibus, neque omnes scrupulos satis expedire.
