Sed tamen cùm & Nicæni Patres, & hic sive verus, sive, quod ego potius reor, fictitius Gregorius hanc methodum adhibuerint, patet ex eorum sententia posse & debere veterum auctorum scripta nonnunquam longè aliter quàm sonant accipi. Unde sequitur intellectu esse difficillima. Jam apud te expendas velim, an non ex tot locis qui hodie in nostris de fide disputationibus ultro citróque afferuntur, multos esse probabile sit, qui comparatè, id est planè aliter quàm litera fert, sint accipiendi. Jam ut Patrum Rhetorica homiliis & sermonibus ad populum habitis caliginem multam affudit, sic eorum Dialectica
units.tr: Gregory, Pope of Rome, to Augustine's question about the degrees of kinship within which marriage may be contracted. This, as Bede attests, he had once answered: It is necessary that now the third or fourth generation of the faithful be allowed to join themselves freely, for the second, which we have mentioned, must altogether abstain. Who, reading this, would not think it was his mind that persons who are related in the third degree and beyond may lawfully be joined in marriage among Christians? But in the centuries that followed Gregory, when it had been decided to extend the prohibition of marriage as far as the seventh degree of kinship, and that indulgence of Gregory's had begun to displease, there was found someone who would interpret it as granted not generally to all the faithful, but specially to the one nation of the English, recently converted to Christ, and who, so that this gloss might be the more easily admitted, attached it to Gregory himself: under his name, a letter to Felix, bishop of Messana, in which he brings in his earlier law, given by himself to Augustine, softened and diluted by this explanation. As for what he wrote (he says) to Augustine, bishop of the English nation, your own pupil, as you recall, concerning the union of kinship in marriage, you may know that I wrote it specially, and not generally, to him and to the English nation, which had lately come to the faith, lest, fearing for the more distant things, it should withdraw from the good it had begun, and not to the others. Baronius holds the letter in which these things are contained to be true and genuine. We agree with our Blondel, who, with clear and unanswerable arguments, has shown that it is spurious, and woven together from the badly sewn patches of various authors, some of them more recent than Gregory. Yet it is old, and was not composed yesterday or the day before. Therefore Baronius, and whoever admits it as truly Gregorian, must necessarily confess that the words of Gregory quoted above have the sense which the letter gives them. We, who think the letter is fictitious, grant that the impostor who once produced it thought that Gregory's law could be bent in this way, and that others (that is, almost all the men of the Papal communion who consider the letter genuine) think the same. I know that these solutions, both of this Pseudo-Gregory and of the Nicene Fathers, are not free of their difficulties, nor do they fully clear away every scruple. But since both the Nicene Fathers and this Gregory, whether genuine or, as I rather suppose, fictitious, have used this method, it is clear from their judgement that the writings of the ancient authors can and must sometimes be understood quite differently from what they sound. From this it follows that they are most difficult to understand. Now I would have you consider whether, among so many passages that are today cited back and forth in our disputations about the faith, it is not likely that many must be taken comparatively, that is, quite otherwise than the letter bears.

units.la: T quæ de controversiis & polemicè scripserunt sexcentis difficultatibus implicavit. Quippe dum disputant tanta animi contentione in scopum quem sibi proponunt feruntur, ut, de cæteris securi, haud raro imprudentes ea effutiant quæ cum cæteris Religionis Christianæ capitibus pugnant. Fit etiam nonnunquam ut, dum totis viribus errorem quempiam oppugnant, in contrarium, eique oppositum, impingere videantur. Vehemens cum adversariis contentio, (verba sunt Theodoreti) fecit ut modum excederent, quod & iis qui arbores colunt evenire solet, cùm enim incurvum plantam viderint, non solùm ad rectam normam exigunt, sed in alteram quoque partem ultra directum inflectunt, ut per nimiam in contrarium inflexionem ad rectum flatum perducatur. Sic Dionysii Alexandrini sibi objecta, tanquam Arianismo difertissimè faventia verba, explicabat, ut supra vidimus, Athanasius. Non scripsit (inquit) simpliciter, quasi fidem expositurus, sed occasione temporis & persona; ut agricola qui alias atque alias arbores aliter pro subjecti soli ratione curat, minimè culpari debet, quod hanc amputet, illam inserat, illam plantet, aliam rursus evellat, sed potius ob multiplicem solertiam in admiratione esse. Deinde subdit Dionysium illa scripsisse occasione erroris Episcoporum quorundam Pentapoleos, qui in Sabellii sententia erant, per dispensationem, ut loquitur, id est, non simpliciter, sed quodammodo tantùm. Quæ autem (inquit) scribuntur aut fiunt per œconomiam, malignè non sunt accipienda, nec ad cujusque libitum trahenda. Alibi sic solvit Patrum Antiocenorum dictum quoddam, negantium Filii consubstantialitatem, ostendit enim ipsis propositum tantùm fuisse Pauli Samosateni sententiam confutare, qui Patris & Filii unam eandémque esse personam, non verò utriusque distinctam subsistentiam, vo-
units.tr: Just as the Fathers' rhetoric has cast much darkness over their homilies and sermons delivered to the people, so their dialectic has entangled with six hundred difficulties what they wrote in controversies and polemically. For while they dispute with such intensity of mind, they are carried so eagerly toward the goal they have set themselves that, being careless of everything else, they often blurt out, heedlessly, things that clash with the other heads of the Christian religion. It also sometimes happens that, while they attack some error with all their strength, they seem to rush into the opposite error and into what is opposed to it. The vehement contention with adversaries (these are the words of Theodoret) has caused them to exceed the measure, as also happens to those who tend trees: when they see a plant bent, they not only bring it to a straight line, but bend it beyond the true line into the other direction, so that by bending it too far the other way it may be brought to an upright state. In this way Athanasius, as we saw above, explained the words of Dionysius of Alexandria which were objected to him as most plainly favouring Arianism: He did not write (he says) simply, as one about to set out the faith, but according to the occasion and the person; just as a farmer, who tends now one tree and now another in different ways according to the nature of the soil, ought not to be blamed for cutting off this one, grafting that, planting one, and uprooting another again, but should rather be admired for his manifold skill. Then he adds that Dionysius wrote those things on the occasion of an error of certain bishops of the Pentapolis, who held the opinion of Sabellius, by dispensation, as he puts it, that is, not simply but only in a certain way. Whatever is written or done (he says) by way of dispensation is not to be taken maliciously, nor twisted to each man's liking. Elsewhere he resolves in this way a certain saying of the Antiochene Fathers, who denied the consubstantiality of the Son; for he shows that their purpose was only to refute the opinion of Paul of Samosata, who held that Father and Son are one and the same person, and not two distinct subsistences, but…

units.la: Id. ep. de Syn. Arim. & Seleuc. T.1. p. 919. B. lebat. Eadem methodo Basilius exponit quod scripserat Gregorius Neocæsariensis, Patrem & Filium cogitatione noitra duas, at hypostasi unum esse; respondet enim, sic locutum non dogmatice, sed disputando. Unde apparet in scriptis ejusmodi sententiam adversus quam Patres pugnant esse normam & mensuram eorum omnium quæ affirmanr aut negant: hinc variantur sensus eorum, licet nonnunquam iisdem vocibus eos exprimant, quas adhibere solent hæretici. Cùm disputanr adversus Valentinianos aut Manichæos, videntur cum Pelagianis facere. Eadem ratione sicubi manus cum Pelagianis conferunt, videntur cum Manichæis sentire. Si adversus Arium feruntur, videntur à Sabellio minus esse alieni. Vicissim cùm Sabellium adoriuntur, ad Arium accedere videntur, ut animadvertit Episcopus Birontinus, de Augustino in primis. Id ipsum quotidie accidit iis qui ad populum verba faciunr; si in avaros invehuntur, parum abest quin prodigos commendent; ubi verò prodigos, ac nimium profusos insectantur, putes eos sordibus & tenacitati velificari. Sic apud Protestantes, qui inanes & evanidas illas figuras, quas Romani Sacramentariis nescio quibus commentitiis tribuunt, à se amoliuntur, ii ita interdum agunt, ut prima fronte videri possint Eucharistiæ realitatem, quam vocant, statuere. Cùm autem adversus transubstantiationem realémque inclufionem disputant, ipsos à Sacramentariis istis stare juranres. Inter Opera Athanasii extat Tractatus quidam, in quo neque nitorem, neque nervos, neque acumen jurc desideres. Cæterum ejus scriptor duarum in Christo naturarum distinctionem tanto nisu constiruit, † ut ad Nestorii placita deflectere videatur, si ea tantùm legås quæ initio disputationis habentur. At postremum caput ostendit * auctorem in recta fuisse sententia. Si tempore, vel quapiam alia injuria ultimum hoc caput intercidisset, non poterat Scriptor ille, propter periculofas locutiones quas, æstu disputationis, quam adver-
units.tr: Id. ep. de Syn. Arim. & Seleuc. T.1. p. 919. B. lebat. Basil uses the same method to explain what Gregory of Neocaesarea had written, that the Father and the Son are two in our thought, but one in hypostasis. He answers that this was said not dogmatically but in debate. From this it appears that, in writings of this kind, the opinion against which the Fathers contend becomes the rule and measure of everything they affirm or deny. Hence their meanings shift, although they sometimes express themselves in the same words that heretics are accustomed to use. When they dispute against the Valentinians or the Manichaeans, they seem to side with the Pelagians. By the same reasoning, wherever they join hands with the Pelagians, they seem to hold the views of the Manichaeans. If they are aimed against Arius, they seem not far removed from Sabellius. Conversely, when they attack Sabellius, they seem to draw near to Arius, as the Bishop of Birontium observes, especially in the case of Augustine. The same thing happens every day to those who address the people. If they inveigh against the avaricious, they come close to commending the prodigal; but where they attack the prodigal and the excessively lavish, you would think they were steering towards meanness and stinginess. So among the Protestants: in removing from themselves those empty and vanishing figures which the Romanists attribute to I know not what fictitious Sacramentarians, they sometimes act in such a way that at first sight they may seem to establish what they call the reality of the Eucharist. But when they dispute against transubstantiation and the real inclusion, they are seen to be swearing that they stand apart from those Sacramentarians.

units.la: * Id. p. 328. sus Eutychianos susceperat, abreptus, adhibet, Nefto‑ rianus non haberi. Eadem de causa Julius Episcopus Romanus in oppositum errorem, Eutychianum, fcili‑ cet, impingere videbatur in Epistola illa quam scribit Gennadius † fuisse olim utilem adversus eos qui duas personas in Christo ponebant, nunc autem (inquit ille) perniciosa probatur, fomentum enim est Eutychiane & Timotheane impietatis. Quod ipsum fecit ut alii scriptores, Gennadio recentiores, † Julii eam esse negaverint, ei‑ que ab hæreticis suppositam fuisse censuerint. Eadem Patrum istorum ratio fuit quæ est gubernatoris, inter duos oppositos scopulos, alterum extantem ac conspi‑ cuum, alterum sub aquis latentem, navigantis; Dum ab eo quem videt totus cavet, facilè in cum quem non animadvertit impingit; ut navem, si non frangl, certè quati ac lædi necesse sit. Sic Doctores isti, quos Pauli Samosatoni, aut Nestorii scopuli non latebant, sed qui‑ bus Arii vel Eutychetis Syrtes, nullo tum naufragio infames, ignotæ erant, dum totis viribus in illis, à quibus sibi metuebant, fugiendis laborant, facere non potuerunt quin, si in has non inciderint, ad eas tamen proximè accesserint, de quibus, scilicet, nihil dum suspicabantur. Attende nunc quanta nobis cautione opus sit apud istos tam multis spinis obsitos scriptores versantibus, quamque acri judicio distinguenda apud eos sint & causa à probationibus,& rei caput ac summa à parergis, & hyperbolæ & meioscs orationis, ab ipsa auctorum sententia. Atque hinc porro expende non verum atque æquum sit uno aut altero verbo,quæ imprudentibus con‑ tra Valentinianos & Marcionitas, vel Nestorianos & Eutychianos disputantibus exciderint, ea decidi ac ju‑ dicari quæ nunc inter nos vel de libero arbitrio, vel de proprietatibus carnis Christi, vel de ipsius Eucharistia disputantur.
units.tr: * Id. p. 328. That writer, carried away by the heat of the dispute he had undertaken against the Eutychians, uses dangerous expressions, and for that reason could not be held free of Nestorianism. For the same reason, Julius, the Roman Bishop, seemed to fall into the opposite error, the Eutychian one, in that letter which Gennadius writes was once useful against those who posited two persons in Christ: but now (he says) it is judged harmful, for it is a source of encouragement to the Eutychian and Timotheian impiety. This very fact led other writers, later than Gennadius, to deny that the letter was Julius's, and to think it had been foisted upon him by heretics. The method of these Fathers was like that of a helmsman sailing between two opposed rocks, one standing out and plainly visible, the other lying hidden beneath the waters. While he takes every care to avoid the one he sees, he easily runs against the one he does not notice, so that the ship, if not broken, must necessarily be shaken and damaged. So these teachers, for whom the rocks of Paul of Samosata or of Nestorius were not hidden, but for whom the quicksands of Arius or Eutyches, not yet notorious for any shipwreck, were unknown, while they labour with all their strength to flee those things they feared, could not help but come, if not into these dangers, at least very near to those of which, of course, they had no suspicion. Consider now how great a caution we need when we deal with writers so thickly beset with thorns, and how keen a judgement is required to distinguish among them the cause from the proofs, the main point and substance of a matter from its digressions, the hyperboles and understatements of speech, and the author's actual opinion. And from this, further, weigh whether it is right and fair that what was said carelessly, with one or two words, by men disputing against the Valentinians and Marcionites, or the Nestorians and Eutychians, should be decided and judged in relation to the questions now debated among us, whether about free will, the properties of the flesh of Christ, or the Eucharist itself.

units.la: Sed antequam missum hoc argumentum facio, notandum quoque est institutorum sive consuetudi‑ num, tam in rebus fecularibus, quàm in Ecclesiasticis in primis mutationem, significationis item vocabulorum variationem, non parum conferre ad difficultates quas in legendis & intelligendis Patribus offendimus. Nemo est in utrisque partibus qui mundi, imò & Ecclesiæ ipsius, faciem penè totam immutatam fuisse vel nescìat vel neget. Doctrinam nunc non moror; de cortice & toga Ecclesiæ tantùm mihi sermo est. Quid factum est vetere disciplina? quid severitate, & canonibus antiquis? quid Baptismi & Eucharistiæ adeo mysticis cærimoniis? quid ritibus in Clericorum ordinatione observatis? Omnia illa defossa sunt. Alia ætas, scilicet, alios mores postulavit. Cùm ergo Veterum libri ad ista quæ nos latent allusionibus scateant, necessariò consequitur ut laboriosum sit admodum sensum eorum in ejusmodi locis percipere. Sed longè major confusio à vocibus ipsis, quas, sed mutata significatione, retinuimus. Papam, Patriarcham, Missam, Oblationem, Stationem, Processionem, Peccata mortalia, Pœnitentiam, Confessionem, Satisfactionem, Meritum, Indulgentiam, cum Veteribus dicimus, & sexcentas hujusmodi voces usurpamus, sed sensu, ab eo quem tum habebant non minùs alieno, quàm illorum ætas distat à nostra. Sicut olim sub Imperatoribus Romanis Magistratuum, rerúmque veteris Reipublicæ, diu fuere in usu nomina. Sed sensu longè alio ab eo quem sub illa obtinebant. Cùm in veterum locum quempiam incidimus in quo Romanus Episcopus Papa vocatur, confestim tota illa ambitiosa Pompa quæ Papas hodie vel cingit, vel affectatur, etiam credo, ne quid deest, Prætoriana Helvetiorum cohors, etiam equitum præcurrentium turma nobis in mentem venit; cùm vel mediocriter in librorum istorum lectione versatis Papæ nomen, quibusvis Episcopis tributum olim fuisse, notum sit. Ita si occurrit exomologesis vel confessio, illico nobis hominem in genua provolutum, confessariâ peccata in aurem immurmurantem, videre videmur. Sic & auditum Missæ vocabulum nobis aures & animum illico ferit, quasi Universa Liturgia, cæremoniæque Eucharisticæ omnes eædem tum fuissent quæ hodie; cùm apud utrarumque partium eruditos constet, voces istas ex illo tempore & antiquam amissse & novam nactas esse significationem. Sed hæc quidem hactenus satis, & forsan plus satis, de obscuritate veterum Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum. Ex quibus concludimus, longè majoris molis esse quàm vulgus putat, ex Patrum scriptis pernoscere quid senserit illorum temporum Ecclesia de iis religionis capitibus quæ hodie controvertuntur.
units.tr: But before I set aside this argument, it must also be noted that the change of institutions or customs, in secular affairs as much as in ecclesiastical ones above all, and likewise the variation in the meaning of words, contribute no little to the difficulties we encounter in reading and understanding the Fathers. No one on either side is unaware or denies that the face of the world, and indeed of the Church itself, has been almost wholly altered. I am not now dwelling on doctrine; my concern is only with the bark and the cloak of the Church. What has become of the ancient discipline? What of its severity and its ancient canons? What of the rites of Baptism and the Eucharist, so full of mystical ceremonies? What of the rites observed in the ordination of the clergy? All those things have been buried. Another age, of course, demanded other customs. Therefore, since the books of the ancients teem with allusions to those things which are hidden from us, it necessarily follows that it is very laborious to grasp their meaning in such passages. But a far greater confusion arises from the very words which we have retained while their meaning has changed. We say, with the ancients, Pope, Patriarch, Mass, Oblation, Station, Procession, mortal sins, Penance, Confession, Satisfaction, Merit, Indulgence, and we use countless words of this kind, but in a sense as foreign to that which they then had as their age is distant from ours. Just as once under the Roman emperors the names of magistrates and of the offices of the old republic remained long in use, but in a sense far different from that which they held under that republic. When we come upon some passage of the ancients in which the Roman Bishop is called Pope, at once that whole ambitious pomp which surrounds or courts the Popes today comes into our minds, even, I think, the Praetorian cohort of Swiss guards, and the troop of outriders going before, lest anything be lacking; although it is known even to those moderately versed in reading these books that the title Pope was once given to any bishop whatever. So too, if exomologesis or confession occurs, at once we seem to see a man prostrate on his knees, whispering his sins into the ear of a confessor. Likewise the word Mass strikes our ears and minds at once, as if the whole Liturgy and all the Eucharistic ceremonies had then been the same as they are today; although it is agreed among the learned on both sides that these words have since then lost their ancient meaning and acquired a new one. But so much for these matters, and perhaps more than enough, concerning the obscurity of the ancient ecclesiastical writers. From them we conclude that it is a far greater task than the common people think, to learn from the writings of the Fathers what the Church of those times believed about those heads of religion which are disputed today.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Ratio VI. Patres sæpè quæ ipsi credunt tacere, & quæ non credunt dicere; seu aliorum, nomine tacito, sententias referant, ut in Commentariis; seu contra adversarios disputent, ubi nihil non adhibent quod ad argumentum suum faciat, seu ad captum auditorum se accommodent, ut in Homiliis.
units.tr: Reason VI. The Fathers often keep silent about what they themselves believe and report what they do not believe. They either relate the opinions of others without naming them, as in their Commentaries; or they argue against adversaries, using everything that bears on their case; or they adapt themselves to the understanding of their hearers, as in their Homilies.

units.la: PAtrum scripta pleraque sunt trium generum. Vel enim sunt Commentarii in S. Scripturam, vel homiliæ è suggestu ad populum habitæ, vel disputationes adversus hæreticos. Vidimus quantum tenebrarum in scripta primi & secundi ordinis inferant ornamenta Rhetorica, quantumque obscuritatis Dialecticæ tricæ & acumina in scripta postremi generis affundant. Videamus jam an, cùm Patrum sermones ex ista ealigine eduxerimus, eorumque sensum accuratè perceperimus, certò tandem constituere liceat, quæ fuerit eorum sententia. Enimvero id mihi vehementer optandum videtur. Sed si vera sunt quæ ipsi de natura & ratione suarum & lucubrationum narrant: vereor ne etiamsi hoc, quod dixi, assecuti fuerimus, multa tamen adhuc nobis superfit de vera eorum sententia dubitatio. Nam quod pertinet ad Commentarios, qui de locis Scripturæ controversis nobis sæpe consulendi sunt, en quid de iis scribat Hieronymus, Latinorum omnium doctissimus,quiq; paucis Græcorum hac in parte concedit. Commentarii (inquit) quid operis habent? Alterius dicta ediderunt: quæ obscure dicta sunt plano sermone manifestant, multorum sententias replicant,& dicunt; hunc locum quidam sic ediderunt; alii sic interpretantur; illi sensum suum & intelligentiam his testimoniis, & hac nituntur ratione firmare, ut prudens Lector cum diversas explanationes legerit & multorum vel probanda vel improbanda didicerit, judicet quid verius sit,& quasi bonus trapezita,adulterina moneta pecuniam reprobet. Num diversa interpretationis & contrariorum inter se sensuum tenebitur reus qui in uno opere, quod ediderit, expositiones posuerit plurimorum? Et quæ eodem loco sequuntur. In eundem sensum loquitur variis operum suorum locis. * Hic est Commentariorum mos (inquit) † & explanationum regula, ut opiniones ediscerent. Et hoc non solum Sanctarum interpretes Scripturarum, sed secularium quoque litterarum explanatores faciunt,tam Latinæ linguæ quam Græcæ. Fateor valde miram esse hanc commendandi rationem. Quid enim certi, quid comperti haurire lector potest ex hujusmodi variarum opinionum in acervum ita congestarum farragine, nullo indicio demonstretur aut innuatur, quæ sit earum vel sequenda, vel fugienda, quæ probabilis,quæ necessaria, quæ ad rem denique, & quæ non? Sed quandoquidem sic Hieronymo libuit, quæcunque causa ad id cum induxerit, facile est videre ipsum pro suis non agnoscere quæcunque in Commentariis suis ponit. Et cum generaliter loquatur de forma & conditionibus Commentariorum, dubium non est quin cæteri Patres in eadem de commentariorum legibus, sententia fuerit, suosque qui inter eorum opera nobis supersunt, ad hanc normam composuerint. Unde videre est quòd quamvis in ejus generis scriptis sententia vel explicatio nobis occurrat liquidò tradita, non ideo sequitur tamen auctorem reipfa in ea fuisse sententia. Forsan non suam ex alio interprete refert. Quod fi nonnisi ex liquidis limpidisque fontibus haurire studuissent Patres, nullâsque nisi probatæ pietatis, fidei, & doctrinæ Scriptorum, vel opiniones, vel oppofitiones, in suis commentariis referrent, minùs periculi effet à multiplici confusaque farragine quam congerunt. Nam etsi restaret dubium an genuina effet sententia Patris cujus nomen præfert, attamen, fi ejus non effet, constaret fani alicujus auctoris esse, æqualisque, vel parum disimilis auctoritatis. Sed quod rei caput est, nullo discrimine, jejunis, imò quandoque periculosis & ex auctoribus suspectis, infamiaque apud Ecclesiam laborantibus desumpris expositionibus commentarios suos referciunt. Saepe monet Hieronymus (& quisquis cum cum cuta evolvet id facile animadverter) commentarios suos qui maximam & sedatissimam operam ejus pattern constituunt, totos contextos esse, ex Originis, Didymi, Apollinaris & aliorum expositionibus, qui jam tum male audiebant, quod in protrudendis propriis sententiis esset audaciores quoque, ut est apud Hieronymum ingenium suum facerent Ecclesiae Sacramenta. Hoc sane mirandum est. Nemo illo acrius in isto Auctores invehitur, qui sanctae illius societatis inter ipsum, Theophilum & Epiphanium adversus Origenem, ejusque discipulos, initae facile princeps esset. Nemo unquam tam acerbe Ruffinum excepit, propter propinata Latinis Origenis toxica in libris quos ex eo interpretatus fuerat. Et tamen in ejus Commentariis parum abest quin Origenis explicationes utramque paginam faciant, quas non temperatas lectoribus imprudentibus & nulla antidoto praemunitis offert. Sic in Commentariis in Prophetas perpetuo congerit varias, etiam Judaeorum, expositiones, ita ut tibi, dum Hieronymum, docent
units.tr: The writings of the Fathers are mostly of three kinds. They are either commentaries on Holy Scripture, or homilies delivered from the pulpit to the people, or disputations against heretics. We have seen how much darkness the ornaments of rhetoric bring into writings of the first and second kinds, and how much obscurity the quibbles and subtleties of dialectic pour into the last kind. Let us now see whether, once we have drawn the Fathers' words out of this darkness and grasped their meaning accurately, we can at last determine with certainty what their opinion was. Indeed, this seems to me greatly to be wished for. But if what they themselves say about the nature and purpose of their writings is true, I fear that even if we achieve what I have said, a great deal of doubt about their true opinion will still remain for us. For as regards commentaries, which we often have to consult on the disputed passages of Scripture, consider what Jerome, the most learned of all the Latins and second to few of the Greeks in this respect, writes about them. What is the work of commentaries (he says)? They publish the sayings of another. They make plain in plain speech what has been said obscurely, they repeat the opinions of many, and say: one man has explained this passage thus; others interpret it thus; those men rest their own sense and understanding on these testimonies and this reasoning, so that the wise reader, when he has read the different explanations and has learned what may be approved or rejected in the views of many, may judge which is truer, and, like a good money-changer, reject the counterfeit coin. Will he who has put forth in a single work the explanations of many be held guilty of diverse interpretations and of senses contrary to one another? And what follows in the same place. He speaks to the same effect in various places of his works. This is the custom of commentaries (he says) and the rule of explanations, that they should learn the opinions. And this is done not only by the interpreters of the Holy Scriptures, but also by the expounders of secular literature, both Latin and Greek. I confess that this way of recommending a work is very strange. For what certain or ascertained knowledge can a reader draw from such a heap of varied opinions piled together in this way, with no indication or hint showing which of them are to be followed or avoided, which are probable, which necessary, and which, in short, pertinent to the matter and which not? But since Jerome chose to write thus, whatever the reason that led him to it, it is easy to see that he did not acknowledge as his own everything he puts into his commentaries. And since he speaks in general about the form and conditions of commentaries, there is no doubt that the other Fathers held the same view about the rules of commentaries, and composed those of their works that survive for us according to this pattern. Hence it may be seen that, although some opinion or explanation appears clearly set forth in writings of this kind, it does not follow that the author was in fact of that opinion. Perhaps he is reporting someone else's view and not his own. If the Fathers had striven to draw only from clear and limpid sources, and had recorded in their commentaries only the opinions or objections of writers of proven piety, faith and learning, there would be less danger than from the manifold and confused mass they heap together. For although it might remain doubtful whether an opinion was genuinely the view of the Father whose name it bears, yet, if it was not his, it would at least be certain that it belonged to some sound author of equal or not very different authority. But, what is the main point, they fill their commentaries without any discrimination with expositions drawn from thin, indeed sometimes dangerous, authors of suspect character who labour under infamy in the Church. Jerome often warns (and whoever reads his commentaries with care will easily notice it) that his commentaries, which make up the greatest and most careful part of his labour, are made up entirely of the expositions of Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris and others, who already at that time were ill-spoken of, because they were rather bold in putting forward their own opinions, so that, as Jerome has it, they made the sacraments of the Church their own cleverness. This is indeed remarkable. No one attacked those authors more sharply than he did, he who was easily the chief in that holy alliance he formed with Theophilus and Epiphanius against Origen and his disciples. No one ever reproved Rufinus so bitterly for the poisons of Origen that he had poured out to the Latins in the books he had translated from him. And yet in his commentaries Origen's explanations fill nearly every page, which he offers to readers unwary and unprotected by any antidote, unmoderated. Thus in his commentaries on the Prophets he constantly gathers various expositions, even those of the Jews, so that while you hear Jerome teaching pure doctrine, you often hear him with a Jew, or with a heretic.

Si Patribus, cujus essent expositiones quas afferunt nos monere visum fuisset, & sigillatim auctorum quos sequuntur nomina recensere, ea, quam amplexi sunt, Scripturas interpretandi ratio, longè plus utilitatis, minúsque confusionis attulisset: Hæc enim nominis indicatio, quanti faciendæ essent sententiæ & expositiones illæ præmonstrasset: sed id ratò observant, ut animadvertere est in expositionibus Hilarij, Ambrosij & aliorum, qui Origenem & alios quos compilant Scriptores ne semel quidem nominare dignantur. Apud Ambrosium certè non solùm periodos, sed & paginas integras ex Basilio reperias, at, ni me fallit memoria, nullibi ejus nomen occurrit. Alienas sententias quasi suas proponunt; non ideo tamen se teneri putant ut eas nobis tanquam idoneas & convenientes præstent.
units.tr: If the Fathers had thought it worth warning us whose the expositions they bring forward were, and had listed by name the authors they follow, the method of interpreting Scripture which they adopted would have brought much more usefulness and much less confusion. For the naming of the authors would have shown how much weight those opinions and expositions deserved. But they seldom take this care, as may be seen in the expositions of Hilary, Ambrose and others, who do not even deign to name once Origen and the other writers they plunder. In Ambrose, certainly, you will find not only sentences but whole pages taken from Basil, and yet, unless my memory fails me, his name occurs nowhere. They put forward the views of others as if they were their own; yet they do not consider themselves bound to present them to us as sound and suitable.

units.la: Hieronymus Commentario in Epistolam ad Galatas vult Petrum à Paulo œconomicè reprehensum non quod revera eum reprehensibilem existimaret, sed ut ea reprehensionis larva & hypocrisi (cùm interea præclarè inter se conveniret) Gentiles ædificarentur & seductentur, ut (inquit) hypocrisis observanda legis, quæ nocebat iis qui ex Gentibus crediderant, corruptionis hypocrisi emendaretur, & utrumque populus salvus fieret, dum & qui circumcisionem laudant Petrum sequuntur, & qui circumcidi nolunt Pauli prædicant libertatem. Augustinus cùm hanc sententiam non probaret, scripsit ea de re ad Hieronymum leniter & graviter, suo more, modestè in medium assers rationes propter quas ab eo dissentiret. Extant adhuc utriusque Epistolæ. Ad hæc Hieronymus multa & quidem mirifica respondet. Inprimis verò negat se præstare debere ea omnia quæ in libro scripsit: quod docet id se jure facere, quædam verba ex sua in illum præfatione refert, quæ memoranda & consideratione dignissima sunt. Nam post indicata Origenis, Didymi, Apollinaris, Theodorii Heracleotæ, Eusebij Emiseni, Adrexandi hæretici, & aliorum scripta, subditItaque, ut simpliciter fateare, legi hæc omnia, & in mente mea plurima coacervans accito notario, vel mea, vel aliena dictavi, nec ordinis, nec verborum interdum, nec sensuum memor. Nonne insignis est, & magni facienda dignaq; quam imitemur, hæc S. Scripturæ explicandi ratio? Tum conuersa ad Augustinum oratione, si quid igitur (inquit) reprehensione dignum putaueras in explanatione nostra eruditionis tuæ fuerat quaerere ut ... in ea quæ scripsimus habeantur in Græcis: ni si illi non dixissent, tunc meam propriè sententiam condemnares. Alibi in eundem sensum respondet Rufsino criminanti quædam à Commentario in Prophetiam Danielis, ab ipso perperam (suo judicio) scripta. Hac ratione ut pernoscamus quæ Hieronymus ex sententia sua in Commentariis scripserit, evolvendi nobis erunt omnes isti Scriptores Græci veteres, adeoque faciendum erit quod fieri non potest cum pleraque ista Scripta perierint, nec quicquam Commentatori tribuendum erit quantumlibet ab eo diserte affectum & confirmatum, nisi prius certò constituerimus nihil de eo apud Veterum ullum extare, à quibus iste expositiones suas mutuatur est, nam si apud ullum eorum explicationum eius vestigia occurrant, pro certo habeto nihil eas ad Hieronymum pertinere, qui nihil aliud fuit quàm istorum notarius, vel librarius, vel certè interpres. Agnoscens quidem ex eiusmodi centonibus quàm scitè Patres ex tot variis Scriptoribus hinc inde decerpta contexuerint, sed ad ipsi in eadem fuerint sententia necne, haud facilius inde cognoscees quàm de fide & opinione librarij ex libro quem describit, vel de sententia interpretis ex scripto quod ex una lingua in aliam transfert, unde sequitur testimonia ex eiusmodi scriptis desumpta, sive pro nobis, sive contra nos, nullius pene esse momenti. Nec id Cardinalem Bellarminum latuit qui ad Iocum ex quodam Hieronymi libro sibi obiectum respondet. Hieronymus eo loco ex aliorum sententia locutus est, est, ut saepe facit in commentariis Epistolae ad Ephesios, & in alijs locis. Eadem ratione Perronius ad obiectionem quā pro Scripturarum Veteris Testamenti canone ex Hilario aduersus Ecclesiam Romanam Protestantes petunt, respondet confidenter, obseruationes eo loco ab Hilario factas eius non esse sed Origenis, Commentario in primum Psalmum, cuius partem Hilarius in suum in Psalmos prologum transtulit; tametsi nihil ille de Origene toto hoc loco dicat, neque usquam significet exsuapte, an Origenis fide ea tradiderit quae illic de Scripturis habet. Haec vero Perronij responsio eo solo nititur, quod Hieronymus variis in locis testatur Hilarium suorum commentariorum maximam partem ex Origene transtulisse. Quandoquidem ergo, teste Hieronymo, haec est omnium in genere commentariorum apud Veteres ratio; quomodo nobis constare poterit an illi, quae in iis habentur ex sua sententia tradiderint, an ex quopiam alio transcripserint? Quandiu vero de hoc ambigitur, quae vis, quiue usus esse possit testimonium quae ex iis seu in hanc, seu in illam partem in controuersiis nostris desumuntur? Atque ita manifestum est hanc methodum, quam Patres in suis Scripturae expositionibus secuti sunt, dubia reddere ea ipsa quae omnium differtissime docent.
units.tr: In his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, Jerome holds that Peter was rebuked by Paul in a managed way, not because Paul truly thought him blameworthy, but so that under the cover and pretence of that rebuke (although meanwhile they agreed excellently with each other) the Gentiles might be built up and not led astray. As he puts it: the pretended observance of the law, which harmed those of the Gentiles who had believed, was corrected by a pretended correction, and both peoples were saved, since those who praise circumcision follow Peter, and those who do not wish to be circumcised proclaim the liberty of Paul. Augustine, not approving this opinion, wrote about the matter to Jerome gently and seriously, in his own manner, modestly setting forth the reasons why he dissented from him. Both letters still survive. To these Jerome replies with many remarkable points. Above all, he denies that he ought to answer for everything he wrote in the book, and he shows that he is right to do so, quoting some words from his preface to that work, which are worth recalling and very worthy of consideration. For after listing the writings of Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris, Theodore of Heraclea, Eusebius of Emesa, the heretic Alexander, and others, he adds: So, to speak plainly, I have read all of these, and gathering a great deal into my mind, I dictated, with a notary called in, some things that were mine and some that were another's, sometimes not mindful of the order, nor of the words, nor even of the senses. Is not this a notable method of explaining Holy Scripture, and one worth great esteem and worth imitating? Then, turning his speech to Augustine, he says: If therefore (he says) you thought anything in our explanation worthy of reproof, you should have asked ... in those things which we have written, let them be held to be from the Greeks; unless they had not said them, then you would condemn my own opinion properly. Elsewhere he replies to the same effect to Rufinus, who accused him of certain things written in his Commentary on the Prophecy of Daniel, which he had (in Rufinus's judgment) written wrongly. By this reasoning, if we are to learn what Jerome wrote in his commentaries from his own opinion, we must go through all those early Greek writers, and so we must do what cannot be done, since most of those writings have perished. Nothing is to be ascribed to the commentator, however clearly he sets it out and confirms it, unless we have first ascertained with certainty that nothing of it exists among the ancients from whom he borrows these explanations. For if traces of such explanations occur in any of them, be assured that they do not belong to Jerome, who was nothing more than their copyist, or scribe, or at least translator. Indeed, from patchwork of this kind you may recognise how skilfully the Fathers wove together passages gathered here and there from so many various writers; but whether they were of the same opinion as those writers you will learn no more easily from this than you would learn a scribe's belief from the book he copies, or an interpreter's opinion from a work he translates from one language into another. Hence it follows that testimonies taken from writings of this kind, whether on our side or against us, are of almost no weight. Nor was this hidden from Cardinal Bellarmine, who, replying to a passage objected to him from a certain book of Jerome, answers: Jerome in that place spoke from the opinion of others, as he often does in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and in other places. On the same reasoning Perronius, replying to the objection which the Protestants press against the Roman Church from Hilary on the canon of the Old Testament Scriptures, confidently answers that the observations made by Hilary in that place are not his but Origen's, from his Commentary on the First Psalm, part of which Hilary transferred into his own prologue to the Psalms; although Hilary says nothing about Origen in the whole passage, nor anywhere indicates that he delivered from his own view, or from Origen's faith, what he holds there about the Scriptures. But Perronius's answer rests on this alone: that Jerome testifies in various places that Hilary transferred the greater part of his commentaries from Origen. Since, then, according to Jerome, this is the practice of all commentaries among the ancients, how can it be established for us whether they delivered in them what is their own opinion, or copied it from someone else? And as long as this remains in doubt, what force or use can be had from the testimonies drawn from them, whether for this side or that, in our controversies? And so it is plain that this method, which the Fathers followed in their expositions of Scripture, makes doubtful the very things which they teach most clearly of all.

units.la: Sed illi fortasse in suis saltem ad populum concionibus & homiliis diligentiores fuere, & vel in huiusmodi saltem scriptis ea tantum adhibuere quae ipsimet sentirent & crederent. An ergo hic certi esse poterimus ipsos ex animo loqui, linguamque, non alienam, sed suam sententiam exponere? Putauerit quidem aliquis in loco tam sacro, unde greges sibi commissos docebant, nihil unquam ab ipsis proponi debuisse quod non censerent veritissimum. Sed praeterquam quod supra ostendimus ipsos, non semper omnem veritatem palam fecisse, sed eius partem quandam propter Ethnicos, vel imperitos silentio texisse; Cardinalis Perronius magnus ille
units.tr: But perhaps they were more careful in their sermons and homilies to the people, and at least in such writings used only what they themselves thought and believed. Can we then be certain that they spoke from the heart, setting out not someone else's language but their own opinion? Someone might think that in so sacred a place, from which they taught their flocks, nothing should ever have been put forward that they did not judge most true. But apart from what we showed above, that they did not always reveal the whole truth openly and instead veiled part of it in silence on account of the heathen or the unlearned, Cardinal Perron, that great and careful investigator of antiquity,

units.la: & curiosus Antiquitatis indagator, eos his ipsis de causis, paulò etiam ulteriùs progressos docet. Cùm enim ad populum, in quo erant & Catechumeni, Scripturam exponebant, si forte in locum qui de Sacramentis ageret inciderent, tum ne ea mysteria aperire paulum declinabant, & pro genuina & reali expositione quam in pectore clausam cohibebant, allegoricam & symbolicam ac, ut loquitur Cardinalis, accessoriam & collateralem asserebant, qua rudiorum animum arte aliqua explerent. Nam si, cùm de hoc argumento se offerebat agendi occasio, prorsùs tacuissent, mirum id auditoribus visum fuissent, suspicionique, imo & offensioni locum dedisset. Vt ergo & exterorum expectationi satisfacerent, & mysterium tamen in occulto continerent, eos hac ratione eludebant, id scilicet proponentes, non quod ipsi optimum & verissimum existimabant, sed quod suo proposito maximè conuenire judicabant. Sic pueros nucibus aut ludicro aliquo oblectamento fallimus ac lactamus, ut eos à rerum maioris momenti cupiditate auocemus. Qui ergo, quæ iis locis apud Patres habentur, pro nativis solidisque expositionibus, genuinisque ipsorum sententiis accipiunt, illi verò multum errant, & umbram pro corpore amplectuntur. His artibus lusisse Sanctos istos viros vix credibile esset, nisi fidem faceret tantus Cardinalis, quo etiam auctore hæc impræsentiarum proferimus, & ex eodem sequentia hæc exempla damus. Augustinus cum in sextum caput loannis incidisset, in quo (ut ille quidem putat) de Eucharistia agitur, tot allegorias, tot ænigmata & ambages ei mysterio obtendit, ut, si fides Cardinali habenda sit, ne una quidem Augustini extet toto tractatu xxvi. periodus quæ non effugium aliquod elusionemve, ac veræ, perfectæque de hoc capite definitionis dissimulationem & imminutionem aliquam contineat. Sic ille panem qui de cælo descendit, interpretatur, donum Spiritus Sancti. Datum, inquit, Dominus Spiritu Sanctum, dixit sc. se esse panem qui de cœlo descendit. Tu, præeunte & tam disertè docente sanctissimo Doctore, putabis hunc esse genuinum loci sensum. Sed cave ne sic putes, nam ex Calvino ostendit Cardinalis id fieri non posse. Eodem quoque modo recipit quod idem Augustinus subdit, aliquando post Hunc (inquit) cibum & potum societatem vult intelligi corporis & membrorum suorum, quod est sancta Ecclesia in prædestinatis & vocatis & justificatis & glorificatis sanctis & fidelibus ejus. Quis (nisi Perronius prærmonuisset exististimaturus fuit Scriptorem istum (adeo religiosum ut in gravem cum Hieronymo contentionem venerit, quod iste simulationem Paulo ausus esset tribuere) hic docuisse hanc esse mentem Domini, nisi eam revera esse sensisset? Cardinalis tamen pleraque sibi à Protestantibus ex eodem Auctore objecta hanc ipsa ratione solvit; ut verbi gratia hunc locum. Credere in Christum est manducare panem vivum: & hunc item; Qui credit in eum manducat, invisibiliter saginatur, quia & invisibiliter renascitur. Et hunc denique: Si quis manducat ex ipso pane non morietur, sed quod pertinet ad virtutem Sacramenti, non quod pertinet ad visibile Sacramentum: qui manducat intus non foris, qui manducat in corde, nonqui premit dente. Contendit Cardinalis Augustinum his omnibus locis veram plenam & integram definitionem istius carnis & sanguinis Christi manducationis supprimere, eiusque loco meditationem hanc allegoricam & accessoriam Catechumenis obtrudere, ut eorum oculos perstringeret, curiosiratémque cluderet. Eadem animaduersione soluit locos allatos ex Theodoreto, & Gregorio Nazianzeno, quem dicit Eucharistiam corporis & sanguinis Christi antitypum vocare, eadem ratione qua Abraham cùm inter iufideles versaretur, Saram sororem suam dicebat, veri quidem aliquid dissimulans, nihil tamen falsi enuntians. Pari modo hæc è Clementis Pædagogo explicat. Caro & sanguis Christi fides est] & promissio. Denique ut paucis absolvam hac observatione ita delectatus
units.tr: teaches that for these very reasons they went even further. For when they expounded Scripture to the people, among whom were also catechumens, if by chance they came upon a passage dealing with the sacraments, they took care to avoid opening those mysteries. In place of the genuine and real exposition, which they kept shut up in their breast, they set forth an allegorical and symbolic one, and, as the Cardinal puts it, accessory and collateral, by which they might satisfy the minds of the less instructed by some device. For if, when the occasion to treat this subject presented itself, they had kept altogether silent, this would have seemed strange to the hearers and would have given rise to suspicion, indeed to offence. So, in order both to satisfy the expectation of outsiders and yet keep the mystery hidden, they put them off in this way, proposing not what they themselves thought best and truest, but what they judged best suited to their purpose. Thus we beguile and amuse children with nuts or some playful diversion, so as to turn them away from the desire for things of greater importance. Those, therefore, who take what is found in the Fathers in such passages for native and solid expositions and their genuine opinions are greatly mistaken, and they embrace a shadow for the body. It would hardly be credible that those holy men played such tricks, were it not that so great a Cardinal vouches for it. It is on his authority that we now put this forward, and from him we take the following examples. Augustine, when he came to the sixth chapter of John, in which (as that author indeed thinks) the Eucharist is discussed, set so many allegories, enigmas and circumlocutions before that mystery that, if the Cardinal is to be believed, not a single sentence of Augustine's whole treatment of twenty-six sections exists which does not contain some evasion or dodge, and some dissimulation and diminution of the true and complete definition of this passage. Thus he interprets "the bread which came down from heaven" as the gift of the Holy Spirit. "The Lord," he says, "gave the Holy Spirit; he said that he himself is the bread which came down from heaven." You, following so holy a teacher who teaches so clearly, will think this is the genuine sense of the passage. But beware of thinking so, for the Cardinal shows from Calvin that this cannot be. In the same way he accepts what the same Augustine adds a little later: "This food and drink he wills to be understood as the fellowship of his body and members, which is the holy Church, among the predestined, called, justified and glorified saints and his faithful." Who (unless Perron had forewarned us) would have thought that this writer, so pious that he fell into a serious dispute with Jerome because he dared to attribute dissimulation to Paul, had taught here that this was the mind of the Lord, unless he had truly thought so? Yet the Cardinal resolves most of the objections that Protestants raise from the same author by this very method: for example this passage, "To believe in Christ is to eat the living bread"; and this one too, "He who believes in him eats, and is invisibly fed, because he is also invisibly born again." And finally this: "If anyone eats of the bread itself, he will not die; but this pertains to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: he eats within, not without; he eats in the heart, not he who presses with the tooth." The Cardinal contends that Augustine in all these passages suppresses the true, full and complete definition of this eating of the flesh and blood of Christ, and in its place foists on the catechumens this allegorical and accessory meditation, so as to dazzle their eyes and shut off their curiosity. With the same observation he resolves the passages cited from Theodoret and Gregory Nazianzen, whom he says calls the Eucharist the antitype of the body and blood of Christ, for the same reason that Abraham, when he was among unbelievers, called Sarah his sister, concealing indeed something true yet uttering nothing false. In the same way he explains these words from Clement's Paedagogus: "The flesh and blood of Christ is faith and promise." Finally, to conclude briefly, Perron, so delighted with this observation,

units.la: quæ de controversiis & polemicè scripserunt sexcentis difficultatibus implicavit. Quippe dum disputant tanta animi contentione in scopum quem sibi proponunt feruntur, ut, de cæteris securi, haud rarò imprudentes ea effutiant quæ cum cæteris Religionis Christianæ capitibus pugnant. Fit etiam nonnunquam ut, dum totis viribus errorem quempiam oppugnant, in contrarium, cique oppositum, impingere videantur. Vehemens cum adversariis contentio, (verba sunt Theodoreti) fecit ut modum excederent, quod & iis qui arbores colunt evenire solet, cùm enim incurvam plantam viderint, non solùm ad rectam normam exigunt, sed in alteram quoque partem ultra directum inflectunt, ut per nimiam in contrarium inflexionem ad rectum statum perducatur. Sic Dionysii Alexandrini sibi objecta, tanquam Arianismo difertissimè faventia verba, explicabat, ut supra vidimus, Athanasius. Non scripsit (inquit) simpliciter, quasi fidem expositurus, sed occasione temporis & personæ; ut agricola qui alias atque alias arbores aliter pro subjecti soli ratione curat, minimè culpari debet, quod hanc amputet, illam inserat, istam plantet, aliam rursus evellat, sed potius ob multiplicem solertiam in admiratione esse. Deinde subdit Dionysium illa scripsisse occasione erroris Episcoporum quorundam Pentapoleos, qui in Sabellii sententia erant, per dispensationem, ut loquitur, id est, non simpliciter, sed quodammodo tantùm. Quæ autem (inquit) scribuntur aut fiunt per œconomiam, maligne non sunt accipienda, nec ad cujusque libitum trahenda. Alibi sic solvit Patrum Antiochenorum dictum quoddam, negantium Filii consubstantialitatem, ostendit enim ipsis propositum tantùm fuisse Pauli Samosateni sententiam confutare, qui Patris & Filii unam eandémque esse personam, non verò utriusque distinctam subsistentiam, vo- Theod. dial. 3. e. 30. Tom. 4. edit. Sermondi. p. 170. Ath. ep. de fid. Dion. Alex. T. 1. p. 551. C. Max. D. Max. E. lebat. Eadem methodo Basilius * exponit quod scripserat Gregorius Neocæsariensis, Patrem & Filium cogitatione no ultra duos, at hypostasi unum esse; respondet enim, sic locutum non dogmatice, sed disputando. Unde apparet in scriptis ejusmodi sententiam adversus quam Patres pugnant esse normam & mensuram eorum omnium quæ affirmant aut negant: hinc variantur sensus eorum,licet nonnunquam iisdem vocibus eos exprimant,quas adhibere solent hæretici. Cùm disputant adversus Valentinianos aut Manichæos, videntur cum Pelagianis facere. Eadem ratione sicubi manus cum Pelagianis conferunt, videntur cum Manichæis sentire. Si adversus Arium feruntur, videntur à Sabellio minus esse alieni. Vicissim cùm Sabellium adoriuntur, ad Arium accedere videntur, ut animadvertit Episcopus Bitontinus, de Augustino in primis. Id ipsum quotidie accidit iis qui ad populum verba faciunt; si in avaros invehuntur, parum abest quin prodigos commendent, ubi verò prodigos, ac nimium profusos insectantur, putes eos sordibus & tenacitati velificari. Sic apud Protestantes, qui inanes & evanidas illas figuras, quas Romani Sacramentariis nescio quibus commentitiis tribuunt, à se amoliuntur, ii ita interdum agunt, ut prima fronte videri possint Eucharistiæ realitatem, quam vocant, statuere. Cùm autem adversus transubstantiationem realemque inclusionem disputant, ipsos à Sacramentariis istis stare jurares. Inter Opera Athanasii extat Tractatus quidam, in quo neque nitorem, neque nervos, neque acumen juris desideres. Cæterum ejus scriptor duarum in Christo naturarum distinctionem tanto nisu constituit, † ut ad Nestorii placita deflectere videatur, si ea tantùm legas quæ initio disputationis habentur. At postremum caput ostendit * auctorem in recta fuisse sententia. Si tempore, vel quapiam alia injuria ultimum hoc caput intercidisset, non poterat Scriptor ille, propter periculosas locutiones quas, æstu disputationis, quam adver- T 2 * Basil. ep. 64. T.2. p 849. B. sus Eutychianos susceperat, abreptus, adhibet, Neftorianus non haberi. Eadem de causa Julius Episcopus Romanus in oppositum errorem, Eutychianum, scilicet, impingere videbatur in Epistola illa quam scribit Gennadius † fuisse olim utilem adversus eos qui duas personas in Christo ponebant, nunc autem (inquit ille) perniciosa probatur, fomentum enim est Eutychiana & Timotheana impietatis. Quod ipsum fecit ut alii scriptores, Gennadio recentiores, † Julii eam esse negaverint, eique ab haereticis suppositam fuisse censuerint. Eadem Patrum istorum ratio fuit quae est gubernatoris, inter duos oppositos scopulos, alterum extantem ac conspicuum, alterum sub aquis latentem, navigantis; Dum ab eo quem videt totus cavet, facile in eum quem non animadvertit impingit; ut navem, si non frangl, certè quati ac laedi necesse sit. Sic Doctores isti, quos Pauli Samosatceni, aut Nestorii scopuli non latebant, sed quibus Arii vel Eutychetis Syrtes, nullo tum naufragio infames, ignotae erant, dum totis viribus in illis, à quibus sibi metuebant, fugiendis laborant, facere non potuerunt quin, si in has non inciderint, ad eas tamen proximè accesserint, de quibus, scilicet, nihil dum suspicabantur. Attende nunc quanta nobis cautione opus sit apud istos tam multis spinis obsitos scriptores versantibus, quamque acri judicio distinguenda apud eos sint & causa à probationibus,& rei caput ac summa à parergis, & hyperbolae & meiosces orationis, ab ipsa auctorum sententia. Atque hinc porro expende non verum atque aequum sit uno aut altero verbo,quae imprudentibus contra Valentinianos & Marcionitas, vel Nestorianos & Eutychianos disputantibus exciderint, ea decidi ac judicari quae nunc inter nos vel de libero arbitrio, vel de proprietatibus carnis Christi, vel de ipsius Eucharistia disputantur.
units.tr: has entangled in six hundred difficulties those who wrote about controversies and in a polemical manner. For while they dispute with such intense contention, they are carried toward the goal they set themselves, so that, careless of the rest, they often blurt out, without thinking, things that clash with the other heads of the Christian religion. It also sometimes happens that, while they attack some error with all their strength, they seem to fall into the opposite, and into what is opposed to it. Vehement contention with adversaries (these are Theodoret's words) has made them go beyond the measure, as happens with those who cultivate trees: when they have seen a bent plant, they not only straighten it to the right rule, but bend it also the other way beyond the straight, so that by excessive bending in the opposite direction it may be brought to an upright state. Thus Athanasius explained the words of Dionysius of Alexandria that were objected to him, as if they openly favoured Arianism, as we saw above: He did not write, he says, simply, as one about to set out the faith, but on account of the time and the person; just as a farmer who tends different trees differently according to the nature of the soil ought not to be blamed for cutting this one back, grafting that one, planting another and uprooting yet another, but rather be admired for his manifold skill. Then he adds that Dionysius wrote those things on account of the error of certain bishops of the Pentapolis, who held the opinion of Sabellius, by dispensation, as he puts it, that is, not simply but only in a certain manner. But what is written or done by way of economy, he says, must not be taken maliciously, nor twisted to each person's liking. Elsewhere he resolves in this way a saying of the Antiochene Fathers that denied the consubstantiality of the Son; for he shows that they had intended only to refute the opinion of Paul of Samosata, who held that Father and Son were one and the same person, and not a distinct subsistence of each (Theod. dial. 3, c. 30; Athanasius, ep. de fide). Basil uses the same method to explain what Gregory of Neocaesarea wrote, that Father and Son are one in hypostasis but not more than two in thought (Basil, ep. 64); for he replies that he spoke not dogmatically but in disputation. Hence it appears that in writings of this kind the opinion against which the Fathers fight is the norm and measure of everything they affirm or deny; hence their meanings vary, although sometimes they express them with the same words that heretics are accustomed to use. When they dispute against the Valentinians or Manichaeans, they seem to agree with the Pelagians. By the same method, wherever they join hands with the Pelagians, they seem to think with the Manichaeans. If they attack Arius, they seem not far from Sabellius. Conversely, when they assail Sabellius, they seem to approach Arius, as the Bishop of Bitonto observed, especially of Augustine. The same thing happens every day to those who preach to the people: if they inveigh against the covetous, they come close to commending the prodigal; but where they attack the prodigal and the excessively lavish, you would think they were steering toward meanness and stinginess. So among Protestants, who strip away from the Eucharist those empty and evanescent figures which the Romanists attribute to I know not what fictitious Sacramentarians, some act in such a way that at first sight they might seem to establish the reality, as they call it, of the Eucharist. But when they dispute against transubstantiation and real inclusion, you would swear they stood with those Sacramentarians. There is extant among the works of Athanasius a certain treatise, in which you will find neither polish, nor sinew, nor acuteness of argument. Its author establishes the distinction of the two natures in Christ with such effort that he seems to lean toward the opinions of Nestorius, if you read only what is found at the beginning of the disputation. But the last chapter shows that the author was of sound opinion. If through time or some other injury this final chapter had perished, that writer could not have been considered a Nestorian, on account of the dangerous expressions which, carried away by the heat of the dispute he had undertaken against the Eutychians, he uses. For the same reason Julius, Bishop of Rome, seems to fall into the opposite error, Eutychianism, in that letter which Gennadius writes: once it was useful against those who posited two persons in Christ, but now it is proved pernicious, for it is a fomentation of Eutychian and Timothean impiety. This led other writers, later than Gennadius, to deny that this letter was Julius's, and to think it had been foisted upon him by heretics. The method of these Fathers was the same as that of a navigator who sails between two opposing rocks, one standing out and conspicuous, the other lying hidden under the waters: while he takes all care to avoid the one he sees, he easily runs into the one he does not notice, so that his ship, if not broken, must necessarily be shaken and damaged. Thus those teachers, to whom the rocks of Paul of Samosata or Nestorius were not hidden, but for whom the Syrtes of Arius or Eutyches, not yet infamous for any shipwreck, were unknown, while they labour with all their strength to shun those things they feared, could not help but, if they did not fall into these, at least come very near to those of which they suspected nothing. Now consider how great a caution we need when dealing with writers so beset with many thorns, and with how keen a judgement we must distinguish in them the cause from the proofs, the head and sum of the matter from digressions, hyperbole and understatement of speech, and the author's own opinion. Then, from this, weigh further whether it is true and fair that what was let fall through one or another word by those disputing unwarily against the Valentinians and Marcionites, or the Nestorians and Eutychians, should be decided and judged in relation to what is now disputed among us, whether about free will, about the properties of Christ's flesh, or about the Eucharist itself.

units.la: Sed antequam missum hoc argumentum facio, notandum quoque est institutorum sive consuetudinum. mum, tam in rebus fecularibus, quàm in Ecclesiasticis in primis mutationem, significationis item vocabulorum variationem, non parum conferre ad difficultates quas in legendis & intelligendis Patribus offendimus. Nemo est in utrisque partibus qui mundi, imò & Ecclesiæ ipsius, faciem penè totam immutatam fuisse vel nesciat vel neget. Doctrinam nunc non moror; de cortice & toga Ecclesiæ tantùm mihi sermo est. Quid factum est vetere disciplina? quid severitate, & canonibus antiquis? quid Baptismi& Eucharisticę adeo mysticis cærimoniis? quid ritibus in Clericorum ordinatione observatis? Omnia illa defossa sunt. Alia ætas, scilicet, alios mores postulavit. Cùm ergo Veterum libri ad ista quę nos latent allusionibus scateant, necessariò consequitur ut laboriosum fit admodum sensum eorum in ejusmodi locis percipere. Sed longè major confusio à vocibus ipsis, quas, sed mutata significatione, retinuimus. Papam, Patriarcham, Missam, Oblationem, Stationem, Proceffionem, Peccata mortalia, Pœnitentiam, Confessionem, Satisfactionem, Meritum, Indulgentiam, cum Veteribus dicimus, & fexcentas hujusmodi voces usurpamus, sed sensu, aboeo quem tum habebant non minùs alieno, quàm illorum ætas distat à nostra. Sicut olim sub Imperatoribus Romanis Magistratuum, rerúmque veteris Reipublicæ, diu fuere in usu nomina. Sed sensu longè alio ab eo quem sub illa obtinebant. Cùm in veterum locum quempiam incidimus in quo Romanus Episcopus Papa vocatur, confestim tota illa ambitiosa Pompa quæ Papas hodie vel cingit, vel affectatur, etiam credo, ne quid defit, Prætorianâ Helvetiorum cohors, etiam equitum præcurrentium turma nobis in mentem venit; cùm vel mediocriter in librorum istorum lectione versatis Papæ nomen, quibusvis Episcopis tributum olim fuisse notum fit. Ita fi occurrit exomologesis vel confessio, illico nobis hominem in genua provolutum, confeffariòe rum & lucubrationum narrant: vereor ne etiamsi hoc, quod dixi, assecuti fuerimus, multa tamen adhuc nobis superfit de vera eorum sententia dubitatio. Nam quod pertinet ad Commentarios, qui de locis Scripturæ controversis nobis sæpe consulendi sunt, en quid de iis scribat Hieronymus, Latinorum omnium doctissimus,quiqi paucis Græcorum hac in parte concedit. Commentarii (inquit) quid operis habent? Alterius dicta edidTerunt: quæ obscure dicta sunt plano sermone manifestant, multorum sententias replicant,& dicunt; hunc locum quidam sic ediderunt; alii sic interpretantur; illi sensum suum & intelligentiam his testimoniis, & hac nituntur ratione firmare, ut prudens Lector cum diversas explanationes legerit & multorum vel probanda vel improbanda didicerit, judicet quid verius sit,& quasi bonus trapezita,adulterina monetæ pecuniam reprobet. Num diversa interpretationis & contrariorum inter se sensuum tenebitur reus qui in uno opere, quod edidTerit, expositiones posuerit plurimorum? Et quæ eodem loco sequuntur. In eundem sensum loquitur variis operum suorum locis. * Hic est Commentariorum mos (inquit) † & explanationum regula, ut opiniones edidTerint. Et hoc non solum Sanctarum interpretes Scripturarum, sed secularium quoque litterarum explanatores faciunt,tam Latinæ linguæ quam Græcæ. Fateor valde miram esse hanc commentandi rationem. Quid enim certi, quid comperti haurire lector poterit ex hujusmodi variarum opinionum in acervum ita congestarum farragine, nullo indicio demonstretur aut innuatur, quæ sit earum vel sequenda, vel fugienda, quæ probabilis,quæ necessaria, quæ ad rem denique, & quæ non? Sed quandoquidem sic Hieronymo libuit, quæcunque causa ad id eum induxerit, facile est videre ipsum pro suis non agnoscere quæcunque in Commentariis suis ponit. Et cum generaliter loquatur de forma & conditionibus Commentariorum, dubium non est quin cæteri Patres in eadem de commentariorum legibus, sententia fuerit, suosque qui inter eorum opera nobis supersunt, ad hanc normam composuerint. Unde videre est quòd quamvis in ejus generis scriptis sententia vel explicatio nobis occurrat liquidò tradita, non ideo sequitur tamen auctorem reipfa in ea fuisse sententia. Forsan non suam ex alio interprete refert. Quod fi nonnisi ex liquidis limpidisque fontibus haurire studuissent Patres, nullâsque nisi probatæ pietatis, fidei, & doctrinæ Scriptorum, vel opiniones, vel oppofitiones, in suis commentariis referrent, minùs periculi esset à multiplici confusaque farragine quam congerunt. Nam etsi restaret dubium an genuina esset sententia Patris cujus nomen præfert, attamen, si ejus non esset, constaret fani alicujus auctoris esse, æqualisque, vel parum difimilis auctoritatis. Sed quod rei caput est, nullo discrimine, jejunis, imò quandoque periculosis & ex auctoribus suspectis, infamiaque apud Ecclesiam laborantibus desumptis expositionibus commentarios suos referiunt. Sæpe monet Hieronymus (& quisquis eum cum cura evolvet id facilè animadvertet) commentarios suos qui maximam & fedatiffimam operum ejus partem constituunt, totos contextos esse, ex Originis, Didymi, Apollinaris & aliorum expositionibus, qui jam tum malè audiebant, quod in protrudendis propriis sententiis essent audaciores quodque, ut est apud Hieronymú ingeniū suum facerent Ecclesiæ Sacramenta. Hoc sanè mirandum est. Nemo illo acrius in isto Auctores invehitur, qui sanctæ illius societatis inter ipsum, Theophilum & Epiphanium adversus Origenem, ejusque discipulos, initæ facilè princeps esset. Nemo unquam tam acerbè Ruffinum excepit, propter propinata Latinis Origenis toxica in libris quos ex eo interpretatus fuerat. Et tamen in ejus Commentariis parum abest quin Origenis explicationes utramque paginam faciant, quas non temperatas lectoribus imprudentibus & nulla antidoto præmunitis offert. Sic in Commentariis in Prophetas perpetuo congerit varias, etiam Judæorum, expositiones, ita ut tibi, dum Hieronymum docent
units.tr: But before I set this argument aside, it must also be noted that changes in institutions and customs, both in secular affairs and above all in ecclesiastical ones, and likewise changes in the meaning of words, contribute not a little to the difficulties we meet in reading and understanding the Fathers. No one on either side is unaware of, or denies, that the face of the world, and even of the Church itself, has been almost wholly changed. I am not now dwelling on doctrine; my discussion concerns only the bark and the toga of the Church. What became of the ancient discipline? What of its severity and the old canons? What of the rites of Baptism and the Eucharist, so mystical in their ceremonies? What of the rites observed in the ordination of clergy? All of that has been buried. Another age, of course, demanded other customs. Since therefore the books of the ancients abound in allusions to things that are hidden from us, it necessarily follows that grasping their meaning in such passages is very laborious. But a far greater confusion arises from the words themselves, which we have retained though their meaning has changed. We say Pope, Patriarch, Mass, Oblation, Station, Procession, mortal sins, Penance, Confession, Satisfaction, Merit, Indulgence, along with the ancients, and we use six hundred such words, but in a sense as foreign to the one they then had as their age is distant from ours. Just as under the Roman emperors the names of magistrates and of the things of the old Republic long remained in use, but in a sense very far from that which they had under it. When we come upon some passage of the ancients in which the Roman bishop is called Pope, at once that whole ambitious pomp which surrounds or aspires to the Popes of today comes into our minds, even, I think, the Praetorian guard of Swiss and the troop of outriders going before, lest anything be lacking; whereas it is known even to those moderately versed in reading these books that the name Pope was once given to any bishops whatever. So if exomologesis or confession occurs, at once we picture a man prostrate on his knees, recounting his misdeeds to the ears of his confessor... I fear that even if we have achieved what I have said, much doubt about their true opinion still remains for us. For as regards the Commentaries, which we must often consult on the disputed places of Scripture, see what Jerome, the most learned of all the Latins, who yields to few of the Greeks in this part, writes of them: Commentarii (he says) what work do they contain? They publish the words of another; they make plain in plain speech what has been said obscurely, they repeat the opinions of many and say: one has published this passage thus; others interpret it so; these men seek to confirm their sense and understanding by these testimonies and this reasoning; so that the prudent reader, having read the various explanations and learned what is to be approved or disapproved by many, may judge what is truer, and like a good money-changer, reject the counterfeit coin. Will he be held guilty of diverse interpretations and of contrary senses among themselves, who in one work he has published has set out the expositions of many? And what follows in the same place. He speaks to the same effect in various places of his works: * This is the custom of commentaries (he says) † and the rule of explanations, that they publish opinions. And this is done not only by the interpreters of the Holy Scriptures but by the explainers of secular literature too, both Latin and Greek. I confess this method of commenting is very strange. For what certain or established knowledge can the reader draw from such a heap of various opinions piled together, when nothing indicates or hints which of them is to be followed or avoided, which is probable, which necessary, and which, in the end, pertinent to the matter and which not? But since Jerome has chosen to do so, whatever cause led him to it, it is easy to see that he does not acknowledge as his own whatever he puts in his Commentaries. And since he speaks generally of the form and conditions of commentaries, there is no doubt that the other Fathers held the same view about the rules of commentaries, and composed those works of theirs that survive among us to this pattern. Hence it is clear that although in writings of this kind an opinion or explanation presents itself to us plainly stated, it does not follow that the author was in fact of that opinion. Perhaps he is reporting it from another interpreter, not his own. But if the Fathers had only striven to draw from clear and limpid springs, and had recorded in their commentaries only the opinions or objections of writers of approved piety, faith and teaching, there would be less danger from the manifold and confused heap they gather together. For even if it remained doubtful whether the opinion was genuinely that of the Father whose name it bears, yet if it were not his, it would at least be certain that it belonged to some sound author of equal or not very different authority. But, what is the heart of the matter, they set down their expositions without any distinction, taken from thin and sometimes even dangerous sources, from authors under suspicion who labour under infamy in the Church. Jerome often warns (and whoever reads him carefully will easily notice it) that his commentaries, which make up the greatest and most tedious part of his works, are entirely pieced together from the expositions of Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris and others, who by then were already ill regarded, because they were bolder in putting forward their own opinions and because, as Jerome has it, they made the sacraments of the Church serve their own wit. This is truly astonishing. No one attacked those authors more fiercely than he, though he was easily the foremost in that holy alliance formed between himself, Theophilus and Epiphanius against Origen and his disciples. No one ever took Rufinus to task so bitterly for the poisons of Origen which he had served up to the Latins in the books he had translated from him. And yet in his Commentaries Origen's explanations come close to filling every page, and he offers them without moderation to unwary readers who have no antidote to protect them. So in his Commentaries on the Prophets he constantly gathers various expositions, even Jewish ones, so that while they teach you, you think you are hearing Jerome teach, when often the matter is with a Jew or a heretic.

units.la: Vide G.E. Comm. in Nah. T.5.2.391. A.B. docentem audire te putas, sæpe cum Iudæo, aut cum hæretico res sit. Si Patribus, cujus essent expositiones quas afferunt nos monere visum fuisset, & sigillatim auctorum quos sequuntur nomina recensere, ea, quam amplexi sunt, Scripturas interpretandi ratio, longè plus utilitatis, minúsque confusionis attulisset: Hæc enim nominis indicatio, quanti faciendæ essent sententiæ & expositiones illæ præmonstrasset: sed id raro observant, ut animadvertere est in expositionibus Hilarij, Ambrosij & aliorum, qui Origenem & alios quos compilant Scriptores ne semel quidem nominare dignantur. Apud Ambrosium certè non solùm periodos, sed & paginas integras ex Basilio reperias, at, ni me fallit memoria, nullibi ejus nomen occurrit. Alienas sententias quasi suas proponunt; non ideo tamen se teneri putant ut eas nobis tanquam idoneas & convenientes præstent. Hieronymus Commentario in Epistolam ad Galatas vult Petrum à Paulo œconomicè reprehensum non quod revera eum reprehensibilem existimaret, sed ut ea reprehensionis larua & hypocrisi (cùm interea præclarè ipsis inter se conveniret) Gentiles ædificarentur & servarentur, ut (inquit) hypocrisis observandæ legis, quæ nocebat iis qui ex Gentibus crediderant, corruptionis hypocrisi emendaretur, & utrumque populus salvus fieret, dum & qui circumcisionem laudant Petrum sequuntur, & qui circumcidi nolunt Pauli prædicant libertatem. Augustinus cùm hanc sententiam non probaret, scripsit ea de re ad Hieronymum leniter & graviter, suo more, mollitè in medium afferrens rationes propter quas ab eo dissentiret. Extant adhuc utriusque Epistolæ. Ad hæc Hieronymus multa & quidem mirifica respondet. Inprimis verò negat se præstare debere ea omnia quæ in libro scripsit: quod docet id se jure facere, quædam verba ex sua in illum præfatione referre, quæ memoratu & consideratione dignissima sunt. Nam posit indicata Origenis, Didymi, Apollinarii, Theodorii Heraclœotæ, Eusebij Emi-
units.tr: See G.E. Comm. in Nah. T.5.2.391. A.B. If the Fathers had thought fit to tell us whose expositions they were offering, and to list by name the authors whom they follow, the method of interpreting Scripture which they adopted would have brought far more usefulness and far less confusion. For such an indication of names would have shown how much those opinions and expositions were to be valued. But they rarely observe this, as may be seen in the expositions of Hilary, Ambrose and others, who do not deign even once to name Origen and the other writers they plunder. In Ambrose, certainly, you will find not only sentences but whole pages taken from Basil, yet, unless my memory fails, his name nowhere occurs. They put forward other people's opinions as if they were their own, yet they do not think themselves bound to present them to us as sound and fitting. Jerome, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, holds that Peter was rebuked by Paul in a prudent, economical manner, not because he truly thought him blameworthy, but so that by this mask and pretence of rebuke (since meanwhile they agreed excellently with each other) the Gentiles might be edified and saved; so that (he says) the hypocrisy of observing the law, which harmed those of the Gentiles who had believed, might be corrected by the hypocrisy of correction, and both peoples might be saved, while those who praise circumcision follow Peter and those who do not wish to be circumcised proclaim the liberty of Paul. Augustine, not approving this opinion, wrote to Jerome on the matter, gently and seriously, in his own manner, softly setting before him the reasons why he dissented. Both letters still survive. To these Jerome replies with many and indeed remarkable things. Above all he denies that he ought to answer for everything he wrote in the book. He says he is entitled to do so, and he quotes certain words from his own preface to that book, which are most worthy of mention and consideration. For after listing the writings of Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris, Theodore of Heraclea, Eusebius of Emesa
