units.la: V seni, Adrexandi hæretici, & aliorum scripta, subditItaque, ut simpliciter fateare, legi hæc omnia, & in mente mea plurima coacervans accito notario, vel mea, vel aliena dictavi, nec ordinis, nec verborum interdum, nec sensuum memor. Nonne insignis est, & magni facienda dignaq; quam imitemur, hæc S. Scripturæ explicandi ratio? Tum conuersa ad Augustinum oratione, si quid igitur (inquit) reprehensione dignum putaueras in explanatione nostra eruditionis tuæ fuerat quærere ea quæ scripsimus habeantur in Græcis: ni si illi non dixissent, tunc meam propriè sententiam condemnares. Alibi in eundem sensum respondet Ruf-
units.tr: "...the writings of Alexander the heretic and of others. So that you may frankly confess it: I read all of these, and, gathering a great deal into my mind, I dictated them with a secretary, whether my own material or another's, sometimes forgetful of their order, their wording, and their sense. Is this not a remarkable method of explaining Holy Scripture, one worth admiring and imitating? Then, turning his words to Augustine, he says: 'If, therefore, you thought anything in our explanation deserved reproof, you should have asked for the passages we wrote to be checked against the Greeks; unless they had said those things, you would then be condemning my own opinion.' Elsewhere he answers in the same vein Rufinus, who accused him of certain things written in his Commentary on the Prophecy of Daniel, which were (in Rufinus's judgement) wrongly written by him."

units.la: sino criminanti quædam à Commentario in Prophetiam Danielis, ab ipso perperam (suo judicio) scripta. Hac ratione ut pernoscamus quæ Hieronymus ex sententia sua in Commentariis scripserit, evolvendi nobis erunt omnes isti Scriptores Græci veteres, adeoque faciendum erit quod fieri non potest cùm pleraque ista scripta perierint, nec quicquam Commentatori tribuendum erit quantumlibet ab eo diserte assertum & confirmatum, nisi priùs certò constituerimus nihil de eo apud Veterum ullum extare, á quibus iste expositiones suas mutuatur est, nam si apud ullum eorum explicationum eius vestigia occurrant, pro certo habeto nihil eas ad Hieronymum pertinere, qui nihil aliud fuit quàm istorum notarius, vel librarius, vel certè interpres. Agnoscès quidem ex eiusmodi centonibus quàm scitè Patres ex tot variis Scriptoribus hinc inde decerpta contexuerint, sed ad ipsi in eadem fuerint sententia, necne, haud facilius inde cognosces quàm de fide & opinione librarij ex libro quem describit, vel de sententia interpretis ex scripto quod ex una lingua in aliam transfert, unde sequitur testimonia ex eiusmodi scriptis desumpta, siue pro nobis, siue contra nos, nullius pene esse momenti. Nec id Cardinalem Bellarminum latuit qui ad locum ex quodam Hieronymi libro sibi obiectum respondet. Hieronymus eo loco ex aliorum sententia locutus est,. est, ut saepe facit in commentariis Epistolae ad Ephesios, & in alijs locis. Eadem ratione Perronius ad obiectionem quā pro Scripturarum Veteris Testamenti canone ex Hilario aduersus Ecclesiam Romanam Protestantes petunt, respondet confidenter, obseruationes eo loco ab Hilario factas eius non esse sed Origenis, Commentario in primum Psalmum, cuius partem Hilarius in suum in Psalmos prologum transtulit; tametsi nihil ille de Origene toto hoc loco dicat, neque ut piam significet exsuapte, an Origenis fide ea tradiderit quae illic de Scripturis habet. Haec vero Perronij responsio eo solo nititur, quod Hieronymus variis in locis testatur Hilarium suorum commentariorum maximam partem ex Origene transtulisse. Quandoquidem ergo, teste Hieronymo, haec est omnium in genere commentariorum apud Veteres ratio; quomodo nobis constare poterit an illi, quae in iis habentur ex sua sententia tradiderint, an ex, quopiam alio transcripserint? Quandiu vero de hoc ambigitur, quae vis, quisve usus esse potest testimonium quae ex iis seu in hanc, seu in illam partem in controversiis nostris desumuntur? Atque ita manifestum est hanc methodum, quam Patres in suis Scripturae expositionibus secuti sunt, dubia reddere ea ipsa quae omnium dissertissime docent.
units.tr: "In this way, if we are to learn what Jerome wrote in his Commentaries according to his own judgement, we shall have to unroll all those early Greek writers, and this would have to be done even though most of those writings have perished. Nor should anything be attributed to the Commentator, however clearly he asserts and confirms it, unless we first establish with certainty that nothing of it exists among the ancients from whom he borrowed his expositions. For if traces of those explanations occur in any of them, be assured that they do not belong to Jerome, who was nothing more than their copyist, or scribe, or at least their translator. You will indeed recognise from such patchwork how skilfully the Fathers wove together passages picked here and there from so many different writers; but whether they themselves held the same opinion, you will learn no more easily from this than you could learn the faith and opinion of a scribe from the book he copies, or the opinion of a translator from a work he renders from one language into another. It follows that testimonies drawn from writings of this kind, whether for us or against us, are of almost no weight at all. Nor did this escape Cardinal Bellarmine, who, replying to a passage from one of Jerome's books objected to him, says: 'Jerome there speaks in the sense of others,' as he often does in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians and in other places. By the same reasoning Perron, answering confidently the objection that Protestants draw from Hilary against the Roman Church for the canon of the Old Testament Scriptures, says that the observations made there by Hilary are not his but Origen's, from his Commentary on the first Psalm, a part of which Hilary transferred into his own prologue to the Psalms. Yet Hilary says nothing about Origen in the whole passage, nor does he indicate in his own person whether he delivered from Origen's faith those things he has there about the Scriptures. Indeed Perron's answer rests on this alone: that Jerome testifies in several places that Hilary took the greater part of his commentaries from Origen. Since, therefore, according to Jerome this is the practice among the ancients in commentaries of every kind, how can we be sure whether they delivered in them what was their own opinion, or copied it from some other source? And as long as this remains in doubt, what force or what use can there be in the testimonies drawn from such works, to support either side in our controversies? Thus it is plain that this method which the Fathers followed in their expositions of Scripture renders doubtful the very things they teach most eloquently."

units.la: Sed illi fortasse in suis saltem ad populum concionibus & homiliis diligentiores fuere, & vel in huiusmodi saltem scriptis ea tantum adhibuere quae ipsimet sentirent & crederent. An ergo hic certi esse poterimus ipsos ex animo loqui, linguamque non alienam, sed suam sententiam exponere? Putauerit quidem aliquis in loco tam sacro, unde greges sibi commissos docebant, nihil unquam ab ipsis proponi debuisse quod non censerent verissimum. Sed praeterquam quod supra ostendimus ipsos, non semper omnem veritatem palam fecisse, sed eius partem quandam propter Ethnicos, vel imperitos silentio texisse; Cardinalis Perronius magnus ille
units.tr: "But perhaps they were at least more careful in their sermons and homilies addressed to the people, and in such writings used only what they themselves thought and believed. Can we then be sure here that they spoke from the heart, setting forth not another's but their own opinion? One might suppose that in so sacred a place, from which they taught the flocks committed to them, nothing should ever have been put forward that they did not judge to be most true. But apart from what we have shown above, that they did not always make the whole truth plain, but kept part of it hidden in silence on account of the heathen or the unlearned, Cardinal Perron, that great and inquisitive investigator of antiquity, ..."

units.la: & curiosus Antiquitatis indagator, eos his ipsis de causis, paulò etiam ulterius progressos docet. Cùm enim ad populum, in quo erant & Catechumeni, Scripturam exponebant, si forte in locum qui de Sacramentis ageret inciderent, tum ne ea mysteria aperire paulum declinabant, & pro genuina & reali expositione quam in pectore clausam cohibebant, allegoricam & symbolicam ac, ut loquitur Cardinalis, accessoriam & collateralem asserebant, qua rudiorum animum arte aliqua explerent. Nam si, cùm de hoc argumento se offerebat agendi occasio, prorsus tacuissent, mirum id auditoribus visum fuissent, suspicioniq; imo & offensioni locum dedisset. Vt ergo & exterorum expectationi satisfacerent, & mysterium tamen in occulto continerent, eos hac ratione eludebant, id scilicet proponentes, non quod ipsi optimum & verissimum existimabant, sed quod suo proposito maximè conuenire judicabant. Sic pueros nucibus aut ludicro aliquo oblectamento fallimus ac lactamus, ut eos à rerum maioris momenti cupiditate auocemus. Qui ergo, quæ iis locis apud Patres habentur, pro nativis solidisque expositionibus, genuinisque ipsorum sententiis accipiunt, illi verò multum errant, & umbram pro corpore amplectuntur. His artibus lusisse Sanctos istos viros vix credibile esset, nisi fidem faceret tantus Cardinalis, quo etiam auctore hæc impræsentiarum proferimus, & ex eodem sequentia hæc exempla damus. Augustinus cum in sextum caput Ioannis incidisset, in quo { ut ille quidem putat) de Eucharistia agitur, tot allegorias, tot ænigmata & ambages ei mysterio obtendit, ut, si fides Cardinali habenda sit, ne una quidem Augustini extet toto tractatu x x v i. periodus quę non effugium aliquod elusionemve, ac veræ, perfectæque de hoc capite definitionis dissimulationem & imminutionem aliquam contineat. Sic ille panem qui de cælo descendit, interpretatur, donum Spiritus Sancti. Datur, inquit, Dominus Spiritu Sanctum, dixit ... se esse panem qui de cœlo descendit. Tu, præeunte & tam diserte docente sanctissimo Doctore, putabis hunc esse genuinum loci sensum. Sed cave ne sic putes, nam ex Calvino ostendit Cardinalis id fieri non posse. Eodem quoque modo recipit quod idem Augustinus subdit, aliquando post Hunc (inquit) cibum & potum societatem vult intelligi corporis & membrorum suorum, quod est sancta Ecclesia in prædestinatis & vocatis & justificatis & glorificatis sanctis & fidelibus ejus. Quis (nisi Perronius præmonuisset exi-stimatum tuus fuit Scriptorem illum (adeo religiosum ut in gravem cum Hieronymo contentionem venerit, quod iste simulationem Paulo ausus esset tribuere) hic docuisse hanc esse mentem Domini, nisi eam revera esse sensisset? Cardinalis tamen pleraque sibi à Protestantibus ex eodem Auctore objecta hanc ipsa ratione solvit; ut verbi gratia hunc locum. Credere in Christum est manducare panem vivum: & hunc item; Qui credit in eum manducat, invisibiliter saginatur, quia & invisibiliter renascitur. Et hunc denique: Si quis manducat ex ipso pane non morietur, sed quod pertinet ad virtutem Sacramenti, non quod pertinet ad visibile Sacramentum: qui manducat intus non foris, qui manducat in corde, non qui premit dente. Cōtendit Cardinalis Augustinum his omnibus locis veram plenam & integram definitionem istius carnis & sanguinis Christi manducationis supprimere, eiusque loco meditationem hanc allegoricam & accessoriam Catechumenis obtrudere; ut eorum oculos perstringeret, curiositatemque eluderet. Eadem animaduersione soluit locos allatos ex Theodoreto, & Gregorio Nazianzeno, quem dicit Eucharistiam corporis & sanguinis Christi antitypum vocare, eadem ratione qua Abraham cùm inter iusfideles versaretur, Saram sororem suam dicebat, veri quidem aliquid dissimulans, nihil tamen falsi enuntians. Pari modo hæc è Clementis Pædagogo explicat. Caro & sanguis Christi fides est & promissio. Denique ut paucis abiolvam hac observatione ita delectatus est, ut eam pene ad omnia patrum loca inculcet. Itaque hic uere primatius ac pene unicus fons est ex quo celeberrimus disputator, suas illas famosas, & omnium sermone jactatas solutiones hausit. Non jam disquiro eane obscuratio omnibus quibus à Petronio adhibetur. Patrum locis congruat, non enim dubito quin paulo seriores rerum aestimatores viri fidem in multis sint desideraturi.) Sed utcunque sit, hoc nunc quidem satis est, quod ille statuit Patres in suis apud plebem concionibus & tractatibus hac methodo frequenter uti, cum inde liquido sequatur, nobis non posse constare eos solidas & idoneas eas explicationes & sententias apud seipsos censuisse, quas in hoc scriptorum genere adhibent. Quemadmodum enim Cardinalis Augustini, Gregorij, Theodoreti & Clementis locorum vim infringit, eodem jure, si Protestantibus objicias locos quosdam ex Homiliis Chrysostomi & Eucherij peritos qui videntur adversus eorum sententiam disserti; nonne regerere possunt Patres istos, de his rebus apud plebem agentes, ea oeconomia usos, ut dicerent, non quod optimum & veritissimum censerent; sed quod magis ad aliorum aedificationem faceret? Metuisse ne sicca & cruda veritatis declaratione frigescerent populorum studia? Cum (inquiunt) multo probabilius esset timere ne Sacramenta in contemptum venirent, quam ne adorarentur, ut revera Patres longe studiosius huius Sacramenti materiam, & contemptui per se obnoxiam, dissimulant, quam ejus formam, cuius natura venerabilis est, quo fit ut saepe & manifeste dicant esse corpus Christi, cum plerumque esse aut fuisse panem taceant.
units.tr: "...teaches that they went even further for these very reasons. For when they expounded Scripture to the people, among whom were also catechumens, if by chance they came upon a passage dealing with the sacraments, they would then shy away from unveiling those mysteries, and in place of the genuine and real exposition, which they kept shut up in their breast, they put forward an allegorical and symbolic one, and, in the Cardinal's words, an 'accessory and collateral' one, by which they might satisfy the minds of the less instructed by some art. For if they had kept entirely silent when the opportunity to deal with this subject presented itself, that would have seemed strange to the hearers and would have given rise to suspicion and even offence. So, in order both to satisfy the expectations of outsiders and yet keep the mystery hidden, they eluded them in this way, proposing not what they themselves judged best and most true, but what they thought best suited their purpose. Thus we deceive and amuse children with nuts or some other playthings, so as to draw them away from desire for things of greater moment. Those, therefore, who take what is found in such passages among the Fathers for native and solid expositions and their genuine opinions are greatly mistaken, and embrace a shadow for the body. It would scarcely be credible that these holy men played such tricks, were it not vouched for by so great a Cardinal, on whose authority we are also bringing forward these things at present, and from whom we give the following examples. When Augustine came to the sixth chapter of John, in which (as that writer thinks) the Eucharist is treated, he put forward so many allegories, enigmas, and circumlocutions concerning that mystery that, if the Cardinal is to be believed, there is not even one sentence of Augustine in the whole twenty-sixth tractate that does not contain some evasion or trick, and some concealment or diminishing of the true and perfect definition of this matter. So he interprets 'the bread which came down from heaven' as the gift of the Holy Spirit: 'The Lord gives the Holy Spirit,' he says, 'when he said ... that he is the bread which came down from heaven.' You, guided by and taught so eloquently by that most holy Doctor, will suppose this to be the genuine sense of the passage. But beware of supposing so, for the Cardinal shows from Calvin that this cannot be. In the same way he accepts what the same Augustine adds, sometimes, after: 'By this food and drink he wishes the fellowship of his body and members to be understood, which is the holy Church among the predestined, the called, the justified, and the glorified saints and his faithful.' Who (unless Perron had warned us that this is considered) would have thought that this writer, so pious that he entered into a serious dispute with Jerome because the latter dared to ascribe dissimulation to Paul, taught here that this is the mind of the Lord, unless he had truly thought it so? Yet the Cardinal solves most of the objections that the Protestants raise from the same author by this very method; for example this passage: 'To believe in Christ is to eat the living bread'; and this one too: 'He who believes in him eats, is invisibly fed, because he is also invisibly born again'; and finally this: 'If anyone eats of that bread itself he will not die, but this refers to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament; he eats inwardly, not outwardly; he eats in the heart, not he who presses with the tooth.' The Cardinal contends that in all these passages Augustine suppresses the true, full, and entire definition of this eating of the flesh and blood of Christ, and in its place thrusts upon the catechumens this allegorical and accessory meditation, so as to dazzle their eyes and elude their curiosity. With the same observation he resolves the passages cited from Theodoret and from Gregory Nazianzen, whom he says calls the Eucharist the antitype of the body and blood of Christ, for the same reason that Abraham, when he was among the uncircumcised, called Sarah 'his sister', concealing indeed something true, yet uttering nothing false. In the same way he explains these words from Clement's Paedagogus: 'The flesh and blood of Christ is faith' and promise. Finally, to be brief, he has been so delighted with this observation that he presses it almost into all the passages of the Fathers. Thus this is truly the first and almost the only source from which that most famous disputant drew those celebrated solutions of his, which are on everyone's lips. I am not now inquiring whether this obscuring, which is applied by Perron to all the passages of the Fathers, is in agreement with them; for I do not doubt that more sober judges of things will in many cases find his good faith wanting. But however that may be, it is enough for the present that he holds the Fathers frequently used this method in their sermons and treatises before the people. For it clearly follows from this that we cannot be sure they judged those explanations and opinions, which they employ in this kind of writing, to be solid and suitable for themselves. For just as the Cardinal breaks the force of the passages of Augustine, Gregory, Theodoret and Clement, so by the same right, if the Protestants object to him certain passages from the homilies of Chrysostom and Eucherius which seem to argue skilfully against their view, could not those Fathers, who were speaking of these things before the people, be thrown back on them, as having used that economy so as to say not what they judged best and most true, but what was more conducive to the edification of others? Did they fear that the enthusiasm of the people would grow cold if the truth were declared dry and crude? When (they say) it would be far more probable that they feared the sacraments would come into contempt, rather than that they would be adored; as indeed the Fathers much more diligently conceal the matter of this sacrament, which is in itself liable to contempt, than its form, whose nature is venerable. Hence they often and plainly say it is the body of Christ, while for the most part they are silent that it is or was bread."

units.la: Supererat e Scriptis Patrum tertium genus, polemicum scilicet, cum adversus fidei suae adversarios, Ethnicos, Iudaeos, vel haereticos disputant. Supra vidimus quantam obscuritatem in hanc partem mentis contentio inferat, quod quidem vitium ex sola animi perturbatione, minime vero ex ullo proposito quo tenebris potius tiùs quàm perspicuitati studerent ortum habuit. Nam cùm omnium studiorum, sive animi affectuum, ea sit indoles, ut iis animus nonnihil perturbetur, fierìque aliter nequeat, licet à sanctissimis, quin dum in controversiis magni momenti versantur (quales sunt quæ ad religionem spectant) commoveantur percellanturque mirandum non est, si in his rebus, Patrum dissertationes iis moribus & quasi coloribus nonnunquam inspergi & variari videamus, quibus plerumque suffunduntur eorum ora quorum animi ejusmodi studiis commoventur. Sed præter turbas quas Patribus incogitantibus per se attulerunt istæ animi concitationes, notandum est præterea in hoc capite eorum sive propositum, sive disputandi methodum magnas in ejusmodi Scripta difficultates invexisse. In hoc namque Scriptorum genere fas esse existimabant quicquid ad causam facit adhibere, utut aliàs infirmum & à nostra etiam sententia alienum, pariterque quicquid susceptæ causæ repugnat repudiare ac refutare, licèt aliàs verum & admittendum. Sed ne hæc observatio miranda & incredibilis videatur, age, eos ipsos hac de re differentes audiamus. En tibi ergo Hieronymi, Patrum omnium Censoris longè accuratissimi verba. Is enim cùm in se, tum in cæteros summam illam ingenij vim qua excellebat convertens, plura huius generis de Patrum stilo, methodo, ingenio ac sententiis quàm quisquam alius observauit. Simul dicimus(inquit)plura esse videlicet genera dicendi, & intercatera aliud esse γυμναστικῶς scribere, aliud διαλεκτικῶς. In priori vagam esse disputationem, & adversario respondentem nunc hac, nunc illà proponere; argumentari ut libet, aliud loqui, aliud agere, panem, ut dicitur, ostendere, lapidem tenere. In sequeti autem aperta frons, & ut ita dicam ingenuitas necessaria est. Aliud est quærere, aliud definire, il altero pugnandum in altero docendum est. Tu me stantem in prælio, & de vita periclitantem siud: ostua magister doceas? Noli ex obliquo & unde non putaris vulnus insligere, directo percute gladio.
units.tr: There remained a third kind of writing from the Fathers, namely the polemical, in which they dispute against the adversaries of their faith: pagans, Jews, or heretics. We have seen above how much obscurity the heat of contention introduces into the mind's judgement. This fault arises from the agitation of the mind alone, and not from any intention to prefer darkness to clarity. For every kind of study, or of the affections of the soul, has such a nature that the mind is somewhat disturbed by it and cannot be otherwise. It is therefore no wonder that, when even the most holy men are engaged in controversies of great weight, such as those concerning religion, they are moved and stirred. In these matters we see the Fathers' discourses sometimes sprinkled and varied with those tones and, as it were, colours with which the faces of those whose minds are stirred by such zeal are usually suffused. But besides the disturbances that these agitations of mind brought upon the Fathers without their intending it, we must also note that in this matter their purpose, or their method of disputing, has raised great difficulties in such writings. In this kind of writing they thought it lawful to use whatever serves their cause, however weak it might be otherwise and even foreign to their own opinion. Likewise they thought it lawful to reject and refute whatever opposes the cause they had undertaken, even if it were otherwise true and admissible. But lest this observation seem strange and incredible, come, let us hear these very men differing on this point. Behold, then, the words of Jerome, by far the most careful critic of all the Fathers. For he, turning upon himself and upon others that great power of intellect in which he excelled, observed more such things about the style, method, character and opinions of the Fathers than anyone else. "At the same time," he says, "we must remember that there are several kinds of speaking, and that one thing is to write gymnastically [γυμναστικῶς], another to write dialectically [διαλεκτικῶς]. In the former the discussion wanders, and answering the opponent one now puts forward this, now that; one argues as one pleases, says one thing and does another, shows bread, as they say, while holding a stone. In the latter, however, an open front and, so to speak, frankness is necessary. It is one thing to ask, another to define; in the one we must fight, in the other we must teach. Why do you, a master, teach me, standing in battle and in danger of my life, as if I were a boy? Do not strike the wound from the side, where you think it cannot be inflicted, but strike with a direct sword."

units.la: {a} Hieron. epist. ad Pammach. T. 1. p. 136. A. turpe tibi est hostem dolis ferire, non viribus, quasi non hoc ars summa pugnantium sit, alibi minari, alibi percutere: legite, obsecro vos, Demosthenem. Legite Tullium, ac ne forsan Rhetores vobis displiceant, quorum artis est verisimilia magis quàm vera dicere. Legite Platonem, Theophrastum, Xenophontem, Aristotelé & reliquos qui de Socratis fonte manentes diversis cucurrere rivulis, quid in illis apertum, quid simplex est? Qua verba non sensuum? Qui sensus non victoria. Origenes, Methodius, Eusebius, Apollinaris multis versuum millibus scribunt adversus Celsum & Porphyrium. Considerate quibus argumentis & quam lubris problematibus Diaboli spiritu contexta subvertant, & quia interdum coguntur loqui, non quod sentiunt, sed quod necesse est dicunt adversus ea quae dicunt Gentiles. Taceo de Latinis scriptoribus Tertulliano, Cypriano, Minutio, Victorino, Lactantio, Hilario, ne non tam me defendisse quàm alios videar accusasse. Hactenus Hieronymus. Quod vero de Paulo subjicit quem iisdem quoque artibus usum putat, de eo non est disputandi locus, quod nunc de Patribus solis, non autem de Apostolis agimus. Patres quidem diserte testatur in disputationibus suis aliud nonnunquam dicere, aliud in pectore clausum gerere panem ostendere, manu lapidem tenere, alibi vulnus intentare, alibi infligere, cogi interdum verba sua, non ad id quod sentiunt, sed ad id quod necessitas postulat inflectere. Idipsum, ut à nobis supra observatum est, de Dionysio Alexandrino agnoscebat Athanasius, eum, scilicet, scripsisse, non simpliciter quasi quid sentiret declarasset, sed coactum veluti occasione propter eos quibusdam negotium erat. Neque aliud volebat Basilius, cùm in responsione pro Gregorio Neocaesariensi distinguebat inter dogmatice differere & disputare Eodem redit quod dicunt aliquid per dispensationem vel œconomiâ scribere; his enim verbis significant apud te quod sentias cohibere, déque eo vel detrahere, vel addere certis quibusdam de causis, si quando de eo contendere necesse sit. Quemadmodum cùm quandoque accidit ut aqua sursum ascendat, spatium quod alioqui vacuum futuri um esse, repleat, non ideo eum motum illi naturalem & usitatum esse inferes. Idem Patribus, in disputationum augustiis versantibus.accidit, ut vitandi ( ut ita dicam) cuiusdam vacui,à quo sibi metuebant, gratia, motum suum naturalem genuinámque sententiam nonnunquam omitterent, & in contrariam tantisper concederent, dum se expedirent. Sed hoc vel tacente Hieronymo) ipsi eorum tractatus disertè satis loquuntur. Hæc enim vis eos nonnunquam subegit varias secùmque pugnantes sententias diversis in locis sequi, frigidùmque & calidum ex eodem ore efflare,& identidem, vel rationi, vel Scripturæ, vel reliquis Patribus adversari. Quis enim tam hebes (inquit idem Hieronymus) & sic in scribendo rudis est, ut idem laudet & damnet? ædificata destruat, & destructa ædificet? At Patres id frequenter faciunt, sequitur ergo ad id suo quodam consilio adactos fuisse, idque œconomicè & per dispensationem, ut loquuntur, fecisse, quandoquidem prudentes, eruditòsque viros fuisse constat. Exempli gratia Hieronymus peregrinationes ad loca sancta, ut ad Hieriosolymorum urbem adeo commendat, ut dicere non dubitet, adorasse ubi steterunt pedes Domini, & quasi recentia natiuitatis & crucis ac passionis vidisse vestigia, partem pietatis esse. Qui conueniunt ista cum iis tam multis quæ in contrariam sententiam habet epistola ad Paulinum. Quorsum inquies (verba sunt claudentis quæ de hoc argumento dixerat) hæc tam longo repetita principio? videlicet ne quicquam fidei tuæ deesse putes, quia Hierosolymam non vidisti, nec nos idcirco meliores existimes quod huius loci habitaculo fruimur. Planè ad Gregorij Nisseni mentem, qui de hoc argumento epistolam scripsit, eorùmque sententiam refellit qui †partem pietatis existimant Hierosolymam videre. Iudicet nunc æquus Lector quibus quantisque difficultatibus Patrum scripta hæc methodus involvat atque implicet. Qui enim cognoscere poteríinus ex animò ne ij loquantur, an secus? scriónè rem agant, an tentandi & experiundi tantùm gratia? fallendinè an alendi causa panem ostendant? Num quæ adhibent problemata solida sint, an lubrica, dogmaticè ne an œconomicè loquantur? Profectò Senatus judicia si in hanc formam conciperentur, nullam unquam litem decidərent. Quod enim excipit Hieronymus; Debuerat (inquit) prudens & benignus Lector etiâ ea quæ videntur dura aßimare de cæteris,& non in uno atque eodem libro criminari me diversas sententias protulisse, id, inquam, verum quidem est, sed difficultatem non tollit: frequenter enim, utut folers & industrius sit lector, impossibile est ut de eâ re judicium ferat, ut, exempli gratia, si desint ea ex quibus judicium instituì vult Hieronymus. Si ex Auctore, cujus is locus est qui explicandus proponitur, nihil nobis præter ipsum locum superest, vel certè præter caput tractatúmve in quo is Auctori excipit. Quàm multa hujus generis occurrunt in hodiernis de religione controversiis; Quid item facimus, aut quò nos convertemus, si ex Patre, qui nobis explicandus est, nullus alius nobis restat de eodem argumento locus, saltem qui sit perspicuus, vel è Scripto quod non sit gymnasticum vel polemicum; Quis judex sidebit in his contradictionibus? Sed quod longè difficillimum est ipsa illa quæ instituendo & formando judicio nostro præscribit Hieronymus non omnibus eadem placent: sed ut sunt singulæ rum studia, ita aliis arridént, aliis displicent, & quæ huic dura ac scabra videntur, eadem malius lævia ac facilia censet, pro partium quisque suarum ingenio. Itaque nonjam de partium dogmatis ex Patrum sententia, sed planè contra de horum sententia ex illarum studiis judicandum erit. Neque l.en'gnitas illam quam in nobis Hieronymus requirit vel hilum promovebit, imò vereendum est ne ipsa plurimum noceat. Nam quo majori benignitate Patrem quempiam complexi fuerimus, tanto majori ope & cura nitemur,ut ejus sensum ab ea sententia quam aversamur, licèt licet forsan ejus ipsamet genuina fuerit, abducamus ut in locis illis quos proximè ex Hieronymo & Gregorio Nysseno retulimus, id ipsum Protestantibus durum & intolerabile videtur, quod eorum aduersariis suaue & acceptum est. Alter in eo loco explicando sudat, qui alteri planus ac facilis est. Qui huic textus Auctoris est, alteri glossæ instar habetur. Quisque pro suo in utrumque hunc Scriptorem studio contendit eos in suam sententiam trahere, id est, à propria dimouere, cum fieri non possit ut utramque utérque amplexus sit. Unde videre est ex verbis Patrum, licet dissertissimis, de eorum sententia nobis constare non posse, siue Scripturas explicent, siue de suggestu populum doceant, siue de fide contra aduersarios decernent.
units.tr: {a} Jerome, letter to Pammachius, vol. 1, p. 136 A. It is shameful for you to strike your enemy with tricks rather than with strength, as if this were not the highest art of fighters: to threaten in one place and strike in another. I beg you, read Demosthenes. Read Tully, and do not be displeased with the rhetoricians, whose art is to say things that are likely rather than true. Read Plato, Theophrastus, Xenophon, Aristotle and the others who, flowing from the fountain of Socrates, ran off in different little streams. What is plain and simple in them? What words are not wrapped in meanings, and what meanings are not wrapped in victory? Origen, Methodius, Eusebius and Apollinaris write many thousands of verses against Celsus and Porphyry. Consider with what arguments, and with what slippery problems woven by the spirit of the Devil, they overturn them, and how, because they are sometimes compelled to speak not what they think but what they must say, against what the Gentiles say. I say nothing of the Latin writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Victorinus, Lactantius, Hilary, lest I seem less to have defended myself than to have accused others." Thus far Jerome. What he adds about Paul, whom he thinks used the same arts, is not a matter for discussion here, since we are now dealing with the Fathers alone and not with the Apostles. Jerome clearly testifies that the Fathers in their disputations sometimes say one thing while keeping another locked in their breast, that they show bread while holding a stone in hand, that elsewhere they threaten a wound and elsewhere inflict it, and that they are sometimes forced to bend their words, not to what they think, but to what necessity demands. Athanasius acknowledged the same thing, as we have observed above, about Dionysius of Alexandria: that he wrote not simply declaring what he thought, but as if compelled by the occasion on account of certain people who were giving him trouble. Basil also meant no other thing when, in his reply on behalf of Gregory of Neocaesarea, he distinguished between teaching dogmatically and disputing. What they say, that someone writes by dispensation or economy, comes to the same thing. For by these words they mean that you restrain what you think, and that, for certain reasons, you either subtract from it or add to it, whenever it is necessary to contend about it. Just as when it sometimes happens that water rises upward and fills a space that would otherwise be empty, you should not infer that this motion is natural and usual for it. The same thing happened to the Fathers when they were engaged in the narrow confines of disputation: for the sake of avoiding a certain vacuum, as I may say, which they feared, they sometimes set aside their natural motion and genuine opinion, and for a while yielded to the contrary, until they could extricate themselves. But this is said quite plainly in their own treatises, even if Jerome were silent. This force has indeed sometimes driven them to follow various opinions in different places, opinions that contradict one another, to breathe out cold and hot from the same mouth, and repeatedly to oppose reason, Scripture, or the other Fathers. "For who," says the same Jerome, "is so dull and so unskilled in writing as to praise and condemn the same thing, to destroy what he has built and to build what he has destroyed?" Yet the Fathers often do this. It follows, therefore, that they were driven to it by some plan of their own, and that they did it economically and by dispensation, as they say, since it is established that they were prudent and learned men. For example, Jerome so commends pilgrimages to holy places, and especially to the city of Jerusalem, that he does not hesitate to say that "it is a part of piety to have worshipped where the feet of the Lord stood, and to have seen, as it were, the fresh traces of his birth, cross and passion." How do these things agree with the many others that he holds to the contrary in his letter to Paulinus? "Why," you will ask (these are the words of one concluding what he had said on this subject), "why this long-drawn-out beginning? Surely lest you think anything is lacking in your faith because you have not seen Jerusalem, and lest you think us the better because we enjoy the dwelling of this place." Clearly this is against the mind of Gregory of Nyssa, who wrote a letter on this subject and refutes those who think that "it is a part of piety to see Jerusalem." Let the fair reader now judge with what great difficulties this method involves and entangles the writings of the Fathers. For how can we know from their minds whether they speak sincerely or otherwise? Whether they are doing a thing seriously, or only for the sake of trying and testing? Whether they show bread for the sake of deceiving or of feeding? Whether the problems they put forward are solid or slippery, and whether they speak dogmatically or economically? Truly, if the judgements of the Senate were framed in this form, they would never decide any suit. For what Jerome replies, "A prudent and kindly reader ought to judge even those things which seem harsh about the others, and not accuse me in one and the same book of having put forward different opinions," is true, I grant, but it does not remove the difficulty. For, however diligent and industrious the reader is, it is often impossible for him to form a judgement on the matter, for example if the things on which Jerome wants the judgement to be based are missing: if, from the author whose passage is put forward for explanation, nothing is left to us except the passage itself, or certainly except the chapter or treatise in which he is answering his opponent. How many things of this kind occur in the religious controversies of our own day! What, too, shall we do, or where shall we turn, if, from the Father whom we must explain, no other passage on the same subject remains to us, at least none that is clear, or drawn from a writing that is not gymnastic or polemical? What judge will sit in judgement on these contradictions? But what is by far the most difficult is that the very things which Jerome prescribes for forming and training our judgement do not please everyone. Rather, as each one's studies are, so they are pleased by some and displeased by others, and whatever seems harsh and rough to one, the same another judges smooth and easy, according to the character of each one's party. Therefore the question will not be judged from the Fathers' opinions concerning the dogmas of the parties, but, quite on the contrary, the Fathers' opinions will have to be judged from the studies of those parties. Nor will that kindness which Jerome requires of us advance the matter in the slightest; rather, we must fear that it will do the greatest harm. For the more kindly we embrace some Father, the more eagerly and carefully we will strive to draw his meaning away from the opinion we dislike, even if, perhaps, that opinion was truly his own. In the passages which we have just cited from Jerome and Gregory of Nyssa, this very thing seems hard and intolerable to the Protestants, which is pleasant and acceptable to their adversaries. One sweats in explaining a passage that is plain and easy to another. What is the text of the author to one is regarded by another as a gloss. Each man, according to his own zeal for each of these writers, strives to draw them to his own opinion, that is, to remove them from their own, since it is impossible for each to embrace both. Hence it may be seen that from the words of the Fathers, however eloquent they are, we cannot be certain of their opinion, whether they are explaining the Scriptures, teaching the people from the pulpit, or deciding matters of faith against adversaries.

units.la: Hanc autem esse etiam plerorumque Pontificiorum de Patrum obscuritate sententiam docent Iesuitarum qui cæteris fere in illis partibus vulgò præferri solent, voces ac testimonia. Nam ex eo Sodalitio scriptor non ignobilis Adamus tradit quid Augustinus de gratia & auxiliis senserit, id ab Ecclesia præsente melius nos discere quàm ex ipsius Augustini libris. Itaque ex huius quidem hominis scitis, frustra Augustini, frustra aliorum Patrum monumenta leguntur ac teruntur, ut eorum quæ fuerit de controuersiis religionis capitibus sententia discamus ac pernoscamus; missō hoc immenso quidem sed tamen casso & inutili labore; rectà adeunda est Ecclesia præsens, id est, ea quæ nunc Romæ præsidet. Illa una est quæ latentes Patrum sensus eruere, quæ caliginem & tenebras quibus eorum oratio tecta atque involuta est discutere queat. Quod si ab isto quæsieris unde scire licebit quæ sit præsentis Ecclesiæ de istis iudicium (non enim cuiusvis est Romam ire; aut Papalis, quæ istic sedet, Maiestatis responsa consulráque de singulis, ut emergunt, dubitationibus, impetrare) Non dubito quin te sit ad suæ Societatis Patres statim amendaturus, quum isti, scilicet, iactant summi Christiana religionis Pontificis oraculum
units.tr: That this is also the view of most Papists about the obscurity of the Fathers is taught by the sayings and testimonies of the Jesuits, who are commonly preferred above almost all others in those parts. For a writer of no small reputation, Adam, hands down from that Society that what Augustine thought about grace and the auxiliary gifts, we learn better from the present Church than from Augustine's own books. Thus, on this man's authority, the works of Augustine and of the other Fathers are read and worn out in vain, if we wish to learn and fully understand what their opinion was on the controverted heads of religion. Setting aside this immense but empty and useless labour, we must go straight to the present Church, that is, the one that now presides at Rome. This alone can draw out the hidden meanings of the Fathers and dispel the darkness and shadows in which their language is covered and wrapped. But if you ask this man how we can know the judgment of the present Church on these matters (for it is not for everyone to go to Rome, or to obtain from the Papal Majesty that sits there its answers and counsel on each doubt as it arises), I do not doubt that he will at once send you back to the Fathers of his own Society, since they boast, of course, of the oracle of the supreme Pontiff of the Christian religion.

units.la: {a} P. Adam dans fes nouvelles leurs. esse. Certè cùm anonymus quidam Scriptor, ex eorum Theologorum numero quos vulgò lansènistas vocant, Adamì mentem ita accepisset; alter, ex eadem societate, Collegij Blesensis Rector, nomine Brisacerius, respondet, se suósque Augustini & cæterorum Patrum liberos legendos quidem putare ac censere, sed ita tamen ut eorum sensum ex præsentis Ecclesiæ, Scholasticorumque usu etque ore petant, neque inficiatur, quin hactenus summi Pontificis oracula dici possint illi suæ Societatis Scholastici Theologi, quod ij Pontifici sint oris & organorum vice, quorum ille ministerio interpretatur, scilicet, easquas declarare vult de rebus Divinis sententias. Denique, exempli causa, affert duas nescio quas recentissimas cujusdam de sua Societate Catecheses, quas quicunque legerint, eos facilè sanè ac expedito compendio in octo decemve paginis reperturos ait quicquid Augustinus de gratia vere ac catholicè sensit. Non jam queror quòd apertè nobis isti, dum sic agunt, illudunt, qui Patrum, ad quos provocant, sententiam ex sua interpretatione pendere volunt; quod nihil aliud est quàm summam & ultimam de iis, quæ cum illis nobis sunt, controversiis iudicandi potestatem sibi ipsis attribuere atque vindicare. Illud unum observo, si ex Patrum scriptis planè liquidòque intelligere non possunt lectores quæ eorum fuerit de iis quæ tractant ac disputant, sententia: si ut quid senserint discamus, ad præsentis uno quoque sæculo Ecclesiæ tribunal, & hoc nostro, ad Iesuiticum sodalitium, unicum scilicet summi Christianorum Pontificis oraculum, confugiendum est. Omnino consequens esse ut statuamus Patrum libros magna obscuritate laborare.
units.tr: {a} P. Adam, in his new letters. Certainly, when an anonymous writer, from the number of those theologians whom they commonly call Jansenists, had understood Adam's mind in this way, another man, from the same Society, the Rector of the College of Blois, named Brisacier, replies that he and his people think the books of Augustine and the other Fathers should indeed be read and considered, but so that they seek their sense from the usage and mouth of the present Church and of the Scholastics. He does not deny that, up to this point, those Scholastic theologians of his Society can be called the oracles of the supreme Pontiff, because they are in the place of the Pontiff's mouth and organs, by whose ministry he interprets, namely, and wishes to declare the opinions on divine matters. Finally, for example, he cites two I know not what very recent Catechisms by a certain man of his Society, which, he says, whoever reads them will find, by an easy and convenient summary, in eight or ten pages whatever Augustine truly and catholically thought about grace. I do not now complain that these men, in acting thus, openly mock us, since they want the opinion of the Fathers to whom they appeal to depend on their own interpretation. This is nothing other than attributing to themselves and claiming for themselves the final and supreme power of judging the controversies that we have with them. This one thing I observe: if the readers cannot understand from the Fathers' writings, plainly and clearly, what their opinion was on the matters they treat and dispute, and if, in order to learn what they thought, we must flee to the tribunal of the Church present in each age, and in ours to the Jesuit Society, the sole oracle of the supreme Pontiff of Christians, then it follows entirely that we must conclude the books of the Fathers labour under great obscurity.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Ratio VII. Patres in iisdem fidei capitibus non semper perstitisse, sed è quibusdam suis sententiis nonnun- quam discessisse, prout exercitatione, vel aetate eorum maturuerat judicium.
units.tr: Argument VII. The Fathers did not always persist in the same articles of faith, but sometimes departed from some of their own opinions, as their judgment matured with practice or with age.

units.la: EX omnibus auctoribus Ecclesiasticis soli Veteris & Novi Testamenti scriptores rerum divinarum notitiam praeter ordinem, afflatu coelesti, sunt consecuti. Reliqui omnes institutione, lectione, meditatione, ut moris est, eam adepti sunt. Haec scientia iis in mentem momento non venit, ut superioribus, sed per gradus crevit, paulatimque prout aetate proficiebantur, usu & experientia incrementa accepit, unde fit ut scripto eorum eiusdem vel ponderis vel pretii non sint omnia. Quis enim non videt ea quae quasi ludentes inter pueritiae vel adolescentiae oblectamenta, effuderunt, longè minoris esse momenti quàm ea quae aetate maturiore scripserunt? Quis exempli gratia epistolam illam quam dum esset adolescens, imò penè puer, primo impetu lascivientis aetatis, calentibus adhuc Rhetorum studiis atque doctrinis, ad Heliodorum misit, cum gravissimis scriptis quae cano capite, arata rugis fronte, maturo ingenio, consummatisque studiis Ecclesiae dedit? Patres in veritatis cognitione cum aetate, studiisque profecisse, luculento exemplo docuit Augustinus, cum quaecunque tota vita scripserat, in seipsum recensuit et excusat, in iisque ingenuè & bona fide notavit quid quid animadversione dignum visum est in Retractationum libris, omnium, quae posteriorati reliquit, illustrissimo praeclarissimoque non solùm de Christiana, sed etiam candidissimi modestissimique pectoris mea certè sententia, monumento. Refeirt Hieronymus Origenem, longo ante tempore, in senectute sua, epistolam scripsisse ad Fabianum Romanum T. x. p. 80. næ urbis Episcopum, in qua testabatur pœnitere se multorum quæ docuerat & scripserat ; Nec dubitandum est quin simile quid plerisque Patribus acciderit, ut quæ pro veris aliquando tradiderant, ea postea improbauerint. Ex hac autem obseruatione nascitur nobis nona difficultas in propositio nostro inquirendi de Patrum sumper controuersiis nostris genuina sententia. Cùm enim eorum quæ scripserunt ilta sit ratio, liquidò patet, si ex eorum sententiæ pugnare nobis animus est, necesse est ut nobis constet, non solùm quòd in ea fuerint, sed etiam quòd in ea ad mortem usque perseuerauerint.
units.tr: Of all the ecclesiastical authors, only the writers of the Old and New Testaments attained the knowledge of divine things by heavenly inspiration, apart from the ordinary way. All the rest acquired it, as is customary, by instruction, reading and meditation. This knowledge did not come to them all at once, as it did to the earlier writers, but grew by degrees, and gradually, as they advanced in age, it received increase through use and experience. Hence it follows that not all their writings are of equal weight or value. For who does not see that those things which they poured out as boyish sport, among the amusements of childhood or youth, are of far less importance than those they wrote in riper age? Take, for example, that letter which, while he was still a youth, indeed almost a boy, in the first rush of wanton age, with his zeal for the studies and doctrines of the rhetoricians still glowing, he sent to Heliodorus, compared with the most weighty writings which, with white head and furrowed brow, with mature judgment and studies brought to completion, he gave to the Church. That the Fathers advanced in knowledge of the truth with age and study, Augustine taught by a striking example: he reviewed and excused, in his whole life's writings, whatever he had written, and in the books of his Retractations he candidly and in good faith noted whatever seemed worthy of correction. That work, in my own judgment, is the most illustrious and renowned monument left by any writer after him, not only to Christian learning but to the most candid and modest heart. Jerome reports that Origen, long before, in his old age, wrote a letter to Fabian, bishop of the city of Rome (T. x. p. 80), in which he testified that he repented of many things he had taught and written. Nor should we doubt that something similar happened to most of the Fathers, so that they later disapproved of what they had at one time handed down as true. From this observation arises for us a ninth difficulty in our present inquiry into the genuine opinion of the Fathers on our controversies. For since this is the nature of what they wrote, it is clear that if we wish to fight with their opinions, it is necessary for us to be certain not only that they held them, but that they persevered in them to the end of their lives.

units.la: Vnde Vincentius Lirinensis in decantatissimo loco de Scriptorum Veterum sententiis ac controuersiis nostras decidendas, adhibendis vult ut ea tantum rata & fixa habeamus quæ ipsi constanter, ut loquitur, decuerint & in quibus permanserint. Idipsum suo exemplo peri spicuè docet Cardinalis Perronius, Nam in controuersia de Diuinarum Scripturarum canone (quem in Ecclesia Occidentali eundem semper fuisse contendit cum eo qui constitutus est in Concilio Carthaginensi iii. in quo Macchabæorum libri Canonicis accensentur) cùm se urgeri sentiret variis locis qui ex Hieronymo in contrariam sententiam afferuntur, hunc nodum ut soluat, respondet interalia, Patrem istum ea scripsisse quæ ipsi objiciuntur, cùm nondum studiorum suorum maturitatem omnem assecutus esset, eumq; postea, accuratius de veritate sensus Ecclesiæ edoctum, sententiam mutauisse, eaq; omnia, quæ in genere & sigillatim in tribus prologis scripserat, in quibus Machabæos è Canone eliminat, reuocasse. Et ad aliam obiectionem pro eadem sententia ex Gregorii Magni Commentariis petiram respondet eodem modo, S. Gregorium, cùm ista scripsit, nondum Papam fuisse, sed Diaconum tantùm. Legatumq; Constantinopoli apud Græcos egisse. Vel infirmæ mæ sunt solutiones iltæ, vel profecto de nullius Patris testimonio considere possumus, nisi prius nobis constet, non solùm ipsum nunquam sententiam revocauisse, verùm etiam ea de quibus agitur,adultis maturisque studiis scripsisse. Atque ita rursus in novum Labyrinthum incidimus. Primùm enimuncde & quomodo arcanum istud explicabimur, cuius vix ullum vestigium apparere potest, Patrem,scilicet,qui objicitur sententiam quæ opponitur in senectute non mutasse. Si omnes,aut potuissent, aut voluissent Augustini modestiam imitari mirùs laboris nobis incumberet : Sed vix ullus, siue olim, siue hisce temporibus qui hoc exemplum sibi imitandum duceret, repertus est. Vnus Cardinalis Bellarminus nostris temporibus modestiam illam multis, ferro seculis mortuam & sepultum suscitandam sibi censuit, edito Retractationum libro, qui tamen variè ab utriusque religionis eruditis acceptus est. Sed si, ut visum est Cardinali Perronio, nullius Patris sententia fidem facere potest, nisi consummatis studiis quid sentiret scripserit, nulla mihi spes est hac via posse nos quicquam progredi. Quicquid enim opponas promptum erit non minus his quàm illis ad singula quæque testimonia regerere. Quis scinus num Doctoris illius maturuissent studia, cùm Tractatum istum edidit ; Quis præstabit non iisdem soiibus qui ipsi postea illuxerunt mentem perinde ut caput, ir carnu sse?neque sententiam, unà cum pilis, mutasse? At ejus nihil apparet in Scriptis ipsius. Esto. Quot Scriptores, non retractatis libris de sententia in qua olim fuerant, discesserunt ; Nonne perire potuit liber in quo à Vetere sententia se recessisse significavit? Si illa fois fuisset Retractationum Augustini, & nouissimorum quorundam ejus operum, quæ fuit sexcentorum aliorum non minoris momenti, cùm ejus tum cæterorum Patrum, quæ tempus absumpsit, pro indubitato haberemus ipsum humanorum operum prævisionem prædestinationis causam statuisse, cùm apud. ipsum, in quodam è prioribus eius operibus hæc legamus. Non elegit Deus opera cuiusquam in præscientia quæ ip-se daturus est, sed fidem elegit in præscientia, ut quem sibi credituruʒm esse præsciuit ipsum elegerit, cui Spiritum Sanctum daret, ut bona operando etiam vitam æternam consequeretur. Pelagianis & Semi-Pelagianis essent ista argumento invicto Augustinum cum ipsis sensisse. Sed ex eius Retractationibus, aliisque operibus id salsissimum esse discimus, magnùmque istum virum omnibus postea expensis alirer omnino judicasse. Nondum (inquit) diligentiùs quæsieram, nec adhuc inveneram qualis sit electio gratiæ de quâ dicit Apostolus, Reliquiæ per electionem gratiæ salvæ factæ sunt, quæ utique non est gratia, si eam merita ulla præcedant, ne iam quod datur, non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum, reddatur potiùs meritis quàm donetur. Quis scit num è Patribus istis, quorum sententias adeo fidenter adhibemus, aliquis non retractarit ea quæ hodie in operibus eorum legimus? & annon errore superstitè, pœnitentiæ monumenta tempus è medio sustulerit? Quis item certò observauit quo vitæ suæ tempore scripserint? utrum veris sint, an Autumni quæ ex eo promuntur poma? acerba, an mitia? Omnis ista historia obscurissima est, cùm pleraque ætatis auctorum ne minimam quidem notam præferant. Quædam sunt in quibus aliquid eiusmodi videtur obseruari posse, Sed quicquid id sit, adeo dubium & incertum est, ut eruditissimi & clarissimi quique in iis cognoscendis aliquando errarent. Denique quis nescit non deesse arbores quæ fructum ferant in æstate, imò ineunte æstate, imò vix desito vere. Fructus intempestiui & serotini non sunt mitissimi, plerumque potiùs putrescunt quàm maturefcunt tempore. Eadem est humanorum ingeniorum, ac proinde Patrum ratio. Nec desunt quorum Ætas quam Autumnus longè feracior fuit. Nam Hyemem, id est, postremam ætatis nostræ partem, ut plurimum sterilem esse notum est, vel, si quid præter naturæ ordinem conetur, netur,fructus edere, quàm in Vere ipso, longè crudiores & acerbiores. Cùm ergo plerumque de huiusmodi rebus neque ex historia, neque ex Auctorum scriptis judicium firmum ferre liceat, praetereáque certa & indubitata non sint quae apud Scriptores ipsos occurrunt, in hoc capite ut in superioribus concludamus difficillimum esse certò & sigillatim statuere quid super controversiis quae hodie inter Christianos agitantur Veteres senserint.
units.tr: Hence Vincent of Lérins, in his much-celebrated passage on deciding our controversies by the opinions of the ancient writers, wishes us to hold as settled and fixed only those things which they, as he puts it, constantly held and in which they persisted. Cardinal Perron clearly showed this by his own example. For in the controversy over the canon of the divine Scriptures (which he maintained had always been the same in the Western Church as that fixed at the Council of Carthage III, where the books of the Maccabees are counted among the canonical books), when he felt himself pressed by various passages from Jerome cited for the contrary opinion, to untie this knot he answered, among other things, that this Father wrote the things objected to him before he had attained full maturity of his studies, and that later, more accurately instructed in the truth of the Church's sense, he changed his opinion and recalled all those things he had written, both in general and in particular, in the three prefaces in which he removes the Maccabees from the Canon. And to another objection drawn from the commentaries of Gregory the Great, in support of the same opinion, he answered in the same way: that St. Gregory, when he wrote those things, was not yet Pope but only a deacon, and had acted as legate at Constantinople among the Greeks. Either these solutions are weak, or indeed we can rely on the testimony of no Father unless it is first established for us that he never revoked his opinion, and that the matters in question were written in mature and completed studies. And so again we fall into a new labyrinth. For first, how and by what means shall we explain that secret, of which hardly any trace can appear: namely, that the Father who is objected to did not change in old age the opinion opposed to ours? If all men were able, or willing, to imitate the modesty of Augustine, our labour would be lighter; but scarcely anyone, whether in former times or in these, has been found who thought that example worth imitating. Cardinal Bellarmine alone, in our own times, thought fit to revive that modesty, long dead and buried for many centuries, by publishing a book of Retractations, which nevertheless has been received in various ways by the learned of both religions. But if, as seemed right to Cardinal Perron, no Father's opinion can carry weight unless he wrote what he thought after his studies were complete, I have no hope that by this road we can make any progress at all. For whatever you may bring forward will be as ready to be turned back against these as against those, on every single testimony. Who knows whether that teacher's studies had matured when he published that treatise? Who will guarantee that he did not change his opinion, along with his hair, when the same light dawned on his mind that later came to his head and his beard? But nothing of this appears in his writings. Granted. How many writers, without retracting their books, departed from the opinion in which they had once been? Could not a book in which they signified that they had departed from their earlier view have perished? If we had the Retractations of Augustine, and some of his last works, and those of six hundred others of no less weight, both his and those of the other Fathers, which time has consumed, we would hold it for certain that he made his foreknowledge of human works the cause of predestination, since in one of his earlier works we read these words: "God did not choose the works of anyone in foreknowledge which he himself is to give, but he chose faith in foreknowledge, so that he chose the one whom he foreknew would believe, to whom he would give the Holy Spirit, that by doing good he might also attain eternal life." Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians would have this as an unanswerable argument that Augustine agreed with them. But from his Retractations and other works we learn that this is most false, and that this great man, having weighed everything afterwards, judged quite otherwise. "I had not yet (he says) inquired more diligently, nor had I yet found what kind of election of grace it is of which the Apostle speaks: 'a remnant is saved by the election of grace,' which certainly is not grace if any merits precede it, lest what is given, not according to grace but according to debt, be rendered to merits rather than bestowed." Who knows whether some of those Fathers, whose opinions we so confidently use, did not retract the things which we read today in their works, and whether time, through a surviving error, has not removed the monuments of their repentance? Who also has certainly observed at what time of life they wrote? Whether they are true, or autumn fruits gathered from it: sour, or mild? All that history is most obscure, since most writers of that age bear not even the slightest mark of date. There are some cases in which something of this kind seems able to be observed, but whatever it is, it is so doubtful and uncertain that the most learned and most famous men have sometimes erred in recognising it. Finally, who does not know that there are trees bearing fruit not only in summer but at the beginning of summer, or just after spring? Untimely and late fruits are not the mildest; they more often rot than ripen in season. The reasoning is the same for human minds, and therefore for the Fathers. Nor are there lacking those whose age was far more fruitful in autumn: for winter, that is, the last part of our life, is well known to be mostly barren, or if it tries to produce anything beyond the order of nature, its fruits are far cruder and more sour than those of spring itself. Since, therefore, for the most part a firm judgment about such matters can be formed neither from history nor from the writings of authors, and since what occurs in the writers themselves is neither certain nor indubitable, let us conclude in this chapter, as in the previous ones, that it is most difficult to determine with certainty and particularly what the ancients thought about the controversies which are debated today among Christians.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Ratio VIII. Necessarium, & idem tamen difficillimum esse ut certò statuamus quid de suis ipsorum singulis sententiis Patres censuerint, & an eas ut ne- cessarias, an ut probabiles tantum, & quo in gradu necessitatis, vel probabilitatis eas habuerint.
units.tr: Proposition VIII. It is necessary, and yet most difficult, to establish with certainty what the Fathers thought of each of their own opinions: whether they held them as necessary or only as probable, and to what degree of necessity or probability they held them.

units.la: PRopositiones veras non omnes esse ex aequo veras Logicorum est pronuntiatum. Illarum enim quaedam sunt contingentes, ut in Scholis loquuntur, aliae verò necessariae: Et rursus cùm hae tum illae magis vel minùs necessariae, ut eas mirabiliter distinguit Philosophus in tribus illis necessitatis gradibus quos explicat priori de demonstratione libro. Unde fit ut earum cognitio vel ignoratio majoris aut minoris sit momenti in disciplinis ad quas pertinent: cùm quaedam sint (quales sunt quae principia dicuntur) adeo necessariae ut ignorari nequeant quin tota scientia in qua locum habere debent evertatur: quaedam verò ejusmodi ut ignorari possint, imò & earum contradictoriae pro veris assi mari nullo periculo. Hae, exempli gratia, in Physicis sunt prioris ordinis. Notum esse, omne corpus locum occupare & similes. Nam amabo te qualis esset Physica quæ huiusmodi principia negaret, vel quæ iis contradiceret? Sed quæ sequuntur sunt posteriores ordinis. Præcisè quinque tantùm esse Sensus in natura animali. Cælum esse ex materia elementari, & aliæ. Nam etsi propositiones istæ ut plurimum veræ habeantur, non sunt tamen adeò necessariæ ut non possit esse Physicus, qui non solùm eas nesciat, sed etiam qui earum contradictorias ponat. Si quæ autem sit disciplina in qua hæc observatio accuratè sit tenenda, ea est, mea sententia, Religio Christiana; permagnum enim discrimen est inter veritates quibus constat, cùm longè sint aliæ aliis magis necessariæ, ut clarè docet Origenes Homil. 27. in Matthæ. Confer inter sehas duas propositiones. Hanc Christus est Deus, & hanc alteram. Christus mortem pertulit natus annos triginta quatuor, aut triginta quinque. Quis, etsi ambæ veræ sint, inter utramque tamen summum esse discrimen non videt? Prior enim necessariò vera est, id est, ita ut fieri non potuerit quin Christus esset Deus, cùm hominis salus, quæ finis est Religionis, optinerinon posset alio modo. Posterior verò, etsi vera sit, & satis aperte ex Scriptura deducatur non est tamen necessaria. Poterat enim Christus, sic ei visum fuisset, mortem obire quadragesimo, aut quinquagesimo ætatis suæ anno, nullo salutis nostræ, quam sibi finem constituerat, dispendio. Pro varietatis huius ratione diversi in Religione momenti est agnitio aut ignorario duarum istarum propositionum. Prior non poterit ignorari, multo minùs negari quin totus pereat Christianismus, posterior ignorari, imò & rejici poterit sine magno periculo. Ut ergo liquidò nobis constet quid super capitibus hodie in Religione controversis senserint Patres, statuendum est non solùm, num ea crediderint, vel secus, sed præterea quo loco ea habuerint, num pro necessario, vel probabiliter tantum, veris sive falsis; imò etiam quo in gradu necessitatis aut probabiliatis. Ntatis ea constituerint. Hanc inquisitionem necessariam esse luculenter docuit Cardinalis Perronius erudita illa Epistola quam ad Casaubonum in Magnae Britanniae Regis gratiam scripsit. Quum enim Princeps ille Catholici nomen sibi vendicaret, quod sibi esse eadem de rebus fidei sententia, quae quinque antiquissimorum seculorum Patribus fuisset, consequentiam illam in dubium vocat Cardinalis, dum inter alia regerit, non satis esse, ad communionem cum Veteribus colendam, ea quae crediderunt credere, sed necessarium esse eadem ratione & eodem gradu quibus crediderunt ea credere existimare, scilicet, tanquam ad salutem necessarium, quod illi ad salutem necessarium censuerunt, & quasi utile ad salutem, quod illi utile existimauerunt, & quod licere credere & fidei non repugnare arbitrati sunt, id eodem numero habere. Subiungit deinde prolixam & exquisitam illam distinctionem variorum necessitatis graduum qui possunt & debent in propositionibus circa religionem usurpari. Beasset nos doctus ille Praesul si ex ea occasione ad quae fidei capita ea observatio posset applicari nos docuisset. Sic enim quod hominum maximam partem latet ab eo didicissemus, quo videlicet gradu unumquodque fidei Christianae caput, sive ab Ecclesia Romana, sive a Veteribus Patribus habendum sit, quae absolute, & quae secundum quid & certis quibusdam conditionibus sint in religione necessaria; quae praeterea necessitate medii, vel necessitate praecepti, ut loquitur, necessaria sint, id est, quae observanda sunt ratione usus, quod nempe sint media quae ad salutem conducunt, vel ratione praecepti tantum, quod imperata sint ab auctoritate quapiam cui morem genere tenemur: quae deinceps sint capita illa, quae omnes & singuli fideles diserte credere tenentur, & quae satis sit in turba & fide implicita credere denique quae omnibus facienda incumbant, & quae satis sit probare, facere non sit necesse. Vtcumque sit, perspicuum est ex iis quae dicit, ad certo pernoscendum quid senserint Patres, & maximè in capitibus quæ hodie in controuersiam vocantur, oportere ut nobis constet quo gradu ea crediderint. Maximè verò factam à Vetere Ecclesia hanc distinctionem apparet, ex eo quod eius semper magnam atque præcipuam rationem habuit; ultro admissis aut reiectis ad se accedentibus, primò, secundùm ea quæ credebant, aut non credebant, deinde secundum varias rationes quibus credebant vel non credebant. Qui enim quæ necessaria apud se containebant repudiabant, vel qui tanquam necessaria urgebant ea quæ probabilia tantùm existimabantur, eos communione sua mouebat. Qui verò ignorabant, aut in dubium vocabant, vel etiam rejiciebant ea quæ ipsa vera quidem, sed non necessaria censebat, maxima semper cum benignitate excipiebat. Clarè id patet ex Epistola Irenæi ad Victorem Episcopum Romanum, apud Eusebium in historia Ecclesiastica. Testatur enim Sanctus ille vir, varietatem siue discrepantiam illam, quæ etiam ante Victorem, de die Paschatis inter Episcopos Asiæ & Ecclesiam Romanam fuerat, non obstitisse quominus pacem & concordiam inter se colerent, adeo ut vel ea de causa, vel propter ullas etiam alias varietates, nullus Asiæ Episcopus è communione Romana unquam reiectus sit. Contra verò Polycarpum, cùm tempore Aniceti Papæ Romam adventasset, postquam de rebus de quibus inter eos non conueniebat inter se disseruissent, quamuis utrumque in sententia perstitissent, concordiam tamen utrumque illibatam inter se seruasse, unaq; communicasse, imò Anicetum præ reuerentia qua Polycarpum prosequebatur, ei concessisse ut in Ecclesia sua Eucharistiam celebraret. Tertullianus libro de præscriptionibus aduersus hæreticos postulat tantùm ut regula fidei (quam vocat) maneat in forma sua, & ordine suo; qua salua concedit cuique quærere & tractare, & omnem libidinem curiositatis effundere, quod certo argumento est, ipsum in communionem recepisse eos etiam qui
units.tr: It is a saying of the logicians that not all true propositions are equally true. Some are contingent, as the schools put it, while others are necessary. Again, both kinds are necessary to a greater or lesser degree, as the Philosopher distinguishes admirably in the three degrees of necessity he explains in the first book of the Posterior Analytics. Hence the knowledge or ignorance of such propositions matters more or less in the disciplines to which they belong. Some propositions (such as those called first principles) are so necessary that they cannot be ignored without overturning the whole science in which they should have a place. Others can be ignored, and indeed their contradictories may be held as true without any danger. In physics, for example, the first kind includes that it is known that every body occupies a place, and similar statements. For, I ask you, what kind of physics would deny such principles or contradict them? But what follows belongs to the second kind: that there are exactly five senses in an animal nature, that the heavens are made of elemental matter, and others. For although these propositions are usually held to be true, they are not so necessary that there cannot be a physicist who not only does not know them but even holds their contradictories. If there is any discipline in which this distinction must be carefully observed, it is, in my judgement, the Christian religion. For there is a very great difference among the truths of which it consists, since some are far more necessary than others, as Origen clearly teaches in Homily 27 on Matthew. Compare two propositions: this one, Christ is God, and this other one, Christ suffered death at the age of thirty-four or thirty-five. Who does not see that there is the greatest difference between them, even though both are true? The first is necessarily true, that is, it could not have been otherwise than that Christ was God, since the salvation of man, which is the end of religion, could not be obtained in any other way. The second, although it is true and is deduced from Scripture quite plainly, is not necessary. For Christ could, had it so pleased him, have died in his fortieth or fiftieth year, without any loss to our salvation, which he had set as his goal. Because of this difference, knowing or not knowing these two propositions is of different importance for religion. The first cannot be ignored, and much less denied, without the whole of Christianity perishing; the second may be ignored, and even rejected, without great danger. So, if we are to be clear about what the Fathers thought on the chapters now disputed in religion, we must determine not only whether they believed them or not, but also what standing they gave them: whether as necessary, or only as probable, true or false; and indeed to what degree of necessity or probability they assigned them. That this inquiry is necessary has been learnedly shown by Cardinal Perron in that erudite letter which he wrote to Casaubon for the favour of the King of Great Britain. For when that prince claimed the name of Catholic, on the ground that his opinion on the matters of faith was the same as that of the Fathers of the first five centuries, the Cardinal calls that inference into doubt. Among other things he replies that it is not enough, in order to keep communion with the ancients, to believe what they believed; it is necessary to believe those things in the same manner and to the same degree in which they believed them. That is, one must regard as necessary for salvation what they regarded as necessary for salvation, regard as useful for salvation what they regarded as useful, and hold as equal what they judged lawful to believe and not contrary to faith. He then adds a long and exact distinction among the various degrees of necessity which may and must be used in propositions concerning religion. That learned prelate would have made us happy if, on this occasion, he had also taught us to which articles of faith this observation could be applied. For then we would have learned what most men do not know: to what degree each article of the Christian faith is to be held, whether by the Roman Church or by the ancient Fathers; which are necessary absolutely, and which only in a certain respect and under certain conditions in religion; which are necessary by the necessity of means, and which by the necessity of precept, as they say, that is, which are to be observed because they are means that lead to salvation, and which only because they have been commanded by some authority to which we are bound to obey; which are those articles that all and each of the faithful are expressly bound to believe; which it is enough to believe in a general way and by implicit faith; and finally which things must be done by everyone, and which it is enough to approve without it being necessary to do them. Be that as it may, it is plain from what he says that, in order to know clearly what the Fathers thought, and especially on the chapters now brought into controversy, we must be sure to what degree they believed them. It is especially clear that the ancient Church made this distinction, since it always took it into great and special account. Among those who came to her, she admitted or rejected them first according to what they believed or did not believe, and then according to the various reasons for which they believed or did not believe. For she set herself against those who rejected what she held to be necessary, or who pressed as necessary what was thought only probable. But those who did not know, or called into doubt, or even rejected what she judged to be true but not necessary, she always received with the greatest kindness. This is clear from the letter of Irenaeus to Victor, Bishop of Rome, preserved in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History. That holy man testifies that the variance or disagreement about the day of Easter, which had already existed between the bishops of Asia and the Church of Rome even before Victor, did not prevent them from keeping peace and concord with one another; so much so that, for this reason or for any other variance, no bishop of Asia was ever cut off from the Roman communion. On the contrary, when Polycarp came to Rome in the time of Pope Anicetus, after they had discussed among themselves the matters on which they did not agree, both remained in their opinions, yet both kept their unity unbroken and shared communion with each other. Indeed, out of reverence for Polycarp, whom he greatly honoured, Anicetus allowed him to celebrate the Eucharist in his church. Tertullian, in his book on prescription against heretics, asks only that the rule of faith (as he calls it) remain in its form and its order. Provided this is kept, he allows each person to inquire and discuss, and to pour out every desire of curiosity. This is certain evidence that he received into communion even those who...

units.la: Tertull. de præscript. adu. hæret. 14. & 15. qui praeter regulam fidei nonnulla alia proferebant, sed ea lege, ut probabilia tantum censerentur neque cum fidei norma pugnarent. Auctor Apologiae pro Origene, quam sub nomine Pamphili Ruffinus edidit, idem obseruat. Cum enim agnoscat Origenem quasdam opiniones priuatas & eas quidem valde alienas & peregrinas vel probasse, vel docuisse, vel certè in medium protulisse,de animę humanæ, priusquam nascatur, statu,& de natura astrorum, contendit tamen huiusmodi opinionibus hominem haereticum non fieri, imò & de his capitibus inter Ecclesię Doctores sententiis variari. Sed & in ipsa Ecclesia Romana idem etiam discrimen apertissimè hodie obseruatur. Feruntur enim in ea Dominicanorum & Franciscanorum contradictoriæ de conceptione B. Virginis sententiæ, quam sine peccato conceptam hi quidem aiunt, illi verò negant. Sed, quod magis mirum videatur, tolerantur eiusmodi sententiæ contradictoriæ super quibusdam capitibus quę, si in seipsis considerentur, maximi censeri possunt esse momenti. Exempli gratia. Potest quilibet in Ecclesia Romana credere, Crucem esse Latrię cultu adorandam: potest etiam si videatur in contraria esse sententia, nullo periculo, vel è communione Ecclesię, vel spe salutis excidendi. Et tamen rem, ut par est, expendenti, videri potest non de nihilo agi. Si enim prior sententia vera est,qui posteriorem amplectuntur haud leuiter peccant, dum obiectum adorationę dignum non adorant. Si salsa est,qui in ea sunt longè omnium grauissimè peccant, cum sint horrendæ idololatrię rei. Quid maioris momenti est quàm fundamentum ipsum & caput totius potestatis Ecclesiasticæ super cuius authoritate, vertitur fides vniuersa,& in quam Ecclesiæ totius moles recumbit? Et tamen super tanii momenti argumento sententiæ contradictoriæ feruntur; aliis Papæ, aliis Concilio hanc dignitatem tribuentibus. Si illorum sententia vera est, horum fides fundamento eruoti obnoxio nititur; si horum sententia vera est, illorum fides pendet à causa non infallibili, ac proinde nulla est. Vtrisq; consulitur dum dicitur interea dum Ecclesia harum sententiarum neutram de fide esse definiit, haereticum non esse qui falsam credat sicut nec simpliciter orthodoxum qui vera amplectatur. Cùm ergo de communione Ecclesiæ agatur, & de salute quæ ab ea pendet, pro certo nobis statuendum est, quo in ordine ea capita quæ hodie reluctantibus Protestantibus obtruduntur Patres habuerint, simpliciter ne, vel magis, an minus, ea existimaverint necessaria. Quandiu enim de eo liquidò non constabit, Protestantes, (quamvis concederent (à quo tamen multum absunt) à Patribus, tanquam vera ea credita fuisse, negabunt tamen sead ea credenda obligari, cùm omnes in religione sententiæ de fide non sint, earúmque aliæ sint necessariæ, aliæ verò minimè. Contendent item ejusdem generis esse ista cum iis quæ inter Dominici & Francisci gregales, interque Sorbonam & Canonistas controvertuntur, de quibus cuique, prout libet, apud se statuere licet. Firmabunt item responsionem suam ex eo quod Concilium Tridentinum manifestè hanc distinctionem inter Patrum sententias instituit: Cùm enim anathema dixisset iis qui parvulis necessariam esse Eucharistiæ communionem dicunt, declarat tamen, anathema illud nihil ad Patres pertinere qui in ea sententia fuerunt, quia sui facti probabilem causam, pro illius temporis ratione, habuerunt, nullàque salutis necessitate id fecerunt. Quod si certo quodam gradu quis errare potest, & quidem errores à Conciliis damnatos, sine anathematis periculo sequitur veritates quasdam posse ignorari, imò & in controversiam vocati, nullo itidem periculo. Quis fidem faciet (subjicient Protestantes) capita quæ repudiamus non esse eiusmodi? Imò licet vera essent, non licere ab iis recedere?
