Neminem esse puto qui jam non videat Ecclesiæ Romanæ doctores ad adversarios suos Patrum auctoritate reuincendos te-
units.tr: Tertullian, On the Prescription against Heretics, chapters 14 and 15, who put forward some other things besides the rule of faith, but on the condition that these were regarded only as probable and did not conflict with the norm of faith. The author of the Apology for Origen, which Rufinus published under the name of Pamphilus, makes the same observation. For while he acknowledges that Origen had either approved, taught, or at least put forward certain private opinions, and indeed very alien and foreign ones, about the state of the human soul before it is born and about the nature of the stars, he nevertheless contends that a person does not become a heretic by holding such opinions. Indeed, on these heads too the opinions of the teachers of the Church vary. The same distinction is also very plainly observed today even in the Roman Church itself. For contradictory opinions circulate in it among the Dominicans and the Franciscans about the conception of the Blessed Virgin: the former say she was conceived without sin, the latter deny it. But, what may seem more remarkable, contradictory opinions are tolerated on certain heads which, if considered in themselves, may be thought to be of the greatest moment. For example, anyone in the Roman Church may believe that the Cross is to be adored with the worship of latria; he may also, if he sees fit, hold the contrary opinion, with no danger of being cut off either from communion with the Church or from hope of salvation. Yet, to someone weighing the matter as it deserves, it can appear that no trivial thing is at stake. For if the former opinion is true, those who embrace the latter do not sin lightly, since they do not adore an object worthy of adoration. If it is false, those who hold it sin most gravely of all, since they are guilty of horrible idolatry. What is of greater moment than the foundation itself and the head of all ecclesiastical power, on whose authority the whole faith turns and on which the whole mass of the Church rests? And yet contradictory opinions are carried on concerning so weighty a matter: some ascribe this dignity to the Pope, others to the Council. If the opinion of the former is true, the faith of the latter rests on a foundation liable to collapse; if the opinion of the latter is true, the faith of the former hangs on a cause that is not infallible, and so is no faith at all. Both sides are accommodated by saying that, since the Church has not defined either of these opinions as a matter of faith, one who believes the false one is not a heretic, nor is one who embraces the true one simply orthodox. Since therefore the question concerns communion with the Church and the salvation that depends on it, we must establish with certainty in what order the Fathers held those heads which are now forced upon the reluctant Protestants: whether they regarded them as simply necessary, or more or less so. For as long as this is not clearly settled, the Protestants (though they would concede, from which, however, they are far removed, that the Fathers held these things as true) will nevertheless deny that they are bound to believe them, since not all opinions in religion are matters of faith, and some are necessary while others are by no means so. They will also contend that these are of the same kind as those things disputed between the Dominicans and the Franciscans, and between the Sorbonne and the Canonists, on which each may decide for himself as he pleases. They will also strengthen their answer by the fact that the Council of Trent plainly drew this distinction among the opinions of the Fathers. For when it had pronounced an anathema on those who say that communion of the Eucharist is necessary for infants, it declared nonetheless that this anathema does not touch the Fathers who held that view, because they had a probable reason for their practice, given the circumstances of that time, and did it with no necessity of salvation. And if one may err to a certain degree, and indeed (errors condemned by Councils excepted) may follow certain opinions with no danger of anathema, then it follows that some truths may be unknown, and even called into controversy, with equal lack of danger. Who will persuade us (the Protestants will add) that the heads we reject are not of this kind? Or that, even if they were true, it is not lawful to depart from them? I think there is no one who does not already see that the teachers of the Roman Church, in order to refute their adversaries by the authority of the Fathers, must show that the disputed heads were held by the ancients not only as true but also as necessary, and indeed with the same degree of necessity with which they themselves hold them.

units.la: P rr n.R j l. 4 in praefat p.7.s. neri demonstrare capita quæ controuertuntur, non solum ut vera Veteres habuisse; sed etiam ut necessaria, & quidem eodem necessitatis gradu quo ipsi habent. Videtur autem in hoc maxima verbi difficultas, imò omnium quas superioribus capitibus attulimus longè im,editissima. Neque mihi alio ad id probandum exemplo opus est quam eo ipso de quo nuper dixi mus. Patres enim Tridentini. nulla necessitate salutis, sed probabilem tantum ob causam Veteres, parvulos usu rationis carentes ad Eucharistiæ communionem suscipiisse decernunt. Atqui non modo magna subest de hac re dubitandi occasio; sed ex ipsis Patrum monumentis certò constare videtur ipsos, quod Tridentinæ Synodi pace dictum sit, parvulorum tinctorum communionem planè censuisse necessariam, sic enim de ea re loquuntur. Augustinus, imò præfatus, ex antiqua & Apostolica traditione Ecclesiæ Christi institutum tenere præter Baptismum & participationem Dominicæ mensæ, non solum ad regnum Dei, sed nec ad salutem & vitam æternam posse quemquam hominum pervenire, Quod postquam (ut quidem ipsi videbatur) ex Scripturas confirmasse, subdit. Si ergo ut tot & tanta Divi na Testimonia connincunt, nec salus nec vita æterna sine baptismo & corpore & sanguine Domini (sic enim Eucharistiam ex solemni illius seculi usu appellat cuiusque sie Ecclesiæ est frustra sine his promittitur parvulis, Et tribus antè capitibus, de his apud Ioannem Domini verbis agens. Nisi manducaueritis carnem meam & biberitis sanguinem meum, non habebitis vitam in vobis (quæ tum in eo loco, tum alibi de communione Eucharistiæ intelligit), fuse disputauerat ea non minus ad parvulos quam ad adultos pertinere. An quisquam etiam (inquit) hoc dicere audebit, quod ad parvulos hæc sententia non pertineat, possint, sine participatione corporis hujus & sanguinis in se habere vitam? Et sic constat ter octo aut decem aliis operum eius locis quos longum esset referre. Innocentius I. Papa æqualis ejus, in eadem fuit sententia. Nam Baptismum parvulis esse nenulla fit præ istis difficultas, Vbi iam hominem qui in opus adeo difficile adeòque intricatum incumbere velit inveniemus; Quis sibi successum non defuturum putet, ubi ejusmodi Concilium frustra fuit ? Vel ipsa rei tam arduæ spes non videtur arrogantia carere. Primò, quo gradu, siue necessitatis, siue probabilitatis suas sententias habeant perraro Patres docent, & si quando docent, ea est ipsorum (quod supra monuimus) phrasis atque oratio, ut nonnisi post accurratum examen de iis certi quippiam constituere liceat. De vltibus, quoties ea suadere volunt, tanquam de necessariisferè loquuntur. At ut fidem & studia nostra à rebus avocent, quas simpliciter falsas aut inutiles existimant, de iis sic loquuntur quasi planè horrendæ perniciosæque essent. Si quis (inquit Ignatius) Dominicam diem aut Sabbathum, uno excepto, (co scilicet quod Pascha antecedit) jejunarit, hic Christi interfectior est, Quis ad voces adeo tragicas non expauescat? Quis non totius religionis Christianæ summam agi putet? Atqui de ea tantum observatione agitur quæ & iuris positiui est, & in vna modò, vt plerique censent Ecclesiæ parte vigebat; quæ deniq; adeo non habebatur vsus necessarij, vt vix in primo probabilium gradu poneretur, nunc verò etiam prorsus in de suetudinem apud Latinos abierit. Hic mos apud Patres frequens est, maximè apud Tertullianum, Ambrosium & Hieronymum, qui cùm ingenio sint feruido ac concitatos quam in partem propendent eo tanto impetu feruntur, vt quos quidem laudant eos inter Angelos, quos verò vituperant, inter Diabolos collocare videantur: Ita quæ credenda putant, non aliter commendant, quàm si totidem essent Christianismi fundamenta, quæ rejiciunt acrefutant, non aliter explodunt quàm si merum atheismum spirarent. Hieronymus certè, ut Furiam, nobilem viduam Romanam à fecundis nuptiis auocet, non aliter agit quàm si eam à patricidio dehortaretur. Hic in memoriam redeant oportet obscuritatis Patrum causæ. (& in primis eorum Rhetorica)quæ hic supra omnia alia argumenta locum habent.
units.tr: P rr n.R j l. 4 in praefat p.7.s. Yet the greatest difficulty of the matter seems to lie here, indeed the most intractable of all the difficulties we have brought up in the earlier chapters. Nor do I need any other example to prove this than the very one of which I have just spoken. For the Fathers of Trent decree that the ancients admitted infants who lack the use of reason to communion of the Eucharist for a probable reason only, not from any necessity of salvation. Yet not only is there a great occasion for doubt on this matter; it also seems certain from the very monuments of the Fathers (with due respect to the Synod of Trent be it said) that they thought the communion of baptized infants wholly necessary, for they speak of it in this way. Augustine, the aforesaid author, after he had (as he himself thought) confirmed this from Scripture, adds: If, therefore, as so many and so great divine testimonies prove, neither salvation nor eternal life can be had without baptism and the body and blood of the Lord (for so he calls the Eucharist, after the solemn usage of that age) it is in vain promised to infants without these. And in three earlier chapters, when he treats of the words of the Lord in John, Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in you (which he understands, both in that place and elsewhere, of communion in the Eucharist), he had argued at length that these words pertain no less to infants than to adults. Will anyone dare to say (he asks) that this saying does not pertain to infants, that they can have life in themselves without participation in this body and blood? And so it is established in eight or ten other places of his works, which would be long to recount. Innocent I, the Pope who was his contemporary, was of the same opinion. For that baptism is necessary for infants there is no difficulty before these... Where now shall we find a man who would set himself to so difficult and so intricate a task? Who would think that success will not fail him, where such a council was in vain? Even the hope of so arduous an undertaking does not seem free of arrogance. First, the Fathers very rarely teach in what degree, whether of necessity or of probability, they hold their opinions; and when they do teach it, their manner of speech and phrasing is such (as we noted above) that nothing certain can be settled about them without a careful examination. When they wish to recommend such things, they speak of them almost as of necessary things. But in order to draw our faith and efforts away from things which they regard as simply false or useless, they speak of them as if they were utterly horrible and pernicious. If anyone (says Ignatius) fasts on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except the one only (namely the one that precedes Pascha), he is a murderer of Christ. Who does not tremble at words so tragic? Who does not think that the whole sum of the Christian religion is at stake? And yet the matter concerns only an observance which is of positive law, and which, as most think, prevailed in only one part of the Church; which, moreover, was not held to be of such necessary use that it was placed even in the first rank of probable things, and which now has entirely fallen into disuse among the Latins. This manner is frequent among the Fathers, especially among Tertullian, Ambrose and Jerome, who, being of fiery and excitable temperament, are carried with such great impetus to whichever side they incline, that those whom they praise seem to be placed among the Angels, and those whom they blame among the Devils. Thus they commend the things they believe to be credible no differently than if they were the foundations of Christianity, and they refute and explode the things they reject no differently than if they breathed pure atheism. Jerome, for example, in order to turn Furia, a noble Roman widow, away from a second marriage, acts no differently than if he were dissuading her from parricide. Here we must call to mind the obscurity of the Fathers' cause (and above all of their rhetoric), which here has a place above all other arguments.

units.la: Vnica restat via qua nobis constare possit quo loco ac numero singula doctrinæ Christianæ capita posuerint, Symbola nempe, & fidei expositiones siue totius Ecclesiæ, siue singulorum, & Conciliorum siue conuentuum Ecclesiasticorum. Probabile enim est eos pro necessariis habuisse ea capita quæ eiusmodi monumentis consignarunt, & quorum contraria anathemate inusserunt. Hac via constare nobis potest necessaria ab iis habita fuisse pleraque ea fidei capita de quibus hodie inter nos conuenit. Iam ab initio quædam exposuimus, nam pleraque in eorum symbolis habentur, & in eorum Conciliis decreta & quæ repugnant diserte damnata sunt. Quod vero ad ea capita pertinet quæ hodie controuersa sunt vix quicquam hac via promouebimus. Nullum enim eorum, vel in regula illa fidei quam tanti fecit Tertullianus, vel in Symbolo Nicæno, vel in Constantinopolitano, vel in Canonibus Ephesinis, vel in Chalcedonensibus comparet. Primum Concilium Ario, secundum Macedonio, tertium Nestorio, quartum Eutycheti anathema dixerunt. Dogmata sunt pleraque ab vtraq; partium recepta. Addequod nec in duobus quidem sequentibus Conciliis habentur controuersa hodie capita; Non in secundo Concilio Constantinopolitano, in quo damnata sunt Theodori, Theodoreti & Ibæ scripta quædam, vt à nobis supra dictum est. Non in Constantinopolitano III. a.d. 681. contra Monothelitas habito. Et tamen sex illa priora Concilia, si septimi patribus fides habeatur, confirmarunt & constituerunt quaecunque a principio temporum, siue scripto, siue traditione non scripta Ecclesiæ tradita sunt. Vnde sequeretur ea fidei capita, quæ in iis non habentur, neque scriptis, neque alia ratione à principio tradita fuisse. Othough demum seculo, eoque; admodum adulto, in apertum erumpit ex capitibus controuersis vnum, de imaginibus, scilicet quod
units.tr: The only way left by which we can determine at what place, and in what order, the early writers set down the individual articles of Christian doctrine is through the creeds and expositions of faith, whether of the whole Church or of individual writers, and through the decrees of councils or ecclesiastical assemblies. For it is probable that they regarded as necessary those articles which they committed to such records, and against whose contraries they pronounced anathema. By this method we can establish that most of those articles of faith on which we agree today were regarded as necessary by them. From the beginning we have set out some of these, for most of them are found in their creeds, and in their councils decrees were issued and what was contrary to them was expressly condemned. But as for those articles that are disputed today, we will make little progress by this route. For none of them appears in that rule of faith which Tertullian held in such high esteem, nor in the Nicene Creed, nor in the Constantinopolitan, nor in the canons of Ephesus or Chalcedon. The First Council pronounced anathema on Arius, the Second on Macedonius, the Third on Nestorius, the Fourth on Eutyches. Most of their dogmas were accepted by both parties. Moreover, not even in the two following councils are the articles disputed today found: not in the Second Council of Constantinople, in which certain writings of Theodore, Theodoret and Ibas were condemned, as we said above; nor in the Third Council of Constantinople, held in 681 against the Monothelites. And yet those first six councils, if credence is to be given to the fathers of the Seventh, confirmed and established whatever has been handed down to the Church from the beginning of time, whether in writing or by unwritten tradition. From this it would follow that those articles of faith which are not found in these councils were not handed down from the beginning, either in writing or in any other way. Only at last, in the eighth century, and that quite far advanced, did one of the disputed articles break out into the open, namely that concerning images, which was decided and determined in various and contradictory ways

units.la: Synod.7 Act. 6. Refut. Synod Iconocl. ( &c. ) general. 7 3. quod varie & contradictorie decisum & determinatum est in Synodis Constantinopolitana, Nicæna & Francofurtensi. Synodorum enim illarum secunda usum & cultum quem prima aboleuerat restituit, tertia verò ea in quibus utraque modum excesserat aliquomodo correxit. Imò in scriptis singulorum, quæ pleraque solent esse longè fusiora canonibus Synodorum, de capitibus illis alrum est silentium. Epiphanius opus suum aduersus hæreses duabus clausit dissertationibus. Altera mores & disciplinam Ecclesiæ temporis sui refert, in qua multa, ab institutis quæ hodie apud nostrum utrosque sunt in usu, discrepare ultro fateor. Altera fusa fidei Ecclesiæ expositio continetur, quam sanctus ille Antistes vocat veritatis firmamentum, immortalitatis spem & confirmationem. Et tamen ex omnibus capitibus quæ hodie sunt in controversia, nullum ibi animaduertere est, præter localem Christi ad inferos descensum, quod quàm parui sit momenti omnes norunt. In Actis VI. Synodi extat Sophronij Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani epistola Synodica, in qua, pro more, fusissimè & sigillatim fidem exponit, & tamen ne unum quidem capitum hodie controversorum ponit. Qui hæc attentius obseruabit & considerabit, ex eo silentio argumentabitur, capita ista in Ecclesiæ fide tum temporis nulla fuisse, neque ut videtur absque recta ratione. Mihi verò satis est superioribus concludere quod instituì, esse, si non omnino impossibile, saltem difficillimum, constituere quo gradu, siue necessitatis, siue probabilitatis Veteres Patres unum quodque caput eorum quæ hodie controvertuntur habuerint, quandoquidem ea neque in fidei suæ expositionibus, neque in Conciliorum suorum canonibus, qui sunt veluti catalogi eorum quæ necessaria censuerunt, unquam posuerunt.
units.tr: Synod. 7 Act. 6. Refut. Synod Iconocl. (&c.) general. 7 3. in the Councils of Constantinople, Nicaea and Frankfurt. For the second of those synods restored the use and worship of images which the first had abolished, and the third in some measure corrected those points where each had gone too far. Indeed, in the writings of individual authors, which are usually much more extensive than the canons of synods, there is silence about those articles. Epiphanius closed his work against the heresies with two treatises. The first recounts the morals and discipline of the Church of his own time, in which I freely admit there is much that differs from the institutions now in use among both our peoples. The second contains a full exposition of the faith of the Church, which that holy bishop calls the firmament of truth, the hope and confirmation of immortality. And yet, among all the articles that are today in controversy, there is none to be found there except the local descent of Christ into hell, and everyone knows how little importance that has. In the Acts of the Sixth Council there is extant the synodal letter of Sophronius, Patriarch of Constantinople, in which, as is customary, he sets out the faith very fully and point by point, and yet he does not set down even one of the articles controverted today. Whoever observes and considers these things more carefully will argue from that silence that these articles were not part of the Church's faith at that time, and not, as it seems, without good reason. For my part, it is enough for me to conclude from what has been said above what I set out to show: that it is, if not altogether impossible, at least most difficult, to determine to what degree, whether of necessity or of probability, the ancient Fathers held each of the articles now under dispute, since they never included them either in their expositions of faith or in the canons of their councils, which are, as it were, catalogues of what they judged necessary.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Ratio ix. Necessarium esse ut nobis constet ratio, non solum de unius aut plurium Patrum, sed etiam de totius veteris Ecclesiæ sententia, quod diffi- cillimum est, pernoscere.
units.tr: Reason 9. It is necessary that we should be sure of the reasoning not only about the opinion of one or several Fathers, but also about the opinion of the whole ancient Church, which is very hard to ascertain.

units.la: QVi SS. Patrum plurimi scripta faciunt, quique ea in controversiis sæpissimè adhibent monent sententiæ eorum pondus & pretium ex eo esse quod sint totidem publicæ & communis Ecclesiæ fidei testimonia, cui soli summam in judicando auctoritatem tribuunt. Singulos enim si seorsum consideres, quatenus unius sui ingenii viribus nitebantur, potuisse eos falli non negant. Inde autem sequitur, ut eorum sententiæ nobis usui esse possint, non satis esse ut nobis constet eorum revera esse, eumque esse sensum qui dicitur, sed opus esse etiam ut certò sciamus, num cum sui temporis Ecclesia senserint. Quemadmodum Senatoris unius sententia vim Senatusconsulti non habet, nisi eadem sit totius, vel certè maximæ partis Senatus, sententia. Atque hinc in novas difficultates relabimur. Unde enim & qua ratione nobis constabit Ecclesiam, quæ Iustini, Hieronymi, vel Augustini temporibus in terris militabat eadem in omnibus de religione sensisse cum unoquoque eorum? Non repugno quin ii magna charitate arserint, summoque studio corpus & fidem Ecclesiæ ubicunq; ea occurrebat amplexi sint. Sed in capitibus, de quibus quid suæ esset sententiæ nondum significaverat, non poterant illi, ut ut maximè vellent, ejus auctoritatem pro suæ sententiæ norma sequi. Cùm ergo agunt de rebus judicatis, & disertè & positivè ab Ecclesia Christiana siue sui seculi, siue superiorum receptis & creditis, vehementer probabile est eos cum illa sentire, adeo ut in ejusmodi capitibus eorum sententia pro fidei Ecclesiæ testimonio possit haberi. Eos enim documenta Ecclesiæ publica ignorasse, aut cognita secutos non fuisse, parum fit verisimile. Exempli gratia, cum Athanasius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus & alij de Filio Dei agunt, fidem sententiamque Ecclesiæ in his sequuntur, nam de hoc capite certa & indubitata erat Ecclesiæ sententia, adeo ut quicquid de eo dicunt pro fidei Ecclesiæ testimonio habendum sit. Eadem est ratio reliquorum omnium capitum, seu de iis constituissent Concilia universalia, seu in Symbolis haberentur, seu in quocunque alio publico fidei Ecclesiasticæ monumento extarent. Si intra hos limites se Patres continuissent, neque ad alia, de quibus non haberetur certum Ecclesiæ judicium, uuquam excurrissent, generalis esset hæc regula, statimque ac aliquid apud ipsos occurreret, pro totius ipsorum temporis Ecclefiæ sententia haberi posset. Verum ingenij humani curiositas, hæreseœn impudentia, & seu ipsorum, seu aliorum conscientiæ infirmitas, variæque aliæ causæ, partim volentes abripuerunt, partim vel invitos compulerunt ceegerúntque longiùs progredi, in rerum nondum universali & publico omnium Christianorum consensu constitutarum veritate inquirenda; qua quidem in investigatione necesse habuerunt ingenij sui luce uti, & in medium privatam suam sententiam afferre, quam quæ subsecuta est Ecclesia deinceps vel amplexata est vel repudiauit. Neque verò necesse est in hac observatione probanda immorari quæ apud utrosque in confesso est, & ex qua ipsi Ecclesiæ Romanæ doctores passim varios è Patribus objectos locos solvunt. Bellarminus in primis, qui Ioannem Papam xxii. hac ratione excusat: docuerat isanimas Deum non visuras, nisi post resurrectionem. Respondet id tum licuisse sine periculo hæreseœs, cùm nulla adhuc præcessisset Ecclesiæ definitio. Eandem medelam adhibet Nicolai I. sententiæ parum (ut vel ipse judicat) probabili, contendentis Baptifimum in nomine Iesu Christi, tacitis reliquis S. Trinitatis personis, collatum valere. Non invenitur (inquit Bellarminus) nlla certa definitio Ecclefix de hac re. Et quantumlibet periculosa & proxime ad hæresin accedens ei videatur eorum opinio, qui existimant Papam Romanum posse hæreticum fieri, Adriano tamen ut ita sentiat concedit, neque eum hoc nomine inter hæreticos censer,quod de eo capite nihil adhuc Ecclesia certi definivisset: Idem in alia magni momenti controversia, de libris Canonicis Veteris Testamenti,cùm urgeretur auctoritate Hieronymi, qui Tobiam,Sapientiam, Ecclesiasticum, & Maccabæos è canone rejicit adversum Ecclesiæ Romanæ sententiam, quæ eos pro canonicis haberi jubet, eadem ratione se expedit. Admitto igitur (inquit) Hieronymum in ea fuisse opinione,quia nondum generale Concilium de his libris aliquid statuerat. Cùm ergo liquidò constet, cùm ex consensu partium, tum ex rei ipsius consideratione. Patres priuatas suas opiniones plurimas in medium attulisse, quásque non aliunde quàm à seipsis habuerant, neque ex Ecclesiæ Schola hauserant, quis non videt, antequam eorum sententiis fidem habeamus, oportere ut nobis constet cujusnam indolis sint, an ex sua ipsorum privata, an verò ex recepta sui seculi sententia locuti sint, cùm nemo non agnoscat, quæ prioris sunt ordinis, necessariò à nobis fidem non exposcere, quod hujus generis pleraque possint, imo & nonnulla debeant, nulla religione repudiari? Hieronymum Sanctorum mortuorum reliquias religiosè venerantem Protestanti objicis. Quid scio (inquit ille) annon hæc privata Hieronymi sententia fuerit? Si Bellarminum hujus Patris auctoritas (quod nulla scilicet Ecclesiæ declaratione niteretur) non permovit,ut in ejus de Veteris Testamenti Canone sententiam concederet cur mihi hæc eiusdem sententia, nullo alio fundamento nixa, suadebit venerandas colendásque reliquias? Idem & quidem admodum probabiliter variis ex Patribus petitis testimoniis
units.tr: Many who write on the holy Fathers, and who very often use their writings in controversies, point out that the weight and value of their opinions lies in this: they are so many public testimonies of the common faith of the Church, to which alone they grant the highest authority in judging. For if you consider each of them separately, insofar as he relied on the strength of his own intellect alone, they do not deny that he could be mistaken. It follows that their opinions can be of use to us only if it is not enough for us to be sure that they really are theirs and that they have the meaning ascribed to them; we must also know for certain whether they held the view of the Church of their own time. Just as the opinion of one senator does not have the force of a decree of the Senate unless it is also the opinion of the whole Senate, or at least of its greatest part. And from here we fall back into new difficulties. For how and on what grounds shall we be sure that the Church, which militated on earth in the times of Justin, Jerome or Augustine, thought the same about religion in all matters as each of these men did? I do not deny that they burned with great love and, with the greatest zeal, embraced the body and faith of the Church wherever it was found. But on those heads on which the Church had not yet declared its opinion, they could not, however much they wished, follow its authority as the rule of their own opinion. Therefore, when they treat of matters judged by the Christian Church of their own age, or of earlier ages, and received and believed expressly and positively, it is highly probable that they agree with it, so that on such heads their opinion can be taken as a testimony of the Church's faith. For it is hardly likely that they were ignorant of the public documents of the Church, or that, knowing them, they did not follow them. For example, when Athanasius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine and others treat of the Son of God, they follow the faith and opinion of the Church, for on this head the opinion of the Church was certain and undoubted, so that whatever they say about it must be held as a testimony of the Church's faith. The same reasoning applies to all the other heads, whether universal Councils had settled them, or whether they were contained in the Creeds, or stood in any other public monument of ecclesiastical faith. If the Fathers had kept within these limits, and had never ventured into other matters on which no certain judgment of the Church existed, this would be a general rule, and as soon as something appeared in their writings it could be taken as the opinion of the whole Church of their time. But the curiosity of the human mind, the boldness of heretics, the weakness of the conscience of themselves or others, and various other causes, partly carried them away willingly and partly compelled them, even unwilling, to go further, in inquiring into truths not yet settled by the universal and public consensus of all Christians. In that inquiry they were necessarily obliged to use the light of their own intellect and to bring forward their private opinion, which the Church that followed either embraced or rejected. Nor is it necessary to linger over proving this observation, which is agreed on by both sides, and by which the very teachers of the Roman Church everywhere answer the various passages of the Fathers cited against them. Bellarmine above all, who excuses Pope John XXII in this way: he had taught that souls would not see God until after the resurrection. He replies that this was then permitted without danger of heresy, since no definition of the Church had yet preceded it. He applies the same remedy to the opinion of Nicholas I, which is hardly probable (as he himself judges), that baptism conferred in the name of Jesus Christ alone, the persons of the Holy Trinity being passed over in silence, is valid. "No certain definition of the Church is found" (says Bellarmine) "on this matter." And however dangerous and close to heresy the opinion of those seems to him who think the Roman Pope can become a heretic, he nevertheless concedes to Adrian that he may hold such a view, and does not count him among heretics on this account, because the Church had not yet defined anything certain on that head. Likewise in another controversy of great importance, concerning the canonical books of the Old Testament, when he was pressed with the authority of Jerome, who rejects Tobit, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus and the Maccabees from the canon, against the opinion of the Roman Church, which orders them to be held as canonical, he extricates himself by the same reasoning. "I grant therefore" (he says) "that Jerome was of that opinion, because a general Council had not yet decided anything about these books." Since therefore it is clear, both from the agreement of the parties and from the nature of the matter itself, that the Fathers brought forward very many of their private opinions, which they had not obtained from anywhere but themselves and had not drawn from the school of the Church, who does not see that before we give credit to their opinions it is necessary for us to be sure of what kind they are, whether they spoke from their own private view or from the accepted opinion of their age? For who does not recognise that those of the former sort cannot rightly demand our faith, since many of this kind can and indeed some must be rejected without any scruple? You object to the Protestant that Jerome reverently venerated the relics of the holy dead. "What do I know" (he says) "whether this was not Jerome's private opinion? If the authority of this Father did not move Bellarmine to agree with his opinion on the canon of the Old Testament (since it rested, of course, on no declaration of the Church), why should this same opinion, resting on no other foundation, persuade me to venerate and worship relics?" The same objection may quite probably be made, with testimonies drawn from various Fathers.

units.la: {a} Id. b. d. c. 11. §. Bellarminus, ibid. Konicem. {b} Ibid. 1. §. 4. exhi. {c} Bel. de Verbo Dei 1. 1. c. 10. §. ultimo. moniis obijcere licet. Itaque & ad confirmandum fidem tuam; & ad præcludendum adversatio hoc effugium docendum est in primis, quam profers Patris cujusvis sententiam, non eius priuatam, sed totius in qua floruit Ecclesiæ communem fuisse, quod meo iudicio maxima parte non minùs difficile est demonstrare, quàm quicquid eorum de quibus hactenus disseruimus. Media enim quibus facilè huiusmodi cognitionem consequamur desunt nobis, si qua verò superstunt, ea ut plurimum infirma sunt & parum valent. Si quid inter duo hæc sententiarum genera discriminis Patres statuissent, singulisque locis quid à se, quid ab Ecclesia haberent monuissent, vel saltem alterum tanquam dubium, alterum verò tanquam certum proposuissent (quod nonnunquam facit Origenes) graui nos difficultate liberassent tametsi nec sic quidem omni nos labore leuassent, quod ii, ut alibi docebimus, ea Ecclesiæ nonnunquam tribuant, à quibus illam alienam fuisse constat: Sed hanc illi distinctionem perraro adhibent & priuatas suas sententias eadem fiducia qua publicè receptas obtrudunt; Imò nonnunquam, quod omnibus rerum quarumlibet auctoribus à natura inditum est, vehementius quæ suo marte percepere, quàm ea quæ aliunde habent commendant. Sic pauca apud eorum unumquemque occurrunt quæ nobis in hoc argumento facem præferant. Superesset alia via ut scilicet quæ hinc inde docent ea cum sententiis publicæ in Ecclesia receptis conferremus, eàq; sanè & compendiosa & certa foret, si, præter ipsorum libros, extarent periculosa & indubirata monumenta eorum omnium quæ ad fidem pertinere singulis seculis credita sunt? Hæc verò si extarent ne necesse quidem esset in evolvendis Patrum scriptis tempus & operam ponere, quæ profectò non alio consilio versamus nisi ut inde discamus quid Veteres Christiani de omnibus iis religionis capitibus senserint quæ inter nos hodie controverruntur. Verùm nemo nescit hanc viam nobis obstructam esse. Nam si Symbola & Canones sex priorum Conciliorum vniversalium & quarumdam Synodorum provincialium exceperis, nulla hujusmodi nobis monumenta supersunt. At (vt superiori capite à nobis jam dictum est) neque in Symbolis, neque in Canonibus Consiliorum, quid suæ esset sententiæ, super capitibus hodie in religione controversis Ecclesiæ declarauit. Sequitur ergo hac via non posse nos scriptis Patrum privatas eorum sententias ab iis secernere quæ, vnà cum cæteris Christianis, communi ac publica fide crediderunt. Quod si nobis ex Scriptore aliquo fide digno constaret hæc ipsa, quæ hodie in quæstionem vocantur, olim á Vetere Ecclesia fuisse decisa in eius sententiam Patres concessisse admodum verisimile foret, sicque licet decreta ipsa non extarent, nihilominus Patres, quibus ea nota & credita fuissent, eorum sensum in scriptis suis nobis tradidisse exstimare aliquomodo teneremur, At nullos est Auctor apud quem simile quid occurrat; contra vero ipsa totius Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ series docet liquidò prioribus Christianismi seculis nihil huiusmodi agitatum fuisse, tantum abest ut aliquid super his controversiis vetus Ecclesia pronunciarit, unde apparet, si quæ apud Patres occurrunt, quæ ad eas pertinere videantur, ipsos, non ex Ecclesiæ documentis (quæ non dum quid super istis capitibus suæ esset fidei notum fecerat) sed ex proprio sensu, priuatâque sua ipsorum meditatione hausisse. Frustrà hic obiceris, licèt ex unius & alterius Patris testimonio constare non posse de sententia Ecclesiæ. attamen plurimos Patres ejusce rei idoneos esse testes, Primò enim Canus auctor est Latinos non multos, non plurimos, sed O M N E S Patres requirere; Tridentina (inquit) Synodus communem T A N T V M O M N I V M Patrum intelligentiam procerta veri norma habendam definivit. Si ita est nullum unquam hæc disquisitio exitum habitura est. Quis enim Patrum illa de re hodie controversa sensum O M N I V M explorare potest
units.tr: {a} Id. b. d. c. 11. §. Bellarminus, ibid. Konicem. {b} Ibid. 1. §. 4. exhi. {c} Bel. de Verbo Dei 1. 1. c. 10. §. ultimo. may be objected. Therefore, both to confirm your faith and to close off this evasion of the adversary, it must be taught above all that when you bring forward the opinion of any Father, it was not his private opinion but the common opinion of the whole Church in which he flourished. In my judgment this is no less difficult to demonstrate for most cases than any of those matters we have discussed so far. For the means by which we could easily attain such knowledge are lacking to us, and if any remain, they are for the most part weak and of little value. If the Fathers had made some distinction between these two kinds of opinion, and had noted in each place what they held from themselves and what from the Church, or at least had put forward the one as doubtful and the other as certain (as Origen sometimes does), they would have freed us from a heavy difficulty, although even so they would not have spared us all labour, because, as we shall teach elsewhere, they sometimes attribute to the Church things from which it is known that the Church was alien. But they very rarely use this distinction, and they press their private opinions with the same confidence with which they put forward what is publicly received. Indeed, as nature has implanted in all authors of whatever matters, they commend more vehemently what they have perceived by their own effort than what they have from elsewhere. So few passages occur in each of them which could carry a torch for us in this question. There would remain another way, namely that we compare what they teach here and there with the opinions received publicly in the Church; and this would certainly be both short and sure, if, besides their books, there existed reliable and undoubted records of all the things that were believed in each age to pertain to faith. If these records existed, there would be no need at all to spend time and labour in unrolling the writings of the Fathers, which we undertake for no other purpose than to learn from them what the ancient Christians thought about all those heads of religion which are disputed among us today. But no one is unaware that this way is blocked to us. For if you except the Creeds and the Canons of the six earlier universal Councils and of certain provincial Synods, no such monuments survive to us. But (as we have already said in the previous chapter) neither in the Creeds nor in the Canons of the Councils has the Church declared its opinion on the heads now disputed in religion. It follows, therefore, that by this way we cannot separate from the writings of the Fathers their private opinions from those which they believed, together with the other Christians, in common and public faith. But if it were established for us from some trustworthy writer that these very matters which are now called into question were decided long ago by the ancient Church, it would be quite probable that the Fathers agreed with its opinion; and so, even if the decrees themselves did not survive, we would nevertheless be obliged in some way to suppose that the Fathers, to whom they were known and believed, had handed down their sense to us in their writings. But there is no author in whom anything of this kind occurs. On the contrary, the whole sequence of ecclesiastical history clearly teaches that nothing of this kind was discussed in the earlier centuries of Christianity; so far is the ancient Church from having pronounced anything on these controversies. From which it appears that if any passages occur among the Fathers which seem to pertain to them, they drew them not from the documents of the Church (which had not yet made known what it held on these heads), but from their own sense and their own private meditation. It is vain for you to object here that, although the opinion of the Church cannot be established from the testimony of one or another Father, nevertheless very many Fathers are fit witnesses of this matter. For first, Canus is the authority that the Latins require not many, not most, but ALL the Fathers; "The Council of Trent" (he says) "defined that only the common understanding of ALL the Fathers is to be held as the certain rule of truth." If this is so, this inquiry will never come to an end. For who can explore the opinion of ALL the Fathers on that matter which is disputed today?

units.la: De loc. Theol. l. 7. c. 3. col. 5. test? cum eorum ne millesima quidem pars quicquam litteris mandaverit; qui vero scripserunt aliquid, ij vel interciderint, vel de paucis, certòrari de omnibus religionis capitibus scripserint; Sed etsi non omnium quidem (quod haberi non potest) sed plurium tamen testimonium teneamus, idcirco clara erit atque comperta Ecclesiæ veteris fides. Nam si uni & alteri accidere potuit, ut ad privatas aliquas opiniones delaberentur; profecto nihil vetat, quo minus alij, etiam fortasse multi, sese iis comites addiderint, & propria præeuntium placita sequuti fuerint. Huc accedit quod cum illius temporis Ecclesia quid suæ esset sententiæ super capitibus hodie controversis nondum aperuisset; profecto non plures magis, quàm pauci id eo tempore nobis exhibere potuerunt. Qui quod adhuc latebat vidissent; qui ex norma quæ nondum apparebat, de fide sua constituissent? Chiliastæ non unius aut alterius patris testimonia congerunt, sed frequentissimos eosque celeberrimos & antiquissimos auctores secum, ut infra videbimus, sententes adducunt. Respondent pleriq; cum tum temporis nihil dum super hoc capite Ecclesia statuisset, horum pronuntiata fidem non facere. Unde liquet nobis non magis ex magno quàm ex exiguo Patrum numero de fide Ecclesiæ constare, necessariùmque esse ut ea in Concilio universali, vel alia quapiam ratione suam de qualibet quæstione mentem ipsa significaverit priùs quam sciamus idem ne de ea senserint Patres, nec ne. Quæ cùm ita se habeant, nobis de suis tumulis suscitanda erit tota vetus Ecclesia, dèque singulis quæstionibus interrogandā, ad quas definiendas singulorum hodie Patrum testimonia afferuntur: Neque enim certò aliter statuere licebit, an quæ de illis apud eos occurrunt privatorum an totius Ecclesiæ sint sententiæ, id est, idoneæque sint quæ fidem faciant an secus. Unde quivis, vel mediocri judicio præditus, nullo negotio intelligere potest, non tantùm difficile esse, sed planè impossibile eam ex scriptis Patrum elucidationem haurire quæ ad omnes in tanti momenti rebus scrupulos ex animis nostris evellendos idonea sit.
units.tr: ...for scarcely the thousandth part of them committed anything to writing; and those who did write something either perished, or wrote about a few matters only rather than about all the heads of religion. But even if we hold the testimony not of all (which cannot be had) but of many, the faith of the ancient Church will nevertheless be clear and established. For if it could happen to one or two to fall into some private opinions, there is certainly nothing to prevent others, perhaps even many, from attaching themselves to them as companions and following the private opinions of those who went before. Add to this that, since the Church of that time had not yet declared its judgment on the heads controverted today, the Fathers could present to us no more, indeed scarcely more than a few, of such opinions. For how could they have seen what was still hidden, or settled their faith by a rule that did not yet appear? The Chiliasts do not heap up the testimonies of one or two Fathers, but, as we shall see below, bring forward as their supporters very many, and very famous and most ancient authors. Most of them reply that, since at that time the Church had not yet decided anything on this head, the pronouncements of these men do not establish faith. Whence it is plain to us that the faith of the Church is established no more by a great number of Fathers than by a small number; and that it is necessary that the Church herself should make known her mind on any question, in a universal council or by some other means, before we can know whether the Fathers too thought the same about it or not. Since these things stand so, the whole ancient Church would have to be raised from its tombs for us, and questioned about each single question for which the testimonies of individual Fathers are today brought forward to settle it. For otherwise we cannot be certain whether what occurs in them on those matters are the opinions of private persons or of the whole Church, that is, whether they are suitable to establish faith or not. Hence anyone endowed with even moderate judgment can understand without any difficulty that it is not only hard but plainly impossible to draw from the writings of the Fathers an elucidation suitable for tearing from our minds every doubt on matters of such great importance.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Ratio x. Acgerrimè sciri posse num Patrum de hujus seculi controversiis sententiæ ab Ecclesia vniuersali, an ab eius parte tantùm receptæ fuerint. Id ipsum tamen scitu pernecessarium esse, vt locorum qui ex iis proferuntur vsus aliquis apud nos esse possit.
units.tr: Argument 10. It can be known with the greatest difficulty whether the opinions of the Fathers on the controversies of this age were received by the universal Church or only by a part of it. Yet this is most necessary to know, if the passages cited from them are to have any use among us.

units.la: AT si ex difficultatibus istis præter spem omnem Patris alicujus beneficio emergere concederetur, ex eoque statuere possemus, non modo quid ipse, sed quid ejus temporis Ecclesia de fide sensisset, nondum tamen omnibus ambagibus, incommodisque defuncti essemus. Nam præter quàm quòd Patrum in his assertionibus fides non raro titubat; si vel hujus qui de communi Ecclesiæ sententia testabitur, certa & indubitabilis auctoritas fuerit, illud tamen insuper inquirendum superesset, quænam fuerit ea Ecclesia quam dicit, num vniuersalis, an particularis tantùm, num totius orbis, an urbis vnius, provinciæ, regionisve. Id levis non esse momenti vel ex eo apparet, quod Ecclesiæ vniversalis, de fide opiniones infallibiles & necessariò veræ habentur, cùm de Ecclesiis particularibus idem non sit judicium, obnoxiæ enim errori censentur. Cùm ergo hic de fide agatur, eámque fundamento inconcussò niti oporteat, nobis in primis necesse est de vniuersalis Ecclesiæ sententia constare, quod in hoc argumento parum valeat singularum seorsum Ecclesiarum sententia. Hanc autem Ecclesiæ vniuersalis à particulari distinctionem necessariam esse exeo manifestum est, quòd cùm opiniones, tum mores & instituta passim & apud plerosque Christianos recepta, non semper tamen in quibuslibet particularibus Ecclesiis locum habuerint, ut nec, quæ in particularibus quibusdam Ecclesiis in usu fuerunt, eundem apud reliquas omnes obtinuerint. Sic ex historia constat Ecclesias minoris Asiæ alio quàm cæteros Christianos die Pascha celebrasse; idque licèt parvi, ut videtur, momenti non minimas tamen turbas dedit. Victor enim P. R. tantilli discriminis causa Asiam excommunicauit. Fartium singulæ suas rationes afferebant, traditionémque Apostolicam, tantáque animorum contentione sententiam suam utrăque confirmabant, ut cum universali Ecclesia singulæ sentire exîstimari potuerint; Cùm tamen unius tantùm partis ea esset sententia. Maxima Christianorum pars hæreticorum Baptismum valere exîstimabat, neque eos qui abdicata hæresi in communionem suam concedebant rebaptizabat, ut ex eo patet quod Cyprianus agnoscit in ipsis Africæ Ecclesiis eum morem alias obtinuisse. Et tamen ex omni ætatum memoria in contraria fuisse cùm sententia, tum praxi Cappadociæ Ecclesias testatur Firmilianus, ipse Cappadocum Cæsareæ Archiepiscopus; imò idipsum cum Galatiæ & Ciliciæ Ecclesiis in media Synodo Iconij habita definiuisse; eodémque fere tempore Cyprianus cum Africæ Episcopis eam sententiam palam professus est. Extant etiam num Acta Synodi Carthaginensis in qua 87. Episcopi, unanimi suffragio, id ipsum constituerunt. Tertulliano superstite Romæ scortatores & adulteri, pœnitentia quadam, quæ ipsis imponebatur, defuncti, ad Ecclesiæ communionem admittebantur, Tertullianus, Montanista factus, reclamat vehementissimè, librúmque, qui etiam num extat, pro contraria sententia edidit. Quis cum legens non exîstimet apud omnes tum Catholicos usu receptum fuisse huiusmodi peccatores ad pœnitentiam & pacem Ecclesiæ admittere? Et tamen ex qua-
units.tr: BUT if, beyond all hope, some Father were granted to us by whose help we could emerge from these difficulties, and we could from him establish not only what he himself but what the Church of his time thought about the faith, we would still not be free of all ambiguities and inconveniences. For apart from the fact that the faith of the Fathers in these assertions often wavers, even if the testimony of one who bears witness to the common opinion of the Church were of certain and indubitable authority, there would still remain the further question of which Church he means: whether it is the universal Church or only a particular one, the whole world or a single city, province or region. That this is no matter of slight importance appears even from this, that the opinions of the universal Church on faith are held to be infallible and necessarily true, whereas the judgment is not the same for particular Churches, which are thought liable to error. Since therefore here the question concerns faith, and that ought to rest on an unshaken foundation, we must above all be assured of the opinion of the universal Church, and in this argument the opinion of individual Churches taken separately is of little weight. That this distinction between the universal and the particular Church is necessary is clear from the fact that opinions, customs and institutions widely received among most Christians have not always held place in every particular Church, just as what was in use in certain particular Churches has not prevailed among all the rest. Thus history shows that the Churches of Asia Minor kept Easter on a different day from other Christians; and although this seems a matter of small importance, it nonetheless caused no small disturbance. For Victor, bishop of Rome, excommunicated Asia over so slight a difference. The parties each gave their own reasons, and each confirmed its view by Apostolic tradition, with such heat of spirit that each could be thought to agree with the universal Church, though that opinion belonged to only one part. The greatest part of Christians held that baptism by heretics was valid, and did not rebaptize those who, having renounced heresy, were admitted to their communion; as Cyprian acknowledges, this custom prevailed in the very Churches of Africa. Yet Firmilian, himself archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, testifies that from all the memory of ages the Churches of Cappadocia held the contrary both in opinion and in practice; indeed, in a full synod held at Iconium they defined the same thing together with the Churches of Galatia and Cilicia. At about the same time Cyprian, with the bishops of Africa, openly professed that opinion. The acts of the Synod of Carthage, in which 87 bishops with one voice decided the same thing, are still extant. While Tertullian was still alive at Rome, fornicators and adulterers who had died were admitted to the communion of the Church after some penance was imposed on them; Tertullian, having become a Montanist, protested most vehemently and published a book, which still survives, in favour of the contrary view. Who, reading this, would not think that among all Catholics it was the accepted practice to admit such sinners to penance and to the peace of the Church? And yet from a certain letter of Cyprian it is clear that some Catholic bishops of Africa held the contrary view.

units.la: dam Cypriani epistola constat nonnullos Catholicos Africæ Episcopos in contraria sententia fuisse. Imò lesuita Petavius existimat ad lenitatem illam nonnihil tardius & longo post tempore Hispaniensis Ecclesiæ Antistites infractos fuisse, & pristinam reveritatem, quæ ejusmodi peccatores ex Ecclesiæ communione in perpetuum rejiciebat, ad Paciani Barcinonensis Episcopi usque tempora inter eos viguisse, qui veniæ & absolutionis Ecclesiasticæ spem omnem præcidit idololatris, homicidis & adulteris, ut cuilibet ex eius ad pœnitentiam Paraenesi constare potest. Anno Domini 364. Synodus Laodicena decernit ut Ecclesiis libri qui sunt extra canonem non legantur, solos canonicos Veteris & Noui Testamenti legendos definiens, quos deinde recenset, Veteri Testamento nonnisi viginti duos adscribens, suppressis iis, quos Cardinalis Perronius posthumos vocat, Ecclesiastico, Sapientia, Macchabæis, Iudith, & Tobia. Et hic quidem Canon cum reliquis ejusdem Concilij Canonibus insertus fuit in Codice Ecclesiæ universalis, in quo hic habetur num. 163. adeo ut non minus quàm cæteri pro ecclesiæ catholicæ norma habitus sit. Quis ergo hanc Canonis Scripturarum declarationem tum temporis ab omnibus Christianis Ecclesiis receptam certò non patet? Non sic tamen visum est Patribus Africanis, Carthagine in Synodo congregatis, Anno Domini 397. Nam inter libros quos in Ecclesiis legi concedunt Macchabæos, Iudith, Tobiam, Ecclesiasticum & Sapientiam recensent, hòsque duos posteriores Salomoni adscribunt. Quis nescit, controversiam quæ prioribus seculis fuit inter Occidentis & Orientis Ecclesias, de ieiunio Sabbathi, illisfas esse, his verò ncfas esse sabbatho ieiunare contendentibus? Unde præsfractus ille Synodi Constantinopolitanæ In Trullo canon 55. Quoniam intelleximus in Romanorum civitate, in sanctâ Quadragesima diebus, præter Ecclesiasticam nobis traditam conveniētiam, Sabbath bis ieiunari, visum est sanctâ Synodo ut in Romana EccleEcclesia inconcusse observetur Canon qui dicit· Si quis clericus,inveniatur in Sancta Dominica die ieiunans, vel in sabbatho praeter unum & solum deponatur. Si vero est deplebe, communione moveatur. Nemini ignotum est quàm variafuerit apud diversas olim Ecclesias jejunij ante paschalisratio; quod vel ex sanctissima illa Irenæi ad VictoremP.R.epistola intelligitur,cujus partem Eusebius historiæsuæ inseruit. Quis nescit Græcæ Ecclesiæ de libero arbitrio & prædestinatione sententias & voces plurimumab iis differre quæ universa ecclesia de his capitibus, cùm viventes,tum etiam mortuo Augustino credidit &docuit ; Iam quod pertinet ad Disciplinam Ecclesiasticam hæc habet Anastasius ad Canonem vi. Concilijvii generalis, quo præcipitur Metropolitanis, ut singulis annis prouinciarum Synodos convocent. Non te moveat, inquit,si hanc definitionem minimè nos habeamus,cùminter earum nonnullas quas inter canones habemus in auctoritatem non recipiamus sicut quasdâ ex Conciliis. Alia namque apud Græcos tantùm:alia verò apud certas tantùm provincias in abservantiam Ecclesiarum assumuntur. Sicut Laodicensis Concilij 16.&17. Regula,quae apud Græcos tantum servantur, ut ea quae& Africani Concilij 6. & 8 Capitula quae nulla provincia servare nisi Africana dignoscitur. Possem huc multa alia exempla congerere, sed haec sufficiunt, ut doceamus sententias & consuetudines,à quibusdam ecclesiis recebpras, non statim omnium fuisse. Unde sequitur non quaecunque constat de sententia aut disciplina Veteris Ecclesiae fuisse, ea statim pro lege universali habenda. Probaturi Protestantes sententiam suam de Canone Scripturarum, Synodum Laodicenam, de qua supra, in medium afferunt, Tu respondes eam fuisse ecclesiarum sententiam revera, sed quarundam tantum & particularium. Nunc non quæro, vera nec ac firma sit tua hæc responsio,nec-ne. Satis est quod ex ea evidenter sequitur tibi, priusquam Patris cujuspiam sententia in rem tuam uti possis, ante omnia probandum esse, non solùm
units.tr: Indeed the Jesuit Petavius thinks that the Bishops of the Spanish Church were somewhat slower to adopt that leniency and, long afterwards, the former strictness, which cut such sinners off from the communion of the Church for ever, prevailed among them until the time of Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, who cut off every hope of pardon and ecclesiastical absolution from idolaters, murderers and adulterers, as anyone can see from his exhortation to repentance. In the year of the Lord 364 the Synod of Laodicea decreed that books not in the canon should not be read in the Churches, defining that only the canonical books of the Old and New Testament should be read. It then lists them, assigning only twenty-two books to the Old Testament, and suppressing those which Cardinal Perron calls apocryphal: Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, the Maccabees, Judith and Tobit. This canon was inserted, together with the other canons of the same council, into the Code of the universal Church, where it stands at no. 163, so that it has been held as a rule of the Catholic Church no less than the others. Who then does not plainly see that this declaration of the canon of Scripture was received at that time by all Christian Churches? Yet the African Fathers, gathered in synod at Carthage in the year of the Lord 397, did not think so. For among the books which they allow to be read in the Churches they list the Maccabees, Judith, Tobit, Ecclesiasticus and Wisdom, and they ascribe the last two to Solomon. Who does not know that the controversy in earlier centuries between the Churches of the West and the East was whether fasting on the Sabbath was lawful, the one side contending that it was lawful and the other that it was unlawful? Hence the famous 55th canon of the Constantinopolitan Synod In Trullo: "Since we have learned that in the city of Rome, in holy Lent, the Sabbath is fasted twice, contrary to the ecclesiastical custom handed down to us, it has seemed good to the holy Synod that in the Roman Church the canon be inviolably observed which says: If any clergyman is found fasting on the holy Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except one only, let him be deposed; if he is a layman, let him be cut off from communion." No one is unaware how varied the custom of fasting before Easter was among various Churches in former times; this is clear even from that most holy letter of Irenaeus to Victor, bishop of Rome, a part of which Eusebius inserted in his history. Who does not know that the opinions and the terms of the Greek Church on free will and predestination differ very much from those which the universal Church believed and taught on these heads, both while Augustine lived and after his death? As for ecclesiastical discipline, Anastasius on the sixth canon of the seventh general council, which orders the metropolitans to convene provincial synods every year, says this: "Do not be disturbed, he says, if we do not hold this definition, since among those canons we have we do not receive as authoritative some of the canons of councils. For some are used only among the Greeks, and others are adopted for observance only in certain provinces, by the Churches. Thus the sixteenth and seventeenth rules of the Council of Laodicea are kept only among the Greeks, and the sixth and eighth chapters of the African council are known to be observed by no province except the African." I could heap up many other examples, but these suffice to show that opinions and customs received by certain Churches were not at once those of all. It follows that whatever is known to have been the opinion or discipline of the ancient Church is not at once to be held as a universal law. When the Protestants wish to prove their view of the canon of Scripture, they bring forward the Synod of Laodicea mentioned above; you reply that this was indeed the opinion of the Churches, but only of some and of particular ones. Now I do not ask whether this reply of yours is true and firm or not. It is enough that from it there clearly follows, for you, that before you can use the opinion of any Father in your cause, you must first prove above all not only

units.la: Aa 3, quod is cum fui temporis Ecclesia senserit, sed eam, cum qua sentit, Ecclesiam universalem fuisse, non particularem tantum. Protestantibus objicis Epiphanium testari Ecclesiam ad summos Presbyterij, Episcopatus, &c. ordines non nisi cœlibes, aut qui ab uxoribus abstinerent, admisisse. Vt valeat hoc eius testimonium in primis docendum est Ecclesiam esse universalem de qua istic Epiphanius verba facit. Nam (inquiunt Protestantes) ut su apud Laodicenos singularem fuisse contendis de Scripturarum Canone opinionem; quidni fieri potuit ut Cyprus suas quoque habuerit proprias ac peculiares de Clericorum ordinatione constitutiones? Eadem est cum rituum & observationum tum sententiarum Veteris Ecclesiæ ratio. Quàm autem difficile sit res adeo confusas explicare, publicum a privato, provinciale a nationali, nationale ab universali secernere, quilibet poterit secum reputare, nemo tamen nisi expertus intelligere. Fac animo obversetur civitas a mille annis solo æquata, cujus nihil præter rudera huc illuc dispersa ac dissipata superfit, cætera dumis, vepribus & spinis obsidentibus. Tum finge hominem qui ubi publicæ, ubi privatæ ædes, qui illarum, qui harum lapides fuerint, distinctè tibi ostendere tibi aggrediatur, ac in confusis indigestisque istis acervis, in quibus omnia simul permixta jacent, alia ab aliis secernere, & ordine cuncta suo collocare moliatur. Non absimile mihi videtur ejus consilium qui velit certò inter Veteris Ecclesiæ sententias distinguere. Antiquitas illa jam vndecim aut duodecim seculis effluxit, ex ea nihil præter parietinas & rudera in Scriptoribus illius ævi nobis superest: quæ vero restant iniquissimè a tempore accepta sunt, ut supra ostendimus. Qui audemus in tam incondita rerum farragine spetare, ut ea quæ publicis templis ornamento fuere, ab iis ex quibus privata sacella constructa fuere internoscantur? Maximè cum privati quique ambitiosè studuerint quæ sua erant pro publicis venditare. Quæ enim Provincia, quæ Ciuitas, quis Doctor non sua pro Apostolicis, priuata pro publicis, propria pro communibus venditauit? Quis non laborauit, ut sui suorumque vel sensus vel ritus pro universalibus haberentur? Hieronymus quidem id studium velut pium omnibus permittit. Vnaquaque provincia (inquit) abundet in sensu suo, & praecepta Majorum leges Apostolicas arbitretur. Agere ipsum de quibusdam rerum per se adiaphorarum observationibus non nego, sed quod in rebus eiusmodi largitur, in omnibus usurpatum est. Nolo hic alias rationes persequi sigillatim, quae hanc investigationem difficilem efficiunt; magna enim eorum pars quae hactenus deferui huc referenda essent. Nam si, ut docuimus, quis Veterum sensus sit Scriptorum liquidò pernoscere difficile sit; longè difficilius erit certò constituere, an opiniones eorum Ecclesiis in quibus vixerunt propriae & peculiares fuerint, an verò universales eo quo floruerunt seculo. Quae enim in illo tenebras offundunt, possunt & in hoc locum, eúmque majorem obtinere. Si animus sit liquidò peruidere quàm laboriosum sit hoc opus, pellege, sodes virorum utriusque religionis doctorum super huiusmodi argumentis dissertationes; Tanta occurret dubitationum, opinionum ac contradictionum varietas, ut statim sis intellecturus inter difficultates quae Antiquitatem evolventibus negotium facessunt hanc inter principes connumerandam.
units.tr: Aa 3, that he thought so with the Church of his own time, but that the Church with which he agrees was universal and not merely particular. You object to the Protestants that Epiphanius testifies that the Church admitted to the highest orders of presbyter, bishop, etc. only men who were unmarried or who abstained from their wives. For this testimony to have weight, it must first be shown that the Church of which Epiphanius speaks there is the universal Church. For (the Protestants will say) just as you contend that the opinion on the canon of Scripture was peculiar to the Laodiceans, why could it not be that Cyprus too had its own particular regulations on the ordination of clergy? The reasoning is the same for the rites and observances, and for the opinions, of the ancient Church. How difficult it is to explain matters so confused, to separate the public from the private, the provincial from the national, and the national from the universal, anyone may reflect for himself, though no one understands it unless he has experienced it. Imagine before your mind a city levelled to the ground a thousand years ago, of which nothing remains except ruins scattered here and there and dissipated, the rest beset by brambles, thickets and thorns. Then imagine a man who sets out to show you clearly where the public buildings were and where the private houses, and which stones belonged to which, and who tries to separate one from another in those confused and disordered heaps, in which everything lies mixed together, and to set all things in their proper order. His undertaking seems not unlike that of one who would determine with certainty what belongs to the opinions of the ancient Church. That antiquity has now passed away for eleven or twelve centuries; of it nothing remains to us except the crumbling walls and ruins in the writers of that age; and what does remain has been handed down to us in a most unfair way, as we have shown above. How dare we hope, in such a disordered heap of things, to distinguish those things which were an ornament to the public temples from those with which private chapels were built? Especially since private individuals have eagerly striven to pass off what was their own as public. For what province, what city, what teacher has not passed off his own as Apostolic, his private things as public, his proper things as common? Who has not laboured that his own opinions or rites, or those of his people, should be held as universal? Jerome indeed allows this zeal to all, as if it were a pious thing: "Let each province, he says, abound in its own sense, and regard the precepts of its elders as Apostolic laws." I do not deny that he is speaking of certain observances that are in themselves indifferent, but what he grants in matters of that kind has been claimed in all matters. I do not wish here to pursue in detail the other reasons which make this investigation difficult, for the greater part of those I have so far passed over would have to be referred here. For if, as we have taught, it is difficult to know clearly what the sense of the ancient writers is, it will be far more difficult to determine with certainty whether their opinions were peculiar and particular to the Churches in which they lived, or universal in the age in which they flourished. For the things which cast darkness on the one question can also, and to a greater degree, occupy the other. If you wish to see clearly how laborious this work is, read, I beg you, the dissertations of learned men of both religions on such arguments. So great a variety of doubts, opinions and contradictions will meet you that you will at once understand that this difficulty, which troubles those who unroll antiquity, must be counted among the foremost.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Ratio xI. Fieri non posse ut super vno eorum capitum quæ sunt hodie in controversia clarè liquidóque per- noscamus quæ totius Veteris Ecclesiæ, sive vniuersalis, sive particularis sen- tentia fuerit.
units.tr: Argument XI. It cannot be that we know clearly and plainly, about any one of those articles which are today in controversy, what the opinion of the whole Ancient Church was, whether universal or particular.

units.la: ANtequam ad alteram partem nos conferamus non videtur à propósito nostro alienum ut hoc postremò moneamus; si vel cæteræ hactenus commemoratæ difficultates, quæ & multæ & arduæ sunt, nullæ essent, haudquaquam tamen ex Patrum libris certò ac liquidò intelligi posse,quæ veteris olim Ecclesiæ, siue Vniversalis, siue etiam alicuius particulatis, fuerit de hodiernis controversiis sententia. Cuius propositionis ut veritas pateat termini quibus constat explicandi sunt. Qui Ecclesiam dicunt, (maximè in hisce controversiis) ij vel omnes eos intelligunt qui se in Ecclesiæ communione viuere profitentur, cuiuscunque sortis & dignitatis sint, vel certè, sensu minùs lato, eos omnes qui Ecclesiæ præsunt, eamque repræsentant, id est, Clerum. Siue de Ecclesia universali sermo sit, seu de aliqua particulari, ut exempli gratia de Gallicana, aut Carthaginensi, ex vocibus utroque hoc sensu accipi possunt. Nam per ecclesiam universalem intelliguntur, vel in genere omnes qui ecclesiæ Christianæ communionem amplectuntur, sive clerici sint, siue laici, siue clerici soli, siue ecclesiastici, ut hodie quidem eos dici mos obtinuit. Nam prioribus Christianissimi seculis Ecclesiastici vocabantur omnes Christiani qui in Catholicorum communione vitam instituebant. Ita quoque Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis nomine significantur, vel in genere omnes fideles in peculiari Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis communione viventes, vel, sensu angustiori, Episcopus Carthaginensi cum toto suo clero. Iam si priori sensu Ecclesiæ nomen sumatur, vix quemquam fore puto qui contendat nobis ex testimoniis certò constare posse quæ singulis seculis Ecclesiæ fuerit de omnibus Christianæ religionis capitibus sententia. Possumus quidem, quæ verorum Ecclesiæ membrorum fides fuerit, rationando colligere. Cùm enim capita quædam sint ad constituendum ejusmodi hominem necessaria requisita, omnino necesse est hæc ipsa veram Ecclesiam, sive universalem, sive particularem credidisse. Enim verò id in primis non ad omnia religionis capita refertur, sed ad ea tantum quæ sunt necessaria, præter quæ multa sunt alia de quibus differentire licet, salva, non solùm Ecclesiæ communione, sed & hæreditatis æternæ spe. Deinde ejusmodi ratiocinatio non valet nisi eorum ratione qui sunt genuina Ecclesiæ membra. Qui verò Christiani, non revera, sed sola tantùm professione sunt, eos profecto neque servari, neque ea fide quæ ad salutem requiritur præditos esse, necesse est. Possunt sub ejusmodi larva omnis generis opiniones, etiam maximè impiæ, latere. Denique quod maximè ad rem nostram facit, hæc cognitio ratiocinatione paratur, cùm de ea nunc agamus quæ ex citatis & interrogatis testibus habetur, qui de ea re, quam scire auemus, certiores nos facere possunt. Cùm Patres eo consilio scripserint ut nos docerent, non tam quæ sui seculi esset, quam quæ omnium esse debeat fides, pro certo tenendum est, non esse ab iis prodita quæcunque de sui temporis scitis ac placitis cognita habebant, huc accedit quòd vel ex charitate, vel ex prudentia sua dissimulasse eos verisimile est quæcunque aliorum sive doctorum, sive etiam coætuum dogmata ipsi velut falsa respuebant, fecisseque eos in dogmatis, quod à se in ritibus factum testatur Augustinus. Quod (inquit) instituitur præter consuetudinem, ut quasi observatio sacramenti sit, approbare non possum, etiam si multa huiusmodi propter nonnullarũ, vel sanctarum, vel turbulentarum personarũ scandala, liberius improbare non audeo. Atque huc pertinet illud Hieronymi de quorumdam magni nominis Patrum placitis, quae licet (inquit) non sequamur, tamen damnare non possumus. Sed fac eos nulla hujus generis ratione deterritos bona fide in id incubuisse, ut suae Ecclesiae sententiam simpliciter traderent; equidem non video qui hoc accurate praestare potuerint. Quaeso enim, cum Ecclesia ex tam multis hominibus, tam inter se & ingenio, & natura, & consilio, & intelligentia discrepantibus constet, qua ratione potuerunt Patres certo cognoscere quae singulorum esset de religione sententia? Verbi gratia, an tu Cyprianum existimas omnium suae Dioecesis hominum, quas nobis referret, sententias ad unguem tenuisse? Quis in ista quae in ejus communione agebat populi turba neminem fuisse docebit, qui ab ipso ulla in re dissentiret? Hodie quidem, ut vetera mittamus, perspicuum est nullam, quantum vis exiguam, esse parœciam in qua singulis de omnibus omnino religionis capitibus cum pastore conveniat. Sed si Dioecesin totam excutias, atque praetermissis iis quos vel tenerior aetas, vel mentis stupor, vel profligata nequitia de religione securos faciunt, ceteros pro ratione diversarum circa sacra sententiarum in suas quasdam classes distribuas, non dubito quin onnium minima futura sit; quae de omnibus ac singulis religionis capitibus plane penitusque cum Episcopo consentiet. Quicquid ille de religione secutus fuerit, vix dimidiae dioecesios sententiam repraesentabit. Non aliter olim quam hodie res humanae comparatae erant: imo de religione longe olim liberatione quam nunc sententiae fuere, quod Ecclesia Romana nondum eam inter Christianos auctoritatem exerceret, quanta multis postea artibus sensim comparatam, nunc usurpat. Non ea tum sive a Pastoribus, sive a Principibus in coercenda opinionum diversitate adhibebatur quae nunc passim obtinet suppliciorum asperitas: unde colligendum restat longè majorem olim fuisse apud unius Ecclesiæ homines sententiarum diversitatem, quàm nunc est, adeóque longè difficilius fuisse Pastoribus omnes singulorum opiniones vel investigare, vel literis mandare. Sed in re obvia diutiùs immorari supervacaneum est. Expendamus potius quod hic multos obiecturos non dubito, nimirum nihil necesse esse ut singulorum sententias varietate penè infinitas, incertas, plerasque, & nullo fundamento nixas, in numerato habeamus, satis esse ut nobis constet quæ populi Christiani Pastorum & Præsulum, id est Ecclesiæ secundo sensu acceptæ, sententia fuerit. Ego verò dubito num id satis sit. Si enim Ecclesiæ est fidem nostram fulcire & regere (quod volunt hujus responsionis auctores) etiam plebis suæ erunt aliquæ in hoc negotio partes. Fateor equidem privatorum opiniones varias esse, & quorundam ex ipsis intelligentiam admodum mediocrem; imò aliquando penè nullam. Sed verendum est ne hæc quoque ratio Clerī ipsius partem auctoritate, quam sibi in his rebus arrogat, exuat, cùm negari non posset, quin sæpissimè apud illum eadem quæ apud plebem ipsam insciitia & nequitia sit. Quis non videt, si captum spectes, privatos interdum in Ecclesia reperiri qui Pastores ipsos doctrina & pietate antecellant? Patrum istorum de quibus agimus nonnemo docuit nos, Plerumque Clerum errauisse: Sacerdotis nutauisse sententiam; divites cum seculi istius terreno regno sensisse, populum fidem propriam reservauisse. Cum aliquando contingere posset, cùm sæpe contigerit, ut Clerus prava senserit, dum plebs in vera fide perstitit, patet, ut mihi quidem videtur, non omnino negligendam populi de rebus Divinis sententiam. Cyprianus quidem docet Ecclesiam sui temporis magnam variis in locis ejus rationem habuisse, adeo ut nihil quod esset alicujus momenti absque fidelium sententia gereretur, ut in ejus epistolis videre est. Certè quæstio de Baptismo hæreticorum, de qua supra nonnihil iam diximus, in Synodo, Carthagine, præsente etiam plebis maxima parte agitata fuit. Sed hoc sanè, quia controversum est, nunc mittamus. Concedamus quod isti volunt, satis esse si nobis constet de Ecclesiæ secundo sensu acceptæ, id est, Cleri sententia. Atqui & Cleri ipsius quæ fuerit singulis seculis de regiligione sententia intelligere ac certò per-. noscere si non est ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων, difficillimum certè esse patet. Non enim in Clero quàm in populo minor sententiarum discrepantia atque varietas, quin & sæpe, major est. Ingenia enim studiis exculta subtilitate delectantur, ex qua plerumque existit opinionum diversitas. Quis hodie, non dicam unius regni, multò minùs totius Christianisimi, sed unius tantum urbis Clericorum de omnibus religionis capitibus sententias recensere queat? Nunquam sententiarum in religionis negotio uniformitas apud Christianos acriori studio conservata retentáque est quàm nostro seculo, quo ad eam rem non censuras &c. anathemata duntaxat, sed etiam ferrum & ignes adhiberi videmus. Quàm multi tamen iis ipsis locis ubi maxime sæuitur, etiam Romæ, penè in ipsius Papæ, ut sic dicam, sinu reperiuntur qui longè in alia quàm, vel collegæ, vel præpositi sui sunt de religione sententia. In Gallia, in qua Dei beneficio libertas major est, non temerè quatuor è Clero, paulo eruditiores ac emunctiores, reperies ex quibus duo non sint qui aliquid singulare, supra Ecclesiæ suæ vulgus, de aliquo religionis capite sapiant. Hic eos omnes qui, magno numero, cùm Cassandro sentiunt, quique quicquid in Patrum monumentis, quæ tantùm non adorant, offendunt, pro universali veterum Christianorum sententia exosculantur, oratos velim, ut in seipsos oculos convertant, & apud se expendant, quam multas foveant opiniones, non solum diuersas, sed plane pugnantes cum ea Ecclesia, in cujus communione vitam instituunt, cujus se membra profitentur, & in qua reipsa tolerantur. Tantum est istorum ab aliis Romanis discrimen, ut Rempublicam in Republica, Ecclesiam in Ecclesia constituere videantur. Attamen cum earum quas sequuntur partium doctores vel in definitionibus, vel in concionibus ad populum, vel in scriptis suis Ecclesiae suae sententiam exponunt, varietas illa non apparet, una caeterorum fides vrgetur; quae Caffandri sequacium est, licet multum diversa, quasi ne tantillum quidem ad Ecclesiam Romanam pertineret; silentio premitur, etsi nos, qui nunc in vivis sumus, eam a multis praestantibus e Clero ipso viris retineri & foveri non lateat. Si clancularia illa secta, quae se reliquo, cujus se partem profitetur, corpore saniora sentire existimat, paulatim, vel per se ipsa extinguatur, vel ui opprimatur, omnis ejus memoria sic peribit, ut posteri (nisi forsan diuini fuerint) quae fuerit istorum de religione sententia nunquam sint intellecturi. Nemo tum temporis non existimabit Romanam hujus seculi Ecclesiam eadem per omnia sensisse quae in Concilij Tridentini decretis, & in aliis ejusmodi monumentis leget. Et tamen ex iis ipsis quos Roma unxit & inaugurauit, quôsque opimis suis sacerdotiis alit, nonnullos novimus, quorum de fide sententia longe alia est quam quae apud illam obtinet. Statuamus ergo suos Caffandros, aliosque ejusmodi, qui non eadem cum vulgo sentiunt, veterem Ecclesiam habuisse, quos ipsa quoque paulatim absorpsit & sepelivit, ita ut ne vestigium quidem eorum superfit. Antiquus Christianismus vel alius, vel idem qui hodie obtinet, reuerat fuit. Si alius, Sophistarum est, ut specie tenus idem fit allaborare, fœdáque salsacia tot in eam rem ex Antiquitate testimonia congerere. Si idem fuit, iisdem proculdubio casibus obnoxius, eandem opinionum varietatem in Cleri sui animos ingessit. Ipsae illae opiniones ac caerimoniae quibus hodie offenduntur Caffandrinae potuerunt olim paris moderationis ingeniis graves & incommode videri. Non est probabile nulla fuisse istis seculis ingenia quae nostrorum, vel folertiam æquarent, vel morositate laborarent. Sed hoc iam non ago, neque ultra in hoc argumento pergere animus est. Satis est quod ostendi in Veteri Ecclesia, unius urbis, vel nationis, multò magis orbis totius universum clerum non necessario eadem per omnia & in singulis capitibus de religione sensisse; Vnde sequitur nobis constare non posse, an quas apud Patres legimus sententias ab omnibus & singulis Ecclesiarum Pastoribus receptæ tum temporis fuerint. Hoc unum inde colligere licet, ipsos aliósque quosdam, eósque (si ita lubet) clarissimos, in hac vel illa sententia fuisse.
