Quemadmodum quæ Bellarminus & alij de Eucharistia scripsere argumento etiam posteris, istos, & multos alios, in Ecclesia Romana, in illa sententia fuisse. Sed quemadmodum, qui ex scriptorum istorum libris concludet, neminem nunc esse in Clero Romano qui aliter quàm isti de hoc capite sentiat, is vehementer errabit, sic verendum est ne eodem modo hallucinemur, dum ex eo quod apud unum aut alterum è Patribus legimus, statim argumentamur hanc ipsorum sententiam ab omnibus in Ecclesia Christiana receptam fuisse. Temerarium est octo vel decem, vt sanctos & eruditos, pro omnibus totius Ecclesiæ doctoribus, qui ipsorum seculo vixerunt, sponsores accipere: pauciores sunt quàm ut de re tanta fideiubeant.
units.tr: Before we turn to the other part, it does not seem foreign to our purpose to add this last point. Even if the other difficulties mentioned so far, which are many and serious, did not exist, still it could by no means be known with certainty and clarity from the books of the Fathers what the opinion of the old Church, whether universal or even of some particular church, was on today's controversies. To make the truth of this proposition plain, the terms it uses must first be explained. Those who speak of the Church (especially in these controversies) mean either all who profess to live in communion with the Church, of whatever rank or dignity they are, or, in a narrower sense, all who preside over the Church and represent it, that is, the clergy. Whether the discussion concerns the universal Church or some particular one, such as the Gallican or the Carthaginian, the word may be taken in either sense. For by the universal Church are meant either, in general, all who embrace the communion of the Christian Church, whether clergy or laity, or the clergy alone, who are now commonly called "ecclesiastics." For in the earliest and most Christian centuries, all Christians who lived in the communion of the Catholics were called "ecclesiastics." So too the name of the Church of Carthage signifies either, in general, all the faithful living in the particular communion of the Church of Carthage, or, in a narrower sense, the bishop of Carthage with his whole clergy. Now if the name of the Church is taken in the former sense, I doubt that anyone will contend that from the testimonies we can know for certain what the opinion of the Church was in each century on all the heads of the Christian religion. We can indeed gather, by reasoning, what the faith of the true members of the Church was. For since certain qualifications are necessary to constitute such a person, it must follow that those who had them believed what the true Church, whether universal or particular, believed. But this reasoning applies, first, not to all the heads of religion, but only to those which are necessary, apart from which there are many others on which one may disagree without losing not only communion with the Church but also the hope of eternal inheritance. Second, such reasoning holds only for those who are genuine members of the Church. Those who are Christians not in truth but only in profession, must certainly be neither saved nor endowed with the faith required for salvation. Under such a mask every kind of opinion, even the most impious, can lie hidden. Finally, and most to the point for our purpose, this knowledge is not gained by reasoning, since we are now speaking of that which is had from cited and questioned witnesses, who can inform us about the matter we wish to know. Since the Fathers wrote with the intention of teaching us not so much what the faith of their own age was as what the faith of all ought to be, it must be held for certain that they did not hand down whatever they knew of the views and opinions of their own time. Moreover, it is likely that, whether from charity or from prudence, they kept silent about whatever doctrines of others, whether teachers or even assemblies, they themselves rejected as false. And that they did so in doctrine, as Augustine testifies that they did in ceremonies, is clear: "What is introduced contrary to custom, so that it becomes as it were an observance of a sacrament, I cannot approve, even though I do not dare to censure many such things too freely, on account of the scandals of certain persons, whether holy or troublesome." To this belongs also Jerome's remark about the opinions of certain Fathers of great name: "Although we do not follow them, yet we cannot condemn them." But grant that they, undeterred by any such consideration, sincerely set themselves to hand down simply the opinion of their own Church. Truly I do not see how they could have done this accurately. For I ask: since the Church consists of so many people, differing among themselves in talent, nature, judgement and understanding, by what reasoning could the Fathers know for certain what the opinion of each one was on religion? For example, do you think that Cyprian kept to the very letter the opinions of all the men of his diocese, which he might report to us? Who will show that, in that crowd of people which lived in his communion, there was no one who dissented from him in anything? Today, to pass over ancient times, it is plain that there is no parish, however small, in which every single person agrees with the minister on all the heads of religion without exception. But if you examine the whole diocese, and set aside those whom a tender age, or dullness of mind, or abandoned wickedness has made careless about religion, and sort the rest into certain classes according to their differing opinions about sacred matters, I do not doubt that the class which agrees completely with the bishop on every single head of religion will be the smallest of all. Whatever the bishop followed in religion, it will scarcely represent the opinion of half his diocese. It was no different in old times than it is now in human affairs; indeed, on religion, opinions were once far more free than they are now, because the Roman Church did not yet exercise among Christians that authority which, gradually acquired by many arts, it now claims. Nor was there then that harshness of punishments which now prevails everywhere, whether applied by ministers or by princes to restrain the diversity of opinions. From this it remains to be concluded that there was once far greater diversity of opinions among the people of a single Church than there is now, and so it was far harder for ministers either to investigate or to commit to writing the opinions of each individual. But it is idle to linger long on a matter so obvious. Let us rather weigh what many will object, I do not doubt: namely, that it is not necessary for us to have in hand the opinions of individuals, which are almost infinite in variety, uncertain, mostly without foundation; it is enough that we know what was the opinion of the Christian people's ministers and bishops, that is, of the Church taken in the second sense. Yet I doubt whether this is enough. For if it is the Church's task to support and govern our faith (as the authors of this answer maintain), then the people too will have some part in this business. I grant indeed that the opinions of private persons vary, and that some of them have quite moderate understanding, and sometimes almost none. But we must fear lest this same reasoning should also strip the clergy of the authority they claim for themselves in these matters, since it cannot be denied that very often among them there is the same ignorance and wickedness as among the people themselves. Who does not see, if you look at ability, that private persons are sometimes found in the Church who surpass the ministers themselves in learning and piety? One of those Fathers we are discussing has taught us: "For the most part the clergy have erred; the priest has wavered in his opinion; the rich have thought with the earthly kingdom of this age; the people have kept their faith intact." Since it could happen sometimes, and often has happened, that the clergy held wrong views while the people remained in the true faith, it is clear, as it seems to me, that the opinion of the people about divine matters is not to be wholly disregarded. Cyprian indeed teaches that the Church of his time took great account of the people in many places, so that nothing of any importance was done without the consent of the faithful, as may be seen in his letters. Certainly the question of the baptism of heretics, of which we have already said something above, was debated at the Synod of Carthage, with the greater part of the people also present. But since this is disputed, let us set it aside now. Let us grant what these men want, that it is enough for us to know the opinion of the Church taken in the second sense, that is, of the clergy. But to understand and know for certain what the opinion of the clergy itself was on religion in each century, if it is not [ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων] out of the impossible things, is plainly most difficult. For there is no less discord and variety of opinions among the clergy than among the people; indeed it is often greater. For minds trained in study delight in subtlety, and from this there usually arises a diversity of opinions. Who today, not to say of a whole kingdom, much less of all Christendom, but of a single city, could recount the opinions of the clergy on all the heads of religion? Never has uniformity of opinion in religious matters been maintained and preserved among Christians with more zeal than in our own age, in which we see that not only censures, anathemas and the like are employed, but also the sword and fire. Yet how many are to be found in those very places where the cruelty is greatest, even at Rome, almost in the very bosom, so to speak, of the Pope himself, who hold a view on religion far different from that of their colleagues or superiors! In France, where by God's kindness liberty is greater, you will not easily find four clerics, somewhat more learned and refined, of whom two at least do not hold something peculiar, beyond the common people of their Church, on some head of religion. I beg all those here who, in large numbers, agree with Cassander, and who embrace as the universal opinion of the ancient Christians whatever they find in the writings of the Fathers, which they almost worship, to turn their eyes upon themselves and consider within themselves how many opinions they cherish, not only different but plainly at war with that Church in whose communion they live, whose members they profess themselves to be, and in which they are in fact tolerated. So great is the difference between these men and other Romanists that they seem to set up a Republic within a Republic, a Church within a Church. Nevertheless, when the teachers of their party explain the Church's opinion, whether in decrees, in sermons to the people, or in their writings, that diversity does not appear; one faith alone is pressed, while the faith of Cassander's followers, though very different, is passed over in silence, as if it had nothing whatever to do with the Roman Church, although we who are now alive know well that it is maintained and cherished by many eminent men of the clergy themselves. If that secret sect, which thinks it holds healthier views than the body of which it professes to be a part, is gradually extinguished, either by itself or by force, all memory of it will so perish that posterity (unless perhaps they are divine) will never understand what their opinion on religion was. Then nobody will think otherwise than that the Roman Church of this age thought in all things as the decrees of the Council of Trent and other such monuments show. And yet we know that among those whom Rome has anointed and installed, and whom she feeds with her rich benefices, there are some whose view of the faith is quite different from that which prevails there. Let us therefore suppose that Cassander and others of his kind, who do not think with the common people, belonged to the ancient Church, and that the Church gradually absorbed and buried them, so that not even a trace of them remains. The ancient Christianity was either different from what holds today, or the same. If different, it is the work of sophists to pretend it is the same, and to heap together so many testimonies from Antiquity for this purpose, and that is a foul trick. If it was the same, it was without doubt subject to the same conditions and produced the same diversity of opinions in the minds of its clergy. Those very opinions and ceremonies which Cassander's followers today find objectionable may once have seemed burdensome and inconvenient to minds of equal moderation. It is not probable that there were no minds in those centuries which equalled ours in acuteness or suffered from peevishness. But I am not now pursuing this, nor do I intend to go further in this argument. It is enough to have shown that in the Ancient Church, not even the whole clergy of one city or nation, much less of the whole world, necessarily thought alike in all things and on every head of religion. Hence it follows that we cannot know whether the opinions we read in the Fathers were received by all and each of the ministers of the Churches at that time. This much alone may be gathered from them: that these writers, and certain others, and those (if you like) most famous, held this or that opinion. Just as, with regard to what Bellarmine and others have written about the Eucharist, it would be a mistake for posterity to conclude, from the books of those writers, that there is no one now in the Roman clergy who thinks otherwise than they did on this head, so we must fear that we may be equally misled when, from what we read in one or another of the Fathers, we at once argue that their opinion was received by all in the Christian Church. It is rash to take eight or ten, however holy and learned, as sponsors for all the teachers of the whole Church who lived in their age; there are too few of them to give surety for so great a matter.

units.la: Duo sunt quæ aduersus ista obijci possunt. Prius est, quòd si aliæ inter veteres, de capitibus de quibus hodie controvertitur, sententiæ fuissent præter illas quas in monumentis, vel quorundam, vel omnium Patrum legimus; futurum ut earum vel mentio, vel refutatio in iis occurreret. Sed jam supra huic objectioni obviam itum. Monuimus enim Patres hanc diuersitatem dissimulauisse, partim prudentia, ne eos qui secum non sentiebant in se provocarent, dissidiáque quæ sopita cupiebant, exacerbarent, partim item charitate, benignè ferentes ea quæ lethalia non censebant De diuersitatibus quæ ipsis innotuerunt ago, cùm plurimæ quæ ipsos laterent, esse potuerint. Quæ ratio persuadet Monachum, exempli gratia, in seculo constitutum, in instituendis ad pietatem aliquot cum viris tum mulieribus occupatum, omnium sui seculi Præsulum sententias ad unguem calluisse? Quis fidem faciet cum in quibusdam aliquando non carpsisse quod Ecclesia in sexcentis aliis patienter ferebat? Quis idoneè cauebit cum ipso Christianos ejus temporis omnes sensisse, nihilque ab ejus opinionibus alienum fuisse? Possevinus, ut solvat quod iis libris objicitur qui Dionysij Areopagitæ nomine circumferuntur, nullam scilicet Hieronymum fecisse ipsorum mentionem, respondet, mirum non esse hominem latitantem in mundi angulo scripta ista, quæ Ariani ubique dispersi supprimebant, latuisse. Nonne pariter dici poterit, non mirandum esse quod vel idem Hieronymus, vel Epiphanius, vel similes Auctores singulis in muneribus propositivæ suis occupati, nescierint nonnullas aliquorum Præsulum opiniones, quas fortasse ipsi auctores, seu charitate, seu prudentia, seu quod se dicendi facultate, auctoritateque destituros sentirent, seu quapiam alia de causa, apud se reconditas continebant? Altera objectio ex eadem ratione desumitur; Istos veteris Ecclesiæ Doctores quas privatas opiniones, ab iis quas hodie in Patrum monumentis legimus diversas apud se fovebant eas non peruulgasse. Sed primò, non cujusvis est singulares sententias vulgare, sed neque, ubi vires adsunt, statim adest animus. Variæ rationes obstare potuerunt. Qui sapiunt & pij sunt, ut plurimum concordiæ sunt studiosi, turbásque vitant, quoad fieri potest, eóque fit ut verissimæ sententiæ non semper superiores evadant. Sapientia enim quæ pro veritate stat patiens est & benigna; temeritas verò quæ mendacij causam agit ferox est, clamosa & ambitiosa. Præterea dubitandum non est, quin ob rationes supra allatas, multa diversitatis istius monumenta perierint, vel tempore absumpta, vel hominum fraude suppressa, ne veritatis, quam extinctam volebant, vestigia ulla extarent. Qualiter nunc apud Latinos fieri videmus, ut quicunque, etiam à suis, libri contra dogmata, quæ vulgo, ac præsertim in Papali Curia placent, scripti atque editi fuerint, eos Inquisitores & Censores quæsitissima diligentia aboleant; Vt exempli causa quæ vel Ambrosius Catharinus, vel Iulianus Colen, vel Martinus Eisengrenius, auctores caeteri Romani, de Certitudine gratiæ recenti memoria eruditissime disputaverant, ea optimi illi librorum carnifices exitio devovent, unâque omnia litura delent Sic ejusdem Catharini quæstiones de verbis, quibus Christus Eucharistiæ Sacramentum confecit, nec non Christophoris capite Fontium doctissimum de eodem argumento libellum iidem quoque severissime prohibuerunt. Sic denique ne plura congeram, Sigeberti & aliorum veterum, itidemque Widdringtoni, & aliorum recentiorum libros contra temporalem Papæ potestatem editos & edendos, aut omnino supprimunt atque intervertunt, aut expunctis, quæ sibi displicent purgatos, quin & interdum adjectis, quæ sibi placent auctos in publicum exire patiuntur; qua de re insignis extat ipsius Widdringtoni querela; Tam ipse Pontifex (inquit) quam locorum ordinarij, atqVe hæretica prauitatis Inquisitores fatis sunt solliciti, ne libri aliqui, qui potestati Pontificiæ ullo modo derogare videntur, in publicum prodeant, & si prodierint, vel omnino supprimantur: vel à nemine absque facultate speciali, eaque in scriptis habita perlegantur, donec expurgati fuerint. Atqui ita difficillimum est hisce præsertim temporibus, aut in libris Catholicorum clausulam ullam reperire, quæ temporalem Pontificis potestatem in controversiam vocandi vel tantillam speciè habeat aut certò cognoscere, quid librorum auctores circa ejusmodi potestatem senserint, sed potius quam opinionem libroru censortes secuti fuerint, cum illi non semper proprijs, sed istorum verbis loqui, suamq; sententiam proferre, quamvis inviti supissime compellantur. Hactenus Widdringtonus. His Latinorum tinorum artibus, si conatus (quod Deus avertat (successerint, nemo non videt brevi futurum,ut quos in Ecclesia Romana & nos & parentes nostri scimus bene multos fuisse, qui gratiæ certitudinem propugnarent, qui Eucharistiæ consecrationem prece, non verbis illis, hoc est corpus meum,&c. fieri defenderent; qui denique potestatem Papæ temporalem negarent, ii vel deletis, vel interpolatis ipsorum monumentis, aut planè nulli fuisse, aut (quod gravius est) etiam sententiam suæ contrariam tenuisse videantur. Sed missis recentioribus, ad vetera redeamus, de quibus, quod nuper affirmavi, id nunc aliquot exemplis illustrandum est. Epiphanius adversus Aërium,quem in hæreliarcharum numerum refert, Episcopum ex Pauli sententia & rei ipsius institutione Presbytero antecellere contendit, fuíèque probat. Sigillatimque quæ in contrarium afferuntur obiectiones omnes confutat. Locum integrum perlege. Facile, ni fallor Epiphanio credes in ea tum sententia fuisse omnes Ecclesiæ doctores, quod non fit verisimile tantum, tamque illustrem Præsulem quam impugnat opinionem tanta acceptitate repudiaturum atque insectaturum fuisse, si quis ex ipsius collegis eam probasset. At ecce tamen Hieronymum illustrissimum Occidentis nostri lumen, Epiphanii æqualem & amicum summum, virtutisque ejus admiratorem singularem, qui liquidò docet, apud Veteres eosdem Episcopos, & Presbyteros fuisse, quia illud nonmen dignitatis hoc gratis erat. Ac ne quis existimet ista.
units.tr: There are two objections that can be raised against these points. The first is that if other opinions on the chapters now in dispute had existed among the ancients, besides those we read in the writings of some or all of the Fathers, then mention or refutation of them would have occurred in those writings. But this objection has already been met above. We noted that the Fathers passed over this diversity in silence, partly out of prudence, so as not to provoke those who did not agree with them and not to inflame disputes they wished to keep quiet, and partly out of charity, bearing patiently with things they did not judge to be deadly. I am speaking of the differences that came to their knowledge, since there could have been very many that lay hidden from them. Does this reasoning not persuade us that a monk, for example, living in the world and busy with the moral instruction of many men and women, could not have known every opinion of the bishops of his own age exactly? Who will vouch for it, when he once failed to criticise in some matters what the Church patiently tolerated in six hundred others? Who can safely guarantee that all the Christians of that time thought alike, and that nothing was foreign to his own opinions? Possevinus, to answer the charge brought against the books circulated under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, namely that Jerome made no mention of them, replies that it is no wonder that a man hiding in a corner of the world should have failed to learn of writings which the Arians, scattered everywhere, suppressed. Could it not equally be said that it is no wonder that Jerome, or Epiphanius, or similar authors, busy with their own particular tasks, should not have known some opinions of certain bishops, which perhaps those authors themselves kept hidden, whether out of charity, or prudence, or because they thought they lacked eloquence and authority, or for some other reason? The second objection rests on the same reasoning: that these teachers of the early Church did not publish the private opinions which they held and which differ from those we read today in the writings of the Fathers. But first, it is not for everyone to make known individual opinions; and even where the ability is present, the will is not always there straight away. Various considerations could stand in the way. Wise and godly men, as a rule, are keen to keep the peace and avoid strife as far as possible, and so it happens that the truest opinions do not always prevail. For wisdom that stands for the truth is patient and kind, whereas rashness that serves a lie is fierce, noisy and ambitious. Moreover, there is no doubt that, for the reasons given above, many records of this diversity have perished, either consumed by time or suppressed by human fraud, so that no trace might remain of a truth which they wished to extinguish. We see this happening now among the Latins: whatever books, even by their own people, have been written and published against doctrines that are generally pleasing, and especially pleasing in the Papal Curia, the Inquisitors and Censors abolish with the most careful diligence. For example, the works which Ambrosius Catharinus, Julian of Cologne, Martin Eisengrein, and other Roman authors had recently and most learnedly disputed on the Certainty of Grace, those excellent butchers of books have condemned to destruction, and they erase them all with the pen. In the same way they have strictly forbidden Catharinus's questions on the words with which Christ consecrated the sacrament of the Eucharist, as well as the very learned little book on the same subject by Christopher Fontius, chapter by chapter. Finally, not to heap up more examples, they either wholly suppress and destroy the books of Sigebert and other ancients, and likewise those of Widdrington and other more recent writers, which were published or are to be published against the temporal power of the Pope; or they allow them to go out to the public purged of whatever displeases them, and sometimes even enlarged with additions that please them. On this matter Widdrington's own complaint is notable: The Pope himself, he says, as well as the local ordinaries and the inquisitors of heretical depravity, are quite anxious that no books which seem in any way to derogate from papal power should come before the public; and if they have appeared, they are either wholly suppressed, or are not to be read by anyone without special permission, and that given in writing, until they have been purged. And yet at present it is most difficult to find in the books of Catholics any clause which has even the slightest appearance of calling the temporal power of the Pope into question, or to know for certain what the authors of books have thought about such power; rather, the censors have followed the opinions of the books, since the authors, unwillingly though they are often compelled to, do not always speak in their own words but in those of others, and express their opinion through them. So far Widdrington. If these arts of the Latins were to succeed (which God forbid), no one fails to see that soon those who, as both we and our parents know, were in the Roman Church quite numerous, who defended the certainty of grace, who maintained that the consecration of the Eucharist is effected by prayer and not by those words this is my body, etc., and who finally denied the temporal power of the Pope, would appear either to have been non-existent, or, what is more serious, to have held an opinion contrary to their own, because their writings had been erased or tampered with. But, setting aside more recent authors, let us return to the ancient ones, about whom what I lately asserted must now be illustrated by some examples. Epiphanius, writing against Aërius, whom he counts among the leaders of heresies, contends and proves that a bishop, by the teaching of Paul and by the very institution of the thing, stands above a presbyter. He refutes all the objections brought against this, one by one. Read the whole passage. You will easily believe, unless I am mistaken, that in Epiphanius's time all the teachers of the Church held that view; for it is not merely unlikely that so illustrious a bishop, whom he attacks, would have rejected and assailed an opinion with such vehemence, had any of his colleagues approved it. And yet there is Jerome, the most illustrious light of our West, Epiphanius's contemporary and close friend, and his particular admirer, who plainly teaches that among the ancients the same men were bishops and presbyters, because that name of dignity was then merely a matter of fact. And lest anyone think that these things...

units.la: Cc num acerbissimè excepit, variisque ejus opinionibus nigrum Theta præfixit, eáque tanquam pestilentes infamavit. Non legimus tamen eundem à reliquis Patribus pro hæretico habitum. Sed de ejusmodi exemplis susiùs infra agendum erit. Hoc solum nunc notandum venit. Si libri Hieronymi quos proximè citavimus perisse nemihem futurum qui non ex epiphanio condemnaret omnes penè veteres ecclesiæ Doctores de episcopi supra Presbyterum jure atque auctoritate censuisse. Hæc ergo cùm ita se habeant quis asseveraret ausit tot opiniones passim apud Patres, minùs præfractè quàm ista ab epiphanio rejecta fuit, repudiatas, à nullo illorum temporum Doctore retentas fuisse? Nonne fieri poterit ut eas multi in tigu foverint? ut à scribendo abstinuerint? Denique ut quæ de iis fortasse scripserant atque ediderant interciderint? Quàm pauci sunt in ecclesia qui velint aut possint scribere? Supra monuimus objici Protestantibus Hieronymum religiosum reliquiarum cultum laudate & probare. Sed ipse testatur episcopos fuisse qui contra cum Vigilantio sentirent, & cos (quæ solennis est viri Rhetorica) celeris ejus consortes vocat. Quis scit qui qualésque viri fuerint, & annon digni qui pluris fierent? Quæ enim Hieronymus vel in ipsos proprie, vel in tota hac contra Vigilantium causa scripsit, ea felle ac bile usq; adeo scatent, ut ejus testimonio fidem omnem derogent. Quàm longè hæc pateant lectori non stulto expendendum relinquo. Cùm ergo fieri nequeat ut nobis ex Patribus certò constet, quæ fuerit sententia Veteris ecclesiæ, seu universalis, seu particularis, seu eam pro omnibus in universum fidelibus, seu pro Præsulibus & Verbi Ministris tantùm accipias, concludo, ut supra, ad probandam veritatem eorum capitum quæ hodie inter Christianos vocantur in controversiam veterum Scripta parum valere.
units.tr: Epiphanius harshly rebuked him, and marked several of his opinions with a black theta, and denounced them as pestilential. We do not read, however, that the same Jerome was regarded as a heretic by the other Fathers. But more on examples of this kind will be discussed below. The only point to note here is this. If the books of Jerome which we have just cited had perished, there would be no one who would not, on the strength of Epiphanius alone, condemn almost all the ancient teachers of the Church for judging that bishops have authority and right above presbyters. Since these things stand as they do, who would dare to assert that so many opinions found scattered among the Fathers, which were rejected by Epiphanius with less severity than these, were repudiated and held by no teacher of that time? Could it not be that many cherished them in silence? That they abstained from writing? Or that what they perhaps wrote and published was lost? How few people in the Church are willing or able to write! We have noted above that Protestants are objected to for praising and approving Jerome's religious veneration of relics. But he himself testifies that there were bishops who thought otherwise than he did, and, in the manner of his famous rhetoric, he calls them the swift companions of Vigilantius. Who knows who and what sort of men they were, and whether they were not worthy of more esteem? For what Jerome wrote against them directly, or throughout this whole cause against Vigilantius, is so full of gall and bile that it takes away all credit from his testimony. How far these things extend I leave for the consideration of a reader who is not a fool. Since, therefore, it cannot be established for us from the Fathers with certainty what the opinion of the ancient Church was, whether universal or particular, whether you understand it as applying to all the faithful in general or only to bishops and ministers of the Word, I conclude, as above, that the writings of the ancients carry little weight in proving the truth of those chapters which are now called into controversy among Christians.

units.la: LIBER
units.tr: BOOK

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS.
units.tr: BOOK II.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Patres tantæ auctoritatis non esse vt nostras de Religione controversias possint decidere. Ratio I. Patrum de fide Ecclesiæ testimonia non esse semper certa verâque.
units.tr: The Fathers are not of such authority that they can settle our controversies about religion. First reason: the testimonies of the Fathers concerning the faith of the Church are not always certain and true.

units.la: ACTENVS ostendimus quàm difficile sit certò explorare quæ Patrum fuerit de hodiernis controversiis sententia. Quòd ex antiquissimis seculis pauca supersint scripta, caque ejusmodi quæ, vt plurimum, de argumentis à controversiis nostris alienissimis agunt: item quod eorum scriptorum quæ extant fides eo parum certa sit, quod & multa Patribus falsò afficta opera, & genuini eorum libri multipliciter viriati sint: Tum quod eorumdem oratio obscura sit atque ambigua. Adhæc quòd alienam non raro potius quam suam sententiam exhibeant. Quòd in multis deficiant, verbi gratia quòd quo gradu fidei unumquodque dogma tenendum sit non doceant, quòd in dubio relinquant an ex sua ipsorum, an ex universalis, an verò ex particularis alicujus Ecclesiæ sententia loquantur. Harum objectionum minima ad eorum infirmandum testimonium satis est, quod valere non aliter poterit, nisi id esse constet ab omni hac labe purum atque immune, quia de fide agitur quam firmo fundamento niti decet. Quisquis ergo ex Patris alicuius loco pugnare instituit, primò, probare tenetur, Scriptorem, ex quo locum profert, prioribus Christianis nimis seculis vixisse & docuisse; deinde operis illius quod citatur auctorem certò esse; locum ipsum, qui in medium affertur, sincerum, nullóque modo depravatum esse; firmandus deinde est qui loci illius esse dicitur sensus, sic ut constet eum non alienam, sed auctoris ipsius sententiam continere. Tum demonstrandum sic authorem sensisse ac scripsisse iam maturo ingenio ac judicio; neque unquam postea mentem mutasse, vel sententiam retractasse. Præterea dispiciendum erit quo gradu eam tenuerit, id est, an ut necessariam, an ut probabilem duntaxat, an solus, an cum Ecclesia, vel universali, vel particulari. Magnum sanè & penè infinitum laborem: quo fit ut vix iperem nos unquam certò explorare atque assequi posse quæ veterum fuerit vera atque liquida de hodiernis controversiis sententia. Sic ergo absoluta est princeps nostra quæstio. Patrum videlicet allegationes non esse medium idoneum & sufficiens ad demonstrandam veritatem eorum de religione capitum quæ Ecclesia quidem Romana statuit atque definit, Protestantes verò repudiant. Quis enim videt hoc probationis genus non minoribus difficultatibus laborare quam quæstionem ipsam? eiusmodique testimonia de obscuritate cum ipsis dogmatis, quæ erant illustranda, certare? Ne tamen videamur temerè, & absque causa idonea, methodum hanc damnare, age, missa nunc omni ista sententiarum in veteribus obscuritate, fingamus facile esse scitu quid de istis controversiis senserint Patres, & expendamus jam secundo loco num ea sit ipsorum auctoritas quæ nos obstringat ad illa omnia amplectenda, nullóque alio præeunte examine credenda, quæcunque credidisse ipsos nobis certò constiterit.
units.tr: So far we have shown how difficult it is to determine with certainty what the Fathers thought about present-day controversies. Few writings survive from the earliest centuries, and most of those deal with subjects far removed from our controversies. Moreover, the trustworthiness of the writings that do survive is weakened because many works have been falsely ascribed to the Fathers and their genuine books have been corrupted in many ways. Their style is obscure and ambiguous. Often they present the opinions of others rather than their own. In many cases they fall short: for example, they do not teach with what degree of faith each doctrine is to be held, and it remains uncertain whether they speak from their own opinion, from that of the universal Church, or from that of some particular Church. Even the least of these objections is enough to weaken their testimony, since it can have no force unless it is clear that it is free and pure of every such blemish, for the matter at issue is faith, which ought to rest on a firm foundation. Therefore whoever sets out to argue from a passage of some Father must first prove that the writer from whom he quotes lived and taught in the earliest Christian centuries; next, that the work cited is certainly his; and that the passage itself, which is brought forward, is genuine and in no way corrupted. Then the meaning ascribed to the passage must be established, so that it is clear that it contains not someone else's opinion but the author's own. It must further be demonstrated that the author thought and wrote thus when his mind and judgment were mature, and that he never afterwards changed his view or retracted his opinion. Besides this, one must examine with what degree of conviction he held it: whether as necessary, or merely as probable; whether alone, or together with the Church, either universal or particular. This is a great and almost endless labour, and so I can hardly hope that we could ever ascertain with certainty, and reach, what the true and clear opinion of the ancients was on present-day controversies. Thus our principal question is settled: the citations of the Fathers are not a suitable and sufficient means of demonstrating the truth of those doctrines of religion which the Roman Church has established and defined, and which the Protestants reject. For who does not see that this kind of proof labours under no smaller difficulties than the question itself, and that such testimonies compete in obscurity with the very doctrines they were meant to clarify? Yet, lest we seem to condemn this method rashly and without good cause, let us, setting aside all this obscurity in the opinions of the ancients, suppose that it is easy to know what the Fathers thought on these controversies. We shall then examine, in the second place, whether their authority is such as to bind us to embrace all those things, and to believe them without any further examination, whatever we have been made certain they believed.

units.la: Duo sunt locorum qui apud Patres occurrunt genera. Nam vel ut testes narrant, quæ in sui seculi Ecclesia credebantur aut gerebantur, vel ut Doctores quid ipsi sentiant exponunt: Inter ista duo magnum discrimen est. Nam in teste requiritur fides, in Doctore eruditio. Ille probitatis & veracitatis suæ opinione ac fama; hic verò rationum momentis persuadet. Patres testes sunt, cum Ecclesiam sui temporis in hac vel illa sententia fuisse simpliciter affirmant. Doctores sunt cum suggestum, ut ita dicam, consCendentes, sententias suas ipsi edidisse runt, eâsque Scripturæ aut rationi superstruunt. Iam quod ad testimonia pertinet quæ de sui temporis Ecclesiæ fide perhibent, haud satis scio an omnia pro veris certisque habenda sint. Hoc scio, quantumlibet fidem mereantur, exigui tamen usus in hac causa futura. De priori dubitare me cogit quod etiam studiosissimos Patrum admiratores concedere videam eos, licet de iure, vel nunquam, vel rarissimè, errent, falli tamen & errare sæpissime ubi de facto quæritur. Ius enim est quid universale & unius generis; at factum mixtum est, & veluti inclusum variis circumstantiis singularibus quæ facilè possunt ignorari, aut malè acceptæ malæ referri, etiam à perspicacissimis ingeniis. Scire autem quæ singulis seculis fuerit Ecclesiæ sententia, cognitio facti est, non iuris; historia est, non fidei caput. Videntur ergo Patres falli potuisse dum quæ huiusmodi sunt exponunt, unde sequitur eorum in hoc rerum genere testimonia nequaquam esse admittenda velut absolutè vera. Neque vero est quod calumnieris, sic Patres malæ fidei damnari. Sæpe enim accidit ut viri, etiam optimi, ea se vidisse innocenter testentur, quæ se vidisse putant, tametsi eos falsò id putasse certis postea documentis deprehendatur. Neminem bonitas quantumvis eximia facit infallibilem Patres, qui homines fuerunt; nihil vetat in rebus eiusmodi potuisse & falli ipsos, & alios absque dolo malo fallere, si qui ipsorum testimonio fidem simpliciter habent; sed neque dubium aut obscurum est, non fuisse illos ab omnibus affectibus ac studiis immunes. Nemo autem nescit quos colores, quamque à rerum natura alienos animi studia atque affectus plerumque invehant, adeo ut res ipsæ, vel optimis quibusque, plane aliæ quàm sunt appareant. Patres interdum sententiæ alicujus studio tenebantur, interdum & ab alia aliqua abhorrebant: facilè hac ratione inducebantur, ut Ecclesiam in ea esse sententia existimarent; in quam ipsi arcano animi motu propenderent, cámque ab iis abhorrere sibi fingerent quæ ipsi odissent; maximè cum alias non deesset probabilis ratio, quæ, ut id crederent, suaderet, nihil enim facilius persuadetur quàm quod placet.
units.tr: There are two kinds of passages found among the Fathers. For they either relate, as witnesses, what was believed or done in the Church of their own time, or they set out, as teachers, what they themselves think. There is a great difference between these two. For in a witness what is required is trustworthiness, while in a teacher it is learning. The former persuades by the reputation of his honesty and truthfulness; the latter persuades by the weight of his arguments. The Fathers are witnesses when they simply affirm that the Church of their time held this or that opinion. They are teachers when, as it were, they mount the platform and put forward their own opinions, building them upon Scripture or reason. Now as far as the testimonies are concerned, which they give concerning the faith of the Church of their own time, I scarcely know whether all of them should be regarded as true and certain. This I do know: however much they deserve credit, they will be of little use in this cause. My doubt about the first kind arises because I see that even the most devoted admirers of the Fathers concede that, though they err never or very rarely in matters of right, they are very often mistaken and go astray when the question is one of fact. For a right is something universal and of one kind; but a fact is mixed, and as it were enclosed in various singular circumstances, which can easily be overlooked, or, when badly understood, badly reported, even by the most perceptive minds. To know what the opinion of the Church was in each century is a knowledge of fact, not of right; it is a matter of history, not a article of faith. It seems, then, that the Fathers could have been mistaken when they set out such things, and it follows that their testimonies on this kind of matter must by no means be accepted as absolutely true. Nor is there any reason for anyone to accuse me of condemning the Fathers as acting in bad faith. For it often happens that men, even the best of them, bear witness innocently to things which they think they have seen, although it is later shown by certain evidence that they were wrong to think so. No degree of goodness makes the Fathers, who were men, infallible. Nothing prevents them, in matters of this kind, from being deceived themselves, and from deceiving others without evil intent, if anyone simply trusts their testimony. Nor is it doubtful or obscure that they were not free from all passions and partialities. And no one is unaware what colours, and how alien to the nature of things, the inclinations and passions of the mind usually bring in, so that the facts themselves appear, even to the best men, quite different from what they are. Sometimes the Fathers were held by a devotion to one opinion, and sometimes they shrank from another. By this means they were easily led to think that the Church held that opinion towards which they themselves were inclined by some hidden movement of the mind, and that the Church abhorred what they themselves hated. This was especially so since there was often a plausible reason, which would persuade them to believe it, for nothing is more easily believed than what pleases us.

units.la: Ita Philistrius, Brixiensis Episcopus, quæ ipse non probabat ea in hæreseon censum, veluti à publica Christianorum omnium fide aliena, retulit, adeo fallaci & futili interdum judicio, ut quæ ille jugulat, Ecclesiam quoque damnasse ab omni veri specie abhorreat. Nam si ei credimus hæretici fuerunt qui Epistolam ad Hebræos, non Pauli, sed aut Barnabæ Apostoli, aut Clementis de urbe Roma Episcopi, esse dicunt, Hæretici sunt, & errorem, si istum audimus, patiuntur non modicum qui non putant omnes Psalmos ab uno Davide scriptos fuisse. Hæresis est, ut hic quidem censet, stellas in cœlum infixas putare; non de thesauris, locisque absconditis, atque à Deo dispositis, in vesperum jussu Divino repente procedere, statutisque horis suo lumine cursum, ministerium-que sinum indictum agnoscere, quod (inquit) contrarium alienúmq; fidei Catholicæ invenitur. Quis Ecclesiam illius seculi adeo delirâm & amentem fuisse crediderit, ut illa, & alia ejus generis plurima, quæ referre longum est, inter hæreses deputaverit, & qui sic sentiunt eos Catholicorum cœtu & nomine exclruserit? Hic quoque pertinet, ut mihi quidem videtur, quod Hieronymus tetatur, Christi Ecclesiam credidisse animam humanam immediatè à Deo creari, cùm eam in corpus infundit. Atqui de eo ambigit Augustinus, quin & palàm propendet in adversam sententiam, quæ statuit animam cum corpore simul seri, & de patre in filium transire. Hoc veò vero satis ostendit tum remporis Ecclesiam nihil dum de ea re definiviße. Ea enim fuit Augustini modestia, ut sine injuria dici nequeat, eum receptam in ecclesia sententiam, ut privatæ indulgeret, reliquisse. Sed Hieronymus, commotiore in Ruffinum animo, sententiam, quod Ecclesiastici in qua plerosque esse videbat ejus temporis Doctores, tota Iesu Christi ecclesia receptam facile sibi persuaderi passus est. Id vero aliis adeo non persuasit, ut etiam annis post ejus mortem amplius quàm quadragentis, Prudentius Tricaslinus episcopus, vir suis temporibus celeberrimus, hac de re sic scripserit, utrum anima de anima, ut caro de carne, nascatur, magna (inquit) quaestio est, à Patribus diu multumque discussa, sed absque certa definitione relicta. Ex eodem fonte manavit Ioannis Thessalonicensis episcopi error (ii tamen error est) dicentis Ecclesiam censere Angelos non omnino esse incorporeos & invisibiles, sed habere corpora minuta & tenuia, quasique ignea & aerea, Qui enim Concilia generalia Romae ediderunt, privata hanc ejus fuisse sententiam existimant. Si ita se res habet (neque jam id execuere necesse habeo) apparet sententiae istius amorem, auctorem iilnum, ut eam ecclesiae tribueret impulisse. Nec minus tamen a Synodo septima ma- gni factus est auctor ille, imo inter Patres & cum Patris elogio, citatus est. Eadem ratione a piphanium excusò qui docet ecclesiam ab Apostolica traditione habere quod ter in hebdomade convenire ad sacram synaxin, quod Petavius an satis certò constet se haud scire dicit. Ita Augustinus non semel testatur hanc universam ecclesiam, ante Cypriani tempora, fuisse consuetudinem, ut venientes ab haereticis, à quibus essent baptizati, in ecclesia absque novo Baptismo reciperentur. Firmilianus, cujus locus postea afferetur, in Ciliciae & Cappadociae ecclesiis alium ab omni memoria morem fuisse docet. Idem Augustinus Hieronymianam Scripturarum interpretationem cum LXX. seniorum versione comparans. Ecclesia (inquit) Christi tot hominum auctoritati, ab Elea[zar]o tunc Pontifice ad hoc tantum opus electorum neminem iudicant praeferendum. Suum nobis & sibi consentientium iudicium pro Ecclesiarum illius temporis judicio obtrudit. Ecclesiae enim ipsae, ubi & quando sic judicarunt? Nullum Ecclesiarum istius seculi fuisse huius generis judicium satis ostendit vel sequentium Ecclesiarum fides; quae Hieronymi versionem, septuaginta abdicatis, tandem praetulit. Fulgentius suum & Augustini de puerorum sine baptismo extinctorum aeternis cruciatibus dogma velut certum fidei caput, proponit, & inter ea censet quibus qui contradixerit haereticus & Christianae fidei inimicus haberi debet, ut est à Petavio obseruatum. Firmissimè (inquit) tene, & nullatenus dubites, &c. etiam parvulos, &c. qui sine sacramento sancti baptismatis de hoc seculo transeunt ignis aeterni sempiterno supplicio puniendos. At id dogma neque ab antiqua Ecclesia unquam definitum fuisse vel posteriorum seculorum contraria doctrina satis docet. Venerabilis Bedae errores, quos alibi notat & castigat Petavius, ejusdem sunt commatis. Habet (inquiebat) Ecclesiae fides Dominum in carne paulo plus quam XXXIII. annis usque ad sua tempora passionis vixisse. Et mox. Sancta siquidem Romana & Apostolica Ecclesia hanc se fide tenere & ipsis testatur indiculis quae suis in cereis annuatim inscribere solet, ubi tepus Dominicae passionis in memoriâ populis revocans numerum annorum triginta semper & tribus annis minorem quam ab eius incarnatione Dionysius ponat, annotat. Idem eodem loco docet. Quod Dominus XV. Luna feria VI. crucè ascenderit, &c. nulli licere dubitare Catholico. Fuse docet Petavius has duas sententias, quas tanquam de fide Ecclesiae essent, tradit Beda, nihil minus esse quam quod ille dicit. Ejusmodi multa in Scriptis Patrum obseruabunt curiosi. Sed haec (meo judicio) satis probant me non sine ratione ambigere, num tanquam certò vera admittenda ea omnia sint testimonia quae Patres de Ecclesiae sui temporis fide perhibent. Sed etsi, intacto Patrum honore, concesserimus quicquid de rebus eiusmodi testantur, extra omnem dubitationis aleam esse positum, ne sic quidem id videtur magni ad rem nostram usus futurum. Primo enim raro simpliciter docent, quae fuerit de capitibus hodie controversis Ecclesiae sui temporis sententia. Id enim Historici est, non Doctoris, cuius est in pietate & religione instituere, probare, hortari, in vitia & errores in vehi, quid faciendum aut credendum sit exponere, non vero quid credatur aut fiat narrare. Sed etiam tum cum de fide & doctrina sui temporis testantur, de ea tantum quae palam erat, atque adeo ipsis nota esset, agere possunt; neque ad latentia aut ignota trahendum est eorum testimonium. At, ut demonstravimus, quid Christiani omnes, qui tum temporis in viuis erant, imo quid pastores qui ipsis praeerant de fide sentirent, compertum habere non potuerunt: privatorum quorumdam tantum potuit ipsis nota esse sententia. Cum ergo etiam ij qui maximi Ecclesiae authoritatem faciunt, singularum Ecclesiarum fidem errori obnoxiam esse fateantur, facile est videri Patrum testimonia, quae sententias non certo veras exhibent, quaeque adeo examinari & probari debent (tantum abest ut ad nostram fidem firmandam & probandam idonea sint) exigui esse in hoc argumento usus. Quantumvis autem Ecclesia Romana singularum ecclesiarum de fide sententias nunquam fallere censeret (quod tamen non docet) medium tamen hoc apud Protestantes esset inefficax quos omnes norunt in alia esse sententia. Certum autem est ex rebus confessis, & ab adversario, quem persuasum vis, aguitis, petendas esse probationes; alias, ut a sententia discedat, nunquam impetrabis. Cum ergo Patrum de fidei & Disciplinae ecclesiasticae sui temporis statu testimonia eiusmodi sint, superest ut alia ipsorum effata expendamus, quae non tanquam rerum a se visarum testes, sed tanquam rerum quas ipsi crederent, credendaque existimarent doctores, pronunciarunt. Enim vero ut ut sancti & eruditi fuerint, homines tamen fuisse, ac proinde erroti obnoxios, negari non potest, maximè cùm de rebus fidei, adeo supra hominum capitum posítis, sermo sit. Solus Dei Spiritus mentes & calamos eorum in omnem veritatem deducere potuit, eosque qua ratione sanctis Apostolis & Prophetis Veteris Novíque Testamenti libros scribentibus adfuit, ab omni errore immunes praestare. Nullo autem modo nobis constare potest Spiritum Dei perpetuam lucem mentibus ipsorum affudisse, rerúmque omnium de quibus agebant veritatem eos docuisse, neque id ipsi sibi sumunt, nemóque, quod sciam, id iis tribuit, praeter Decreti Gloss atorem, qui in Scriptis Patrum omnia usque ad ultimum jota teneri jubet, hoc nomine ab Alphonso de Castro & Melchiore Cano Theologis Hispanis merito castigatus; cui tamen hoc in delirio succinit etiam Lucas Tudensis Episcopus, aperte significans Canonicorum Patrum (sic enim appellat) dicta veneranda esse sicut Evangelium Dei, quasi per Spiritum Sanctum prolata, & ad eorum libros impudenter detorquens quae de Canonicis Scripturis dixerat Augustinus; Ego sic eis libris, qui iam canonici appellantur, didici hunc timorem honoremque deferre, ut nullum eorum scribendo errasse audeam credere, &c. Sed cum istorum somnia omnes nunc explodant, jam coeptam disputationem itaque pertexamus. Cùm nonnisi rebus veris fidem adhibere teneamur, apparet quandiu non constat veras esse Patrum sententias, iis nos nec posse nec debere credere. Cùm autem ex nuda ipsorum authoritate de eo constare non possit, necesse est ut alia via ad hanc inquisitionem contendamus; homines enim fuerunt, iisque non semper Spiritu ex alto afflati. Recurrendum est ergo, vel ad Scripturam sacram, vel ad ratiocinationem, vel ad traditionem, vel ad Ecclesiae, quae nunc in terris versatur, institutionem, vel ad quampiam aliam quam ipsi adhibuerint rationem. Unde apparet nudam eorum assertionem non esse idoneam quae sententia alicui pro funda-
units.tr: So Philistrius, bishop of Brescia, listed among heresies whatever he did not himself approve, as if it were alien to the public faith of all Christians. His judgement was so deceptive and trivial at times that the condemnation he pronounces on certain things would shock anyone as lacking all semblance of truth, even when he attributes it to the whole Church. For if we believe him, those are heretics who say that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not Paul's but the work of either the Apostle Barnabas or Clement, bishop of the city of Rome. And those who do not think that all the Psalms were written by David alone are, if we listen to him, in no small error. It is a heresy, so he holds, to think that the stars are fixed in the heavens, and not that they come forth suddenly each evening from storehouses and hidden places appointed by God, at the command of God, and at their appointed hours, by their own light, acknowledge their course and service as assigned to them; which (he says) is found to be contrary to and alien from the Catholic faith. Who could believe that the Church of that age was so mad and deranged as to count among heresies this and very many other things of the same kind, which would take too long to list, and to have cut off from the company and name of Catholics those who think thus? Here too, as it seems to me, belongs what Jerome asserts: that the Church of Christ believed the human soul to be created immediately by God when he infuses it into the body. Yet Augustine hesitates on this point, and indeed he openly inclines to the opposite view, which holds that the soul is produced together with the body and passes from father to son. This alone sufficiently shows that the Church of that time had not yet defined anything about this matter. For Augustine's modesty was such that it cannot be said without injustice that he abandoned the opinion received in the Church in order to indulge a private view. But Jerome, with his mind more stirred up against Rufinus, allowed himself to be easily persuaded that the opinion that the ecclesiastical writers, in which he saw most of the teachers of his time, was received by the whole Church of Jesus Christ. Yet this did not persuade others at all, so that even more than four hundred years after his death, Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, a man most famous in his own times, wrote on this subject thus: whether the soul is born from the soul, as flesh from flesh, is a great question (he says), long and much discussed by the Fathers, but left without certain definition. From the same source flowed the error of John, bishop of Thessalonica (though it is an error), who says that the Church holds that angels are not wholly incorporeal and invisible, but have small and thin bodies, somewhat fiery and airy. Those who published the general councils at Rome think this was merely his private opinion. If that is so (and I have no need now to go further into it), it is plain that love of this opinion impelled that author to attribute it to the Church. Nevertheless, that same author was made a great authority by the Seventh Synod, and he is even cited with the title of Father. In the same way Epiphanius is excused, who teaches that the Church has from apostolic tradition that it meets for the holy synaxis three times a week; Petavius says he does not know whether this is sufficiently certain. Thus Augustine testifies more than once that, before the time of Cyprian, it was the custom of the whole Church that those coming from heretics by whom they had been baptized were received into the Church without a new baptism. Firmilian, whose passage will be cited later, teaches that in the churches of Cilicia and Cappadocia there was a different custom, unknown from memory. Augustine, comparing Jerome's translation of the Scriptures with the version of the Seventy elders, says: the Church of Christ, for so many men of authority, judges that none of the chosen men at that time, from Eleazar the high priest, is to be preferred for this work alone. He thrusts upon us his own judgement and that of those who agree with him as though it were the judgement of the Churches of that time. For where and when did the Churches themselves so judge? That there was no such judgement among the Churches of that century is sufficiently shown even by the faith of the later Churches, which at last preferred Jerome's version, setting aside the Seventy. Fulgentius sets forth his own dogma, and that of Augustine, about the eternal torments of children who die without baptism, as a certain article of faith, and counts among those things whoever contradicts them ought to be held a heretic and an enemy of the Christian faith, as Petavius has observed. Hold most firmly (he says), and do not doubt in any way, etc. even the little ones, etc. who pass from this age without the sacrament of holy baptism are to be punished with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire. But that this dogma was never defined by the ancient Church, or was contrary to the teaching of later centuries, is sufficiently taught by the facts. The errors of the venerable Bede, which Petavius notes and rebukes elsewhere, belong to the same category. The faith of the Church (he said) holds that the Lord lived in the flesh a little more than thirty-three years, up to the time of his passion. And soon after: The holy Roman and Apostolic Church testifies that it holds this faith, and it notes this in the calendars which it is accustomed to inscribe every year on its wax tablets, where, recalling to the people the time of the Lord's passion, it always records the number of years as thirty-three, fewer than Dionysius sets down from his incarnation. In the same place he teaches also: that the Lord was crucified on the fifteenth day of the moon, on a Friday, etc., it is not permitted for any Catholic to doubt. Petavius at length shows that these two opinions, which Bede hands down as if they were of the faith of the Church, are anything but what he says. Curious readers will observe many such things in the writings of the Fathers. But these things (in my judgement) sufficiently prove that I do not doubt without reason whether all the testimonies which the Fathers bear to the faith of the Church of their time are to be admitted as certainly true. But even if, leaving the honour of the Fathers intact, we were to concede whatever they testify about such matters as placed beyond all risk of doubt, even so this would not seem to be of great use for our purpose. First, they rarely simply teach what the opinion of the Church of their time was on the chapters controverted today. For that belongs to the historian, not the teacher, whose task is to instruct, prove and exhort in piety and religion, to inveigh against vices and errors, and to set forth what must be believed or done, not to narrate what is believed or done. But even when they bear witness to the faith and teaching of their own time, they can treat only of what was public and therefore known to them; and their testimony must not be dragged into things hidden or unknown. But, as we have shown, they could not have ascertained what all Christians who were alive at that time, or even what the ministers who presided over them, thought about the faith; only the opinions of some private persons could have been known to them. Since therefore even those who give the greatest authority to the Church admit that the faith of individual churches is liable to error, it is easy to see that the testimonies of the Fathers, which set forth opinions not certainly true, and which must therefore be examined and tested (so far are they from being fit to strengthen and prove our faith), are of little use in this matter. However much the Roman Church may hold that it never deceives concerning the opinions of individual churches on the faith (which it nonetheless does not teach), this means would nevertheless be ineffective among Protestants, whom all know to hold another opinion. It is certain, however, that from things admitted, and from the adversary whom you wish to persuade, proofs must be sought; otherwise you will never obtain his withdrawal from his opinion. Therefore, since the testimonies of the Fathers on the state of faith and of church discipline in their own time are of this kind, it remains for us to weigh their other sayings, which they pronounced not as witnesses of things they had seen, but as teachers of things which they themselves believed and thought ought to be believed. For indeed, however holy and learned they were, it cannot be denied that they were men, and therefore liable to error, especially since the matter concerns faith, which rises so far above human understanding. Only the Spirit of God could lead their minds and pens into all truth, and, in the way he was present with the holy Apostles and Prophets who wrote the books of the Old and New Testament, render them free from all error. But it cannot in any way be established for us that the Spirit of God poured perpetual light into their minds, and taught them the truth of all the things about which they were speaking; nor do they claim this for themselves, and no one, so far as I know, attributes it to them, except the author of the Decretum Gratiani, who orders that all the Fathers' writings are to be held down to the last iota, a claim rightly rebuked by the Spanish theologians Alphonsus de Castro and Melchior Cano; yet in this madness Lucas, bishop of Tuy, also echoes him, openly signifying that the sayings of the canonical Fathers (for so he calls them) are to be venerated just as the Gospel of God, as if uttered through the Holy Spirit, and shamelessly twisting to their books what Augustine had said of the canonical Scriptures: I have so learned to bear this fear and honour toward those books which are now called canonical, that I dare not believe any of them to have erred in writing, etc. But since everyone now explodes these dreams, let us continue the discussion we have begun. Since we are bound to give assent only to true things, it is evident that, as long as it is not established that the opinions of the Fathers are true, we can neither be obliged nor ought to believe them. But since this cannot be established from their bare authority, we must necessarily seek another way to this inquiry; for they were men, and not always inspired by the Spirit from on high. We must therefore have recourse either to holy Scripture, or to reasoning, or to tradition, or to the institution of the Church now living on earth, or to some other method which they themselves used. From this it is clear that their bare assertion is not fit to be laid as the foundation of any opinion.

units.la: Gloss in Dec. D 9.c.1. Alph. de Cast f.11 ad verf.haeref.c. 7.p.71. edit. Venit. an 1546. Mulch. Can.l.7.loc. Theol.c.3.n.4. I.b. contr. Albig. c.8. Biblio. Patr T.4. pars.1 p.650. E.D. fundamento substernatur. Præjudicium quidem eorum assertio aliquod afferre potest quod fidem provocet, cùm, qua sunt apud nos existimatione, non facilè credamus viros tantos eam sententiam sequuturos fuisse quæ falsa sit: quod argumentum probabile est duntaxat, cum auctor, de quo agitur, merus est homo; at ubi de fide agitur, nullomodo admittendum est, cum fides non probabilitate aliqua, sed veritate necessaria niti debeat. In hoc negotio ea est Patrum quæ reliquorum Doctorum ratio; adeo ut tanti sit eorum assertio, quanti sunt ratio & auctoritas qua ipsam firmant atque fulciunt. Hunc insuper usum habent, quòd eorum nomine percellantur mentes nostræ, attentiúsque expendant quæ docent, cùm rebus falsis tam præstantes viros fidem adhibuisse non fiat verisimile. Sic in scientiis humanis longè diligentiùs Aristotelis, quam cujusvis alius Philosophi, qui minoris fiat, sententia expenditur, quòd apud omnes ferè præjudicatum sit non solere stupendo illi ingenio ea quæ veris adversantur probari. Cæterum si rem ipsam instituto accuratiori examine se aliter habere deprehensum fuerit, nuda ejus auctoritas nihil persuadet: hic enim quod sapienter ipse dixit locum habet. Sanctum esse veritati cujuslibet amicitia anteponere. Sunto ergo si placet Patres eodem in Philosophia Christiana loco quo in seculari est Aristoteles, fatebor eorum de religione sententias reverenter esse habendas atque expendendas: fatebor de veris maximis, ac præcipua eruditionis ac sanctitatis fama florentibus, non esse temerè quicquâ secius suspicandum, neque eorum placita absque graui & evidenti ratione erroris aut vanitatis, præsertim in re momentosa, insimulanda, ita tamen ut meminerimus eos homines fuisse, qui nonnunquam vel memoriæ, vel intelligentiæ, vel judicij errore labi possent. Expendenda deinde sunt eorum scripta ad principia ex quibus conclusiones suas eliciunt, neque ipsis fides nostra prius superstruenda quàm de eorum veritate nobis certò constiterit. Si mihi non de Patribus, sed de quibusvis aliis sermo esset, nihil ad superiora adderem; cùm haec facis, ut videtur, doceant ipsorum auctoritatem tantam non esse, ut necessariò in eorum sententiam concedere teneamur: Sed quia de Patribus quaeritur, quos quanti faciat Ecclesia nemo nescit, age, ne quis nos criminetur aut suspicetur de honore iis debito quicquam detractum vel decerptum velle, hoc ipsum argumentum paulò accuratius excutiamus, & ex rei ipsius rationibus ostendamus, Patrum, vel in seipsis, vel nostri respectu, majorem non esse auctoritatem quàm eà est quam hactenus ipsis tribuimus.
units.tr: Gloss in Dec. D 9.c.1. Alph. de Cast f.11 ad verf.haeref.c. 7.p.71. edit. Venit. an 1546. Mulch. Can.l.7.loc. Theol.c.3.n.4. I.b. contr. Albig. c.8. Biblio. Patr T.4. pars.1 p.650. E.D. It is true that their assertion may create some prejudice that unsettles faith, since, given the esteem in which they are held among us, we do not readily believe that men so great would have followed an opinion that is false. That argument is probable only, because the author in question is a mere man; but where faith is concerned it must in no way be admitted, since faith ought to rest not on some probability but on necessary truth. In this matter the judgement of the Fathers is the same as that of the other teachers: their assertion is worth exactly as much as the reason and authority by which they confirm and support it. It has this further use, that our minds are stirred by their names and weigh more carefully what they teach, since it is not likely that men of such standing gave their trust to falsehoods. So in human sciences the opinion of Aristotle is weighed far more carefully than that of any other philosopher, the one who is held in less esteem, because almost everyone has taken it for granted that a mind so remarkable would not be likely to approve what is contrary to the truth. But if, on closer examination of the matter itself, it is found to be otherwise, his bare authority persuades no one; here what he wisely said applies: It is holy to put friendship with the truth before friendship with anyone. Let the Fathers then, if you please, hold in Christian philosophy the same place that Aristotle holds in secular philosophy. I will admit that their opinions on religion are to be received and weighed with reverence; I will admit that, in the case of men of the greatest truth and of pre-eminent learning and holiness, we should not lightly suspect anything the less, nor charge their decisions with error or vanity without a grave and evident reason, especially in a weighty matter; yet we should remember that they were men, who could sometimes slip through error of memory, of understanding, or of judgement. Next, their writings must be weighed against the principles from which they draw their conclusions, and our faith must not be built upon them before we have been made certain of their truth. If I were speaking of some other writers and not of the Fathers, I would add nothing to what has been said above; for these things, as it seems, show that their authority is not so great that we are bound to agree with their opinion of necessity. But since the question concerns the Fathers, whom the Church values as highly as anyone knows, come, so that no one may accuse us or suspect us of wishing to take away or diminish anything from the honour due to them, let us examine this very question a little more carefully, and show from the reasons of the matter itself that the authority of the Fathers, whether in themselves or with respect to us, is not greater than what we have hitherto ascribed to them.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Ratio II. Patres ipsos negare nudis suis assertionibus absolutè standum esse in iisque de religione ipsi in medium afferunt.
units.tr: Reason II. The Fathers themselves state that their bare assertions are not to be accepted absolutely, and they bring forward for discussion the things they say about religion.

units.la: QVæ sit Veterum Scriptorum auctoritas nemo nos certius docere poterit quam ipsi Veteres, quibus sua meliùs quàm nobis perspecta fuisse clarum & indubitatum est. Aurem ergo ipsorum de ea testimoniis prebeamus, &, si tanti apud nos sunt quanti eos esse profitemur, ipsorum hac in parte iudicium revereamur, ipsisque neque majorem neque minorem honorem quàm expetunt exhibeamus. Cùm, propter capitis secundi Epistolae Pauli ad Galatas supra memoratam expositionem, ortum esset inter Augustinum & Hieronymum, duo splendidissima Ecclesiae Latinae lumina, nonnihil controversiae, illæ, ut ab ea se, qua urgebatur, sex aut septem Scriptorum Graecorum ab Hieronymo obiectorum auctoritate, liberaret, quanti omnia id genus Scripta faceret his ipsis verbis exponit. Ego inquit, fateor caritati tuae solis eis Scripturarum libris, qui iam Canonici appellantur, didici hunc timotimorem honoremque deferre, ut nullum eorum auctorum scribendo aliquid errasse firmissimè credam. Ac si aliquid in eis offendero literis quod videatur contrarium veritati, nihil aliud quàm vel mendosum esse codicem, vel interpretem non assecutum esse quod dictum est, vel me minime intellexisse non amibigam. Alios autem ita lego ut quantalibet sanctitate doctrináque prœpolleant, non ideo verum putem, quia ipsi ita censeerunt, sed quia mihi, vel per illos auctores Canonicos, vel probabili ratione, quòd à vero non abhorreat, persuadere potuerunt. Nec te, mi Frater, sentire aliquid aliter exissimo: prorsus, inquam, non te arbitror sic legisse libros tuos velle, tanquam Prophetarum vel Apostolorum, de quorum scriptis quod omni errore careant dubitare nefarium est. Deinde postquam locis ab Hieronymo allatis alios quosdam oppositi, ita pergit. Quanquam, sicut paulo ante dixi, tantummodo Scripturis Canonicis hanc ingenuam debeam servitutem quæ eas solas ita sequar, ut conscriptores earum nihil in eis omnino errasse, nihil fallaciter posuisse non dubitem. Hæc autem monuisse tanti referre existimavit vir sanctus, ut eadem ipsum alibi inculcare ac denuo repetere non piguerit. Lectorem oro ne molestè ferat si locum ea de re unum aut alterum, tametsi paulò longiores, hic descripsero. Quod genus literarum, inquit, de libris agens quos scribimus non cum auctoritate imperandi, sed eo consilio ut exercitatione proficiamus, non cum credendi necessitate, sed cum judicandi libertate legendum est: cui tamen ne intercluderetur locus & adimeretur posteris ad difficiles quæstiones tractandas atque versandas linguæ ac stili saluberrimus labor, distinctâ est à posteriorum libris excellentia canonica auctoritatis Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quæ Apostolorum firmata temporibus, per successiones Episcoporum & propagationes Ecclesiarum tanquam in sede quadam sublimiter constituta est, cui serviat omnis fidelis & pius intellectus. Ibi, si quid absurdum moverit, non licet dicere, auctor hujus libri non tenuit veritatem: sed aut codex mendosus est, aut interpres errauit, aut tu non intelligis. In opusculis autem posteriorum quæ libris innumerabilibus continentur, sed nullo modo illi sacratissima Canonicarum Scripturarum excellentia coaquantur etiam in quibuscunque eorum invenitur eadem veritas, longe tamen est impar auctoritas. Itaque in eis, si qua forte propterea dissere putantur a vero, quia non ut dicta sunt intelliguntur, tamen liberum ibi habet lector audiendi iudicium, quo vel approbet quod placuerit, vel improbet quod offenderit, et ideo cuncta ejusmodi nisi vel certa ratione, vel ex illa canonica auctoritate defendantur, ut demonstretur, sive omnino ita esse, sive fieri potuisse quod vel disputatum ibi est, vel narratum, sicut displicuerit, aut credere noluerit, non reprehenditur. Sed et in opere de Baptismo idem Augustinus Donatistis Cypriani, et Synodi cuiusdam Carthaginensis nomina objectantibus in hanc sententiam sermone sane luculento respondet; Quis (inquit) nescit sanctam Scripturam Canonicam, tam veteris, quam novi Testamenti certis suis terminis contineri, eamque omnibus posterioribus Episcoporum litteris ita praponi, ut de illa omnino dubitari, et disceptari non possit, utrum verum, vel utrum rectum sit, quicquid in ea scriptum esse constiterit. Episcoporum autem litteras, quae post confirmatum canonem vel scriptae sunt, vel scribuntur, et per sermonem forte sapientiorem cuiuslibet in ea re peritioris, et per aliorum Episcoporum graviorem auctoritatem, doctioremque prudentiam, et per Concilia licere reprehendi, si quid in eis forte a veritate deviatum est? Et ipsa Concilia, quae per singulas regiones, vel provincias fiunt plenariorum Conciliorum auctoritati, quae fiunt ex universo orbe Christiano, sine ullis ambagibus cedere? ipsaque plenaria saepe priora posterioribus emendari, cum aliquo experimento rerum aperitur, quod clausum erat, et cognoscitur quod latebat, sine ulla typho sacrilega superbia, sine ulla inflata cervice arrogantia, sine ulla contentione livida invidia, cum sancta humilitate, cum pace catholica, cum caritate Christiana? Sed et sequens locus dignus videtur, qui hic quoque describatur: Neque (inquit) quorumlibet disputationes, quamvis Catholicorum et laudatorum hominum, velut Scripturas Canonicas habere debemus, ut nobis non liceat salva homohonorificentia, quæ illis debetur hominibus, aliquid in eorum scriptis improbare atq; reprehendere, si forte inveniremus, quod aliter senserint, quàm veritas habet, divino adiutorio vel ab aliis intellecta, vel à nobis. Talis ego sum in scriptis aliorum; tales volo esse intellectores meorum. Atq; hæc hactenus Augustinus; quibus, ut in multis aliis locis quos prolixum esset huc referre, diserte docet Patrum in scriptis suis assertiones, non ipsorum auctoritate, sed rationib. quas afferunt nitisde fide non esse nisi Scripturæ aut rationi consonent, & ex utraque esse examinandas, cum hominum sint qui falli potuerunt. Unde liquidò sequitur quam nunc adhibent methodum ad demonstrandam veritatem non sufficere. De opinione quadam vel de alicujus Scripturæ sensu ambigitur. Affertur ad eam rem Patris sententia, planè contra quàm vult hic Augustinus, ut de Patribus ex Scriptura, non verò ex Patribus de Scriptura fiat judicium. Enimvero, ex Sancti istius viri sententia, etsi Patris alicujus assertio non minùs diserta esset adversùs Protestantes quàm sunt Concilii Tridentini canones, non erunt tamen illi reprehendendi si negaverint se ei fidem ante habituros, quàm vel ratione certa, vel Literarum Canonicarum auctoritate confirmata fuerit, quod si præstitum fuerit se ad eam admittendam ita demum paratos fore. Si ita se res habet, nihil hic faciunt auctorum nomina; in rationum ab iis allatarum ponderibus totum negotium vertitur; pensandum, non qui sint auctores, sed quàm solida sint quibus nituntur argumenta, & inspiciendum quale sit quod offertur, non quæ sit vel facies, vel manus offerentis, ac, ut verbo dicam, à personis ad res tota disputatio referenda est. Neque verò Hieronymus aliter instituendum censuit; sunt enim hæ ejus voces præfatione in secundum Commentarium in Hoseam. Tunc (id est postquam reversa fuerit terra in terram suam, post obitum videlicet) sine nomine minùs dignitate sola iudicantur ingenia, nec considerat qui legturus est cuius, sed quale sit quod lecturus est. Sive sit Episcopus
units.tr: No one can teach us more reliably what the authority of the ancient writers is than the ancients themselves, who are clearly and beyond doubt better acquainted with their own position than we are. So let us lend them our ear on this matter, and if they are as important to us as we profess, let us respect their judgment in this part and give them neither more nor less honour than they themselves ask for. When, on account of the exposition of the second chapter of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians mentioned above, some controversy arose between Augustine and Jerome, the two most brilliant lights of the Latin Church, Augustine, to free himself from the authority of six or seven Greek writers that Jerome had put forward against him, explains in these very words how much he values writings of that kind. I confess, he says, to your charity that I have learned to show reverence and honour only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing anything. And if in them I come upon anything in the letter that seems contrary to truth, I do not doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not grasped what was said, or I have not understood it at all. But I read other writers so that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not think something true simply because they have held it, but because they have been able to persuade me, either through those canonical authors or by a probable argument, that it does not depart from the truth. Nor do I suppose, my brother, that you think otherwise. I do not think, I say, that you have read your books in such a way as to want them taken as those of the Prophets or Apostles, about whose writings it is impious to doubt that they are free from all error. Then, after citing some other passages from Jerome, he goes on: Although, as I said a little earlier, I owe this free servitude only to the canonical Scriptures, so that I follow those alone in such a way that I do not doubt that their writers erred in nothing and put nothing falsely in them. A holy man thought it worth while to point these things out, so that he did not mind inculcating them elsewhere and repeating them again. I beg the reader not to take it amiss if I copy out here one or two passages on this matter, although they are rather long. Writings of this sort, he says, speaking of the books we write, are to be read not with the authority of command, but with the purpose of making progress by practice, not with the necessity of believing, but with the freedom of judging. Yet, so that the way is not closed to this, and the most wholesome labour of language and style is not taken away from later generations for handling and turning over difficult questions, the canonical authority of the Old and New Testament has been distinguished by its excellence from the books of later writers. Confirmed by the times of the Apostles, it has been set up on high, as on a certain throne, through the succession of bishops and the spread of churches, and every faithful and pious understanding should serve it. There, if anything absurd should stir us, we may not say that the author of this book did not hold the truth; rather, either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator erred, or you do not understand. But in the minor works of later writers, which are contained in innumerable books, and which are in no way to be compared with that most sacred eminence of the canonical Scriptures, even if the same truth is found in them, their authority is far lower.
