units.tr: {1} Jerome, Comm. on Hosea 2, end of the preface, vol. 5, p. 1144. Whether he be bishop or layman, emperor or lord, soldier or slave, whether he lies in purple and silk or in the coarsest cloth, he will be judged not by the difference of honour but by the merit of his works. He is speaking either of right or of fact. Either he teaches that things ought to be done this way, or he simply reports that they are commonly done this way. If his words are to be taken in the first sense, he entirely abolishes all authority derived from the names of writers, and decrees that nothing is to be considered apart from the merits of the work itself, that is, its reasons and arguments. If his words are taken in the second sense, their meaning will seem false, since it is certain that men generally attend to the titles of books rather than to the matters they discuss. But however they are taken, it is plain that Jerome approves this method of proceeding, and that it did not displease him in the slightest. So if you wish to abide by his judgement, pray send away for a moment the great names of Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom and Cyril. Let the dignities and insignia of such great men withdraw, their fillets, perhaps, their mitres, their sacred palls. Look not at what they did but at what they say; weigh not the merits of persons but the force of arguments. So Father Jerome bids. Hence I cannot but wonder at those who, though most versed in reading the ancients, fill the judgement of their readers with oratorical declamations, while they praise the authors whose testimonies they use so extravagantly that they sometimes even relate how illustrious the family was from which those authors sprang, how liberally they were educated, and further how keen their intellect, what splendour of see, what height of dignity, and what glory of deeds they flourished in. Whether this is permitted by the precepts of rhetoric I do not now inquire; this one thing I say, and rightly and deservedly, as it seems to me: such things do not agree well with the opinion of Jerome just cited. But let us now proceed to clearer passages, so that we may see more certainly what was the view of that greatest Aristarchus of antiquity on this subject. I know, he says, writing to Theophilus, the Alexandrian patriarch, that I stand differently towards the Apostle [Paul] and the other commentators: they always say true things, while these, like men, err in some matters. Could he have taught what we were saying above more clearly? And in the sixty-fifth epistle, when he had discussed the errors of Origen, others have erred, he says, both Greeks and Latins, whose names there is no need to bring forward, lest we seem to defend him not by his own merit but by the error of others. In these words he decided that opinions must be judged by the weight of reasons. And a little later: So I shall read him (Origen) as I read the others, because they erred as the others did. Elsewhere too, speaking generally of ecclesiastical writers, those very men whom we today call Fathers, and of the lapses and errors that occur in their books, he says: It may happen that they either erred simply, or wrote in another sense, or their writings were gradually corrupted by ignorant copyists, or certainly, before Arius, that noonday demon, was heard in Alexandria, they spoke some things innocently and too carelessly, things that could not escape the calumny of perverse men. A most excellent passage, which briefly but clearly and forcefully proves most of what we have set out so far in this treatise. Now consider, I beg you, with how much caution one must read and weigh these authors, and how carefully one must examine whether their scribes erred in their writings, whether they themselves spoke obscurely, whether they arranged the feelings of their minds carelessly, or expressed them wrongly through error. Elsewhere, after reporting the opinions of various authors on a certain question about which he had been asked, in order to choose the most suitable, he adds: Nor is the opinion of the teacher to be weighed as prejudged, as with the disciples of Pythagoras, but the reasoning of the teaching. These words clearly confirm that the sense of that passage is what we cited above from the second Commentary on Hosea. Then he adds these words: My purpose is to read the Ancients, to test each thing, to keep what is good, and not to depart from the faith of the Catholic Church. This follows the rule which he himself lays down in Epistle 76: I think that Origen, on account of his learning, must sometimes be read in the same way as Tertullian, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinaris and some ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin, so that we may choose their good points and avoid what is contrary, according to the Apostle who says: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. He repeats this everywhere, and with great freedom he often wields the censor's rod against the opinions and expositions of his predecessors, frankly setting out what he thinks of each. Blessed Cyprian, he says, never discoursed on the Divine Scriptures, crowned with the famous martyrdom of Victorinus; what he does not understand he cannot express. Would that Lactantius had been able to confirm our doctrines as easily as he overthrew those of others. Arnobius is uneven and excessive, and confused without any division of his work. Saint Hilary is raised on the Gallic buskin, and is sometimes entangled in long periods, and is far from the understanding of simpler brethren. I shall not relate what he says elsewhere about Origen, Theodore, Apollinaris, the Chiliasts, and others to whom he was openly opposed, whom he everywhere takes up most harshly, although he does not conceal that these men were otherwise of the highest talent, and (as regards Origen, than whom hardly anyone was more blemished) that he wrote expressly that after the Apostles, no one except an ignorant man denies him to be the teacher of the Churches. But to speak only of those whose names never suffered any infamy in the Church, listen, I beg you, to how he treats Rheticius of Autun, an ecclesiastical author, in order to soothe him: There are innumerable things, he says, in his Commentaries which have seemed to me to be foul. And a little later: He seems to have gone so wrong on the rest that no one can judge of his errors. He rejects their opinions or expositions with the same freedom, and indeed sometimes not without the sting of biting words. He vigorously defends the Hebrew truth of the Old Testament, and contends that the version of the Septuagint Interpreters swarms with countless errors, although almost all the most ancient Fathers, and those who were still living at that time, and, to name no more, Augustine, were of a quite different opinion, and considered the work of the seventy elders to be divine. He dismisses as a fable the story of the seventy cells in which, inspired from heaven, they put together the version of the Bible, and sometimes mockingly ridicules it as false. Mocking his detractors, he says: Let them dwell in the seventy cells of the Alexandrian lighthouse, so that they may neither lose the sails from the ships nor sigh over the losses of ropes. Their expositions, when they please him less, he rejects without any scruple. The other Fathers thought that the name Israel means a man seeing God. He himself reproves this. Although, he says, they are of great authority and eloquence, and their shadow overwhelms us, those who have rendered Israel as "a man, or mind, seeing God", we are led more by the authority of Scripture and of the Angel, or of God who called him Israel, than by the eloquence of any secular writer. These words, and Hieronymus himself, did not prevent Augustine from falling into the same error: He interprets, he says, Israel as "seeing God". So also in Epistle 146, which is to Damasus: Some, more superstitiously than truly, not considering the text of the Psalm: "My heart has uttered a good word" [Ps. 45:1], think it is understood as the person of the Father. Yet this was the very opinion of almost all who lived around the time of Arius. Almost all of them thought that Adam was buried on Mount Calvary, the place where the Lord was crucified. Jerome not only rejects this opinion, but also mocks it without any restraint. Some of those same ancients, out of pious affection for the Apostle Peter, used to say that Peter denied not God but man, and that the sense is, "I do not know the man, because I know God". How trivial this is) is Jerome's judgement) a prudent reader understands. They so defend the Apostle that they make him guilty of lying to God. For if he did not deny Him, then the Lord who had said, "Amen I say to you," etc., lied. With the same freedom he rebukes Ambrose, who took Gog in Ezekiel as the nation of the Goths, and the Fathers who, in order to indulge more freely in allegories, understood flesh by Bozrah in Isaiah, although it signifies a firm and fortified place. It would be easy to collect many other things of this kind, but these are enough as a sample. For who does not now see that those holy men, the Fathers who went before us, did not acknowledge themselves to be judges and arbiters of the matters pertaining to religion in the Church? That they did not hold their assertions as oracles, but reserved for themselves the freedom, which Augustine concedes to all of us, of judging them from reason and from Scripture? Nor ought we to be troubled by the fact that somewhere Jerome seems to except the works of Athanasius and Hilary, when he instructs Paula, the daughter of Laeta, to run through the epistles of the one and the books of the other with an unoffended foot. Let her delight, he says, in the treatises and the minds of those in whose books the piety of faith does not waver; let her read the rest in such a way that she judges rather than follows. For first, however many writings of the Fathers contained no error at all (as there is no doubt that very many of this kind exist), it does not follow that their authority is infallible. For there are also among more recent writings some in which neither side can be charged with any mark of error concerning the faith, and yet which of us would wish to grant them the power of judging matters of faith? The truth is indeed the same (as Augustine warned above), but the authority is not always the same as that found in the canonical books. Next, if the trust that Baronius placed in the doctrine of the Holy Trinity must be restricted to Jerome's final statement (for it was about this that the Catholics and Arians were contending most vehemently at that time), then if it is taken generally, it will be found false. For there are some passages in Hilary in which piety clearly wavers, as we shall show below; and even granting that Jerome understood it in general (for, not to conceal anything, his words seem to suggest this), it is not incredible that this happened to him in this place, what he himself notes has happened to others more than once, namely that he slipped in some error of judgement. For it must not be supposed that this was Jerome's mind, that we should make him more important than he himself made the rest. Augustine certainly denied that he himself thought recently that Jerome had felt differently about this matter. But we shall both safely and gladly assent to Augustine, and with him fully judge that Jerome did not wish his books to be read as those of the Prophets and Apostles, but to be valued under that rule by which he valued the writings of the other Fathers. And if we detract from the trust in Augustine, let us at least keep that trust in Jerome himself, in the second Commentary on Habakkuk: These things, he says, I have said briefly. But if anyone finds things more subtle and truer than these, let him give his assent to that explanation rather than mine. And in his Commentary on Zephaniah, in the same way: I have said these things as I could, serving the allegorical interpretation. But if anyone finds things more probable and reasoned than those we have set forth, let the reader be led rather by his authority. And elsewhere in the same sense: I have spoken these things as I was able, as far as the powers of my little talent could bear, briefly touching on the various opinions of the Hebrews and of ours. If anyone says something better, or rather truer, we shall gladly yield to the better. So he speaks. By these words, as you see, he puts no chains on our minds or tongues, so that we would never dare to disturb what he himself has once said, or to inquire into their reasons. Let us use the freedom which the Fathers themselves grant us. Let us give them trust (but as they themselves wish) in matters which they build upon the reason of Scripture. Unless they themselves had been versed in the writings of those who went before them, the dreams of Origen, Apollinaris and others of that kind would long ago have overthrown the whole Christian faith. But neither the fame of learning, nor the brilliance of holiness, nor other such gifts, in which no one would deny that those most ancient men excelled, have so dazzled the eyes of posterity that they have not separated the true and sacred things which their elders taught from the vain and false things which the same men added. Therefore neither should the eminence of those who flourished before us deter us from omitting or even rejecting, with the good pardon of the authors, whatever is weak or trivial in their opinions. They themselves freely acknowledge that they are men, and think nothing human foreign to themselves. We shall be inexcusable if we accept their opinions without prior examination, after such kind and frank admonitions. I (he says) count it a favour if someone, reading my writings, tells me what moves him [Augustine]. First, because I may be mistaken in those things which I know; many things they pass over, many things sound different to some people. To this I refer the zeal of the Ancients in warning their contemporaries not to proceed without prior…

units.la: Ambrosius) beneficio annumero si quis mea legens scripta dicat mihi quo videatur moveri. Primum quia in iis quae scio falli possum, multa aut praetereunt, multa quibusdam aliter sonant. Eo refero Veterum studiū in monendis suis seculi hominibus ne sine praevio examine dicta sua susciperent. Unde Origenes. Qua audientes ut diligenter attendant, & accipiant gratiam Spiritus, de qua dictum est, discretio Spiritum, ut probati trapezita facti diligenter observent quādo falsus sim magister, quando vero predicē qua sunt pietatis ac veritatis. Cyrillus eodem prorsus modo quarta Catech. pagin. 15. Cathechesi. Ne mihi ista dicenti simpliciter credideris, in demonstratione eorum quae tibi annuntio accipias è Divinis Scripturis; fidei enim nostrae conservatio non est ex eloquentiae facultate, sed ex demonstratione Divinarum Scripturarum. Si tum cùm viua vox eorum in Ecclesia persōnabat nolebant Patres sibi fidem haberi de ulla re quam ex Scripturis non demonstrassent, quanto minus voluisse censen-di sunt, ut nos absque hac demonstratione eas sententias admittamus quae hodie in mutis eorum Scriptis, praesertim tam multipliciter, quod supra ostendimus, depravatis & interpolatis, occurrunt? Enim vero cùm hinc sanctos illos viros se esse homines errori obnoxios expendenda esse dicta sua, non pro oraculis habentes clamantes audio, inde verò egregia illa sequentium saeculorum effata oculis meis obversantur, Eorum dicta esse vniversalis Ecclesiae legem, & necessarium esse ea sequi, non tantum quantum ad sensum, sed etiā quantum ad verba, & quaecunque dicunt usque ad ultimum iota retinenda esse. Cùm, inquam, ista animo expendo, ac inter se contendo, venit in mentem Pauli & Barnabae historia, quibus culn Licaonij honores divinos per fas nefasque exhibere vellent, repugnasse summa vi sanctissimos viros leginus, & vestes, quod impatientissimè ferrent tibi cultum uni Dei Maiestati debitum tribui, lacerasse, consciissque tunicis clarissima ad turbas voce inclamasse, Viri, quid haec facitis? & nos mortales sumus, similes vobis homines.' Cùm enim unius Dei verbi sit certò & necessa‐ rio verùm, esse,cúmque huiusmodi esse oporteat id ver‐ bum quo fides nostra nititur, quis non videt hominem in gloriæ Deo debitæ possessionem mitti, & in eius lo‐ cum quasi evehi, cùm ejus verba pro norma & funda‐ mento fidei nostræ, & pro judice controversiarum ha‐ bentur, quæ de ea moventur? Itaque si sancti illi viri quæ hic apud nos geruntur ea de beatis in quibus cum Domino suo vitam agunt sedibus vident, non equidem dubito quin falsum illum honorem qui ipsis reclaman‐ tibus defertur molestissimè ferant, eúmque probro du‐ cant, quem scilicet intelligunt sibi tribui non posse, sine redemptoris, cui salutem suam acceptam debent, inju‐ ria, glorias-que eius, quam millies seipsis potiorem ha‐ bent, detrimento. Quod si è tumulis, in quibus quic‐ quid eorum mortale fuit jacet, vocem edere possent nobis proculdubio ob tantum errorem succenserent gra‐ vissimè, verbaque quondam S.Pauli inclamarent. Viri, quid hæc facitis? nos quoq; homines, similes vobis æque mor‐ tales, iisdemque vobiscum affectibus obnoxij sumus. Verùm quid opus est eorum sepulchra refodere, vel sanctas eo‐ rum animas de cœlo in terram devocare, cùm voces illæ tam clarè etiamnum in iis ipsis libris personent, quos per summam imprudentiam super folio uni Dei verbo debito collocamus? Quæ fuerit Augustini, quæ Hiero‐ nymi summorum totius Ecclesiæ Occidentalis virorum de hoc capire sententia supra vidimus. Nulla est invidia cum tantis heroibus sentire, vel quid cum eis sentias li‐ berè eloqui.
units.tr: "I count it a kindness," says Ambrose, "if anyone reading my writings tells me where he thinks they need correcting. First, because I can be wrong in what I know; many things are passed over, and many sound differently to some people." To this belongs the care the ancients took, in warning the people of their own age, not to accept their teaching without prior examination. Hence Origen: "Let those who hear these things attend carefully and receive the grace of the Spirit, of which it is said, 'the discerning of spirits,' so that, having become approved money-changers, they may diligently observe when I am a false teacher and when I speak what is true of piety and truth." Cyril, in exactly the same way, in his fourth Catechesis, page 15: "Do not simply believe me when I say these things; receive the proof of what I announce to you from the Divine Scriptures. For the preservation of our faith rests not on skill in eloquence but on the demonstration from the Divine Scriptures." If, while their living voice sounded in the Church, the Fathers did not want to be believed about any matter they had not proved from Scripture, how much less can it be supposed that they wanted us to admit, without such proof, those opinions which now occur in their silent writings, especially so many of them corrupted and interpolated in many ways, as we have shown above? Indeed, when I hear those holy men crying out that they are men liable to error, and that their words are to be weighed and not held as oracles, and then those famous sayings of later centuries rise before my eyes, that "their words are the universal law of the Church, and it is necessary to follow them not only as to their sense but also as to their words, and every word they use is to be kept down to the last iota," then, I say, when I weigh these things in my mind and set them against each other, there comes to mind the story of Paul and Barnabas. When the people of Lycaonia wished to pay them divine honours by right or wrong, we read that those most holy men resisted with the utmost force, tore their garments, and, with a loud voice, cried out to the crowds, since they could not bear with the greatest impatience that worship due to the majesty of the one God should be given to them: "Men, why are you doing these things? We too are mortals, men like you." For since the word of the one God is certainly and necessarily true, and since the word on which our faith rests must be of this kind, who does not see that a man, when his words are taken as the rule and foundation of our faith and as the judge of the controversies raised about that faith, is put into the possession of the glory due to God and is, as it were, raised into his place? So if those holy men see from their blessed seats, where they live with their Lord, what is done here among us about them, I do not doubt that they would bear with great displeasure the false honour paid to them against their protests, and would count it a disgrace; for they understand that it cannot be given to them without injury to the Redeemer, to whom they owe their salvation, and without loss to his glory, which they hold to be a thousand times greater than themselves. And if they could raise their voice from the tombs in which whatever was mortal in them lies, they would doubtless be very angry with us for so great an error and would cry out the words once spoken by St Paul: "Men, why are you doing these things? We too are men, mortal like you, and subject to the same passions as you." But why need we dig up their graves, or call their holy souls down from heaven to earth, since those very voices sound so clearly even now in the books which, through the greatest folly, we place upon a pedestal next to the one Word of God that is due to it alone? What was the opinion on this matter of Augustine and Jerome, the greatest men of the whole Western Church, we have seen above. There is no envy in agreeing with such heroes, or in freely saying what you think along with them.

units.la: Sed antequam ultra pergamus operæ pretium est paucis expendere ac dissoluere quiddam quod hoc loco non sine aliqua veri specie objici posse videtur. Nam si non ea est Patrum in fide definienda quæ iis vulgò tribuitur auctoritas, cur ergo, inquis, Patrum sententiis ac testimoniis in suis de religione disputatio‐ nibus utuntur & Athanasius & Cyrillus, & ipse ille qui nuper à nobis memoratus est Augustinus ? Præterquam quòd rectè nonnulli annotarunt, eos non aliter ferè quàm ab adversariis provocatos in hanc arenam descendere, hoc insuper moneo, nos, tametsi negemus Patrum auctoritatem ad fidei caput probandum sufficere, non ideo tamen prohibere quominus illi legantur & allegentur. Sapientum Ethnicorum Scripta, Sibyllarum oracula, & è libris Apocryphis petita testimonia sæpe citant Patres. An ideo ista pro fidei fundamentis habuere, quibus religionem nostram tutò superstrui putarent? Absit ut de iis tam malè sentiamus. Verbo Divino fides illorum nitebatur; sed ut fulgorem eius in aperto ponerent, disciplinas scientiásque humanas perscrutabantur, & hac inquisitione ostendebant lumen illud ex alto sibi revelatum etiam in scholis humanis, ut ut caliginosis, aliquo gradu lucere ac veluti micare, si nulla nisi humana testimonia attulissent, ne unum quidem ad fidem convertissent; Sed postquam è revelatione Dei fidei nostræ argumentum hauserant, sapientiæ fuit, eius, non quidem veritatem, sed splendorem ex scintillis illis quę in animis hominum emicabant probare. Eandem ferè Augustinus, Athanasius, Cyrillus & multi alii in Patribus citandis rationem sequuti sunt. Postquam enim gratiæ Divinæ necessitatem, & efficaciam, confubstantialitatem Filij cum Patre, & unionem duarum in Christo naturarum Divinæ revelationis auctoritate constituerunt, varios è superioribus Doctoribus locos deinceps, veluti auctarium & corollarium, afferunt, ut docent illa dogmata ita clarè in verbo Dei haberi, ut ab omnibus majoribus in eo visa & agnita fuerint; utili sanè consilio, & ad fidei nostræ solatium accommodatissimo. Quid enim animo fideli suavius atque jucundius accidere potest quàm si recognoscat viros Ecclesiæ principes, sanctitate & doctrina celeberrimos, jam olim in eadem, de Christo ejúsque gratia, sententia fuisse quæ hodie apud nos obtinet? Sed ex eo non sequitur, sanctos {a}ctos viros ea fidei capita, etiam nullo in Scripturis Canonicis fundamento niti, neque vspiam alibi quàm in Majorum suorum Scriptis extare comperissent, ea nihilominus, sola Majorum auctoritate permotos, credituros & amplexuros fuisse. Palàm testificatur Augustinus, cùm ita se res habet, nulla invidia posse eos rejici, neque tum sine nimia credulitate admitti. Niminæ enim credulitatis est aliquid sine ratione credere. Quod verò sine Scriptura vel ratione in medium asserturi, id discrètè negat Augustinus hujus esse auctoritatis ut credi debeat. Hominum ergo afferuntur testimonia, non ad probandam fidei veritatem, sed ad eam illustrandam, vbi semel probata est. At nonjam de illis capitibus, quæ in Ecclesia Romana creduntur & decentur illustrandis agitur, de rebus ipsis quæritur quarum veritas in controversiam vocatur. Docete nos (inquiunt Protestantes) vel ex Scripturis vel ex necessariis rationibus esse aliquod Purgatorium, Eucharistiam non esse panem, Papam esse Ecclesiæ Monarcham, si hoc semel præstiterit non repugnamus quin deinceps suo ordine quæratur num tertio & quarto seculo eadem veritas, de qua inter nos convenerit, in confesso fuerit, Vt hinc incipiatis non finit ipse rerum naturalis ordo. An res sit statuendum est prius quàm an credita fuerit inquiramus. Quid enim juvabit demonstrasse sic sensisse Veteres, si nulla apud eos extat ratio qua ad idem sentiendum commoveri queamus; Quid verò erit incommodi si in ea fuisse sententia Veteres nescianus, modo tamen se ita habere apud nos constet; Iam quod à nonnullis, vt Patres de controversiis summi judices constituantur, asserti video, Sisinnium, scilicet, Nouatianum, ejusque Episcopum Agellium, auctores fuisse Constantinopolitano Archiepiscopo Nectario, & Imperatori Theodosio vt quaererentur ab Arianis reciperentne eos qui ante oborta Ecclesiæ dissidia interpretes ac doctores fuissent Scripturæ sacræ, id est, num eorum judicio stare vellent, id, inquam, totum nullius apud nos momenti esse decet. Consilium enim fuit hominis veteratoris, & quidē schismatici quē merito suspiceris dolo, ac istis solenni fraude vel grassari, vel ludere potius voluisse, quàm ex æquo & bono in hoc negotio versari. Si ea fuit legitima methodus, cur tot Catholicis Episcopis non venit in mentem ? Nesciebant illi, scilicet, quibus armis adversus Ecclesiæ hostes pugnandum esset. Unus repertus est adolescens schismaticus, qui nostros veram disputandi artem docerer. Quæ si probata fuit cur Gregorius Nazianzenus, cur Basilius, cur alii sexcenti, qui in confutandis illorum temporum Arianis operam posuerunt, Scripturas ferè solas contra hæresin adhibent? Nimirum sancti illi viri dum sic agebant & Christiano candori obsequebantur, qui præter Deum nullum alium habet fidei ducem ac magistrum, & Ecclesiæ sapientissimè consulebant. Nam si auctoritatibus humanis decidenda fuisset ea controversia non video qui verè præstari ac demonstrari potuerit quod ille de Novatiani grege nugator iactabat, Neminem unquam Veterum ausum fuisse dicere Filium Dei ex aliquo principio ducere originem, cum in antiquissimorum Patrum libris duræ & incommodæ de hoc argumento locutiones etiam nunc occurrant. Quin & Veterum testimoniis pugnasse ut plurimum Arianos ex Athanasio, Hilario, ailisque nonnullis discimus. Sed nimium diu immoror in ea refellenda historia quam Cardinalis ipse Baronius explodit velut fabellam, à Sozomeno Novatiano in Schismatis sui gratiam confictam. Vincentij cujusdam Lirinensis, è libello quodam quem plurimi fecit Gennadius, locus videtur majori consideratione dignus. Isergo postquam dixit se de iis tantum Patribus agere qui in fide & communione catholica sancte, sapienter, constanter viventes, docentes, & permanentes, vel mortiin Christo fideliter, vel occidi pro Christo feliciter meruerint, subjungit, quibus hac lege credendi est, ut quicquid vel omnes, vel plures, uno eodemque sensu, manifeste, frequenter perseveranter, velut quodam consentiente sibi magistrorum consilio, accipiendo, tenendo, tradendo firmaverint, id pro indubitato ratióque habeatur. Verùm quam nonnulli Patribus tribuunt summam in fidei negotio auctoritatem locus iste adeo non confirmat, ut me quidem de ea vehementer dubitare cogat. Ex istis enim patet hunc Scriptorem (non quaero iam quo animo atque consilio (id in primis optasse, ut apud Patrum tribunal omnes de religione controversiæ judicarentur, idque ut impetraret omnibus modis contendisse, quo eorum de rebus Divinis judicium infallibile censeretur. Atqui tota istius in hoc argumento oratio sic æstuat, sic anxia, sic perplexa est, ut satis appareat hominem id quod cupiebat sensisse ac vidisse ipsum à vero alienum esse. Tam sollicitè enim propositionem suam circumscripsit, ut si in Patrum sententiis verè inveniantur conditiones, quascunque iste requirit, vix putem quemquam fore adeo cautum ac suspicacem, qui in eorum sententia, his quidem legibus, non conquiescat. Sed ex alia parte, quas Vincentius iste, ad hoc ut Patribus tutò credamus, exigit conditiones eas in unum concurrere usque adeo difficile est, ut nulla spes sit hæc unquam, quæ ipse fingit exempla, in rebus humanis repertum iri. Primò non aliorum in hoc negotio testimonia adhiberi vult quàm eorum qui, non solum vixerint, sed etiam docuerint, &, quod majus est, permanserint in fide, atque adeo in communione catholica. Sed ne sic quidem satis se tutum putavit. Itaque novo quodam trium (ut sic dicam) adverbiorum vallo se munivit, ut scilicet ij quos ad dicendum testimonium admittit, vixerint, & docuerint sanctè, sapienter, & constanter. Sed nondum finis: his omnibus illud postremò adjicit, ut vel pro Christo, vel certè in Christo, mortui sint. Si vixerint, & non docuerint, vixerint & docuerint, sed non permanserint; vixerint & docuerint & permanserint in fide, sed non in communione; aut in communione, sed non in fide Ecclesiæ catholicæ; aut si in ea vixerint & docuerint sancte, sed non sapienter; vel contra sapienter, sed non sancte: Denique si praestitis istis omnibus, neque in Christo, neque proChristo mortui fuerint, non possunt, (si quid iste noster Legislator sapit) testimonium in hac causa dicere. Hic quidem tuto, ni fallor, poterat consistere ac quiescere, neque opus erat ut anxie etiam testium testimoniorumque istorum numerum praescriberet. Quis enim est Christianus qui non ultro fidem adhibeat sententiae eius viri, qui sancte, sapienter, & constanter vixerit & docuerit, & permanserit in fide & communione Catholica? Iste quidem, quem talem esse sciero, non dubitabo quin vera de religione dicturus sit. Quomodo enim sapienter & constanter docuisset, si falsa ulla dogmata docuisset? Nihil ergo homo iste aliud spondet nisi suturum ut non fallamur si modo nulla nisi sancta & vera dogmata admittamus. Sic solent pueri ludere, dum te negant moriturum, si modo cibum semper sumpseris. Neminem nunc putem tam duro & iniquo esse animo, qui non ultro de fide sua sit compromissurus apud hominem quem compertum habuerit ejusmodi revera esse, qualem nobis describit noster ille Lirinensis. Sed cum in primis de teste constare debeat, priusque sciendum sit, qui qualisque sit, quam ipsum audiamus, superest ut, antequam Patri ulli aurem praebeamus, certo atque indubitato teneamus eum iis omnibus quas Vincentius requirit conditionibus verè praeditum fuisse. Amabo, quis ea de re nobis constabit? Quis nobis fidem faciet vel Athanasium, vel Cyrillum, vel alium quemvis veterum Scriptorum vixisse, docuisse permansisse, mortuum esse, sancte, sapienter, constanter in fide & communione Ecclesiae? Non aliter de his cuiquam constare potest nisi qui in istorum Patrum vitam & doctrinam accuratissime inquisierit. Atqui id nunc post duodecim undecim ve secula inquirere & ferum est, &, (ut loquuntur) impossibile. Ac ut possibile esse finxeris, supervacancum canteum quidem futurum nulliúsque ad Vincentianas rationes usus manifestum est. Patres enim testes advocat ut ex iis veritatem discat. Vt autem legitimè inquiramus an iis conditionibus, de quibus supra actum est, præditi fuerint, ante omnia necessarium est ut de veritate ipsa nobis constet. Hanc nisi teneas scire non potes an sancte, & sapienter docuerint. Quod si apud te quæ sit veritas jam constitutum est, ut ad eam discendam ipsos audias nihil opus est. Usui tamen esse poterunt in illustranda & confirmanda hactenus cognita veritate, non ut ignotam ex iis discas. Quod si alio sensu pronuntiatum illud intelligas, sapientiámque, sanctitatem, fidem & communionem catholicam, de quibus agit, pro umbra tantum, rerúmque istarum corrice, promiscuáque, leui & ex fama tantùm audita rei notitia accipias, falsum erit evidenter quod ille pronuntiat. Qui enim specie tenus tantum, & non reipsa conditionibus illius præditi sunt, ij nô sunt idonei qui testimonium dicant, multò minùs qui de rebus fidei judicio vltimo, & à quo provocare non liceat, statuant. Itaque Vincentiana propositio, si præcisè ut sonat, accipiatur, supervacanea aut impossibilis est. Sin de eius sensu aliquid remittas, falsa. Eadem consideranda se se offerunt circa conditiones quas in testium istorum numero & testimoniis requirit. Vim enim leges non concedit, nisi iis rebus quas, vel omnes, vel plerique asseruerint.Si per hæc vel omnes Patres qui fuerunt, vel eorum saltem maximam partem intelligit, ad impossibile nos adigit. Patrum enim qui fuerunt pars maxima & forsan potissima nihil scripserunt: ex iis qui scripserunt,quam multos vel tempus absumpsit, vel hominum fraus suppressit, aut depravauit? Prorsus ergo impossibile est vt quæ, vel omnium, vel plerorumque Patrum sententiæ fuerint hoc sensu pernoscamus. Quod si hanc Patrum, vel universalitatem, vel maximam saltem partem, ad eos qui hodie extant, id est quorum monumenta supersunt, vel quotum in historiis scriptisve aliorum mentio fir, restringas, restabit constituendum, an nulla aetatis distinctione omnes promiscue sententiam rogari velis, an in varias classes pro seculorum ratione distribui malis, ita ut in unum conjungantur ij omnes qui eodem seculo vixerint, firmumque & ratum habeatur quod eorum maxima pars confirmaucrit. Utrumvis eligas, judicium de fide Christiana fortuitum fiet; ex variis enim casibus quibus aut perierint, aut conseruati fuerint Patrum libri, pendebit. Esto enim praeclara haec methodo dogma aliquod controversum comprobatic Vincentius; tam optatum successum igni, aeri, aquis, tineis, vel cariei, quae Scriptoribus peperцerint, aut eos qui cum adversariis suis faciebant absumpserint, debebit. Abique his foret in haereticorum censum referendus fuit. Sic eadem pene ratione fidei capita definiuntur qua lites olim nescio quis decidisse dicitur, forte, scilicet, atque alea, jactis tesseris lusoriis. Expende sodes qui quantumque labor futurus sit, omnium seculorum Patres, vel sparsos in unum colligere, collectosque promiscue nullo discrimine consulere, vel pro aetatum ratione in certas classes distributos sententiam rogare. Quid vero fiet si (quod nonnunquam accidere posse infra docebimus) plerorumque sententiae, vel Scripturae, vel Ecclesiae adversari comperientur? Sed & iniquissimum est eorum aequari sententias qui doctrina, sanctitate, integritate metito denique, valde dispares fuerint Rhericium, verbi gratia, illum quem falso sugillat Hieronymus eodem cum Augustino suffragij jure gaudere, vel Philastrium & Hieronymum eodem ordine censeri. Et inter Patres cuius unius sententia pondere & pretio centum alios vincit. Decernit tamen Vincentius suffragia non expendi, sed numerari, tantique esse jubet apud nos aereos, quanti aureos nummos. Denique ut Patres ipsos caeteraque inter se aequales fuisse fingamus, Patrum certe sententiae aequari non possunt, immani ut plurimum discrimine inter se distinctæ, quarum aliæ, ut ita dicam,pro tribunali, inspectis omnibus litis firmamentis atque documentis, auditis ambabus partibus, accuratéque expensis totius causæ momentis, rite ac legitimè pronunciatæ; aliæ temerè ac tumultuariè, ab aliud agentibus effusæ potiùs quam dictæ sunt.At Vincentius, ut ab hoc postremo incommodo sibi cavERET, decernit ut maximæ istius partis, quam ad eiusmodi auctoritatis fastigium evehit, sententia firmata fuerit manifestè frequenter & perseveranter; ita demum pro indubitata certa, ratáque habeatur. En tibi novus labor, noua de integro superanda difficultas. Amabo enim, cum Patres istos é sepulchris excitauerimus, ut nos quid de religione olim senserint doceant, qui nobis constare poterit an quæ in eorum libris nunc legimus huiusmodi sint quæ manifestè frequenter & perseveranter firmauerint,necne? Quod si in eo,quod ille fingit, Patrum Concilio, iis suffragii jus suam vel manifestè expressisse, vel frequenter confirmauisse, vel denique constanter retinuisse,tuam fidem,lector, quis denique ex tanto numero supererit, cui suffragij ius tutò deferri possit? Fidei quidem symbola, ac prima quatuor Concilia, quæ Protestantes ipsi quoque agnoscunt, suum in hoc iudicio locum habebunt atque tuebuntur. Cætera verò Patrum dicta pro sententiis ac iudiciis in hac causa censeri his profectò legibus non licet, vt vel ex iis patet quæ in priori operis parte disputauimus. Atque ita iam, ni fallor, satis manifestum est Vincentianam illam methodum, vel plane impossibilem, vel valde periculosam esse. Quo sapientissimum Augustini de Patrum auctoritate iudicium magis magisque confirmatur; Cùm enim qui aliter de iis judicat Vincentius, in ea se incommoda induerit quibus efficitur ut eius sententia, vel liquidò falsa sit, vel certè obscura & inanis, vel denique maximis periculis obnoxia, apparet eam ex uno auctoris studio, non ex ulla solida ratione natam esse: In qua expendenda paulo diutius immorari libuit, quòd eam multis, & quidem eruditis, nimium placere videam. Alioqui post luculentissima Augustini & Hieronymi judicia nihil erat quod de vnius Lirinensis Monachi sententia laboraremus.
units.tr: But before we go further, it is worth weighing briefly and dissolving something that may seem to be objected here, and not without some appearance of truth. For if the authority of the Fathers in defining the faith is not what it is commonly held to be, why, you ask, did Athanasius, Cyril, and that Augustine just mentioned by us use the sayings and testimonies of the Fathers in their disputations about religion? Apart from the fact that some have rightly observed that they entered this arena only because they were challenged by their opponents, I add this: although we deny that the authority of the Fathers is sufficient to prove an article of faith, we do not for that reason forbid them to be read and cited. The Fathers often cite the writings of the pagan sages, the oracles of the Sibyls, and testimonies taken from the Apocryphal books. Did they therefore regard these as foundations of faith, on which they thought our religion could safely be built? Far be it from us to think so poorly of them. Their faith rested on the Divine Word; but in order to set its brightness in plain view, they searched through human disciplines and sciences, and by this inquiry they showed that the light revealed to them from on high also shines, and as it were glimmers, to some degree in human schools, however dim these may be. If they had brought forward no human testimonies at all, they would not have converted a single person to the faith. But once they had drawn the argument for our faith from the revelation of God, it was a matter of wisdom to show, not the truth of that revelation, but its splendour, from the sparks that shone out in the minds of men. Augustine, Athanasius, Cyril, and many others followed almost the same method in citing the Fathers. For after they had established, on the authority of Divine revelation, the necessity and efficacy of divine grace, the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, and the union of the two natures in Christ, they then brought forward various passages from the earlier teachers as an appendix and corollary, to show that these doctrines are so clearly contained in the Word of God that they were seen and acknowledged in it by all the greater men. This was certainly a useful plan, and very well suited to the comfort of our faith. For what can happen more pleasantly and agreeably to a faithful mind than to recognise that the leading men of the Church, most celebrated for holiness and learning, held long ago, concerning Christ and his grace, the same view that now prevails among us? But it does not follow from this that holy men, had they found that those articles of faith had no foundation in the canonical Scriptures and existed nowhere except in the writings of their predecessors, would nevertheless have believed and embraced them on the sole authority of their predecessors. Augustine openly testifies that, when matters stand thus, these articles cannot be rejected without any ill feeling, nor could they then be admitted without excessive credulity. For it is excessive credulity to believe anything without reason. And as for what is brought forward without Scripture or reason, Augustine wisely denies that it has the authority to be believed. Human testimonies are therefore adduced, not to prove the truth of the faith, but to illustrate it once it has been proved. But our present concern is not with those articles which are believed and observed in the Church of Rome, to be illustrated; the question is about the matters themselves, whose truth is being called into dispute. Teach us, the Protestants say, either from the Scriptures or from necessary reasons, that there is some Purgatory, that the Eucharist is not bread, that the Pope is the Monarch of the Church; if you once accomplish this, we do not object to inquiring afterwards, in its proper order, whether the same truth on which we have agreed was accepted in the third and fourth centuries. Let your starting point be this: the natural order of things does not allow anything else. We must determine whether a thing is so before we inquire whether it was believed. For what will it help to have shown that the ancients thought thus, if no reason survives among them by which we can be moved to think the same? And what harm will there be if we do not know that the ancients held that view, provided it is established among us that the matter is so? Now as for what I see asserted by some, that the Fathers are constituted supreme judges of controversies: they say that Sisinnius, Novatian, and Agellius their bishop were the authors of the proposal to the Constantinopolitan Archbishop Nectarius and the Emperor Theodosius that the Arians should be asked whether they would accept those who before the rise of the Church's disputes had been interpreters and teachers of holy Scripture, that is, whether they would abide by their judgement. I say that this whole matter ought to be of no weight at all among us. For it was the counsel of a crafty man, and indeed a schismatic, whom you may rightly suspect of having wished to rage, or rather to play, with trickery and that customary deceit, rather than to act fairly and justly in this business. If that was a legitimate method, why did it not come into the minds of so many Catholic bishops? Did they, forsooth, not know with what weapons they should fight against the enemies of the Church? Only one schismatic youth was found to teach our side the true art of disputing. If this method was approved, why did Gregory Nazianzen, why Basil, why so many hundreds of others, who laboured to refute the Arians of those times, rely almost entirely on Scripture against the heresy? Surely those holy men, while acting thus, were both following Christian sincerity, which has no leader and master of faith besides God, and consulting the Church most wisely. For if that controversy had been decided by human authorities, I do not see how it could truly have been established and demonstrated what that trifler of Novatian's flock boasted: No one of the ancients ever dared to say that the Son of God derives his origin from some beginning, since harsh and inconvenient expressions on this subject still occur even now in the books of the most ancient Fathers. Indeed, we learn from Athanasius, Hilary, and some others that the Arians mostly contended with the testimonies of the Fathers. But I have lingered too long in refuting that story, which Cardinal Baronius himself explodes as a fable, invented by Sozomen in favour of Novatian's schism. The passage of a certain Vincent of Lérins, from a little book which Gennadius held in high esteem, seems worthy of greater consideration. He, after saying that he treats only of those Fathers who, living, teaching and persisting holily, wisely and steadfastly in the faith and Catholic communion, have deserved either to die faithfully in Christ or to be happily slain for Christ, adds: they are to be believed on this condition, that whatever all, or many, have affirmed with one and the same sense, clearly, frequently, and persistently, receiving, holding and handing it down, as if with the consenting counsel of their teachers, is to be regarded as beyond doubt and reason. But the passage does not confirm at all what some attribute to the Fathers, namely supreme authority in matters of faith; indeed it makes me very doubtful of that authority. For from these words it is plain that this writer (I do not ask now with what mind and purpose) above all desired that all controversies about religion should be judged before the tribunal of the Fathers, and strove by every means to obtain this, so that their judgement on divine matters might be regarded as infallible. And yet the whole of his discourse on this subject is so agitated, so anxious and so perplexed that it sufficiently appears that the man, in sensing and seeing what he desired, was himself far from the truth. For he hedged his proposition about so carefully that, if in the sayings of the Fathers the conditions that he requires are truly found, I can hardly think that anyone would be so cautious and suspicious as not to rest content with their judgement under these laws. But on the other hand, that the conditions which Vincent demands, so that we may safely believe the Fathers, should all concur in one case is so difficult that there is no hope of ever finding, in human affairs, the examples he invents. First, he wishes that the testimony of none be admitted in this business except of those who not only lived but also taught, and, what is greater, persisted in the faith and thus in the Catholic communion. But even so he did not think himself safe enough. So he fortified himself with a new rampart of three adverbs, as it were, so that those whom he admits to give testimony must have lived and taught holily, wisely, and steadfastly. But there is still more: to all this he finally adds that they must have died either for Christ or at least in Christ. If they lived and did not teach; or lived and taught but did not persist; or persisted in the faith but not in communion; or in communion but not in the faith of the Catholic Church; or if they lived and taught holily but not wisely, or conversely wisely but not holily: finally, if, having fulfilled all these conditions, they did not die either in Christ or for Christ, then (if our legislator knows what he is about) they cannot give testimony in this cause. Here, I think, he could safely have stopped and rested, nor was there any need for him to prescribe so anxiously even the number of these witnesses and testimonies. For who is the Christian who would not readily give credit to the opinion of a man who lived holily, wisely and steadfastly, and taught and persisted in the faith and Catholic communion? I, for my part, when I know a man to be such, will not doubt that he will say true things about religion. For how could he have taught wisely and steadfastly if he had taught any false doctrines? So this man promises nothing other than that we shall not be deceived, provided we admit only holy and true doctrines. Children play in this way when they deny that you will die, provided you always eat. I think no one now is of so hard and unjust a mind that he would not willingly pledge his faith before a man whom he knew to be really such as our Lérinian describes. But since, first of all, the witness must be known, and it must be known who and what sort of person he is before we hear him, it remains that, before we lend an ear to any Father, we hold it certain and beyond doubt that he was truly endowed with all the conditions that Vincent requires. Pray, who will establish this for us? Who will make us believe that Athanasius, or Cyril, or any other of the ancient writers lived, taught, persisted, died holily, wisely, steadfastly in the faith and communion of the Church? Nothing of this can be known to anyone except one who has investigated the life and teaching of those Fathers most accurately. But to inquire into this now, after eleven or twelve centuries, is both savage and, as people say, impossible. And even if you pretend it is possible, the inquiry would be superfluous, and it is clear it would be of no use for Vincent's principles. For he summons the Fathers as witnesses so that from them we may learn the truth. But in order to inquire lawfully whether they were endowed with those conditions described above, it is first of all necessary that we be certain of the truth itself. If you have not got this, you cannot know whether they taught holily and wisely. But if you have already settled for yourself what the truth is, you have no need to hear them in order to learn it. They may nevertheless be of use in illustrating and confirming a truth already known, though not for learning an unknown one from them. But if you understand that statement in another sense, and take wisdom, holiness, faith and Catholic communion, of which he speaks, merely as a shadow and a vague outline of those things, and a knowledge of the matter acquired superficially and only from hearsay, then what he asserts is plainly false. For those who possess these conditions only in appearance, and not in reality, are not fit to give testimony, much less to pronounce on matters of faith with a final judgement from which there is no appeal. Thus Vincent's proposition, if taken exactly as it sounds, is either superfluous or impossible; but if you relax something of its meaning, it is false. The same things present themselves for consideration with regard to the conditions which he requires in the number and the testimonies of these witnesses. For the law grants force only to those matters which either all, or most, have asserted. If by these words all he means all the Fathers who have existed, or at least the greater part of them, he drives us to the impossible. For the greatest and perhaps most important part of the Fathers who existed wrote nothing; and of those who did write, how many has time consumed, or the fraud of men suppressed or corrupted? It is therefore utterly impossible for us to learn, in this sense, what was the opinion of all or of most of the Fathers. But if you restrict this universality or greater part of the Fathers to those who survive today, that is, whose monuments remain, or of whom mention is made in histories or in the writings of others, there will remain the question whether you wish to ask the opinion of all of them without any distinction of age, or prefer to distribute them into various classes according to their centuries, so that all those who lived in the same century are joined together, and what the greater part of them affirmed is held firm and valid. Whichever you choose, the judgement on the Christian faith will become a matter of chance; for it will depend on the various accidents by which the books of the Fathers either perished or were preserved. For suppose that Vincent proved some disputed dogma by this excellent method: such a desired outcome he would owe to fire, air, water, moths, or decay, which have spared some writers, or consumed those who were opposed to their own adversaries. Without these, he would have had to be counted among the heretics. In this way the articles of faith are defined almost by the same method by which, they say, someone once decided lawsuits: by chance, I suppose, and dice, the gaming tables being cast. Consider, I beg you, how great the labour would be, either to gather together the Fathers of all centuries, scattered as they are, and to consult them collected together without any distinction, or to ask the opinion of them distributed into fixed classes according to their ages. What then will happen if (as we shall show below that it sometimes can happen) the opinions of most of them are found to be opposed to Scripture or to the Church? But it is also most unjust to equate the opinions of those who differed greatly in learning, holiness and integrity, and in the end in merit: for example, to allow Rhetorius, whom Jerome falsely disparages, the same right of voting as Augustine, or to count Philastrius and Jerome in the same rank. And among the Fathers, the opinion of one single man, by its weight and worth, outweighs a hundred others. Yet Vincent decrees that votes are not to be weighed but counted, and bids that they be worth among us as much as bronze coins are worth as much as gold ones. Finally, even if we pretend that the Fathers themselves and the others were equal to one another, the opinions of the Fathers certainly cannot be made equal: they are for the most part distinguished from one another by an enormous difference. Some were pronounced, as it were, from the tribunal, with all the grounds and documents of the dispute examined, both parties heard, and all the weight of the whole cause carefully weighed, duly and lawfully; others were poured out rashly and in a confused manner by men doing something else, rather than spoken. But Vincent, in order to guard himself against this last inconvenience, decrees that the opinion of that greatest part, which he raises to such a height of authority, must have been affirmed clearly, frequently and persistently; only then is it to be held as certain, firm and valid. See, here is a new labour, a new difficulty to be overcome from the beginning. For, I beg you, when we have raised those Fathers from their tombs so that they may teach us what they once thought about religion, how will it be established for us whether the things we now read in their books are of this kind, that they affirmed clearly, frequently and persistently, or not? And if in that Council of the Fathers, which he imagines, those who had the right of voting either clearly expressed it, or frequently confirmed it, or finally kept it constantly, reader, which of such a great number will remain at last, to whom the right of voting can safely be entrusted? The creeds of the faith, and the first four Councils, which the Protestants themselves also acknowledge, will certainly have their place and hold their ground in this judgement. But the other sayings of the Fathers cannot be counted as opinions and judgements in this cause under these laws, as is clear even from what we argued in the earlier part of this work. And so, I think, it is now sufficiently plain that the Vincentian method is either utterly impossible or very dangerous. By this the most wise judgement of Augustine on the authority of the Fathers is more and more confirmed. For since Vincent, who judges otherwise about them, has entangled himself in such difficulties that his opinion becomes either plainly false, or at least obscure and empty, or finally exposed to the greatest dangers, it appears that it arose from the sole zeal of its author and not from any solid reason. I was pleased to linger a little longer over weighing it, because I see that it pleases many, and indeed learned men, too much. Otherwise, after the most splendid judgements of Augustine and Jerome, there was nothing for us to trouble ourselves about in the opinion of a single monk of Lérins.

units.la: Sed antequam caput hoc concludo juvat in ipso Vincentio vtramque, id est suam & Augustinianam methodum experiri. Negat Augustinus nos ulla cuiuscunque auctoris sententia teneri, nisi quæ vel Scripturarum canonicarum authoritate, vel aliqua ratione probabili constituta confirmatáque fuerit. Hic verò Lirinensis eremites quam vel Scripturam vel rationem attulit qua suam illam assertionem nobis probaret? Eam ergo liberum est ex Augustini lege & praxi repudiare, præsertim cùm repudiandæ certa ratio sit, cuius constituendæ nulla, vel ab ipso auctore, allata est. Vides ex Augustini decreto nullam esse apud nos debere sententiæ Vincentianæ authoritatem, quantumlibet fuisse finxeris auctoris inter Patres nomen. Sed jam de Vincentio ex propria ipsius sententia judicemus. Vetat Scriptoribus fidem adhiberi, nisi qui ad mortem usque sanctè & sapienter vixerint & docuerint. Quis idoneè cauebit ipsum sic & vixisse & docuisse? Quis confirmabit non fuisse eum hæreticum hæreticorumve fautorem? Iste enim, quisquis de cætero fuerit, Semipelagianis, qui tum in Galliis Augustini memoriam proscindebant, quinque ab Ecclesia damnati sunt haud obscurè fauet, & ex Commonitorio apparet, quo loco licet tacitis virorum nominibus innuit, quæ Prosper & Hilarius apud Cœlestinum de Gallorum Massiliensium nouiratibus criminati erant, ea falsa fuisse, & Gallis per calumniam afficta. Quin & hunc earum adversus Augustinum objectionum auctorem fuisse quas Prosper confutat & Vincentianas inscribit nomen ipsum clamat. Suspicionem etiam plurimum augent laudes quas in istum confert Gennadius, quem constat in eadem facta fuisse; ut vel ex eo patet, quod tanti facit Pelagianorum Patriarcham Ruffinum, Aquileensem presbyterum; cum eum non minimam partem Doctorum Ecclesiae vocat, aperteque eius adversarium Hieronymum tanquam invidum, & calumniatorem criminatur; tum ex eo quod Augustino iniquissimus est, & in cum sane impudenter torquet S. Spiritus apud Salomonem dictum. In multi loquio non deerit peccatum. Quo fit ut satis mirati nequeam Cardinalis Peronij temeritatem, qui hunc scriptorem ut plurimum cum Sancti Vincentij Lirinensis elogio laudatae, pessimo exemplo, in Doctorum numerum referens Scriptorem de haeresi suspectum. Cum ergo is fuerit Vincentius, non est mirandum quod tanti faciat Patrum judicia, quorum auctoritate nemo nescit Pelagianos & Semi-Pelagianos abusos fuisse. Cum enim iis qui de hoc argumento ante Pelagij tempora scripserant multa incautius excidissent, quae orthodoxis negotium facessebant, ea in compendium suum vertebant Pelagiani & Massilienses. Sed etsi Vincentio nihil eorum defuisset quae in aliis ipse ad hoc requirit, ut testimonium in hoc negotio idoneum ferre possint, ne sic quidem vllius ponderis esse poterit ista eius sententia, quae apud eorum qui ipso superiores fuerunt Patrum neminem occurrit; praesertim diserte repugnantibus Augustino & Hieronymo, in locis quos supra ex ipsis protulimus, quae denique obscuritatibus & ambiguitatibus inexplicabilibus laborat. Itaque quamvis sanctus & doctus, quamvis Episcopus, quamvis confessor & martyr (quod non est) fuisset, ista tamen eius sententia, (ut ipsius verba hic usurpem) inter proprias & occultas & privatas opiniunculas a communis, publica & generalis sententia auctoritate secreto sit. Stemus ergo potius in hoc argumento Augustini judicio, cuius & ratio evidens, & auctoritas infinitis parasangis Vincentiana superior est. Nulli ergo Patrum sententiae, quam ex Scriptoribus Canonicis vel probabili ratione non confirmaverint, in posterum fidem adhibeamus.
units.tr: But before I conclude this chapter, it is worth testing both methods, his own and Augustine's, on Vincent himself. Augustine denies that we are bound by the opinion of any author unless it is established and confirmed either by the authority of the canonical Scriptures or by some probable reason. But what Scripture or what reason did this Lérins hermit offer to prove to us his assertion? We are therefore free, by Augustine's rule and practice, to reject it, especially since the ground for rejecting it is clear, while the author himself offered no ground for establishing it. You see from Augustine's decision that Vincent's opinion should carry no authority with us, however great the name of author among the Fathers you may imagine it to be. But let us now judge Vincent by his own opinion. He forbids that writers be believed unless they have lived and taught holily and wisely until death. Who can properly guarantee that he himself lived and taught in this way? Who will confirm that he was not a heretic or a supporter of heretics? For whatever else he was, he clearly favours the Semipelagians, who at that time in Gaul were tearing down the memory of Augustine and were condemned by the Church as the Five Articles. The Commonitorium shows this. In it, though without naming the men, he hints that the charges which Prosper and Hilary brought to Celestine about the new teachers of the Gallic Massilians were false and were slandered against the Gauls. Indeed, the name Vincentian, which Prosper gives to the objections he refutes against Augustine, proclaims that Vincent was the author of them. The praises which Gennadius heaps on him also greatly increase the suspicion, since it is agreed that Gennadius was of the same party. This is clear from the fact that he esteems so highly the patriarch of the Pelagians, Rufinus, the presbyter of Aquileia, calling him no small part of the teachers of the Church, while he openly accuses Jerome, Rufinus's adversary, of being envious and a slanderer. It is clear too from the fact that he is most unfair to Augustine, and shamelessly twists against him the saying of the Holy Spirit in Solomon: In a multitude of words there will not be lack of sin. So I cannot sufficiently marvel at the rashness of Cardinal Perron, who, to the very great discredit of his own example, numbers among the teachers this writer, who is suspected of heresy, while for the most part praising him with the commendation of Saint Vincent of Lérins. Since Vincent was such a man, it is no wonder that he esteems so highly the judgements of the Fathers, by whose authority, as everyone knows, the Pelagians and Semipelagians abused. For when those who had written on this subject before the time of Pelagius had said many things rather carelessly, things which caused trouble for the orthodox, the Pelagians and the Massilians turned these to their own purpose. But even if Vincent had lacked none of those qualities which he himself requires in order that men may give a fitting testimony in this matter, still that opinion of his could carry no weight at all. It does not occur among any of the Fathers who were before him, and it is plainly opposed by Augustine and Jerome in the passages we cited above. Finally, it suffers from obscurities and ambiguities that cannot be resolved. So, although he were holy and learned, although a bishop, although a confessor and martyr (which he was not), yet his opinion (to use his own words here) is secretly set apart from the common, public and general judgement, among the private and hidden little opinions of his own. Let us therefore rather stand in this matter by the judgement of Augustine, whose reasoning is evident, and whose authority is far superior to Vincent's by infinite leagues. Therefore let us in future give no credence to any opinion of the Fathers which they have not confirmed from the canonical writers or by some probable reason.

units.la: Ratio iii. Patres ea ratione scripsisse ut manifestum sit iis inter scribendum, de Religione pronunciare non fuisse propositum. Eorum in quibus lapsi sunt, & errauerunt exempla quædam.
units.tr: Reason 3. The Fathers wrote in such a way that it is clear to their readers that they did not intend to pronounce on religion. Some examples of places where they slipped and erred.

units.la: VErum quisquis diligenter eam rationem experiderit qua Patres in scribendo vsi sunt, is nullum aliud in hac causa testimonium desiderabit. Scriptorum ipsorum ratio satis perspicuè testatur plerorumque eam mentem fuisse non ut placita nobis sola dicentium auctoritate suffulta pronunciarent, sed tantum ut suas in varias Religionis partes nobiscum meditationes communicarent, ea lege vt liberum nobis esset eas, prout commodum videretur, examini subjicere, admittere, vel repudiare. Diserte id professus est supra Hieronymus, cùm ageret de ingenio & ratione commentariorum in S. Scripturam. Si aliud fuisset eorum consilium, tempus non triuissent (quod plurimum faciunt) in colligendis variis aliorum sententiis. Hæc diligentia in Doctore laudem meretur; in iudice ridicula est. Neque verò eorum stilus judici convenit. Illa quæ Patribus familiaria sunt, partim, ut supra diximus ex ornamentis Rhetoricis, partim ex Dialecticis tricis & aculeis contexta involucra nullum in iudicium sententiis locum habent. Quis enim pigmenta ejusmodi in Senatusconsulto, vel in nudo testimonio adhibentem ferat? Sed illa præsertim incuria, securitas, & negligentia, quæ in iis libris cernitur (qui nobis pro norma fidei nunc obtruduntur) hoc ipsum quod diximus luculentissimè docet. Credibilene est homines adeo exquisita sanctitate illustres, si veram & perfectam fidei normam posteris tradere in animo habuissent, in tanti momenti negotio adeo perfunctorie versaversaturos fuisse? Nec sanè, sine summa eorum injuria, fingi potest ipsos aliter in id indubituros quàm oculis apertis, mente composita & attenta, summâque cum omnium animi facultatum contentione, ne quid eis excideret quod, vel ab ipsorum sapientia, vel à fidelium commodis alienum esset. Iudices, quorum vel mediocris est æquitas, non aliter de Titij Mæviique bobus, fundo, aut stillicidiis pronunciant. Quanto magis eadem maturitas, eademque gravitas hic requiritur, ubi agitur de fide, de anima & de salute æterna totius generis humani? Absit ut existimemus sanctos istos viros de huiusmodi causa, nisi summa cum diligentia, tum attentione judicare instituisse. At manifestum est pleraque quæ supersunt eorum volumina vel negligenter, vel (ut mollius dicam) secuè conscripta fuisse, sive ipsam rerum inventionem, sive ordinem aut elocutionem spectes. Si ergo eius sanctitas & sapientiæ, qua floruerunt, laudi faucmus, profectò statuendum est nunquam eos hoc consilio ita scripsisse, ut judicio omni provocatione majori, de fidei capitibus decidérent; vel ut quæ dixissent, ea à nobis haberentur pro totidem Senatusconsultis, vel edictis Prætoriis. Fatendum est quod res est, eorum monumenta nihil aliud esse quàm litteraria varię indolis, ex concursu variarum occasionum nata opuscula, pro temporis, ingenij, & ætatis ratione magis minúsve elucubrata. Quanquam autem ille accurationis & maturitatis neglectus satis per se pateat cuilibet non ofcitanter Patres legenti, attamen, ne quid sine probatione affirmare videar, huc quædam eius specimina in medium afferre constitui.
units.tr: Whoever carefully considers the method the Fathers followed in writing will need no other witness in this matter. The method of their writings bears clear witness that most of them did not mean to lay down opinions supported only by the authority of those who speak them. They meant rather to share with us their own reflections on the various parts of religion, on the condition that we remained free to examine them as we thought fit, and either to accept or to reject them. Jerome stated this openly above, when he discussed the nature and method of his commentaries on Holy Scripture. If their purpose had been otherwise, they would not have spent so much time (as they very largely did) in gathering the varied opinions of others. This diligence earns praise in a teacher; in a judge it is ridiculous. Nor does their style suit a judge. The ornaments that are familiar to the Fathers, partly drawn, as we said above, from rhetorical embellishment and partly from the dialectical tricks and barbs woven into their wrappings, have no place in judicial sentences. For who would tolerate such decoration in a decree of the Senate, or in a bare piece of testimony? Moreover, the carelessness, the complacency and the negligence that can be seen in those books (which are now thrust upon us as the rule of faith) most clearly teach the very point I have made. Is it credible that men so remarkable for their exquisite holiness, if they had intended to hand down to posterity a true and perfect rule of faith, would have treated a matter of such great importance so perfunctorily? Nor, without great injustice to them, can it be imagined that they would have approached it otherwise than with eyes open, mind composed and attentive, and with the utmost effort of all their mental powers, lest anything slip from them that was unworthy of their wisdom or harmful to the interests of the faithful. Judges who have even moderate fairness do not pronounce otherwise on the oxen of Titius and Maevius, on a piece of land, or on the right of dripping water. How much more, then, is the same ripeness and the same seriousness required here, where the subject is faith, the soul and the eternal salvation of the whole human race? Far be it from us to think that those holy men undertook to judge such a matter except with the greatest care and attention. Yet it is plain that most of the volumes they have left were written carelessly or (to put it more gently) hastily, whether one looks at the invention of the material, its arrangement or its expression. If, therefore, we give praise to their holiness and to the wisdom for which they flourished, we must surely conclude that they never wrote with the intention of deciding, on the articles of faith, matters beyond all possibility of challenge; nor that what they said should be held by us as so many decrees of the Senate or edicts of the praetor. We must admit what is the truth: their monuments are nothing other than literary works of varied character, little pieces arising from the coming together of various occasions, elaborated more or less carefully according to the time, the talent and the age of their authors. Although this lack of accuracy and maturity is sufficiently evident in itself to anyone who reads the Fathers with attention, nevertheless, so that I may not seem to assert anything without proof, I have decided to bring forward some specimens of it here.

units.la: Primò ergo inter Patrum opera non pauca occurrunt raptim scripta; quædam etiam ex tempore effusa, adeòque eiusmodi ut admodum probabile sit auctores ipsos multa in iis fuisse emendaturos, si recognoscere licuisset. Hieronymus Prologo in quasdam homilias quas è Græcis Latinas fecefat dicit, Origenem eas ex tempore in Ecclesia peroravisse. De his ille nos monuit: sed quàm multa sunt ejusdem generis inter Chrysostomi, Augustini & aliorum sermones, quos cum vulgo putemus maturè & per otium meditatos, digestos & elaboratos, vero fortasse propius est subitò, ex aliqua occasione in lucem ediros, citiúsque naros quàm conceptos. Hieronymus non semel testatur se quæ scribit raptim & properanter dictasse. Ita ad finem prolixæ illius epistolæ quam ad Fabiolam misit, se eam ad unam lucubrationem culam,cùm jam funis solveretur è littore, & naturæ crebriùs inclamarent propero sermone dictavisse air. Et (quod longè majoris est momenti) trium Salomonis voluminum Proverbiorum, Ecclesiastæ & Canticorum interpretationem, tridui opus vocat, quibus tamen accuratè & arrentè legendis (propter difficultates quibus scatent, siue voces & phraseologiam, siue res ipsas spectas) vix mensis vnus satis sit. Er tamen, si vera sunt Ecclesiæ Romanæ decreta, exiguum illud tridui opus adeo fausto fidere natum est, ut non solùm probarum & maximi factum sit, sed etiam à Concilio Tridentino in Canonem relatum. An Domini nostri consilium fuerit, ut hic Hieronymi tam præceps labor pro suo verbo haberetur, quæranr quibus vel lubet vel vacat. Ego sanè certò posse videor negare Hieronymum id unquam vel cogitasse vel sperasse futurum, ut in isto ordine collocaretur aliquando istud suum opus, quòd non sit verisimile ipsum, in eo elucubrando opusculo, quod tanti olim futurum prævideret, non alia quanto plus & temporis & operæ posituru fuisse. Ita fir interdum ut res quibusdamsupra spem & vota cedant.
units.tr: First, then, many of the Fathers' works contain things written in haste; some were even poured out extemporaneously, and so of a kind that it is very probable their authors would have corrected much in them, had they been allowed to revise them. Jerome, in the preface to certain homilies which he turned from Greek into Latin, says that Origen had delivered them extempore in the Church. He warned us of this himself. But how many sermons of the same kind are there among those of Chrysostom, Augustine and others, which we commonly think were thought out in good time and at leisure, digested and polished, whereas in truth they were perhaps more often brought suddenly to light on some occasion, and sooner spoken than composed! Jerome more than once testifies that what he writes he dictated hastily and in a rush. Thus at the end of that long letter which he sent to Fabiola, he says that he dictated it in a single hurried night's work, when the rope was already being loosed from the shore, and nature kept crying out more and more loudly, with a hurried speech. And (what is of far greater importance) he calls his interpretation of the three books of Solomon, the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, a work of three days; yet to read these accurately and carefully (on account of the difficulties with which they abound, whether one looks at the words and phraseology or at the matters themselves) hardly one month would be enough. And yet, if the decrees of the Roman Church are true, this little work of three days was so happily born that it was not only approved and held in the highest regard, but was also placed in the canon by the Council of Trent. Whether it was the intention of our Lord that this headlong labour of Jerome should be held as his own word, let those inquire who wish or have the leisure. I for my part seem to be able to say with certainty that Jerome never thought or hoped that his work would one day be placed in that order; for it is not likely that he, in drafting a little work which he foresaw would someday be of such importance, would not have spent more time and effort on it. So it happens at times that some things turn out beyond hope and wish.

units.la: Idem de alio suo opere inquir. Extemporalis est dictatio, & tanta ad lumen lucernulæ facilitate profusa, ut notariorum manus lingua præcurreret, & signa ac furra verborum volubilitas sermonem obrueret. Alibi, opus maioris momenti, Commentarios scilicet in Matthæum, eadem ratione excusat; quod temporis angustiis coactus fuerit eos summa celeritate dictare. Et Præfatione in secundum. dum Commentarium in Epistolam ad Ephesios narrat, sic in scribendo interdum perfingulos dies usque ad numerum mille versuum pervenire. Breviter ne si omnes ejusmodi locos commemoravero lectori taedium afferram, Hieronymo solennis est illa excusatio; vel ab ea orditur, vel in eam desinit in plerisque suis lucubrationibus; vel urget tabellarius, vel ipse allis occupationibus avocatur, vel aliqua alia de causa festinare cogitur, omnia subito & cursim facit. Interdum animus morbo dejectus jacet, interdum lingua ex Hebraicarum vocum pronunciatione rubiginem contraxit; stilus nonnunquam solito tardior est. Tuam fidem, Lector, si quicquid scribit pro oraculo habendum putavit, nisi quaedam excusari, quaedam condonari voluit, quid iltis omnibus opus fuit? Quis unquam judicem temporis angustias excusantem audivit? Haec in judice defensio crimen est; quod hoc ipsum, cursim nempe & festinanter judicare, sit culpa gravissima. Mihi quidem Patres isti judicum dignitati, quas nos eos, velint, nolint, donamus, non videntur clarius renuntiare potuisse, quam dum ira scribunt ac loquuntur. Sed vel tacente Hieronymo (quanquam quae ille de se nos monet ad judicandum de caeteris Patribus facem praeferre debent (quam parum temporis ac curae in plerisque operibus suis adhibuerint Patres ipsa per se loquuntur. Alias qui tantis, tamque in omni litterarum genere versatis Scriptoribus, tot, sive in Historia, sive in Grammatica, sive in Philosophia, sive in aliis Disciplinis errores, licet leviusculi, excidisse ent? Eorum quaedam exempla hic referam, non ut quicquam de magnorum istorum virorum laude deterram, veluti eos minutiarum istarum rudes & imperitos fuisse putem, sed ut eos in scriptis suis non semper omnes ingenii sui vires explicuisse doceam, & quandoque, neque totam suam industriam, usque omnes suas horas iis condendis adhibuisse. Patrachronismos immensos & frequentes hic mitto, ut quum Iustinus scribit Davidem mille & quingentis annis ante vixisse quàm Christus homo factus crucifigeretur; cùm ex setie temporum & historiis, quâ sacris, quâ profanis, facile fit colligere à morte Davidis usque ad Christum natum circiter mille & viginti quinque aut triginta annos tantum effluxisse. Cum Epiphanius scribit Mosem anno ætatis trigesimo ex Ægypto profectum cum Israelitis mare rubrum pedibus ingressum, testante contra S. Scriptura tum octoginta annos natum fuisse. Cùm refert Hierosolymorum sub versionem ad quintum & sexagesimum annum à Christi passione. Chrysostomus scribit suo tempore quingentesimum agi annum ab Hierosolymæ à Tito excisæ clade. Item à quo Paulus vixit annos præteriisse quingentos. Alibi quadringentos annos ab illis temporibus ad suam memoriam putat. At vero constat annos ab illius urbis clade ad Chrysostomi exilium non plures quam 353. aut 354. effluxisse, quod & ipse semel tetigit, scribens 300. annos esse & amplius à quo Hierosolyma excisa erant. Idé alibi Ezechiam mille post Davidis mortem annis vixisse ait, & inter quos ne 400. quidem annos intercessisse constat. Et in genere veterum omnium Chronologia minutum in modum involuta, & supina, & incondita est, & pleraque à vera temporum ratione alienissima ut notantur & fusè probant recentiores omnes Scaliger, Petavius & alii. Sed cùm hæc præ summa tenuitate nonnunquam perspicacissimos fugiant, & in iis aliquando etiam diligentissimi quiqi hallucinentur, pluribus in iis inquirendis supersedeo. Sed en tibi in aliis argumentis quæ horum Scriptorum securitatem perspicuè evincant. Iustinus agens de Versione Septuaginta interpretum dicit Ptolomæum Egypti Regem legatos ad Herodem Iudæ regem misisse, cùm extra dubium sit Legatos istos missos fuisse ad summum Sacerdotem Eleazarum, ducentis & quod excurrit annis, antequam Herodes regnaret in Iudæa. Epiphanius tribus aut quatuor locis docet Peripateticorum & Pythagoreorum eandem fuisse in
units.tr: He says the same about another of his works: It is an extempore dictation, poured out with such ease by the light of a little lamp that the hands of the notaries were outrun by the tongue, and the rapid flow of words overwhelmed the signs and the writing. Elsewhere, for a work of greater importance, namely his commentaries on Matthew, he makes the same excuse, saying that he was forced by the shortness of time to dictate them with the utmost speed. And in the preface to the second book of his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians he relates that in writing it sometimes, for each single day, he reached as many as a thousand verses. In short, lest I weary the reader by recounting all such passages: that excuse is customary with Jerome; he either begins with it or ends with it in most of his compositions. Either a messenger is pressing him, or he himself is called away by other occupations, or for some other reason he is compelled to hurry, and does everything suddenly and cursorily. Sometimes his spirit lies cast down by illness; sometimes his tongue has contracted a rust from pronouncing Hebrew words; sometimes his pen is slower than usual.
