If Jerome, reader, had wished whatever he wrote to be held as an oracle, why would all these excuses have been needed, some to be pardoned and some to be forgiven? Who has ever heard a judge pleading the shortness of time in his own defence? In a judge, such a defence is itself a crime, since to judge in this very way, that is cursorily and hastily, is the gravest fault. To me indeed those Fathers, in respect of the dignity of judges which we, whether they wish it or not, bestow upon them, do not seem able to have declared it more clearly than when they write and speak in anger. But even without Jerome's testimony (although what he tells us about himself ought to shed light for judging the other Fathers), the Fathers themselves show by their own words how little time and care they devoted to most of their works. Otherwise, how could such writers, so great and so versed in every kind of learning, have fallen into so many errors, whether in history, in grammar, in philosophy or in other disciplines, however slight those errors may be? I will set out some examples of them here, not to detract in any way from the praise of these great men, as if I thought them unskilled and ignorant of such trifles, but to show that they did not always set forth all the powers of their minds in their writings, and sometimes did not devote all their diligence, nor all their hours, to composing them. I pass over here the great and frequent parachronisms, such as when Justin writes that David lived fifteen hundred years before Christ, made man, was crucified; whereas from the sequence of times and from histories, both sacred and profane, it is easy to gather that only about one thousand and twenty-five or thirty years had elapsed from the death of David to the birth of Christ. When Epiphanius writes that Moses, in his thirtieth year, left Egypt and walked with the Israelites through the Red Sea on foot, whereas Holy Scripture testifies on the contrary that he was then eighty years old. When he reports that the overthrow of Jerusalem took place in the sixty-fifth year after the passion of Christ. Chrysostom writes that in his own time five hundred years had passed since the ruin of Jerusalem by Titus; likewise that five hundred years had passed since Paul lived. Elsewhere he thinks that four hundred years lay between those times and his own memory. Yet it is certain that from the destruction of that city to the exile of Chrysostom no more than 353 or 354 years had passed, which he himself touched upon once when writing that it was 300 years and more since Jerusalem had been destroyed. Elsewhere again he says that Hezekiah lived a thousand years after the death of David, whereas it is certain that not even four hundred years lay between them. And in general the chronology of all the ancients is involved in a minute and careless manner, is confused and inaccurate, and for the most part wholly alien to the true reckoning of times, as all the more recent scholars, Scaliger, Petavius and others, note and prove at length. But since these matters, because of their extreme subtlety, sometimes escape even the most perceptive, and since even the most diligent men are at times mistaken about them, I refrain from inquiring into many of them. Yet here is evidence from other arguments which clearly proves the carelessness of these writers. Justin, speaking of the Version of the Seventy interpreters, says that Ptolemy, king of Egypt, sent envoys to Herod, king of Judaea; whereas it is beyond doubt that those envoys were sent to the high priest Eleazar, more than two hundred years before Herod reigned in Judaea. Epiphanius teaches in three or four places that the sect of the Peripatetics and that of the Pythagoreans were the same among the Gentile philosophers; [those who are known even to boys, and who disagreed no less sharply than the Stoics with the Epicureans]. Augustine, however, says that Aristotle taught that the soul is a fifth body, because in the matter...

units.la: a Epiph. in Anacephal. p.122. Ex Epiph. adv. haeres. Iud. 9. in Gentilium Philosophia sectam: quos vel pueris notum est, non minùs intense dissensisse quàm Stoicos ab Epicureis. Augustinus verò ait tradere Aristotelem animam esse quintum corpus, quia in re deceptum eum suisse & ex Aristotele ipso patet cuius superstunt nobilissimæ de anima disputationes, & à Ludovico Viue & Leonardo Cocquæo scholis in ipsum locum obsaruatum est. Idem Epiphanius præter totius veteris Historiæ fidem scribit ex mysteriis ab Orpheo & aliis Athenas invectis derivatas esse varias sectas sententiasque Philosophorum, Stoicos immortalitatem animorum & Metempsychosin credidisse, quod utrumque falsum est: Nabuchodonosorem, captis Hierosolymis, coloniam in regionem Samaritanorum deduxisse, cùm longe antea Salamanassaris temporibus ea deportatio facta fuisset. Quid quod fallitur etiam in rebus quæ paulo antequàm nasceretur acciderunt? Vt cum Arium mortuum fa- cit ante Concilium Nicænum, historiamq; Meletij & schismatis cuius ille auctor fuit, omnino perperam refert. Quales sint ipsius etiam Augustini errores: vt cùm Cresconio objicienti Litteras à Synodo Sardicensi Donatistis missas respondet; Disce ergo quod nescis: Sardicense Concilium Arianorum fuit, quod notum iam diu est, ut habemus, contractu maximè contra Athanasium Episcopum Alexandrinum. Hæc ille, contra omnium Ecclesiasticæ historiæ Scriptorum fidem, qui Sardicensem Synodum & Catholicorum, & pro Athanasio fuisse testantur. Idem de Basilio & Gregoria Nazianzeno, Insignes (inquit) viri & iam clara praediti sanctitate, & sicut feruntur etiam carne germani. Atqui Basilij frater, non Nazianzenus, sed Nyssenus Gregorius & ferebatur & revera erat. Idem in suis adversus Donatistas disputationibus constanter vetur rem certò exploratam ponit, hanc ante Cyprianum fuisse universæ Ecclesiæ consuetudinem, ut ab hæreticis baptizati sine baptismo admitterentur. At Firmilianus certissimus suorum temporum testis, disertissimè affirmmat alium fuisse Ecclesiarum Cappadociæ & Ciliciæ jam inde ab initio morem; Nos (inquit) veritati & consuetudinem iungimus; & consuetudini Romanorum consuetudinem, sed veritatis opponimus, ab initio hoc tenentes quod à Christo & ab Apostolo traditum est. Nec meminimus hoc apud nos aliquando cæpisse, cum semper iste observatum sit, ut nonnisi unam Dei Ecclesiam nosse mus & sanctam Baptisma nonnisi sanctæ Ecclesiæ computaremus. Idem nobis pro comperto narrat Epiphanius de 80. hæresibus opus, sex libris distinctum, historica narratione commemorate omnia, nulla disputatione adversus errorem pro veritate decertare: brevesque esse libellos, qui si in unum redigantur, nec ipsum fore suis longitudine comparandum. Quæ quam sint à vero aliena, etiam hodie superites Epiphanianum opus, loquitur Augustiniano multis partibus prolixius, & perpetua contra singulas fere hæreses disputatione decertans.
units.tr: a Epiph. in Anacephal. p.122. From Epiphanius, Against Heresies, Jude 9, concerning the sects of Gentile philosophy: as even children know, they disagreed no less sharply than the Stoics disagreed with the Epicureans. Augustine, however, says that Aristotle taught that the soul is a fifth body, and that he was mistaken in this. Aristotle's own writings show it, since his most noble disputations on the soul survive, and Ludovicus Vives and Leonardus Coquaeus have pointed out the error in their commentaries on that passage. Epiphanius likewise writes, contrary to the whole testimony of ancient history, that the various sects and opinions of the philosophers were derived from the mysteries that Orpheus and others brought to Athens. He says that the Stoics believed in the immortality of souls and in metempsychosis, and both claims are false. He says that Nebuchadnezzar, after taking Jerusalem, settled a colony in the region of the Samaritans, though that deportation had been made long before, in the time of Shalmaneser. Why should I speak of his errors even in events that happened shortly before he was born? He makes Arius die before the Council of Nicaea, and he reports the history of Meletius and of the schism of which Meletius was the author entirely wrongly. Augustine's own errors are of the same kind. When he answers Cresconius, who objected to letters sent to the Donatists by the Council of Sardica, he says: Learn therefore what you do not know: the Council of Sardica was a council of the Arians, which has long been known, as we have it, gathered chiefly against Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria. He says this against the testimony of all the writers of ecclesiastical history, who attest that the Council of Sardica was both Catholic and held in defence of Athanasius. He says the same about Basil and Gregory Nazianzen: Distinguished men, already endowed with clear sanctity, and, as they are reported, even brothers in the flesh. Yet Basil's brother was not Nazianzen but Gregory of Nyssa, and that was both the report and the truth. Again, in his disputations against the Donatists, Augustine constantly takes it as a firmly established fact that before Cyprian it was the custom of the whole Church to admit without baptism those baptized by heretics. But Firmilian, the most reliable witness of his own times, expressly states that the churches of Cappadocia and Cilicia had from the beginning a different custom. We (he says) join truth and custom; and we set the custom of the Romans, which is custom, against truth, holding from the beginning what was handed down by Christ and the Apostle. Nor do we remember that this began among us at any time, since it has always been observed that we know only the one Church of God, and we count baptism as belonging only to the holy Church. Epiphanius, in his work on eighty heresies, divided into six books, likewise tells us as a known fact that he recounted everything in historical narrative and did not contend against error with any disputation on behalf of truth, and that his little books, if gathered into one, would not be comparable in length to Augustine's. How far these claims are from the truth is shown by the Epiphanian work itself, which survives today; it is much longer than Augustine's in many parts and contends in continuous disputation against almost every heresy.

units.la: Narrat Iustinus ut rem certissimam sub Claudio Cæsare Simoni Mago erectam fuisse Romæ, inter duos pontes in amne Tiberi, statuam cum hac inscriptione, SIMONI DEO SANCTO: Sed hodie inter eruditos constat inscriptionem fuisse Dei cuiusdam minorum gentium apud Romanos, in hæc verba, SEMONI SANCO DEO, quam bonus iste Pater perperam legerat Semoni pro Simoni & sanco, pro sancto accipiens.
units.tr: Justin reports, as a most certain fact, that under the emperor Claudius a statue was erected at Rome to Simon Magus, between two bridges on the Tiber, with this inscription: TO SIMON THE HOLY GOD. But today it is established among scholars that the inscription belonged to a certain god of the lesser peoples among the Romans, and read: TO SEMO THE HOLY GOD. That good father had misread it, taking Semo for Simon and sanco for sancto.

units.la: Eusebius, & post Eusebium Hieronymus, non semel referunt Iosephum Iudæorum scriptorem vernaculum asseruisse, illo tempore quo crucifixus est Dominus, ex adytis templi virtutum cœlestium erupisse voces dicentium migremus ex his sedibus. Atqui constat Iosephum ista referre ad tempora postrema obsidionis, quæ accidit annis, post mortem Domini, quadraginta. Idem, & plerique omnes Patres, velut rem certam narrant Philonem Iudæum in libro de vita contemplativa Ascetarum Christianorum instituta describere. Et tamen ipse Philonis liber, qui etiamnum extat, satis clamat ipsum agere de Essæis quæ vna fuit ex tribus Iudæorum sectis; minimè verò de Christianis, vt Scaliger & alij multi annotarunt.
units.tr: Eusebius, and after him Jerome, more than once report that Josephus, the Jewish writer, asserted that at the time the Lord was crucified, voices of heavenly powers were heard coming from the inner sanctuaries of the temple, saying, Let us depart from these seats. Yet it is clear that Josephus refers this to the last stages of the siege, which took place forty years after the death of the Lord. Again, Philo the Jew, in his book on the contemplative life, is said by almost all the Fathers, as a certain fact, to describe the institutions of Christian ascetics. Yet Philo's book, which still survives, clearly shows that he is speaking of the Essenes, one of the three sects of the Jews, and by no means of Christians, as Scaliger and many others have observed.

units.la: Ambrosius vt supra attigimus per Gog & Magog apud Ezechielem Gothos qui tum temporis orbem Christianum inundarant parùm consideratè intelligit. Eadem securitate alibi dicit Zachariam, Ioannis Baptistæ Patrem, Iudæorum summum sacerdotem fuisse, Idemque etiam tradunt Augustinus & Chrysostomus, quod salsissimum esse euidenter probat Baronius.
units.tr: Ambrose, as we touched on above, understands rather carelessly that the Goths, who at that time were overrunning the Christian world, are meant by Gog and Magog in Ezekiel. With the same carelessness he says elsewhere that Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was high priest of the Jews. Augustine and Chrysostom also hand this down, and Baronius clearly proves that it is most absurd.

units.la: Non sunt meliora quæ sequuntur. Epiphanius docet fluuium Phison de quo Moses in descriptione Eden, eundem esse qui ab Indis & Æthiobibus Ganges appellatur, à Græcis Indus quique magna Æthiopia penetrata, tandem intra Gades in ingentem Oceanum erumpit. Miranda sanè, si quæ vnquam fuit, Geographia, & quæ integro fermè hemisphærio disjunctos locos confundit.
units.tr: What follows is no better. Epiphanius teaches that the river Pishon, of which Moses speaks in describing Eden, is the same river that the Indians and Ethiopians call the Ganges, the Greeks the Indus; that it penetrates great Ethiopia and finally breaks out into the vast Ocean near Gades. Surely this is a remarkable geography, if ever there was one, which confuses places separated by almost a whole hemisphere.

units.la: Basilius, scriptor cætera præstantissimus, à Danubij fontibus paulò proprius aberrauit, quem in Pyrenæorum montium radicibus oriri tradit. Eridanum verò (quod prodigiosum est) ex Riphæis vltra Scythiam interiam montibus. Hæc flumina mihi in memoriam revocent quod Patres omnes vnanimi consensu Gheon Paradisi terrestris pro Nilo accipiunt; quod Cardinalem Perronium sic fefellit, vt id ipsum, velut ex S. Scripturæ auctoritate obtrudere, eíque, tanquam in specie absurdum, impingere non dubitet, quanquam ab eo errore alienissimæ. Siue enim Hebræos, siue Græcos, siue Latinos codices consulas, de Nilo Paradisi terras alluente apud eam altum Silantium. Finxerant quidem sibi Patres Nilum vnum esse è fluuiis quos Paradiso Moses assignat, sed præter omnem rationem, vt disputauit Scaliger & Petauius aguouit.
units.tr: Basil, otherwise the most excellent of writers, strayed rather far from the sources of the Danube, which he says rise at the foot of the Pyrenees. And he says the Eridanus (which is prodigious) rises in the Riphaean mountains beyond interior Scythia. These rivers bring to mind that all the Fathers unanimously take the Gihon of the earthly paradise to be the Nile. This so deceived Cardinal Perron that he does not hesitate to press it upon others as if it were the authority of Holy Scripture, and to thrust it on them as something absurd in itself, although he is most remote from that error. For whether you consult the Hebrew, the Greek or the Latin manuscripts, you will find nothing about the Nile watering the lands of Paradise, beside which there is a deep silence. The Fathers had indeed imagined that the Nile is one of the rivers that Moses assigns to Paradise, but this is contrary to all reason, as Scaliger argued and Petavius acknowledged.

units.la: Patrum Philosophia non minus aliquando miranda est quam geographia, vt cùm plantas sensu & intelligentia præditas esse contendit Tertullianus. Cùm Epiphanius docet vitam hominis mortui instaurari sine animaposse. Cùm Ambrosius narrat solem ad sui temperiem alimentum aquarum sibi sumere, indéque fieri ut eũ aliquando madidum atque rorantem videamus. Cùm alii formamcœli sphæricam acriter negant †ut Chrysostomus,* voluntque cameram esse quam potens aquæ, illi basisinstar substratæ, ut auctor Quæstionum quæ lustini nomine circumferuntur. Alij in mundi rotunditatem invehuntur, Antipodésque dari præfractè negant, adeo vt penè qui in contraria sunt sententia pro hæreticis habeant. * Cujusmodi est & Gregorii magni deliratio, somniantis in Sicilia & vicinis insulis Ætnæ, & similium montium incendia tormentorum infernalium ollas cruciare, quæ scilicet laxatis (inquit) quotidie finibus excrescunt, ut mundi termino appropinquante; quanto certum est illic amplius exurendos colligi, tanto & eadem tormentorum loca amplius videantur aperiri. Sed hæc non sunt simpliciter imperitiæ peccata; errores sunt ex rationis & judicij defectu nati.
units.tr: The philosophy of the Fathers is sometimes no less wonderful than their geography. Tertullian, for example, contends that plants are endowed with sense and intelligence. Epiphanius teaches that the life of a dead man can be restored without a soul. Ambrose says that the sun takes water to itself as nourishment to maintain its warmth, and that this is why we sometimes see it wet and dripping. Chrysostom and others sharply deny that the heavens are spherical, and want the sky to be a vault, with a mighty body of water spread beneath it like a base, as the author of the Questions circulated under Justin's name holds. Others rush against the roundness of the world and stubbornly deny that there are antipodes, so that they almost count as heretics those who hold the opposite view. Such too is the raving of Gregory the Great, who dreams that the fires of Etna and similar mountains in Sicily and the neighbouring islands are the furnaces that torment the infernal punishments, which, as he says, with their boundaries loosening daily, grow larger, so that as the end of the world draws near, the more it is certain that more are gathered there to be burned, by so much the more the same places of torment seem to be opened. But these are not simply sins of ignorance; they are errors born of a lack of reason and judgement.

units.la: Jam in Grammaticam propter linguæ Hebraicæ imperitiam multo etiam crebrius quàm in cæteras artes peccant: ut cum Optatus, Vigilius, Isidorus, PseudoAnacletus nomen Cephas à Græca voce κεφαλὴ deducunt; etsi hæc caput, Cepha verò) quod est Syriacum) petram significet; quod ipse Evangelista disertè monuerat. Similis est Lactantij & Ambrosij error dum, vocis Hebraicæ Pascha, quæ transitum proprie sonat, originem repetunt à verbo Græco πάσχειν, quod est pati; quos in hac parte præeuntes secutus est Innocentius Papa III. serm. 1. in Concil. Lateran. Etiam absurdior atque incredibilior est Gregorij I. quantumvis magni, hallucinatio in Cornustibio (quod unius è lobi filiabus nomen est apud Latinum interpretem sid enim ille sic accipit ac si esset ex cornu & tibia compositum. Quia percornu (inquit) tibiam vnum verbum ex viroque composuit (Interpres Latinus) vtrumq; verbum per vnam orationis partem in Latina lingua a transfusum quo voluit genere licitè vocauit. Movebat enim hominem quod ille non Cornutibiam, sed Cornusflibium dixisset. Bonus Papa vel nescivit, vel certè non attendit, quid esset Latinè flibium; quod nunc etiam pueri sciunt. Eiusdem est commatis quod illud è Cantico Salomonis exponens. Botrus cypri dilectus meus mihi; Cyprum, de Insula Cypro, accipit, in qua (inquit) uberiores vineæ quam alibi nascuntur, nescions id hic plantæ odoratissimæ nomen esse. Sed tam puerilīter istum labi non indignum fortasse fuit, qui litteras fastidit & pro nugis habet, iisq; fludere episcopum, impium & profanum putat; & alibi penè gloriatur se artem loquendi, quam magisteria disciplinæ exterioris insinuant, seruare despexisse, non barbarismi confusionem devitare, situs, motúsque prepositionum, casúsque seruare contemnere, quia indignum (inquit) vehementer existimo, ut verba cœlestis oraculi restringam sub regulis Donati; quasi verò humani Diviniq; sermonis leges addiscere & observare, id sit Cœlestia oracula Donato subjicere. Linguarum quidem eruditionem eo usque contempsit ut Græcam tametsi ante Pontificatum Constantinopoli complures annos Apocrisiarius vixerit, ne attingere quidem voluerit; quam se scire non semel negat: Nos (inquit) nec Græcum novimus, nec aliquod opus aliquâ do Græce conscripsimus. Nonnullos huius generis aliorum errores supra observavimus ab Hieronymo notatos, cui sanè plurimum debet Ecclesia, tum quod in accurate addiscenda lingua Hebraica labori non pepercit, tum quod nullos reveritus, omnes ejusmodi lapsus liberè reprehendit. Reliqui omnes, paucis exceptis, ut in tenebris versantes, prætentant viam. Inde tot ineptæ nominum propriorum, quæ in Scriptura occurrunt etymologiæ. Quis sine stupore legere posset quod habetur de nomine Iesu apud Irenæum? Iesus (inquit) nomen secundum propriam Hebræorum linguam litterarū est duarum & dimidiæ...... & Hh 2 secundum antiquam Hebraicam linguam cælum est. Quæ in ipso Matthæi Evangelij initio disertè non docuisset Angelus, Christum ideo Iesum dictum, quod servaturus esset populum suum à peccatis ipsorum. Ejusdem commatis est quod alibi docet nomen Adonai aliquando nominabile & admirabile significare, aliquando autem duplicata littera delta cum aspiratione, vt puta Addhonei, præsinientem & separantem terram ab aqua, & similia etyma vocum Sabaoth & Iaoth. Ejusmodi furfuris sunt quæ eodē libro reliquis omnibus tam veteribus quam recentioribus ne fando quidem audita aperit mysteria. Deum Hebraicè Barneth dici, antiquásque & primas Hebrœorum literas sacerdotales nuncupatas decem numero esse, & scribi quasque per quindecim. Clemens Alexandrinus ex eodem fonte hauserat id quod mirificè docet de derivatione vocis Abraham. Exponitur(inquit) Pater electuosoni, & nominis Rebecca, quod dicit item exponi Dei Glorio. Hilarius Sehon infructuosæ arboris interpretationem esse dicit. Sed nos Hieronymus monet eum sermonis Hebræi ignarum fuisse, & Græcarum literarum aurulàm quandam tantum cepisse,& ab Heliodoro presbytero,quo familiariter vtebatur, quæ intelligere non poterat, quomodo ab Origene essent dicta quæsisse: cùm autem is parum ingenuè in eo negotio versaretur, inde accidisse ut nonnulli ejusmodi errores in sancti istius viri Commentariis occurrant. Theophilus Antiochenus ante Melchisedecum Ierulalem dictam Ierosolyma, ab eoqi deinceps Hierusalem dictam; mirum sanè figmentum: explicet ejus rationem qui potest, & erit mihi magnus Apollo. Mera somnia narrat Ambrosius lectoribus suis de explicatione nominum Chorat & Oreb, quorum illud intellestum,hoc vero omne cor, aut quasi cor asserit significare; & in Psal. 118. dum exponit nomina Hebraicorum elementorum à quibus initium sumunt versiculi singulorum octonariorum ex quibus secundùm ordinem Alphabeti Hebraici Psalmus ille constat. Sed ferri non potest cùm,licèt Græcè sciret, vocem ἐοία, ex ἀεὶ semper & ἔστι existens componit; non enim impune ferret qui in prima linguæ Græcæ schola sic erraret. Petrus cognomento Chrysologus Mariam Hebraicè Dominam Latinè nuncupari scribit,quod longè aliud esse omnes sciunt. Philastrius velut rem certam narrat, & quidem( ne eum sine auctore loqui putes) Hesiodi Græci Poetæ testimonio firmat, Paganos ita dictos esse à Pagano rege Deucalionis & Pyrrhæ filio: quæ totidem sunt somnia & Hesiodo & omnibus eruditis inaudita. Hieronymum verò. non equidem nego ejusmodi nonnulla in Operibus suis effudisse, sed non tam imprudentem quam ludentem ut cum vocem Latinam nugæ ab Hebræa ﬠ noghè,quæ Sophoniæ cap.3. v.8. legitur derivatiću m ulquè ab Hebræis Pauli Philemonis,Onésimi, Timothei & aliorum vocabulorum quæ purè puta Græca sunt,significationem repetit.
units.tr: Moreover, in grammar, because of their ignorance of the Hebrew language, they err much more often than in the other arts. Thus Optatus, Vigilius, Isidore and the so-called Anacletus derive the name Cephas from the Greek word κεφαλὴ, "head" [κεφαλὴ]; yet Cepha, which is Syriac, means a rock, as the Evangelist himself had clearly pointed out. Lactantius and Ambrose make a similar mistake when they trace the Hebrew word Pascha, which properly means passing over, to the Greek verb πάσχειν, "to suffer" [πάσχειν], which means to suffer. In this matter Pope Innocent III followed them as leaders, in his first sermon at the Lateran Council. Gregory I, however great he was, is even more absurd and incredible in his blunder over Cornustibium, which is the name of one of the daughters of Job in the Latin translation. He took it as if it were compounded of cornu and tibia. "Because," he says, "he made one word out of both, cornu and tibia," (the Latin translator says) "he rightly called each word by whatever gender he wished, transferring them into Latin as one part of speech." For it troubled the man that the translator had written not Cornutibia but Cornusflibium. The good Pope either did not know, or certainly did not notice, what flibium means in Latin; even boys know this now. Of the same kind is his explanation of the verse from the Song of Solomon, "My beloved is unto me a cluster of Cypress": he takes Cyprus to be the island of Cyprus, "in which," he says, "vineyards grow more fruitful than anywhere else," not realising that here it is the name of a most fragrant plant. But perhaps it was not unworthy that a man who scorns letters, and regards them as trifles, and thinks it impious and profane for a bishop to babble, should slip so childishly. Elsewhere he almost boasts that he has disdained to keep the art of speaking, which the teachings of outward learning instil; that he has not avoided the confusion of barbarisms, nor cared to keep the position and motion of prepositions and the cases, because (he says) I think it highly unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus. As if to learn and observe the laws of human and divine speech were to subject the heavenly oracles to Donatus! He so despised the study of languages that, although for several years before his papacy he had served as apocrisiarius at Constantinople, he did not even want to touch Greek, which he more than once declares he does not know: We (he says) know neither Greek, nor have we written any work in Greek. I have already noted some errors of this kind of other men, which Jerome pointed out; the Church certainly owes him very much, both because he spared no labour in learning the Hebrew language accurately, and because, reverencing no one, he freely reproves all such slips. All the rest, with few exceptions, grope their way as if in darkness. Hence come so many silly etymologies of the proper names that occur in Scripture. Who could read without astonishment what is found about the name Jesus in Irenaeus? Jesus (he says) is, according to the proper language of the Hebrews, a name of two and a half letters...... and, according to the ancient Hebrew language, is heaven. The angel would surely have made this plain in the very beginning of Matthew's Gospel, if it were so, when he taught that Christ was called Jesus because he would save his people from their sins. Of the same kind is what he teaches elsewhere, that the name Adonai sometimes signifies wonderful and admirable, and sometimes, with the letter delta doubled and aspirated, as in Addhonei, signifies separating and dividing the earth from the water; and similar etymologies of the words Sabaoth and Iaoth. Of this sort of chaff are the mysteries which, in the same book, he discloses, things never heard of, not even whispered, by all the others, both old and recent. He says that God is called Barneth in Hebrew, that the first and most ancient Hebrew letters are called priestly and are ten in number, and that they are all written through fifteen. Clement of Alexandria drew from the same source when he wonderfully taught the derivation of the name Abraham: It is explained (he says) as "father of a multitude," and the name Rebecca, which, he says, is likewise explained as the glory of God. Hilary calls Sehon the interpretation of an unfruitful tree. But Jerome warns us that this man was ignorant of the Hebrew language and had only a little knattering of Greek letters, and that he asked Heliodorus, a presbyter with whom he was on intimate terms, what he could not understand, namely how Origen had explained these things. Since Origen had handled the matter rather dishonestly, it happened that some errors of this kind appear in the commentaries of that holy man. Theophilus of Antioch says that Jerusalem was called Ierulalem before Melchizedek, and was afterwards called Hierusalem by him: a truly strange fiction. Let whoever can explain its reasoning, and I shall call him a great Apollo. Ambrose tells his readers pure dreams about the explanation of the names Chorat and Oreb, of which he asserts that the former means understanding and the latter every heart, or as it were a heart; and in Psalm 118, where he explains the names of the Hebrew letters with which the verses of each eight-line stanza begin, the stanzas of that psalm following the order of the Hebrew alphabet. But it cannot be tolerated that he, although he knew Greek, composes the word ἐοία [eoia] from ἀεὶ [always] and ἔστι [is]; for he would not have got off lightly had he made such a mistake in the first class of a Greek school. Peter, surnamed Chrysologus, writes that Mary is called Lady in Latin, though everyone knows it is something quite different in Hebrew. Philastrius relates as a settled fact, and lest you think he speaks without an authority, confirms it by the testimony of the Greek poet Hesiod, that the Pagans were so called from Pagan, king and son of Deucalion and Pyrrha: these are dreams just as much as the rest, unheard of by Hesiod and by all learned men. As for Jerome, I do not deny that he poured out some such things in his works, but he was not so much careless as playing, when he derived the Latin word nugae from the Hebrew, and gave the meaning of the Hebrew word read in Zephaniah 3:8, and of the names Paul, Philemon, Onesimus, Timothy and other words which are purely Greek.

units.la: Iam tametsi Patres in S. Scripturis essent vetsatissimi; eásque longè maiori venetatione quàm reliqua omnia scripta prosequerentur,sæpe tamen in iis allegandis hallucinantur. Sic Justinus locum è Sophonia citat qui apud Zachariam habetur, & alibi Ieremiam pro Daniele ponit. Ita Hilarius monet Paulum Actor. 13. quædam verba ex primo Psalmo afferre quæ tamen in secundo reperiuntur : cùm contra Paulus de primo Psalmo nihil dicat, sed disertè secundum designet. Epiphanius ex Actor. cap.27. v.37. refert in navi quæ naufragio periit fuisse cum Paulo aliquando 70. circiter animas; nonnunquam 80. cùm disertè dicat Lucas fuisse 276. Alibi ex historia Evangelica refert Iesum Christum dixisse matri suæ Noli me tangere, cùm tamen non legamus iis verbis usum nisi ad Mariam Magdalenam. Hieronymus laborat in concilianda Pauli ex Habacuco allegatione cum textu Hebraico, quasi eum Apostolus in hæc verba citasset. Iustus ex fide mea viuet,cùm contra certissimum sit Apostolum & primo capite ad Roman. & in Epist.ad . Galat simpliciter sic referre. Iussus ex fide vivet, minimè verò, Iussus ex fide mea vivet. Athanasius in Synopsi (vel quisquis ejus operis auctor est) recensens libros Divinos tertium Esdiae, ex communi omnium Christianorum sententia Apocryphum pro primo, quem omnes cùm Christiani, tum Iudaei, in Canone esse agnoscunt evidenter accipit. Potest huc referri (si tamen opus tam infscitum inter Patrum monumenta collocandum est) error qui in Epistola Gregorij Papae secundi occurrit ubi bonus Pontifex acriter invehitur in Regem Oziam propter comminutum serpentem aeneum, quemque ideo fratrem Leonis Imperatoris iconoclastae vocat, convitio ex auctoris mente, infando, quo illum putabat scelestissimis & perditissimis principibus accenseri. At S. Scriptura, non Oziam, sed Ezechiam, serpentem aeneum confregisse docet, idque ei non probro, sed laudi vertit.
units.tr: Although the Fathers were very well versed in the Holy Scriptures, and attended to them with far greater reverence than to all other writings, they nevertheless often go astray in citing them. Thus Justin cites a passage from Zephaniah which is found in Zechariah, and elsewhere puts Jeremiah for Daniel. Likewise Hilary observes that Paul, in Acts 13, quotes certain words from the first Psalm, which are nevertheless found in the second; whereas Paul says nothing about the first Psalm, but clearly designates the second. Epiphanius, from Acts 27:37, reports that there were about seventy souls in the ship that perished in the shipwreck with Paul, and at other times eighty, although Luke expressly says there were 276. Elsewhere, from the Gospel history, he reports that Jesus Christ said to his mother, Touch me not, although we do not read that these words were used except to Mary Magdalene. Jerome labours to reconcile Paul's citation from Habakkuk with the Hebrew text, as if the Apostle had quoted it in these words: The just shall live by my faith; whereas it is most certain that the Apostle, both in the first chapter of Romans and in the Epistle to the Galatians, cites it simply thus: The just shall live by faith, and by no means The just shall live by my faith. Athanasius in his Synopsis (or whoever is the author of that work), in listing the divine books, clearly takes Third Esdras, which all Christians, and Jews too, acknowledge as apocryphal by the common judgement of all, to be the first book in the canon. This may be referred here (if indeed so unlearned a work is to be placed among the monuments of the Fathers): the error that occurs in the letter of Pope Gregory II, where the good Pontiff sharply inveighs against King Uzziah because he broke the bronze serpent, and on account of this calls him brother of the iconoclast Emperor Leo, reproaching him, in the author's mind, with an unspeakable crime, as if he were numbered among the most wicked and abandoned princes. But Holy Scripture teaches that it was not Uzziah but Hezekiah who broke the bronze serpent, and it turns this to his praise, not his disgrace.

units.la: Memoriae autem lapsus si quis referre omnes velit ei vix satis fuerit ulla memoria, adeo frequentes occurrunt in libris Patrum Gregorius Nazianzenus scribit, & quidem duobus diversis locis, Davidem in eum animadvertisse qui Absalomi mortem ipsi nuntiavit. Nempe quod apud Scripturam de eius supplicio legerat, qui Saulem à se interfectum Davidi nuntiaverat, id nostrer imprudens ad Absalomi interfectorem transtulit; quod etiam est à Iacobo Billio eius interprete & scholiaste annotatum. Narrat alicubi Ambrosius quod etiam aquila, cùm fuerit mortua, ex suis reliquiis renascetur. Quis non videt illum Phoenicem intelligere? sed alibi hanc ipsam de Phoenice fabulam referre volens, dicit hoc relatione crebra & Scripturarum auctoritate cognoscI, nempe quę apud auctores vel ethnicos vel certè Ecclesiasticos de Phoenice legerat, ea Scripturis imputat; quo modo, sed multis post seculis, Innocentius Pontif. Rom. III. velut ex Divinis libris citat quae habentur in Augustinianis; cùm (inquit) Sacra Scriptura dicat auctoritas, quod injuriam facit Martyri qui orat pro Martyre. Haec verò ut omnes sciunt non
units.tr: If anyone wished to report all the lapses of memory, no memory would be large enough, so frequently do they occur in the books of the Fathers. Gregory Nazianzen writes, and in two different places, that David took offence at the man who brought him news of Absalom's death. Our author had indeed read in Scripture of the punishment of the man who told David that he had killed Saul, and he carelessly transferred this to the slayer of Absalom. James Billius, his translator and commentator, has also noted this. Somewhere Ambrose relates that even the eagle, when it has died, will be reborn from its remains. Who does not see that he means the Phoenix? But elsewhere, wishing to recount this very fable of the Phoenix, he says I know this from frequent report and the authority of the Scriptures. He thus ascribes to Scripture what he had read about the Phoenix in authors, whether pagan or at least ecclesiastical. In the same way, though many centuries later, Innocent III, Pope of Rome, cites as from the divine books what is in fact found in Augustine: since (he says) Sacred Scripture says the authority, that does injustice to a martyr who prays for a martyr. But these things, as everyone knows, are not

units.la: Athan. in Synops. p. 59. & 84. non Scriptura sacra, sed Augustini dicit auctoritas, sermo ne xvii. de verbis Apostoli. Ambrosius vero de quo coeperam dicere, errore non absimili haec verba, in hoc ipsum te suscitaui ut ostendam in te virtutem meam a Deo ad Mosem dicta fuisse docet. Sed Pharaonem non autem Mosem his verbis a Deo compellatum legimus. Idem Judaeis tribuit quod de Iesu Christi discipulis narrat Ioannes, cap.9. petiisse scilicet ipsos a Domino, Magi ster, hic peccavit an parentes eius, ut sic caecus nasceretur? Aitu, vt reor, Rhetorices rapiebatur cum alibi vni ex Maccabaeis fratribus, qui sub Antiocho passi sunt, orationem tribuit in qua mentio fit Ioannis & Iacobi filiorum tonitrui, Christi Apostolorum, qui tamen nonnisi longo post tempore, ut cuivis notum est, in vivis fuerunt. Lapsus est item memoria Tertullianus cum Mosi creatorem dixisse refert, Non te contempserunt, sed me. Huc quoque pertinet quod Chrysostomus Sophoniam cum dicit qui est Habacuc, & Paulum apud Gallionis tribunal verbedonec natum ex B. Virgine Filium vidit,nescivisse tanta gloria eam esse celebrandam,nec quicquam de ea intellexiffe nisi filiam fuisse Ioachimi & Annæ, Elizabethæ cognatam, & de dono & familia Davidis. Sed postea cognovisse tantum illam in terris decus esse consecutam ut ad eam Angelum suum Deus miserit,eámque felectam fuisse ut haberetur ei Divinitus is honor, tantumque gratiæ consequeretur.
units.tr: Athan. in Synops. p. 59. & 84. says that it is not Holy Scripture but the authority of Augustine, in sermon 17 on the words of the Apostle. Ambrose, of whom I had begun to speak, through a not dissimilar error teaches that the words I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I may show my power in you were spoken by God to Moses. Yet we read that these words were addressed by God to Pharaoh, not to Moses. He likewise attributes to the Jews what John narrates of the disciples of Jesus Christ in chapter 9, namely that they asked the Lord, Master, did this man sin, or his parents, that he was born blind? I think he was carried away by rhetorical zeal when elsewhere he assigns to one of the Maccabean brothers, who suffered under Antiochus, a speech in which mention is made of John and James, the sons of thunder, the apostles of Christ, who yet, as everyone knows, lived only a long time afterwards. Tertullian's memory also slipped when he reports that the Creator said to Moses, They have not despised you, but me. To this also belongs what Chrysostom says: that Zephaniah is the one who is Habakkuk, and that Paul was beaten before the tribunal of Gallio. And that Mary, until she saw the Son born of the Blessed Virgin, had not known that she was to be celebrated with such glory, and had understood nothing of her beyond her being the daughter of Joachim and Anna, a relative of Elizabeth, and of the gift and family of David. But afterwards he came to know that she had attained such honour on earth that God sent his angel to her, and that she was chosen so that this honour was divinely given to her and she obtained such great grace.

units.la: Verùm hujusmodi errorum, qui in Patrum libris occurrunt, catalogum non perteximus: sufficit hoc specimen, ut, quod aiunt, ex vngue leonem noscamus. Vnum tantum hîc addam, præter securitatem illam adeo frequentem,qua,nullo discrimine, quicquid in mentem venit,aut quod alii affirmarunt, in chartam fine examine effundunt,follenne etiam illis esse(quod tamen ludicum personæ quam ipsis tribuimus non bene convenire videtur) ludere & meditationes allegoricas texere,puerorum nostrorum chartaceis ludicrisque ædiculis neque firmiores neque solidiores, quas Perronius nostras bilares locos vocat. Equidem scio allegoriam esse uilem, & sæpe necessariam,sed ea lege ut fit sobria,clara & solida; sed non alias hic denoto quàm quæ textui vim faciunt, eumque (fi ita loqui licet) obtorto collo quolibet trahunt, Scripturámque in vanos fumos converterunt. His tamen scatent Patrum scripta. De Origenis ejusque discipulorum in hoc argumento licentia sæpe queritur Hieronymus,qui tamen ipse sæpe & fine modo hic peccat. Si cui id observare cordi fit legat, sodes, epistolam eius 146. in expositione parabolæ de filio prodigo, legat item quæ habet genealogiam Prophetæ Sophoniæ & de vrbe Damasco: in historiam Abifag Sunamitidis: de viginti quinque viris & duobus principibus quorum Ezech. 11. fit mentio: de eversione Tyri Egypti, & Affur, quam prænuntiat idem Propheta: quæ de Numeris & Dario philosophatur : quæ irem adeo subtiliter disserit super mandato Domini, ut ci qui ceciderit derit nos in dexteram maxillam obvertamus & alteram & alias ipsius ejusdem generis meditationes. Hilarius adeo ista scribendi ratione delectatur, ut dum Scripturam interpretatur fere in ea totus sit, utque ad eam sibi viam sternat fingit nonnunquam in Scripturis absurdas quaedam & impossibilia, quae tamen nulla sunt, ut, hac data porta, ad allegorias confugere possit: ut in Psal.136. negat explicari posse quod ibi haberur Iudaeos super flumina Babylonis sedisse & flevisse,& in salicibus suspendifse organa sua: quasi in regione quam Euphrates & Tygris affluebant nullus fuisset amnis, nulla salix, nullae arbores aquaticae. Ibidem velut nodum nactus vindice dignum haeret ac rogat, quaenam a Propheta filia Babylonis dicta sit, & cur misera dicatur; quae sane difficultas adeo est solutu facilis, ut ne pueros quidem in ea explicanda ad allegorias confugere necesse fuerit. In Psal. 146. per nubes quibus Deus Coelum operit intelligit Prophetas, & per pluviam quam parat terrae doctrinam Evangelicam, & per montes in quibus producitur foenum Prophetas & Apostolos, & per jumenta homines; & per pullos corvorum Gentiles; asseritque haec aliter, id est, ad literam, intelligere non tantum erroris, sed irreligiositatis extrema esse. Quid est de Scriptura ludere si hoc non est? Alibi per volatilia caeli, de quibus Dominus dicit quod non serunt neque congregant in horrea, immundos spiritus intelligit, & Angelorum coelestium claritates per lilia agri quae non laborant neque nent. Vereor ne Lectoris patientia abuti videar si hic describfero quaecunque ille habet mirifica de historia duorum daemoniacorum quos Dominus sanavit in regione Gerasenorum, de porcorum per praeceps in mare casu, de fuga pastorum, & de legatione missa ad Dominum ne urbem adiret, vel si totam ejus expositionem attulero in v.29.cap.10. Matth. Nonne duo passeres asse veneunt? Per duos passeres intelligit peccatores corpore & anima constantes, qui licet nati sint ad volandum pennis spiritualibus, minimo se vendunt peccato, & vnum fiunt, animæ subtilitate in naturam corporum ingravescente, & alia ejusmodi figmenta, quæ lectores cordatos non tam ædificare quàm in stuporem dare possunt. Neque gravior in hoc genere aut modestior fuit Ambrosius. Allatis enim his Domini verbis. Si habueritis fidem sicut granû sinapis, dicetis huic monti tollere, & jactare in mare. Huic, cui? daemonio iuquit à quo ipse invasus fuerat & oppressus. Cui vacabit plura exempla videre, legat sermones ejus in Psal. 118. Opus alias præstans sanè & eloquentia sanèque doctrina refertum, lectúsque adeo dignissimum. Difficilius fortasse fuerit quæ non raro idem in Scripturæ verbis ludit legitimè purgare. Vt cum ea Valentiniano & Gratiano tribuit quæ de Christo & Ecclesia dicuntur in Cantico Cantico-rum. Quis dabit te frater fratrem mihi, lactentem uberà matris meæ? Inveniens te foris osculabor te, assumàte & inducam te in domum matris meæ, & in secretum ejus quaeconcepit me. Potum dabo tibi à vino operosi unguenti, a fluxu malorum granatorum meorum. Læva ejus sub caput meum, & dextera ejus complectatur me. Promittit (inquit Ambrosius) fratri augusta memoria Gratianus præsto sibi fructus diversarum esse virtutum. Et ad eundem finem plerosque istius sacri Cantici locos adhibet, ea licentia quam ipsi etiam Poetæ vix ludentes usurparet. Quæ in hanc rem ex Gregorio Nazianzeno, Augustino, maximè in Psalmorum enarratione, quos ille, neglecta litera, contortis allegoriis, sæpe frigidis & dilutis, vexat verius quàm interpretatur; ex Gregorio Romano I. cujus moralis in Iobum expositio tota ex hujus generis fumis contexta est; & aliis plerisque Patribus afferre possem sciens volens mitto. Taceo & de fabulis, ad allegoricum genus accedentibus, quibus non pauci è Veteribus sua opera assitim exornarunt. Notatos eo nomine jam supra diximus à Melchiore Cano Gregorium & Bedam. Ille quidem & in Dialogis & alibi non semel fabulosis narrationibus ita impense gaudet ut Paganicum figmentum, jampridem
units.tr: But we have not drawn up a catalogue of such errors as occur in the books of the Fathers; this specimen is enough, so that, as they say, we may know the lion from its claw. I will add just one thing here, besides that frequent carelessness by which, without any discrimination, they pour onto paper whatever comes into their heads or what others have affirmed, without examination. It was also customary for them (though this does not seem to suit well the character of the judges we ascribe to them) to play and to weave allegorical meditations, no firmer or more solid than the paper and playful little houses of our children, which Perron calls our bilares locos. I indeed know that allegory is a cheap thing and often necessary, but on the condition that it be sober, clear and solid. Here, however, I mean nothing other than those allegories that do violence to the text and drag it, if one may speak so, by the twisted neck wherever they please, and turn Scripture into empty smoke. Yet the writings of the Fathers abound in such things. Jerome often complains of the licence of Origen and his disciples in this matter, though he himself often and immoderately errs here. If anyone cares to observe this, let him read, please, his letter 146, on the exposition of the parable of the prodigal son. Let him read likewise what he has on the genealogy of the prophet Zephaniah and on the city of Damascus; on the history of Abishag the Shunammite; on the twenty-five men and the two princes mentioned in Ezekiel 11; on the overthrow of Tyre, of Egypt and of Assyria, which the same prophet foretells; what he philosophizes about the Numbers and about Darius; and how subtly he discourses on the Lord's command that to one who strikes us on the right cheek we should turn the other also, and other meditations of the same kind. Hilary is so delighted with this manner of writing that while interpreting Scripture he is almost wholly given over to it. To pave his way to allegory he sometimes invents absurd and impossible things in Scripture, which in fact are not there, so that, with this door opened, he can take refuge in allegories. Thus on Psalm 136 he denies that what is said there can be explained, namely that the Jews sat down by the rivers of Babylon and wept, and hung their harps on the willows, as if in a region watered by the Euphrates and the Tigris there had been no river, no willow, and no water-trees. In the same place, as if he had caught a knot worthy of a champion, he sticks fast and asks which daughter of Babylon the prophet meant, and why she is called wretched. This difficulty is in fact so easily solved that not even boys would need to resort to allegories to explain it. On Psalm 146 he understands by the clouds with which God covers the heavens the prophets, by the rain which he prepares for the earth the evangelical doctrine, by the mountains on which the hay grows the prophets and apostles, by the beasts men, and by the young ravens the Gentiles. He asserts that to understand these things otherwise, that is, literally, is not only error but the utmost irreligiousness. What is this but playing with Scripture? Elsewhere, by the birds of the air, of which the Lord says that they neither sow nor gather into barns, he understands unclean spirits, and by the lilies of the field, which neither toil nor spin, the brightnesses of the heavenly angels. I fear I may seem to abuse the reader's patience if I set down here all the wonderful things he has on the story of the two demoniacs whom the Lord healed in the country of the Gerasenes, on the rush of the swine headlong into the sea, on the flight of the herdsmen, and on the embassy sent to the Lord asking him not to enter the city; or if I were to bring forward his whole exposition of Matthew 10. 29: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? By the two sparrows he understands sinners who consist of body and soul, who, although born to fly on spiritual wings, sell themselves for the smallest sin and become one with it, the soul being weighed down by the subtlety of the body's nature; and other fictions of this kind, which can astonish thoughtful readers rather than edify them. Ambrose was no more serious or restrained in this genre. Having cited these words of the Lord, If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, Be removed, and be cast into the sea, he says: "To this one"? To what? To the demon, by whom he himself had been seized and oppressed. Whoever has the leisure to see more examples should read his sermons on Psalm 118. This is otherwise an outstanding work, indeed full of eloquence and sound teaching, and most worthy of being read. It will perhaps be more difficult to clear properly of blame what the same man often plays with in the words of Scripture. For example, he attributes to Valentinian and Gratian what is said of Christ and the Church in the Song of Songs: Who will give you to me as a brother, sucking the breasts of my mother? Finding you outside I will kiss you, and I will lead you into the house of my mother, and into the secret chamber of her who conceived me. I will give you to drink of the wine of my spiced ointment, of the juice of my pomegranates. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me. Ambrose says: "The august memory of Gratian promises to his brother the ready fruits of various virtues." To the same end he applies many passages of that sacred Song, with a licence which even the poets themselves would hardly use in jest. What might be added on this matter from Gregory Nazianzen and from Augustine, especially in his exposition of the Psalms, which, neglecting the letter and with contorted allegories, often cold and watery, he harasses rather than interprets; from Gregory the Great, whose moral exposition of Job is wholly woven from this sort of smoke; and from many other Fathers, I could bring forward. Knowingly and willingly I pass them over. I also pass over the fables that approach the allegorical kind, with which not a few of the Ancients have adorned their works. We have already said above that Melchior Cano named Gregory and Bede on this account. Gregory in particular, both in his Dialogues and elsewhere, delights so intensely in fabulous narratives that the pagan fiction, long since

units.la: ² pridem & à Plutarcho & à Luciano commemoratum, de quodam ad inferos, per Genij errorem, ob nominis ambiguitatem decepti, evocato, & deinde ad superos à Iudice, agnitô ministri sui errore, remisso, totum veluti rem Constantinopoli verè gestam referre non dubitaverit, affirmaréque se eam ab ipso, cui ista contigerant, accepisse. Neque aliud est inter hos fabulatores differimen, nisi quod quem Plutarchus Antyllum, Lucianus Demylum dicunt, hunc nostER Stephanum vocat.
units.tr: Already long ago related by both Plutarch and Lucian, of a certain man who, deceived by the ambiguity of a name through a spirit's mistake, was summoned to the underworld, and then sent back to the upper world by the Judge once his minister's error was recognised. Stephen does not hesitate to report the whole story as though it had really happened at Constantinople, and he affirms that he received it from the very man to whom these things befell. Between these storytellers the only difference is that the man whom Plutarch calls Antyllus and Lucian calls Demylus, our Stephen names.

units.la: Sed in istis diutius haerere nihil necesse est, quòd abundè sint quæ hactenus attulimus, ex quibus prudens Lector satis, ni fallor, intelliget hanc docendi rationem: luculentissimè significare sanctis illis Patribus, cùm libros ita scripserant, nunquam fuisse consilium ut de fide nostra judicarent, vel dogmata quæ hodie controvertuntur deciderent. Eos ego conficeor magnis ingenij dotibus, acumine, sagacitate, & summa ad pernoscendum verum perspicacitate; adhæc, pietate, sapientia, & eruditione singulari excelluisse. Sed qui vel plurimum iis artibus pollent frustra sunt, nisi cas omnes serio & ex animo adhibeant, præsertim in negotio difficillimo, adhæc tanti momenti, ut nemo unquam ad id expendendum & judicandum satis diligentiæ & attentionis attulerit. At ex iis quæ disputavimus manifestum esse arbitror, Patres ad scribendum ne quaquam attulisse summam hanc curam atque contentionem. Non sunt ergo quę illi scripserunt ulla de rebus Theologicis judicia, vel decreta. Fateor leves istos errores nihil de ea opinione debere detrahere in qua sunt apud nos Patres magno suo merito, propter acumen & vim ingenij incredibilem. Facilè concedo eos si mentem intendissent ab hujusmodi erratis facilè cavere sibi potuisse, in quæ non aliter ipsos incidisse judico, quàm ex quadam incogitantia, quæ in omni artium genere etiam verissimis & peritissimis quibusque obrepere interdum solet. Etiam hoc, fi cupis, largiar, viros summos hos & similes nævos suis operibus prudentes de industria inspersisse, ut luderent, & nobis cruces figerent: quod Grammaticos de suo Virgilio dixisse memini. Sed quocunque consilio secerint, cùm, ut apparet, fecerint, certum est nunquam iis in mentem venisse ut religionis leges & fidei decreta conderent. Quotquot occurrunt in Patrum operibus innocui errores, lapsus, lusus, & alia eiusmodi, iis nos veluti totidem vocibus ipsi jubent alios judices quærere; negant se pro tribunali sedere, aut magistratum agere, familiares esse quos fundunt sermones, non prætorias sententias. His si subjungas quæ tam disertè celeberrimi quique supra in hanc rem dixerunt, videbis hoc eos velle & cupere, non ut suas opiniones pro oraculis, & decretis habeamus, sed ut de iis ex Scriptura & ratione iudicemus tanquam de doctorum hominum placitis, qui quidem pietate & doctrina excelluerunt, sed ita tamen ut homines fuerint, errori obnoxij, neque semper quid verum, quid de jure Divino esset liquidò pervidere potuerint, qui fortasse in hoc ipso negotio quid valerent offendere noluerint & parcè viribus suis vsi sint, minusque attentionis & diligentiæ, temporisque in eo posuerint, quàm fuerant adhibituri si seriò in hanc causam incumbere omnésque ingenii vires in ea explicare decrevissent.
units.tr: But there is no need to dwell longer on these things, since what we have brought forward so far is abundant. From it the prudent reader will, unless I am mistaken, understand well enough this manner of teaching: it was made most clear by those holy Fathers, when they wrote their books in this way, that it was never their intention to judge our faith or to settle the doctrines that are disputed today. I grant that they excelled in great gifts of mind, in keenness, sagacity and the highest perspicacity in discerning the truth, and besides in piety, wisdom and singular learning. But those who are most powerful in these arts achieve nothing unless they apply all of them seriously and wholeheartedly, especially in a most difficult matter of such importance that no one has ever brought enough diligence and attention to weighing and judging it. From what we have discussed, however, I think it is clear that the Fathers, in writing, did not bring this highest care and effort at all. Therefore the things they wrote are not any judgments or decrees concerning theological matters. I admit that these slight errors ought in no way to detract from the esteem in which we rightly hold the Fathers, on account of their acuteness and incredible force of mind. I readily concede that, had they applied their minds, they could easily have guarded themselves against errors of this kind, into which I judge they fell only through a certain inattention, which in every kind of art tends sometimes to creep in even upon the most accurate and most skilled. Even this I will grant, if you like: that these great men, and others like them, deliberately sprinkled such blemishes into their works, prudently, in order to play and to set traps for us, as I recall Grammarians said of their own Virgil. But whatever their intention, since it is apparent that they did so, it is certain that it never entered their minds to frame laws of religion and decrees of faith. Whatever innocent errors, slips, playful remarks and other things of this sort occur in the works of the Fathers, they bid us, as it were in so many words, to seek other judges for them. They deny that they sit on a tribunal or act as magistrates; the discourses they pour forth are familiar talk, not praetorian sentences. If you add to these what the most celebrated men mentioned above have said so plainly on this matter, you will see that they wish and desire this: not that we should hold their opinions as oracles and decrees, but that we should judge them from Scripture and reason, as the opinions of learned men who indeed excelled in piety and learning, yet were men nonetheless, prone to error, and not always able to see clearly what is true and what is by divine right. Perhaps in this very matter they were unwilling to test what they were capable of, used their powers sparingly, and gave less attention, diligence and time to it than they would have given had they resolved to bend seriously to this cause and to bring all the powers of their intellect to bear on it.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Ratio IV. Patres siue seorsum singulos, siue coniunctim plures, in variis religionis capitibus errâsse.
units.tr: Argument IV. That the Fathers, whether taken singly or several together, erred in various heads of religion.

units.la: QVæ duobus superioribus capitibus disseruimus sufficere arbitror ut quivis moderato ingenio præditus apud se constituat, non tantum esse in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus, quam vulgus existimat, Patrum au-ctoriƈtoritatem. Poterunt ergo, quiqui sint æqui Lectores, hoc & sequens caput prætermittere, quod utrumque pæne invitus subjicere cogor, ut iis, qui se studiis suis abripi patiuntur, excusationem omnem præcidam. Ea, quibus in hac causa laborant, præjudicia, obstabunt ne rationis lucem videant, vocésque Patrum ipsorum audiant, ac forsan ne quid de honore, quo reclamantes eos prosequi decreverunt, imminuant, co venient ut modestiæ & animi demissioni quæ veritatis sunt pronunciata tribuant. Istorum pertinacia, non vestra necessitas, me nonnihil de ea reverentia remittere subegit qua Veteres prosequor. Ut enim invicta horum hominum duritics penitus frangatur, operæ pretium est etiam superioribus graviora Patrum errata retegi, quos qui intellexerint in multis magni momenti capitibus lapsos fuisse spes est, vel invitos, co tandem compulsum iri, ut ipsi agnoscunt nos non frustra neque temerè à summis illis viris fuisse admonitos, ne suis opinionibus, nisi quas verbo Dei, aut quapiam alia veritate subnixas constaret, fidem adhiberemus. Ægre quidem,&,quod ait Poeta αἰκστη Συ-μοῦ hanc disputationis partem aggredior. Grave enim est, & à pudore nostro alienum, hominum, præsertim sanctorum & merito venerabilium, nævos ac labes spectare ac ostentare. Sed cùm apud me reputo nobis nihil esse debere veritate & proximorum salute carius, ac vbi ea agitur sanctum esse in hujusmodi causa carissima quæque contemnere ac proculcare, huc facilè adducor, ut credam ipsos Patres, si nunc superessent, gratiam nobis de conatu hoc nostro habituros, nostræque in homines Christianos caritati gratulaturos, quos ut ab errore tenterrimo abducamus nævos etiam suos nudare audeamus. Neque enim temerè factum est, ut his infirmitatibus laborarent etiam laudatissimi viri, sed certo ac sapienti Divinæ providentiæ consilio, ut homines eos fuisse ex his intelligeremus. Si cui tamen hic noster conatus displicuerit, illů ego iterum obsecro atque obtestor ut cogitet, ne una eorum quibuscum mihi res est, quorumque sententiam confuto pervicacia, solo veritatis, & quidem gravissimæ, docendæ studio, ad hanc (si tamen ira appellanda est) irreverentiam compelli. Si exemplis me tueri vellem posset Cardinalem Perronium auctorem laudare, qui ut probaret, jure ab Ecclesia Romana prohibitum ne quis, non impetrata prius venia, libros Divinos legat, non dubitavit Scripturæ, non quidem errores (qui revera nulli sunt) sed falsas errorum & contradictionum species quæ nonnullos in sacris litteris offendant colligere, & capite integro exponere. Quanto æquius est hanc nobis veniam concedi ut Patrum, quorum dignitas atque honos immenso quodam intervallo infra Dei Majestatem ac reverentiam subsidit, hallucinationes, si quæ sunt, notemus; ac legentium oculis exponamus, ut gravi eorum morbo medeamur, quorum immoderatum est in Antiquitatis monumenta studium? & adversariis quidem hoc quo uno fere nituntur errorum suorum præsidium eripiamus? nostros vero confirmemus, ne ad nudum Patrum nomen temere expavescant? Maximi Regis vox fuit nulla re magis aut suam mortalitatem argui, aut adulatorum, à quibus Deus salutabatur, impudentiam refelli, quam vilissimis, & maximè pudendis naturæ suæ necessitatibus. Cum ergo tanti nostra interfuit scire Patres homines fuisse, nulla sit religio, si quid ij humani passi sunt, id bona fide promere & lectoribus spectandum objicere, ut argumento invicto omnem adulatorum pervicaciam frangamus. Ne pigeat in sanctorum virorum arcana irrumpere, & infirma indagare, ne Divinam esse pesthac putemus eorum auctoritatem. Cum autem partim ex ipsorum Patrum literis, partim ex veteris historiæ monumentis constet eos non plane ab iis affectibus fuisse immunes qui plerumque miseros mortales transverso agunt, testor, imprimis, me nulla hinc argumenta allaturum, vel hanc infirmitatis humanæ partem vexaturum, quam ego libenter patior æternis silentij"tenebris obscuratam jacere, neque repugno quin Patrum innocentia arque sanctitas summa, & omnibus suis numeris (quantum quidem fert humanæ naturæ modus)absoluta fuisse credatur. Non animi, sed mentis lapsus,non morum,sed opinionum peccata persequar.
units.tr: I think that what I have argued in the two preceding chapters is enough to convince any reasonable reader that the authority of the Fathers counts for less in matters of religion than the common people suppose. So fair readers may, if they wish, skip this chapter and the next, which I am almost reluctant to add, and I cut off every excuse from those who let themselves be carried away by their studies. The prejudices under which they labour in this matter will stop them from seeing the light of reason and from hearing the Fathers' own voices. Perhaps, too, they will not want to diminish the honour with which they have resolved to regard them, in spite of all objection. They will therefore come round to attributing to modesty and humility what is said for the sake of truth. It is their obstinacy, not any need of yours, that has compelled me to relax somewhat the reverence with which I treat the ancients. To break the invincible hardness of these men completely, it is worth exposing the more serious errors of the Fathers as well as those already mentioned. I hope that those who recognise that the Fathers slipped into error on many matters of great importance will at last be forced, even against their will, to acknowledge that we were not wrongly or rashly warned by those great men not to give credence to their opinions unless they were shown to rest on the Word of God or on some other truth. I approach this part of the discussion with reluctance, and, as the poet says, αἰκστη Συ-μοῦ. It is a heavy task, and foreign to our sense of decency, to look upon and display the blemishes and stains of men, especially holy men who deserve veneration. But when I reflect that nothing should be dearer to us than truth and the salvation of our neighbours, and that where these are at stake it is right in such a cause to despise and trample on even what is most dear, I am readily led to believe that the Fathers themselves, if they were alive now, would thank us for this effort and rejoice in our charity towards Christian men, whom we dare to expose even the blemishes of the Fathers in order to lead them away from a most dangerous error. Nor did it happen by chance that even the most praised men were afflicted with these weaknesses; it was by the sure and wise counsel of divine providence that we might understand them to be men. If anyone is displeased with this effort of mine, I beg and entreat him once more to consider that I am not driven to this irreverence (if indeed it should be called anger) by obstinacy, or by a desire merely to teach the truth, and that of the most serious kind, against those with whom I have to deal and whose opinions I refute. If I wished to defend myself by examples, I could cite Cardinal Perron as an authority. He, to prove that the Church of Rome rightly forbids anyone to read the divine books without first obtaining permission, did not hesitate to gather together in a whole chapter not indeed errors (for there are none in reality) but the false appearances of errors and contradictions which trouble some in the Sacred Writings. How much more fair it is that we be granted this indulgence: to note the delusions of the Fathers, if there are any, whose dignity and honour sink far below the majesty and reverence of God, and to set them before the eyes of readers, so that we may cure the grave disease of those whose study of antiquity is immoderate! Should we not also take from our adversaries the one thing on which their errors almost entirely rest, and make our own people secure, so that they are not rashly terrified by the mere name of the Fathers? The saying of a great King was that nothing shows more clearly both his own mortality and the shamelessness of the flatterers who hailed him as a god than the meanest and most shameful necessities of his nature. Since, therefore, it is so important to us to know that the Fathers were men, there is no reason for scruple if we honestly bring out whatever human frailties they suffered and place them before the reader to be examined, so that we may break the obstinacy of flatterers with an unanswerable argument. Let us not be ashamed to break into the secrets of holy men and to search out their weaknesses, lest we think their authority henceforth divine. But since it is clear, partly from the writings of the Fathers themselves and partly from the records of ancient history, that they were not wholly free from those passions which commonly drive wretched mortals off course, I declare first of all that I shall bring no arguments from this source, nor shall I harass that part of human weakness which I gladly allow to lie covered in the eternal darkness of silence. Nor do I object if it is believed that the innocence and holiness of the Fathers were of the highest degree and complete in every respect, so far as the measure of human nature allows. I shall pursue not the lapses of the spirit but of the mind, not the sins of conduct but the errors of opinion.

units.la: Omnium Patrum antiquissimus est Iustinus, magni apud Veterum historias nominis, non solum propter ignem rerum Divinarum & Philosophiæ cognitionem, sed etiam propter zelum illum quem luculentissimè & magna cum laude exseruit, cùm mortem pro Christo fortiter oppetiit. In huius tamen viri operibus, quàm multa occurrunt vel levia vanàque, vel etiam periculosa; Accipe quæ scribat de postremis temporibus quæ judicium, mundìque supremum diem anteibunt. Ego (inquit)& si qui per omnia recte sentientes Christiani sunt & carnis resurrectione futuram novimus,& mille annos in Hierusalem instaurata & exornata & dilatata,sicut Prophetæ Ezechiel & Esaias & aliy promulgant. His subjicit locum ex Esaiæ 63. vaticinium ex Apocalypsi. Christi fideles annos mille Hierosolymis peractures esse, ac postea universalem & sempiternam omnium unanimiter simul resurrectione& judicium futurum. Ex his verbis apparet manifestè ipsum cum Chiliastis sentire, antequam resurrectio penitus perficiatur, Hierosolymis fideles annos mille regnaturos. Quæ tamen sententia ab universæ Occidentis Ecclesiæ Christianis,quasquunque partes sectentur,tanquam falsa repudiatur. Alibi videtur sensisse essentiam Dei esse finitam; probat enim adversus Iudæum, de Patre non fuisse dictum,Dominus pluit super Sodomam ignem & sulphur,alias (inquit) in cœlis non fuerit. Quæ habet de Angelis,rametsi istis leviora, sunt tamen & ipsa quoque absurdissima; Deus (inquit) hominum ipsorum, atque eorum quæ sub cælo sunt,providentiam Angelis ad hac dispositis attribuit: Angeli autem ordinationem sive dispositionem eam transgressi,cùm mulierum concubitus causa,amoribus sunt vieli,,tum filios; procrearunt, eos qui daemones sunt dicti. Nescio an & ista quae alibi habet facile fit cuipiam persuasum: Omnes animas iustorum & Prophetarum sub potestatem malignorum Angelorum cadere, ideoque Dominum in crucem in manus Patris spiritum suum depositie. Quod dogma, quamvis mirificum & a piorum sensu abhorrens, diu tamen iuter Christianos haesisse apparet ex Anastasio Antiocheno qui cum sexto saeculo vixerit, eadem tamen sequitur quae Iustinus: Τὸ πνεῦμα (inquit) ὑπῆρχεν πάσης ἀψυχῆς ... quia Scriptura haufterat qui supra Iustinus quae secunda Apologia docet. Quicunque cum ratione vixere Christiani sunt, quāvis Atheis & nullius numinis cultores habiti sint, quamvis inter Graecos fuere Socrates Heraclitus, atque iis similes: in ter barbaros autem Abbraham & Ananias & Azarias, &c. quod eodem loco & paulo post item repetit. Qui cum ratione vixerunt, atque etiam nunc vivunt Christiani, & extra metum atque perturbationem omnem sunt.
units.tr: The oldest of the Fathers is Justin, of great renown in the histories of the ancients, not only for his knowledge of divine things and of philosophy but also for that zeal which he displayed most brilliantly and with great praise, when he bravely faced death for Christ. Yet in the works of this man, how many things occur that are trivial and vain, or even dangerous! Consider what he writes about the last times, which will precede the judgement and the final day of the world: "I, and all who think rightly in every respect as Christians do, know that there will be a resurrection of the flesh and a thousand years in Jerusalem, rebuilt, adorned and enlarged, as the prophets Ezekiel, Isaiah and others proclaim." To this he adds a passage from Isaiah 63 and a prophecy from the Apocalypse, that the faithful of Christ will spend a thousand years at Jerusalem, and that afterwards there will be one universal and everlasting resurrection and judgement of all together. From these words it is plain that he agrees with the Chiliasts, that before the resurrection is fully accomplished the faithful will reign a thousand years at Jerusalem. Yet this opinion is rejected as false by Christians of the whole Western Church, whatever parties they follow. Elsewhere he seems to have held that the essence of God is finite; for in his dispute with the Jew he argues that it was not said of the Father, "The Lord rained fire and sulphur upon Sodom," otherwise (he says) he would not have been in heaven. What he says about the Angels, though lighter than these things, is also most absurd: God (he says) assigned the providence of men themselves and of those things which are under heaven to Angels appointed for this purpose; but the Angels, transgressing that ordering or arrangement, were captivated by love for the embraces of women, and begot children, who are called demons. I do not know whether what he says elsewhere is easily persuasive to anyone: that the souls of all the just and of the Prophets fell under the power of evil Angels, and that therefore the Lord committed his spirit into the Father's hands when he was on the cross. This dogma, though wonderful and abhorrent to the sense of the pious, seems to have stuck for a long time among Christians, as appears from Anastasius of Antioch, who lived in the sixth century and nevertheless follows what Justin follows: "The spirit (he says) was [the cause] of every soul ..." [Τὸ πνεῦμα ὑπῆρχεν πάσης ἀψυχῆς], because Scripture had taken in what Justin teaches above in his Second Apology. "Whoever lived with reason are Christians, though they were thought to be atheists and worshippers of no divinity: among the Greeks Socrates and Heraclitus and those like them; among the barbarians Abraham and Ananias and Azarias, etc." He repeats this in the same place and again a little later: "Those who lived with reason, and those Christians who live even now, are free from all fear and disturbance."

units.la: Irenaeus Episcopus Lugdunensis, qui ipsum proximè secutus est, in eadem est cum eo sententia, de statu animarum statim à morte usque ad diem judicii. Ad finem enim illius praeclari operis quod adversus haereses elaboravit, cum dixisset Dominum usque ad tertiam diem commoratum fuisse in inferioribus terrae, ubi animae mortuorum erant, quem locum, virae, quam in terris degimus, opponit, subjungit. Manifestum est quia discipulorum ejus propter quos & haec operatus est Dominus, anima abiit in invisibilem locum definitum ea a Deo, & ubi usque ad resurrectionem commorabuntur, suspensu resurrectionem; post recipientes corpora & perfecte resurgentes, hoc est corporaliter, quemadmodum & Dominus resurrexit, sic veniunt ad conspectum Dei. Atque hanc suam sententiam Valentinianorum & Gnosticorum opinioni, quam capitis
units.tr: Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons, who came next after him, holds the same opinion as he does concerning the state of souls from the moment of death until the day of judgement. For at the end of that famous work which he wrote against the heresies, after saying that the Lord remained until the third day in the lower parts of the earth, where the souls of the dead were, he sets against this the life we lead on earth and adds: It is clear that the soul of his disciples, for whose sake the Lord also did these things, departed into an invisible place fixed by God, and there it will remain until the resurrection, awaiting the resurrection; afterwards, receiving their bodies and rising perfectly, that is bodily, just as the Lord rose, so they come to the sight of God. And he sets this opinion of his against the opinion of the Valentinians and Gnostics, which he related at the beginning of the chapter.

units.la: Irenaeus lib.5. contra haeres. c.36. pitis initio retulit,opponit. Affirmabant autem illi fe simul atque mortui fuissent supergressuros cœlum & Demiurgum, & ad matrem, vel ad ipsum, qui ab ipsis fingebatur, Patrem. Quam quidem sententiam eodem planè modo,loco supra ex libro adversus Tryphonem citato rejicit Iustinus. Unde patet( ut cætera argumenta mittamus) ipsum de statu animarum post mortem in eadem fuisse cum Irenæo sententia. Iam Irenæus in hoc quoque lapsus est quod , secundo libro eiusdem adversus hæreses operis, acriter contendit Dominum non ætate seniorem, & quadraginta aut quinquaginta annos natum fuisse cum docuit & mortem perpessus est; quam sententiam, tametsi cum historia Evangelica haud leviter neque obscurè pugnantem,probabilibus & levibus argumentis conatur confirmare: quòd cùm venisset omnes infantes & parvulos & pueros & seniores per semetipsum salvare,omnem ætatem in seipso sanctificare debuerit. Eo item trahit verba Iudæorum ad Dominum.Quinquaginta annos nondum habes & Abrahamum vidisti? Denique refert S. Ioannem tradidisse senioribus in Asia Christum ætatem habuisse provectiorem cum docebat, natum scilicet quadraginta aut quinquaginta annos. Quod quidem commentum Baronius adeo absurdum putavit, ut præter omnium Irenæi exemplarium fidem, & satis perspicuum orationis eius contextum, nativámque cùm ingenij tum stili eius indolem, non dubitarit afferere, totum hunc locum ab imperito quopiam vel veteratore Irenæi textui assutum, ejúsque certò non esse. Sed videtur ipse non magna cum ratione in hanc suspicionem venisse, ut clarè docuit in suis ad Epiphanium notis Petavius Iesuita. Utcunque sit,colligere est Baronium non impossibile esse censuisse, quod priore huius tractatus parte disputavimus, fœdè interpolata pleraque Veterum Patrum monumenta fuisse,multis additis,pluribúsque per fraudem detractis. Eodem loco statuit & probat Irenæus animas characterem corpoin quo etiam adaptantur, cuslodire eundem corpore solutas licet, & habere hominis figuram, vt etiam cognoscantur. Omitto quid cap.49. ejusdem libri videtur significare neutri Christi naturæ Patrem horam & diem m judicij manifestauisse, etsi ægrè ad bonum sensum ista reduci posse videantur. Taceo item quod cùm ipse tum Lustinus adeo incautè de naturæ humanæ in salutis negotio viribus loquuntur. Sentio enim, cum Cassandro, omnes istos locos posse & debere explicari ex Scriptorum ipsorum proposito, quod non aliud fuit quàm confutare suitemporis hæreticos, qui cùm necessitatem naturalem in homine statuerent, cum omni electione & judicio spoliabant.
units.tr: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 5, ch. 36. ...which he related at the beginning of the chapter and opposes. Those men asserted that as soon as they died they would pass beyond the heaven and the Demiurge, and go to the Mother, or to the very Father who was imagined by them. Justin rejects this same opinion in exactly the same way, in the passage cited above from his book against Tryphon. So it is clear (to set aside other arguments) that Justin held the same view as Irenaeus about the state of souls after death. Irenaeus also erred in this, that in the second book of the same work against the heresies he vigorously maintains that the Lord was not older in age, but was about forty or fifty years old when he taught and suffered death. He tries to confirm this opinion, which fights not lightly nor obscurely against the Gospel history, with probable and slight arguments: since he came to save all infants, little children, boys and old men through himself, he had to sanctify every age in himself. He also draws to this the words of the Jews to the Lord: "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Finally, he reports that St John handed down to the elders in Asia that Christ, when he taught, had reached a more advanced age, namely about forty or fifty years old. Baronius thought this fiction so absurd that, against the testimony of all the manuscripts of Irenaeus and the quite clear context of his discourse, and the native character both of his mind and of his style, he did not hesitate to assert that this whole passage was stitched into Irenaeus's text by some unskilled person or forger, and is certainly not his. But he himself seems to have come to this suspicion without great reason, as the Jesuit Petavius clearly showed in his notes to Epiphanius.
