However that may be, it may be gathered that Baronius judged it not impossible (what we argued in the earlier part of this treatise) that most of the monuments of the ancient Fathers had been foully interpolated, with many additions and many passages removed by fraud. In the same place Irenaeus states and proves that souls keep the character of the body in which they are also fitted, even when loosed from the body, and that they have the figure of a man, so that they may be recognised. I pass over what ch. 49 of the same book seems to mean, namely that the Father revealed the hour and day of judgment to neither nature of Christ, although these things seem to be brought to a good sense only with difficulty. I likewise say nothing of how both he and Justin speak so carelessly about the powers of human nature in the business of salvation. For I think, with Cassander, that all those passages can and should be explained from the very purpose of the writers, which was nothing other than to refute the heretics of their own time, who, while they set up a natural necessity in man, stripped him of all choice and judgment.

units.la: Neque vero Clementis Alexandrini quæ summa fuit eruditio obstitit quominus in varios errores incideret. Docet is variis in locis Gentiles ante Christum natum justificatos fuisse per philosophiam, quæ tum erat ipsis (inquit (ad justitiam necessaria, at nunc tantum est ad Dei cul-tum vtilis; quæ Græcis fuerit quod Lex Hebraeis pædagogus scilicet ad Christum, vt quæ Græcos olim justificarit, cum eis deta fuerit vt esset proprium ipsorum sœdus, & fundamentum Philosophiæ quæ est secundum Christum. Sibi fingit deinde Dominü nostrū descendisse ad inferos vt prædicaret mortuis, multósque servasse, eos omnes videlicet qui crediderunt. Apostolos itē eo descendisse & post mortem similiter prædicasse Euangelii iis qui ex Gentibus apti erāt ad conversionem. Censet alioqui Deum injustum & personarum acceptorem, futurum, si damnasset eos qui ante Christi adventum vixerunt. Nam (inquit) si iis qui erant in carne propteres annunciavit Evangelium ne injuste condemnarentur, quomodo non iis etiam qui excesserunt ante ejus adventū propter eandem annuntiavit causam? Ex his & similibus rationibus concludit necesse fuisse vt omnium tam Gentilium quam Iudæorum animæ Domini prædicationem audi ent, ejusque dispensationis beneficio frueren-tur, vt illic (id est in inferis) audita prædicatione, aut ostenderent pœnitentiam [illegible, ~10 letters]iam. tiam, aut propterea quod non credidissent iustiu fatererentur esse supplicium. Passim etiam ex ejus operibus pater sentire eum omnes poenas, quas Deus hominibus infligit, ipsis esse salutares, adeo ut ab eo nonnisi ad institutionem & emendationem immittantur; quo in censu etiam ca supplicia collocat quae damnati apud inferos luunt. Unde etiam est quod alibi docet, per ignem expurgationem eorum qui male vixerunt fieri; quo refert conflagrationem a Stoicis creditam, & sententias quasdam Platonis, & Philosophi cujusdam Ephesij (id est Heraclíti.) Ex quibus intelligimus Clementem in ea quoque sententia fuisse, quam ipsius discipulus Origines sequitur passim, docens inferorum poenas omnes esse purgatorias, nonnadeo aeternos, sed aliquando desituras, postquam, scilicet, qui damnati sunt, eo igne satis excocti & purgati fuerint. Sed & cum lustino quidem docet Clemens Angelos amore mulierum correptos iis arcana multa, quae legenda fuerant, reuelasse, ab Irenaeo vero sententia Dominum usque ad quadraginta annos vitam in terris produxisse sententis longissime discedans tradit Christum annum integrum in carne praedicasse, & uno & trigesimo aetatis suae anno mortuum fuisse. Sed nullum operae pretium fuerit in hoc Scriptore diutius immorari, apud quem utrique confitemur multa parum sana occurrere.
units.tr: Nor did Clement of Alexandria's learning, great as it was, prevent him from falling into various errors. In several places he teaches that the Gentiles before the birth of Christ were justified through philosophy, "which was then necessary to them for righteousness (he says), but now is useful only for the worship of God; and which was to the Greeks what the Law was to the Hebrews, a tutor, that is, leading to Christ, since it justified the Greeks of old, when it was given to them so that it might be their own covenant and the foundation of the philosophy which is according to Christ." He then imagines that "our Lord descended into hell to preach to the dead, and saved many, namely all those who believed. The Apostles likewise went down there and after death similarly preached the Gospel to those among the Gentiles who were fit for conversion." He moreover thinks that God would be unjust and a respecter of persons if he had condemned those who lived before the coming of Christ. "For (he says) if he proclaimed the Gospel to those who were in the flesh, so that they might not be unjustly condemned, why did he not likewise proclaim it for the same cause to those who departed before his coming?" From these and similar reasons he concludes that the souls of all, Gentiles as well as Jews, must have heard the preaching of the Lord and enjoyed the benefit of his dispensation, "so that there (that is, in the underworld), once the preaching had been heard, they might either show repentance, or, because they had not believed, acknowledge that the punishment was just." Everywhere in his works it may also be seen that he holds that all the punishments which God inflicts on men are salutary to them, so that they are sent by him only for instruction and correction; and in this class he also places those punishments which the condemned suffer in the underworld. Hence it is that he also teaches elsewhere that the purging of those who have lived badly is effected by fire; to this he refers the conflagration believed in by the Stoics, and certain sayings of Plato, and of a certain philosopher of Ephesus (that is, Heraclitus). From these things we understand that Clement held also that opinion which his disciple Origen follows throughout, teaching that all the punishments of the underworld are purgatorial, and not eternal, but will at some time cease, once, that is, those who have been condemned have been sufficiently burned and cleansed by that fire. But Clement also, like Justin, teaches that the angels, seized by love of women, revealed many secrets which ought to have been kept hidden; and, departing far from Irenaeus's view that the Lord lived on earth until about forty years of age, he holds that Christ preached for a whole year in the flesh and died in the thirty-first year of his life. But it would be worth nothing to linger longer over this writer, in whom we both admit that many unsound things occur.

units.la: Tertuliani ad Montanistas defectio de ea, qua apud Ecclesiam propter pietatis fervorem eruditionemque cum nulla alia conferendam, pollebat auctoritate & gratia plurimum detraxit. Sed praeter quam quod aliquam operum suorum partem in Catholicorum communione elucubravit, considerandum est praeterea Montanismum illum, quem secutus est, disciplinam Ecclesiasticam tantum sollicitasse, fidem non violasse; Tertullianus autem qui ingenio esset tetrico & morosò, quam quidem Montanistae affectebant disciplinam austeram & severam facile probavit: quod vero pertinet ad ipsa fidei dogmota, ipse non semel testatur se in eadem siue norma, siue fide cum Catholicis constanter permanere. Vnde aculeatæ hæ voces quas in orthodoxos intorquet. Hi paracleto controversiam faciunt, propter hoc noua prophetia recusantur non quod alium Deum prædicent Montanus & Priscilla & Maximilla, nec quod Iesum Christum soluant, nec quod aliquam fidei aut spei regulam euertant, sed quod plane doceant sapius jejunare quàm nubere. Idipsum apparet ex uniuerso contextu librorum quos Montanista scripsit, in quibus de sola disciplina contra Catholicos pugnat, quod non & ita pridem pro suo canone confessus est novissimum operum eius editor. Sed licèt ab Ecclesiæ, (apud quam magno fuit olim in pretio) fide & doctrina non desciuerit, quot tamen in eius opera-ribus peregrinæ & absurdæ opiniones occurrunt? Nihil nunc de iis dicam quæ de persona Filij (quod jam supra me dixisse memini) nimium profectò securè atque periculosè loquitur, quàm stupenda philosophatur de natura Dei, quem videtur affectibus humanis, irę, odio, dolori obnoxium facere? cui tribuit substantiam corporeā, adeo vt, si ipsi fides, nemo negaturus sit Deum esse corpus, quo fit vt minùs mirum videri debeat quod tam fidenter asserat, nullam substantiam esse quæ non sit corporea, ¹ vel quòd cum lustino & Clemente Alexandrino Angelis amorem in mulieres carnalem tribuat. ᵇ Vnde hæc verba in libro de velandis virginibus. Debet adumbrari facies tam periculosa, quæ vis; ad cælum scandala jaculata est. His positis nemo item mirari debet eius de animæ humanæ natura sententiam, quam corporalem esse statuit c certâque figura atque effigie conformatam; de substantia pa-ris in filij corpus propagatam, satam & genitam cū corpore, & una redundantem & alia ejusmodi somnia quætamen in libro de anima tanta vi, contentione, subtilitate & eloquentia tuetur, vt vix in tota Antiquitate quicquam occurrat ornatius atque elegantius. Cæterum hic quoque non minùs quàm Irenæus, omne animâ ex hac vita migrantem, subterraneo quodam carcere includit in quo vult eam sequestrari vsque ad diem judicij, nulli enim ex ejus sententia patet cœlum terra adhuc saluam, ne (inquit) dixerim clausa. Solis martyribus concedit vt in paradisum ingrediantur (quem tamen sub cœlo & ipsum collocat) vt in eo vsque ad postremum judicium viuant. Tota (inquit) paradisi clavis sanguis tuus est, statuitq; locum illum, in quo sequestrantur animæ, vsque ad finem clausum manere; decernens de cætero, planè præter Iustini mentem, omnes animarum humanarum apparitiones, illusiones & Diaboli fraudes esse; hanc item animarum sequestrationem permansuram donec noua Ierusalem tota ex gemmis & margaritis constructa per miraculum de cœlo descendat in mille annos permansura, (in ea vitam omnibus bonis & gloria cumulatissimam viuentibus, interea dum sanctorum concludatur sanctorum resurrectio pro meritis maturius vel tardius resurgentiu. Vnde explicandum est quod alibi docet, modicum quodque deluctum mora resurrectionis illic luendum. Post ipsos mille annos, &c. tunc & mundi destructione, & judicy conflagratione commissa, futurū vt in atomo in angelicam substantiam de mutemur. Taceo inuectibus auersus repetitas nuptias, & quam de toto nuptiarum negotio iniquè sentiat, sunt enim commenta ista è disciplina Paracliti Montanici. Sed magno numero consentientes habuit catholicos in eo quod de Baptismo hæreticorum docuit, scilicet habendum esse, adeo vt qui ab eorum communione veniebant, ante baptizandos, quàm admittendos censeret. Apud nos (inquit) Ethnico par, imo & super Ethnicum hæreticus, etiā per Baptismā veritatis vtroque homine purgatus admittitur. Fideles veio adeo non inuitat vel vrget ad Baptismum jam inde à prima infantia suscipiendum, quod hodie fit, vt concedat, imo & auctor sit pueris & ipsis adolescentibus vt pro cuiusque conditione ac dispositione, etiam atate cunctetur Baptismum accipere, quod ille vtilius esse judicat. Quemadmodum autem in hoc
units.tr: The defection of Tertullian to the Montanists, which robbed him of much of the authority and favour he had enjoyed in the Church, on account of his fervour of piety and a learning matched by no other, has to be weighed. But apart from the fact that he composed some part of his works while still in communion with the Catholics, it must be considered that the Montanism which he followed troubled only ecclesiastical discipline, and did not violate the faith. Tertullian, however, who had a harsh and morose temperament, readily approved the austere and severe discipline which the Montanists favoured. As for the dogmas of the faith themselves, he himself more than once testifies that he remained constantly with the Catholics in the same rule and the same faith. Hence those biting words he hurls at the orthodox: "These men make a controversy with the Paraclete; on this ground the new prophecy is rejected, not because Montanus and Priscilla and Maximilla preach another God, nor because they dissolve Jesus Christ, nor because they overturn any rule of faith or hope, but because they plainly teach that one should fast more often than marry." The same appears from the whole context of the books which he wrote as a Montanist, in which he fights against the Catholics only over discipline; this the latest editor of his works has likewise admitted, having long ago so declared in his own account of the canon. But although he did not desert the faith and doctrine of the Church (among whom he was once held in great esteem), how many foreign and absurd opinions nonetheless occur in his works! I will now say nothing of those things which he says about the person of the Son (as I recall having said above) with far too much rashness and danger; nor how wonderfully he philosophises about the nature of God, whom he seems to make liable to human passions, anger, hatred and grief. To God he attributes a corporeal substance, so that, if one believes him, no one will deny that God is a body; and this makes it less surprising that he so confidently asserts that there is no substance which is not corporeal, or that, with Justin and Clement of Alexandria, he ascribes to the angels a carnal love of women. Hence these words in his book On the Veiling of Virgins: "The face which has such power ought to be shadowed, which has hurled scandals up to heaven." Given these things, no one should likewise be surprised at his opinion about the nature of the human soul, which he holds to be corporeal and formed with a definite shape and likeness, propagated from the substance of the father into the body of the son, sown and begotten together with the body and passing over with it, and other dreams of this kind. Yet in his book On the Soul he defends these with such force, contentiousness, subtlety and eloquence that hardly anything more ornate and elegant can be found in all antiquity. Yet here too, no less than Irenaeus, he shuts up every soul that migrates from this life in a certain subterranean prison, in which he wants it kept apart until the day of judgment; for according to his view the heaven is not yet open to any, "lest (he says) I should say shut." He concedes to martyrs alone that they enter paradise (which he too places under the heaven), there to live until the last judgment. "The whole key of paradise (he says) is your blood." He holds that the place in which souls are kept apart remains closed until the end, and, decreeing otherwise, quite contrary to Justin's mind, that all apparitions of human souls are illusions and deceits of the Devil; and that this separation of souls will last until the new Jerusalem, built entirely of gems and pearls, descends from heaven by a miracle, and will last for a thousand years (during which life, filled with every good and glory, is lived by all the good), while "the resurrection of the saints is kept back, so that they may rise sooner or later according to their merits." Hence what he teaches elsewhere must be explained: that "each small delay of the resurrection is to be paid there." After those thousand years, and so on, then, with the destruction of the world and the conflagration of judgment accomplished, it will come about that "in an atom they are changed into an angelic substance." I pass over his repeated invectives against second marriages, and how unjustly he thinks of the whole matter of marriage; for those notions come from the discipline of the Montanist Paraclete. But he had a great number of Catholics agreeing with him in what he taught about the baptism of heretics, namely that it must be held valid, so that those who came over from their communion were to be baptised before being admitted. "With us (he says) a heretic is admitted on a par with a Gentile, or even above a Gentile, when he has been cleansed in both man and woman by the baptism of truth." But he does not invite or urge the faithful to receive baptism from the very first infancy, as is done today, so that he even concedes, indeed is the author for boys and for young men themselves, that they may delay receiving baptism according to each one's condition and disposition, even into adult age; which he judges more useful. But just as in this matter he approaches the view of the Anabaptists, so in other matters too he agrees with them, most of all in this, that he denies that a Christian may exercise any judicial office.

units.la: argumento ad Anabaptistarum sententiam accedit, sic & in aliis ipsi cum illis convenit, vt in hoc maximè quod Christiano licere negat vllum judiciarium munus a exercere. Neque, inquit, judicet de capite alicujus, &c. neque damnet, &c. neque vinciat, neque recludat aut torqueat. Sed & bellare vetat vel ad militiam nomen dare diserte scribens, omnem militem Dominum in Petro exarmando discinxisse. Haec est Tertulliani disciplina quo fit ut eorum vel studium vel certè oscitantiam mirer qui ex Scriptoris mitissimi planéque innoxii loco vno, sed perpetram intellecto, colligere non dubitant censuisse ipsum capitalibus poenis in haereticos esse saeviendum, à qua immanitate haud propius cum abfuisse certum est quàm coelum distat à terra. Addo, antequam ad reliqua pergo, censere ipsum c Christum mortem pertulisse trigesimo aetatis anno, quod tamen adversa fronte cum Evangelio pugnat; & sibi fingit d gratiam coelestem & spiritum Prophetiae in Ioanne Baptista, post totius Spiritus in Dominum translationem defecisse.
units.tr: In this matter he comes close to the opinion of the Anabaptists, and in other points too he agrees with them, most of all in denying that a Christian may hold any judicial office. "He shall not," he says, "judge concerning the life of anyone, etc.; nor condemn, etc.; nor bind, nor shut up or torture." He also forbids warfare, and writes plainly that "the Lord, in disarming Peter, ungirded every soldier." This is Tertullian's teaching. I marvel either at the zeal or at the sheer carelessness of those who do not hesitate to infer, from one passage of this most gentle and wholly harmless writer, read carelessly, that he thought heretics should be punished with capital penalties. He was as far from such savagery as heaven is from earth. Before I go on to the rest, I add that he held Christ suffered death in the thirtieth year of his age, which clashes head-on with the Gospel. He also imagines that heavenly grace and the spirit of prophecy failed in John the Baptist after the whole Spirit had been transferred to the Lord.

units.la: Hujus vnicus admirator Cyprianus, vt etiam eum propeter excellentiam magistrum vocitare soleret, c ista- rum sententiarum quasdam liberè sequutus est, ac, inter cæteras, proximam de rebaptizandis hæreticis, mordicus tenuit, consentientibus ferè clarissimis quibúsque illius memoriæ viris, Firmiliano Cappadociæ Metropolitano,& Dionysio Alexandriæ Episcopo,cum Africæ, Cappadociæ, Pamphyliæ & Bithiniæ Conciliis, tametsi vehementer obsisteret & in iras atque anathemata nequicquam prorumperet Stephanus Episcopus Romanus, qui & ipse propriam fovebat, non multo probabiliorem, sententiam. Omnes enim nullo discrimine hæreticos absque Baptismo admittebat, vt ex LXXIV. Cypriani i epistolæ initio apparet. At Ecclesia quinque & sexaginta, vel circiter annis post Stephanum, Sa-
units.tr: Cyprian, his only great admirer, who used to call him master on account of his excellence, freely followed some of these opinions. Among others he held stubbornly to the nearer view on rebaptizing heretics, with the agreement of almost all the most famous men of that age: Firmilian, Metropolitan of Cappadocia, and Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, and the councils of Africa, Cappadocia, Pamphylia and Bithynia. Stephen, Bishop of Rome, strongly resisted, and vainly broke out into wrath and anathemas; he too cherished his own opinion, which was not much more probable. For he admitted all heretics without any distinction and without baptism, as appears from the beginning of Cyprian's seventy-fourth epistle. But the Church, some sixty-five years or so after Stephen, Sa-

units.la: i Cypr. ep 74 vbi referuntur hæc Stephani verba: si ergo a quacunque hæresi venerit ad nos nihil innovetur, nisi quod traditum est, vt manus illi imponantur in poenitentiam. Et ibid. p. 94 B. mosatenianorum Baptismum irritum pronuntiavit, qua ratione videri posset reliquos absque baptismo admittendos censuisse. Sed secundi Concilij oecumenici Patres intra hos limites se non continuerunt: non mittendos ... nus enim quam Gentiles ipsos rebaptizari voluerunt omnes qui à communione Eunomianorum, Montanistarum, Phrygum, Sabellianorum, & aliorum haereticorum ad Ecclesiam Catholicam se recipiebant. Solos Arianos, Macedonianos, Sabbatianos, Novatianos, Quartodecimanos & Apollinaristas ab ea lege immunes non rebaptizandos constituerunt, ut patet ex istius Concilij codicibus Graecis Can. VII. qui etiam habetur in Codice Graeco Ecclesiae vniversalis n° clxx. Ita & Stephanus & Cyprianus suas vterque habuerunt privatas de hoc argumento sententias, quod omnium simpliciter haereticorum baptismum ille quidem admitteret, hic vero repudiaret; quem duae Synodi oecumenicae simpliciter neque admittunt, neque rejiciunt; sed aliorum quidem admittunt, aliorum vero repudiant. Caeterum Stephano (ut mihi quidem videtur) Cyprianus eo praeferendus est quod cum vtergq; erraret, hic quidem aliter sentientes ferebat, vt ex Synodo Carthaginensi constat & ab Hieronymo confirmatur. Stephanus vero, vt erat, Firmiliano teste, feruidus & iracundus omnes, qui à sententia sua recedebant communione sua summouebat. Idem Beatus Martyr in fui seculi errore vel sabatur, putans omnibus baptizatis, ne pueris quidem exceptis, Euchatiftiam esse ad salutem necessariam, ut apparet ex Epistola. lix. in qua cum lxv. Episcopis pueros recens natos ad Baptismum & Euchatiftiam admittit, contra cujusdam Fidi sententiam qui nonnisi Octavo die pueros ad ista Sacramenta admittebat. Patet idem ex eo quod alibi narrat de puella, quae licet per aetatem loqui non posset, attamen insigni miraculo repulit à se sanctificatum in Domini sanguine potum quem Diaconus reluctanti in os infundebat in coetu fidelium, conscientia quadam facti, & quasi se eo indignam existimasset quod paulò ante delata fuisset ad idolum quoddam,&panem meromixtum de immolatione accepisset. {b} Manabat autem error ille ex eo quod Eucharistiam non minùs quam Baptismum ad salutem necessarium arbitrabantur, vt facile est colligere ex ejusdem Auctoris verbis lib. 3. de tetam ad Quirinum, cujus cùm hanc {c} epigraphen fecisset. Ad regnum Dei nisi baptizatus & renatus fuerit quis pervenire non posse vt id probet,citat primo ex Iean,3. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu non potest introire in regnum Dei; deinde statim subjicit ex ejusdem Evangelij cap.6.nisi aderitis carnem filij hominis,& biberitis sanguinem ejus non habebitis vitam in vobis. Illum locum ad Baptismum, hunc ad Eucharistiam referens, quòd vtrumque ad regenerationem necessariam existimaret. Omitto nonnulla quae ipsi quandoque in hoc de haereticorum Baptismo argumento excidunt,ex quibus videri potest ejus sacramenti efficaciam ex ministri sanctitate & integritate pendere voluisse.{d} Iam de Origine nobis agendum esset; sed quandoquidem ex quo è vivis excessit ejus multi ingenium & doctrinam infamarunt, alij contra acriter defenderunt, intactum eum sinemus neque nos in controversiam tanta vtrimque animorum contentione agitatam immittemus Vnum tantum ex eo exemplo notandum venit, neque antiquitatem,neque eruditionem neque sanctitatem necessario obstare quominus homines in insulsos & graves errores incidant, quippe cùm inter antiquissimos sit Origines, & paucis annis tertij seculi dimidium praetergressus sis; neque ei caetera, hoc est vitae innocentiam, &summam doctrinam vel infensissimi hostes inviderint aut negarint. Quae verò de ipsius casu narrat {e} Ehiphanius ea visi laudem nihil prorsus imminuunt, primò quod etiamsi constarer rem ita gestam fuisse, vt perhiber Epiphanius, non desint fidelium exempla qui grauissimae tentationi succubuerunt, vt ex Petri exemplo
units.tr: (i) Cyprian, Epistle 74, where these words of Stephen are reported: "If therefore anyone comes to us from any heresy, nothing is to be changed except what has been handed down, that hands be laid on him for repentance." And ibid., p. 94 B. He pronounced the baptism of the Samosatenians void, by which reasoning it might seem that he judged the rest to be admitted without baptism. But the Fathers of the second ecumenical council did not keep within these limits. They wished all who came over to the Catholic Church from the communion of the Eunomians, Montanists, Phrygians, Sabellians and other heretics to be rebaptized, no less than the Gentiles themselves. They exempted from this rule only the Arians, Macedonians, Sabbatians, Novatians, Quartodecimans and Apollinarists, ordering that these not be rebaptized, as is clear from the Greek codices of that council, Canon VII, which is also found in the Greek Codex of the universal Church, no. 170. Thus both Stephen and Cyprian had their own private opinions on this question: the one would simply admit the baptism of all heretics, the other would simply reject it. Two ecumenical synods neither simply admit nor simply reject them, but admit some and reject others. Moreover, to Stephen (as it seems to me) Cyprian is to be preferred, because though both erred, Cyprian bore with those who thought otherwise, as the Council of Carthage establishes and Jerome confirms. But Stephen, as Firmilian testifies, was fervent and hot-tempered and removed from his communion all who departed from his opinion. The same blessed martyr also slipped into the error of his age, thinking the Eucharist necessary to salvation for all the baptized, infants not excepted. This appears from Epistle 59, in which, together with sixty-five bishops, he admits newborn infants to baptism and the Eucharist, against the opinion of a certain Fidus, who admitted children to these sacraments only on the eighth day. The same appears from what he tells elsewhere of a girl who, though too young to speak, with a remarkable miracle refused the drink sanctified in the Lord's blood, which the deacon poured into her unwilling mouth in the assembly of the faithful. From some awareness of the deed, she seemed to think herself unworthy, because shortly before she had been taken to a certain idol and had received bread mixed with what had been sacrificed. (b) That error arose from their thinking the Eucharist no less necessary to salvation than baptism, as is easily gathered from the words of the same author in Book 3 of the Testimonies to Quirinus. Having made this heading (c) "Unless a man is baptized and born again, he cannot come to the kingdom of God," he proves it by citing first John 3: "Unless a man is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God"; then straightaway he adds from the sixth chapter of the same Gospel: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." He refers the former passage to baptism and the latter to the Eucharist, since he thought both necessary to regeneration. I omit some things that sometimes slipped from him on this question of heretics' baptism, from which it can be seen that he wished the efficacy of that sacrament to depend on the holiness and integrity of the minister. (d) Now we ought to deal with Origen. But since, from the time he passed from life, many have defamed his genius and learning, while others have fiercely defended him, we shall leave him untouched and not enter into a controversy stirred on both sides with such heat of minds. Only one thing from that example needs noting: neither antiquity, nor learning, nor holiness necessarily prevents men from falling into foolish and grave errors. Origen is among the most ancient writers, and he lived only a few years past the middle of the third century. Nor did even his most bitter enemies grudge or deny his other qualities, namely the innocence of his life and his great learning. As for what Epiphanius (e) relates of his fall, those things do not in the least diminish his praise. First, even if it were established that the thing happened as Epiphanius reports, there are not lacking examples of believers who succumbed to a very grave temptation, as the example of Peter

units.la: apparet: tum, ne quid dissimulem,placet mihi Baronij sententia, totam istam narrationem commentitiam esse docentis,natam ex eorum odiis,qui magni & admirabilis istius viri gloriam ferre non potuerunt, & vel Epiphanij libris inde per fraudem assutam, vel quod potiùs reor, & probabilius est ab Epiphanio temerè creditam,& literis mandatam; qualia habet nom pauca vir, sanctus quidem, sed interdum profectò nimium credulus, vt vel postremus eius interpres confitetur. Cùm ergo Origenes: tantis donis licèt instructus, plurima tamen procuderit, & defenderit peregrina & absurda dogmata, quæ acriter, nec immeritò ab Ecclesia posteriorum seculorum repudiata sunt; hoc exemplo docemur Doctores, vel antiquissimos, doctissimos, atque sanctissimos posse in errores etiam tetros incidere. Nulla enim ratio est cur quod Origeni in multis accidit, idem cuivis non possit in quibusdam accidere.
units.tr: shows. Then, not to conceal anything, I am pleased with Baronius's opinion, that the whole story is fabricated, born of the hatred of those who could not bear the glory of that great and admirable man. Either it was inserted fraudulently into Epiphanius' books, or, what I rather think and is more probable, it was rashly believed by Epiphanius and committed to writing. He has several such things, being a man holy indeed but at times clearly too credulous, as even his latest translator confesses. Since Origen, though furnished with such great gifts, nevertheless produced many things and defended foreign and absurd doctrines, which the Church of later centuries rejected sharply and not undeservedly, we are taught by this example that even teachers who were most ancient, most learned and most holy can fall into errors that are even foul. For there is no reason why what happened to Origen in many matters should not be able to happen to anyone in some matters.

units.la: Sed neque dissimulandum est eos qui adversus Origenem scripserunt non fuisse in his disputationibus tanta fœlicitate versatos, vt, dum huius errores oppugnant, in nullos ipsi incurrerint. Methodius ā istorum primipilaris apud Epiphanium docet homines post resurrectionem & vltimum judicium æternùm in terra habitaturos, & Angelorum more, sine ulla mutatione, in immortalitatis statu optima quæque facturos. Ipse quoque cum aliis Angelos mulierum amatores ᵇ fingit, Providentissimque Dei nonnisi causas vniuersales curare statuit, ᶜ & particularia quæque Angelis committere. Quas sanè sententias qui recte expenderit, non minùs perniciosas Scripturæque adversas judicabit, quam eas ipsas quas in Origene notat atque reprehendit.
units.tr: But it must not be concealed that those who wrote against Origen were not so fortunate in these disputes that, while attacking his errors, they fell into none themselves. Methodius, the foremost of these men, teaches in Epiphanius that men will dwell on the earth for ever after the resurrection and the last judgment, and that in the state of immortality, like the angels, without any change, they will do all the best things. He himself, along with others, imagines that angels are lovers of women, and he decides that God's providence takes care only of universal causes and entrusts each particular matter to the angels. Anyone who weighs these opinions rightly will judge them no less pernicious and contrary to Scripture than the very ones he notes and reproves in Origen.

units.la: Iisdem de causis Eusebium, Didymum, Apollinarem & alios ejusmodi omitto, licet enim Veteres sint; vulgò tamen haud magni fiunt, propterea quòd apud maximam Ecclesiæ partem malè audierint. Antiquissimi enim (quanquam non minoribus nævis laboraverit corum fides tamen æquius à posteris accepti sunt, seu quòd ætate longè superiores eorum qui in cæteros censuram exercuerunt odia & invidiam minùs excitarint, seu quòd propter exi<.stimationem in qua apud Ecclesiæ vulgus erant ipsis parcitum sit.
units.tr: For the same reasons I pass over Eusebius, Didymus, Apollinaris and others of that sort. Although they are ancient, they are generally not held in high regard, because they have a bad reputation with most of the Church. The earliest writers, though their faith was not free of no small blemishes, have been received more fairly by posterity, either because they lived so long before those who took up censure of others and so stirred up less hatred and envy, or because they were spared on account of the reputation they enjoyed among the common people of the Church.

units.la: Lactantius Firmianus licet à veterum paucis de erroribus accusatus, ab iis tamen immunis non fuit. Iamdudum Hieronymus gravissimum notavit. Lactantius (inquit) in libris suis, ut maximè in epistolis ad Demetrianū, Spiritus sanctl omnino negat subsistantiam, &, errore Iudaico, dicit eum, vel ad Patrem referri, vel ad Filium, & sanctificationem utriusque persona sub ejus nomine demonstrari. Cæteri sunt leviores, eíque cum multis aliis Patribus communes: ut quod, verbi gratia docet Angelos mulierum congressibus inquinatos, & inde nescio quod genus dæmonum terrenorum natum. Idem quod disserit omnes( animas) in una communi custodia detineri, donec tempus adveniat quo maximus Iudex meritorum faciat examen. Christum ante ultimum judicium in terras venturum, & eos qui tum superstites futuri sunt non morituros, sed permille annos infinitam multitudinem genera turos, vitámque in civitate ornatissima acturos pacatam, omnibúsque commodis uberrimè affluentem, sub Christi & sanctorum quorumdam à mortuis suscitatorum regno.
units.tr: Lactantius Firmianus, though accused of error by few of the ancients, was not free from it either. Jerome long ago noted a very serious one: Lactantius (he says) in his books, especially in the letters to Demetrianus, altogether denies the subsistence of the Holy Spirit, and by a Jewish error says that he is referred either to the Father or to the Son, and that the sanctification of both persons is shown under his name. His other errors are lighter and are shared with many other Fathers. For example, he teaches that the angels were defiled by intercourse with women, and that from this some kind of earthly demons, I know not what, were born. He also argues that all souls are held in one common custody until the time comes when the greatest Judge makes the examination of merits. He holds that Christ will come to earth before the last judgment, and that those who are then alive will not die but will beget an infinite multitude for a thousand years, and will live in a most splendid city in peace, richly flowing with every blessing, under the reign of Christ and of certain saints raised from the dead.

units.la: Quid quod noster Hilarius qui circa medium seculum quartum florebat suos etiam manes passus est, nævis & ipse aspersus eo insignioribus quo pluris à Veteribus factus est? Errorum omnium perniciosissimus is est quòd naturam Christi humanam nullo dolorum vel cruciatuum sensu affectam fuisse existimat. Passus quidem( inquit) Dominus Iesus Christus dum caditur, dum suspenditur, dum crucifigitur, dum moritur, sed in corpus irruens passio, nec tamen naturam passionis exercuit, dum & pœnali ministerio illa defuit, & virtus corporis sine sensu pœnæ vim in se defevientis excepit. Habuit sanè illud Domini corpus doloris nostri naturam, si corpus nostrum id natura habet ut calcet undas,& super fluctus eat;& non deprimatur ingressus, neque aqua insistentis vestigiis cedant, penetret etiā solida, nec clausa domus obstaculis arceatur. Et paulo post.Et homo ille de Deo est, habens ad patiendum quidem corpus, ut passus est, sed naturam non habens ad dolendum. Natura enim propria ac sua corpus illud est, quod in cœlestem gloriam transformatur in monte.Id ibid.In quem quāvis aut ictus incideret, aut vulnus descenderet, aut nodi concurrerent, aut suspensio elevaret, afferrent quidē hac impetum passionis, non tamen dolore passionis inferrent: ut telū aliquod aut aquam perforās, aut ignem compungens, aut aera vulnerans. Omnes quidē has passiones natura sua infert ut perforret, ut cōpungat, ut vulneret, sed naturā suam in hac passio illata non retinet, dū in natura non est vel aquā forari, vel pungi igne, vel aera vulnerari, quāvis natura telis sit vulnerare & cōpungere & forare. Et ne putes illa ei subito ex impudenti aliquo animi impetu excidisse, eadē variis in locis repetit. Vt Cōmentario in Psal.53.Suscepta, inquit,voluntarie est (passio) officio quidem satisfactura pœnali, nō tamen pœna sensu læsura patientē. Et alibi quoq;Putatur dolore quia patitur, caret vero doloribus ipse quia Deus est. Apud te jam reputa quo ista evadant, et quæ futura sit nostra salus, si passio Christi, quæ ejus unicum fundamentum est, evanida tantum fuit, & inanis, sine vllo doloris sensu, passionis imago. Ac ut, .. repositio semel vno absurdo, aliud sequatur necesse est, sua illa privata opinione ad totam passionis Dominicæ pervertendam historiam inductus est. Fingit enim caliginosæ illius noctis, in qua Dominus propter assensas noxas traditus est gravissimos angores, grumosq; illos sanguinis, non à doloribus aut cruce illa cui affigendus erat manasse (& sanè cum ex ejus sententia nullus Christo dolor incumberet, nihil erat quod eo commoveretur, sed à metu quo afficiebatur, ne discipuli sui, qui se cæsum & crucifixum erant contemplaturi, Deum negarent, & ficin Spiritum Sanctum peccarent, & hanc rationem in Petro servatam, qui cum eum negaretur effet, sic negavit,non novi hominem,quia dictum aliquod in filium hominis remittitur. Illa vero Domini verba, Pater mi si possibile est transeat a me calix iste, nostra ita accipit,non ut Dominus a se passionem deprecetur,sed ut optet discipulos,postquam ipse passus fuerit,eadem quoque ratione similia pati. Transeat, inquit, calix a me, id est quomodo a me bibitur,ita ab iis bibatur,sine spei diffidentia,sine sensu doloris,sine metu mortis. Quicquam ne fingi potuit, vel frigidius,vel dilutius,vel a simplicitate & veritate Evangelica magis alienum ? Satis autem mirari non possumus,quod postquam Christi carnem in spiritum ita transformavit, alibi animas nostras in corpora immutet. Nihil est(inquit) quod non in substantia sua & creatione corporeum fit,&c. Nam & animarum species, sive obtinentium corpora sive corporibus exulantiis,corpoream tamen natura sua substantiam sortiuntur. Censet Baptismum ab omnibus peccatis nos minime mundare, & omnibus postremo die per ignem transeundum decernit. Haec enim ejus sunt. In quo (die judicii) nobis est indefessus ille
units.tr: What of our Hilary, who flourished about the middle of the fourth century? He too has suffered his own shades, and he is stained with blemishes all the more conspicuous because the Ancients held him in such high esteem. The most pernicious of all his errors is that he thinks the human nature of Christ was affected by no sense of pain or torment. The Lord Jesus Christ indeed suffered (he says) when he was struck, when he was hanged, when he was crucified, when he died; but the suffering, falling upon the body, did not exercise the nature of suffering, since it lacked the penal service, and the power of the body received the force of what was bearing down upon it without any sense of punishment. That body of the Lord certainly had the nature of our pain, if our body has by nature the power to tread on the waves and walk over the billows, and the step is not sunk, and the traces of his feet do not yield to the water, and he penetrates even solid things, and a closed house is not kept out by obstacles. And a little later: That man is of God, having a body capable of suffering, as he suffered, but not having a nature capable of feeling pain. For that body is by its own proper nature the body which is transformed into heavenly glory on the mountain. The same in the same place: Into whatever blow or wound might fall upon him, or whatever knots might gather, or whatever hanging might lift him up, they would indeed bring the force of suffering, but would not inflict the pain of suffering: as a weapon piercing water, or pricking fire, or wounding air. All these sufferings by their nature perforate, prick and wound, but in that suffering which is inflicted he does not keep his nature, since it is not in the nature of water to be pierced, or of fire to be pricked, or of air to be wounded, although the nature of weapons is to wound, prick and pierce. And lest you think these things slipped from him suddenly in some rash impulse of mind, he repeats the same things in various places. So in his Commentary on Psalm 53: The suffering, he says, was undertaken voluntarily, to satisfy by its office the penalty, but not to harm the one who suffers by the sense of punishment. And elsewhere also: He is thought to grieve because he suffers, but he himself is free from grief because he is God. Consider for yourself where these things lead, and what our salvation would be if the passion of Christ, which is its sole foundation, was only an empty appearance, a semblance of suffering without any sense of pain. And as one absurdity is followed by another, he was led by his private opinion to pervert the whole history of the Lord's passion. For he imagines that the grievous agonies of that dark night, in which the Lord was betrayed on account of the sins of others, and those clotted drops of blood, did not flow from the pains or from the cross to which he was to be fastened (and indeed, since on his view no pain weighed upon Christ, there was nothing that could move him, but rather from the fear by which he was seized, lest his disciples, who were about to behold him beaten and crucified, should deny God, and sin against the Holy Spirit; and he thinks this reason was observed in Peter, who, when he was denied, so denied, I do not know the man, because some word is remitted against the Son of Man). But those words of the Lord, My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me, he takes thus: not that the Lord prayed to be spared the suffering, but that he wished his disciples, after he himself had suffered, to suffer similar things in the same way. Let the cup pass from me, he says, that is, as it is drunk by me, so let it be drunk by them, without distrust of hope, without a sense of pain, without fear of death. Could anything more frigid, more diluted, or more alien to Gospel simplicity and truth have been devised? We cannot sufficiently wonder, however, that after he so transformed the flesh of Christ into spirit, he elsewhere changes our souls into bodies. Nothing is (he says) which is not corporeal in its substance and creation, etc. For the kinds of souls, whether they hold bodies or are exiled from bodies, nevertheless by their nature receive a corporeal substance. He holds that baptism does not cleanse us at all from all sins, and he decrees that all must pass through fire on the last day. For these are his words: On that day (of judgment) for us there is that tireless

units.la: Id. ibid. sol. 33. A. Transeat calix a me, id est, quomodo a me bibitur, ita ab iis bibatur, sine spei diffidentia, sine sensu doloris, sine metu mortis, &c.
units.tr: Id. ibid. sol. 33. A. Let this cup pass from me, that is, as it is drunk by me, so let it be drunk by them, without distrust of hope, without a sense of pain, without fear of death, etc.

units.la: Id. fer. in Matth. Can. 5. sol. 7. A. col. 1.
units.tr: Id. fer. in Matth. Can. 5. sol. 7. A. col. 1.

units.la: Id. in Psalm. 112. lib. Gimel. sol. 53 B. col. 1. ignis obeundus in quo subeunda sunt gravia illa expianda animæ supplicia. Beatæ Mariæ animam gladius pertransibit vt revelentur multorum cordium cogitationes. Si in judicij severitatem capax illa Dei Virgo ventura est, desiderare quis audebit à Deo judicari? Nescio an suo tempore multos in sententiam induxerit, nostro quidem frustra eam Franciscanis, frustra cæteris B. Virginis ab omni peccatis labe immunitatem defendentibus occinerent.
units.tr: Id. in Psalm. 112. lib. Gimel. sol. 53 B. col. 1. There is a fire to be undergone, in which those heavy punishments of the soul to be expiated must be endured. A sword will pierce the soul of the blessed Mary, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. If that Virgin of God is to come to the severity of judgment, who would dare to desire to be judged by God? I do not know whether he persuaded many of this opinion in his own time; but in ours, they sing it in vain to the Franciscans, and in vain to the others who defend the immunity of the blessed Virgin from every stain of sin.

units.la: Basilius Cæsareæ in Cappadocia laudatissimus Episcopus suos tamen & ipse nævos habet. Nam eo manifestè propendet, vt quicunque non simpliciter à schismate, sed ab hæresi ad Ecclesiam veniunt, ij rebaptizentur; vt aliqui hæretici sine baptismo suspiciantur non concedit, nisi ad vitandum scandalum, ἐπειδὴ δὲ (inquit) ὅλως ἐδόξει που τῷ κῷ τῷ Ασίαν οἰκονομίας ἕνεκα τῶν πολλῶν διχαθῶν αὐτῷ τὸ βάπτισμα, ἔσω δίχτον. Quoniam autem Asianis quibusdam placuit propter quandam dispensationem· vt vt eorum(hæreticorum) baptisma reciperetur, esse receptû. Prope accedit ad suì Firmiliani sententiam. Notavit Petavius,& viri maximi nomini adeo non pepercit, ut in has eius ad Amphilochium epistola multa mirifica, & si verum quaerimus parum catholica continerì exserte sensit. sed & Basilius videtur ab Origenis de purgatorio ipsius gehennæ igne dogmate non admodum abhorruisse. Certè vix'aliter explicari possunt quæ in Isaiæ cap.quartum philosophatur, eos ipsos qui ad mortem voluntariè peccant igne purgari constituens. Origeni quidem & ipsum & summum eius amicum Gregorium Nazianzenum multum tribuisse loquitur Philocalia communis utriusque ex Origene labor.
units.tr: Basil, the most praised bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, nevertheless has his own blemishes. For he clearly inclines to this, that those who come to the Church not simply from schism but from heresy should be rebaptized; and he does not allow that some heretics are to be regarded as without baptism, except to avoid scandal: Since, however, it seemed good to some of the Asians, for the sake of a certain economy, that their baptism should be received, let it be received. [Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὅλως ἔδοξέ που τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν οἰκονομίας ἕνεκα τῶν πολλῶν δεχθῆναι αὐτῶν τὸ βάπτισμα, ἔστω δεκτόν.] He comes close to the opinion of Firmilian. Petavius has noted this, and spared no reverence for so great a man's name, so that he plainly perceived in this letter of his to Amphilochius that it contains many marvellous things, and, if we seek the truth, little that is catholic. But Basil also seems not to have greatly shrunk from Origen's doctrine of a purgatorial fire, the fire of Gehenna itself. Certainly the things he philosophizes on in the fourth chapter of Isaiah can hardly be explained otherwise, when he holds that even those who sin willingly unto death are purged by fire. The Philocalia, the common labour of Basil and Gregory from Origen, indeed tells us that both Origen himself and his great friend Gregory of Nazianzus owed him much.

units.la: Gregorius verò magnum & ipse Ecclesiæ Græcanicæ decus Origenici istius dogmatis clara expressaque vestigia non uno in loco exhibet. Nam cum ignem vindicantem & punientem alicubi memorasset,& à purgante distinxisset, dixisseque illum nunquam extingui, sed perennare cum ipsis qui puniuntur, peccatoribus, eam sententiam veluti paulò diriorem & inhumaniorem corrigens statim hæc addit; nisi cui tamen hoc quoque loco id humanius, ac ut Deo qui punit dignum est, intelligere placeat. Eodem referendum videtur quod oratione præcedenti Novatianos, si in ichismate perseverent sine resipiscentia, baptizatum iti ait igni; qui postremus est baptismus, inquit, nec solum acerbior, sed etiam diuturnior, pœnas etiam impœnitentibus denuntians, diuturnas quidem & acerbas, non tamen æternas.
units.tr: Gregory of Nazianzus, the great ornament of the Greek Church, also shows clear and express traces of this Origenist doctrine in more than one place. When he has mentioned somewhere the avenging and punishing fire, and distinguished it from the purging fire, and said that it is never extinguished but lasts on together with the sinners who are punished, he corrects that opinion as somewhat harsh and inhuman, and at once adds: unless someone is pleased to understand this also in that place more humanely, and as is worthy of God who punishes. To the same point seems to belong what he says in the preceding oration about the Novatians: if they persist in schism without repentance, they are baptized with fire, which is the last baptism, he says, and not only more bitter but also more lasting. He threatens even the unrepentant with punishments, lasting and bitter indeed, but not eternal.

units.la: Gregorius Nyssenus episcopus, Basilij natura quidem frater disciplina verò filius, eadem, & quidem multò apertius, sequitur; idque fatetur Nilus Thessalonicensis Archiepiscopus. Germanus episcopus C.P. qui A.D.680. florebat tres Nysseni libros hoc errore inspersos concedebat, sed eos ab hæreticis vitiatos fuisse hariolabatur, non ab ipso auctore ita scriptos; quod ultimum est eorum effugium qui stulta & absurda pertinacia sibi persuadere volunt.
units.tr: Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, brother of Basil by nature but his son in discipline, follows the same view, and indeed much more openly. Nilus, archbishop of Thessalonica, admits this. Germanus, bishop of Constantinople, who flourished in A.D. 680, granted that three books of Nyssen were tainted with this error, but he guessed that they had been corrupted by heretics and were not written thus by the author himself. That is the last refuge of those who, in a foolish and absurd obstinacy, want to persuade themselves of something.

units.la: LI 3 suadent nihil à Veteribus sciptum esse à præsenti ipsorum fide aliunum. Cæterum tam multa sunt & totis Nysseni orationibus ita penitus infixa huius delirij venena vt parum sit verisimile ea ab alia esse quam ab autoris mente & manu. Videat qui volet librum ejus de anima & resurrectione. Orationem Catecheticam & de iis qui præmaturè abripiuntur; item orationem de mortuis, ac denique opusculum in illud Apostoli, Tunc ipse Filius subjicietur Patri, quo clarissimè constituit totū dogmatis Origenici mysterium. Sed & in aliis Origenem sequitur, ut cùm quæ Moses de duabus arboribus in medio Edene conuitis narrat, totámque Paradisi historiam allegoricè non ad litteram intelligendam esse contendit, cum pelliceas tunicas quibus Adam à Deo vestitus est de corpore, siculnet folia de gloriis, honoribus & deliciis secularibus interpretatur, cùm corpora Sanctorum post resurrectionem ad aeriam tenuitatem atque subtilitatem contextum iri docet, quæ omnia planè esse Origenis sciunt qui in eo versati sunt. Sed & singularia habet Gregorius non pauca, & à communi fide abhorentia. Nam & peccatum originis eo aperti&ime tollit quod negat ... Parvulos indigere sanitate quæ fit per purgationem, quod neque ab initio morbum in animam susceperint; & mediationis Christi necessitatem evertit, cùm eius incarnatione opus futurum fuisse negat fi omnes Heliæ, Eliæ, Ezechieli similes forent; & triduum mortis Domini ab Euchariistia aspicatur, quòd in ea jam mortuum fuisse ph. T.1.p.45. Christum velit; quòd quam sit absurdum omnes videant.
units.tr: Those who would persuade us that nothing written by the Ancients is foreign to their present faith are mistaken. Moreover, the poisons of this delirium are so many, and so deeply fixed through all the orations of Nyssen, that it is hardly credible they came from anyone but the author's own mind and hand. Let whoever wishes look at his book on the soul and the resurrection, the Catechetical Oration, the work on those who are snatched away prematurely, likewise the oration on the dead, and finally the little work on the Apostle's words, "Then the Son himself will be subjected to the Father," in which he sets out most clearly the whole mystery of the Origenist doctrine. He also follows Origen in other matters: he contends that what Moses relates about the two trees in the middle of Eden, and the whole history of Paradise, is to be understood allegorically and not literally; he interprets the leather tunics with which God clothed Adam as the body, and the fig leaves as worldly glories, honours and pleasures; and he teaches that the bodies of the saints after the resurrection will be woven into aerial thinness and subtlety. Everything of this kind is known by those versed in Origen to be plainly his. Gregory also has not a few peculiar views, far removed from the common faith. He most openly removes original sin by denying that ... infants need the health that comes through purgation, since they did not take the disease into their soul from the beginning. He overturns the necessity of Christ's mediation, denying that his incarnation would have been needed had all men been like Elijah, Elisha and Ezekiel. And he separates the three days of the Lord's death from the Eucharist, because he wishes Christ to have been already dead in it (ph. T.1.p.45). How absurd this is, everyone can see.

units.la: Ambrosius, firmissimum Ecclesiæ sui temporis columen, ne ipse quidem omni planè errore caruit. Cum Hilario consentit, omnec in uciversum ignis examen subituros; justos inde liberatum iri, infidelis in eo æternum mansuros. Post consummationem seculi (inquit) misffit Angelis qui segregent bonos & malos hoc futurum esse baptisma, quando per caminum ignis iniquitas exuretur, ut in regno Dei fulgeant justi sicut sol in regno Patris sui. Et si aliquis fit Petrus fit, ut Ioannes baptizatur hoc igni Veniet ergo Baptista magnus (sic enim eum nomino, quomodo nominavit Gabriel, dicens, hic erit magnus) videbit multos ante Paradisi stantes vestibulum, movebit romphaeam versatilem, dicet iis qui a dextris sunt, nō habentibus gravia peccata, intrate, &c. Et alibi ab eo examine nullum nisi Christum eximit. Omnes oportet perigne probari quicunque; ad Paradisum requirere desiderant. Non enim otiose scriptum est quod ejectis tundem sen. Adam & Eua de Paradiso fede, posuit Deus in exitu paradisi 476. gladium igneum, versatile. Omnes oportet transfire per flammas sive ille Ioannes Evangelista sit, quem ita dilexit Dominus, ut de eo diceret ad Petrum, &c. sive ille sit Petrus, qui claves accepit regni coelorum, qui super mare ambulavit, oportet dicat transivimus per ignem & aquam & induxisti nos in refrigerium. Sed Ioanni cito versabitur igneus gladius quia in eo nō invenitur iniquitas quem dilexit aquitas, &c. Sed ille Petrus examinabitur ut argentum; ego examinabor, ut plumbum; donec plumbum tabescat, ardebo: si nihil in me argenti inventum fuerit; heu me! in ultima inferni detrudar, aut ut stipula totus exurar. Resurrectionem vero mortuorum non simul & semel futuram arbitratur, sed paulatim longo & statuto ordine, ita ut qui ciediderunt primi resurgant pro meritorum ratione. Eo referendum est quod alibi habet. Beati qui habent partem in prima resurrectione, isti enim sine iudicio veniunt ad gratiam. Qui autem non veniunt ad primam resurrectionem, sed ad secundam reservantur, isti vrentur donec impleant tempora inter primam & secundam resurrectionem, aut si non impleverint diutius in supplicio permanebunt. An vero bono sensu accipi possit quod videtur docere, adulterium antequam lex Moisis promulgaretur, non fuisse illicitum, lectorum iudicium esto. Consideremus primum (inquit) quia Abraham, ante legem Moysi & ante Evangelium fuit nondum interdictum adultes- 176, rium videbatur. Pæna criminis ex tempore legis est quæ crimen inhibuit,nec ante legem vlla rei damnatio est sed lege.
units.tr: Ambrose, the firmest pillar of the Church of his time, was not himself entirely free of error. He agrees with Hilary that all will undergo the trial of fire; the just will be freed from it, while the unfaithful will remain in it for ever. "After the consummation of the age," he says, "God will send angels to separate the good from the bad. This will be the baptism, when iniquity is burnt up in the furnace of fire, so that the just may shine in the kingdom of God as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. And if anyone is Peter, or John, he is baptized in this fire. The great Baptist will therefore come (for so I name him, as Gabriel named him when he said, 'He shall be great'); he will see many standing before the vestibule of Paradise, he will move the turning sword, and he will say to those on the right, who have no grave sins, 'Enter,' and so on. And elsewhere he exempts from that trial no one but Christ. All must be proved through fire, whoever desire to come to Paradise. For it is not idly written that when Adam and Eve were cast out of Paradise, God placed at the exit of Paradise a fiery sword, turning. All must pass through the flames, whether that is John the Evangelist, whom the Lord loved so much that he said of him to Peter, etc., or whether it is Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, who walked upon the sea; he must say, 'We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.' But the fiery sword will turn quickly for John, because no iniquity is found in him whom righteousness loved, etc. But Peter will be tested as silver; I will be tested as lead. Until the lead melts away, I will burn; if no silver is found in me, alas! I shall be thrust into the depths of hell, or I shall be wholly burnt up like straw." Ambrose does not think the resurrection of the dead will be single and simultaneous, but gradual, in a long and fixed order, so that those who have died first rise according to the measure of their merits. To this belongs what he says elsewhere: Blessed are those who have a part in the first resurrection; for they come to grace without judgment. But those who do not come to the first resurrection, but are reserved for the second, will be burnt until the times between the first and second resurrection are fulfilled; or if they are not fulfilled, they will remain longer in punishment. Whether what he seems to teach, that adultery was not unlawful before the law of Moses was promulgated, can be taken in a good sense, let the reader judge. Let us consider first (he says) that Abraham, before the law of Moses and before the Gospel, the adulterer did not yet seem forbidden; the penalty of the crime comes from the time of the law which forbade the crime, and before the law there is no condemnation of the thing, but it comes from the law.

units.la: Item an quæ libro de Institutione virginis, † & passim alibi disserit, ea nullam nuptiarum honestati labem afpergant. Expendant etiam coradti Lectores plus ne soliditatis an subtilitatis attulerit ad expositionem arcus in nube quem Deus Noacho promisit,ut esset in signum fœderis quod cum ipso & cum orbe vniverso pangebat. Vehementer enim negat ista quæ promittit Deus de Iride intelligenda,sed ea ad nescio quem alium arcum allegoricum contendit referenda. Absit, inquit, ut hunc arcum Dei dicamus ; hic enim arcus,qui Iris dicitur,per diem videri solet, per noctem non apparet,& deinceps per hunc arcum intelligit invisibilem Dei virtutem per quam omnia continet moderatúrque mensúra quadam quam extendit & remittit pro Divina voluntate. Neque postremò scio an quod ille primo de Spiritu Sancto libro docet ulla idonea ratione probari possit,plenum scilicet esse Baptismatis Sacramentum, nuncupato tantum Filio, vel Spiritu Sancto, & tacitis Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis personis reliquis.
units.tr: Likewise, let the reader ask whether what he discusses in the book On the Instruction of a Virgin, and elsewhere, casts no stain on the honour of marriage. Let the careful readers also weigh whether he brought more solidity or more subtlety to his exposition of the bow in the cloud, which God promised to Noah as a sign of the covenant he made with him and with the whole world. For he strongly denies that what God promises should be understood of the rainbow, and contends that it refers to I know not what other allegorical bow. Far be it from us, he says, to call this the bow of God; for this bow, which is called Iris, is usually seen by day and does not appear by night. Through this bow he understands the invisible power of God, by which he contains and governs all things with a certain measure, which he extends and withdraws according to the divine will. Finally, I do not know whether what he teaches in the first book On the Holy Spirit can be proved by any suitable reasoning: namely, that the sacrament of baptism is complete when only the Son or the Holy Spirit is named, and the remaining persons of the Holy Trinity are passed over in silence.

units.la: Epiphanius verò ut ingenio erat simplici & aperto,&, si dicere licet in cauto , & nimis credulo,sic acer fuit & vehemens in iis omnibus retinendis quæ sancta & vera esse in animum induxerat, ideóque facilius abreptus est ad multa admittenda tanquam solida quæ, ut semel susceperat,non facilè dimittebat, sed retinebat mordicus. Non exiguo volumine & multo otio opus esset ad ea omnia recensenda quæ notari ex eo possent. Si cui in ea inquirere cordi est adcat Dionysij Petavij recentissimi interpretis notas; castigat enim eum sæpenumero , ac nonnunquam quidem acriter. Perobscura atque impedita , imo falsa esse quæ ille de anno & die quo natus est Dominus noster Iesus Christus differir, nullúmque Sphyngis ænigma eius oratione perplexius esse non dubitat pronunciare. Nec sanè injuria , sinatalis eius anni ratio habeatur, Quod verò ad ipsum diem pertinet Christi natalem, an is, scilicet, Ianuarij sextus fuerit, quod cum Ecclesia Ægyptiaca sequitur Epiphanius, x an verò Decembris vigesimus quintus (quod hodie volunt) non puto sine temeritate quicquam ea de re posse affirmari; eum harum sententiarum neutra ullo y idoneo fundamento nitatur. Sed & falso esse Petavius contendit quæ narrat Epiphanius in Ecclesia initiò decrevisse Apostolos ut Iudaico ritu Pascha celebraretur, aut cum iis etiam Christianis atque episcopis qui Iudaicè, ac minimè legitimo tempore fungerentur. Nescio item cui fundamento superstruere potuerit commentum quod pro re certissima obtrudere non dubitavit. Diabolum ante Christi advenum miserlcordiæ nonnihil se consecuturum sperasse, ideoque contumeliosam in Dominum suum iactare vocem, vel rebellare non fuisse ausum; Verum ubi suam ad obtinendam salutem conversionem à Christo repudiari infe lix animadvertit, illico os contra Dominum aperuisse, ac maledicentiam omnem evomuisse.
units.tr: Epiphanius, however, as he had a simple and open nature, and, if I may say so, a somewhat cautious and overly credulous one, was keen and vehement in retaining everything he had persuaded himself was holy and true. He was therefore more easily carried away into admitting many things as solid, and once he had taken them up he did not readily let them go but held on to them tenaciously. A large volume and much leisure would be needed to list all that could be noted in him. If anyone cares to inquire into these matters, let him consult the notes of Dionysius Petavius, the most recent editor, for he rebukes Epiphanius very often, and sometimes sharply. Petavius does not hesitate to say that what Epiphanius writes about the year and day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was born is very obscure and entangled, indeed false, and that no riddle of the Sphinx is more perplexing than his discourse. Nor is this without justification, if one considers the year of his birth. As for the day of Christ's birth itself, whether it was 6 January, which Epiphanius follows with the Egyptian Church, or 25 December (which they now want), I do not think anything can be affirmed about this without rashness, since neither opinion rests on any sound foundation. Petavius also contends falsely what Epiphanius relates: that in the Church the Apostles at first decreed that the Passover be celebrated in the Jewish manner, or with those Christians and bishops who observed it in the Jewish way and at a wholly improper time. I know not on what foundation he could build the fiction which he did not hesitate to thrust forward as a most certain fact: that the devil, before the coming of Christ, hoped to obtain some measure of mercy, and therefore did not dare to utter a insulting word against his Lord or to rebel; but when he saw that his conversion, by which he sought to obtain salvation, was unhappily rejected by Christ, he at once opened his mouth against the Lord and poured out all his slander.

units.la: Ioannes Chrysostomus iisdem quoque temporibus vixit, florentissimus & absque controversia doctissimus ac facundissimus scriptor. Ei tamen multa excidisse, vel falsò, vel certè incautiùs dicta & veniam poscentia quis neget? Quale est quod somniat Dauidem eos Psalmos qui quinquagesimum proximè consequuntur humana simpliciter intelligentia scripsisse vacuus erat.
units.tr: John Chrysostom lived in the same times, a most flourishing writer and beyond dispute among the most learned and eloquent. Yet who would deny that many things slipped from him, either falsely or at least too carelessly, so that he must ask pardon for them? Such is his dream that David wrote the Psalms which closely follow the fiftieth by merely human understanding; he was empty-headed.

units.la: Idem peccatum originale videtur nescivisse nam & peccatum nobis natura inesse negat, & parvulos peccato carere ait, & illud Pauli Rom. 5. 19. per inobedientiā unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, admodū diluutè interpretatur, ac si Apostolus vellet homines Adq scelere, non peccato quidè ipsū, sed morti fuisse subiectos.
units.tr: The same man seems to have been ignorant of original sin. For he denies that sin is inborn in us by nature, says that infants are free from sin, and explains very loosely that saying of Paul, Rom. 5. 19, "by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners", as if the Apostle meant that men were made subject to death because of Adam's crime, not to sin itself.

units.la: Rom. 5. 19. Illo enim peccante ac mortali effectio, & qui ex eo orti sunt tales esse nihil absurdum. At ex illius inobedientia altera pec-
units.tr: Rom. 5. 19. For it is no absurdity that, when he sinned and became mortal, those who sprang from him should be such. But that from his disobedience others

units.la: catorem extitisse, id vero quam obsecro congruentiam consequentiamq; haberet? Itaque alibi, quod Christus e virgine natus fit, hanc duntaxat affert rationem, quod Dominum in mundum magnificentius atque augustius quam nos ingredi deceret: non quòd eum a labe originali purum & intactum nasci necesse esset: quod utique si scivisset, id omnino in hac quæstione commemoratorus fuisse videtur. Huc quoque ea pertinent quæ idem multis in locis de natura & liberi arbitrij viribus multo quam deprium eruditis observata sint, mitto. Iam eum quoque clarum est iustorum animas coelo ante supremam resurrectionis diem excludere & preces pro ipsis damnatis approbasse, ac velut utiles commendasse, quod videntur quoque sentire & Augustinus & Damascenus & alij. Loca sigillatim describere longum est, quæ in margine annotavimus; ea videat qui volet.
units.tr: became sinners, what congruity or consequence would that have, I beg you? Hence elsewhere, on Christ's being born of a virgin, he gives only this reason: that it was fitting for the Lord to enter the world more magnificently and nobly than we do, not that he had to be born pure and untouched by original stain. Had he known that, he would surely have mentioned it in this question. To this belong also the things he observed in many places about nature and the powers of free will, far more learnedly than others; I pass them over. Moreover, it is clear that he holds the souls of the righteous are shut out of heaven until the last day of the resurrection, and that he approved prayers for the damned themselves and commended them as useful, as Augustine, Damascene and others also seem to think. To describe the passages one by one would be long; let whoever wishes look at those we noted in the margin.

units.la: Hieronymus, liberrimus ac gravissimus Antiquitatis censor, quam in alios feliciter exercuit Criticem ejus in se quoque adhibendæ occasionem aliquoties præbuit. Primò enim Origenis de damnatorum purgatione & salute delirium, æquè ac præceptor Nazianzenus, Basilius, Nyssenus, Commentario in Amos quæ videtur diserte scribens hæreticos & omnes peccatores liberatum iri, ut tortem raptum de incendio poll quam extrema ignis medicina exusti purgatique tucrint. Alios, non omnes quidem damnatos, sed eos tamen qui Christianissimum professi fuerint, servatum tandem illi quando iri non obscure significat, quam in sententia fuisse suo tempore quoque modo etiam Gnostici tollatur Augustinus. Hieronymi verba sunt peccatorum atque imperium & tamen Christianorum quorum opera in igne probanda sunt, moderatam arbitramur, & mixtam clementiæ sententiam, dicit. Quo & ille locus pertinet, ubi ab Origenis opinione suam sic distinguit, ut ipse Diabolum quidem & omnes impios & prævaricatores perire perpetuo. Christianos vero (si in peccato præventi fuerint) salvandos esse post pœnas dicat. Sed neque video qui probari vel purgari, aut excusari possit quod idem alibi Hieronymus adeo fidenter de Dei providentia disserit, curare quidem ipsum omnes & singulos homines, relinqua vero, sive inanimata, sive ratione carentia, non item. Absurdum est (inquit) ad hoc Dei deducere Majestatem ut sciat per momenta singula quot nascantur culices, quot vel moriantur, quot cimicum & vulicum & muscarum sit in terra multitudo, quanti pisces in aqua natent, & qui de minoribus majorum præda recedere debeant. Non simus tam fatui adulatores Dei, ut, dum potentiam ejus ad ima detrahimus, in nos ipsos injurios simus. Eandem rationabilem quam irrationabilem providentiam esse dicentes. An hæc sententia stare possit equidem in præsentiarum non dispuco, sed tamen hoc dico, ægerrime posse ex hoc Iesu Christi pronuntiato probari: Nonne duo passerculi asserio venundantur? & unus ex eis non cadet in terram sine Patre vestro. Verum ut posset illa sententia, vel defendi, vel certe excusari, negari tamen non potest quin Hieronymus modum excesserit, cum tanquam fatuos & ridiculos eos sugillat, qui malunt infinitam Dei scientiam adorare, quam eam veluti finitam circumscribere. Si quid iudico multo minus est in hoc ab absurditate & ineptia, quàm in illo quod sequitur, a temeritate periculi. Ille ipse qui hic ... atiam & providentiam Dei circumscribit, alibi sanctorum animarum post discessum suum præsentiam in infinitum extendit, adeo ut eas nullis spatiis, nulloque loco circumscribi, vel contineri velit, idque propter rationem sanè mirandam. Sequuntur Agnum quoconque vadit. Si Agnus ubique, ergo & hi ... T. 1. qui cum Agno sunt ubique esse credendi sunt. Nulla est tam ... gnis solutione Dialectica quæ ferat hominem ita argumentantem, & Christi Divinitatem cum ejusdem humanitate confundentem, & ex iis quæ de hac dicuntur, quæ illius sunt propria, concludentem. Alibi ut omnes cujusdam allegoriæ partes ad propositum suum accommodet, spiritus iustorum consummatorum. Angelósque adeo ipsos peccato obnoxios facit.t Mitto quæ passim probra iactat adversus conjugium in genere, & secundas nuptias in specie, quæ tam sunt acerba ut, vel adhibitis omnibus lenimentis atque malacticis, quæ ipse ad hunc usum in Epistola ad Pammachium suggessit, vix videantur posse à Tertulliani sensibus vindicari, quos Ecclesia, tanquam in nuptiarum honestatem contumeliosos, & Scripturarum auctoritati adversos, damnauit. Exempli gratia, quo melle, quove saccharo condiri possunt quæ ille ad Futiam scribit. Nontam laudandam, si & si Christiana non servet quod per tanta seculs gentiles feQuæ repetit iisdem verbis epistola sequente ad Ageruchiam, ut eam ad idem propositum hortetur, adhibitis etiam quibusdam imaginibus non admodum honestis, adeo ut in eas quæ nuptias repetunt intorquere non vereatur illud à Petro Apostolo longè alia mente usurpatum prouerbium. Canis revertens ad vomitum, & sus lota ad volutabrum luti. Nonne hoc est secundas nuptias rebus turpibus & fœdis accensere? Ejusmodi sunt quæ alibi habet. Non damno digamos, imo nec trigamos, plus aliquid inferam, etiam scortatorem recipio pœnitentem. Itaque digamos eodem loco habet quo scortatores qui in lustris versantur. Passim id genus sermonibus scatet, quibus condiendis ne uniuersæ quidem in Canariæ satisfiunt. Nisi putaffet aliquid impuri subesse in nuptiis, non iam cunctabundus & restitans (quod facit ) sed ultro & alacriter pronunciasset, Adamum & Evam etiamsi non peccassent conjugio tamen suo usuros fuisse, de quo nemo dubitabit qui secundum Genesēos caput à v.18. ufque ad finem attentè expenderit. Id tamen definire non est ausus Hieronymus, veritus nequid impuri primæve hominum integritati, affricaret si ullum nuptiarum usum tum futurum fuisse concederet. Neque sanè fœlicius eloquitur quæ planè eodem modo sentit de carnium usu, qui cùm ante diluvium nullus fuisset, postea mortalibus concessus est, eadem (ut quidem ille statuit) ratione qua Iudæis diuortium (scilicet propter duritiam cordis ipsorum) concessum postea fuisse legimus: unde sequitur (quod ipsum neque obscurè significauit) carnium esum à Christo non minus quàm diuortium, & circumcisionem sublatum fuisse. {b}Quod autem nobis obiicit (Iouinianus,inquit)in secunda Dei benedictione comedendarum carnium licentiam datam, quæ in prima concessa non fuerat,sciat quomodo repudiù,juxta eloquium Saluatorii,ab initio non dabatur,sed propter duritiam cordis nostri,per Moysem humano generi concessum est,sic & esum carnium usque ad diluuium ignotum fuisse,post diluuium verò quasi in eremo murmuranti populo coturnices, ita dentibus nostrùm nervos & virulentiam carnù ingesias. Enimuero diuortium est quid in ipso malum, quod viri & fœminæ creationi, & primigeniæ nuptiarum in paradiso institutioni repugnat, ut Diuinè Dominus in disputatione, quam de hoc argumento cum Iudæis habuit,docet. Si ergo ejus generis est carnium usus, in seipso malum & prohibitum quis non videt? Vix durius quid à Marcione & Manichæis dici potuit. Alicubi videtur existimare Evangelicam veritatem non recipere iuramentum; quod quidem dogma cuiusdam cum Scriptura & ratione pugnat. Difficile est etiam eum ab errore de sacramentorum efficacia, cujus supra nonnulla vestigia in Cypriano animaduertimus, excusare: hæc enim sunt ejus verba. Sacerdotes qui Euchariftiæ seruiunt & sanguinem Domini populù ejus diuidut, impiè agunt in legemChristi,putantesEucharistiam imprecantur facere verba,non vitam,& necessariam esse tantum solemnemorationem,& non sacerdotum meritum. De statu fidelium post resurrectionem non nisi cunctanter dicit, non ore rotundo, eorum vitæ sustentandæ cibos necessarios non suturos. Ergo inquies, (hæc ejus verba sunt) & nos post refurrectionem comesuri sumus? Nescio. Non enim scriptum est, & tamen si quaeritur non puto comesuros. In genere au iure probari & cum Domini Iesu disciplina consentanea censeri possit Auctoris istius in disputando frequens methodus equidem nescio. Trahit enim quo iure quisque iniuria adversariorum suorum sententias longissime ultra ipsorum mentem, iisque sensus alienissimos, & qui in eorum verbis nulli sunt affingit, deinde infestis armis atque animis eos aggreditur, adhibitis convicis, dictis aculeatis, multisque ex eruditione seculari, in qua excellebat; petitis figuratis morsibus. Augustinus cum illo disputans docebat sacras Iudaeorum caerimonias, etsi Christi adventu sublatas, potuisse nihilominus Christianismi initio ad tempus custoditi, ab iis qui eam Parentibus acceperant, etiam cum in Christum credidissent, ea lege ut in iis non constituerent (pem salutis, quoniam per Dominum Iesum salus ipsa quae ipsis caerimoniis & sacramentis significabatur adveneram. Quae suit doctrina sancta est & convenit cum iis quae docet Paulus priore ad Corinthios & alibi de libertate Christiana, per quam possumus aut debemus rebus, quae per se sunt adiaphorae, uti vel abstinere, prout proximorum nostrorum aedificatio postulat. Haec ita accipit Hieronymus s quasi sentiret Augustinus eos qui ex Iudaeis crederent legi esse subjectos; solos Gentiles fide in Christum legis onere liberos fieri. Hinc arrepta occasione farcastice & salse quantum potest ei illudit. Hoc si placet, inquit, quod placet, ut quicunque credunt ex Iudaeis debitores sint legis scindendae, Iu, ut Episcopus in toto orbe notissimus, hoc scribant ea promulgare sententiam & in assensum tantum omnes Episcopos trahere. Sed illi cum viro reserat, cui facile fuit verba ab iniqua, quae ipsis affingebatur, explicatione vindicare & in os adversarii perperam sibi impacta regerere, ut cuivis notum esse potest ex praestanti & divina religione quam iis omnibus opposuit quae ille in epistola sua scripserat. Cum Ruffino res longe aliter cessit: Tum enim Hieronymus cum homine futili pugnabat, & palo vulnera infligebat, cuius & causa ipsa fortasse deterior, industria quidem certè ad suf defensionem nulla erat. Hieronymus postquam miserum hominem à capite ad calcem liberaliter defricuit, & quibus potuit aculeis compunxit ac transfixit, postremò assumat libro primo extremo, se Deum reveritum ab ultione abstinere neque æstuanti pectori verba commodare, & cum Psalmista, ponere custodiam ori suo. Alibi fusè ipsum monet in superstua crimini objectione non esse verandum, hæc non certhas Ecclesiasticas, sed judicum libellos debere continere. Hoc unum denuntio (inquit) & repetens iterum, iterumque monebo, cornutam bestiam petit. Erit ramen fortasse cui mirum videbitur ista cornua tot vigiliis, tot ieiuniis lachrymisque Bethleemitis, & eremi Saracenicæ maceratione bus non potuisse retundi. Ad quod quidem quid respondeam nihil habeo, nisi Deum arcano & sapientissimo judicio fuisse sanctos isto viros, licet charitate, patientia, animisque lenit re instructissimos, affectibus iis nonnunquam abripi, ut vel hinc pateret unum Deum perfectæ sanctitatis arcem tenere: hominibus verò, quantacunque virtute excellere censeantur, adhærere semper infirmitatis humanæ reliquias. Vtcunque sit, ista disputandi ratio qua Hieronymus in Augustinum utitur facit ut metuam, ne in cæteros productis longius quàm par fuit eorum verbis, nonnunquam iniquior fuerit. Verum hæc ferri fortasse possunt: illud non possumus concoquere, quod ipsos Veteris & Novi Testamenti Scriptores parum reverenter interdum excipit, ut cùm diserte nulla circuitione usus, eam fuisse negat Atheniensis altaris inscriptionem quam dicit apud Lucam Paulus Act.17. Inscripto autem ara, (inquit, non ita erat ut Paulus asseruit).
units.tr: Jerome, the most free and most serious critic of antiquity, whose criticism he happily exercised on others, has on several occasions also given cause for it to be applied to himself. First, in his commentary on Amos, where he seems to write plainly that heretics and all sinners will be set free, like a brand snatched from the fire after being burned and cleansed by the last remedy of fire, he shows the same delirium about the purging and salvation of the damned that his teacher Nazianzen, Basil and Nyssen also showed. Others, not all of the damned but those who have professed the Christian faith, he obscurely indicates will at last be saved; Augustine says this opinion was held in Jerome's own time, in some form, even by the Gnostics.
