The words of Jerome are: "We judge that the sentence concerning sinners and wicked men, and yet Christians whose works are to be tested by fire, is a moderate and mixed sentence of mercy." To the same effect is the passage where he separates himself from Origen's opinion in this way: "the devil indeed, and all the impious and transgressors, will perish forever; but Christians (if they have been overtaken in sin) are to be saved after their punishments." But I do not see how it can be defended, or even excused, that the same Jerome elsewhere speaks so confidently about the providence of God, saying that God indeed cares for all and each man, but not for things that are lifeless or without reason. "It is absurd (he says) to ascribe to the Majesty of God such knowledge that he knows moment by moment how many gnats are born, how many die, how great is the multitude of bedbugs, lice and flies on the earth, how many fish swim in the water, and which of the smaller creatures ought to withdraw as prey of the larger. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we lower his power to the depths, we become unjust to ourselves, saying that providence is rational or irrational." Whether this opinion can stand, I do not now dispute; but I say this, that it could hardly be proved from this saying of Jesus Christ: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father." Yet, however that opinion might be defended, or at least excused, it cannot be denied that Jerome went beyond due measure when he mocks as foolish and ridiculous those who prefer to adore the infinite knowledge of God rather than to circumscribe it as if it were finite. If I judge rightly, there is far less absurdity and foolishness in this than in what follows, which carries danger of rashness. That same man who here limits even the knowledge and providence of God, elsewhere extends the presence of the souls of the saints after their departure to infinity, so that he wishes them to be confined by no spaces and no place, and this for a reason truly remarkable: "They follow the Lamb wherever he goes. If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must be believed to be everywhere." There is no dialectical solution so sound that it could bear a man arguing in this way, confusing the divinity of Christ with his humanity, and drawing conclusions from what is said of the one that belong properly to the other. Elsewhere, in order to fit every part of some allegory to his purpose, he speaks of the spirits of the perfected just; and he makes the angels themselves liable to sin. I pass over the reproaches he flings everywhere against marriage in general and second marriages in particular, which are so bitter that, even with all the softenings and mollifying remedies he suggested for this purpose in his letter to Pammachius, they can scarcely be defended from the views of Tertullian, which the Church condemned as insulting to the honour of marriage and opposed to the authority of Scripture. For example, with what honey or what sugar can the things he writes to Furia be seasoned? "It is not to be praised, if a Christian does not keep what the Gentiles have kept for so many ages." He repeats the same words in the following letter to Ageruchia, urging her to the same purpose, and he adds certain images not very decent, so that he does not hesitate to turn against those who marry again that proverb used by the Apostle Peter in a very different sense: "The dog returns to his vomit, and the washed sow to her wallowing in the mire." Is this not to count second marriages among filthy and foul things? Of the same kind is what he says elsewhere: "I do not condemn the twice-married, nor even the thrice-married; I go further and receive even the fornicator who repents." So he places the twice-married in the same class as fornicators who haunt the brothels. Such language is found everywhere, and not even the whole of Canaries suffices to season it. Unless he had supposed that something impure lay in marriage, he would not have hesitated and held back (as he does) but would have declared readily and gladly that Adam and Eve, even had they not sinned, would still have used their marriage; no one will doubt this who weighs carefully the chapter of Genesis from verse 18 to the end. Yet Jerome did not dare to define this, fearing that he would attach something impure to the original integrity of humankind if he granted that any use of marriage would then have existed. Nor does he speak more happily when he holds the same view about the eating of flesh. Since there was none before the flood, it was afterwards granted to mortals, for the same reason (as he judges) that we read divorce was afterwards granted to the Jews, namely because of the hardness of their hearts. From this it follows (which he also did not obscurely indicate) that the eating of flesh was abolished by Christ no less than divorce and circumcision. "As for what Jovinian objects to us, that in the second blessing of God permission to eat flesh was given which had not been granted in the first, let him know that, as divorce, according to the word of the Saviour, was not given from the beginning but was granted to the human race through Moses because of the hardness of our hearts, so also the eating of flesh was unknown until the flood, and after the flood, as to the murmuring people in the wilderness quails were given, so flesh and its virulence were thrust upon our teeth and sinews." Indeed divorce is in itself something evil, which is opposed to the creation of man and woman and to the first institution of marriage in paradise, as the Lord Himself teaches divinely in the dispute he held with the Jews on this subject. If, then, the eating of flesh is of this kind, who does not see that it is in itself evil and forbidden? Scarcely anything harsher could have been said by Marcion and the Manichaeans. Somewhere he seems to hold that "the Gospel truth does not receive an oath," a doctrine which clearly conflicts with Scripture and with reason. It is also hard to excuse him from error about the efficacy of the sacraments, of which we noted some traces above in Cyprian. For these are his words: "The priests who serve the Eucharist and divide the blood of the Lord among his people act impiously against the law of Christ, thinking that the Eucharist is made by the words of prayer, not by life, and that it is only a solemn remembrance, not the merit of the priests." Concerning the state of believers after the resurrection, he says only hesitantly, and not with a firm voice, that they will not have the food necessary to sustain their lives. "Therefore, you will say (these are his words), shall we too eat after the resurrection? I do not know. For it is not written; and yet, if it is asked, I do not think they will eat." I cannot tell whether this method of disputing, frequent in this author, can be approved in general, or be regarded as consistent with the discipline of the Lord Jesus. For he drags the opinions of his adversaries, by whatever right, far beyond their own meaning, attributes to them senses most alien to their words and which are in no way contained in them; then he attacks them with hostile weapons and spirits, using insults, stinging words, and many figurative bites drawn from the secular learning in which he excelled. Augustine, disputing with him, taught that the sacred ceremonies of the Jews, though abolished by the coming of Christ, could nevertheless be kept for a time at the beginning of Christianity by those who had received them from their parents, even when they had come to believe in Christ, on the condition that they did not place hope of salvation in them, since salvation itself, which was signified by those ceremonies and sacraments, had already come through the Lord Jesus. This doctrine is holy and agrees with what Paul teaches in his first letter to the Corinthians and elsewhere about Christian liberty, by which we may or ought to use or abstain from things which are in themselves indifferent, as the building up of our neighbours requires. Jerome took this as if Augustine meant that those of the Jews who believed were still subject to the law, and only Gentiles were freed from the burden of the law by faith in Christ. Seizing on this occasion, he mocks him as sarcastically and wittily as he can: "If this pleases, what pleases you, that all who believe from among the Jews are debtors to keep the law, then let the bishop, who is most famous throughout the whole world, publish this opinion in writing and draw all bishops to his assent alone." But Augustine dealt with a man for whom it was easy to clear his words from the unfair interpretation imposed on them, and to throw back into the adversary's face the blows wrongly aimed at himself, as anyone may know from the excellent and divine piety with which he answered everything that the other had written in his letter. With Rufinus the matter went quite differently. Then Jerome was fighting with a frivolous man and inflicting wounds with a stick; and the cause of that man was perhaps worse, though he had certainly no skill in defending himself. After Jerome had lavishly rubbed the wretched man from head to heel, and pricked and pierced him with what darts he could, at last, at the end of the first book, he takes on himself the role of one who, reverencing God, refrains from vengeance, and does not lend words to his seething heart, but, with the Psalmist, sets a guard upon his mouth. Elsewhere at length he warns himself that in answering a charge of crime he must not be carried away, and that his writings ought to contain not ecclesiastical arguments but the libels of judges. "This one thing I announce (he says), and repeating it again and again, I will warn: he attacks the horned beast." Perhaps there will be some to whom it seems strange that those horns could not be blunted by so many vigils, so many fasts, tears at Bethlehem, and mortifications in the Saracen desert. To this I have nothing to answer, except that God, by his hidden and most wise judgement, allowed these holy men, though most richly endowed with charity, patience and a gentle spirit, to be sometimes carried away by such passions, so that from this it might be plain that God alone holds the citadel of perfect holiness, while remnants of human weakness always cling to men, however much they are thought to excel in virtue. However that may be, the method of disputing that Jerome uses against Augustine makes me fear that, in applying their words to others, he has sometimes been more unfair than was proper. Such things may perhaps be borne; but this I cannot digest: that he sometimes treats the very writers of the Old and New Testaments with little reverence, as when, using no circumlocution, he denies that Paul's account in Acts 17 of the inscription on the Athenian altar was true. "But the inscription on the altar (he says) was not as Paul asserted."

units.tr: Hier. lib. in Ruff. To an unknown God (but thus: to the gods of Europe, Asia and Africa, an unknown and foreign God). Likewise he repeatedly insists that Paul, a Hebrew writing for Hebrews, could not express profound thoughts in a foreign language, made no artful arrangement of words, could not render a hyperbaton, and could not round off a sentence. And elsewhere: He did not speak, as most suppose, out of humility, but truly, saying that he was unskilled in speech, since he could not express in Greek the profound thoughts he had, and could hardly bring out in words what he was thinking, and could not put it into a foreign language so as to be clear to the ears.

units.la: lerandum est) n S. Apostolum disputantem cum Galatis,quos sultos dixerat paulo ante factis sultum nec ad eos vsum ar- gumentis quibus ad Romanos,sed simplicioribus & quæstulis possent intelligere & penè de trivio, adeo ut ni præmisset, secundum hominem dico, sapientibus displicere potuissent.
units.tr: And (what must be borne least of all) he says of the holy Apostle, who was arguing with the Galatians, whom he had called foolish a little before, that he was foolish himself, and that he did not use with them the arguments he used with the Romans, but simpler and more trivial ones, which they could understand, and almost drawn from the street corner, so much so that, had he not prefaced it with "I speak after the manner of men," he might have displeased the wise.

units.la: Quisquis vel primoribus labiis S. Apostoli cum ingenij tum sermonis vim,robur & candorem gustarit, non sine summa animi molestia cum sic exagitari feret,maximè si apud se reputer,ista omnia,etiamsi ratione non carerent (quæ tamen nulla est) imperitis scandalo esse,ac proinde temere non esse effutienda, nec sine summa cautione in medium proferenda.
units.tr: Whoever has tasted, even with the tips of his lips, the force, strength and candour of the holy Apostle's mind and style will bear with no small distress of spirit to see him so harried, especially when he considers that all these things, even if they were not without reason (which in fact they are not), are a stumbling block to the unlearned, and therefore should not be uttered rashly, nor brought forward without the greatest caution.

units.la: Augustini ,fateor, longè major est moderatio. Ubique enim, ut par est,summam erga Divinarum Scripturarum auctores testatur reverentiam, neque unquam de eorum vel stilo, vel sensu nisi cum singulari admiratione loquitur.Sed in iis quæ vel à se,vel ab aliis habuit,suos passum esse manes nemo iure inficiabitur. Ejusmodi est quod adversus pueros ante Baptismum morientes, adeo immisericorditer pronunciat , non solùm visione Dei privandos, quæ sententia vulgo nunc obtinet,sed etiam inferorum igne in æternum cruciandos,° quæ fuit etiam sententia Gregorij Ariminensis ᴾ doctoris Scholastici non ignobilis qui ob id parvulorum tormentum dictus est, similitum propter hujus sententiæ diritatem. Statuit etiam Augustinus Eucharistiam pueris necessariam, ut ad aliud argumentum supra annotavimus. Huic subjicienda est alia opinio in quam evidenter propendet, animam esse ex traduce, & de patre in filium transfire, & ex eius substantia non minùs quàm corpus progigni, minimè verò à Deo immediatè creari & immitti, quæ hodie nostra omnium fides est. Nemo nescit ipsum passim Angelis naturam corpoream tribuere: temerè item affirmare vniversum orbem momento creatum, & sex dierum intervalla, in creatione ad varios gradus cognitionis Angelicæ referre. Censuit item, cum veterum plerisque,Tempus quod inter hominis mortem & ultimum resurrectionem interpositum est animas abditis receptaculis continere. Sed & cum iisdem omnino videtur sentire supremo olim die, omnium etiam sanctissimorum hominum corpora, post resurrectionem, igne lustratum iri. Quid quod dubitat an Sydera ratione & intellectu prædita sint, & ad Ecclesiæ corpus pertineant. Sed nec illud quidem, inquit, certum habeo virum ad eandem Ecclesiæ societatem pertinere ant Solem & Lunam & cunctla sidera; quamvis nonnullis lucida corpora esse, non cum sensu & intelligentia videantur. Alibi incerto itelinquit utrum possit anima, vel hominis simpliciter, vel etiam iusti, cum ex hac vita migraverit, magicis carminibus evocata vivorum apparere conspectibus, etiam corporis lineamenta gestans. Neque item definire audet alibi qualiter liberos suscepturi fuissent primi parentes, si non peccassent, conjugali necne amplexu, an alio aliquo modo. Alibi item relinquit, in medio mundi sive animal sit, an secus? Sed huius quidem generis infinita sunt in Augustini disputationibus, in quibus ille, pro innata modestia, timidiùs & cunctantiùs agit, de rebus, vel claris, vel nullius momenti, dubitans, & nodos, ut videtur, interdum etiam in scirpis quærens, ægrè quicquam definiens & Academicorum more in plerisque fluctuans. Illud sanè mirificum est quod vir, alioqui cautus & à temeritate alienus, dissertissimè affirmat LXX. interpretes Prophetas fuisse, & à Spiritu sancto
units.tr: I grant, indeed, that Augustine's moderation is far greater. Everywhere, as is right, he shows the highest reverence towards the authors of Holy Scripture, and he never speaks of their style or their meaning except with singular admiration. Yet no one can rightly deny that in those views which he held either on his own or from others, he allowed his own opinions to hold sway. Of this kind is what he pronounces so pitilessly against infants who die before baptism: that they are to be deprived not only of the vision of God, which opinion now generally prevails, but also to be tormented for ever in the fire of hell. This was also the opinion of Gregory of Rimini, a Scholastic doctor of no little note, who on this account was called the torturer of infants, as if on account of the harshness of this opinion. Augustine also laid down that the Eucharist is necessary for infants, as we noted above under another head. To this must be added another opinion, towards which he clearly inclines: that the soul is derived by traducianism, passing from father to son and being begotten from his substance no less than the body, and is by no means created and infused immediately by God, which is today the faith of all of us. No one is unaware that he everywhere ascribes a corporeal nature to angels. He also rashly affirms that the whole world was created in an instant, and refers the intervals of six days in creation to the various degrees of angelic knowledge. He likewise held, with most of the ancients, that the time which lies between a man's death and the final resurrection the souls keep in hidden receptacles. But he also seems to hold much the same view that on the last day the bodies even of the most holy men, after the resurrection, will be purified by fire. What of the fact that he doubts whether the stars are endowed with reason and understanding, and belong to the body of the Church? But nor do I hold it certain, he says, that the sun and moon and all the stars belong to the same fellowship of the Church, although some bright bodies do not seem to be without sense and intelligence. Elsewhere he leaves undecided whether the soul, either of a man in general or even of a righteous man, when it has departed from this life, can be summoned by magic incantations and appear to the sight of the living, bearing even the outlines of the body. Nor again does he venture to define elsewhere how the first parents would have begotten children had they not sinned, whether by conjugal embrace or not, or in some other way. Elsewhere again he leaves it open whether the middle of the world is an animal or not. Indeed, there are endless examples of this kind in Augustine's disputations, in which he, from his native modesty, acts more timidly and hesitantly, on matters either clear or of no moment, doubting, and seeking knots, as it seems, even in bulrushes, scarcely defining anything, and in most cases wavering after the manner of the Academics. Truly remarkable is the statement, made most eloquently by a man otherwise cautious and far from rashness, that the Seventy translators were prophets and were inspired immediately by the Holy Spirit in translating the Scriptures; so that whatever readings in their version differ from the Hebrew sources, he would have these come not from the error of the translators but from the very will and command of God. He was led into this opinion because he was too credulous about the commonly told tales of the seventy separate cells of those translators, tales which Jerome sharply censured and ridiculed.

units.la: immediatè afflatos in Scripturis vertendis; ita vt quæcunque apud hos aliter sunt quàm in Hebræis fontibus, ea non ab interpretum errore, sed à Dei ipsius numine ac voluntate esse velit; in quam ille opinionem eo inductus est, quòd vulgari, & ab Hieronymo acriter castigatæ & irrisæ, de suptuaginta diversis istorum interpretum cellulis fabulæ, nimium credulus fuit. † Sed hunc quidem nihil opus est longis sermonibus probare in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus errare potuisse, qui id vltro ipse luculentissimo Retractationum Opere confessus est, quo varia quæ pridem præter, vel contra veritatem scripserat, stili ipse sui mucrone confodit. Non possum tamen dissimulare ipsum ad ingentem illam & ea præclarissimam existimationem quam immortalibus ingenij sui monumentis sibi merito comparavit, multum adjecturum fuisse, si in rebus constituendis & decídendis firmior & constantior fuisset.
units.tr: But there is no need to prove at length, against this man, that he could err in matters pertaining to religion, since he himself has most clearly confessed it of his own accord in his splendid work of Retractations, in which he pierces with the point of his own pen the various things he had earlier written beside or against the truth. Yet I cannot conceal that he would have added much to that immense and, for this reason, most distinguished reputation which he had rightly won for himself by the immortal monuments of his genius, had he been firmer and more consistent in establishing and deciding matters.

units.la: Quisquis attentè in reliquorum Patrum lectione versabitur facilè in eorum scriptis varios ejusmodi errores observabit, adeo ut vix ullum reperire sit, cujus sit aliquod nomen, cui simile quid non exciderit. Nos verò qui hæc inviti expositimus plurimus libenter supersedemus. Quæ enim attulimus ad institutum nostrum satis esse videntur; & in ea ipsa explicare sola nos publicæ utilitatis necessitas coegit, quæ alioqui latere maluissemus. Cùm enim hi ipsi Patrum facilè principes, suoque merito jam inde ab antiquissimis temporibus tota Ecclesia celeberrimi, tam multipliciter in rebus ad fidem pertinentibus hallucinati sint, quid est, quæso, à cæteris expectandum, quorum longè minor est vel sanctitas, vel eruditio, vel fama? Cum Justini & Irenæi, Clementes & Tertulliani, Cypriani & Lactantij, Basilij & Nazianzeni, Hilarij & Ambrosij, Nysseni & Chrysostomi, Hieronymi & Augustini, & Epiphanij, id est, acerrima & præstantissima totius orbis ingenia, in quibusdam impegerint, in alios verò penitus lapsi sint, quid de Leonibus, Gregoriis Romanis, & Damascenis existimandum est, qui istis, vt ævo, ita & ingenio ac sanctitate cedunt? Tum si sancti isti viri in rebus tanti momenti hallucinati sunt, hic de natura Dei, ille de humanitate Christi, alter de animarum nostrarum natura, alij de earum conditione, vel de resurrectione, cur in capitibus de quibus disceptamus hodie falli cosdem potuisse negabimus? Quod in illis tam manifestè ipsis accidit, cur & in his accidere non potuit? Parum verisimile est vt supra monuimus, controversias nostras vnquam ipsis in mentem venisse. Minùs item verisimile est, de iis pronunciare ipsis vnquam propositum fuisse, vt haud ira pridem probavimus. Sed finge eos & habuisse perspecta capita quæ hodie controvertuntur, & in iis explicandis operam posuisse, sententiámque de his suam litteris mandasse, cur eos in his foelicius esse versatos opinabimur, quàm in aliis tam multis de quibus eos præter verum pronuntiasse demonstravimus? Nulla ratio est cur qui in capite de resurrectione erravit, idem de animæ post hanc vitam statu errare non potuerit. Cui ignota fuit natura corporis Christi, is profectò quid sit Christi Eucharistia ignorare æquè potuit. Nulla certa apparet ratio cur aliquod inter ista discrimen fuisse statuamus, fit quidem nonnunquam vt quis in argumento quopiam labatur qui stet feliciter in alio; Nimirum id ita accidit cùm vel in uno bono accuratius & attentius quàm in altero versatur, vel cùm res ipsa, hæc illa facilior & expeditior est; tum enim licèt eandem attentionem in vtroque argumento adhibeas, fieri poterit, vt quod facile est, & expeditum, id assequaris; quod vero difficile est & impeditum, id minime assequaris. Sed harum rationum neutra hic locum habet. Cur enim Patres in quibus errarunt in iis excutiendis minùs attentionis & diligentiæ adhibuissent? Cur in iis de quibus hodie sunt nostræ controversiæ diligentiùs & accuratiùs versati fuissent? Vtraque sugt paris in religione, momenti. Quid enim? Papæne auctoritatem putas periculosius nescīri, quam Dei naturam? animarum in purgatorio poenas, quàm fidelium in resurrectione statum? Eucharistiæ substantiam, quam veras corporis Christi proprietates? nostræ cum Christo communionis sacramentum, quàm ipsum passionis Dominicæ calicem? An pluris est ad salutem scire Christum in altari verè offerri, quàm verè in cruce passum? Quis non videt hæc capita vel paris esse ad religionem utraque momenti, vel si quid est discriminis, omnino pluris esse illa in quibus lapsi sunt Patres, quàm hæc de quibus hodie litigamus? Ergo conclusum esto Patres, si utraque ob oculos habuerunt, eandem in utrisque expendendis curam ac diligentiam adhibuisse; paritérq; adeo in utrisque & falli & verum assequi potuisse. Neque verò est quod quis causetur, illa in quibus falsi sunt, iis difficiliora esse quæ verè judicasse putantur. Qui enim attentè rem ipsam expenderit, reperiet parem esse utrorumque vel facilitatem vel difficultatem; &, si qua fuerit inæqualitas, omnino etiam faciliora ea fuisse in quibus aberrarunt Patres. Quæso enim nonne tam facile est ex ratione & Scriptura constituere num in terris post resurrectionem mansuri sint fideles, quàm definire an iidem post obitum sint in purgatorium profecturi? Difficiliúsque est cognoscere num in Angelos obscœnus amor cadere possit, quàm explorare an Papa, etiam qua Papa est, errori sit obnoxius? Si quis autem hîc objiciat Ecclesiam cùm de his capitibus judicavit, de aliis verò nihil statuit, quas ex illis difficultates amovit, eas in his reliquisse; respondeo idipsum hic supponi quod in quæstione versatur, quódque liquido falsum est. Priorum enim seculorum Ecclesia nihil vnquam publicè & authenticè (quod quidem sciamus) de capitibus hodie controversis pronunciauit, ut supra docuimus. Cùm ergo sancti viri (si adeo harum causarum ulla ipsis vnquam in mentem venit) parem rerum vel facilitatem vel difficultatem in utraque parte nacti sint, adhæc cùm parem animi contentionem ad utrumque genus attulerint, neminem puto non agnoscere ipsos, si in ferenda de prioribus sententia falsi sunt, potuisse eadem ratione in posterioribus à vero etiam aberrare. Quæ autem ex iis nobis superfsunt monumenta exertissime clamant, (ut ex iis paucis quæ proximè ex ipsis retulimus colligere licuit) illos, & quidem nonnunquam graviter, circa capita illa priora erravisse. Superest ergo ut eorum iudicium circa posteriora, de quibus nunc sunt inter nos controversiæ, falli quoque potuisse fateamur. Fingamus ergo in iis locis quæ à Romanis Theologis ex Hilario afferuntur realem Christi in Eucharistia præsentiam verè haberi; fingamus Protestantes homines id agnoscere atque confiteri (quod tu nulla fortasse subtilitate ab iis unquam extorquebis) nihil admodum profecceris, si hoc ipsum, quod tu magnum putas, assecutus fueris. Respondebunt enim Protestantes hunc eundem Hilarium eodem opere statuisse Christi corpus nullo doloris sensu in cruce affectum fuisse. Si in hoc capite aberravit, nihil necesse esse ut in altero scopum attigerit. Quæstio de Christi corpore non minoris est momenti quàm quæ est de Eucharistia, imo clariùs illa habetur in Scriptura, in eáque nihil occurrit, quod vel tantillum ea suadeat quæ de corpore Christi sibi finxit Hilarius. Contra verò quædam in Scripturis leguntur quæ ei de Eucharistia opinioni quæ Hilario tribuitur nonnihil favere, saltem in speciem, videntur. Cùm ergo Hilarius in priori capite, quod & planius & paris momenti est, à vero manifestè aberraverit, quis in posteriori, quod & obscurius difficiliúsque est & multominus ad religionem necessarium, verum vidisse eum præstabit? Idem respondere licet ad reliqua Patrum quæ objiciuntur testimonia, quorum nemo est quæ non suum aliquem de rebus ad religionem pertinentibus errorem vel erraverit, vel errare certè potuerit. Nec puto quicquam esse quod legitimè possit huic responsioni opponi, cùm eam ipsa & Patrum, & partium, inter quas est controversia, praxis liquidò confirmet. Augustinus enim in disputatione cum Hieronymo, cùm sibi objicerentur sex aut septem auctores, non putavit anxiè disquirendum quid illi sensissent, sed simpliciter respondet, quosdam eorum de Ecclesia propter haeresin egressos, alios ab ipso Hieronymo de errore fuisse reprehensos. Quæ quidem responsio nihil valet nisi supponas nullum ejus, qui in aliquo fidei capite erraverit, testimonium, ad fidem firmandam valere. Nicaeni II. Concilij Patres eandem methodo contra Iconoclastas adhibent, quibus Eusebij Caesariensis locum objectantibus, respondent Eusebium Arianum fuisse. b An vera sit responsio & ad rem appositè allata, nil necesse est nunc excutere. Satis est quod isti, dum sic disputant, aperrissimè statuunt, qui in aliquo de religione capite hallucinatus sit, eum nullam in caeteris fidem mereri. Hoc ipsum solenne est Cardinali Perronio, aliisque earundem partium Scriptoribus. Non enim aliter solvunt petitas ex Socrate vel ex Sozomeno Historicis Ecclesiasticis objectiones quàm respondendo istos Scriptores Novatianos fuisse. Qui Concilia generalia Romæ edi curarunt Gelasio Cyziceno, qui Acta c Concilii Niceni scriptis mandavit, fidem ideo omnem abrogant, quòd hæc ejus historia variis laboret erroribus. Cum ergo ejus testimonio Scriptoris, cui error merito possit impingi, nulla sit sententia certò superstruenda, plerorumque Patrum, vel penè omnium, paret nullam esse certam auctoritatem, quorum, scilicet, nullus est cui non possit idem quoque objici. Sed hic fortasse quispiam respondebit complurium Patrum aliam esse rationem, aliam singulorum, fatebiturque singulos quidem errare posse, & satis saepe reipsa errare; negabit fieri posse ut vera non sint quae Patres, vel omnes, vel certè complures, magno consensu docuerint. Aliquid jam ad responsionem istam diximus, cùm VinVincentij Lirinensis de hoc argumento pronunciatum excussimus. Vt paucis expediam idem est ac si quis postquam concessit singulos Senatores posse ægrotare, negaret tamen Senatum universum communi & quasi epidemico morbo posse laborare. Credibilius est, fateor, unum quàm multos ægrotare; quia hoc quàm illud rarius accidit. Sed fieri tamen potest & fit nonnunquam ut multi eodem morbo laborent, præsertim si morbus sit epidemicus, vel nondum probè cognitus; cujus generis plerique sunt magnorum virorum errores. Ij enim sub eorum nomine veluti sub ingenti clypeo tuti latent, eóque facilius ab incautis & imprudentibus imbibuntur & contrahuntur. Sed si ratio hic quod res est non persuadet; experientia saltem edocti sapiamus. Certum est enim in quibusdam ex iis erroribus quos supra memoravimus, versatos fuisse, non unum, vel duos, vel tres tantùm Patres, sed multos, sed plerosque, imo non nunquam ejusdem seculi universos, quorum nomina & Scripta ad nos usque pervenerunt. Iustinum cum Chiliastis sensisse supra vidimus, quorum opinio non solum falsa, sed & in consectariis suis periculosa ab omnibus vulgò judicatur. Non unus autem sic sensit; plerique omnes illius seculi doctores in eadem erant sententia, ut ex ejus verbis constat. Sic enim Tryphonem & Iudæos ejus amicos compellat. Tametsi cum quibusdam qui Christiani dicuntur contulistis, & qui hoc ipsum non concedunt, sed Deum Abraha, Deum Isaaci, & Deum Iacobi blasphemare audent, & qui non esse mortuorum resurrectionem, verum statim à morte animas ipsorum assumi in cœlum dicunt, p. 307. 8. ne habeatis eos pro Christianis, perinde ac rem ut par est aestimanti Iudai non sunt Sadducæi & similes sectæ. Per pseudo christianos Valentinianos, & alios Gnosticos intelligit. Deinde sic pergit. Ego verò & qui rectè sentiunt per omnia Christiani, & resurrectionem carnis futuram scimus, & mille annos in urbe Hierosolyma instaurata exornata & dilatata agendos. His verbis omnes suo tempore catholicos in eo errore versatos, solósque hæreticos ab eo alienos fuisse testatur Scio ipsum supra dixisse, multos esse qui sint in pia & pura Christianorum sententia qui hoc non agnoscunt. Verum hæc adeo discrepantia conciliet qui potest. Omnes qui recta sentiunt, sunt in ea opinione, &c, multi qui recta sentiunt sunt ab ea opinione alieni. Iuquitat etiam, cui vacabit, an nullum sit in lustini codicibus mendum. Ficri enim potest ut corruptus sit locus ab hominibus posteriorum temporum mirantibus & indignantibus illam de mille annis sententiam (quæ iampridem apud omnes Christianos pro hæresi habetur) fuisse à tanto martyre omnibus omnino orthodoxis attributam. Ut sit, satis est, quod caput rei est, ex hoc loco constare plerosque illorum temporum cum Doctores, tum fideles in eo errore fuisse. Irenæum qui eo seculo vixit, & Tertullianum qui proximè cum secutus est, in ea sententia fuisse notum est, nullo, quod quidem sciamus tum contradicente. Papiam Hierapolitanum qui A. D. decimo & centesimo florebit eius erroris parentem fuisse Eusebius & Hieronymus h aliisque auctores docent. Sequitur ergo omnium, qui nobis ex eodem seculo supersunt, Patrum in eadem sententia consensum non esse necessarium veritatis argumentum. Quòd si ad seculaa inferiora descendas, reperies cundem errorem à variis magni in Ecclesia nominis Doctoribus diu retentum fuisse. Hieronymus qui hoc delirium passim in suis commentariis strenuè oppugnat ac refellit, id tamen scribit à multis receptum fuisse, & ad superiores, quos iam nominavimus Lactantium addit, & Victorinum, Severum & Apollinarium, quem, inquit alibi, nostrorum, in hac parte duntaxat, plurima sequitur multitudo, ut præsagia mente iam cernam quantorum in me rabies concitanda sit, quia scilicet eam sententiam identidem refutat. Unde patet Hieronymi tempore, id est quinto seculo inente illam sententiam passim in Ecclesia obtinuisse. Certè Ambrosius ab ea non videtur abhorruisse qui non obscurè, quod antea diximus, statuit diversos fore resurgentium gradus. Eam quidem Hieronymus, etsi pro ingenio & more suo, acerrimè neque semel insectetur, penitus tamen damnare non est ausus. Quæ licèt non sequamur, inquit, tamen damnare non possumus, quia multi Ecclesiasticorum virorum & Martyres ista dixerunt, & unusquisque in suo sensu abundet, & Domini cuncta iudicio reserventur. Unde patet (ut id obiter moneam) sententiam de fide aliquam Patres non semper eodem quo nos gradu habuisse. Hieronymo enim tolerabilis error est qui hodie non ferendus censeretur. Si regeratur Ecclesiam sequentium seculorum eum errorem damnavisse; quid hoc aliud est quam agnovisse, sensisseque posteriorem Ecclesiam, quod complurium Patrum consensus non sit idoneum veritatis argumentum? Si aliter censuisset Dionysius Alexandrinus, nunquam ille adversus Irenæum de hoc capite scripsisset, quod ab eo factum testatur Hieronymus, in altero locorum proximè ex eius Commentariis citatorum. Quod si solius auctoritatis ratio habenda est, eam vim non habet Ecclesiæ posterioris iudicium, quæ liquidò ac indubitatò doceat quid in hac quæstione verum sit. Sequentis enim Ecclesiæ præferre sententiam nihil aliud est quàm auctoritatem auctoritati opponere, non autem nodum solvere. Vt non putarunt Dionysius Alexandrinus, Hieronymus, Gregorius Nazianzenus & alij se Iustini, Irenæi, Lactantij, Victorini, Severi & cæterorum vetustiorum auctoritate teneri, ita neque nos ipsorum iudicio obligari par est. Neque enim illis posteri maiorem debent reverentiam, quàm ipsi maioribus suis debuerant. Quinimo videntur ipsi maioribus suis plus deferre debuisse quàm nos ipsis debemus, quia quo magis à tempore Apostolorum recedituř (qui fons est & origo totius Ecclesiasticæ auctoritatis) eo magis decrescit ac minuitur Doctorum Ecclesiasticorum gratia & auctoritas. Si Antiquitas (uti dicebamus) veritatis nota est, nihil est majori veneratione atque honore dignum quàm quod antiquissimum. Hæc instantia, si vel vna esset, satis tamen ostenderet plurium Patrum consensum nullius esse ad fidem constituendum auctoritatis. At aliæ multæ supersunt quarum nonnullas hic subjiciam. Justinum, Irenæum, Tertullianum & Augustinum supra audivimus negantes cœlum ante diem judicij referendum: fidelium interim animas, paucis, peculiari quodam privilegio, exceptis, in quadam subterranea custodia omnes detinendas. Quæstionum & responsionum quæ sub Justini nomine feruntur Auctor in eadem est sententia, vt patet ex responsionibus ad quæstiones IX. & LXXIV. Ac ne tempus in describendis auctorum locis frustra teramus, illud in genere aio, Veterum plerosque hanc sententiam, vel totam, vel certè eius partem secutos esse. Nam præter Justinum, Irenæum, Tertullianum, Augustinum & antiquissimum Quæstionum Justino falsò affictarum Scriptorem, patet Origenem, Lactantium, Victorinum, Ambrosium, Ioannem Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Oecumenium, Aretam, Prudentium, Theophylactum, Bernardum, & inter Papas Clementem Romanum & Ioannem XXII. in ea opinione versatos fuisse. Id testatur diserte Sixtus Senensis, & Stapletonus. Et superioribus addere poterant Nouatianum, Hilarium, Hieronymum, Paulinum Nolæ Episcopum, Claudianum Mamerti Viennensis Episcopi fratrem, & Mosem Bar-cepha Syrum quorum quæ in margine annotavimus loca eandem de animæ adeo sarrectionem statu sententiam præ se ferunt. Quin & mirandus ille ac penè vniuersalis in hoc errore consensus, nullo per annos 1400. contrario Ecclesiæ decreto pulsatus vnquam legitur. Imò ne vllum quidem Patrem apparet in hoc errore confutando operam potuisse. Dionysius Alexandrinus & Hieronymus adversus Chiliastarum errorem scripserunt; De hoc vel planè silvas-
units.tr: Anyone who reads the remaining Fathers with close attention will easily notice errors of this kind in their writings, so much so that it is hard to find any one of them whose name is not attached to some such slip. We who set these things out unwillingly are for the most part glad to pass them over. What we have brought forward seems enough for our purpose, and the necessity of public benefit alone has forced us to explain even these points, which we would otherwise have preferred to leave hidden. For if these very leaders among the Fathers, men famous throughout the whole Church from the earliest times, have gone astray in so many matters touching the faith, what, I ask, should we expect from others, whose holiness, learning and reputation are far inferior? If Justin and Irenaeus, Clement and Tertullian, Cyprian and Lactantius, Basil and Nazianzen, Hilary and Ambrose, Nyssen and Chrysostom, Jerome and Augustine, and Epiphanius (that is, the keenest and most outstanding minds of the whole world) have stumbled in some matters and fallen utterly in others, what should we think of the Leos, the Gregories of Rome, and the Damascenes, who yield to these men in age, and in talent and holiness as well? Again, if these holy men went astray in matters of such great weight, one on the nature of God, another on the humanity of Christ, another on the nature of our souls, others on their condition or on the resurrection, why shall we deny that the same men could have been mistaken in the chapters we are disputing today? What happened to them so plainly in those matters, why could it not happen in these? It is hardly likely, as we pointed out above, that our controversies ever came into their minds. It is less likely still that they ever intended to pronounce on them, as we showed not long ago. But suppose they both had before them the points now in dispute and took pains to explain them, and committed their opinion on them to writing: why should we think they handled these more happily than the many others on which we have shown them to have pronounced falsely? There is no reason why the man who erred on the chapter of the resurrection should not also have erred on the state of the soul after this life. The man who did not know the nature of Christ's body could just as well have been ignorant of what Christ's Eucharist is. No clear reason appears for us to suppose any difference between these. It does sometimes happen that someone slips in one subject while he stands firm in another. That happens when a man deals with one topic more carefully and attentively than with another, or when the matter itself is one thing easier and more straightforward than another; for then, although you bring the same attention to both subjects, you may succeed in what is easy and straightforward, and fail utterly in what is difficult and obstructed. But neither of these reasons applies here. For why should the Fathers have applied less attention and diligence to the matters in which they erred, and handled more carefully and accurately those on which our controversies turn today? Both kinds of question are of equal weight in religion. What then? Do you think it is more dangerous to be ignorant of the authority of the Pope than of the nature of God? Or of the punishments of souls in purgatory than of the state of the faithful at the resurrection? Of the substance of the Eucharist than of the true properties of Christ's body? Of the sacrament of our communion with Christ than of the very cup of the Lord's passion? Or is it more important for salvation to know that Christ is truly offered on the altar than that he truly suffered on the cross? Who does not see that these points are of equal weight for religion, or, if there is any difference, that those on which the Fathers went wrong are clearly weightier than those about which we now dispute? Let it therefore be concluded that if the Fathers had both before their eyes, they brought the same care and diligence to weighing each, and so could equally have been mistaken and yet attained the truth in both. Nor can anyone plead that the points on which they were wrong were harder than those on which they are thought to have judged rightly. For whoever weighs the matter closely will find that the ease or difficulty of each is the same, and that if there is any inequality, those points on which the Fathers went astray were in fact the easier. For is it not as easy to settle from reason and Scripture whether the faithful will remain on earth after the resurrection, as to determine whether the same people will go to purgatory after death? And is it harder to find out whether obscene love can fall upon the angels, than to discover whether the Pope, even as Pope, is liable to error? But if someone here objects that the Church, when it judged on these chapters and said nothing on others, removed the difficulties from the former and left them in the latter, I answer that this assumes the very thing in question, and that it is plainly false. For the Church of the earlier centuries never, so far as we know, publicly and authoritatively pronounced on the chapters that are disputed today, as we have shown above. Therefore, since these holy men (if any of these controversies ever came into their minds at all) found the same ease or difficulty on either side, and since they brought the same effort of mind to each kind, I think everyone will admit that if they were wrong in their judgment on the former, they could by the same reasoning have strayed from the truth in the latter as well. Moreover, the monuments of them that survive cry out most plainly (as the few examples we have just cited make clear) that they erred, and sometimes gravely, on those earlier chapters. It remains, then, that we must admit that their judgment on the later points, which are now in dispute between us, could also have been mistaken. Let us suppose, then, that in the passages which the Roman theologians cite from Hilary, there is truly a real presence of Christ in the Eucharist; let us suppose that the Protestants acknowledge and confess this (which you perhaps could never wring from them by any subtlety). You will have gained nothing of substance, even if you have achieved that very point which you consider great. For the Protestants will answer that this same Hilary, in the same work, held that Christ's body, when on the cross, felt no sensation of pain. If he went wrong on this point, there is no necessity that he hit the mark on the other. The question about the body of Christ is no less important than the question about the Eucharist; indeed the former is taught more clearly in Scripture, and nothing occurs in Scripture that suggests even slightly the notions Hilary invented about Christ's body. On the contrary, certain things are read in the Scriptures which seem, at least at first sight, to favour somewhat that opinion about the Eucharist which is attributed to Hilary. Since Hilary, then, has plainly strayed from the truth in the former chapter, which is both clearer and of equal weight, who will guarantee that he saw the truth in the latter, which is both obscurer and more difficult, and far less necessary for religion? The same answer may be given to the remaining testimonies of the Fathers that are brought against us; there is none of them who has not either erred, or certainly could have erred, in some error of his own on matters pertaining to religion. Nor do I think there is anything that can fairly be set against this answer, since both the practice of the Fathers and that of the parties between whom the controversy lies clearly confirm it. For when Augustine, in his dispute with Jerome, was confronted with six or seven authors, he did not think it necessary to inquire anxiously what they had thought, but simply replied that some of them had departed from the Church on account of heresy, and that others had been rebuked by Jerome himself for error. That reply is worthless unless you assume that the testimony of no one who has erred in some article of the faith has any weight in establishing the faith. The Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea use the same method against the Iconoclasts, who cited a passage of Eusebius of Caesarea; they reply that Eusebius was an Arian. Whether this reply is true and aptly made need not be examined now. It is enough that these men, while they argue in this way, plainly lay down that whoever has gone astray on any chapter of religion deserves no credit in the rest. Cardinal Perron, and other writers of the same party, make exactly this assumption. For they answer the objections drawn from the ecclesiastical historians Socrates and Sozomen in no other way than by replying that these writers were Novatians. Those who had the general councils printed at Rome, and who condemned Gelasius of Cyzicus, who committed the acts of the Council of Nicaea to writing, reject his whole authority for the reason that his history suffers from various errors. Since therefore no opinion can be safely built on the testimony of a writer who may fairly be charged with error, it appears that there is no certain authority in most of the Fathers, or almost all of them, since there is not one of them to whom the same objection cannot be made. But perhaps someone here will reply that the reasoning for several Fathers together is different from that for each one singly; he will admit that each of them could err, and often in fact did err, but will deny that what the Fathers, all or at least many of them, have taught with great agreement can be untrue. We have already said something in reply to this when we examined the pronouncement of Vincent of Lérins on this subject. To put it briefly, it is the same as if someone, having granted that each single senator may fall ill, should nevertheless deny that the whole Senate can suffer from a common and as it were epidemic sickness. It is more credible, I admit, that one man falls ill rather than many, because the latter happens less often. But still it can happen, and sometimes does happen, that many suffer from the same disease, especially if the disease is epidemic or not yet properly understood; and most of the errors of great men are of this kind. For these lie hidden under the names of such men, as under a huge shield, and are therefore more easily drunk in and caught by the unwary and the imprudent. But if this reasoning does not persuade, let us at least grow wise taught by experience. For it is certain that many Fathers, not just one or two or three, but many, and most of them, and sometimes all the writers of the same century whose names and writings have reached us, were involved in some of the errors we mentioned above. We have seen above that Justin held with the Chiliasts, whose opinion is commonly judged by everyone to be false, and in its consequences dangerous. Yet he was not the only one who thought so; almost all the teachers of that age were of the same mind, as is clear from his own words. For he addresses Trypho and his Jewish friends thus: Although you have conferred with some who are called Christians, who do not concede this, but dare to blaspheme the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, and who say that there is no resurrection of the dead, but that their souls are taken straight to heaven at death, p. 307, line 8; do not regard them as Christians, just as the Jews, judging the matter as it ought to be judged, do not regard the Sadducees and similar sects as Jews. By "pseudo-Christians" he means the Valentinians and other Gnostics. Then he goes on thus: But I and all who think rightly in every point are Christians, and we know that the resurrection of the flesh will come, and that a thousand years will be spent in the city of Jerusalem, rebuilt, adorned and enlarged. By these words he testifies that in his time all the catholics were involved in that error, and only the heretics were free of it. I know that he himself said above, that there are many who are in the pious and pure opinion of the Christians and who do not acknowledge this. But who can reconcile such contradictory statements? All who think rightly are in that opinion, etc., and many who think rightly are alien to that opinion. Let whoever has the leisure consider also whether there is any corruption in the manuscripts of Justin. For it may be that the passage was corrupted by men of later times, who were astonished and indignant that the opinion about a thousand years (which for a long time now has been regarded by all Christians as a heresy) should have been attributed by so great a martyr to all orthodox men without exception. However that may be, it is enough, and it is the heart of the matter, that from this passage it is clear that most of the teachers and faithful of that time were in that error. It is well known that Irenaeus, who lived in that century, and Tertullian, who followed soon after him, were of that opinion, and so far as we know no one contradicted them at that time. Eusebius and Jerome and other writers teach that Papias of Hierapolis, who flourished in the year of our Lord 110, was the parent of this error. It follows, therefore, that agreement of all the Fathers who survive from the same century in one opinion is not a necessary argument of truth. But if you go down to the later centuries, you will find the same error retained for a long time by various teachers of great name in the Church. Jerome, who vigorously attacks and refutes this folly throughout his commentaries, nevertheless writes that it was widely accepted, and he adds to the earlier authors we have already named Lactantius, and Victorinus, Severus and Apollinaris, whom, he says elsewhere, a great multitude of our people follow in this part alone, so that I can already foresee in my mind how great a rage will be stirred up against me, because I keep refuting that opinion again and again. From this it is clear that in Jerome's time, that is in the fifth century, that opinion was widely held in the Church. Certainly Ambrose does not seem to have shrunk from it, since he, as we said before, did not obscurely affirm that there will be different degrees among those who rise. Jerome, although in his own manner and vehemence he attacks it most sharply and more than once, nevertheless did not dare to condemn it utterly. Although we do not follow these things, he says, yet we cannot condemn them, because many churchmen and martyrs have said these things, and each man may abound in his own sense, and all things are reserved for the judgment of the Lord. From this it is clear (to note this in passing) that the Fathers did not always hold a point of faith with the same firmness that we do. For the error was a tolerable one for Jerome, while today it would be regarded as not to be endured. If it is objected that the Church of the following centuries condemned that error, what does this amount to except acknowledging that the later Church also perceived and felt that the agreement of many Fathers is not a sound argument of truth? If Dionysius of Alexandria had judged otherwise, he would never have written against Irenaeus on this point, which Jerome testifies he did, in the other passage cited just above from his Commentaries. But if only the question of authority is to be considered, the judgment of a later Church, which clearly and undoubtedly teaches what is true in this question, does not have that force. For to set the opinion of a later Church against it is nothing other than to oppose authority to authority, not to untie the knot. Just as Dionysius of Alexandria, Jerome, Gregory Nazianzen and others did not think themselves bound by the authority of Justin, Irenaeus, Lactantius, Victorinus, Severus and the other older writers, so we too ought not to be bound by their judgment. For later generations do not owe the earlier ones greater reverence than the earlier ones themselves owed to their own forebears. Indeed, they seem to have owed more deference to their forebears than we owe to them, because the further we move from the time of the Apostles (who are the source and origin of all ecclesiastical authority), the more the grace and authority of the ecclesiastical teachers diminishes and declines. If antiquity is (as we were saying) a mark of truth, then nothing is more worthy of veneration and honour than what is most ancient. This single instance, if it were the only one, would still sufficiently show that the agreement of many Fathers has no authority for establishing the faith. But there are many other instances, some of which I shall set out here. We heard above that Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and Augustine deny that heaven is to be opened before the day of judgment, but that the souls of the faithful are all to be kept in some subterranean custody, with a few excepted by a special privilege. The author of the Questions and Answers that circulate under the name of Justin is of the same opinion, as is clear from his answers to questions IX and LXXIV. And lest we waste time in listing the passages of the authors, I say in general that most of the ancients followed this opinion, either wholly or at least in part. For besides Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Augustine, and the most ancient writer of the Questions falsely ascribed to Justin, it is plain that Origen, Lactantius, Victorinus, Ambrose, John Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, Arethas, Prudentius, Theophylact, Bernard, and among the popes Clement of Rome and John XXII were involved in this opinion. Sixtus of Siena and Stapleton state this expressly. And to the earlier writers they could have added Novatian, Hilary, Jerome, Paulinus, bishop of Nola, Claudian, brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, and Moses Bar-Cephas the Syrian, whose passages we have noted in the margin, and which carry the same opinion about the state of the soul and about the resurrection. Indeed, that remarkable and almost universal consensus in this error is never read of as having been challenged by any contrary decree of the Church for 1400 years. Nor does it even appear that any Father bothered to refute this error. units.la: y De Paradiso c.18, T.2. Bibliotb.patr. runt cæteri Patres, suóque silentio errantibus assentiri visi sunt, vel sat habuerunt nonnunquam ex occasione testari se credere sanctorum animas statim à morte & ante resurrectionem Dei visione frui, licèt diserte alteram opinionem minimè rejecerint. Sed antiquissimum esse hunc errorem, vulgóque olim apud Christianos receptum fuisse ex eo præterea patet, quod is etiam hodie ab universa Græcorum Ecclesia defenditur, & ex omni eorum numero qui se Patrum monumenta pro fidei suæ norma habere profitentur soli Latini ab errore discesserunt, contrariámque sententiam ann. demum 1439. in Concilio Florentino, ante annos 212. publicè confirmarunt. In qua Synodo tu quæso Vincentium illum nostrum de Lu incnsi insula medio in consessu constituas, sua illa de quibus supra diximus oracula profantem; rata, scilicet, ac immota esse debere quæcunque Patresuno consensu docuerunt. Palàm est istos Patres huncmerito explosuros fuisse, veluti qui Dei veritatem humanæ auctoritati inepte subjiceret. Veterem enim illiopinionem intellecto eius errore repudiare non dubitaruntnulla eorum ratione habita qui ita olim senserant, quantalibet de cætero esset ipsorum vel antiquitas, velmultitudo, vel eruditio, vel sanctitas. Contrariam verosententiam tametsi illa tantorum virorum pompa carentem, tamen quod vera fit, iidem publicè decreverunt. Ex iis capitibus fidei quæ Protestantibus perfuasuiesse cupit Ecclesia Romana, perpauca esse arbitror quibus probandis tot afferri possint, probabilia in speciem,Patrum testimonia, quot vera & necessaria ad veterisillius erroris defensionem possent congeri, & is tamenerror non solùm in dubium vocatus, sed penitus etiamrepudiatus est. Quis ergo hinc non intelligit Patrum, etiam pluri morum, consensum ad constituendam fidei veritatem haudquaquam satis valere ? Verum ad reliqua pergamus. Hilarij atque Ambrosij sententia de omniumhominum, etiam sanctissimorum, per supremum ignem probatione, quam supra memoravimus, ea & multorum aliorum est cum ipsis communis; Nam eadem & ante eos Origenes † & Lactantius docuerant,& post eos docuerunt Hieronymus, Augustinus, Paulinus Nolanus, Pseudo-Eusebius Emissenus, Cæsarius, Arelatensis, Eligius Noviomensis (si is quidem verò est, quod non videtur; auctor homiliæ octavæ ) Alcuinus & alij. Pseudo-Eusebij verba de illo igne loquentis observanda sunt: Illic iusti velut per amœnos gurgites incendiis naturam suam mutantibus transfmeabunt intacta ignibus CORPORA, ipsis honorificanda pœnis, quia non sunt onerata peccatis. Ita & Cæsarius: Qui modo unum digitum suum in ignem mittere timet, quare non timeat ne necesse sit hunc non parvo tempore cum anima & CORPORE cruciari? Icti pari consensu igne, ultimo die exarsuro, putant omnes homines de mortuis resuscitatos probatum iri, etiam iustissimos, atque sanctissimos. Neque tamen effecit eorum consensus ut non fuerit iam pridem explosa anilis ista de hominum supremis opinio. Bellarminus quidem ait eam manifestum errorem continere. Vidimus supra Tertullianum, Cyprianum episcopum & Martyrem, Firmilianum Cappadociæ Metropolitanum, Dionysium Patriarcham Alexandrinum, cum Synodis episcoporum Africæ, Cappadociæ, Ciliciæ, & Bithyniæ hæreticorum Baptismum rejecisse, ac pro nullo habuisse. Basilius, inter Principes Ecclesiæ Orientalis viros plurimùm eminens, longo post Concilij Nicæni decretum tempore, parumab eadem sententia abest, in epistola ad Amphilochium, quam Canonistæ Græci inter Ecclesiasticas regulas censent. Nemo tamen hunc errorem esse negat. Veterum plurimi, Tertullianus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Lactantius, Africanus Christum à Baptismo suo semel tantum Pascha celebrasse censuerunt, verùm tot Veterum in eandem sententiam consursus, non obstat quominus id falsum sit, imò, ut affirmat Iesuita Petavius, cum Evangelio manifestè pugnet. Mitto quòd Chryfoftomus, Hieronymus, Bafilius, & Patres Concilij Constantinopolitani sub Flaviano Patriarcha, iurare omnino nefas esse sub Novo Testamento videantur existimare. Taceo etiam Athanafium, Basilium, Methodium, teste Ioanne Theffalonicenfi, Angelos corporeos esse sensisse, quibus,vt su-pra vidimus, addi possunt Hilarius, Iustinus, Tertullianus,& alij magno numero, qui obscœno amori obnoxios Angelos censuerunt. Quin & ipse Augustinus idem sensisse videtur. Qui hunc eorum nominibus errorem confirmare vellet, nonne is Romanis ex æquo & Geneventibus scholis ludibrium deberet? Sed non est prætermittendum præter Cyprianum, Augustinum, Innocentium Papam I.quorum testimonia supra retullimus, penè omnes Doctores priorum seculorum credidisse Eucharistiam necessariam esse infantibus, idque observasse Maldonatum scribentem hanc sententiam fexcentos circiter annos viguisse in Ecclesia. Cassander se apud Veteres hanc praxin sæpe adimadvertisse testatur. Et revera Carolus Magnus & Ludovicus Pius, longo post seculum sextum tempore, testantur, referente Cardinale Perronio, hanc consuetudinem suo tempore in Occidente perdurasse. Quinimo eius vestigia inter Christianos, qui cum Ecclesia Latina communionem non colunt, etiamnum videre est. Obseruabat enim Nicolaus de Lyra ab hinc trecentis vel circiter annis Græcos dicere quod hoc sacramentum (Eucharistiæ) tanta necessitatis quòd pueris debet dari sicut Baptismus. Et Patrum nostrorum tempore Ieremias Patriarcha, Græcæ totius Ecclesiæ nomine loquens non solum,inquit, baptizamus infantes, sed etiam eos facimus participes Cœnæ Domini. Et paulo post. Existimamus vtrumque Sacramentum omnibus ad salutem necessarium, Baptismum scilicet & sacrã communionem. Eodem modo Abyssini infantes suos re-
units.tr: y De Paradiso c.18, T.2. Bibliotb.patr. The other Fathers passed over the matter in silence and seemed to assent to the erring, or were content to say now and then, when the occasion arose, that they believed the souls of the saints enjoy the vision of God immediately after death and before the resurrection, though they never expressly rejected the other opinion. That this error is very ancient, and was once widely received among Christians, is further clear from the fact that it is still defended today by the whole Greek Church, and that of all those who profess to hold the monuments of the Fathers as the norm of their faith, only the Latins have departed from the error. Only in 1439, at the Council of Florence, about 212 years ago, did they publicly confirm the contrary opinion. In that Synod, I beg you, place in the midst of the assembly that Vincent of ours from the island of Lérins, pronouncing those oracles of his of which we spoke above, namely that whatever the Fathers have taught with one consent must be held fixed and unshaken. It is plain that those Fathers would have rejected this man, as one who foolishly subjected the truth of God to human authority. For when they recognised the error of that old opinion, they did not hesitate to repudiate it, taking no account of those who had held it in former times, however great might otherwise be their antiquity, their number, their learning or their holiness. The contrary opinion, though lacking that pomp of so great men, they nevertheless publicly decreed, because it is true. Of those articles of faith which the Roman Church wishes to persuade the Protestants of, I think there are very few for which as many Patristic testimonies might be brought forward, plausible in appearance, as could be gathered in defence of that old error that is true and necessary; and yet that error has not only been called into question but utterly repudiated. Who then does not see from this that the consent of the Fathers, even of very many, is by no means sufficient to establish the truth of faith? But let us proceed to the rest. The opinion of Hilary and Ambrose, that all men, even the most holy, are to be tested by the supreme fire, which we mentioned above, is shared with them by many others. For the same view had been taught before them by Origen and Lactantius, and after them by Jerome, Augustine, Paulinus of Nola, Pseudo-Eusebius of Emesa, Caesarius of Arles, Eligius of Noyon (if indeed he is the author, which does not seem to be the case, of the eighth homily), Alcuin and others. The words of Pseudo-Eusebius speaking of that fire are to be noted: There the righteous will pass through the fire, as through pleasant streams, the fires changing their nature, their BODIES untouched by the flames, to be honoured by the punishments themselves, because they are not burdened with sins. So also Caesarius: He who now fears to put one of his fingers into the fire, why does he not fear that he may have to be tormented for no short time, in soul and in BODY? The jurists, with equal agreement, think that all men will be proved, by the fire which will blaze on the last day, to have been raised from the dead, even the most just and most holy. Yet their consensus has not prevented that silly old-wives' notion about the final fate of men from having been long since exploded. Bellarmine indeed says it contains a manifest error. We saw above that Tertullian, Cyprian the bishop and martyr, Firmilian the metropolitan of Cappadocia, and Dionysius the patriarch of Alexandria, together with the synods of bishops of Africa, Cappadocia, Cilicia and Bithynia, rejected the baptism of heretics and held it as nothing. Basil, among the most eminent men of the leaders of the Eastern Church, long after the decree of the Council of Nicaea, is not far from the same opinion, in his letter to Amphilochius, which the Greek canonists count among the ecclesiastical rules. Yet no one denies that this is an error. Many of the ancients, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius, and Africanus, held that Christ celebrated the Passover only once, from his own baptism onwards; but the agreement of so many of the ancients in that opinion does not prevent it from being false, indeed, as the Jesuit Petavius affirms, it plainly clashes with the Gospel. I pass over the fact that Chrysostom, Jerome, Basil, and the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople under Patriarch Flavian seem to hold that it is altogether wrong to swear under the New Testament. I also say nothing of Athanasius, Basil and Methodius, who, as John of Thessalonica testifies, held that angels are corporeal; to whom, as we saw above, may be added Hilary, Justin, Tertullian and many others in great number, who held that the angels were subject to obscene love. Indeed Augustine himself seems to have held the same. Would not he who wished to confirm this error by their names deserve to be mocked alike by the Roman and the Genevan schools? But it must not be passed over that, besides Cyprian, Augustine and Pope Innocent I, whose testimonies we cited above, almost all the teachers of the earlier centuries believed that the Eucharist was necessary for infants, and Maldonatus, writing, observed this, saying that this opinion flourished in the Church for about six hundred years. Cassander testifies that he had often noticed this practice among the ancients. And indeed Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, long after the sixth century, bear witness, as Cardinal Perron reports, that this custom endured in their time in the West. Moreover, its traces may still be seen among Christians who do not keep communion with the Latin Church. For Nicholas of Lyra observed about three hundred years ago that the Greeks say that this sacrament (of the Eucharist) is of such necessity that it ought to be given to children just as baptism is. And in the time of our Fathers, Patriarch Jeremiah, speaking in the name of the whole Greek Church, says: We not only baptize infants, but we also make them partakers of the Lord's Supper. And a little later: We think that both sacraments are necessary to salvation for all, namely baptism and holy communion. In the same way the Abyssinians admit their baptized infants to holy communion.

Antequam enim Concilium Tridentinum, superiore seculo eam damnaret, nemo é Christianis repertus erat qui eam disserte repudiaret. Supta diximus Augustinum sensisse pueros sine baptismo mortuos non privari solùm Dei visione, sed etiam igne cruciari. Id agnoscit Petavius, additque Alcimum Avitum Viennensem Episcopum quin & ipsos Florentinos Patres
units.tr: From this anyone can understand that in this false opinion about the necessity of the Eucharist there were not just three or four of the ancients, but very many, indeed almost all of them. For before the Council of Trent condemned it in the previous century, no one among Christians was found who expressly rejected it. units.la: BEssario Græcorum eruditissimus, quem Eugenius IV. galero Cardinalitio, propter egregiam navatam operam in farciendo schismate Orientem inter & Occidentem, donavit, in Scripto quod de hoc argumento in Concilio Florentino elaboravit, quicquid controversiarum est Græcam inter & Latinam Ecclesiam ad tribunal Patrum evocat. Cùm verò non nescirent, si judicibus inter se non convenit, causam (maximè si ad religionem pertinent) non posse legitimè decidi, obnixè contendit Patribus, non modo secum singulis, sed (quod longè magis arduum est) etiam inter se universis optimè convenire. Itaque si quando ulla in eorum Scriptis sententiarum diversitas occurrat, jubet nos nostram potius ignorantiam accusare, quàm Patribus aliquam inter se contradictionem impingere. Ex hac viri, quo nullus in Synodo Florentina fuit acutior aut doctior, hypothesi, statuendum est, Patres non aliter controversiarum nostrarum judices esse posse, nisi ipsi inter se eadem de religione sentiant, quod sanè per se planum ac perspicuum est. Si enim vel secum ipsi, vel inter se pugnent, nostras controversias adeo non component vel imminuent, ut eas potius magis magisque impediturì & animos nostros in partes scissuri videantur. Sic ergo, ut constet an nostræ controversiæ ad Patrum tribunal, quod vult Bessario, recte referantur, discipiendum est, an eorum (quod idem ait) de religionis capitibus sententiæ nunquam inter se pugnent. Fac ita esse, non ideo sequetur infallibile esse Patrum judicium. Fieri enim poterit ut in iisdem erroribus multi, vel ex compositio, vel casu, vel quapiam alia simili.
units.tr: Bessarion, the most learned of the Greeks, whom Eugenius IV rewarded with a cardinal's hat for his outstanding work in healing the schism between East and West, in the treatise he prepared on this subject at the Council of Florence, summons to the tribunal of the Fathers every controversy between the Greek and Latin Churches. Since he knew that if judges do not agree among themselves a case (especially one touching religion) cannot be decided lawfully, he insisted strenuously that the Fathers agree very well, not only each with himself, but (which is far harder) all of them with one another. So, if any diversity of opinion appears in their writings, he bids us blame our own ignorance rather than charge the Fathers with contradiction. From this hypothesis of that man, who was the sharpest and most learned of all at the Synod of Florence, it must be concluded that the Fathers can be judges of our controversies only if they themselves think the same about religion, which of course is plain and obvious in itself. For if they quarrel either with themselves or with one another, they will not settle or lessen our controversies at all, but will rather seem to make them more and more intractable and to divide our minds into factions. So, to establish whether our controversies are rightly referred to the tribunal of the Fathers, as Bessarion wishes, we must inquire whether their opinions on the heads of religion (as he likewise says) never clash with one another. Grant that they do not: it will not follow that the judgment of the Fathers is infallible. For it may happen that many agree in the same errors, through habit, chance, or some other similar cause.

units.la: a Bessar. orat. de unione, p. 510. ratione conspirent. Sin hoc,quod ait Beffario, falsum fit, certissimè statuendum est alios,quàm Patres, quærendos controversiarum nostrarum iudices. Demonstremus ergo,ut & hoc superioribus nostris probationibus adiiciamus,hoc pronunciatum maiori confidentia quàm veritate prolatum esse, plurimáque de rebus ad religionē pertinentibus extare inter Veteres sententiarum divortia. Nonnulla iam ex aliis occasionibus attigimus quæ satis est breviter hic perstringi.
units.tr: a Bessarion, oration on union, p. 510. If, however, what Bessarion says is false, we must most certainly conclude that other judges than the Fathers must be sought for our controversies. Let us therefore show, so that we may add this to our earlier proofs, that this claim has been made with more confidence than truth, and that very many divergences of opinion on matters pertaining to religion exist among the ancients. We have already touched on some of them on other occasions; it is enough to set them out briefly here.

units.la: Observavimus imprimis memorabile Dionysii Alexandrini,Gregorij Nazianzeni, Hieronymi & aliorum à vetustissimis lustino,Irenæo, Tertulliano & cæteris,quorum ingens numerus fuit,dissidium; hos enim mille ane. delicias,& Hierusalem gemmeam atque adamantinam, cum gloria, & uberrima rerum omnium in terris copia nobis sério polliceri; Illos verò has spes velut commenta, puerorumque & vetularum deliria, ex ludaeorum liene, non ex Apostolorum cerebro enata acriter infectari atque explodere. Illam quoque controversiam attigimus quæ Victori R.Ep.de die Pascbatis cum Asianis fuit. Item quæ Cyprianum cum Stephano de Baptismo hæreticorum commisit. Vtraque sic exstitit, ut res ad anathemata protulerit. Si ostenderit Bellario istos in speciem tantùm, non autem reapse inter se dissensisse, non dubitabo quin aquam & ignem, agnos & lupos & inimicissima quæque inter se sit eadem opera conciliaturus. Vidimus Tertullianum docuisse animam esse ex traduce, id est, de patre in filium generatione naturali propagari, Augustinúmque in eam sententiam propendisse, & cum eo Occidentalium plerosque eadem sensisse, teste Hieronymo. b Ipse vero Hieronymus hanc sententiam rejicit, c censétque animam à Deo immediatè creari, & eodem tempore in corpus infundi, quinimo eam fuisse de hoc argumento totius Ecclesiæ sententiam docet. Idem cum suis auctoribus existimat Petrum à Paulo, quod habetur in epistola ad Galatas, per simulationem reprehensum fuisse, atque ita ex composito inter se lusisse duos istos Apostolos. At Augustinus, cum multis aliis,rem seriò,nullàqj inter Petrum & Paulum collusione gestam contendit, planè ut in Scripturis, simpliciter ac bona fide, narratur. Hæc verò controversia Hieronymi animo sic altè insederat, ut præter epistolas quas multo felle tinctas de hoc argumento scripsit, alibi etiam, & in i· lis quidem Commentariis, quos animo sedato compositssse putatur, Augustinum identidem tacitè perstringere ac vellicare velle videatur. Itaque prorsus insanire cum oporteat qui Patres istos in eadem de hisce capitibus fuisse sententia contendat. Iustinus ipsum Samuelis animam Pythonissæ invocatam Sauli apparuisse vult. Cum lustino sentiunt ex Græcis Origenes & Anastasius Antiochenus; ex Latinis Severus Sulpitius, Zeno Veronensis, Ambrosius & Augustinus eo,licèt aliter aliàs sentiens,prependet. Alij spectrum merum fuisse autumat; ut Tertullianus, Eustathius Antiochenus, Pionius Martyr, Basilius Cæsareensis, Gregorius Nyssenus, Hieronymus, Philatrius Brixiensis, Carolus Magnus. Nonnemo arbitratur traditionis esse Apostolicæ ter singulis hebdomadis ad Eucharistiæ celebrationem convenire. Alter negat. Nonnulli Sabbatho jejunandum sentiunt. Alij eum qui Sabbatho jejunet Christi inter fœtorem dicere non verentur. Sunt qui contendunt Christum mortuum cum natus esset annos quadraginta, aut quinquaginta. Scribunt alij crucifixum fuisse annum agentem trigesimum, vel trigesimum primum. Utrique aperte cum Evangelio pugnant. In eo enim docemur perspicuè Christum post baptismum, id est, ab ætatis suæ anno trigesimo, ad minimum triennio, bien
units.tr: We have observed, first of all, the notable disagreement between Dionysius of Alexandria, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome and others, and the very ancient writers Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and the rest, who were a great number. The latter (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and the rest) seriously promised us a thousand years of delights, a Jerusalem of gems and adamant with glory, and an abundant supply of all things on earth; while the former vigorously attacked and rejected these hopes as fancies and the delusions of children and old women, born from the spleen of the Jews and not from the brain of the Apostles. We have also touched on the controversy that Victor, bishop of Rome, had with the Asians about the day of Easter. Likewise the dispute that set Cyprian against Stephen about the baptism of heretics. Both of these disputes went so far that they brought about anathemas. If Bessarion shows that these men differed only in appearance and not in reality, I shall not doubt that he will, by the same effort, reconcile water and fire, lambs and wolves, and all the most hostile things. We have seen that Tertullian taught that the soul is derived by transmission (ex traduce), that is, propagated from father to son by natural generation; that Augustine inclined to this opinion, and that with him most of the Westerners held the same view, as Jerome testifies. But Jerome himself rejects this opinion, and he holds that the soul is created immediately by God and infused into the body at the same time; indeed, he teaches that this was the view of the whole Church on this question. He thinks, together with his own authorities, that Peter was rebuked by Paul by pretence, as is related in the epistle to the Galatians, and that the two Apostles had thus played a game together by agreement. But Augustine, with many others, maintains that the matter was done in earnest, with no collusion between Peter and Paul, just as it is narrated in the Scriptures, simply and in good faith. Indeed, this controversy had so deeply lodged in Jerome's mind that, apart from the letters he wrote on this subject steeped in much gall, he seems elsewhere, even in those Commentaries which are thought to have been composed in a calmer spirit, to keep secretly trying to attack and taunt Augustine. Therefore, whoever maintains that those Fathers held the same opinion on these questions must surely be mad. Justin wants the spirit of Samuel, called up by the witch, to have appeared to Saul. Origen and Anastasius of Antioch agree with Justin among the Greeks; among the Latins, Severus Sulpicius, Zeno of Verona, Ambrose and Augustine lean that way, though Augustine at other times thinks otherwise. Others judge it was a mere phantom, such as Tertullian, Eustathius of Antioch, Pionius the martyr, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, Jerome, Philastrius of Brescia, and Charlemagne. Some think it is a tradition of the Apostles that they should assemble three times each week for the celebration of the Eucharist; another denies it. Some think one should fast on the Sabbath; others do not hesitate to say that the one who fasts on the Sabbath smells of Christ. There are those who maintain that Christ died when he was forty or fifty years old. Others write that he was crucified in his thirtieth or thirty-first year. Both plainly contradict the Gospel. For we are clearly taught in it that Christ, after his baptism, that is, from the thirtieth year of his age, dwelt on earth for at least three years, or at most five.
