Af-fricanus, ubi supra. nionve; ad summum quinquennio in terris versatum fuisse. Nonnulli ( ut docent nos ipsi illi Græci qui ad Latinos desciverunt d ) in doctrina de Trinitate voces, causas & effectus usurpari concedunt, alij vetant. Alij ordinem & dispositionem quandam inter Trinitatis personas constituunt. Alij ne voces quidem istas ferre possunt. Latini de solo filio dicunt quòd sit Patris imago; Græci & Spiritum sanctum sic dici volunt. Basilius vocem προϐολὴ progenies., è Theologia de Filio exterminat. Alij eam nulla religione admittunt. Dubito an legisset Bessario Hieronymi & Ruffini Invectivas & Apologias, qui tamen ambo Patres & in pretio, licet non eodem à suorum & sequentium temporum. Ecclesia habiti. Sed neque ut opinor eorum meminerat quae in Chrysostomum gesta sunt à Theophilo & Epiphanio quae nihil minùs significant quam bene inter eos convenisse. Sed ad infirmandum audax Græci hominis pronunciatum nullo alio argumento opus est, quam eo ipso in quo nunc ille laborat. Cui enim persuasurus est Patres eadem de processione Spiritus sancti dixisse & scripsisse ? Quibusdam in locis perspicuè eum à Filio procedere statuunt, ut in Basilij loco quem Latini (reclamantibus tamen Græcis & suppositicium criminantibus) ex opere contra Eunomium allegant, ut & Patres. Occidentales in variis locis difertissimis. Sed qua fronte dici possit omnes in hac eadem sententia fuisse equidem non video. Cætera à Græcis obiecta testimonia nunc mitto, quæ Latini ægre, & qua licet diluunt; Patrum non raro & verba & sensus vexantes & contorquentes. Sed Theodoreti ex refutatione Anathematismorum Cyrilli locus difertior est quàm ut eludi queat. Cyrillus Anathema 9. Spiritum Sanctum esse proprium Filij dicerat. f Respondet Theodoretus, impium & blasphemum esse dicere Spiritum S. habere subsistentiam suam à Filio, aut per Filium. Si proprium Spiritum Filij (inquit) & quidem ut ejusdem cum eo natura & ex Patre procedentē divis,

T.1, p. 8<7. {s} On Matthew 6; on Vai. 7; on Ezekiel 13. {t} On heresies, har. 26. {u} On magic, l. 4, c. 27. {x} Epiphanius, Panarion, exposition of the faith, p. 1104. {y} Augustine, letter to Januarius (Fl.) 118, T.3; see Petau on Epiphanius, p. 354. {z} See Petau, p. 359. {a} Epiphanius, Ecclesiastical Roman, op. S.c.d 5, c. 22; Augustine, p. 86. {b} Letter 118; Innocent, l. 1, p. 1, c. 4. {c} Ignatius, p. 4, to Philippians; Canons of the Apostles, d. 7, c. 68; Constitutions of the Apostles, 47, 6, 24; Synod of Trullo, 455; Irenaeus, l. 2, c. 39; Tertullian, Latin; Africanus, as above. or at most five years on earth. Some (as those Greeks who went over to the Latins themselves teach us {d}) concede that the terms cause and effect may be applied in the doctrine of the Trinity, while others forbid them. Others set up a certain order and arrangement among the persons of the Trinity; others cannot even bear these words at all. The Latins say only of the Son that he is the image of the Father; the Greeks want the Holy Spirit to be called this too. Basil banishes the word proboles [προϐολὴ], "progeny," from his theology of the Son. Others admit it with no religious scruple. I doubt whether Bessarion had read the Invectives and Apologies of Jerome and Rufinus, though both were Fathers and held in esteem by the Church, although not in the same way by their own and later times. Nor, I think, did he recall what was done against Chrysostom by Theophilus and Epiphanius, which proves nothing less than that they agreed well with one another. But to weaken the bold assertion of this Greek man, no other argument is needed than the very task in which he is now labouring. For to whom will he persuade that the Fathers said and wrote the same things about the procession of the Holy Spirit? In some passages they plainly state that he proceeds from the Son, as in Basil's passage which the Latins cite from his work against Eunomius (though the Greeks protest and accuse it of being spurious), and as the Fathers do too. The Western writers do so in many very clear places. But I for my part do not see with what face it can be said that all were of this same opinion. I now set aside the other testimonies the Greeks have objected, which the Latins answer with difficulty and only in part, often twisting and distorting both the words and the sense of the Fathers. But the passage of Theodoret from his refutation of Cyril's Anathemas is too clear to be evaded. Cyril, in Anathema 9, had said that the Holy Spirit is the proper possession of the Son. Theodoret replies that it is impious and blasphemous to say that the Holy Spirit has his subsistence from the Son, or through the Son. If (he says) the Spirit is proper to the Son, and indeed of the same nature with him and proceeding from the Father, we shall at once confess this and receive it as a pious word.

units.la: {d} Conc. Flor. Act. 10. T.4. Cir.p.454.C. Cyrill. anath. 9. Theod. refut. Anath. 9. Cyrill. Act. Conc. Ephes. p.3.T.1. Conc. cil.p.164.C. dixit, simul confitebimur & tanquam piam suscipiemus vocem. Siverò tâquam ex Filio, aut per Filium, existentiam habeat, hoc ut blasphemum & impium rejiciemus. Non potuit dubiusfententia illa respui. Quid ad hæc Cyrillus? Ille verò tametsi juveniliter à Theodoreto provocatus, adhæc in causa optima atque æquissima, cùm ab adversario probrosè explosa, impietatisque damnata esset ea sententia, quæ totius, (si Latinis credimus) Ecclesiæ communis erat, tamen molliter & paucis hoc unum respondet, h Procedere quidem ex Deo & Patre Spiritum sanctum, secundum Servatoris vocem, sed non esse à Filio alienū, cum habeat omnia cum Patre. Atqui Theodoretus hic erat hæreseos accusandus, si Ecclesiam quidem illius temporis statuas docuisse Spiritum sanctum ex Filio procedere. Quid est ergo quòd Cyrillus tam patienter audit sententiam verámque sententiam velut impiam & blasphemam proculcari? Cur non indignatur? Cur Ecclesiam (si hæc erat eius fides) non appellat injuriæ suæ vindicem? Cur nihil istorum facit, sed clementi & languido responso adversarium non tam arcet quàm demulcet, sic ut causam prodere potiùs videatur quàm defendere? Nam neque Theodoretus, neque recentiores Græci unquam defenderunt Spiritum Sanctum esse à Filio alienum, qui scilicet Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum unum esse eundémque Deum in secula benedictum vltro confitentur. Quisquis ista omnia accuratè expenderit (non enim hic locus est ea fusiùs excutiendi) agnoscet, opinor, tum temporis nihil adhuc Ecclesiam de eo capite constituisse, vel decrevisse, Illósque Doctores, pro disputationum in quibus versabantur ratione, & tanquam in rebus nondum examinatis & diserte explicatis, quid sentirent privatim litteris ex occasione mandasse, adeo ut me nonnunquam Græcorum & Latinorum miserat in Parribus ad se suâsque partes trahendis nequicquam sudantium; quorum voces, si quid iis insit ambigui; torquent, codices, ubi sibi non favent, ad adversariis depravatos fuisse criminantur. Denique, ubi omnia tentarunt,nihil promovent & lectori,qui quidem stà partium studio alienus, plus tædij quàm fructus aut solidæ ædificationis afferrunt. Atqui longè facilius atque consultius erat id quod res ipsa loquitur, agnoscere; Patres, scilicet, ut de multis aliis religionis capitibus, ita de hoc quoque non unum idemq; sensisse. Quod verò Bessario, ut hoc Theodoreti testimonium eludat, comminiscitur, eum ex Ecclesia propter negatam Spiritus sancti è Filio processionem,ejectum; deinde cantata publicè in Synodo Chalcedonensi palinodia restitutum,hæc nobis Græca fide narrat,eo ipso quod fingitanimi sui vehemens in hanc causam studium apertissimè ostendens. Amabo enim,à quo ille vetere Scriptore habuit Theodoretum, non dicam damnatum vel excommunicatū, sed vel reprehensum aut accusatum,quod de Spiritus sancti processione perperam sensisset?Habemus Acta Concilij Ephefini in quo fuit excommunicatus. Habemus epistolam Cyrilli, qua ad pacem Ecclesiæ admittit Ioannem Patriarcham Antiochenum, omnésque eius socios, quorum Theodoretus facile princeps erat. Habemus Concilium Chalcedonense, in quo Theodoretus,post nonnullos adversariorum clamores, pro episcopo catholico habitus fuit & cum cæteris consedit. Vllúmne in istis omnibus authenticis monumentis verbum de eius sententia circa Theologiam de Spiritu sancto occurrit? Ne Cyrillus quidem, id est ipsemet viri adversarius, eius de hoc capite sententiam damnavit. Sed sat habet excusare, vel si mavis simpliciter defendere suam. Theodoreti in Ephefino & Chalcedonensi Conciliis causa cum hac nihil omnino commune habuit. Agebatur enim tantùm de duabus naturis Iesu Christi, quem Nestorius in duas personas divellebat. Ioannes Patriarcha Antiochenus, Theodoretus & varij alij Orientis Præsules Nestorio nonnihil favebant, vel, vt verius dicam;injuria illum à Concilio Ephesino asse-ctam stum dolebant; & nonnulla in Anathematismis Cyrilli damnabant. Cum hæc in Actis Concilij clara sint omnia, qua fronte dicitur de gradu ideo dejectus Theodoretus quòd male de Spiritus sancti processione sentiret? Verùm de his satis. Nunc illud scire pervelim, quomodo Græcus noster Conciliator D C X X X. Chalcedonensis Synodi Patres, cum Leone Romano episcopo sit reconciliaturus, & XXVIII. illorum canonem cum tam multis huius ad Anatolium, ad Marcianum, ad alios epistolis in vnum redintegraturus? Chalcedonenses Patres Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ thronum supra Alexandrinam & Antiochenam sedes evexerant, eam Romano ipsi throno haud obscurè æquantes: Leo ex alia parte hoc istorum decretum, velut intolerabilem errorem, insectatur. Sed Chalcedone, si placet, prosectus, in Africam noster Eessario naviget, & illarum provinciarum Patres cum Pontificibus Romanis, si potest, conciliet inter se litigantes, cum illi quidem suos clericos Romam provocare vetarent; hi verò contenderent id licere, suique juris esse. Si labor successerit, poterit in componenda Nicænorum & Francofurtensium Patrum lite operam collocare, quos diffidere inter se notum est, quod illi quidem decreverint imaginibus salutationem & adorationis suffitus, & cereorum honorem, hi verò totam Græcorum Synodum repudiarint. Certè vel cæci vident omnes istos Patres adversis pugnantibus inter se discordes esse sententiis, nullámque aliam ad conciliationem viam patere, nisi ut cum suis singuli sententiis admittantur; quod mirabili quodam & hactenus inaudito sapientiæ specimine Constantinopolitani in Tullo Patres sequuti sunt. Admiserunt enim illi simúlque ac semel confirmarunt, Ecclesiæq; regulas esse jusserunt tum Apostolorum, tum concilii Ecclesiasticici canones, hoc est, Sardicensis & Carthaginensis & Laodicenæ Synodorum decreta; Inter quæ tamen haud pauca sunt quæ inter se pugnant. Exempli gratia. Vt ab omnibus episcopis jus esset Romæ appellare Sardicæ constitutum est. At idipsum Chalcedone Constantinopolitanæ sedi attributum est. P Laodicena Synodus nullos in Sanctarum Scripturarum canone agnoscit Macchabæorum, Ecclesiastici, Sapientiæ, Tobiæ & Iudith libros, quos Carthaginensis diserte in Canonem refert. ʳ Boni verò isti Trullani Patres, ut omnibus satisfacerent, nullam istius diversitatis rationem habuerunt; singulos cum suis opinionibus & privatis constitutionibus recipiunt, neminem cogunt ut certæ alicui & communi regulæ acquiescat, & hæc ipsi quæ habent ea etiam ut videtur lege decernunt, ut nulli in eorum quos admittebant sententiam concedere tenerentur, nisi quatenus rationibus suis convenire, & è re sua esse existimarent. Neminem puto fore qui non facilè omnia Patrum scripta, hac quidem lege, pro authenticis recipiat, ut scilicet ipsi integrum & liberum sit quicquid commodum vel incommodum videbitur id pro suo arbitrio vel admittere vel rejicere. Atque ita jam, ni fallor, quicquid opinetur Bessario concludere tutò veréque possumus, Patres, non semper eadem sensisse, de capitibus ad religionem pertinentibus: unde & illud evidentissimè sequitur, non posse eos controversias nostras suo judicio decidere. Cùm enim notum sit eos de tot magni momenti capitibus inter se pugnare, quis fidem faciet inter ipsos de iis quæ hodie controvertuntur convenire? Cur iis in quæstionibus de Eucharistia, de auctoritate Ecclesiæ de potestate Papæ, de libero arbitrio, de Purgatorio non idem accidere potuit quod in his capitibus de quibus proximè egimus accidisse comperitur? præsertim, cùm ea de quibus differentire deprehenduntur, his, de quibus nos litigamus, neque minoris momenti, neque obscuriora sint, ut præcedente capite observatum est. Epiphanij, & Hieronymi de veteri presbyterorū & episcoporum jure voces non minùs inter se pugnant quam Theodoreti & Cyrilli de processione Spiritus sancti dicta. Neque Tertulliani & Damasceni Theodoreti & Eusebij Emeseni, Eusebij Caesareensis & VII ac Synodi de Eucharistia assertiones magis inter se consentaneæ sunt quam Cypriani & Stephani de hæreticorum baptismo sententiæ. Eadem est aliorum fere omnium ratio. Quid ergo est cur de eorum in istis concordia tantopere laboremus? vt etiam velut admotis fidiculis invitos ac repugnantes idem sentire cogamus. Quin ultrò agnoscimus ingenuéque fatemur quod res, eos, ut verbis, sic sensu quoque inter se differre? Nulla nobis religio est eos confiteri aliter atque aliter de iis sensisse de quibus nulla est inter nos controversia. Non video cur gravius sit eos de iis dissensisse quæ nunc sunt inter nos controversa. Sed plura ea de re verba facere nihil necesse est. Satis est Patrum diversas fuisse de religione sententias, inde enim necessarior conficitur non posse nos eorum iudicio in controversiis nostris istare.
units.tr: {d} Conc. Flor. Act. 10. T.4. Cir.p.454.C. Cyrill. anath. 9. Theod. refut. Anath. 9. Cyrill. Act. Conc. Ephes. p.3.T.1. Conc. cil.p.164.C. He said: "We shall at once confess it, and receive it as a pious utterance. But if he has his existence as from the Son, or through the Son, we shall reject this as blasphemous and impious." That opinion could not be rejected as doubtful. What does Cyril say to this? He, although provoked by Theodoret in a youthful manner, and in a cause most good and most just, since that opinion, which (if we believe the Latins) was common to the whole Church, had been scornfully rejected and condemned as impious by his opponent, nevertheless answers this one point mildly and briefly: It is true that the Holy Spirit proceeds from God and the Father, according to the word of the Saviour, but he is not alien from the Son, since he has all things in common with the Father. And yet Theodoret would have been charged with heresy here, if you suppose that the Church of that time taught that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Why then does Cyril so patiently hear a sentence, and a true sentence, trampled down as impious and blasphemous? Why is he not indignant? Why does he not call the Church (if this was its faith) the avenger of its wrong? Why does he do none of these things, but with a gentle and languid reply does not so much ward off his opponent as soothe him, so that he seems to betray the cause rather than defend it? For neither Theodoret nor the more recent Greeks ever defended that the Holy Spirit is alien from the Son, since they freely confess that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and the same God, blessed for ever. Whoever weighs all these things carefully (for this is not the place to examine them at greater length) will recognise, I think, that at that time the Church had not yet settled or decreed anything on that head; and that those teachers, according to the manner of the disputations in which they were engaged, and as if in matters not yet examined and clearly explained, privately committed to writing what they thought, as occasion arose. So I have sometimes pitied the Greeks and Latins, sweating in vain to draw the Fathers to themselves and their side. Whose words, if there is anything ambiguous in them, they twist; and where the manuscripts do not favour them, they accuse those manuscripts of having been corrupted by opponents. Finally, when they have tried everything, they achieve nothing, and bring to the reader, who is indeed free of partisan zeal, more weariness than profit or solid edification. And yet it was far easier and more prudent to acknowledge what the matter itself declares: that the Fathers, as on many other heads of religion, so also on this one, did not all think the same. As for what Bessarion devises to evade this testimony of Theodoret, namely that he was cast out of the Church on account of denying the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, and then restored by a palinode publicly sung in the Council of Chalcedon, he tells us this on Greek authority, and by the very fact that he invents it he clearly shows the vehement zeal of his mind in this cause. Pray, from which ancient writer did he get the idea that Theodoret was not merely condemned or excommunicated, but even rebuked or accused, because he had thought wrongly about the procession of the Holy Spirit? We have the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, in which he was excommunicated. We have the letter of Cyril by which he admits to the peace of the Church John the Patriarch of Antioch and all his companions, of whom Theodoret was easily the chief. We have the Council of Chalcedon, in which Theodoret, after some clamours of opponents, was held to be a catholic bishop and sat down with the others. Does a single word about his opinion concerning the doctrine of the Holy Spirit occur in all these authentic records? Not even Cyril, that is, the man's own adversary, condemned his opinion on this head. Cyril is content to excuse it, or, if you prefer, simply to defend his own. Theodoret's cause at the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon had nothing at all in common with this question. For the matter at issue was only the two natures of Jesus Christ, whom Nestorius was splitting into two persons. John the Patriarch of Antioch, Theodoret and various other prelates of the East favoured Nestorius somewhat, or, to speak more truly, they grieved that he had been unjustly treated by the Council of Ephesus; and they condemned some things in the Anathematisms of Cyril. Since all these things are clear in the Acts of the Council, with what face is it said that Theodoret was deprived of his rank because he thought wrongly about the procession of the Holy Spirit? But enough of these things. Now I would very much like to know how our Greek conciliator is going to reconcile the six hundred and thirty Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon with Leo the Roman bishop, and bring back into one agreement the twenty-eighth canon of that council with the many letters of Leo to Anatolius, to Marcian and to others. The Fathers of Chalcedon had raised the throne of the Church of Constantinople above the sees of Alexandria and Antioch, openly making it equal to the Roman throne itself; Leo, on the other hand, attacks this decree of theirs as an intolerable error. But let our conciliator, if you please, set out from Chalcedon, sail to Africa, and try to reconcile the Fathers of those provinces with the Roman pontiffs, who are quarrelling among themselves: the former forbade their clergy to appeal to Rome, while the latter insisted that this was lawful and within their right. If his labour succeeds, he may take pains to settle the dispute between the Fathers of Nicaea and those of Frankfurt, who are known to disagree among themselves: the former decreed salutation and adoration for images, and the honour of incense and candles; the latter rejected the whole Synod of the Greeks. Surely even the blind see that all these Fathers are at odds, holding opposing and conflicting opinions, and that there is no way to reconciliation open except that each be admitted with his own opinions. This is what the Constantinopolitan Fathers in the Trullan council followed, with a certain wonderful and hitherto unheard-of display of wisdom. For they admitted them all, and at the same time and once for all confirmed them, and ordered that the rules of the Church should be both the canons of the Apostles and the canons of the councils, that is, the decrees of the Synods of Sardica, Carthage and Laodicea. Among these, however, there are not a few which contradict one another. For example: that every bishop should have the right to appeal to Rome was established at Sardica. But that very same right was granted at Chalcedon to the see of Constantinople. The Synod of Laodicea recognises in the canon of the Holy Scriptures none of the books of the Maccabees, Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, Tobit and Judith, which Carthage expressly brings into the canon. Those good Trullan Fathers, in order to satisfy everyone, took no account of this difference; they receive each with his own opinions and private constitutions, they compel no one to acquiesce in some certain and common rule, and they themselves decree by this law, as it seems, that no one among those whom they admitted was bound to concede their opinion, except insofar as they judged it agreed with their own reasons and was to their advantage. I think there will be no one who does not readily accept all the writings of the Fathers on this condition, as authentic: namely, that it should be entirely free for himself to admit or reject whatever seems to him convenient or inconvenient, at his own discretion. And so now, unless I am mistaken, we can conclude safely and truly, whatever Bessarion may think, that the Fathers did not always think the same on the heads pertaining to religion. Whence it also follows most clearly that they cannot decide our controversies by their judgment. For since it is known that they disagree among themselves on so many matters of great moment, who will give assurance that they agree among themselves about those things which are disputed today? Why could it not happen in the questions about the Eucharist, the authority of the Church, the power of the Pope, free will and Purgatory, what is found to have happened in those heads which we have just discussed? Especially since the things on which they are found to differ are neither of less moment nor more obscure than those for which we contend, as was observed in the preceding chapter. The sayings of Epiphanius and Jerome on the ancient right of presbyters and bishops contradict each other no less than the sayings of Theodoret and Cyril about the procession of the Holy Spirit. Nor are the assertions of Tertullian and Damascene, of Theodoret and Eusebius of Emesa, of Eusebius of Caesarea and of the Seventh Synod on the Eucharist more consistent with one another than the opinions of Cyprian and Stephen on the baptism of heretics. The reasoning is almost the same for almost all the others. Why then do we labour so greatly for their agreement on these matters, so as to compel them, as if with stretched strings, unwilling and resisting, to think the same? Indeed, do we not willingly acknowledge and frankly confess that they differ from one another in matter as well as in words? We have no scruple about admitting that they thought differently on matters about which there is no controversy between us. I do not see why it should be more serious that they disagreed on those things which are now in controversy among us. But there is no need to say more on this point. It is enough that the Fathers held diverse opinions on religion; for from this a stronger conclusion follows, that we cannot rest our controversies on their judgment.

units.la: Hactenus de Patrum in exponenda Scriptura diversitate, vel nihil, vel certè paucissima diximus. Atqui id magni in primis momenti est, & præ cæteris memorabile. Si enim Iudices nostri constituantur, subinde ac pene assiduè consulendi erunt de locis quorum sensus apud nos controvertitur. Quid fiet si de horum expositione apud ipsos Patres non maior quàm apud nos consordia sit? Hic ex Evangelio secundùm Ioannem locus Ego & Pater unum sumus magni est momenti in disputationibus contra Sabellium & Arium. Vin' tu eius generinum sensum doceri, ne perversa expositione in istorum scopulos inpingas? Si Patres adis, reperies nobilem hunc locum ab aliis ad animi & voluntatis vnionem ab aliis ad essentiæ & naturæ vnitatem referri. Hic alter ex eodem Evangelio locus Pater maior me est, dignus est qui accuratè expendatur in quæstione de Divinitate Iesu Christi. Atqui & hunc ipsum Patres aliter atque aliter interpretantur; Sunt enim qui Patrem Filio sim{y}pliciter qua Filius est, maiorem intelligi volunt, sunt qui catenus tantum quatenus homo est Filius. Hæc Ioannis verba. Verbum caro factum est magni sunt usus in controversiis cum Nestorio & Eutychete. Si Patrum arbitrio rem committis, alij hæc Ioannis cum illis Paulinis conferunt. Christus factus est peccatum & execratio. Cyrillus vero ab ea expositione cavendum præcipit. Infinitum est quæcunque huc pertinent, omnesque Patrum in exponenda Scriptura diversitates ac pugnas, referre. Si cui plura exempla videre libeat, recentiorum interpretum Commentarios adeat, eorum quidem qui Parrum in Scripturam interpretationes colligere ac in unum comportare diligenter solent. Cuius generis sunt Maldonatus in Euangelia, Toletus in Ioannem, Iustinianus in Paulum, & alii penè innumerabiles. Animadvertet vix ullum esse vetusculum quem Patres omnes eodem sensu acceperint. Sed & eorum expositiones non modo inter se pugnare, sed quod sanè grauissimum est, plerasque frigere comperiet, raróque apud eos occurrere solidam illam simplicitatem ac sobrietatem, quæ in iis requiritur, quicunque in sacris literis versantur. Cùm ergo non minùs Scripturæ interpretationibus, quàm sententiis, inter se discrepent Patres, conclusum esto non tantam esse eorum in dirimendis nostris controversiis auctoritatem ut ab ea provocare sit nefas, quod quæ inter ipsos repetitur sententiarum repugnantia, satis arguit non esse eos infallibiles, quales tamen esse necesse est huius causæ judices, ad ea confirmanda dogmata quæ adversus Protestantes Ecclesia Romana hodie propugnat.
units.tr: Hitherto we have said either nothing, or very little, about the diversity of the Fathers in expounding Scripture. Yet this is of great importance above all, and more memorable than the rest. For if our judges are to be appointed, they will have to be consulted again and again, almost constantly, on the passages whose meaning is disputed among us. What will happen if there is no greater agreement among the Fathers themselves about the exposition of these passages than there is among us? Take the passage from the Gospel of John, "I and the Father are one", which is of great weight in disputes against Sabellius and Arius. Do you want its meaning taught to you, so that you do not stumble on their rocks through a faulty exposition? If you consult the Fathers, you will find that some refer this noble text to the unity of will and affection, others to the unity of essence and nature. Another passage from the same Gospel, "The Father is greater than I", deserves careful weighing in the question of the divinity of Jesus Christ. Yet the Fathers also interpret this very text in different ways: some want the Father to be understood as greater than the Son simply as the Son is Son, others only in so far as the Son is man. These words of John, "The Word was made flesh", are of great use in controversies with Nestorius and Eutyches. If you commit the matter to the judgment of the Fathers, some compare these words of John with those of Paul, "Christ was made sin" and a curse. Cyril, however, instructs us to beware of that exposition. It would be endless to report everything that bears on this, and all the diversities and conflicts of the Fathers in expounding Scripture. If anyone would like to see more examples, let him consult the commentaries of more recent interpreters, those who are accustomed to gather with diligence the Fathers' interpretations of Scripture and bring them together into one place. Of this kind are Maldonatus on the Gospels, Toletus on John, Justinianus on Paul, and others almost innumerable. He will notice that there is scarcely any passage which all the Fathers have understood in the same sense. Moreover, he will find that their expositions not only conflict with one another but, what is most serious, that most of them are feeble, and that that solid simplicity and sobriety which is required in all who engage with the sacred writings rarely appears among them. Since, then, the Fathers disagree among themselves no less in their interpretations of Scripture than in their opinions, let it be concluded that their authority is not so great in settling our controversies that it would be wrong to appeal to it. For the contradiction of opinions repeated among them sufficiently shows that they are not infallible, and yet such infallibility is necessary in the judges of this cause, if the Roman Church is to establish the dogmas it now defends against the Protestants.
