units.la: Ratio VI. Neque Protestantes, neque Pontificios agnoscere Patres iudices rerum ad religionem suam pertinentium, hosque non minus quam illos qui ad palatum suum non faciunt nulla religione repugnare. Satisfit duabus quaestionibus quae ex superioribus omnibus oriuntur.
units.tr: Argument VI. Neither the Protestants nor the Papists acknowledge the Fathers as judges of matters pertaining to religion, and they reject them no less than those who do not suit their taste. Two questions arising from all the foregoing are answered.

units.la: HActenus demonstrauimus Patrum scripta, non tantam in seipsis habere auctoritatem, ut pro rebus iudicatis haberi possint quae apud eos de nostris in religione controversiis extant. Iam quae nostri ratione sit eorum auctoritas disputandum. Licet enim iudicium in se aequum & validum sit, & a iudice legitimo recte atque ex ordine pronuntiatum, litem tamen non decidit, nisi haec eius auctoritas ab utraque partium agnoscatur, aut saltem (ut sit in rebus ad hanc vitam pertinentibus) iis viribus instructus sit iudex, quae possint pervicaces in ordinem cogere. Hic vero cum religio agatur, res sancta ac Divina, quae non imperari sed persuaderi debet, vis nullum in hoc iudicij genere locum habere potest. Etsi enim vi quis adigi possit ut summam se Patrum monumentis auctoritatem deferre profiteatur, ipsorum tamen fides nullius animo hoc modo infigetur. Haerebunt semper in mentis penetralibus dissidia, ex quibus ea evelli necesse est, ut vera de rebus ad religionem pertinentibus pax atque concordia constituatur. Itaque ut recte ac feliciter decidantur huius generis controversiae necesse est utrique litigantium parti imprimis certum ac persuasum esse, iudicem qui sedet ea praeditum esse auctoritate quae ad conflandum hoc iudicium necessaria est. Fac Patres quae de hac causa sentiebant ea clare ac liquido pronunciasse (quod non ita esse demonstravimus.) Fac Patres (quod ipsum quoque quàm dubium fit docuimus) tanta dignitate atque auctoritate præditos fuisse, ut ab eorum placitis nulla detur provocatio. Nullius tamen erunt ista usus, nisi hanc revera esse Patrum auctoritatem utraque pars litigantium consentiat. Veteris Testamenti Scriptura Diuinitus inspirata & summa auctoritate prædira est, adeo ut quicquid dicit de fide, ac necessariò credendum sit. Nihil tamen illa ethnico persuadebit, quia quæ apud nos tanta est, apud illum nulla est auctoritas. Eadem Noui Testamenti erga Iudæum ratio est. Novi enim fœderis libri eam quidem in se habent auctoritatem quæ ad decidendas Ecclesiæ cum Iudæo controversias necessaria est; cæterum nihil efficient quandiu nullam apud Iudæum auctoritatem habebunt. Itaque ridiculus esset & qui ex Vetere Testamento aduersus Gentilem, & qui ex Nouo aduersus Iudæum argumenta peteret ad veritatem fidei nostræ apud utrumque probandam. Finge ergo Patrum scripta super controversiis nostris esse clara & perspicua, imò, (si ita vis) diuinitus esse inspirata summáque adeo auctoritate prædita. Ne sic quidem ex iis controversiæ nostræ decidi poterunt, quamdiu sublimem i lamm iraadamque iis auctoritatem vel utraque, vel certè altera pars negabit. Nunc ergo consideremus quanti utrique Patres faciant, an iis summum constituendæ ac definiendæ religionis ius tribuant? an saltem Patres ut arbitros inter se admittant quorum placita firma & immota manere debeant? Protestantes quidem quibus, ex iustæ disputationis legibus, nulla decet nisi confessa principia proponi, faris constat nihil minùs Patribus tribuere quàm eiusmodi auctoritatem. Ecclesiæ enim Gallicanæ, initio suæ confessionis, testantur se agnoscere libros sacræ Scripturæ esse canonicos, id est, se eos pro fidei suæ norma & regula habere. Libros verò Ecclesiasticos esse quidem utiles, sed non eiusmodi, ut ex iis constitui possit aliquis fidei articulus. Quæ enim credunt Scripturam ( que paulò post testantur ) b compleƈti quicquid ad cultum Dei & salutem hominum requiritur nullo adeo iudice opus habent, frustráque ad Veterum auƈtoritatem confugerent, quorum, quantacunque fingatur auƈtoritas, nunquam tamen eo assurget ut non longè subsistat infra verbi Domini maiestatem. Eædem deinceps Ecclesiæ profitentur, se ex ea norma doƈtrinam Christianam reformare velle, omnésque fidei articulos quos ipsa ponit firmiter retinere, quoscunque autem ea non habet constanter repudiare, quantumcunque excellat & emineat auƈtoritas quæ vel hos ad fidem hominum adjecit, vel illos substulit. Neque hominibus (inquiunt c) neque ipsis Angelis fas est quicquam ei verbo adŷrere, vel detrahere, vel quicquam prorsus in eo immutare, ex quo efficitur neque antiquitatem, neque consuetudines, neque multitudinem, neque humanam sapientiam, neque iudicia, neque edićta, vel decreta nulla, neque concilia, neque visiones, neque miracula Scripturæ illi Divinæ opponere licere : sed potius omnia ad eius regulam & præscriptū examinari & exigi oportere. Hanc sunt diserta Protestantium verba, ut ij, nisi huic fidei, quæ totius reformationis veluti fibula atque fundamentum est, nuntium remittant, non possent Patres, qui secundo, tertio, quarto, & sequentibus seculis vixerunt, vel ut iudices, vel etiam, quod leuius est, ut testes fidei suæ agnoscere. Omnes enim constituunt puram illam ac genuinam doƈtrinam, quam olim Apostoli & præ dicarunt, & Novi Test.libris consignarunt, sensim & sine sensu labem contraxisse, tempore, quod omnia immutat, non nihil alieni & impuri paulatim admiscente, nunc ludaicum aliquod, vel ethnicum dogma, nunc observationem aliquam cutisam, nonnunquam cultum superstitiosum, hos stipulam, illos fœnum, nonnullos lignum super fundamentum superædificasse; donec illud religionis Christianæ, ut sic dicam, corpus, ita pedetentim immutatum, tandem omnino aliud fieret ab illo quod olim fuerat. Quod enim ex auro & argento ædificium fuerat, postremo ex ruderibus, ex gypso, ligno, cœno & eiusmodi vili materia constare deprehenditur. Quemadmodum vidi mus, inquiunt, tiuos, quo magis à scaturigine sua recedunt, eo plus sordium, & alieni vitiosíque liquoris contrahere. Vt homo, quo magis ætate provehitur, eo plus amittit de natiua illa ingenuitate quæ in puero elucebat. Mens cum corpore immutatur, studium, ars, fucus, omnia paulatim incrustant, adeoque dissimilem personam inducunt, ut non amplius is sit qui fuit prius. Idipsum contendunt accidisse in Christianismo, eoque illustrem è posteriore Pauli ad Thessalonicenses epistola locum referunt, de insigni apostasia, cuius quidem fundamenta iam tum clam substruebantur, sed quæ tamen non nisi longe post tempore revelanda & in apertum proruptura esset; ut videmus maxima quæque, siue in natura, siue in rebus & calamitatibus humanis concipi foueriique lentè & paulatim, ininterdumque totis antequam in lucem edantur seculis.
units.tr: Hitherto we have shown that the writings of the Fathers do not have so much authority in themselves that what they say about our controversies in religion can be regarded as settled. Now we must discuss what authority they have in our judgment. For although a judgment may be fair and valid in itself, and pronounced by a lawful judge in due order, it does not settle a dispute unless its authority is recognised by both parties, or at least (as in matters pertaining to this life) the judge is equipped with the force that can compel the obstinate to obey. But here, since religion is at issue, a holy and divine matter that must be persuaded rather than imposed, force can have no place in this kind of judgment. For although someone may be compelled to profess that he grants the monuments of the Fathers the highest authority, their faith will not be implanted in his mind in this way. Disagreements will always remain in the inner recesses of the mind, and they must be uprooted if true peace and concord about matters pertaining to religion is to be established. Therefore, if such controversies are to be settled rightly and happily, it is necessary, above all, that each of the litigating parties be certain and convinced that the judge who sits has the authority that is necessary to conduct this judgment. Suppose the Fathers had declared clearly and plainly what they thought about this cause (which we have shown is not so). Suppose the Fathers (whose own status we have also shown to be doubtful) were endowed with such dignity and authority that no appeal from their decisions is allowed. Still, these would be of no use unless both litigating parties actually agree that this is indeed the authority of the Fathers. The Scripture of the Old Testament is divinely inspired and possesses supreme authority, so that whatever it says about faith must necessarily be believed. Yet it will persuade no Gentile, for what has such great authority among us has none among him. The same holds for the New Testament with respect to the Jew. For the books of the New Covenant have in themselves that authority which is necessary for settling the Church's controversies with the Jew; but they will accomplish nothing so long as they have no authority with the Jew. Thus whoever would derive arguments from the Old Testament against the Gentile, or from the New against the Jew, to prove the truth of our faith to either, would be ridiculous. So suppose the writings of the Fathers on our controversies were clear and perspicuous, indeed (if you like) divinely inspired and possessed of such supreme authority. Even so, our controversies could not be settled by them as long as either both parties, or at least one, deny that they have that lofty pre-eminence and authority. Let us now consider how highly each side esteems the Fathers, whether they grant them the supreme right to establish and define religion, or at least admit the Fathers as arbiters among themselves, whose opinions ought to remain firm and unshaken. As for the Protestants, to whom, by the laws of proper debate, only admitted principles ought to be put forward, it is plain that they attribute nothing less to the Fathers than such authority. For the Gallican Churches, at the beginning of their Confession, testify that they acknowledge the books of Holy Scripture to be canonical, that is, that they hold them as the norm and rule of their faith. But ecclesiastical books they say are indeed useful, yet not of such a kind that any article of faith can be constituted from them. For since they believe that Scripture (which they affirm a little later) comprehends whatever is required for the worship of God and the salvation of men, they have no need of any judge, and they would be fleeing in vain to the authority of the ancients, whose authority, however great it is supposed to be, will never rise so high as not to remain far below the majesty of the Word of the Lord. The same Churches then profess that they wish to reform Christian doctrine by that norm, that they firmly retain all the articles of faith which it contains, and that they constantly reject whatever it does not contain, however much the authority that has either added these to human faith or removed those may excel and stand out. Neither men (they say) nor even the Angels themselves are permitted to add anything to that Word, or take away from it, or change anything at all in it; from which it follows that neither antiquity, nor customs, nor multitude, nor human wisdom, nor judgments, nor edicts or decrees of any kind, nor councils, nor visions, nor miracles may be set against that Divine Scripture; but rather that all things ought to be examined and tested by its rule and prescription. These are the plain words of the Protestants. Therefore, unless they were to renounce this faith, which is as it were the clasp and foundation of the whole Reformation, they could not acknowledge the Fathers who lived in the second, third, fourth and following centuries either as judges or, what is less, as witnesses of their faith. For they all maintain that the pure and genuine doctrine which the Apostles once preached and committed to the books of the New Testament gradually and imperceptibly contracted a stain, as time, which changes all things, little by little mixed in something foreign and impure: now some Jewish or Gentile dogma, now some carnal observance, sometimes superstitious worship; some building on the foundation wood, hay, stubble, and others gold, silver and precious stones, until that body of the Christian religion, as I may say, was so gradually altered that at last it became wholly different from what it had once been. For the building which had been of gold and silver was at last found to consist of rubble, plaster, wood, mud and such cheap material. Just as we see, they say, that streams, the further they recede from their source, the more filth and foreign and corrupt liquid they take on; as a man, the further he advances in age, the more he loses of that native innocence which shone in the boy. The mind changes along with the body; study, art, and pretence gradually encrust everything, and so they produce a persona so unlike the former that he is no longer the one he was before. They maintain that the same has happened in Christianity, and they cite as evidence the passage from Paul's later Epistle to the Thessalonians, concerning the notable apostasy, whose foundations were indeed secretly being laid even then, but which was not to be revealed and break out into the open until long after. Just as we see that the greatest things, whether in nature or in human affairs and calamities, are conceived and nourished slowly and gradually, and often for whole ages before they come to light.

units.la: Ex hac hypothesi quæ, ut mihi videtur, Protestantium omnium communis est, omnino sequitur doctrinam Ecclesiæ iam secundo seculo nonnihil labis contraxisse, peregrinis quibusdam in eius seu fidem seu cultum adscitis; tertio item seculo aliquid aliud vitii ei astrictum esse: itidemque quarto & quinto & sequentibus seculis, paulatim degenerare nativa illa religionis sinceritate & simplicitate, & identidem ad eam adhærescentibus novis sordibus, donec tandem ad postremum corruptionis & depravationis gradum delapsa est, in quo se eam repperisse contendunt, indeque Scriptura duce in eundem illum statum restituisse in quo fuerat ab initio collocata; Itaque religionem ex quo, ut sic dicam, cardine hominum fraude & insciitia labentibus tot seculis paulatim deiecta fuerat, in eo ipso à se fixam & repositam putant. Quæ cum ita sint, apparet Protestantes, nisi secum ipsi pugnent, concedere non posse, Patres qui ab Apostolis ad nos usque vixerunt, omnium fidei suæ capicap't ım canonem & normam esse. Nam, si vera eorum est de corruptionis progressu hypothesis, secundo, tertio & quarto seculis nonnihil adultera fuerat Ecclesiæ doctrina; quàm verò ipsi amplexi sunt, fidem, ea, quippe ex solis Scripturis hausta, omnino eadem est quæ Apostolorum tempore fuit; siquidem vera sunt quæ de reformatione docent. Vnde sequitur, si hæc eorum fides ad Patrum secundi seculi scripta exigatur, necessario aliquid in iis repertum iri, præter reformatæ doctrinæ capita, quæ à solis habent Apostolis, & quo magis ad inferiora secula devolvemur, eo plura huius generis occursura, quod, ex commemorata eorum hypothesi, corruptio una semper cum tempore sua incrementa acceperit. Si enim cum Patrum istorum fide ita convenit Protestantium doctrina, ut nihil supra, nihil etiam minus contineat, è duobus alterum necessariò sequetur, vel illam fidei & disciplinæ corruptionem, quam in Ecclesia accidisse iidem Protestantes statuunt, diversam esse ab apostasia à Paulo prædicta, cuius mysterium suo jam tempore cœpisse operari ipse testatur Apostolus, vel certè nunc factam ab ipsis reformationem non esse sin- ceram & simplicem Christi & Apostolorum doctrinam, quæ duo, ut liquet, pugnant cum duabus illis sententiis, quas vulgò apud eos ab omnibus defendi diximus. Superest ergo, ne in istam contradictionem impingant, ut immoti permaneant in ea sententia quam in sua fidei confessione profitentur, nulla esse scripta Ecclesiastica, cuiuscunque seculi sint, quorum tanta sit auctoritas ut iis superstrui, vel ex iis iudicari possint fidei dogmata, Scripturámque solam esse normam ad quam universum istud examen institui & decet & necesse est. Et sanè ita instituunt omnes Protestantium Theologi, quotquot vel legi, vel audivi: idque ex libris Calvini, Buceri, Melanchronis, Luteri, Bezæ, & aliorum discere licet, qui sola Scriptura nituntur, neque usquam, quod sciam docent Patrum auctoritatem idoneam esse fidei. rationem. Non nego primarios quosdam inter ipsorum Scriptores, quales sunt Bucerus, Martyr, Iuellus Episcopus Sarisburiensis, & recentiores fermè omnes, Patrum libros in disputationibus adhibere : sed si eorum mentem atque institutum accuratè inspexeris, reperies eos ad refutandum non ad confirmandum, ad evertandas opiniones Romanas, nos ad suas constituendas Patrum uti testimonio. Illi enim Patrum doctrinam ut Apostolica minus puram esse statuunt, sic à labe & corruptione quæ Romanam posteriorum seculorum fidem & disciplinam peruasiè multum abesse profitentur ac defendunt, quod nimirum Christianæ doctrinæ & puritas immutata, & labes aucta fuit certis quibusdam gradibus, prout tempora, & ab Apostolorum ævo longius discedebant, & ad prædictam à Paulo apostasiam propiùs accedebant. Quo fit ut tametsi Scripturam solam pro fidei suæ fundamento agnoscant, Patrum tamen testimoniis in his disputationibus uti cogantur: Primò quidem ut probent revera in Christianismo accidisse illam de qua diximus doctrinæ sincerioris depravationem: Secundo ut doceant adversariorum suorum errores tum temporis nondum editos in lucem fuisse, sed in suis adhuc sæminibus latuisse. Exempli causa, nondum vetustis illis temporibus receptam fuisse Transsubstantiationem, tametsi iam tum ab imprudentibus, & quorsum res evasura esset ignorantibus, crederentur quæ postea variè à multis tractata & amplificata in transsubstantiationem posteriore exierunt. Ita neque ullam tum fuisse illam quam hodie videmus Papæ Monarchiam, tametsi quædam eius primordia, ac, ut sic dicam, fibræ tum extarent, à quibus originem duxit ingens illa & stupenda, totiusque nunc orbi formidabilis, potentia; Eandem esse eorum quæ à se refutantur Ecclesiæ Latinæ dogmatum plerorumque rationem. Atque hanc revera esse Protestantium in istis mentem satis ex iis libris intelligi potest quos non paucos de hoc argumento scripserunt historicè florice exequentes Christianismi tum in fide, tum in moribus & disciplina inclinationem. Sed & hoc ipsum quod diximus satis esse videtur ad eam, quam tuentur, causam plane penitusque constituendam. Illi enim, cum nihil affirmative tanquam fidei caput ad salutem necessarium doceant, quod non facile fit ex Scriptura probare, nullo alio ad confirmandam fidei suae veritatem principio opus habent. Praeterea cum omnia illa capita affirmativa, quibus eorum fides continetur, apud Ecclesiam Romanam fere sint in confesso (quod in huius operis initio diximus, nihil eos necesse est in iis demonstrandis laborare. In omni enim disputatione non demonstrantur, sed sumuntur ac (ut loqui solemus) supponuntur ea de quibus ambae partes consentiunt. Si quis tamen scire vellet quae fuisset de iis capitibus Patrum sententia, facile Protestantibus esset ostendere eos de his omnibus idem secum sensisse. Exempli causa, quod sit Deus; quod Christus salutem nobis quaesiuit, quod idem Baptismum & Eucharistiam instituerit, & similia dogmata, quorum breve specimen initio huius disputationis dedimus. Iam quod pertinet ad caetera quae Ecclesiasticae fidei dogmatis praeter ista accensentur, satis est Protestantibus ea argumenta solvere, quae pro illis a Romanis Theologis afferuntur, docereque talia nullo fundamento niti, meritoque adeo Christianorum religione excludi. Atque hic proprie locus est quo Patrum testimonia a nostris adhibentur, ut demonstrent de istis Romanorum hodie propriis dogmatis longe aliter sensisse Veterem olim Ecclesiam. Quod ergo nostri illi homines Patres in hac disputatione itaque usurpant ac laudant, ex eo quidem apparet ipsos negare hodiernam Romanorum fidem plane penitusque eandem esse quae Veterum Christianorum olim fuit, praesertim primis quatuor aut quinque, a Christo in terris nato, seculis, quod ipsum sane superiori Ecclesiarum reformatarum, de Christianismi corruptione hypothesi plane consentancum est ; inde vero nequaquam conficirur Patrum à nostris auctoritatem pro idoneo fidei fundamento haberi, quod recta, ac, ut aiunt, ex diametro cum nostra doctrina pugnat, ut vel nostri Theologi subinde testificantur. Quo fit ut fatis mirari non possim quam quidam ex adversariis sequuntur in disputando rationem, qui cum Protestantibus sic agunt, quasi ex Patribus fidem suam probent, cùm clarum fit eorum consilium ex his, non suam ipsorum fidem constituere, sed adversariorum suorum sententiam subvertere. Cum enim Pontificij doctores contendant Ecclesiam Christianam nunquam in fide erraffe, neque eius aliam unquam fuisse de rebus factis sententiam quàm quæ nunc est ; Protestantibus ex adversa parte fatis est collatis inter fe Patrum & Ecclesiæ Romanæ sententiis demonstrare difcrimen inter eas esse non exiguum. Neque vero illi eo fe obligant ad ea omnia tenenda quæ Patres docuerunt,cùm clarum fit ex eorum hypothesi, ipsam Veterum fidem suos quoque naevos habuisse, tametsi longè minores quàm sunt ij qui in Ecclesiam fequiorum feculorum irrepsisse reperiuntur. Concludamus ergo Protestantes, neque in Patribus, neque in eorum Scriptis, tantam auctoritatem agnoscere, quæ fatis fit ac ultimam, & à qua provocare non liceat, sententiam de hiffce controversiis ferendam. Vnde sequitur Patrum auctoritate, etiamsi revera tanta esset quanta in legitimo iudice requiritur, non potuisse tamen hanc litem decidisatque adeo Ecclesiæ Romanæ Theologos ad alia media confugere debere, ut adversariis suis, ea, de quibus supra egimus,persuadeant.
units.tr: On this hypothesis, which I think is common to all Protestants, it follows entirely that the doctrine of the Church had already contracted some taint in the second century, through certain foreign elements admitted into either its faith or its worship; that in the third century it was again tainted by something else; and that in the fourth, fifth and following centuries it gradually degenerated from its native purity and simplicity, new filth continually adhering to it, until at last it fell to the final stage of corruption and depravity. They claim to have found it in that state, and to have restored it, with Scripture as their guide, to the very condition in which it had been established from the beginning. They think that religion, which had been cast down over so many centuries, little by little, through human fraud and ignorance, from its hinge, so to speak, has been fixed and restored by them to that same point. Given this, it is clear that the Protestants, unless they contradict themselves, cannot concede that the Fathers who lived from the Apostles down to our own time are the rule and standard of all the articles of their faith. For if their hypothesis about the progress of corruption is true, the teaching of the Church was already somewhat adulterated in the second, third and fourth centuries; but the faith they have embraced, drawn as it is from Scripture alone, is wholly the same as it was in the time of the Apostles, provided that what they teach about the Reformation is true. Hence it follows that, if their faith is tested against the writings of the Fathers of the second century, something will necessarily be found there beyond the heads of the reformed doctrine, which they hold from the Apostles alone; and the further we descend into later centuries, the more such things will turn up, since, on their own hypothesis, corruption has always grown with time. For if the doctrine of the Protestants agrees with the faith of those Fathers so exactly that it contains nothing more and nothing less, then one of two things must necessarily follow: either the corruption of faith and discipline which the same Protestants say occurred in the Church is different from the apostasy foretold by Paul, whose mystery, as the Apostle himself testifies, had already begun to work in his own day; or else the reformation now made by them is not the sincere and simple doctrine of Christ and the Apostles. These two conclusions clearly clash with the two opinions which, as I said, are commonly defended among them by everyone. What remains, then, if they are not to fall into this contradiction, is that they stand firm in the position they profess in their confession of faith: that there are no ecclesiastical writings, of whatever century, of such authority that the articles of faith can be built upon them or judged by them, and that Scripture alone is the norm to which the whole of this examination ought and must be referred. And indeed all the Protestant theologians, as many as I have read or heard, proceed in exactly this way. This can be learned from the books of Calvin, Bucer, Melanchthon, Luther, Beza and others, who rest on Scripture alone and nowhere, so far as I know, teach that the authority of the Fathers is a suitable ground of faith. I do not deny that some of their leading writers, such as Bucer, Martyr, Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury, and almost all the more recent ones, use the books of the Fathers in their disputations. But if you look closely at their purpose and method, you will find that they use the testimony of the Fathers to refute, not to confirm: to overthrow Roman opinions, and not to establish their own. For they hold that the doctrine of the Fathers was less pure than the Apostolic, yet they profess and defend that it was far removed from the taint and corruption which has widely infected the faith and discipline of the Roman Church in later centuries; namely, that the purity of Christian doctrine was changed and its taint increased by certain stages, as times passed and as they moved further from the age of the Apostles and nearer to the apostasy foretold by Paul. Hence it happens that, although they acknowledge Scripture alone as the foundation of their faith, they are nevertheless compelled to use the testimonies of the Fathers in these disputations: first, indeed, to prove that the aforesaid corruption of the purer doctrine really occurred in Christianity; and second, to show that the errors of their opponents had not yet been brought to light at that time, but were still lying hidden in their seeds. For example, Transubstantiation was not yet received in those ancient times, although things were already being believed by people who were rash and ignorant of where the matter would end, and these, handled and enlarged in various ways by many afterwards, issued in transubstantiation. Likewise, the papal monarchy which we see today did not yet exist, although some of its beginnings and, so to speak, its fibres were already present, from which sprang that huge and amazing power, now formidable to the whole world. The same account, they say, holds for most of the doctrines of the Latin Church which they refute. That this really is the Protestants' mind on these matters can be understood well enough from the many books they have written on this subject, historically and eloquently tracing the drift of Christianity, both in faith and in morals and discipline. But what we have said seems enough by itself to establish the cause they defend, fully and thoroughly. For since they teach nothing affirmatively as an article of faith necessary to salvation which cannot easily be proved from Scripture, they have no need of any other principle to confirm the truth of their faith. Moreover, since almost all those affirmative articles by which their faith is contained are admitted by the Roman Church (as we said at the beginning of this work), they need not labour to demonstrate them. In every dispute, what both sides agree on is not demonstrated but taken for granted, and, as we are accustomed to say, presupposed. If anyone wished to know what the Fathers thought about those articles, it would be easy for the Protestants to show that they held the same view as themselves on all of them. For example, that there is a God; that Christ won salvation for us; that he instituted both Baptism and the Eucharist; and similar doctrines, of which we gave a brief sample at the beginning of this disputation. As for the other things counted among the dogmas of ecclesiastical faith beyond these, it is enough for the Protestants to answer the arguments which the Roman theologians bring forward for them, and to show that such things rest on no sound foundation and therefore rightly stand outside the religion of Christians. And this is properly the place where our side uses the testimonies of the Fathers, to show that the ancient Church thought quite differently about those doctrues which the Romans now hold as peculiar to themselves. So when these men of ours use and praise the Fathers in this way in the dispute, it indeed shows that they deny that the present faith of the Romans is wholly and entirely the same as that of the ancient Christians, especially in the first four or five centuries after Christ was born on earth. That agrees fully with the earlier hypothesis of the reformed Churches about the corruption of Christianity. But it by no means follows from this that the authority of the Fathers is held by our side to be a suitable foundation of faith, since it runs straight against our doctrine, as even our own theologians sometimes testify. So I cannot sufficiently wonder at the method of disputing that some of our opponents follow, who deal with the Protestants as if they proved their faith from the Fathers, when it is clear from this that their purpose is not to establish their own faith but to overthrow the opinion of their adversaries. For since the Papist teachers contend that the Christian Church has never erred in faith, and that its opinion on the matters at issue has never been other than what it is now, it is enough for the Protestants on the other side to show, by setting the opinions of the Fathers and of the Roman Church side by side, that there is no small difference between them. Nor do they bind themselves thereby to hold everything the Fathers taught, since it is clear from their own hypothesis that the faith of the ancients too had its blemishes, though far smaller than those which are found to have crept into the Church of later centuries. Let us conclude, then, that the Protestants acknowledge in the Fathers and their writings no authority which is sufficient and final, and from which there is no appeal, for pronouncing judgement on these controversies. Hence it follows that even if the authority of the Fathers were really as great as is required in a lawful judge, it could still not have settled this dispute; and so the theologians of the Roman Church must have recourse to other means to persuade their adversaries of the matters we have discussed above.

units.la: Verum quid fiet si ne ipsa quidem Ecclesia Romana in Patribus eiusmodi auctoritatem agnoscat? Neminem tam peruicacem futurum arbitror qui non conficeatur hanc eius methodum, qua fidem suam ex Patrum testimoniis probat,non solum non sufficere,sed etiam omnino alienam esse & incommodam. Quis enim ferat sibi eius hominis ad fidem faciendam testimonium obtrudi, cujus apud utrumque fides sit dubia & sublesta? Videamus ergo an Ecclesia Romana Patribus, tantum tribuat, quantum se iis tribuere hac methodo præ se ferre videtur. Enimvero non pauci eius Doctores variis occasionibus satis aperrè docent Patres non pluris à se quàm à Protestantibus fieri. Nam hi quidem Patrum auctoritatem Scripturæ sic subjiciunt, ut nihil pro cerro atquo indubitato admittant, quod Scriptura non nitatur, ea verò omnia rejicienda putent, quæ præter aut contra ipsam adstruuntur. Illi vero Patrum sententias ab uniuscuiusque seculi Ecclesiæ iudicio pendere volunt, sic ut quæcunque hæc vel probat vel damnat, ipsi quoque pariter vel admittant vel respuant. Discrepant quidem inter se in eo quòd alii Scripturæ, alii præsenti sui seculi Ecclesiæ summam auctoriratem tribuunt. Sed in eo utrique conueniunt, quod eam auctoritatem non minus hi quam illi Patribus negant, adeo ut incassum terant tempus, dum causam in hoc secundario & obnoxio tribunali agunt in quo plurimum valent rabularum artes, ac vitiligantium tricæ ac captiones: in quo ægre iudicia consequaris, ægriúsque impetrata intelligas; in quo denique de controversiis sententia fertur non summa, sed à qua utraque pars litigantium putat alio se provocare iure posse: cùm facile fuisset omissis adeo longis & molestis ambagibus, recta ad summum, siue Scripturæ, siue Ecclesiæ tribunali pergere, in quo & forensibus technis minus est loci, & sententiæ feruntur clariores & liquidiores,& quidem (quod summum est) hujusmodi à quibus nulla datur provocatio.
units.tr: But what if the Church of Rome itself does not acknowledge any such authority in the Fathers? I think no one will be so stubborn as not to confess that this method of hers, by which she proves her faith from the testimonies of the Fathers, is not only insufficient but also wholly foreign and unsuitable. For who would tolerate having the testimony of a man forced upon him to establish faith, when that man's reliability is doubtful and shaky to both parties? Let us see, then, whether the Church of Rome grants the Fathers as much as she seems, by this method, to claim for them. Indeed, not a few of her teachers, on various occasions, plainly teach that the Fathers are not valued by her any more than by the Protestants. For the Protestants subordinate the authority of the Fathers to Scripture so that they admit nothing as certain and indubitable that Scripture does not rest upon, and they think that everything is to be rejected which is asserted beside or against Scripture itself. The Papists, on the other hand, want the opinions of the Fathers to depend on the judgment of the Church of each century, so that whatever this Church either approves or condemns, they too likewise either admit or reject. They disagree indeed in this, that some ascribe the highest authority to Scripture, others to the Church of their own age. But in this they agree, that both alike deny that authority to the Fathers, so that they waste their time in vain while they plead their cause before this secondary and unreliable tribunal, where the tricks of lawyers and the snares and captious quibbles of wranglers prevail most; where judgments are hardly obtained and hardly understood when obtained; where, in short, the decision on controversies is pronounced not as final, but one from which each party of the litigants thinks it can appeal to another law. Yet it would have been easy, leaving aside such long and troublesome circumlocutions, to go straight to the highest tribunal, whether of Scripture or of the Church, where there is less room for legal technicalities and the sentences handed down are clearer and more plain, and indeed (which is the greatest thing) are of such a kind that no appeal is allowed from them.

units.la: Sed ne sententiam istam Ecclesiæ Romanæ Doctoribus falso tribuere videamur, age, ipsosmet loquentes audiamus. Cardinalis Caietanus Præfatione in Pentateuchum de suis in Scripturam Commentariis agens, inquit d, occurrit novus sensus textui consonus, nec à Sacra Scriptura, nec ab Ecclesiæ doctrina dissonus, quàvis
units.tr: But lest we seem to attribute this opinion to the teachers of the Church of Rome falsely, come, let us hear them speaking for themselves. Cardinal Cajetan, in the preface to his Commentaries on the Pentateuch, speaking of his commentaries on Scripture, says:ᵈ "If a new sense should occur that agrees with the text, and is neither foreign to Sacred Scripture nor at variance with the doctrine of the Church, although it is strange to the torrent of holy teachers..."

units.la: d Thom. de vita Si quando, inquit, occurrit novus sensus textui consonus, nec à Sacra Scriptura, nec ab Ecclesiæ doctrina dissonus, quàvis Pentat. à torrentè doctorum sacrorum alienus, rogo lectores omnes ne præcipites detestentur, sed æquos se præbeant censores. Meminerint tur suum unicuique tribuere. Solis Sacræ Scripturæ authoritas reservata authoritas hæc est, ut ideo sic credamus esse, quia ipsi ita scripserunt. Alios autem (inquit Augustinus) ita lego ut quantalibet sanctitate doctrinaque prapolleant, non ideo credam sic esse, quia ipsi ita scripserunt. Nullus itaque detestetur nonnum S. Scripturæ sensum ex hoc quod dissonat priscis doctoribus, sed scrutetur perspicacius textum ac contextum Scripturæ, & si quadrare invenerit, laudet Deum qui non alligavit expositionem S. Scripturarum priscorum doctorum sensibus, sed Scripturæ ipsi integræ, sub Catholicâ Ecclesiæ censura. Melchior C nus Episcopus Canariensis postquam dixit ex Augustino hanc felicitatem Deum in solis Divinis voluminibus inesse voluisse, ut in iis non esset quicquam erroris, subjungit, cæteroqui nemo quantumvis eruditus & sanctus non interdum allucinatur, non alicubi caveat, non quandoque labitur. Et postquam eorum exemplorum quæ supra commemoravimus, nonnulla attulit, locum sic concludit. Legentur itaque à nobis Patres veteres cum reverentia quidem, sed ut homines cum delectu atque judicio. Et paulo post addit, Reliqui Scriptores sancti inferiores & humani sunt, &ficiunt quæ interdum, ac monstrum quandoque pariunt, præterponentem ordinem institutumque naturæ. Et ibidem Ad reverenda sequi maiores nostros per omnia, & in illorum vestigiis nos quoque pedes nostros figere, ut pueri faciunt per lusum, nihil videtur esse aliud quam ingenia nostra damnare, iudicio nos privare nostro & facultate inquirenda veritatis. Sequamur veteres bene habet, sed ut duces non ut domini. Ambrosius Catharinus eodem modo. Veritas quod sanctorum dicta vel scripta in se non sunt firma authoritatis, ut in singulis teneantur illis præbere assensum. Et Iesuitæ ipsi satis in variis locis docent se à Patrum authoritate non adeo pendere ac vulgo creduntur. Hæc sunt Peravij in Epiphaniam ingenuæ voces. Nos ea quæ par est moderatione in divinorum hominum, sed hominum, errores ac lapsus, non tam inquirimus, quàm oblatos ultro, ac vel invitis occurrentes, ne cui fraudi sint patefacimus: tueri autem ac defendere nihilo magis quàm eorum vitia, si quae fuerint debemus. Item alibi. Idem testatur se observasse plerique veterum Patrum in variis fidei capitibus usuvenisse ut ante errorum atque haeresewn quibus ea sigillatim oppugnabantur originem, nondum satis illustrata ac patefacta rei veritate, quaedam scriptis suis asperserint, quaecum orthodoxae fidei regulâ minimè consentiant. Et revera saepius cùm sententias, tum explicationes eorum rejicit, ac nonnunquam quidem satis du è, ut supra de ipsius Epiphanio ostendimus. Cum sibi alicubi Patrum nonnullorum de cujusdam apud Lucam loci expositione auctoritatem cum sua ipsius sententia pugnantem objecisset, nulla eorum habita ratione respondet. Nec est quod certorum Patrum opponatur auctoritas, qui non aliud affirmare possunt quàm quod ex Luca didicerunt, nec est ulla ratio cur ex illorum verbis Lucam interpretemur potius, quàm ex Luca quae ab illis asseruari videtur. Haec ille praeclarè, ut videtur, & magno cum iudicio scribit, tum iis quae supra ex Augustino retulimus plane consentanea, tum ad plerasque nostras controversias utilissima, de quibus, cùm nihil ipsi Patres statuere potuerint, nisi quod à Scriptura haberent, verius est ex eruditissimi istius Iesuitae sententia, eorum testimonia in hisce capitibus ex Scriptura, quàm Scripturam ex ipsis explicari. Idem in alio opere P, hodiernum Ecclesiae Romanae in administrandâ poenitentia usum aduersus Arnaldum Veterem Patrum praxin objicien-tem defendens, docet Patrum traditioni & antiquitati praeferendam esse praesentem recentiorum in uno quoque saeculo temporum consuetudinem, quam scilicet, ex Ioanne Fischero, vult à Spiritu sancto Ecclesiam regente profiscisci. Neque caeteri Iesuitae aliter loquuntur. Maldonatus, quo nemo est Protestantium acrior aut infensior adveríarius, cùm retulisset Patrum quorundam sententiam existimantium perperam respondisse Z bedæi filios, cùm interrogati a Domino, num possent poculum, quod ipse bibiturus esset, bibere, & baptismate, quo ipse baptizatus esset, baptizari, dixerunt se posse, subdit ille. Malle se credere eos nec temere, nec inscienter, sed amanter & vere respondisse . E alibi ad vers.11. cap.9. Matthæi s allatis expositionibus multorum, imò penè omnium Patrum negatse adduci posse ut eam interpretationem sequatur. Et tamen observanda loci istius sensum hodie in controversiam vocari. Non video quomodo fit iste Protestantibus persuasurus, ut, quem ipse tam securè hic contemnit plurium de aliis locis consensum, necessario sibi sequendum putent. Alibi verò idem etiam durius ad verba Christi maximè omnium controversiarum Porta inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Quorum verborum (inquit) sensus non videtur mihi esse quem omnes præter Hilarium, quos legisse memini, auctores putant. Item alibi ad vers.11. cap.11. Matthæi. Qui est minimus in regno cœlorum major est Ioanne Baptista, allatis variis veterum expositionibus. Habet (inquit) ex multis opinionibus quam elegat lector, sed si meam quoque sententiam audire, libere fatebor in nulla prorsus earum meum qualecunque iudicium acquiescere, Idem ad 6. Ioan. Ammonius, Cyrillus, Theophylactus & Euthymius respondent, non omnes trahi, quia non omnes digni sunt, quod nimis affine est Pelagianorum errori. Salmeron magni, inter Iesuitas nominis. Argumenta petunt (adversarii) à doctorum antiquitate cui semper maior honor habitus est quàm novitatibus. Respondetur quamlibet ætatem antiquitati semper detulisse, &c. Sed illud asserimus quo iuniores eo perspicaciores esse doctores. Et contra hanc quam obiectant multitudinem respondemus (inquit) ex verbo Dei, Exod.23. In iudicio, plurimorum non acquiesces sententiis, ut à vero devies. Caussinus quo nemo inter Iesuitas Francicè eloquentior habetur. Augustinum (imò & ipsum Paulum) in iis quæ de gratia scripserunt excessus &c. & intemperantiæ cujusdam accusaie non veretur, criminis inuidiam allegorico metaphoræ splendore mitigans. Ingentes illi viri (inquit) totidem sunt magna & immensa maris, quæ arcano spiritus impetu percita intumescunt, & in unum littus ita penitus feruntur, ac tota incumbunt, ut alterum ei oppositum siccum destituant. Vt Oceanus postquam exæstuans hanc plagam longè lateq; inundauit, mox paulatim in alveos sibi à Deo definitos redit. Ita nostri illi ubi in spiritus rebelles, veritati immorigeros effusi longius excurrerunt, mox se recolligunt, seq; ad eum placida æqualitatis modum referunt, qui domum Dei ædificet. His imaginibus non obscurè significar Cauffinus vario ac inæquali motu ferri sanctissimos illos viros; interdum intra veritatis & Spiritus Sancti fines fluere? interdum extra prorumpere; ultra veri vias nonnunquam abripi, mox ad se redire. Socij sui mentem aperitius nuper edidérunt ex eodem sodalitio Pater quidam Adamus, nam in opere edito scripsit. Augustini libris tenebris & caligine quadam tegi, doctrinam (le gratia scilicet) involutum esse & impeditam & hujusmodi quæ se cum ipsa pugnare videatur. Non eam fuisse ... Augusti in eligendis constituendis sententiis felicitatem, ut non sit nobis liberum ab ejus auctoritate discedere, & alia quam quæ ipse definiit sequi. Augustinum vel noluisse animi sui sensum clare simpliciter eloqui, vel certe conantem id tamen minime esse assecutum, ut plane intelligi posset quod voluerit: Illum dum adversus Pelagium ardentius pugnat, in extremis quoddam valde periculosa delatum esse, satisque consilare eum de gratia & prædestinatione cum excessu locutum. Itaque Augustini de eo argumento opiniones diras & agrestes alibi vocat. Quin & hunc Iesuitam eo progressum refert quidam eius adversarius, ex Iansenistarum, (ut vocant) Theologorum numero, ut in Sermone apud plebem Parisiensem 2. D. 1650. habito, publicè dixerit Augustinum obscurum esse & involutum; Augustinum ut erat Afer, ardenti ingenio, modum sæpe excessisse, dum gratia hostes impugnat, ultra veri fines abreptum fuisse. Iidem Ianselarminus Medinam affirmare S.Hieronymum idem omnino Baronius ubi de Veteribus Galliorum & Germaniae episcopis agit, qui ante annos 800. sub Carolo & eius filio Ludovico Pio Ioannem & summo consensu, tum universi in Synodo Francofordiensi, in qua erant numerorum recenti, tum singuli in suis opusculis, ut Agobardus, Hincmarus, Valafridus Strabo, alii, Nicenae alterius Synodi num & insolens de imaginum veneratione ac cultu dogma refutarunt, non dubitat, pro summa sua in Antiquitatem reverentia, scribere eos omnes Ex hoc uno discere licet quanti isti veterum Patrum auctoritatem faciant, quos, si quid contra suum Pontificem tendant infinire & putant, & libere pronunciant. Sirmondus (quo nemo ut opinor in istis partibus fuit modestior, hic tamen & ipse erupit; neque se continere potuit quia proderet, quam nihili apud se suosque sit antiquitatis indicium, quoties a Papae Urbici placitis discederet. Nam eorundem illorum Patrum sententiam, quos insanisse Baronius rotunde dixit, hic noster quanta mis aliquanti sobrios, & orru ac gente Gallus, non est tamen verius dilertissimis verbis Gallorum haeresin appellare. Sed ad Baronium redeo; qui Patres liberrime passim reprehendit ac refutat, quoties ii aliud, quam quod ipse probat, sentiunt. Petri Damiani Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalis, viti & doctrinae & sanctitatis nomine apud Latinos iam ab annis paene fexcentis celeberrimi, cum plurima Baronius ex epistola ad Firminum Episcopum, Hildebrandino & Bonifaciano dogmati de temporali Papae imperio repugnantia recitasset; Hucusque (inquit) de his Petrus Damiani; cui Catholica dogmata penitus adversantur, quibus haeresis errore notantur omnes, qui ab Ecclesia Romana,cathedra Petri,è duobus alterum gladium auferunt, nec nisi spiritualem concedunt: iterumque mox non paucis interiectis: Errore igitur lapsus convincitur Petrus (excusare eum nec debemus, nec possumus) quem communi, & Catholicae totius Ecclesiae consensu constat esse damnatum. Hinc Baronii in Petrum censuram memorat, ac probat, Bellarminus. Utrque autem omnes fere in hoc uno Petro veteres Ecclesiae Christianae scriptores, multos etiam Romae episcopos haereseos aperte damnant Athanasium, Ambrosium, Hieronymum, Augustinum, Gregorium Turonensem, Othonem Frisingensem, Nicolaum I. Ioannem VIII. Celestinum III. & alios, qui nonnisi gladium, armaque spiritualia Ecclesiae concedunt; ut notavit, suisseque probavit vir Romanae communionis nostrae memoria doctissimus Rogerus Widrinctonus Anglus. Iam idem quoque Baronius Vsuardo & Adoni, celeberrimis noni seculi scriptoribus, superbissimè alicubi inequitat, quòd in dubio reliquerint an Sanctissimae Virginis Mariae corpus post ejus mortem in coelos fuerit subvectum; eosque tametsi putet in hanc sententiam falso Hieronymi nomine deceptos venisse, excusatione tamen indignos esse pronunciavit, quòd à praeeunte Romanae Ecclesiae exemplo ac iudicio hac in parte defecisse ipsi videantur. Neque verò antiquioribus parcit. Theodoretum virum eruditissimum, verba Pauli ad Colossenses de religione Θρησκεία Angelorum, velut in haereticos dicta, qui Angelos olim colerent, accipientem negat feliciter afecutum esse Pauli sensum, ait errore semel lapsum in alium graviorem impegisse; quòd scribat, scilicet, de his haereticis intelligendum esse Laodicenae Synodi Canonem XXXV. ac denique nimis incaute, quae à Catholicis essent instituta, haereticis tribuisse, dum tradit Oratoria in ea Asiae regione S. Michaeli Archangelo sacra ab haereticis erecta fuisse. Iste scilicet mille & amplius post Theodoretum annis natus, melius quàm ipse nouit quae tum essent in Phrygia ab haereticis, vel à Catholicis erectae aedes. Cum Epiphanio non auso affirmare B. Virginem esse mortuam paulo agit benignius . Hanc enim de Mariae obitu dubitationem, tametsi ab Ecclesia admitti neget, Epiphanio tamen condonandum esse edicit; quod aliis sanctissimis atque eruditissimis viris, aeque ac Epiphanio, saepe accideriit, ut dum ardentiori studio in hostes inuehuntur, vehementiori impetu in contrariam partem acti lineam veritatis transgressi esse videantur. Pari alibi indulgentia in Gregorium Turonensem vtitur, cuius culentissimum de Dionysii Parisiensis in Gallias sub Decio, A. D. 250. aduentu testimonium, (quem ipse A. D. 109. passum esse vult) cum aliter non posset refellere, haec eius simplicitati tam multa facile admittenti dondanda esse scribit. Sed & Hieronymo ipsi, "diuinam ab Hebraeos epistolam a Latinis inter Scripturas canonicas recipi semel atque iterum negati, idem Annalium Parens liberrime obloquitur, falsumque id esse contendit quod ille de rebus sui seculi suaeque Ecclesiae non semel tradidit, quem tamen, quod hominem, credo, iracundum sciret, ita placare conatur, ut hunc eius errorem Eusebio imputet cui ille, scilicet, nimis credulus fuerit . Nempe, si hunc sequimur, Hieronymus Eusebio pridem mortuo de Romanorum sententia atque consuetudine magis credidit, quam ipsis Romanis apud quos diu vixerat, quorumque pars haud exigua fuerat. Cyprianum, ipsum, sanctissimum Christi martyrem, quod Stephano Episcopo Romano resistere ausus sit, eiusque censuras reprehendere ait idem Baronius satis excandescere ac iurgari, & a conuitiis atque contumeliis disputationem suam exordiri. Sic & Firmilianum Caesareae in Cappadocia episcopum, virum illius memoriae laudatissimum, paria de Stephani censuris cum Cypriano sententem ait iracund a igne inflammatum & furore concitum in contumelias & probra ferri praecipitem, femeli, menti 6.47. tetra offusa caligine falsa a veris minus valuisse distinguere; eaque patentis (vt ipse loquitur) mendacij, tum foedae & in
units.tr: d Thom. de vita: "If ever," he says, "a new sense occurs that agrees with the text, and does not disagree with Sacred Scripture or with the teaching of the Church, although it is foreign to the torrent of the holy teachers, I ask all readers not to condemn it hastily, but to show themselves fair judges. Let them remember to give each his due. The authority of Sacred Scripture alone is reserved for itself, and this authority is such that we believe a thing to be so simply because the writers themselves wrote it. But other writers (says Augustine) I read in such a way that, however eminent they are in holiness and learning, I do not on that account believe it to be so, merely because they wrote it so. Let no one, therefore, condemn any sense of Holy Scripture merely because it differs from the early teachers, but let him examine the text and context of Scripture more keenly, and if he finds that it fits, let him praise God, who has bound the exposition of the Holy Scriptures not to the opinions of the early teachers but to Scripture itself, entire, under the judgment of the Catholic Church." Melchior Canus, bishop of the Canaries, after saying from Augustine that God willed this happiness to be found in the divine books alone, that in them there should be no error whatever, adds: "Otherwise no one, however learned and holy, is not at times led astray, does not sometimes fail to be on guard, does not on occasion slip." And after he has brought forward some of the examples mentioned above, he concludes the point thus: "Let us therefore read the early Fathers, indeed with reverence, but as men, with discrimination and judgment." And shortly afterwards he adds: "The other holy writers are lesser and human, and they make mistakes at times, and sometimes give birth to a monster, departing from the order and institution of nature." And in the same place: "To follow our elders in all things with reverence, and to set our own feet in their footprints, as children do in play, seems to be nothing other than to condemn our own abilities, to deprive ourselves of our own judgment and of the power to search out the truth. Let us follow the early writers, it is well, but as leaders, not as masters." Ambrosius Catharinus says the same: "Truly, the sayings or writings of the saints are not in themselves of firm authority, so that in each case they must be given assent." And the Jesuits themselves teach in various places that they do not depend so much upon the authority of the Fathers as is commonly believed. These are the frank words of Peravius on the Epiphany. We, with the moderation that is fitting, do not so much examine the errors and lapses of divine men, but men, as we reveal those that come freely to hand, or meet us even against our will, lest they be a snare to anyone; yet to defend and uphold them is no more our duty than to defend their faults, if there are any. Likewise elsewhere: the same writer testifies that he has observed that in various articles of faith it has often happened to many of the early Fathers that, before the origin of the errors and heresies against which these articles were attacked one by one had been sufficiently cleared up and the truth of the matter made plain, they let fall some statements in their writings that do not agree with the rule of the orthodox faith. And indeed he often rejects both their opinions and their explanations, and sometimes quite sharply, as we have shown above in the case of Epiphanius himself. When somewhere he had objected to him the authority of certain Fathers on the interpretation of a passage in Luke, which was at odds with his own opinion, he answers without taking any account of them. Nor is the authority of certain Fathers to be set against him, since they can affirm nothing other than what they learned from Luke, and there is no reason why we should interpret Luke by their words rather than interpret their words by Luke, as it seems they were asserting. He writes these things, as it seems, admirably and with great judgment, both entirely in agreement with what we have brought from Augustine above, and most useful for many of our controversies, concerning which, since the Fathers themselves could decide nothing except what they had from Scripture, it is truer, according to the opinion of this most learned Jesuit, that their testimonies in these matters are to be explained from Scripture, rather than Scripture from them. In another work, defending the present usage of the Church of Rome in administering repentance against Arnauld, who objected the ancient practice of the Fathers, he teaches that the present custom of recent times in each age is to be preferred to the tradition and antiquity of the Fathers, a custom which, as he wishes, comes from the Holy Spirit governing the Church, as John Fisher maintains. The other Jesuits speak no differently. Maldonatus, than whom no Protestant is a sharper or more hostile opponent, after he had reported the opinion of certain Fathers who thought that the sons of Zebedee had wrongly answered when the Lord asked them whether they could drink the cup that he himself was about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which he himself was baptized, and they said they could, adds: he would rather believe that they answered neither rashly nor ignorantly, but lovingly and truly. And elsewhere, on Matthew 9:11, after bringing forward the expositions of many, indeed almost all, the Fathers, he denies that he can be brought to follow that interpretation. And yet he says that the sense of that passage is today called into controversy. I do not see how he will persuade Protestants that they should think it necessary to follow him, when he so confidently despises the agreement of so many writers on other passages. Elsewhere, however, he speaks even more harshly on the words of Christ, the most important of all controversies: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it. The sense of these words (he says) does not seem to me to be that which all the authors, except Hilary, whom I remember to have read, think. Likewise elsewhere, on Matthew 11:11: He that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John the Baptist, after setting out various expositions of the early writers: He has, out of many opinions, that which the reader chooses; but if he wishes to hear my own opinion too, I will freely confess that I rest my own judgment, such as it is, in none of them at all. The same, on John 6: Ammonius, Cyril, Theophylact and Euthymius answer that not all are drawn, because not all are worthy, which is too close to the error of the Pelagians. Salmeron, a man of great name among the Jesuits: The adversaries seek arguments (he says) from the antiquity of the teachers, to which greater honour has always been given than to novelties. It is answered that every age has always paid honour to antiquity, etc. But we assert this, that the more recent the teachers, the sharper-sighted they are. And against this multitude which they object to us, we answer (he says) from the word of God, Exodus 23: "In judgment you shall not acquiesce in the opinions of the many, so as to turn aside from the truth." Cassinus, than whom no one among the Jesuits is considered more eloquent in French, does not hesitate to accuse Augustine (indeed Paul himself too) of excess and some intemperance in what they wrote about grace, softening the odium of the charge with the splendour of an allegorical metaphor. Those great men (he says) are like so many great and immense seas, which, stirred by a secret impulse of the spirit, swell up and are carried so completely onto one shore, and so entirely press upon it, that they leave the opposite shore dry. As the ocean, after it has surged and flooded this coast far and wide, soon returns little by little into the channels set for it by God, so those men of ours, when they have poured out into rebellion against the spirit and into disobedience to the truth, and have run too far, soon gather themselves together again and return to that calm level which builds up the house of God. By these images Cassinus clearly signifies that those most holy men are carried with a changing and uneven motion; at times they flow within the bounds of truth and the Holy Spirit, at times they burst out beyond them; sometimes they are swept beyond the paths of truth, and soon they come back to themselves. A certain Father Adam of the same fraternity lately made his colleague's mind more openly known, for he wrote in a published work that Augustine's books are covered with a certain darkness and mist, that the doctrine (of grace, namely) is wrapped up and entangled, and of a kind that seems to contradict itself. That it was not Augustine's good fortune in choosing and establishing opinions, so that it is not open to us to depart from his authority and follow anything other than what he himself has defined. That Augustine either did not want to express the sense of his mind clearly and simply, or at any rate, though he tried, did not succeed at all, so that what he meant could be plainly understood: that while he fought against Pelagius too fiercely, he was carried to some very dangerous extremes at the end, and that he spoke of grace and predestination with too much excess. Accordingly, he elsewhere calls Augustine's opinions on that subject dire and rustic. Indeed one of his adversaries, from the number of the so-called Jansenist theologians, reports that this Jesuit went so far that in a sermon delivered publicly before the Parisian people on 2 December 1650 he said: Augustine is obscure and involved; Augustine, being an African of fiery genius, often exceeded measure while he attacked the enemies of grace, and was carried beyond the limits of truth. Likewise, Bellarmine and Medina affirm that Saint Jerome... and Baronius, where he treats of the ancient bishops of Gaul and Germany, who about 800 years ago, under Charles and his son Louis the Pious, with the greatest unanimity, both all together in the Synod of Frankfurt, in which there were many men of recent memory, and each one singly in their own little works, such as Agobard, Hincmar, Walafrid Strabo and others, refuted the new and unusual dogma of the Second Council of Nicaea concerning the veneration and worship of images, he does not hesitate, out of his great reverence for antiquity, to write that they all... From this one case we may learn how highly these men value the authority of the early Fathers, whom, if they incline in any way against their own Pontiff, they think should be condemned, and they pronounce freely. Sirmond (than whom, I think, no one was more moderate in those parts) nevertheless broke out too, and could not restrain himself, because he would betray how little regard is paid by himself and his people to antiquity whenever it departs from the decrees of Pope Urban. For the opinion of those same Fathers, whom Baronius bluntly called mad, this man of ours, a Frenchman in spirit and by birth, though rather sober, calls by no less distinguished words the heresy of the French. But I return to Baronius, who everywhere freely reproves and refutes the Fathers whenever they think otherwise than he himself approves. Of Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Roman Church, celebrated among the Latins for nearly six hundred years now for his life, learning and holiness, when Baronius had recited many passages from his letter to Bishop Firmin that conflict with the Hildebrandine and Boniface doctrine of the temporal empire of the Pope, he says: "Thus far Peter Damian on these matters, whom Catholic dogmas utterly oppose, by which all are marked with the error of heresy who take away from the Roman Church, the chair of Peter, one of the two swords, and grant only the spiritual one." And again, soon after, with a few things interposed: Peter is therefore convicted of having fallen into error (we neither ought nor are able to excuse him), whom it is agreed by the common and Catholic consensus of the whole Church to have been condemned. Bellarmine also cites and approves Baronius's censure of Peter. Both of them openly condemn as heretics nearly all the early Christian writers in this one Peter, and also many bishops of Rome: Athanasius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory of Tours, Otto of Freising, Nicholas I, John VIII, Celestine III and others, who grant to the Church only the sword and spiritual arms; as the learned Roger Widrington, an Englishman and most learned in the memory of our Roman communion, has noted and proved. Now Baronius also, in one place, most arrogantly sets upon Usuard and Ado, the most celebrated writers of the ninth century, because they left in doubt whether the body of the Blessed Virgin Mary was carried up into heaven after her death; and though he thinks they came to this opinion, deceived by the false name of Jerome, he nevertheless pronounced them unworthy of excuse, because they seem to have departed in this matter from the preceding example and judgment of the Roman Church. Nor does he spare the older writers either. He denies that Theodoret, a most learned man, happily grasped the sense of Paul's words to the Colossians on religion (θρησκεία) of angels, taking them as said against heretics who once worshipped angels; he says that having once fallen into error, he rushed into another, more grievous one; because he wrote that the canon 35 of the Council of Laodicea must be understood of these heretics; and finally that he had too incautiously attributed to heretics what was instituted by Catholics, while he records that oratories in that region of Asia sacred to Saint Michael the Archangel were erected by heretics. That man, indeed, born more than a thousand years after Theodoret, knows better than he did which buildings in Phrygia were then erected by heretics, or by Catholics. With Epiphanius, who did not dare to affirm that the Blessed Virgin had died, he proceeds more kindly. For concerning this doubt about Mary's death, although he denies that it is admitted by the Church, he declares that it is to be pardoned in Epiphanius; because it has often happened to other most holy and learned men, just as to Epiphanius, that while they attack their enemies with a more ardent zeal, they are driven with a more vehement impulse to the opposite side and seem to have crossed the line of truth. Elsewhere he shows the same indulgence to Gregory of Tours, whose very clumsy testimony about the coming of Dionysius of Paris into Gaul under Decius, in the year 250 (whom he wishes to have suffered in the year 109), since he could not otherwise refute it, he writes that these things must be pardoned in his simplicity, who admitted so many things so easily. But also against Jerome himself, who on more than one occasion said that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not received among the canonical Scriptures by the Latins, the same Father of the Annals most freely speaks out, and contends that what he handed down more than once about the affairs of his own age and of his own Church is false; yet, because he knew him to be, I suppose, a hot-tempered man, he tries to soothe him by attributing this error of his to Eusebius, whom he had trusted too readily. Indeed, if we follow this, Jerome, who had long been dead, believed Eusebius more about the opinion and custom of the Romans than the Romans themselves, among whom he had lived for a long time, and of whom he was no small part. Baronius says that Cyprian himself, the most holy martyr of Christ, because he dared to resist Stephen, bishop of Rome, and to find fault with his censures, grew sufficiently heated and quarrelled, and began his disputation with insults and abuse. So too he says that Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man most highly praised in memory, who agreed with Cyprian about the censures of Stephen, was inflamed with a fiery anger and stirred by fury, rushing headlong into insults and reproaches, and a dark mist was poured over his mind so that he could less well distinguish falsehood from truth; and by this, as he himself puts it, of manifest lying, then of foul and in

units.la: Ibid. §.44.46. Ecclesiam Romanam calumnia, & in Stephanum procacitatis damnatiae eo denique provehitur ut virum, quem & doctrina & sanctitate morum nulli propemodum illorum temporum secundum fuisse visum, quem & inter Sanctos ab universa Graecorum Ecclesia coli fatetur naufragium fecisse dicat. Idem alibi Polycratem, Polycarpum,& Irenaeum (quibus viiis nihil fere habet sanctius aut venerabilius omnis Christianorum antiquitas) mendaciarguere non veretur, quòd Ioannem Apostolum tradidisse negarent, ut Pascha die Dominico necessario celebraretur. Sed & quae ab Irenaeo, Tertulliano, Clemente Alexandrino, Basilio, compluribusque aliis de restitutis ab Esdra Scripturis tradita sunt, ipse libere, (neque sane immerito) refellit. Denique quodam loco de Petri a Paulo reprehensi causa agens, omnes auctores (Veteres intelligit) in alterutram sententiam conspirasse, atque in eo convenisse praefatus ut vel ea cuncta simulate peracta (a Petro scilicet & Paulo) fuisse, ac sic nullum fuisse Petri peccatum, vel seriò facta esse, ac sic Petrum errasse senserint; Ipse utramque (id est omnium Patrum; sententiam explicit, & tertiam quandam (quae nullius Patris fuit, sequitur plane mirabilem, dicens, illa nec ex composito ab Apostolis facta, nec ea faciendo Petrum vel minimum deliquisse. Sed quanti & hic & Bellarminus Patrum sive numerum, sive auctoritatem faciant ex disputatione de Honorio Pontifice Romano liquido intelligimus; quem cum haereseos vel damnent, vel damnatum à VI. Synodo agnoscant primo Trullani Patres CCXXVII. adhaec octauae CCCLXX. & praeter hos Hadrianus P.R. II. cum tota illa sua Romana Synodo, cuius in octaua generali fit mentio; denique plurimi singulares illorum & sequentium scriptores, ut Bedae, Anastasius, Hincmarus, Photius, Psellus, Adonis, Humbertus, Marianus Scotus, Cedrenus, Glycas, Vincentius Spergensis Abbas, Chronici Reicherspergensis au- tor; universi (ut liquet) plures quam mille & sexaginta; hos ta'; ihos tamen omnes utTrque ille Cerdinalisr, magna Biniis & aliorum recentiorum caterva stipante, libere refutant, ac vel fefellisse, vel falsas deceptasque fuisse, licet absque ulla rationis aut veri specie ; uno causæ Papalis studio permoti, audacter tamen affirmant pertinaciterque contendunt. Quis enim istos heri & nudiustertius natos res Honorii, ac Synodi Sextæ melius ac certius nosse putet, quam veteres illos, vel eius ævo proximos, vel certe ab eo multo propius distantes ; quam aoftræ memoriæ homines ? Non est absimilis noftratis Peronii inverecundia non in unum, aut alterum, sed in sexcentos, & quidem in celeberrima Synodo Chalcedonensi sedentes Patres; quos ille in euchendo & Romanæ sedi æquiparando throno ƐPO omnes dissimulationis, perfidiæ, prævaricationis, ac turpissimi mendacii damnare non dubitatt, dum eos fingit Anatolii partitim vi & minis, partim fraude & malis artibus circumventos id præter suam voluntatem, ac conscientiam decreuisse, quod ipsi se sponte, & ex animi sui sententia statuisse clara omnes voce, quidam etiam iurati, graviter ac sancte frequentissima Synodo affirmant atque profitentur. " Sunt alia & horum & aliorum Romanorum loca in quibus Patrum sententias magna libertate vel repudiant, vel etiam refellunt. Sed nihil necesse est plura congerere : ex hoc enim specimine quivis non plane habes intelligit istos, dum Patres de nostris controversiis iudices postulant, semper intelligere se eorum iudicia admissuros quidem, sed ea lege tamen, ne quid illi de tota hac causa pronuntient præter suam id est Papæ sui) voluntatem ac sententiam ; Ni fecerint, sibi ut liberum sit atque integrum ab eorum placitis sine fraude discedere, ipsosque iudices non aliter quam insanos atque hæreticos contemnere. Huc denique redit omnis istorum de antiquitatis laudibus atque auctoritate clamor atque strepitus. Hoc vero quid aliud, quæso, est quam & nobis, & suis, & orbi universo palàm illudere?
units.tr: Ibid. §.44.46. The Roman Church is so carried away by calumny and by insolence toward Stephen that it finally goes so far as to say that a man whom almost none of those times was thought second to in learning and sanctity of life, and whom he admits the whole Greek Church honours among the Saints, suffered shipwreck. Elsewhere the same writer does not hesitate to charge Polycrates, Polycarp and Irenaeus (of whom almost nothing more holy or venerable is found in all Christian antiquity) with lying, because they denied that the Apostle John had handed down that the Passover must necessarily be celebrated on the Lord's day. But he also freely (and not undeservedly) refutes what Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Basil, and many others have related about the Scriptures restored by Ezra. Finally, in a certain place, treating the cause of Peter's rebuke by Paul, he prefaces his remarks by saying that all the authors (he means the ancients) have conspired into one of two opinions, and have agreed on this, that either all those things were done feignedly (by Peter and Paul, namely), and so there was no sin of Peter, or they were done in earnest, and so they judged that Peter erred; he himself sets out both (that is, the opinion of all the Fathers) and a certain third opinion (which belongs to no Father), which is plainly remarkable, saying: those things were neither done by agreement among the Apostles, nor by doing them did Peter sin in the least. But how much both he and Bellarmine value the number or the authority of the Fathers, we clearly understand from the dispute about Honorius, Pope of Rome. Whom the Fathers of Trullo, first 227 of them, then the eighth council with 370, and besides these Hadrian II with his whole Roman synod, mentioned in the eighth general council, either condemn for heresy or acknowledge as condemned by the Sixth Synod; and finally very many individual writers of those and later times, such as Bede, Anastasius, Hincmar, Photius, Psellus, Ado, Humbert, Marianus Scotus, Cedrenus, Glycas, Vincent, abbot of Speyer, the author of the Chronicle of Reichersberg; all together (as is clear) more than 1,060. Yet all of these that Cardinal [Bellarmine], with a great crowd of other more recent writers crowding round him, freely refutes, and says they were either mistaken or false and deceived, though without any appearance of reason or truth; moved by the single zeal of the Papal cause, they nevertheless boldly assert and stubbornly maintain it. For who would think that these men, born yesterday and the day before, know the affairs of Honorius and the Sixth Synod better and more certainly than those ancients, who were either near his own time or at least much closer to it than men of our memory? Our Peronius's shamelessness is not unlike this: he accuses not one or two but six hundred Fathers, sitting in the celebrated Council of Chalcedon, of all dissimulation, perfidy, prevarication and most shameful lying, when he exalts and equates the throne with the Roman see; he pretends that they, partly by force and threats, partly by fraud and wicked arts, circumvented by Anatolius, decided against their own will and conscience what they themselves, of their own accord and according to their own judgment, declared with one clear voice (some even under oath) and solemnly and seriously affirm and profess in a very crowded synod. There are other passages, both of these men and of other Romans, in which they either reject or even refute the opinions of the Fathers with great freedom. But there is no need to heap up more: from this sample anyone can plainly see that these men, while demanding the Fathers as judges of our controversies, always intend to accept their judgments, but on this condition, that they pronounce nothing in this whole cause except according to their own will and opinion, that is, the Pope's. If they do not, then it is to be free for them to depart from the Fathers' decisions without blame, and to despise the judges themselves no differently than madmen and heretics. In the end all the clamour and noise of these men about the praise and authority of antiquity comes down to this. But what else, I ask, is this than to mock us, and their own people, and the whole world openly?
