units.la: Sed hanc Romanorum hominum de suis vnius Papæ, pro omni antiquitate, auctoritate sententiam, quia nullus vel simplicius, vel lucentius expressit, quam Cornelius Muffus Bitonninus in Italia episcopus, qui inter Patres Tridentinos non postremus sedit, non videtur prætermittendum viri nobilissimi insigne ea de re testimonium. Sic ergo ille Romam, conuerso ad eam sermone in Paulum Apostolum scribens, affatur. Ad quem inquit Roma, quaerenda sunt divina concilia nisi ab illis qui- bus mysterium Dei dispensatio credita est? Quem ergo pro Deo habemus in his quae Dei sunt quicquid ipse dixerit, tanquam Deum audire debemus. Ego, (vt ingenuè fatear) plus vni summo Pontifici crederem, in his quae fidei mysteria tangunt, quàm mille Augustinis, Hieronymis, Gregoriis, neaicam Ricardis, Scotis, Guilielmis. Credo enim & scio quod summus Pontifex in his quae fidei sunt errare non potest, quoniam auctoritas determinandi quae ad fidem spectant in Pontifice residet. Audacius & imprudentius ista effusa culpiam forsan videbuntur. Sed rem penitus intuenti, rei speciem (quae vt plurimum ad deludendos imperitos accommodata est) contemnati patebit, ni vehementer fallor, Bitonium non minùs verè quàm ingenuè exposuisse quod sit Ecclesiæ Romanæ de Patribus iudicium, quæ cum Papam esse infallibilem, Patres vero errare, & decipi potuisse doceat, qui non videt Papam Patribus apud eam anteponi; Neque verò est quod quis regerat, non ab omnibus Papam infallibilem haberi. Nam præterquam quòd, qui sententiæ illi adversantur, minimam & quæ minimi fit Ecclesiæ Romanæ partem constituunt, iidem ipsi uniuscujusque seculi Ecclesiæ istud ipsum infallibilitatis ius tribuunt, quod Papæ ereptum eunt. Vt si Concilium nunc rite habeatur eius, (vt hi quidem putant) sententia omnibus in vniuersum Patribus superior futura sit. Itaque nullum est aliud horum à Cornelio discrimen, nisi quod quos illi Patres Præsulibus omnibus in Consilio congregatis subjiciunt .
units.tr: But since no one has expressed this opinion of the Romans, that their one Pope stands above all antiquity and all authority, more simply or more clearly than Cornelius Musso, bishop of Bitonto in Italy, who sat among the Fathers of Trent not least, it seems right not to pass over the notable testimony of that most noble man on this matter. So he, turning his speech to Rome and writing to the Apostle Paul, addresses her: "To whom, Rome, must divine councils be sought, unless from those to whom the dispensation of God's mystery has been entrusted? Whatever he himself says in matters that are God's, we must hear as if it were God." I, to confess candidly, would believe the one supreme Pontiff more, in matters that touch the mysteries of faith, than a thousand Augustines, Jeromes, Gregories, Richards, Scotuses, Williams. For I believe and know that the supreme Pontiff cannot err in matters of faith, since the authority of determining what pertains to faith resides in the Pontiff. These statements will perhaps seem too bold and imprudent. But whoever looks into the matter thoroughly will see that the appearance of the thing (which is for the most part designed to deceive the unskilled) is contemptible; unless I am greatly mistaken, Bitonto has set out no less truthfully than candidly the judgment of the Roman Church about the Fathers. For the Church, teaching that the Pope is infallible and that the Fathers could err and be deceived, who does not see that it places the Pope before the Fathers? Nor is there anything one can reply, that not all hold the Pope to be infallible. For apart from the fact that those who oppose that opinion make up the smallest part, and even the smallest part of the Roman Church, the same men attribute to the Church of every age that very right of infallibility which they snatch from the Pope, so that if a council is now lawfully held (as these men indeed think), its judgment will be superior to all the Fathers together. Thus there is no difference between these men and Cornelius, except that those whom he subjects to all the prelates gathered in council,

units.la: hos iste,uno omnes Papa inferiores facit. Vna tantum illa hyperbole, qua mille Augustinos, Hieronymos, Gregorios, ad Pontificis Romani pedes paulo (fareor) superbiùs dejicit, videtur posse culpari, quanquam non desit etiam quod excusēs; solent enim in hos plerumque excessus abripi optima sincerissimaque ingenia. Certe à Bitontini mente non discedit novissimus Cypriani editor, vir, quod omnes sciunt, modestissimus & eruditissimus, qui multa, imo plurima apud Veterum Ecclesiam ab hodierno Romæ & sensu & ritu diuersissima pro suo candore obseruat; sed sic tamen ut antiquis præsentia anteponenda edicat; quod quid aliud quæso est, quàm unum Romæ,siue Præsulem,siue cœtum, omnibus priscis Patribus præferre; Hoc (inquit) certè liceat, scripta priscorum legentibus obseruare, quod illi fecerint dixerintve, unde POSTERIORA probentur fuisse CERTIORA PRIORIBVS & HODIERNA sentiamus esse COMMODIORA PRISTINIS. En quo tandem recidat omnis Romanorum in Patres sedulitas, cura ac reverentia ! ut, scilicet, Romæ ipsa etiam antiquitas cedat ac succumbat, eiusque prostrata atque abjecta maiestatem attollat. Ergo isti, Patres, si verum amamus, eo consulunt, non ut sequantur, sed ut in ordinem cogant. Verùm ipse Ecclesiæ Romanæ usus siue praxis etiam multò clarius ac certius docebit quanti ipsa Patres faciat. Enimuero si veterum auctoritate standum est, ita ut nihil quod confirmarint abrogare, nihil quos ipsos latuerit usurpare liceat, qui fit ut tam multa à Veteribus obseruata occurrant quæ hodie in usu esse desierunt? Ad tria veluti maximè insignia capita revocari potest universa religio, fidem ipsam,cæremonias & disciplinam singula, si placet, strictim & quantum ad institutum nostrum satis est, percurramus; patebit in tribus illis capitibus multa præter Veterum auctoritatem tum abrogata tum instituta.
units.tr: these men make all inferior to the one Pope alone. Only that one hyperbole, by which he casts a thousand Augustines, Jeromes and Gregories somewhat too proudly (I confess) at the feet of the Roman Pontiff, seems open to blame, although there is also something to excuse it; for the best and most sincere minds are usually carried away into such excesses. Certainly the most recent editor of Cyprian, a man, as everyone knows, most modest and learned, does not depart from Bitonto's mind; for out of his candour he observes many, indeed very many, things in the ancient Church that are quite different from the present sense and rite of Rome. Yet he does so in such a way as to declare that present things are to be preferred to ancient ones. What else, I ask, is this than to set one Rome, whether prelate or assembly, above all the early Fathers? "This much at least," he says, "may be allowed to readers who observe the writings of the ancients: that whatever they did or said, by which LATER things are shown to be MORE CERTAIN than EARLIER, and we judge PRESENT things to be MORE CONVENIENT than FORMER." See to what at last the whole zeal, care and reverence of the Romans toward the Fathers comes down! Namely, that even antiquity itself gives way and succumbs at Rome, and that its majesty, once prostrated and cast down, is raised up. So these men, if we love the truth, consult the Fathers not in order to follow them, but in order to put them in their place. But the very practice and usage of the Roman Church will teach much more clearly and certainly how highly it values the Fathers. Indeed, if we must abide by the authority of the ancients, so that it is allowed to abrogate nothing they affirmed and to introduce nothing they did not know, how does it happen that so many things observed by the ancients occur, which today have ceased to be in use? The whole of religion can be referred to three most notable heads: faith itself, ceremonies, and discipline. Let us briefly run through each of these, as far as our purpose requires; it will be clear that under these three heads many things have been both abrogated and instituted, apart from the authority of the ancients.

units.la: Nam quòd ad primum genus pertinet in superioribus. nonnulla iam eius specimina protulimus. Vidimus enim eam de animarum, interea dum resurrectio expectatur, statu sententiam; quae & Veteris Ecclesiae pene totius fuit, & Graecae etiam hodie est, ante annos ducentos in Concilio Florentino damnatam fuisse ab Ecclesia Romana, sententiamque adversam pro fidei Christianae articulo constitutam. Vidimus praeterea amplius quam sexcentis a Christo annis in Ecclesia obtinuisse ut Eucharistia infantibus ad salutem non minus quam ipsa Baptismi lotio necessaria esse crederetur. Id vero dgma nuper a Tridentina Synodo palam explosum est, & qui id docerent anathemari diserte subiecti sunt . Si quis dixerit parvulos antequam ad annos discretionis pervenerint necessariam esse Eucharistiae communionem, anathema sit. Tantum ad demulcendos post tam atrocem contumeliam Patres, aliquid iis Synodus quae dam, ab iis quae se illi liquido & diserte sentire profitentur, alienam, ut supra demonstravimus, quo illata iis injuria adeo non sarcitur, ut potius geminetur. Sic enim non modo velut haereticis traducuntur, sed insuper velut bardi & hebetes illudantur, quibus os oblinire facile fit. Ab ipso item Hieronymo accepimus suo tempore Chiliastas toleratos fuisse. At hodie haereticis accensetur. Tum quidem nemini apud Ecclesiam fraudi erat animae humanae originem ex traduce repetere, eamque opinari de parte in filium per generationem propagari. At id ipsum hodie gravissimus error habetur. Censebant Veteres non posse illesa Scripturarum auctoritate hominis in Ecclesia pendere imagine, neque debere picturas esse in Ecclesia, ne quod colitur & adoratur in particibus depingatur . Plane contraria est Concilii Tridentini sententia, Imagines Christi, Deiparae Virginis, & aliorum sanctorum, in templis praesertim, habendae & retinendae, ibique debitus honor & veneratio impertiendus. Patres quidem nonnulli, ut Chrysostomus (quod supra annotavimus) videntur peccatum originale negasse, alii ab eo sanctos quosdam immunes fuisse putasse, ut Philastrius k, qui pro absurdo habet iustos tot tantosque in iniquitate conceptos dici, cum(inquit)in ventre sanctificati sint, ut Patriarcha, Prophetæ, Iudices, Ieremias, & Ioannes Baptista beatissimus: Sed his exceptis, & similibus, quos perpetam de hoc fidei capite sensisse constat, sunt cæteri omnes quantum quidem ex eorum scriptis colligere possumus, Beatam Virginem in peccato originali conceptam censuerunt 1. Si eos pro iudicibus habuerunt Tridentini, cur veriti sunt ne cum iis in hoc argumento sentire viderentur? Cum enim in decreto suo sta tuissent, peccatum illud, quod propagatione, non imitatione, ab Adamo in omnes transfunditur, omnibus & singulis proprium inesse, declarant postremò, non esse suæ intentionis comprehendere in hoc decreto, ubi de peccato originali agitur, Beatam immaculatam Virginem Mariæ Dei genitricem. Quæ verba nulla ratione ita explicari possunt, quin Patribus omnibus fœdè impingatur error. Si enim Virginem Mariam, sine peccato concesserunt, contradictoriam eius, in qua Patres fuerunt, sententiæ ponunt ac definiunt, quo nihil durius ad Patres erroris arguendos pronuntiari potuit. Si vero simpliciter significant (tametsi verba quibus vsi sunt hunc sensum vixserant) non esse certò verum B. Virginem in peccato conceptam, honesta oratione bonos illos Patres, id quod dubium erat, pro certo affirmasse, & quod probles maticum tantum erat, pro indubitato habuisse dicunt. Synodus Laodicena-Codici Canonum Ecclesiæ uniuersalis infert a veteris Testamenti Canoni non nisi vigiti duos libros adscribit, Tobiam, Iudith, Sapientiam, Ecclesiasticum, & Maccabæorum utrumque præterm itt it, Caneque adeo excludit ". Melito Sardensis Episcopus o, Origenes P, Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus q, Gregorius Nazianzenus r, Hilarius s, Epiphanius t in eadem sunt sententia, quibus etiam succinunt Athanasius u, Rufinus x, & Hieronymus y. Hoc tamen decretum condere non dubitavit Concilium Tridentinum. Si quis libros ipsos integros cum omnibus suis partibus, prout in Ecclesia Catholica legi consueuerunt, & in Veteri vulgata Latina editione habentur, profacris & Canonicis no susceperit, &c. Anathema esto. Praeter quam quod graui iniuria pullant tot antiquissimos clarissimosque Patres, imo & primituam Ecclesiam totam, quae Laodicenum illud decretum inter Canones suos uniuersales retulit, quoddam aliud dogma inter Christianos hactenus inauditum, hic procudunt, dum, scilicet, iubent Bibliorum vulgatam versionem in Ecclesia esse Canonicam & authenticam. Concilij secundi uniuersalis c L. & quatti d c x x x. Patres, existimant Veteres sedem Romanam supra omnes alias euexisse, quod Urbs Roma rerum in seculo potiretur, ac dignitate regia supra omnes alias emineret. Itaque simili de causa sedem Patriarchalem Constantinopolitanam cum illa exaequant, quod in eodem honoris & dignitatis fastigio Urbs Constantinopolis cum vetere Roma constituta esset. Hodie vero anathema, marranata cesfetetur quisquis quippiam eiusmodi doceret, quique Pontificium primatum alio referret, quam ad TV ES PETRVS & PASCEOVES MEAS. Consilium Tridentinum anathema dicit iis qui negant episcopos presbyteris superiores Ea tamen certissima fuit Hieronymi & aliorum multorum patrum sententia. Supra iam à nobis dictum est Romam olim Graecos, quod Spiritum sanctum non de Filio, sed de solo Patre procederre contenderent, excommunicasse. Et tamen Theodoretus qui id ipsum diserte ponit, vt superiore capite vidiOrthodoxus & Catholicus habitus fuit. Nulla ab eo extorta vel quaesita huius sententiae purgatione aut revocatione. Plurima eiusdem generis congeri possent in quibus à Vetere Ecclesia discesserunt Pontificij, sed haec sufficiunt ut pateat istos minimè gentium putare summam esse debere veterum de fidei rebus auctoritatem.
units.tr: For the first kind of error, I have already given some examples above. We saw that the view on the state of souls while the resurrection is awaited was held by almost the whole of the ancient Church and is still held by the Greeks today; yet about two hundred years ago it was condemned by the Roman Church at the Council of Florence, and the contrary view was laid down as an article of the Christian faith. We have also seen that for more than six hundred years after Christ it prevailed in the Church that the Eucharist was believed to be no less necessary to salvation for infants than the washing of Baptism itself. That dogma has recently been openly rejected by the Council of Trent, and those who teach it are expressly subjected to anathema: If anyone shall say that the communion of the Eucharist is necessary for little children before they reach the age of discretion, let him be anathema. The Synod has granted some small concession to soothe the Fathers after so atrocious an insult, namely that it separates them from those who declare that they hold this view clearly and expressly, as we showed above. But the injury done to them is so far from being repaired that it is rather doubled. For they are not only branded as heretics, but are also mocked as dull-witted and stupid, and so are easily silenced. We have also learned from Jerome himself that in his time the Chiliasts were tolerated; today they are counted among the heretics. In the past, no one in the Church was held to be at fault for deriving the origin of the human soul from traducianism, and for thinking that it is passed from parent to child by generation. Yet today that very view is regarded as a most serious error. The ancients held that, without damage to the authority of the Scriptures, the image of man could not be hung in the Church, and that there ought to be no pictures in the Church, lest what is worshipped and adored be depicted in parts. The opinion of the Council of Trent is plainly the opposite: The images of Christ, of the Virgin Mother of God, and of the other saints are to be had and retained, especially in churches, and due honour and veneration are to be paid to them there. Some Fathers, such as Chrysostom (as we noted above), seem to have denied original sin, and others thought that certain saints were free of it, as Philastrius k does, who considers it absurd that so many and such great righteous men should be said to have been conceived in iniquity, since (he says) they were sanctified in the womb, like the patriarchs, the prophets, the judges, Jeremiah, and the most blessed John the Baptist. But leaving aside these and similar writers, whose view on this article of faith is known for certain, all the others, so far as we can gather from their writings, have held that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in original sin. If the Tridentine fathers regarded them as judges, why were they afraid of appearing to agree with them on this point? For having laid down in their decree that that sin, which passes into all men and each one by propagation, not by imitation, from Adam, is proper to all and each, they finally declare that it is not their intention to include in this decree, where original sin is treated, the Blessed Immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God. These words cannot be explained in any way without foully charging all the Fathers with error. For if they grant that the Virgin Mary was without sin, they set down and define the contrary of the opinion held by the Fathers, and nothing harsher could be pronounced to convict the Fathers of error. But if they mean merely (although the words they use have a different sense) that it is not certainly true that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in sin, then they say, with polite phrasing, that those good Fathers affirmed as certain what was doubtful, and held as indubitable what was merely probable. The Synod of Laodicea, in the Code of the canons of the universal Church, assigns to the canon of the Old Testament only twenty-two books, and passes over Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and both books of the Maccabees, and so excludes them. Melito, bishop of Sardis, Origen, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory Nazianzen, Hilary, and Epiphanius are of the same opinion, and Athanasius, Rufinus, and Jerome agree with them. Yet the Council of Trent did not hesitate to enact this decree: If anyone does not receive the books themselves entire, with all their parts, as they have been customarily read in the Catholic Church and are contained in the old Latin Vulgate edition, as sacred and canonical, let him be anathema. Apart from the grave injury this does to so many most ancient and famous Fathers, indeed to the whole primitive Church, which placed that Laodicean decree among its universal canons, it also brings forth here another doctrine hitherto unheard of among Christians, namely that the Vulgate version of the Bibles is to be canonical and authentic in the Church. The Fathers of the second universal council (canon 3) and of the fourth (canon 28) thought that the Roman see was raised above all others by the ancients because the city of Rome held the mastery of the world and was pre-eminent over all others in royal dignity. For a similar reason they placed the Patriarchal see of Constantinople on an equal footing with it, because the city of Constantinople had been established with ancient Rome at the same height of honour and dignity. Today, however, whoever teaches anything of this kind, and who refers the Papal primacy to any other text than You are Peter, and upon you I will build my church and Feed my sheep, is pronounced anathema, maranatha. The Council of Trent pronounces anathema on those who deny that bishops are superior to presbyters. Yet this was the most certain opinion of Jerome and of many other Fathers. We have already said above that Rome once excommunicated the Greeks because they contended that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Son but from the Father alone. And yet Theodoret, who expressly states this very thing, as we saw in the previous chapter, was regarded as orthodox and Catholic. No purgation or retraction of this opinion was extorted from him or sought. Many more examples of the same kind could be gathered in which the Papists have departed from the ancient Church, but these are enough to show that they by no means think that the authority of the ancients in matters of faith ought to be supreme.

units.la: Nunc ad ritus & cærimonias veniamus. Primas tenet Baptismus, qui è conditione naturæ eductos,nos Chri- sto inserit. Olim in Ecclesia in aquam mergebantur qui baptizabantur. Tertulliano, Cypriano, Epiphanio, & aliis testibus ; quin etiam ter mergitari solenne fuisse tradunt Tertullianus, & Hieronymus , qui mos etiam hodie apud Græcos quidem & Russos obtinet : à Romanis verò, quantumuis antiquus & pene uniuersalis, iampridem abrogatus est. Eo fit ut Moscouitæ Latinos rite baptizatos negent, quòd in eorum baptismo minimè adhibita fuerit trina illa mersio quam ipsi, ut potè olim à Ioanne Metropolitano suo, ut putant, Prophetæ præceptam summa religione obseruât, planeque necessariam existimant. Ne Gregorius quidem Monachus Græcus, Florentinæ conciliationis assertor vehemens, negat trinam illam mersionem esse in baptismo necessariam, in responsione ad Marcum Ephesinum Episcopum ı. Egressis è baptismate lactis & mellis in Veteri Ecclesia, prægustanda offerebatur concordia, ut patet, tum ex iisdem auctoribus, tum ex Sufannæ Martyris Vetes ribus apud Baronium Actis, & post baptismum parvulis æquè ac adulris Eucharistia statim porrigebatur, un de restat apud Æthiopes mos Eucharistiam in os in fantium recens baptizatorum ingerendi. Quid apud Antiquitatis adoratores istis ritibus factum est? tantos Antiquitatis adoratores istis ritibus factum est? ubi lac illud? ubi mel? ubi Patrum statim à baptismo Eucharistia? Hæc vero etsi usu apud Veteres olim recepta Romæ pridem sepulta iacent. Olim baptismus puerorum,& adolescentium vulgò differebatur, ut apparet ex historia de Constantino magno, Constantio, Theodosio, Valentiniano & Gratiano epud Ambrosium & I. 4. c. 6. in Gregorij Nazianzeni & Basilij de hoc argumento homiliis. Imò quidam Patres differendum senserunt, ut T. 1. p. 9. de Tertulliano supra obseruauimus: Qui fit ergo ut ne vestigia quidem istius consuetudinis in Ecclesia Romana supersint, ut etiam. veluti parum pium, exhorrescoﬁ tent, si quis eam ad usum revocare vellet? Mitto Baptis⁠ mi tempus, qui in Veteri Ecclesia haud fere alias quàm in Vigiliis Paschatis & Pentecostes administrabatur. Mitto & universam cerei Paschalis cærimoniam & vestes candidas quas baptizari tota post Pascha hebdomada gerebant , quòd hæc levio ra videri possint, quæ tamen si humanæ auctoritatis, non sœrum ipsarum, ratio haberetur, non video cur non æquè retenta fuerint, ac exorcismi & abrenunciationes & cætera huius generis quæ infantibus recens natis omnino, si verum fateri licet, præter decorum & à Veteribus olim adhibita sunt, & nunc à Latinis adhibentur. Sed & Veterum de Baptismi ministro traditio apud istos mutata est. Concilium Carthaginense I v. (ut est à Petavio observatum ) vetabat olim ne mulier baptizare præsumeret. Baptismum ab homine laico ministratum Basilius , in epistola ad Amphilochium, (quam omnis Græcia pro authentica & habuit semper & nunc etiam habet) irritum, ac (ut loquuntur) nullum censere videtur, quod idem quoque Petavius annotavit. Eliberitana quidem Synodus baptismum à bigamo, etiam ingruente necessitate, ministrari disertè vetat . Augustinus vero de baptismo ab homine, qui ipse rinctus non fuerit, ministrato dubitat, an is valere debeat, quod utrumque est ab eodem Iesuita animaduersum . Atqui omnes sciunt apud Romanos hodie licere & mulieribus, & quibusvis viris, laicis, bigamis, catechumenis, imo etiam Iudæis & Paganis baptismum in necessitate administrare. Iam Eucharistiam Cassander liquidò demonstrat ex pane & vino, à pia plebe oblatis, in veteri Ecclesia factam fuisse, panem in varia fructula fi actum, deinde consecratum & fidelibus distributum fuisse. At usus contrarius invaluit, non enim amplius consecratur (ut olim) panis à fidelibus oblatus, sed panis azymus, orbicularis, & in denarij formam effictus, quod acriter in Veteri Romani ordinis expositione reprehenditur. Huc quoque pertinet, quod cum omnis Ecclesia,Græca quidem ad hunc diem, Latina vero ad postrema usque noni sæculi tempora(quod doctissimus irmondus contra Baronium & aliós propria nuper differtatione valide asseruit planeque demonstrauit)eucharistiam in pane fermentato confecisse deprehendatur : Romanos constat iam inde ab undecimo sæculo adulto veterem morem pro sua libidine mutasse, instituisseque ut id sacramentum in azymo (quod apud eos omnes hodie in usu est) celebraretur. Iam is, de quo super diximus, Caffander fuse explicat quomodo in Veteri Ecclesia oratio canonica & Eucharistiæ p.3.64. consecratio clara voce ita recitaretur,ut facile plebs audire & ad eas Amen responder e posset,quas, ut notum est, voce adeo submissa sacerdotes hodie pronuntiant , ut eas nullus audiat , unde fit ut ea Liturgiæ pars secreta dicatur. Supra obseruauimus veteres summo studio sancti istius sacramenti materiam & mysterium texisse, ita ut nunquam illud coram catechumenis, vel infidelibus celebrarent ; nunc verò nullæ sunt huiusmodi in missa Romana cautiones. Etiam Iudæis, Gentilibus & Mahumetanis præsentibus Eucharistia celebratur,nulla veterum istorum canonum habita ratione. Quin & eo progressi sunt, ut veluti Antiquitati, quæ Sacramentum hoc studiosè occultabat, oppere vellent, id hodie publicè ostentent; & per vicos quotidie, quotannis semel atque iterum magna ac singulari pompa , in solennibus supplicationum processionibus gestent ac circumferant: quæ quidem cæremonia inter Christ a ios recentissima est, Veteribus adeo ignota,ut etiam monstri instar apud eos futura fuerit. Ita mirum instituta in auras abiecerunt , quorum nunc locum noua nescio quæ omni antiquitati inaudita occupant. Verùm idem Caffander probat Eucharistiam, non nisi coram iis qui eius participes fiebant olim celebratam fuisse : ceteros vero maturè cessisse. Chrysostomus quidem acerrimè in eos invehitur qui, cùm sacris cœtibus interessent,ad sacram syn-
units.tr: Let us now turn to the rites and ceremonies. First place belongs to Baptism, which admits us into Christ, drawing us out of the condition of nature. In the Church of old, those who were baptized were immersed in water, as Tertullian, Cyprian, Epiphanius and other witnesses attest. Indeed, Tertullian and Jerome report that it was customary to be dipped three times, and this custom still prevails today among the Greeks and the Russians, though among the Romans it has long since been abolished, however ancient and almost universal it once was. As a result, the Muscovites deny that Latins are validly baptized, because the threefold immersion was not at all used in their baptism. They themselves observe that threefold immersion with the utmost reverence, as having been commanded long ago by the Prophet John, as they think, their Metropolitan, and they regard it as plainly necessary. Not even Gregory the Greek monk, a fierce advocate of the Florentine union, denies in his reply to Mark, bishop of Ephesus, that the threefold immersion is necessary in baptism. In the ancient Church, those who came up from baptism were offered a foretaste of milk and honey, as is clear both from the same authors and from the Acts of the martyr Susanna in Baronius. And immediately after baptism the Eucharist was given to infants as well as to adults. From this custom there remains among the Ethiopians the practice of putting the Eucharist into the mouths of newly baptized infants. What has become of these rites among the worshippers of antiquity? Where is that milk? Where is that honey? Where is the Eucharist given by the Fathers immediately after baptism? These customs, though once received in practice among the ancients, now lie long buried at Rome. Formerly, the baptism of children and young people was commonly postponed, as appears from the history of Constantine the Great, Constantius, Theodosius, Valentinian and Gratian in Ambrose, from book 4, chapter 6, and from the homilies of Gregory Nazianzen and Basil on this subject. Indeed, some Fathers thought it should be deferred, as we observed above in volume 1, page 9, concerning Tertullian. How is it, then, that not even traces of this custom survive in the Roman Church, so that people shrink from it as though it were impious, if anyone wished to restore it to use? I pass over the time of baptism, which in the ancient Church was administered almost only at the Easter and Pentecost vigils. I pass over also the whole ceremony of the Paschal candle and the white garments which the baptized wore throughout the whole week after Easter. These may seem trivial matters; yet if the authority of men, not of the things themselves, were taken into account, I do not see why they were not retained just as much as exorcisms and renunciations and the other things of this kind, which, if we may speak the truth, are altogether unbecoming for newborn infants, and which were used by the ancients and are now used by the Latins. But also the tradition of the ancients concerning the minister of baptism has been changed among them. The Council of Carthage (as Petavius has observed) once forbade that a woman should presume to baptize. Basil, in his letter to Amphilochius (which all Greece has always regarded and still regards as authentic), seems to judge baptism administered by a layman to be invalid and, as they say, null; Petavius also noted this. The Synod of Elvira expressly forbids baptism to be administered by a bigamist, even in pressing necessity. Augustine, indeed, doubts whether baptism administered by a man who had not himself been baptized ought to be valid; both points were noted by the same Jesuit. Yet everyone knows that among the Romans today it is lawful, in case of necessity, for women, for any men whatever, for laymen, bigamists, catechumens, and even Jews and pagans, to administer baptism. Now Cassander clearly demonstrates that in the ancient Church the Eucharist was made from bread and wine offered by the devout people; the bread was shaped into various small loaves, then consecrated and distributed to the faithful. But the contrary custom has prevailed: the bread offered by the faithful is no longer consecrated, as it once was, but unleavened bread, round and stamped in the form of a coin, which is sharply rebuked in the exposition of the Roman order. To this also belongs the following fact. Every Church, the Greek indeed to this day, and the Latin up to the last times of the ninth century (as the most learned Irmondus has strongly asserted and plainly demonstrated in a recent separate dissertation against Baronius and others), is found to have celebrated the Eucharist with leavened bread. It is clear that the Romans, from the eleventh century onward, changed the ancient custom at their own pleasure, and instituted that this sacrament be celebrated with unleavened bread, which is now in use among all of them. Now Cassander, whom we mentioned above, explains at length how in the ancient Church the canonical prayer and the consecration of the Eucharist were recited in a clear voice, so that the people could easily hear them and be able to respond Amen to them. Whereas today the priests pronounce these in so low a voice, as is well known, that no one hears them, and hence that part of the Liturgy is called the secret. Above we observed that the ancients, with the greatest care, veiled the matter and mystery of this holy sacrament, so that they never celebrated it before catechumens or unbelievers. But now there are no such safeguards in the Roman Mass. The Eucharist is celebrated even in the presence of Jews, Gentiles and Muhammadans, with no regard at all for those ancient canons. Indeed they have gone so far that, as if they wished to oppose antiquity, which kept this sacrament carefully hidden, they now display it publicly. In solemn processions of supplication, with great and singular pomp, they carry it and parade it through the streets every day, once or twice a year. This ceremony is very recent among Christians and was so unknown to the ancients that it would have seemed a monstrous thing among them. Thus they have cast to the winds the institutions of wonderful antiquity, and in their place occupy the room with I know not what novelties unheard of in all antiquity. Yet the same Cassander proves that the Eucharist was formerly celebrated only in the presence of those who were partakers of it, and that the others withdrew in good time. Chrysostom indeed inveighs most sharply against those who, though they were present at the holy assemblies, did not approach the holy communion.

units.la: xim non accedebant. Etiam hodie in Liturgia Æthiopica finito Evangelio, clamat Diaconus. Exite foras qui non vultis accipere sacramentum. Ite catechumeni.Et denuo post cantatum symbolum, Qui communicare non vultis, discedite." Nunc vero apud Latinos qui Missæ intersunt rari communicant, una iis cura est sacramentum non sumere, sed adorare. Vnde hæ locutiones natæ, Audire Missam, & videre Missam. Dicebat Chrysostomus Quisquis mysteria non participat, impudenter & temere hic adstat, &c. Dic mihi si quis ad convivium vocatus manus lauet & sedeat, & ad mensam se comparet, sed eorum quæ apposita fuerint particeps non fiat. Nonne iniuria afficiet eum a quo vocatus est? Nonne præstitisset nunquam accessisse? Sic tu etiam huc te contulisti, hymnum cum omnibus cecinisti, & in eo quod cum indignus non fecisti, te dignum esse professus es: Quomodo cum manseris mensa particeps non fis? Et quæ sequuntur apud Chrysostomum. Si eiusmodi verba hodie concionator haberet, nonne ridiculus haberetur? Nimirum hodie (quod omnes vident) longè aliter quàm olim viuitur, alia à vetere consuetudo inualuit. Sole meridiano clarius est in uniuersa prisca Ecclesia liquide fidelibus Eucharistiam è sacro coetu domum deferre, eamque donec sumere liceret, clam apud se habere, unde est quod Tertullianus plerisque qui stationum diebus non putabant orationibus interueniendum, quod statio solvëda esset accepto corpore Domini, auctor est, {a}ut acceptum corpus Domini reservët, & sic utrumque salvum fore, & participationem sacrificij, & executionem officij. Idipsum etiam patet ex historia quam narrat Cyprianus, de muliere quadam quæ cùm arcam suam, in qua Domini sanctum fuit, manibus indignis tentasset aperire, igne inde surgente deterrita est, ne auderet attingere: Basilius Cypriano longe recentior in epistola ad Pattitiam scribens te statuer eam consuetudinem suo adhuc sæculo in Ecclesia obtinuisse, quod Petavius etiam diserte confitetur; idque insuper luculentissime confirmat Basilii æqualis
units.tr: Even today, in the Ethiopian Liturgy, when the Gospel is finished the deacon cries out: Get out, you who do not wish to receive the sacrament. Go, catechumens. And again, after the creed has been sung: You who do not wish to communicate, depart. But now among the Latins those who attend the Mass rarely communicate; their only concern is not to receive the sacrament but to adore it. Hence these expressions arose: to hear Mass and to see Mass. Chrysostom said: Whoever does not partake of the mysteries stands here shamelessly and rashly, etc. Tell me, if someone invited to a feast washes his hands and sits down and takes his place at the table, but does not share in what is set before him, will he not do wrong to the one who invited him? Would it not have been better never to have come? So you too have come here, you have sung the hymn with everyone, and in what you did not do because you were unworthy, you have professed yourself worthy: How can you remain at the table and not partake? And what follows in Chrysostom. If a preacher were to speak such words today, would he not be thought ridiculous? Undoubtedly today (as everyone sees) life is lived far differently from formerly, and a different custom has prevailed from the old one. It is clear as midday that throughout the whole primitive Church the faithful plainly carried the Eucharist home from the sacred assembly and kept it privately with them until they were permitted to take it. Hence Tertullian, advising those who on station days did not think they should attend the prayers, because the station had to be ended by receiving the body of the Lord, that they should keep the body of the Lord which they had received, and so both the participation in the sacrifice and the performance of duty would be preserved. The same is also plain from the story that Cyprian relates of a certain woman who, when she tried to open with unworthy hands her chest in which the holy body of the Lord was kept, was deterred by fire rising from it, so that she did not dare to touch it. Basil, writing to Patricia (Pattitia) much later than Cyprian, shows that this custom still prevailed in his own century; Petavius also expressly confesses this. And Ambrose, a contemporary of Basil, confirms this most plainly, when he relates that his brother Satyrus, shipwrecked, feared not death but that he should leave life without the mysteries, and asked from the bishop, since he knew that the bishop had been initiated, that divine sacrament of the faithful, not so that he might thrust curious eyes into its secrets, but so that his faith…

units.la: Ambrosius, dum narrat fratrem suum Satyrum in naufragio constitutum non mortem metuentem, sed ne vacuum mysteriis exiret è vita, quos initiatos esse cognouerat, ab hiu divinum illud fidelium sacramentum poposcisse, non ut curiosos oculos insereret arcanis, sed ut fidei sua consequeretur auxilium; etenim ligari fecisse in orario, & orarium innoluisse collo, atq; ita se deiecisse in mare & ex undis enatasse. Cur hunc morem Roma, si Patres vere veneratur, non seruavit? Cur quod olim adeo frequens fuit nunc adeo improbatur, ut sine sacrilegio, ac huius, ut ait Petavius, sacramenti profanatione ferri non posse videatur, ut ne sanctis monialibus quidem ipsis concedatur ut in coenobio suo, ac ne in choro quidem, aut usquam alibi publicè in Ecclesia sacramentum asservent? Docet praeterea Ambrosius tum temporis fas fuisse Eucharistiam mari deporrare, quem tamen morem, licet antiquum, adeo auersatur Ecclesia Romana, ut religiosum putet sacramentum super ullis aquis, siue in fluvio, siue in mare habere. Illa ipsa consuetudo sacramentum priuatim asservandi, liquidò offendit fideles olim ipsum manibus accepisse, quod etiam ex Tertulliano constat. Inuectus enim in Christianos statuariam, vel picturam, factitantes, criminatur eos quòd eas manus admouerent corpori Domini quibus damonis corpora contulissent, id est quibus idola fabricassent. Cyprianus multa passim habet in hanc rem disertissima id ipsumque testatur Gregorius Nazianzenus Poemate sexagesimo tertio, & Concilij Constantinopoli in Trulla celebrati ab anno Christi DCLXXXX primus, & centesimus canon sancit, ut si quis voluerit communicare de corpore Christi manus in formam crucis figuret, & sic adeat, & suscipiat gratiam communionem: quod etiam usu receptum iam erat Cyrilli Hierosolymitani temporibus. Nemo tamen nescit aliam iam esse communionis istius rationem, & fideles Eucharistiam, non manu, sed ore accipere, in quod ab ipso sacerdote ingeritur. Pervelim etiam doceri quo Veteris Ecclesiae canone in-
units.tr: Ambrose, relating that his brother Satyrus, when he was in a shipwreck, did not fear death but was anxious lest he should depart from life without the mysteries, of which he knew he had been initiated, asked for that divine sacrament of the faithful from him. He did so not so that he might thrust curious eyes into its secrets, but so that he might obtain the help of his faith. For he had himself bound in a cloth, and tied the cloth round his neck, and so threw himself into the sea and swam out of the waves. Why, if Rome truly venerates the Fathers, has it not kept this custom? Why has what was once so common now become so disapproved that it seems it cannot be carried without sacrilege and, as Petavius says, a profanation of this sacrament? Not even holy nuns are permitted to keep the sacrament publicly in their convent, nor even in the choir, nor anywhere else in the Church. Ambrose further teaches that at that time it was lawful to cast the Eucharist into the sea. Yet the Roman Church so abhors this custom, though it is ancient, that it regards it as sinful to keep the sacrament over any waters, whether river or sea. That very custom of keeping the sacrament privately clearly shows that the faithful of old received it into their own hands, which is also evident from Tertullian. For, attacking Christians who make statues or paintings, he accuses them that they applied to the body of the Lord those hands which they had offered to the bodies of demons, that is, the hands with which they had made idols. Cyprian has many very clear passages on this matter, and Gregory Nazianzen attests it in his sixty-third poem. The hundredth canon of the Council of Constantinople, held in the Trullo in the year of Christ 692, lays down that if anyone wishes to communicate of the body of Christ, let him shape his hands in the form of a cross, and so approach and receive the grace of communion. This practice was already in use in the time of Cyril of Jerusalem. Yet no one is unaware that the manner of communion is now different, and that the faithful receive the Eucharist not in the hand but in the mouth, into which it is put by the priest himself. units.la: Cypr. ep. 56. pag. 130. B. lib. de bono patient. Greg. Nazian. carm. 63. Synod. Quinisext. can. 100. stitutæ sint Missæ illæ solitariæ, quæ singulis diebus fiunt & canuntur, in quibus, præter ministrum qui consecrat, nemo communicat, & qui cum reverentia Antiquitati debita convenire possit Concilij Tridentini Canon. a Si quis dixerit missas in quibus solus sacerdos sacramentaliter communicat illicitas esse, ideoque abrogandas esse, anathema sit. Cùm ignotæ fuerint in vetere Ecclesia, ut Cassander, in consultatione ad Imperatorem, fusè probat. b Verùm nihil Antiquitatis studiosos æquè malè habet ac consuetudo illa quam decretis & canonibus distertis Ecclesia Romana in duobus conciliis suis generalibus, altero Constantiæ c, altero Tridentini d habitis inuexit & instituit, de nullo præter eum unum qui consecrat, ad calicis Eucharistici communionem admittendo. Arcet enim ab eo laicos primùm, tum & sacerdotes ipsos, & alios Clericos qui sacramentum non consecerunt, cùm universa Ecclesia antiqua per quadringentos & mille annos ad sacri & benedicti calicis sanctam communionem non minùs utrosque adhibuerit, quàm ad sacri panis participationem, quod duo ista Concilia in Præfatione novellæ suæ constitutionis diserte ipsa confitenture. Imò hic usus etiamnum hodie viget, inter omnes totius orbis Christianos, Russos, Græcosf, Armenos, Æthiopes g, Protestantes h & alios, solis exceptis ex communione Romana Latinis. Peraduius quidem hanc sub utraque communicandi praxin, & Apostolorum temporibus obtinuisse, & pluribus in Ecclesia seculis retentam fuisse confiterur: idque scribit negari non posse nisi ab homine insigniter ac supra omnem modum, vel impudenti, vel certè imperito. Sed præter quàm quòd hanc sub utraque (ut hodie loqui mos est) specie communionem; concedebant veteres, non videntur (quod longè maius est) nisi in casibus quibusdam extraordinariis communionem sub una specie permisisse. Quod si aliter fuisset, non monuisset Leo Papa hac nota Manichæos à Catholicis internoscendos k. Cùm ad legendam infidelitatem suâ nostris audent (inquit) interesse mysteriis, mysteriùs, ita in sacramentorum communione se temperant, ut interdum tutiùs lateant, ore indigna Christi corpus accipiunt, sanguinem autem redemptionis nostrae omnino haurire declinant: quod ideo subjungit Leo) vestram volumus scire sanctitatem, ut vobis huiusmodi homines bis manifestentur indicijs. Si nunc Leo viveret, & istorum missas videret, putaret profecto Romanos suos, exceptis Sacerdotibus conficientibus, omnes esse Manichaeos. Eodem quoque pertinet nobile Gelasij Pontificis Romani decretum Comperimus quod quidam sumpta tantummodo corporis sacri portione a calice sacri cruoris abstineant qui proculdubio (quo a s s. s. 12.) niam nescio qua superstitione docentur obstringi) aut integra sacramenta percipiant, aut ab integris arceantur, quia divisio unius eiusdem mysterij sine grandi sacrilegio non potest provenire. Huc accedit quod Ibae Edesseno Episcopo accusatores inter caetera objiciunt, quod vinum altari tam parcè submi-nistraret, ut cum id aliquando, communicata exigua plebis parte, repente defecisset, qui sanctum corpus diuidebant, eo intrare iusserit, quòd de sanguine Domini nihil superesset. Nihil necesse erat ob vini penuriam mysteriorum celebrationem soluere, si solo pane, sine vini specie, communio fieri potuit. Si apud Constantienses & Tridentinos summa habita fuit Patrum auctoritas, cur illi, quod ab his tam diu tamque constanter seruatum fuit, abrogauerunt? Quomodo item cum debita antiquitati reuerentia hic postremi Concilij Canon conciliari potest? Catholicam non iustis causis & rationibus adductam fuisse, ut Laicos atque etiam clericos non conficientes sub pane tantummodo specie communicaret, aut in eo errasse, anathema sit.
units.tr: Cypr. ep. 56. pag. 130. B. lib. de bono patient. Greg. Nazian. carm. 63. Synod. Quinisext. can. 100. those solitary Masses were instituted, which are said and sung every day, and in which no one communicates except the minister who consecrates, and which can be reconciled with the reverence due to antiquity. The canon of the Council of Trent reads: If anyone says that Masses in which only the priest communicates sacramentally are unlawful, and therefore ought to be abolished, let him be anathema. Since they were unknown in the ancient Church, as Cassander fully proves in his consultation addressed to the Emperor. But nothing troubles lovers of antiquity so much as that custom which the Roman Church, by plain decrees and canons in two of its general councils, the one at Constance and the other at Trent, introduced and established: that no one except the one who consecrates may be admitted to communion of the Eucharistic chalice. For it first excludes the laity, then the priests themselves and other clerics who have not consecrated the sacrament, although the whole ancient Church for four hundred and a thousand years admitted both alike to the holy communion of the sacred and blessed chalice no less than to participation in the sacred bread. The two councils themselves plainly confess this in the preface to their new constitution. Indeed this practice still flourishes today among all Christians of the whole world: Russians, Greeks, Armenians, Ethiopians, Protestants and others, the Latins within the Roman communion alone excepted. Peraudius indeed concedes that this practice of communion under both kinds prevailed even in the times of the Apostles and was retained in the Church for many centuries. He writes that this cannot be denied except by a man remarkably and beyond all measure either shameless or certainly ignorant. But apart from the fact that the ancients allowed communion under both kinds (as it is now customary to say), they do not appear, and this is far more significant, to have permitted communion under one kind except in certain extraordinary cases. If it had been otherwise, Pope Leo would not have warned that the Manichaeans should be distinguished from Catholics by this mark: "When they dare to attend our mysteries in order to conceal their unbelief, they so moderate themselves in the communion of the sacraments that they sometimes lie more safely hidden. They receive the body of Christ with an unworthy mouth, but they entirely refuse to drink the blood of our redemption." Leo adds: "We wish your holiness to know that such people are revealed to you by these signs." If Leo were alive now and saw their Masses, he would surely think that all their Romans, except the priests who consecrate, are Manichaeans. To this also belongs the noble decree of Gelasius, Pope of Rome: We have found that certain people, having taken only a portion of the sacred body, abstain from the chalice of the sacred blood. These, without doubt, are taught to be bound by I know not what superstition. Let them either receive the sacraments entire, or be excluded from them entire, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without great sacrilege. Add to this that among other things the accusers object to Ibas, Bishop of Edessa, that he supplied the altar with wine so sparingly that once, when a small part of the people had communicated and the wine suddenly failed, he ordered those who were dividing the holy body to go in there, because nothing of the Lord's blood was left. There was no need to suspend the celebration of the mysteries for lack of wine, if communion could be made with bread alone, without the form of wine. If among the Constantinians and the Tridentines the authority of the Fathers was held in such high regard, why did they abrogate what these had kept so long and so constantly? How, too, can the last canon of that council be reconciled with the reverence due to antiquity? If anyone says that the Catholic Church was not induced by just causes and reasons to give communion under the bread alone to laity and also to clerics not consecrating, or has erred in this, let him be anathema.

units.la: Ægre enim videtur Ecclesia recens posse absolui, quin antiqua damnetur, cùm factis contradictoriis inter se liquido pugnent: prohibet enim recens quod antiqua concedebat: Imo (ut sane videtur) antiqua prohibebat, quod recens imperat. Quomodo alteram iustas habuisse rationes confirmabis, quin illico alteram iis caruisse, vel iniustas habuisse asseueres, cùm conster, neque tempus, neque ipsum hominum genus à ducentis annis immutatum esse? Nulla enim in recentiorum gratiam fingi potest ratio, quæ veteres non adstrinxerit, neque pariter ulla afferri quæ Veterum contrario instituto faueat, quæ recentiores tenere & fleƈtere non debuerit, adeo ut necessariò oporteat hos vel illos erroris, vel saltem negligentiæ aut inscitiæ reos teneri. Superest ergo ut dicamus Romam, quandoquidem se infallibilem contendit, veterem Ecclesiam inscitiæ vel saltem iniuriæ damnare, quod perpatum mihi convenire videtur iis qui nihil præter antiquitatis reverentiam clamant. Atque hic amplum meditandi campum habent qui verè sunt antiquitatis studiosi: Nam de rationibus quidem (inquiunt) quæ ultimi Concilij Patres permoverunt quomodo iudicare possumus, an ex iustæ sint, necne, cùm nullas illi ediderint? Veterum verò rationes, in quodam libro ad finem operum Cassandri Parisiis excuso expositæ, firmæ sunt & perspicuæ, totaque ut videtur, sapientiam & charitatem redolent, sed nihil necesse est nos in istis diutius immorari. Satis est ad institutum nostrum quod hinc constet Ecclesiam Romanam antiquissimum ritum abrogasse. Præter cærimonias istas apud Patres in Baptismo & Eucharistia receptas, plurimæ aliæ,quæ olim etiam in usu fuerunt, sublatæ sunt. In eo ordine ieiunium Sabbathi non colloco, licèt Romæ obseruatum fuerit præter reliquæ uniuersæ Ecclesiæ morem, quæ illud pro piaculo habebat, hæc enim diuersitas iam ipsius Augustini temporibus cernitur, ac proinde Romæ recentiori tribui non debet. Eadem ratione taceo quæ Firmilianus suo tempore, id est, anno quinquagesimo & ducentesimo à Christo nato,scribebat. Eos qui Romæ essent non ea in omnibus obseruare quæ essent ab origine tradita,& frustra Apostolorum auctoritatem prætendere.Sed hic tacere nō debeo inter'omnes Christianos olim more receptum fuisse, ut, neque die Dominica, neque Paschate ad Pentecostem, in genua procumberent. Id institutum in Ecclesia konmana universa penitus abrogatum est, quod tamen, sive ob antiquitatem, sive ob auctoritatem eorum apud quos receptum & commendatum fuit, nullus pene ritus venerabilior occurrit. Ejus enim memini vetustissimus Quæstionum & responsionum apud Justinum Scriptor, & rationem reddit, probatque ex quodam Irenæi loco & à temporibus Apostolicis initium ejus repetit, Tertullianus quoque meminit, & Epiphanius & Hieronymus, & morem inter Ecclesiæ instituta censent. Ipsa quinctiam (quod longè majus est) sanctissima Synodus universalis Nicæna diserte canone ritum illum confirmavit. Quandoquidem sunt quidam (inquiunt ccexviii. illi venerandi Patres) qui die Dominica genu flectunt & in Pentecostes diebus, ut in omni parœcia (vel hodie loquimur Diœcesi) omnis eodem modo custodiantur, visum est [sanctæ Synodo, ut à fidelibus preces Deo fundantur. Et renovatà & explicata fuit antiqua illa consuetudo ad finem septimi seculi, in Concilio Constantinopolitano quinquesexto, quo prohibitum est ne genua flecterentur iis quatuor & viginti horis, quæ fluunt à Sabbati vespera usque ad vesperam diei Dominicæ. Nemo item nescit abrogatum fuisse jejunium feriæ quartæ, quod tamen in usu fuit apud Veteres, ut patet ex pseudo-Ignatio, Clemente Alexandrino, Petro Episcopo Alexandrino & Martyre, b Epiphanio, c & aliis. Eadem libertate rejectæ sunt vigiliæ in Veteri Ecclesia receptæ, quæque Hieronymus d adversus Vigilantium probavit & defendit, adeo ut Vigilantii in hac parte sententia Hieronymianæ prævaluerit. Idem Hieronymus e alicubi tradit tenere Alexandriam vocat morem (sic tempore receptum, quo ante diem Vigiliarum Paschæ ante noctis dimidium populos dimittere non [...] licebat. Quid factum est instituto isto non simpliciter prisco, sed, si Hieronymo fides, ab Apostolis ipsis derivato? Habemus item ex variis monumentis prohibitionem sanguinis & suffocati diutissimè in Ecclesia viguisse. Primis quidem seculis summo studio observatam fuisse ex Tertulliano & Eusebio satis constat. Concilium Constantinopolitanum quinisextum jubet excommunicari laicos & deponi clericos qui aliter fecerint. Hadrianus I. A. D. 795. mortuus eadem severitate hanc legem apud Latinos praecepisse deprehenditur, ad Egilam Hispanum Episcopum ita scribens. Nos quidem Apostolicis praeceptis imbuti atque eruditi confirmantes pradicamus quod si quis pecudum aut suffocatum manducaverit, non solum eruditionis totius alienus, sed ipsius quoque intelligentia communis prorsus extraneus, sub anathematis vinculo obligatus in laqueos incidat Diaboli. Pamelius in Apologeticum Tertulliani observat non ita diu esse ex quo Christiani vescimur suffocato & morticina carne, & quotquot hac de re supra CCCC. annos scripserunt certum poenitentiae tempus praescribere, si quis Apostolicam legem sacris praevaricatus. Illa tamen, licet antiqua & generaliter recepta, in desuetudinem abiit, sensimque & sine sensu apud Latinos sepulta, adeo ut ne unus quidem (quod sciam) quo tempore, & qua ratione id factum fuerit observarit. Hoc unum satis apparet, non esse amplius in usu. Hoc ipsum & observare est de oratione pro sanctis mortuis, quae in scriptis veterum apertissimè extat. Epiphanius scribit orari pro justis & Patribus ac Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, Evangelistis, Martyribus, Confessoribus, &c. Ut Dominum Jesum Christum singulari honore prosequentes ab caeterorum hominum ordine segregemus. Supersunt & quorumdam ejus argumenti preces, ut in Liturgia Jacobi, in Syriaca Basilii, postquam actum est de Patriarchis, Prophetis, Joanne Baptista, Stephano, Virgine Maria & omnibus
units.tr: The modern Church can hardly be absolved without condemning the ancient one, since its practices plainly contradict each other. The recent Church forbids what the ancient one allowed, and indeed (as it certainly seems) the ancient one forbade what the recent one commands. How will you show that the one had just reasons without at once admitting that the other lacked them, or had unjust ones, when it is clear that neither the times nor the human race itself has changed in the last two hundred years? For no reason can be devised in favour of recent men that did not also bind the ancients, nor can any be offered in support of the ancients' contrary practice that recent men ought not to have held and bent to. So it must be that either one or the other is held guilty of error, or at least of carelessness or ignorance. It remains, then, for us to say that Rome, since it claims to be infallible, must condemn the ancient Church of ignorance or at least of wrong, which seems to me a very plain consequence for those who cry out for nothing but reverence for antiquity. Here those who are truly devoted to antiquity have a wide field for reflection. "As for the reasons," they say, "that moved the Fathers of the last Council, how can we judge whether they were just, since they published none?" The reasons of the ancients, set out in a certain book printed at Paris at the end of the works of Cassander, are firm and clear, and seem to breathe wisdom and charity throughout; but there is no need for us to linger on them longer. It is enough for our purpose that it is evident from this that the Roman Church has abrogated a most ancient rite. Besides those ceremonies received among the Fathers in Baptism and the Eucharist, many others which were also once in use have been abolished. In this category I do not place the fast on the Sabbath, although it was observed at Rome contrary to the custom of the whole rest of the Church, which regarded it as a sin; for this difference is already seen in the time of Augustine himself, and therefore should not be ascribed to the recent Church at Rome. For the same reason I pass over what Firmilian, in his own time, that is in the year 250 after the birth of Christ, wrote: that those at Rome did not observe in everything what had been handed down from the beginning, and vainly pleaded the authority of the Apostles. They who were at Rome did not observe in all things what had been handed down from the beginning, and vainly pleaded the authority of the Apostles. But here I must not be silent that it was once the custom received among all Christians that they should not kneel on the Lord's day, nor from Easter to Pentecost. This practice has been entirely abrogated throughout the Roman Church; yet, whether on account of its antiquity or of the authority of those among whom it was received and commended, scarcely any rite more venerable can be found. For the most ancient writer of the Questions and Answers among the works of Justin recalls it and gives its reason, and by appeal to a passage of Irenaeus he proves that it goes back to Apostolic times. Tertullian also mentions it, and Epiphanius and Jerome, and they reckon the custom among the institutions of the Church. Moreover, the most holy universal Synod of Nicaea itself (which is still more significant) expressly confirmed that rite by a canon. For there are some, say those venerable Fathers (318 of them), who kneel on the Lord's day and in the days of Pentecost; so that, in order that all things may be observed in the same manner in every parish (or, as we say today, diocese), it seemed good to the holy Synod that prayers should be offered to God by the faithful. That ancient custom was also renewed and explained at the end of the seventh century, in the Quinisext Council of Constantinople, which forbade kneeling during those twenty-four hours that run from Saturday evening to Sunday evening. Likewise, no one is unaware that the fast on Wednesday was abrogated, although it was in use among the ancients, as is clear from the pseudo-Ignatius, Clement of Alexandria, Peter, bishop of Alexandria and martyr, Epiphanius, and others. With the same freedom the vigils received in the ancient Church have been rejected, which Jerome approved and defended against Vigilantius, so that Vigilantius's opinion on this point has prevailed over that of Jerome. Jerome also elsewhere records that the custom then held at Alexandria was that, before the day of the Paschal vigil, the people were not allowed to be dismissed before midnight. What has become of that institution, not simply ancient but, if we trust Jerome, derived from the Apostles themselves? We also have from various records that the prohibition of blood and of what is strangled was very long in force in the Church. In the earliest centuries it was certainly observed with the greatest care, as is sufficiently clear from Tertullian and Eusebius. The Quinisext Council of Constantinople orders that laymen be excommunicated and clerics deposed who act otherwise. Hadrian I, who died in 795, is found to have enjoined this law with the same severity among the Latins, writing thus to Egila, bishop of Spain: We, indeed, imbued and instructed in the Apostolic precepts, confirm and proclaim that if anyone eats of animals or of what is strangled, he is not only alien to all instruction but also entirely a stranger to the common understanding itself, bound by the chain of anathema, and falls into the snares of the Devil. Pamelius, in his commentary on Tertullian's Apology, observes: It is not so long since Christians have eaten strangled and carrion flesh, and all who have written on this matter over the last four hundred years have prescribed a fixed time of repentance for anyone who transgressed the Apostolic law. Yet that rule, although ancient and generally received, has fallen into disuse, and has gradually and almost imperceptibly been buried among the Latins, so that not even one person (so far as I know) has noted when and for what reason this happened. One thing alone is sufficiently clear: it is no longer in use. The same is true of prayer for the holy dead, which stands out most plainly in the writings of the ancients. Epiphanius writes that prayers are offered for the just and for the Fathers and Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, Martyrs, Confessors, etc., so that, paying singular honour to the Lord Jesus Christ, we may separate them from the rest of mankind. There also survive prayers of this kind in certain liturgies, as in the Liturgy of James, and in the Syriac liturgy of Basil, after mention has been made of the Patriarchs, Prophets, John the Baptist, Stephen, the Virgin Mary and all

units.la: emnibus sanctis. Memento (inquiunt) etiam Domine eorum qui decesserunt, migraruntque ex hac vita, & Episcoporum orthodoxorum, qui inde à Petro & Jacobo Apostolo ad hunc usque diem rectum fidei verbum clarè fuerunt profes⁠si, & nominatim Ignatij, Dionysii, Julij, ac reliquorum divorum laudabilis memoria. In Liturgia Marci nominatis Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, Martyribus, Confessoribus, Episcopis. Et horum omnium animas (inquiunt) fac requiescere Dominator Domine Deus noster in sanctorum tuorum Tabernaculis, in regno tuo, largiens ipsis promissionum tuarum bona, quæ oculus non vidit, & auris non audivit, & in cor hominis non ascenderunt. Sic in Liturgia Joannis Chrysostomi, offerimus tibi hunc rationalem cultum pro iis qui in fide requieverunt. Et tamen morem istum in Universum adeo antiquavit & improbavit Ecclesia Romana ut non putet, sine sanctorum injuria, hujusmodi pro iis supplicationes fieri posse. Plura hujus generis ritunm Veterum à recentibus discerni⁠ma curiosis observare facile erit.
units.tr: all the saints. Remember also, they say, O Lord, those who have departed and passed out of this life, and the orthodox bishops who from Peter and James the Apostles down to this day have clearly professed the right word of faith, and especially the praiseworthy memory of Ignatius, Dionysius, Julius, and the other divine men. In the Liturgy of Mark, after the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors and Bishops are named: And make to rest, they say, the souls of all of them, O Lord God, Ruler, in the tabernacles of your saints, in your kingdom, granting them the good things of your promises, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man. So too in the Liturgy of John Chrysostom: We offer to you this reasonable worship for those who have rested in the faith. And yet the Roman Church has so entirely abrogated and disapproved this custom in general that it does not think such supplications for them can be made without injury to the saints. It will be easy for curious readers to observe many more differences of this kind between the rites of the ancients and those of the moderns.

units.la: Neque vero major est Romanorum cum Veteribus in disciplina concordia. Primaria fere & plerarumque aliarum origo in ministrorum Ecclesiasticorum electionibus & ordinationibus versatur, quæ disciplinæ & ministerii Ecclesiastici unica sunt basis. Eas in antiquissima Ecclesia partim à populo pependisse constat. Singuli enim fidelium cœtus, vel suos pastores eligebant, vel in oblatorum ad id munus vitam & mores inquirebant, eosque probabant. Pontianus Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis Diaconus narrat q Cyprianum judicio Dei & plebis favore ad officium Sacerdotii & Episcopatus gradum, cum esset adhuc neophytus & ut putabatur, novellus, electum fuisse. Idipsum Cyprianus variis in locis docet: In Epist. LII. hæc habet. Factus est Cornelius Episcopus de Dei & Christi ejus judicio, de clericorum penè omnium testimonio, de plebis quæ tunc affuit suffragio, & de Sacerdotum antiquorum & virorum bonorum collegio, Alibi hæc etiam scribit . Ipsa plebs maximè habet potestatem, vel eligendi dignos Sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi: quod & ipsum videmus de Divina authoritate deferendere, ut sacerdos plebe præsente sub omnium oculis deligatur, & dignus atque idoneus publico judicio ac testimonio comprobetur. Ideoque paulo post subdit. Diligenter de traditione Divina & Apostolica observatione observandum est & tenendum, quod apud nos quoque, & fere per provincias universas, tenetur, ut ad ordinationes rite celebrandas, ad eam plebem, cui præpositus ordinatur, Episcopi ejusdem provinciæ proximi quinque convenient, & episcopus deligatur plebe præsente, qua singulorum vitam plenissime novit, & uniuscujusque actum de ejus conversatione perspexit. units.tr: Nor is there greater agreement between the Romanists and the ancients in discipline. The primary, and almost the origin of most others, lies in the elections and ordinations of ecclesiastical ministers, which are the sole foundation of ecclesiastical discipline and ministry. It is established that in the most ancient Church these depended in part on the people. For each assembly of the faithful either chose its own ministers, or inquired into the life and character of those offered for that office and approved them. Pontianus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, relates that Cyprian was chosen by the judgment of God and the favour of the people to the office of priesthood and the rank of bishop, when he was still a neophyte and, as was thought, a novice. Cyprian himself teaches the same in various places. In Letter 52 he says: Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present, and by the assembly of the ancient priests and good men. Elsewhere he also writes: The people themselves have the greatest power either to choose worthy priests or to reject unworthy ones; which we also see to be derived from divine authority, that a priest be chosen with the people present, before the eyes of all, and be approved as worthy and fit by public judgment and testimony. And so he adds shortly after: Diligently must be observed and held to the divine tradition and Apostolic practice, which is kept also among us and almost throughout all the provinces: that for the due celebration of ordinations, the bishops of the same province nearest to that people over which a leader is to be ordained shall assemble, and a bishop be chosen with the people present, who knows most fully the life of each and has seen the conduct of each from his behaviour. D. xin illis temporibus in usu fuisse, ex historia Ecclesiastica certissime constare, diuq; durasse, & in Canonibus non semel repetitis decretis confirmatam esse, cujusmodi sunt (inquit) Synodi Carthaginensis IV, Arelatensis II, Parisiensis III, Celestini I, & Leonis I, Romanorum Pontificum, aliique complures canones. Inde est quod Episcopus Nicomediensis Eusebius inter alias causas, propter quas vitio ordinatum fuisse Athanasium criminabatur; hoc objiceret, quod ad ejus ordinationem plebis consensus defuisset. Respondent vero Concilii Alexandrini Patres, uno animo a populo Alexandrino cum singularibus pietatis & industriæ testimoniis, ad Episcopatum expetitum fuisse. Sic etiam Julius Ep. Romanus inter cetera quæ Gregorii ad Episcopatum Alexandrinum evecti ordinationi defuisse memorat; hoc in primis monet ipsum a populis non fuisse postulatum. Et perspicuè apparet ex Hieronymo, & ex Actis Concilii Constantinopolitani, & Calcedonensis, & ex Pontificali, & ex variis aliis monumentis hanc electionum atque ordinationum formam & rationem diu in Ecclesia permansisse. units.tr: x Apud Athanasium, Apol. 2, p. 726 B and 727 D: that in those times it was in use is most certainly established from ecclesiastical history; it lasted a long time and was confirmed in the canons by decrees repeated more than once, such as (he says) the Fourth Synod of Carthage, the Second of Arles, the Third of Paris, the decrees of Celestine I and Leo I, Roman bishops, and several other canons. Hence Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, among the other grounds on which he accused Athanasius of having been ordained irregularly, objected this: that the consent of the people was lacking at his ordination. The fathers of the Alexandrian Council, however, reply that he was sought for the episcopate with one mind by the people of Alexandria, who gave particular testimonies of his piety and diligence. Likewise Julius, the Roman bishop, among the other defects he records in the ordination of Gregory, raised to the Alexandrian see, warns above all that he had not been requested by the people. And it is clearly evident from Jerome, from the Acts of the Councils of Constantinople and Chalcedon, from the Pontifical, and from various other records that this form and manner of election and ordination remained for a long time in the Church. Conc. p. 432. nemiuem Laicorum principum semet inferere electioni, vel promotioni Patriarchae, vel Metropolitae aut cujuflibet episcopi, &c. cum nullam in talibus potestatem quemquam potestati vocum, vel caeterorum laicorum habere conveniat, sed potiùs silere, ac attendere sibi, usque quo regulariter a collegio Ecclesiae suspiciat finem electio futuri Pontificis, ac postremò quisquis contra agere tentaverit anathemati subjicit. Hujus canonis, velut globi alicujus e tormento majori effulminati, vi dejecta est Patrum, antiquissimorumque Ecclesiae seculorum auctoritas, quae plebi fideli aliquam in Pastorum suorum electione partem hactenus concesserat. Neque vetus mos post illa tempora resurgere, aut plane restitui potuit. Nunc verò palàm est plebem suo hoc jure penitus fraudari, ut ne minimam quidem partem habeat, non dico in Paparum, vel Primatum, vel Archiepiscoporum, sed nec in minimorum quidem Episcoporum electione. Plebis olim ut in suorum Pastorum electione, sic etiam in aliis omnibus negotiis, quae alicujus essent momenti, suae erant partes. Cum Cypriani aetate excitata fuisset gravissima persecutio, & multi, qui Gentilium violentiae cesserant, peccati conscientia ducti, ad Ecclesiae quidem pacem recipi vellent ac contenderent, sed ita tamen, ut à Canonicis poenis, quae peccatoribus tunc graves atque diuturnae infligebantur, immunes essent, & ad hanc merendam veniam Confessorum gratiam emendicarent Sacerdotumque fidem labefactarent, ut ad communionem absque praevia satisfactione admitterentur. Cyprianus studiosissimus veteris disciplinae assertor advertus hanc antiquae severitatis relaxationem varia scripsit, ex quibus manifestum est plebi Christianae suas in cognitione & definitione causarum sitarum partes fuisse. Epistola enim xi dicit {f} presbyteros illos, qui temere, & praeter disciplinam hujusmodi peccatores admittebant, acturos apud se, & apud Confessores ipsos, & apud plebem universam causam suam. Et ad plebem Carthaginensem {g} Cum, pace, nobis omnibus à Domino prius data, ad Ecclesiam regredi coeperimus, tunc examinabuntur singula PRÆSENTIBUS & JUDICANTIBUS VOBIS. Et hac ipsa epistola, & ad hanc ipsam rem subjicit locum supra à nobis in capite de veterum librorum depravatione allatum. Audiant quaso patienter consilium nostrum, expectent regressionem nostram, & cum ad vos per Dei misericordiam venerimus, convocati coepiscopi plures, secundum Domini disciplinam, confessorum praesentiam, & vestram quoque sententiam, beatorum martyrum litteras & desideria examinare possimus. Hinc est quod alibi testatur ⁠se à primordio episcopatus sui statuisse nihil sine consilio fratrum suorum Presbyterorum & Diaconorum & sine consensu plebis, privata sententia gerere. Cui plura de his doceri cordi erit, adeat epistolam xiv. ejusdem Auctoris & xxviii. de causa Philumeni & Fortunati Subdiaconorum, & xl. de Feliciissimo abstinento. Item lxvii. ad Clerum & plebes in Hispania consistentes conjunctim scriptam, in qua laudat eos quod Episcopos suos gravissimorum peccatorum reos loco movissent. Sed ne quis existimet hoc institutum in sola Ecclesia Carthaginensi in usu fuisse, non omittam Clerum Romanum ipsius consilium probare. Nobis (inquiunt) in tam ingenti negotio placet, quod & tu ipse tractasti prius, Ecclesiae pacem subfinendam, deinde sic collatione consiliorum cum Episcopis, Presbyteris, Diaconis, Confefforibus pariter ac slamibus laicis facta lapsorum tractare rationem. Et (quod mea sententia apprime notandum est) ipse Cyprianus ad Cornelium Episcopum Romanum scribens, dicit apud se non esse dubium quin, pro mutua dilectione quam alter alteri debebat & exhibebat, florentissimo Clero secum Romæ præsidenti, & sanctissimæ atque amplissimæ plebi legeret semper litteras suas. Unde pater Romæ etiam ad plebem delata fuisse negotia Ecclesiastica. Nihil opus est monere quàm nunc contemnatur Veterum in hac re cum auctoritas tum exemplum. Omnes satis per se vident, non solum in consiliis, & in foro Episcoporum nullam haberi plebis rationem, sed & pro hæretico habitum iri, si quis simile mile quippiam agitare aut incœptare audèret. Illud in primis velim apud te reputes, si quis nunc fit Episcopus, vel Archiepiscopus qui ad Pontificem Romanum illa Cypriani ad Cornelium scribat. Frater carissime hortor te, & peto à te, ut quod per te ipsum ut plurimum & cum honore facis, id ipsum à me rogatus facias, scilicet ut hæc mea ad te epistola florentissimo Clero, qui istic tecum præsidet, & sanctissimæ plebi legatur. Si quis inquam Præsul ad hodiernum Papam hæc scribat quo loco habendus sit, & an non mitissime atque optimè secum agi fit existimaturus, si nullam infœlicis epistolæ pœnam graviorem luat, quàm ut ludibrio excipiatur, ac velut morio mente captus, omniumque rerum ignarus contemnatur? Atqui hæc ipsissima sunt Cypriani ad Cornelium Papam verba. Verum ut Episcopi & alii Clerici plebem eo omni jure fraudaverunt, qua apud Veterem Ecclesiam gaudebat, tam in Præsulum electione, quàm in cæteris negotiis Ecclesiasticis, sic etiam ipsis Episcopis & Clericis Romanus Papa, non solum ista miserę plebis spolia, sed omnem pene reliquam potestatem atque auctoritatem detraxit ac eripuit, sibiq; uni totam vindicavit, & quam ab ipsis Christianismi primordiis, ab antiquissimis Ecclesiæ canonibus acceperant, & quam ipsi secutis postea temporibus per varias artes non sine magno labore, magnáq; industria paulatim comparaverant. Ista nescio quo modo intra breve tempus in unam Romam universa confluxerunt. Nicæni CCCXVIII. Patres definiunt Episcopum oportere ab omnibus episcopis, si fieri potest, qui sunt in Provincia ejus ordinari. Si vero hoc difficile fuerit, vel aliqua urgente necessitate, vel itineris longitudine, certè tres Episcopos debere in unum congregari, ita ut etiam caeterorum qui absentes sunt, literis consensum teneant, & ita faciant ordinationem. Potestatem verò, vel confirmationem per singulas provincias pertinere ad Metropolitanum Episcopum. Qui sanè Canon cum more superioribus seculis recepto plane congruit, ut ex loco proximè à nobis, ex LXVIII. Cypriani epistola allato, constat. Imo etiam sequentibus seculis diu observatus fuit, ut patet ex epistola Concilii Constantinopolitani I. ad Papam Damasum & ex oratione dominorum Moderatorum Concilii Chalcedonensis, de juribus quæ ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum in diœcesi sua pertinebant. Et tamen universo orbi notum est, quis sit hodie Ecclesiæ Romanæ usus. Nihil enim vere potestatis vel auctoritatis Metropolitanis eorumque Conciliis, in Episcoporum ordinatione relicqui fecit, ejus vis omnis ab uno Pontifice Romano penderet, & ab iis quibus, seu sponte, seu invitus ejus partem concesserit. Ipsi quidem Præsules non alii quàm ci uni hujus beneficii gratiam habent, neque munus inire licet, quin numerata pecunia urbis Papæ diplomata acceperint, & de Annalis, quas vocant, transfegerint. Neque aliter solent nomina sua inscribere quam hac formula N. miseratione Divina & sanctæ sedis Apostolicæ gratia Episcopus. Quarum quidem formularum nullum apparet in ullis antiquitatis monumentis vestigium. Ex tot Episcopis quorum etiamnum subscriptiones habemus, partim in Conciliis, partim in aliis libris & historiis, nec unus quidem occurrit qui se in solenni nominis sui inscriptione Episcopum Papæ Romani gratia profiteatur. Satis constat in Synodis provincialibus ac diœcesanis tractata olim ac decisa fuisse quævis Ecclesiastica negotia, ut manifestum est ex canonibus & exemplis quæ etiam extant: qualia sunt quæ de Ario & Eutyche apud veteres legimus, quos ab Alexandrina & Constantinopolitana Synodis anathemate percussos scimus. Hę vero hodie Synodi de minoribus tantùm causis cognoscunt; ° si què graviores occurrunt, ex non ab alio quam ab ipso Papa judicantur, neque Synodis per se aliud licet, quàm simpliciter de re inquirere, & quæ cognoverint ad Papam perscribere. Neque quisquam est in Episcopali ordine, quantumvis abjectus, qui in causa graviori & ad dignitatem suam pertinente, ab ullo alio quam à Pontifice Romano judicari possit. In his causis nihil juris est Metropolitano, nihil Primati, nihil Synodo Provinciæ, vel etiam Dioecesēos, quo sensu hæc vox à Veteribus accipiebatur? Præter ordinem quidem interdum à Papa aliqua iis causæ cognitio delegatur, sed ad instruendam duntaxat litem, Romamque mittendam, ubi demum à Pont. Rom. cognoscitur ac decernitur, ut diserte decretum est à Conc. Trid. . Mitto ereptam Episcopis præter veterum canones & morem in plerosque monachos, aliosque clericos, sive seculares, sive regulares, in suis parœciis consistentes inspectionem & jurisdictionem. Item quod Papa omnem in universum absolvendi, & in multis casibus, quos reservatos vocant, dispensandi potestatem, quæ omnium pariter Episcoporum olim fuit, sibi uni vindicavit: quod solus indulgentias largitur, jubilea promulgat, quæ nulla in omnibus antiquissimis seculis fuere. Ac ut paucis rem absolvam, Petavii nobilissimi Jesuitæ testimonium hic recitabo; quo multa hujus generis à suis expuncta exscecutus, Denique (inquit) ut sit finis, vel ex mediocri Patrum lectione certò intelligi cognoscig, potest, Ecclesiastica disciplina (ejus quidem quæ in ritibus atq; consuetudinibus sita est) partem magnam penitus immutatam esse, ejusque praxin nunc plane aliam esse, quàm quæ in primitiva Ecclesia olim fuit. Jam verò quod proprie ad eum disciplinæ ordinem pertinet qui in peccatoribus vel pœnitentiæ subjiciendis, vel ad communionem admittendis versatur, omnis ejus forma plane penitusque interciderit. Sola rei idea in Veterum libris superest, ut, verbi gratia in Gregorii Neocæsareensis, Basilii, & aliorum Epistolis canonicis, & in Conciliis tam œcumenicis quàm provincialibus.
