Ubi nunc sunt notissimi olim apud Veterem Ecclesiam quatuor pœnitentium gradus; quorum alii pro foribus Ecclesiæ flebant, alii cum Catechumenis audiebant, alii ad fidelium pedes provolvebantur, alii ad communes fidelium preces admittebantur; alii denique his omnibus perfuncti ad sacramentorum participationem admittebantur. Tanta olim erat seueritas, ut interdum poenitentia ad octo, decem & viginti annos fieret. Absolutionem autem lapsis non fuisse olim datam, nisi post peractam satisfactionem à Pastoribus juxta canones impositam, & constat ex omnibus antiquitatis monumentis, & confitentur eruditissimi quique Romanarum partium viri, Maldonatus, Petavius, alii quos commemorare longum est, & acriter hodie pugnant illi Theologi, qui ab aliis Jansenii, à se ipsis Augustini discipuli vocantur. Nunc vero etiam pueris notum est peccatores in Papæ communione statim post consessionem absolvi; absolutos demum de injunctis à sacerdote satisfactionibus præstandis cogitare. Quin & inter Jesuitas nuper repertus est qui æstu, & contentionis adversus Jansenistas studio ita abreptus est, ut non dubitarit scribere, satisfactionem ante absolutionem exigere neminem, nisi cum Catholici nominis jactura posse; & si qui ita instituant, eorum disciplinam desperationis esse aditum, indurationis & finalis impœnitentiæ viam, Tartari præcipitium, & cætera quæ referre piget, adeo sunt in sanctissimos Patres contumeliosa, quos certum est illam ipsam pœnitentiæ rationem, quam iste tantopere abominatur, constantissimè commendasse, & accuratissimè secutos esse. Cæterum hanc disciplinam, ubique apud veteres obviam, plane absorpsit quos apud eos nusquam cernitur nupera Romanorum auricularis (ut vocant) confessio. Ac ut illæ veterum saluberrimæ pœnitentibus pœnæ sublatæ sunt, aliæ quædam novæ suffectæ sunt, ad rem (fateor) Romanorum longè utilissimæ, sed peccatoribus perniciosissimæ, quales sunt Interdicta, cùm ob unius aut alterius, vel personæ, vel ordinis culpam, eamque aliquando non tam veram quàm fictam & imaginariam, Rebusplicæ totæ, & Regna integra, in quibus multæ hominum myriades sunt, sacramentorum communione multantur, quibus quasi instrumentis vitam & gratiam Christus miseris mortalibus impertitur, quod non ita pridem nobis pueriis adversus Rempublicam Venetam tentavit urbis Papa Paulus V. Quo in codice habetur adeo ferale institutum, quo animarum innoxiarum myriades propter paucorum peccata ad inferos damnantur; Qui quae sic fxvit potestas Apostolica dici potest, cùm, non ad destructionem, verùm ad aedificationem instituta sit potestas Apostolica? Pervelim item doceri quibus veterum canonibus nitatur cruenta Inquisitionis (ut vocant) disciplina, quae postquam vafris, & Christianissimo indignis, artibus, partim etiam merito horrendis cruciatibus, à misero homine haereseos confessionem extorsit, ad mortem damnat quem institucre debuit, cúmq; Magistratibus secularibus tradit, ac, ut constet Deo non minùs quàm hominibus illudi, diserte rogat, ne reus morte plectatur * sed ea tamen lege, ut nisi ante sextum, aut ad summum septimum diem quaesitissimo supplicio afficiatur, id est, vivus comburatur, idq; sine ulla, vel causae, vel facti cognitione, * ipsi judices omnibus censuris ad hanc carnificinam urgeantur, ac postremò excommunicentur, deponantur, & de omni dignitatis sive in Ecclesia, sive in Republica gradu deiiciantur. Tanta autem est illius instituti immanitas, ut tametsi reus (quod fidem penè superat) culpam agnoscat, poenitentiam profiteatur, poenam deprecetur, séq; omnibus Ecclesiae satisfactionibus etiam laboriosissimis ultro subiciat, nihilo secius tamen poenam capitalem luat, si ex eorum quidem genere fuerit quos relapsos vocant. O inhumanam poenitentiam, Scythisq; & Laestrigonibus solis dignam, Christi verò illius nomine indignissimam, qui jubebat, Apostolum suum non septies tantùm, sed septuagies septies condonare! Sed & ab Antiquitate, cujus isti sic successores & haeredes profiteri non dubitant, plane penitúsq; alienam! Mitissima enim illa antiquitas, cujus nomen tam inverecundè mentiuntur, clarè docuit, b Pietatis proprium esse, non cogere, sed perfuadere, cum Dominus vim non intulerit, sed uniuscujusque arbitrio ut se sequerentur permisserit. Diabolum vero quandoquidem nihil veri haberet, eorum ad quos accedit & a quibus recipitur, bipenni & securi fores infringere: Servatorem vero nostrum adeo esse mitem, ut doceat quidem, si quis vult post me venire, & si quis vult esse meus discipulus, at accedentem ad unumquemque neminem cogere, sed fores pulsare, & dicere. Aperi mihi soror mea, sponsa mea, & ad aperientes ingredi, sed si qui nolint audire, recedere, cum nec telis, nec militibus, nec manu armata veritas annuntietur, sed persuasione & consilio. Haec eadem antiquitas Arianos acriter increpat quod in propaganda & confirmanda religione sua vim adhiberent. Unde didicerunt (sicenim eos compellat) persecutionibus savire? se id habere a sanctis sanè non dixerint, sed a Diabolo traditum acceperunt. Item, jussit quidem Christus fugere, & sanctos fugerunt; at persequi incaptum est Diabolicum, & hoc ipsum adversus omnes expetit. Et alibi testatur, Arianos in hoc ipso quod proscribebant eos qui sententiae suae subscribere nollent (id verò longè minùs fuit quàm vivos exurere) se alienos à Christianismo, & Diaboli, ejusque daemonum amicos prodidisse. Haec eadem Antiquitas, apud alium Veterem Scriptorem, adversus eosdem Arianos qui in mortalibus ad fidem suam trahendis persecutionum terrorem & mundanorum bonorum illecebras adhibebant; in haec epiphonemata crumpit. Nunc proh dolor! divinam fidem suffragia terrena commendant, inopsque virtutis sua Christus, dum ambitio nomini suo concilitur, arguitur Terret exilis & carceribus Ecclesia, credique sibi cogit quae exilis & carceribus est credita, pendet à dignatione communitum, quae persequentium est consecrata terrore. Fugat Sacerdotes, quae fugatis sacerdotibus est propagata. Diligi se gloriatur a mundo, quae Christi esse non potuit, nisi eam mundus odisset. Quo sensu nobilissimus ex eodem genere Auctor scripserat. Fundendo sanguinem & patiendo, magis quam faciendo contumelias, Christi fundatam esse Ecclesiam, persecutionibus crevisse,
units.tr: d Pontif. Rom. in ordinat. Presbyt. sol. 38, vol. 2. vide supra Lib. 6. Conc. VIII. Can. 22. T. 3. Conc. p. 432. Let no lay prince thrust himself into the election or promotion of a Patriarch, a Metropolitan, or any bishop, etc., since it is not fitting for any lay person, whether a prince, a voter, or anyone else, to have any power in such matters, but rather to keep silent and wait until the election of the future Pontiff is regularly announced by the college of the Church; and finally, whoever tries to act otherwise is subjected to anathema. By this canon, as if by a ball struck from a great cannon, the authority of the Fathers and of the most ancient centuries of the Church was overthrown, which had hitherto granted the faithful people some share in the election of their ministers. Nor could the old custom be revived after those times, or be fully restored. Now it is plain that the people are wholly defrauded of this right, so that they have not the smallest part, I do not say in the election of the Pope, or of the Primate, or of the Archbishops, but not even in the election of the least of the bishops. In former times the people had their part not only in the election of their ministers but also in all other matters of any importance. When a very grave persecution had been stirred up in the time of Cyprian, many who had yielded to the violence of the Gentiles, moved by a sense of sin, wished and demanded to be received back into the peace of the Church, but on the condition that they be exempt from the canonical penalties, which were then imposed on sinners, severe and long-lasting, and that they beg for the favour of the confessors to obtain this pardon, and weaken the confidence of the priests, so that they might be admitted to communion without previous satisfaction. Cyprian, a most zealous defender of the old discipline, wrote various things against this relaxation of ancient severity, from which it is clear that the Christian people had their part in the examination and decision of cases. For in his eleventh letter he says that those elders who rashly and contrary to discipline admitted such sinners would have to plead their cause before him, before the confessors themselves, and before the whole people. And to the people of Carthage: When we have begun, with peace first granted to us all by the Lord, to return to the Church, then each case will be examined IN YOUR PRESENCE AND WITH YOU JUDGING. And in this same letter, and on this very matter, he adds the passage which we cited above in the chapter on the corruption of the old books: Let them, I beg, patiently hear our counsel, let them wait for our return, and when we have come to you by the mercy of God, several fellow bishops having been called together, we may examine, according to the discipline of the Lord, in the presence of the confessors and with your judgment too, the letters and desires of the blessed martyrs. Hence he also testifies elsewhere that from the beginning of his episcopate he had resolved to do nothing on his own opinion without the counsel of his brother elders and deacons, and without the consent of the people. Whoever wishes to be taught more on these matters, let him consult the fourteenth letter of the same author, and the twenty-eighth on the case of Philumenus and Fortunatus, subdeacons, and the fortieth on Felicissimus. Likewise the sixty-seventh, written jointly to the clergy and the people standing in Spain, in which he praises them because they had removed their bishops, who were guilty of very grave sins, from their place. But lest anyone think that this practice was in use only in the Church of Carthage, I shall not omit that the Roman clergy approved his counsel. We (they say) are pleased in so great a matter, that you yourself first dealt with it, to keep the peace of the Church, and then, by a consultation of counsels made with the bishops, elders, deacons, confessors, and likewise the lay believers, to deal with the case of the fallen. And (which in my judgment is especially to be noted) Cyprian himself, writing to Cornelius, the Roman bishop, says that he had no doubt that, because of the mutual love which each owed and showed to the other, the most flourishing clergy presiding at Rome with him and the most holy and most honourable people would always read his letters. Whence it appears that at Rome also the ecclesiastical business was referred to the people. There is no need to warn how much both the authority and the example of the ancients in this matter are now despised. Everyone sees for himself that not only in councils and in the courts of the bishops is no account taken of the people, but that anyone who dared to attempt or begin anything like it would be held a heretic. Above all I would have you consider this: if any man is now made a bishop or archbishop and should write to the Roman Pontiff those letters of Cyprian to Cornelius: Most dear brother, I urge you and ask of you that what you do for the most part through yourself and with honour, you would do at my request, namely that this my letter be read to the most flourishing clergy who preside there with you and to the most holy people. If, I say, some prelate were to write these words to the present Pope, what place would he expect to be given him, and would he not think he was dealt with most mildly and kindly if he suffered no heavier penalty for his unhappy letter than to be made a laughing-stock and, like a madman, be scorned as ignorant of all things? And yet these are the very words of Cyprian to Pope Cornelius. But just as the bishops and other clergy have defrauded the people of all that right which they enjoyed in the ancient Church, both in the election of prelates and in other ecclesiastical affairs, so too the Roman Pope has drawn away and snatched from the bishops and clergy themselves not only these spoils of the wretched people but almost all the remaining power and authority, and has claimed it all for himself alone; and what they had received from the very beginnings of Christianity and from the most ancient canons of the Church, and what they had afterwards, in later times, gradually acquired through various arts, not without great labour and great diligence, all this has, I know not how, in a short time flowed together into Rome alone. The three hundred and eighteen Fathers of Nicaea decreed that a bishop ought to be ordained by all the bishops who are in his province, if this can be done. But if this is difficult, either because of some pressing necessity or the length of the journey, then certainly three bishops ought to be gathered together, while those who are absent also hold their consent by letter, and so let them make the ordination. But the power of confirmation belongs, in each province, to the Metropolitan bishop. This canon fully agrees with the custom received in earlier centuries, as is clear from the passage cited just above from the sixty-eighth letter of Cyprian. Indeed it was also long observed in the following centuries, as appears from the letter of the First Council of Constantinople to Pope Damasus, and from the speech of the moderators of the Council of Chalcedon, concerning the rights which pertained to the Patriarch of Constantinople in his diocese. And yet it is known to the whole world what is now the practice of the Roman Church. For she has left to the Metropolitans and their councils no real power or authority in the ordination of bishops; all its force depends on the one Roman Pontiff, and on those to whom, willingly or unwillingly, he has granted a part of it. The prelates themselves have no grace of this benefit from any other than that one, nor is it allowed to take up the office unless they have first received the Pope's city bulls for money paid down, and have transcribed them into the so-called Annates. Nor do they usually inscribe their names otherwise than in this formula: N., by the Divine mercy and the grace of the holy Apostolic See, bishop. Yet no trace of such formulas appears in any monument of antiquity. Of so many bishops whose signatures we still have, partly in councils and partly in other books and histories, not one even occurs who in the solemn inscription of his name professes himself a bishop by the grace of the Roman Pope. It is quite certain that in provincial and diocesan synods all ecclesiastical matters were once discussed and decided, as is clear from the canons and examples which still exist, such as those which we read about Arius and Eutyches in the ancients, whom we know were struck with anathema by the Synods of Alexandria and Constantinople. But today these synods take cognizance only of minor causes; if any more serious ones arise, they are judged by no one but the Pope himself, and the synods are not allowed to do anything more than simply inquire into the matter and report to the Pope what they have learned. Nor is there anyone in the episcopal order, however humble, who can be judged in a more serious case touching his dignity by anyone other than the Roman Pontiff. In these causes the Metropolitan has no right, nor the Primate, nor the synod of the province, nor even of the diocese, in what sense this word was understood by the ancients. Indeed, contrary to the ordinary order, sometimes the Pope delegates to them the hearing of some case, but only to prepare the suit and send it to Rome, where at last it is heard and decided by the Roman Pontiff, as the Council of Trent expressly decreed. I pass over the inspection and jurisdiction, taken from the bishops contrary to the ancient canons and custom, over most monks and other clergy, whether secular or regular, who live in their parishes. Likewise, the Pope has claimed for himself alone the whole power of absolving in general, and of dispensing in many cases which they call reserved, a power which once belonged equally to all bishops. He alone grants indulgences, and proclaims jubilees, which did not exist in any of the most ancient centuries. And to bring this matter to a close, I shall here quote the testimony of the most noble Jesuit Petavius, who, having carried out the expunging of many things of this kind by his own people: Finally (he says), so that there may be an end, it can be clearly understood and known even from a moderate reading of the Fathers that a great part of ecclesiastical discipline (namely that which lies in rites and customs) has been wholly changed, and its practice is now plainly other than what it once was in the primitive Church. Now indeed, as regards that order of discipline which properly concerns the imposing of repentance on sinners or their admission to communion, its whole form has utterly perished. Only the idea of the thing survives in the books of the ancients, for example in the canonical letters of Gregory of Neocaesarea, of Basil, and of others, and in the councils, both ecumenical and provincial. Where now are the four well-known grades of penitents once known in the ancient Church: of whom some wept at the doors of the Church, some listened with the catechumens, some threw themselves at the feet of the faithful, some were admitted to the common prayers of the faithful; and finally others, having gone through all these stages, were admitted to participation in the sacraments. So great was the severity of old that sometimes repentance lasted eight, ten, or even twenty years. That absolution was not given to the lapsed in former times except after the satisfaction imposed by the ministers according to the canons had been completed is clear from all the monuments of antiquity, and it is acknowledged by the most learned men of the Roman party, Maldonatus, Petavius, and others whom it would be long to name; and those theologians who are today called disciples of Jansenius, though they themselves are disciples of Augustine, fight fiercely about it. Now, however, even children know that sinners in the communion of the Pope are absolved immediately after confession, and only afterwards think about performing the satisfactions enjoined by the priest. Indeed, among the Jesuits there has lately been found one who, carried away by heat and by zeal in contention against the Jansenists, did not hesitate to write that no one requires satisfaction before absolution, except at the loss of the name of Catholic; and that if any men so arrange things, their discipline is an approach to despair, a way to hardening and final impenitence, a precipice of Tartarus, and other things which it is distasteful to repeat; these are so insulting to the most holy Fathers, who certainly most constantly commended and most carefully followed that very method of repentance which this man so greatly abominates. Moreover, the modern so-called auricular confession of the Romanists, of which no trace is seen among them, has wholly swallowed up this discipline, which is everywhere found among the ancients. And just as those most salutary penalties of the ancients for penitents were removed, so certain other new ones have been substituted, very useful to the Roman cause (I admit), but most pernicious to sinners, such as the Interdicts: when, because of the fault of one or two, either of a person or of an order, and sometimes not so much a true fault as a fictitious and imaginary one, whole commonwealths and entire kingdoms, in which there are many myriads of men, are punished by withholding communion in the sacraments, by which, as by instruments, Christ grants life and grace to wretched mortals. This the city Pope Paul V attempted against the Venetian Republic not so long ago, when we were boys. In that document is contained so deadly an institution, by which myriads of innocent souls are condemned to hell on account of the sins of a few. What kind of apostolic power can be called this, since apostolic power was instituted not for destruction but for edification? I should also very much like to be taught by what ancient canons the bloody discipline of the so-called Inquisition is supported, which, after it has extorted a confession of heresy from a wretched man by crafty arts, unworthy of a Christian and partly by horrible tortures deservedly so called, condemns to death the man it ought to have instructed, and hands him over to the secular magistrates; and, so that it may be plain that God is mocked no less than men, it expressly asks that the accused not be punished with death, but on this condition, that he be subjected to the most exquisite punishment, that is, burned alive, unless this is done before the sixth or at latest the seventh day, and this without any examination of the cause or the fact; the judges themselves are urged on to this butchery by all censures, and finally are excommunicated, deposed, and cast down from every degree of dignity, whether in the Church or in the Commonwealth. So great is the monstrousness of that institution that, although the accused (which almost passes belief) acknowledges his guilt, professes repentance, begs for punishment, and of his own accord submits himself to all the satisfactions of the Church, even the most laborious, he nevertheless suffers capital punishment, if he is of the kind they call relapsed. O inhuman repentance, worthy only of the Scythians and the Laestrygonians, and most unworthy of that Christ who bade his Apostle to forgive not seven times only but seventy times seven! But it is also wholly and entirely alien to Antiquity, whose successors and heirs these men do not hesitate to profess themselves to be! For that most gentle antiquity, whose name they so shamelessly misuse, clearly taught that it is the mark of piety not to compel but to persuade, since the Lord did not offer force, but left each to follow him by his own choice. The devil, since he had nothing true in him, breaks down the doors with an axe and a hatchet of those whom he approaches and by whom he is received; but our Saviour is so gentle that he teaches indeed, If anyone wishes to come after me, and if anyone wishes to be my disciple, yet he compels no one who approaches, but knocks at the door and says: Open to me, my sister, my bride, and enters to those who open; but if any are unwilling to hear, he withdraws, since truth is proclaimed not with weapons, nor with soldiers, nor with an armed hand, but by persuasion and counsel. This same antiquity sharply rebukes the Arians because they used force in propagating and confirming their religion. Whence, it says, they learned (for so it addresses them) to rage with persecutions? They could not have said that they had this from the saints, but they received it as handed down by the Devil. Likewise, Christ indeed bade them flee, and the saints fled; but to pursue is a devilish undertaking, and this very thing he seeks against all. And elsewhere it bears witness that the Arians, in this very thing that they proscribed those who would not subscribe to their opinion (which was far less than burning them alive), betrayed themselves as strangers to Christianity and friends of the Devil and his demons. This same Antiquity, in another ancient writer, against the same Arians who used the terror of persecutions and the allurements of worldly goods to draw mortals to their faith, breaks out into these exclamations: Now, alas! earthly supports commend the divine faith; Christ, poor in his power, is accused while ambition is sought for his name. The Church, which was entrusted to exile and prisons, is terrified; she is compelled to be believed by those to whom she was entrusted in exile and prisons; she depends on the favour of the powerful, she who was consecrated by the terror of persecutors. She puts priests to flight, she who was propagated by the flight of priests. She boasts that she is loved by the world, she who could not be Christ's unless the world hated her. In the same sense the most noble author of the same kind had written: By pouring out blood and by suffering, rather than by doing injuries, the Church was founded by Christ, grew by persecutions, and was crowned with martyrdoms.

units.la: o Id. cont. Aria. Orat. 1. T. 1. p. 88. A. oi outw ... A. vel. 1. f Hier. ep. 62. ad Theoph. p. 274. B. T.2. ‡ Hilar. l. contr. Auxent p. 86. martyriis coronatum esse. Venerandæ item illius antiquitatis non postremus erat qui Ariano exprobrat, quod ferro in rebus Ecclesiasticis uteretur. Quos (inquit ) non potuerit (Auxentius) sermone decipere, eos gladio putat esse feriendos, cruentas leges ore dictans, manu scribens, & putans quod lex fidem possit hominibus imperare. Ac ne forte exis-timas, quod Ariano vitio vertit, id cum in se suisque probare, alibi narrat se in Galliis professum noluisse communicare cum Episcopis qui devios à fide ad necem petebant. Eadem ratione Marcianus laudatissimæ pietatis Imperator negat se ulli penitus necessitatem præcepisse imponi, qualenus aut subscriberet, aut consentiret invitus (Concilii scilicet Chalcedonensis definitioni) Non enim (inquit) terrore aut violentia aliquos volumus ad viam trahere veritatis. Sanè Hosius Episcopus Cordubensis longè antea testatus erat, Constantem Imperatorem maximè Catholicum neminem coegisse orthodoxum fieri. Nec alia fuit veterum omnium sententia. Sic enim Hilarius Deus cognitionem sui docuit potius quàm exegit, & operationum cœlestium admiratione præceptis suis consilians auctoritatem, coactam confiscandi se aspernatus est voluntatem, &c. Deus universitatis est. Obsequio non eget necessario. Non requirit coactam confessionem. Quibus rationibus, & aliis ejusmodi Constantio Imperatori persuadere conatur. Scriptor iste hominum conscientiis vim non esse afferendam. Ambrosius Christus Apostolos misit ad seminandam fidem; qui non cogerent, sed docerent, nec vim potestatis exercerent. Sed doctrinam humilitatis attollerent. Unde fit ut Cyprianus inter Veteris & Novi fœderis agendi rationes collationem instituens, Tunc quidem (inquit) non obedientes, gladio occidebantur quando adhuc & circumcisio carnalis manebat, nunc autem, &c. spirituali gladio superbi & contumaces negantur, dum de Ecclesia ejiciuntur. Ergo nunc etiam, ut Cypriano credimus, sub Veteri Testamento in Hispania & Italia vivitur, & in aliis quibuscunque provinciis viget Inquisitio. Hoc verò Cypriani dictum difficile cum m Luc. 17. p. 99. T. 5. n Cypr. ep. 62. p. 143.
units.tr: o Id. cont. Aria. Orat. 1. T. 1. p. 88. A. oi outw ... A. vel. 1. f Hier. ep. 62. ad Theoph. p. 274. B. T.2. ‡ Hilar. l. contr. Auxent p. 86. crowned with martyrdom. Nor was the least among that venerable antiquity the man who reproached the Arian for using the sword in ecclesiastical affairs. Those whom he could not deceive by argument (says Auxentius), he thinks should be struck down with the sword, dictating bloody laws with his mouth, writing them with his hand, and thinking that a law can impose faith on men. And lest you perhaps think he approved in himself and his own people what he censured in the Arian, he tells elsewhere that he declared in Gaul that he would not communicate with bishops who sought the death of those who had strayed from the faith. On the same principle the Emperor Marcian, of most praiseworthy piety, denies that he had ever laid any necessity on anyone, that they must either subscribe or consent unwillingly (to the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, that is). For (he says) we do not wish to draw anyone into the way of truth by terror or violence. Indeed, Hosius, bishop of Cordoba, had testified long before that the Emperor Constantius, most Catholic, had compelled no one to become orthodox. Nor was the opinion of all the ancients otherwise. For thus Hilary: God taught the knowledge of himself rather than exacted it, and, recommending his precepts by the wonder of heavenly works, he rejected a will that would be forced into a grudging acknowledgment of himself, etc. God is the Lord of the universe. He does not need obedience. He does not require forced confession. With these arguments, and others of the same kind, he tries to persuade the Emperor Constantius. That writer holds that force is not to be brought to bear on men's consciences. Ambrose: Christ sent the apostles to sow the faith; men who were not to compel but to teach, nor to exercise the force of power, but to exalt the doctrine of humility. Hence Cyprian, comparing the ways of dealing under the Old and the New Covenant, says: Then indeed the disobedient were killed by the sword, while carnal circumcision still remained; but now, etc., the proud and obstinate are cut off by the spiritual sword, when they are cast out of the Church. So now too, if we believe Cyprian, it is the Old Testament that still governs life in Spain and Italy, and the Inquisition flourishes in every other province. But this saying of Cyprian can hardly be reconciled with m Luc. 17. p. 99. T. 5. n Cypr. ep. 62. p. 143.

units.la: Pii Papæ V. sententia conciliare, qui statuit Episcopos posse habere administratros, & lictores ad causas quæ sui juris sunt, & qui in reos lege agant. Quod vero Ecclesia ad brachium seculare passim nunc & vulgo confugit, id non ideo fieri quòd suis ipsa viatoribus & lictoribus, aliisque ejus generis ministris jure careat,sed quòd nullos habeat, vel quòd, si quos habeat, adeo vel infirmos, vel paucos habeat, ut ad compescendos & plectendos reos potestatis temporalis ope atque auxilio uti cogatur. Huic argumento finem imponet locus Tertulliani Scriptoris Latinæ Ecclesiæ antiquissimi, quem ut supra attigimus vult Pamelius sensisse capitis supplicio in hæreticos animadvertendum esse, tametsi ille Christiano non concedat ut,vel in Bello adversus publicos hostes,vel in Magistratu constitutus adversus fontes, ex legibus gladium stringat. En tibi ergo ejus de religione verba. Videte enim(Gentiles affatur )ne & hoc ad irreligiositatis elegium concurrat, admicere libertatem religionis, & interdicere optionem Divinitatis, ut non liceat mihi colere quem velim. Nemo se ab invito coli vellet ne homo quidem. Et aliquot capitibus interjectis. Facile iniquum videtur liberos homines invitos urgeri ad sacrificandum. Nam & alias Divina rei facienda libens, animus inducitur. Et in alio opere, de hoc ipso argumento agens. Humani juris & naturalis potestatis est,unicuique quod putaverit colere, nec alii obest aut prodest alterius religio: sed nec religionis est cogere religionem, quæ sponte suscipi debeat, non vi,cum & hostilia ab animo libenti expostulentur. Mirabili commento hæc Tertulliani loca diluit Pamelius, quæ sic accipit, quasi significarent non esse quidem homines ad religionem directè cogendos esse, tamen si nolint ab hæresi discedere puniendos. Suavis homo non putat eum cogi qui, propositâ capitis pœna,ad aliquid faciendum compellitur. Concilice qui poterit Inquisitionis praxin, & Papärum adversus Henricum VIII. & Elizabetham ejus filiam & Regum nostrorum quosdam fulmina cum constanti hac totius antiquitatis sententia.
units.tr: The sentence of Pope Pius V in the council, which decreed that bishops may have administrators and lictors for cases within their jurisdiction, and officers who may proceed against the accused by law. As for the fact that the Church now everywhere and commonly has recourse to the secular arm, this is not because she lacks by right her own apparitors, lictors and other ministers of that kind, but because she has none, or, if she has some, has them so weak or so few that to restrain and punish the accused she is forced to use the help and aid of temporal power. This argument will be closed by a passage of Tertullian, the most ancient writer of the Latin Church, whom Pamelius, as we touched on above, holds to have meant that heretics must be punished by execution, although Tertullian does not allow a Christian, either in war against public enemies or when holding magistracy, to draw the sword under the laws against his fellow believers. Here then are his words on religion for you. See (he addresses the Gentiles) that it does not also fall in with the praise of irreligion, to admit freedom of religion and to forbid the choice of divinity, so that I may not be allowed to worship whom I wish. No one would wish to be worshipped by an unwilling person, not even a man. And after several chapters have intervened: It seems plainly unjust that free men should be urged, against their will, to sacrifice. For in other matters too, a willing mind is brought to doing divine things. And in another work, treating this very subject: It is a matter of human right and natural power that each may worship what he thinks fit; nor does one man's religion harm or help another's: but it is not the part of religion to compel religion, which ought to be undertaken willingly, not by force, since even hostile acts are demanded from a willing mind. Pamelius dissolves these passages of Tertullian with a wonderful contrivance, taking them as if they meant that men are indeed not to be compelled directly to religion, yet are to be punished if they refuse to depart from heresy. Sweet fellow! He does not think a man is compelled when, with the penalty of death set before him, he is forced to do something. How then will he be able to reconcile the practice of the Inquisition, and the Popes' thunderbolts against Henry VIII and his daughter Elizabeth and certain of our kings, with this constant opinion of all antiquity?

units.la: Jam qui Patrum fidem, cærimonias, & disciplinam adeo securè contemnere ac proculcare deprehenduntur Pontificii,ut quæcunque Veterum minùs placebant, ea summa licentia immutarint vel antiquarint ; qua fronte nobis iidem Antiquitatem laudant ? quo pudore, quave religione eam in controversiis nostris vel testem, vel judicem adhibent ? Illis vero, dum sic agunt, quis non intelligit ea ad amussim congruere quæ Tertullianus in argumento consimili gentilibus olim objecit ? Nunc religiosissimi legum & paternorum institutorum protectores & ultores, respondeant velim de sua fide & honore & obsequio erga majorum consulta, si à nullo desciverunt ? Si in nullo exorbitaverunt, si non necessaria & aptissima quaeque disciplinæ obliteraverunt ? Quonam illæ leges abierunt, &c. Ubi religio, ubi veneratio majoribus debita à vobis ? Habitu, victu, instructu, sensu, ipso denique sermone proavis renuntiastis. Laudatis semper antiquitatem,& novè de die vivitis. Nunc non quæro juréne an injuria ita cum Veteribus agant. Satis est quod eo clarissimè testantur non esse sibi summam Patrum in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus auctoritatem. Quos ergo sic ipsi repudiant, quo jure eosdem Protestantibus obtrudunt ? Quorum tam multas sententias ac cærimonias resciderunt, qua eorumdem auctoritate quicquam in religione constitui posse sperant ? Patres, inquis, Purgatorium ignem esse crediderunt. Esto, inquam, Sed qui Patrum perspicuam de sanctarum animarum ad diem resurrectionis statu sententiam libere explosisti ; cur hanc mihi feres legem, ut quod eos de Purgatorio sensisse putas,id necessario admittam ? Parem esse decet inter se disputantium conditionem. Si tibi licuit illud prius Patrum dogma ad rationis & Scripturæ trutinam expendere; cur me vetas hoc alterum eorumdem placitum ad eandem normam exigere ? Tu verò, si vera loquentem ferre potes, aperte & nobis, & universo hominum generi illudis, qui eosdem illos Patres crepare, & ad ravim laudare, & eorum nominibus omnia tua volumina minua implere non definis, quos indignissimè acceptos abjecisti; quorum auctoritatem in tam multis sprevisti atque conculcasti.
units.tr: Now the Papists are found to despise and trample so carelessly on the faith, ceremonies and discipline of the Fathers that whatever of the ancients displeased them they have changed or revived with the greatest licence. With what face, then, do the same men praise antiquity to us? With what shame, or what piety, do they call it in as witness or judge in our controversies? Indeed, when they act thus, who does not see that what Tertullian once objected to the Gentiles in a similar argument fits them exactly? Now let the most scrupulous protectors and avengers of the laws and of ancestral institutions answer me, I should like to know, concerning their faith, honour and obedience towards their ancestors' decrees: whether they have never departed from them? If they have not strayed in anything, if they have not blotted out any of the most necessary and fitting features of discipline? Whither have those laws gone, etc. Where is the religion, where the reverence owed by you to your ancestors? In dress, food, furnishing, manner of thought, and finally even in speech, you have renounced your forefathers. You always praise antiquity, and live new from day to day. I do not now ask whether they are right or wrong in so dealing with the ancients. It is enough that by this they most clearly testify that for them the supreme authority of the Fathers in matters pertaining to religion does not hold. Whom, then, they thus reject themselves, by what right do they thrust upon Protestants? Having cut away so many of their opinions and ceremonies, how can they hope that anything can be established in religion by the authority of those same men? "The Fathers," you say, "believed that there is a purgatorial fire." Granted, I reply. But you, who freely rejected the Fathers' clear opinion about the state of holy souls until the day of resurrection, why do you impose on me this rule, that I must necessarily admit whatever you think they held about purgatory? The condition of those disputing with one another ought to be equal. If you were allowed to weigh that earlier doctrine of the Fathers in the balance of reason and Scripture, why do you forbid me to test this other opinion of theirs by the same standard? But you, if you can bear someone speaking the truth, openly mock both us and the whole human race: you do not cease to rattle on about those same Fathers, to praise them to the skies, and to fill all your bulky volumes with their names, though you have cast aside with the greatest contempt those whose authority you have spurned and trampled in so many matters.

units.la: Frustra hoc loco objectas Protestantes pleraque illa capita,quæ supra retulimus tecum repudiare,qui scilicet, non Patres,sed Scripturam pro fidei suæ norma habent, neque ex Antiquitate quicquam recipiendum putant, nisi quod idem Scriptura sacra vel contineri vel niti reperiatur.
units.tr: You vainly charge Protestants here with rejecting, together with you, those many heads [of doctrine] which we listed above; for they hold not the Fathers but Scripture as the rule of their faith, and think nothing should be received from antiquity unless it is found to be contained in, or grounded upon, the same holy Scripture.

units.la: Si postremò causeris Patrum in commemoratis nuper capitibus auctoritatem nullius esse momenti, quòd Ecclesia de iis aliter pronuntiarit; eo ipso liquidò id fateris quod ego nunc contendo, non esse, scilicet, Patrum summam in judicandis nostris controversiis auctoritatem. Ecclesiæ verò quam tu hic obtendis, quæ qualisque sit potestas atque auctoritas, non est nostri instituti nunc quærere. Res alterius loci & tituli est. Hoc unum tantum dicam, quamcumque tu Ecclesiæ auctoritatem, seu parvam, seu magnam tribueris, eam nullius esse posse ad componendas nostras controversias usus, nisi primùm & ante omnia constituatur, quænam & ubi sit Ecclesia; Eam enim quæ nunc Romæ id sibi nominis vindicat, Christi Ecclesiam verè esse negant Protestantes ? neque in omnibus his quæstionibus quicquam esse videtur difficilius, quàm ut Christi verè esse Ecclesiam iis persuadeas Papæ Romani,ut vocant,obedientiam. Quam si, scilicet, Ecclesiam esse concederent, ad eam statim, absque ulla controversia aut mora, ultro redirent.
units.tr: If at last you plead that the Fathers' authority on the heads recently mentioned is of no weight, because the Church has pronounced otherwise about them, you thereby plainly confess what I now contend: that the Fathers do not hold supreme authority in judging our controversies. But what power and authority the Church you put forward here has, and of what kind, is not our business to inquire into now; that is a matter for another place and another heading. I will say only this: whatever authority you assign to the Church, whether small or great, it can be of no use for settling our controversies unless it is first and above all established which Church it is, and where it is. For the Protestants deny that the Church which now at Rome claims that name for itself is truly the Church of Christ, and among all these questions nothing seems harder than to persuade those who are in what they call the obedience of the Roman Pope that it is truly the Church of Christ. For if they granted that it was the Church, they would at once, without any controversy or delay, willingly return to it.

units.la: Concludamus ergo non esse Patrum sententiam idoneam, ad eas decidendas controversias, quæ hodie in religione agitantur, medium : primò quòd difficile sit scire quænam illa de qua quæritur, revera fuerit Patrum sententia; tum quod ipsa per se satis non sit ad fidem faciendam, quod Patres errori obnoxii fuerint; ac denique, quod eadem parum sit apud utramque litigantium partem ponderis habitura; cùm ipsius Antiquitatis sententias, cærimonias, & disciplinam altera quidem pars Scripturæ, altera vero Ecclesiæ judicio aperte subiciant.
units.tr: We conclude, then, that the opinion of the Fathers is not a suitable means for settling the controversies now debated in religion. First, it is hard to know what the Fathers really held on the point in question. Second, their opinion is not enough in itself to produce faith, since the Fathers were liable to error. Finally, it would carry little weight with either side in the dispute, because one party subjects the opinions, ceremonies and discipline of antiquity to the judgment of Scripture, and the other to the judgment of the Church.

units.la: Verum ex hac conclusione nasci video duas quæstiones. Cùm enim ex Patribus de capitibus controversis nihil certi constituere queamus, quæri potest primo quâ aliâ viâ ad dirimendas hasce controversias progrediendum sit; tum secundo, quis & qualis possit esse Patrum usus. Ac tametsi neutra quæstio ad institutum proprie nostrum pertineat, tamen, quia neque ab eo plane fuit alienæ, utramque paucis, & quoad fieri poterit breviter exequar. Ad priorem nihil videtur respondeni commodiùs posse, quam quod in hoc ipso argumento Græcis suis olim respondisse reperitur Scholarius Scriptor, Græcus ortu & lingua, sed Latinis acceptissimus, & ab iis, qui Concilia Oecumenica Romæ ediderunt, magno in pretio habitus. Is igitur in Oratione, quam Florentiæ habuit, ut ad componendum Græcorum ac Latinorum dissidium & in quo sapiendo tum maximè laborabatur viam aperiret, primò quidem, (inquit) non decet velle omnia disertis verbis è Scriptura desumere, nam multos hæreticos scimus pratextu hoc usos; sed siquid verbis prolatis sit consequens adaque erit honorandum; Similiter quod veris & confessis visum fuerit repugnans & contrarium, nullo modo erit admittendum. Tum decernit eorum quæ obscurius dicta sunt, sumendas esse ex Scriptura ipsa, veluti magistra, explicationes per ea quæ uspiam clarius illa dixerit. Denique, si quæ videtur esse discrepantia, tollendam esse ait adhibita expositione sic ut tempora, usus ac necessitas, sensuumq. diversitas & hujusmodi alia perpendantur. Deinde docet Patres Nicænos hac ratione verum de Filio Dei fidem ex Scripturis definisse. Mox eadem ad institutum suum referens subjungit, Scripturam manifestè disertèque testari Spiritum San-
units.tr: But from this conclusion I see two questions arising. Since we cannot establish anything certain from the Fathers about the disputed heads, it may be asked, first, by what other way we ought to proceed to settle these controversies; and second, what kind of use the Fathers can have. Neither question properly belongs to my present purpose, but since it is not wholly foreign to it, I shall deal with both briefly and as concisely as I can. For the first question, nothing seems better as an answer than what the writer Scholarius once gave the Greeks on this very subject. He was a Greek by birth and language, but was most welcome to the Latins, and was highly esteemed by those who published the Ecumenical Councils at Rome. In the speech he delivered at Florence, meant to open a way towards composing the disagreement between Greeks and Latins, which at that time was being laboured over above all, he said: first indeed, it is not fitting to wish to take everything in express words from Scripture, for we know that many heretics have used this pretext; but if anything follows from the words quoted, that is to be honoured; likewise, whatever seems opposed and contrary to things true and confessed is in no way to be admitted. Then he lays down that the explanations of things said more obscurely are to be taken from Scripture itself, as from a teacher, through those things which it has said more clearly somewhere. Finally, if there seems to be any discrepancy, he says it is to be removed by applying an exposition in which times, usage and necessity, and the diversity of meanings, and other such things, are weighed. He then teaches that the Nicene Fathers defined the true faith concerning the Son of God from Scripture in this way. Soon, referring the same to his own purpose, he adds: Scripture clearly and expressly testifies that the Holy Spirit

units.la: ctum ... &c. E. ... T. Concil. genit. p.690. 6. edit. vetero Concil. am. Parif. A.1636. T.8. p.921. cium ex Patre procedere, idque communiter & Graecos & Latinos confiteri: non itidem docere an Spiritus Sanctus procedat ex Filio, necne; atque in hoc versari quaestionem quod hoc quidem Latini affirmant Graeci vero negent. Ea ergo (inquit) colligenda est ex quibusdam aliis quae Scriptura dicat aperte; quod deinceps exequitur, & quidem, si quid judico, docte & felicitcr; è perspicuis, hoc quod erat obscurum, illustrans atque definiens. Haec est magni viri sententia, quae Latinis, quorum ille contra suos Graecos partes tuetur, displicere non debet. Ego quidem quid aequius ac verius in hac causa dici possit non video. In omnibus scientiis haec Methodus observatur. De quibus dubitatur, ea ex confessis probantur. Ex certis incerta confirmantur; ex perspicuis obscura illustrantur. Ergo & haec ipsa ratio in controversiis nostris sequenda est. Verbum Dei, utrorumque commune instrumentum est, communes (ut sic dicam) tabulae. Inde ergo quaerendum est, unde fidem & nostram confirmemus, & adversarii refellamus. Exempli gratia, id quod Christus in sacra Coena accepit, panem fuisse verbum Dei diserte dicit. (De eo inter nos omnes convenit.) nusquam vero diserte dicit panem illum vel mutatum fuisse vel in nihilum abiisse. De hoc quaeritur. Oportet ergo (auctore Scholatio) id probare ex aliquibus aliis rebus quae in Dei verbo liquido ponantur. Si probationis labor succedat, vicisti. Sin secus, cur tu quemquam velis id credere, quod ex verbo Dei demonstrare non potes? Ira etiam discertissime docet Scriptura, Christum praecepisse Apostolis suis, ut acciperent, comederent, & biberent quae ipse iis porrexit, cum Eucharistiam instituit. Jussisse ut sacrificarent, neque hic, neque alibi usquam dicit. Haec ergo est quaestio, quam si probare volunt Latini, ex iis eruere ac concludere debent quae perspicue & expresse in Dei verbo ponantur. Scriptura itidem docet Christum esse mediatorem inter Deum & homines, caput Ecclesiae, purgare nos a peccatis nostris suo sanguine. De eo inter nos omnes convenit. Sed nusquam aufquam ponit sanctos mortuos mediatores esse, Papam esse caput Ecclesiæ, animas nostras igne quodam purgatorio peccatorum parte aliqua mundari. De his est omnis quæstio. Ex sapientissimi Scholarii sententia, qui capita ista ponunt, ea illi ex rebus liquidò & disertè in Scriptura constitutis inferre & confirmare tenentur. Ni fecerint, frustra pro veris obtrudunt quæ vera esse non probant. Ac tametsi & in religione, & in omni gravi negotio, satis causæ esse videatur cur aliquid minimè credamus, si nulla causa afferatur, cur id credere debeamus; Si quis tamen, velut ex ἀθεωρίας, quæ nulla ratione fulta, vel demonstrata rejicit, ea insuper falsitatis arguere, certisque argumentis convincere velit, is ex ejusdem Autoris sententia ita progredi debebit. Ille in primis eorum inceptiam atque absurditatem damnat, qui singula totidem Scripturæ verbis probari postulant; quod de iis maximè intelligendum est, quæ propositionibus (ut vocant) negativis continentur, quarum nulla scientia certam rationem habet: id enim infinitum esset, & nullius usus. Sufficit quæ vera sunt ponere. Quemadmodum enim quicquid ex iis legitimè sequitur, verum; sic etiam, quicquid repugnat, falsum est. Vin tu ergo ostendere propositiones, quæ tibi obtruduntur, falsas esse? Eas, cum iis rebus quæ liquidò & disertè in Scripturis habentur, confer; si repugnant, cave fidem ullam adhibueris. Exempli causa: Si Protestantes non satis habeant ea argumenta solvere quibus Latini Purgatorium suum probare frustra conantur, sed id insuper dogma refellere, falsúmque ostendere velint, ut res succedat, totum illud dogma cum iis comparare debebunt, quæ Scriptura tum de statu animarum ex hac vita migrantium, tum de causa & ratione expiationis peccatorum nostrorum & similibus clarè perspicuèque tradidit. Purgatorium si cum his pugnare demonstretur, explodendum erit. Sed non finit hujus opusculi modus plura de his verba facere.
units.tr: ctum ... etc. E. ... T. Concil. genit. p.690. 6. edit. vetero Concil. am. Parif. A.1636. T.8. p.921. proceeds from the Father, and that both Greeks and Latins commonly confess this: he does not teach in the same way whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son or not, and he holds that the question lies in this, that the Latins affirm it while the Greeks deny it. This (he says) is therefore to be gathered from certain other things which Scripture says plainly; and he goes on to do this, and indeed, if I judge rightly, learnedly and happily, illustrating and defining what was obscure from what is clear. This is the opinion of a great man, and it ought not to displease the Latins, whose side he defends against his own Greeks. For my part I do not see what could be said more fairly and truly in this matter. In all sciences this method is observed: what is doubtful is proved from what is granted; the uncertain is confirmed from the certain; the obscure is illuminated from the plain. Therefore this very method must also be followed in our controversies. The Word of God is the common instrument of both sides, the common tablets, so to speak. From it, then, we must seek how to confirm our own faith and refute our opponents. For example, the Lord in the holy Supper took bread, which the Word of God expressly says was bread (on this we all agree). But nowhere does it expressly say that this bread was changed or turned into nothing. This is what is in question. It is necessary, therefore (on Scholarius's authority), to prove this from other things that are plainly laid down in God's Word. If the labour of proof succeeds, you have won; but if not, why should you want anyone to believe what you cannot demonstrate from the Word of God? So too Scripture teaches most explicitly that Christ, when he instituted the Eucharist, commanded his apostles to take, eat and drink what he gave them. Nowhere, neither here nor elsewhere, does it say that he commanded them to sacrifice. This, then, is the question, and if the Latins wish to prove it, they must draw it out of, and infer it from, what is set down plainly and expressly in God's Word. Scripture likewise teaches that Christ is the mediator between God and men, the head of the Church, who cleanses us from our sins by his blood. On this we all agree. But nowhere does it state that dead saints are mediators, that the Pope is the head of the Church, or that our souls are cleansed of some part of their sins by a certain purgatorial fire. On these points the whole question turns. According to the opinion of that most wise Scholarius, those who put forward these heads are bound to infer and confirm them from things clearly and expressly laid down in Scripture. If they do not, they foist on us in vain as true what they do not prove to be true. And although, in religion and in every grave matter, there seems to be sufficient reason not to believe something if no reason is given why we ought to believe it, yet if anyone, from mere unthinking assertion [ἀθεωρίας], rejects what is supported by no reasoning or demonstration, and wishes moreover to prove it false and convict it by sure arguments, then, by the same author's judgment, he must proceed in this way. Scholarius first condemns the folly and absurdity of those who demand that each single point be proved by just so many words of Scripture. This is to be understood chiefly of those things contained in what are called negative propositions, for which no science has a fixed method, since that would be endless and of no use. It is enough to lay down what is true, for just as whatever legitimately follows from these is true, so whatever contradicts them is false. Do you, then, wish to show that the propositions forced upon you are false? Compare them with those things that are plainly and expressly found in the Scriptures; if they contradict them, take care not to give them any credence. For example: if the Protestants are not content merely to answer the arguments by which the Latins vainly try to prove their Purgatory, but also wish to refute that doctrine and show it to be false, then, if they are to succeed, they must compare that whole doctrine with what Scripture has clearly and plainly taught both about the state of souls departing from this life and about the cause and manner of the expiation of our sins, and things like these. If Purgatory is shown to clash with these, it must be rejected. But the limits of this little work do not allow me to say more about these matters.

units.la: Altera verò quæstio nullo negotio solvitur. Veterum enim librorum quòd summam esse & infallibilem auctoritatem negavimus, non ideo illum esse usum negavimus. Si id solum in religione conduceret quod est infallibile, nullius scriptï humani ullus esset usus. Auctorum quì nostro seculo, aut paulo ante, scripserunt nulla est apud utrosque auctoritas. Leguntur tamen eorum opera, & quidem magno cum fructu. Quanto utilior erit Patrum lectio, quorum multo quàm recentium major, plerumque est, certe testatior & manifestior, pietas atque eruditio? Augustinus quidem non ideo veteres contemplsit, quòd quæ scripserant, ea non aliter vera esse putaret, quàm quatenus vel rationis lucè, vel Scripturæ auctoritate niterentur. Idem de Hieronymo dici potest, qui Patres tanti fecit ut penè omnes legerit; tamen li libertrinè eorum lapsus detestetur. Si Patribus, non jam dico praetoriam illam judicandi, quam nunquam sibi arrogârunt, auctoritatem; sed famam omnem, nomenque ipsum detraxeris, non ideo nullius eruntur usus quæ literis mandata reliquerunt. Neque enim eo prosunt ac juvant libri, quòd ab hoc vel illo scripti sunt; sed hoc maxime quòd vera & utilia docent, quòd ab errore avocant, & à vitiis deterrent. Expunge si libet Augustini nomen è fronte præstantissimorum librorum de Civitate Dei, & de Doctrina Christiana: Me utrumque opus, stlamsi auctoris nomen nstieres, docebit tamen egregè, si legeris, mutrâ scire discipline. Cæterorum eadem est ratio. Principio occurrunt in his Patrum monumentis plurimæ eaque graves ad morum sanctitatem, accuratamque disciplinæ Christianæ observationem cohortationes. Multa quoque passim obvia sunt, quibus religionis Christianæ fundamenta, quæ apud omnes sunt in confesso, luculentissimè illustrantur & confirmantur: ad hæc plurima præclara & ad Scripturas & ad mysteria, quæ Scripturis continentur, intelligenda longè utilissima: Quin & ipsa eorum auctoritas magno hic nobis usui esse poterit ad Christianismi veritatem probandam. Quæso enim nonne admirabile est, tam multos, tam acri mente, tam felici ingenio viros, per quingentos & mille annos diversis temporibus & locis natos, disparibus inter se naturis & studiis, ac interdum etiam sententiis, tam constanter, uno veluti animo, unaque voluntate in omnibus Christianismi fundamentis conspirasse & convenisse, unumque (cætera tam diversos) Christum adorare? Ad eandem sanctificationem cohortari? eandem immortalitatem sperare? Eadem Evangelia suspicere? In iis omnes ingentia & sublimia mysteria demirari? Christianismi veritatem satis, fateor, per se commendat ipsa rerum ratio, disciplinæque totius eximia sapientia, ac inusitata, quædam pulchritudo, quæ se ipsa statim sui specie cœlestem divinamque esse prodit, ut nullum aliud certius, aut illustrius argumentum desideretur. Sed neque tamen contemnendum est, quod ejusdem rei non leve, ut opinor, documentum nobis præbet is, de quo dicere cœpimus, Patrum de Evangelii veritate plane admirabilis consensus. Abhorret enim ab omni veri specie tam multos excellentissimo, (quod eorum monumenta loquuntur) ingenio, mente acerrima atque perspicacissima præditos viros tam stolide hallucinatos esse, ut rerum suarum summam, omnésque adeo fortunas suas in Christi disciplina constituerent, pro hac nullum discrimen subterfugere-rent, vitam etiam ipsam ultro ac lætantes profunderent, nisi ejus esset ad afficiendas & percellendas hominum mentes divina quædam vis. Estne credibile his heroibus de Evangelii veritate tam constanter, tamque admirabiliter consentientibus véritora ac certiora vidisse pauculos atheos, adversus sanctissimam disciplinam hic illic subinde tam fœdè tamque incondité obloquentes; ut eorum obtrectatio pro canum latratu, aut suum grunnitu potius habenda sit, quam pro hominum voce atque oratione? Ac horum quidem si vel eo essent, quo sé
units.tr: The second question is resolved without any trouble. For the fact that we deny the ancient books to have supreme and infallible authority does not mean that we deny them any use. If only what is infallible were useful in religion, no human writing would have any use at all. The authors who wrote in our own age, or shortly before, have no authority with either side, yet their works are read, and indeed with great profit. How much more useful, then, will the reading of the Fathers be, whose piety and learning, being far greater than those of more recent writers, are generally more solid, and certainly more evident and manifest? Augustine did not despise the ancients because he thought that what they had written was true only insofar as it rested on the light of reason or the authority of Scripture. The same can be said of Jerome, who valued the Fathers so highly that he read almost all of them, and yet detested their occasional lapses. If you strip the Fathers not indeed of that supreme power of judging, which they never claimed for themselves, but of all their reputation and even their very name, the books they committed to writing do not therefore lose all their use. For books help us not because this or that man wrote them, but chiefly because they teach what is true and useful, call us away from error, and deter us from vices. Strike out, if you like, the name of Augustine from the title of his most excellent books, The City of God and On Christian Doctrine: each of these works will still teach you excellently, if you read them, both kinds of learning, even if you had removed the author's name. It is the same with the others. First of all, in these monuments of the Fathers there occur very many weighty exhortations to the holiness of life and the careful observance of Christian discipline. Also, many passages are found everywhere which illustrate and confirm most brilliantly the foundations of the Christian religion, which all acknowledge. Besides these, there are many excellent things, very useful for understanding both the Scriptures and the mysteries contained in them. Indeed, their very authority will be of great service to us here in proving the truth of Christianity. For tell me, is it not wonderful that so many men, of such keen mind and such happy talent, born at different times and places over five hundred and a thousand years, differing among themselves in natures and pursuits and sometimes even in opinions, should have agreed so constantly, as if with one mind and one will, in all the foundations of Christianity, and that, though so different in other things, they all worship one Christ, exhort to one sanctification, hope for one immortality, revere the same Gospels, and marvel together at the great and sublime mysteries in them? I grant that the very nature of things, and the outstanding and unusual wisdom and beauty of the whole discipline, commend the truth of Christianity well enough by themselves, showing at once by their very appearance that they are heavenly and divine, so that no other surer or clearer proof is needed. Yet we should not despise the proof this matter also gives us, which, I think, is no small one: the remarkable agreement of the Fathers on the truth of the Gospel, of which I began to speak. For it is far from any appearance of truth that so many men, endowed with most excellent talent, as their writings testify, with the keenest and most penetrating minds, should have been so foolishly deceived as to stake the whole sum of their affairs and all their fortunes on the discipline of Christ; that they should have shrunk from no danger for it, and even gladly and willingly poured out their very lives, unless there were in it some divine power to move and strike men's minds. Is it credible that these heroes, agreeing so constantly and so admirably about the truth of the Gospel, saw less truly and less certainly than a few atheists, who now and then here and there so foully and so crudely rail against this most holy discipline, so that their disparagement should be taken as the barking of dogs or the grunting of pigs rather than as human speech and reasoning? And if these men at least were where they boast, falsely and foolishly, that they stand, endowed with wit and acuteness…

units.la: falso stultéque jactant, ingenio, atque acumine prædití, testimonium tamen merito suspectum redderent ipsi eorum mores: neque enim mirandum est, quòd homines vel ambitione vel libidinibus perditi, eam difcipli­nam infament quæ scortatores & lenones & superbos ad Tartarum damnat; quod qui animam in vino & mergit vivens, & evomit motiens,eam religionem odérit, quæ ebrietati æternas pœnas constituit. Nemo mirari debet falsam esse Christi doctrinam eos facilè sibi persuadere, quorum tanti refert eam falsam esse. Si quem diræ hujusmodi nebulonum adversus Religionem Christianam calumniæ commovent, idem facit ac fi de legum, quæ morum sanctimoniam præcipiaut, æquitate ac justitia, ex gaheonum ac preftibulorum sententia judicet. Planè diversa est sanctissimorum virorum ratio, qui Religionis Christianæ veritatem tam constanter docuerunt. Cùm enim & nati & educati in iisdem quibus cæteri mortales, infirmitatibus effent, nullum dubium est quin effent natura & proni in ea vitia quæ sunt à Christo vetita, & aversi ab iis artibus & virtutibus, quæ sunt ab eodem præcepte. Qui ergo, cùm tales effent, Christi tamen disciplinam veram esse affeverarunt,nulla profectò ratio est, cur hoc eorum testimonium fufpectum habeamus. Itaque etiamsi Patribus defuisset summa illa ingenii atque eruditionis excellentia,qua atheos facilè fuperarunt, illorum tamen vel nudæ voces horum testimonio effent anteponendæ. Apparet enim & horum contra Christianam veritatem judicium odii merito sufpectum esse; & illorum de Christi & Evangelii divinitate voces ab omni studio puras & immunes esse.
units.tr: They boast falsely and foolishly that they are endowed with wit and sharpness, yet their own morals would rightly make their testimony suspect. It is no wonder that men ruined by ambition or lust should slander a discipline that condemns fornicators, pimps and the proud to Tartarus, or that a man who drowns his soul in wine while alive and vomits it out while dying should hate a religion that appoints eternal punishments for drunkenness. No one should wonder that those who so readily persuade themselves that Christ's teaching is false are men for whom it matters greatly that it be false. If the dreadful slanders of such scoundrels move someone against the Christian religion, he does the same as one who judged the fairness and justice of laws that prescribe moral purity by the opinion of prostitutes and pimps. The case of the most holy men who taught the truth of the Christian religion so steadfastly is entirely different. For since they were born and brought up among the same weaknesses as other mortals, there is no doubt that they were by nature inclined to those vices that Christ forbids, and averse to those practices and virtues that he commands. Therefore, since they were such men and yet affirmed that Christ's discipline was true, there is certainly no reason why we should regard their testimony with suspicion. So even if the Fathers had lacked that great excellence of wit and learning by which they easily surpassed the atheists, their bare words would still be preferable to the testimony of the atheists. For it is clear that the judgment of the latter against Christian truth is rightly suspect as the product of hatred, while the Fathers' statements about the divinity of Christ and the Gospel are free and exempt from all partisan zeal.

units.la: Illa vero sententiarum de quibusdam religionis capi& shy;tibus à nobis supra memorata diversitas, quæ interdum apud Patres occurrit, adeo nullum ipsorum de Chriftiaæ doctrinæ veritate testimonio pondus detrahit, ut etiam plurimum ad id momenti adjicere videatur quæ eorum scilicet in hac parte consensum omni fyn& shy;cretifmi icretismi suspicione liberat. Sic enim constat eos non ex compacto, neque ex communi aliqua conspiratione eadem de Christo loqui. Nam quos de multis inter se dissentire animadvertis, eos profecto satis intelligi de quibus consentiunt, ea non alios ab aliis accepisse, vel communicatis inter se consiliis constituisse, sed ex rerum ipsarum meditatione & attenta consideratione hausisse. Patrum opera & monumenta, hæc utilitas si vel unica esset, abundè nobis commendaret. Verum ne qui hinc pendet suavissimus fructus, quadam earum opinionum oppositione minuatur atque intercipiatur, quæ apud Patres variæ diversæque occurrunt, illud in primis pro certo statuendum est, nequaquam situm esse Christianismum in argutiis & subtilitate, neque tam in dogmatum numero ac multitudine, quam vi & efficacia. Eorum enim quibus Christianismus continetur plerorumque finis est sanctificatio, hoc est sincerus Dei cultus & vera in homines charitas. Quemcunque rectè & verè de duobus istis capitibus, deque cæteris, quæ ad ea necessaria sunt, sentire compereris, eum pro sanctę illius disciplinæ alumno certissimè habero. Reliqua vero præter hæc, quæ multa sunt & in contemplatione potiùs quam in praxi & usu versantur, si nescierit, non erit ideo contemnendus; imo si curiositate aut quapiam alia causa abreptus in errorem aliquem, circa alia capita, inciderit, tuum est id modestè ferre: Nam ut peccata, sic & errores nostros, Deus nobis condonat. Ligna, fœnum, stipula exurentur: qui ista struxerit servabitur, si modo fundamentum integrum & illæsum servaverit ac retinuerit. Ne commovearis aut tumultueris, si quando vel imperitia, vel etiam error in capitibus illius generis (quæ sunt scilicet præter fundamentum,) apud Patres occurrant; neque tu auctores istos ideo Christianos non fuisse putes, quod in talibus nonnunquam lapsi sint. Hujusmodi enim lapsus potest cadere etiam in præstantissimos Christi
units.tr: That diversity of opinion on certain articles of religion, which I have mentioned above and which sometimes occurs among the Fathers, takes away nothing of the weight of their testimony to the truth of Christian doctrine. Indeed, it seems to add a great deal to it, since it frees their agreement on this point from any suspicion of syncretism. For it is established that they did not speak of Christ in the same way by prior agreement or by some common conspiracy. Those whom you see differing from one another on many points are clearly understood to agree on the points where they do agree, and they did not receive these from one another or settle them by consultation together, but drew them from the meditation and careful consideration of the things themselves. The works and records of the Fathers would commend themselves to us on this ground alone, if it were the only benefit. But lest the sweetest fruit that hangs from them be diminished or cut off by some opposition of opinions, which appear among the Fathers in various and different forms, this must above all be firmly held: Christianity does not consist in subtleties and hair-splitting, nor so much in the number and multitude of dogmas as in their power and efficacy. For the aim of most of the things by which Christianity is contained is sanctification, that is, sincere worship of God and true love toward men. Whoever you find thinking rightly and truly about these two heads, and about the others that are necessary to them, I will hold him most certainly a pupil of that holy discipline. But as for the rest, apart from these, which are many and lie more in contemplation than in practice and use, if he does not know them, he is not therefore to be despised. Indeed, if through curiosity or some other cause he falls into some error about other articles, it is your part to bear it modestly. For God pardons our errors just as he pardons our sins. Wood, hay and stubble will be burned up; he who has built them will be saved, provided only that he has kept and held fast the foundation whole and unharmed. Do not be disturbed or upset if at any time ignorance, or even error, on articles of that kind (which are of course beyond the foundation) occurs among the Fathers; nor should you think that those authors were not Christians because they sometimes slipped in such matters. For such a lapse can befall even the most eminent servants of Christ.

units.la: servos. Vix ulla est facies adeo venusta, quæ omni prorsus nævo & labe careat. Etiam laudatur, etiam amatur ea pulchritudo, quæ tamen suas sed leves habet mendas. Nostra hæc fors est, ut nihil apud nos sit ab omni parte beatum, ut nemo sine venia placeat. Præterea licet & alium insignem fructum ex Patribus percipere. Exurgunt nonnunquam homines carnis suæ sensu inflati, qui ex ingenio, non ex ullis veræ religionis principiis hausta dogmata procudunt. Ad horum hominum compescendam audaciam peropportunè poterit Veterum auctoritas adhiberi. Videlicet si doceas, Patribus penitus ignota fuisse quæ isti obtrudunt dogmata. Quod si demonstrari poterit pro certo id tuendum est ejusmodi dogmata à Christo vel ab Apostolis generi humano nunquam fuisse tradita nulla enim veri specie fingi poterit, sanctos superiorum seculorum doctores, per quos ad nos manavit Christianismus, aliquid eorum latuisse quæ Dominus, quod essent alicujus momenti & ad salutem necessaria, nobis revelavit & commendavit. Equidem non negaverim Patres, fallaci aliqua ratiocinatione, aut speciosa auctoritate deceptos, ea nonnunquam docere quæ Christus nunquam revelavit, & quæ sunt liquidò falsa, nulloque idoneo fundamento nixa, ut allatis exemplis supra ostendimus. Non item inficias ierim ex iis, quæ nobis quidem Christus in Scriptura revelavit, sed quæ non sunt tamen absolutè ad salutarem fidem necessaria, quædam potuisse Patres fugere, vel quòd Scripturarum de talibus sensum, tempus & eventus rerum nondum aperuissent; vel quòd ipsi non satis attentionis ad ea expendenda attulerint; vel quòd aliquo studio affectúve præpediti ea non animadverterint, quæ jam tum elucebant. Sed fugisse ipsos omnes aliquid quod necessario ad fidem pertineret; fieri nequaquam potest. Id enim si ita esset, concedendum esset ipsos salute excidisse, à qua cogitatione plurimum abhorrent omnes boni. Fateor ergo, quod hoc, ni fallor, opere
units.tr: There is hardly any face so lovely that it lacks every blemish and stain. Beauty is praised and loved even though it has its own slight defects. It is our lot, perhaps, that nothing among us is wholly blessed in every part, and that no one pleases without indulgence. Moreover, it is also permitted to gain another notable benefit from the Fathers. Sometimes men arise, puffed up with the sense of their own flesh, who forge doctrines drawn from their own wit and not from any principles of true religion. To curb the audacity of these men, the authority of the ancients can be employed very opportunely. Namely, if you can show that the doctrines they thrust upon us were entirely unknown to the Fathers. And if it can be demonstrated with certainty that these doctrines were never handed down by Christ or the Apostles to mankind, then, since no plausible pretence can be made, it must be maintained that the holy teachers of earlier centuries, through whom Christianity flowed down to us, were not ignorant of anything that the Lord revealed to us and commended as being of some importance and necessary to salvation. Indeed, I would not deny that the Fathers, deceived by some fallacious reasoning or by a specious authority, sometimes taught things that Christ never revealed and that are plainly false and rest on no suitable foundation, as we have shown above with examples. Nor would I deny that, of those things which Christ indeed revealed to us in Scripture but which are not absolutely necessary to saving faith, some the Fathers may have overlooked, either because the Scriptures had not yet disclosed their meaning about such matters, or the time and course of events had not yet done so; or because they did not bring sufficient attention to weighing them; or because, hindered by some zeal or bias, they did not notice what was already shining forth. But that all of them overlooked something that necessarily pertained to faith is by no means possible. For if this were so, it would have to be conceded that they fell from salvation, a thought from which all good men shrink in the strongest terms. I therefore confess that what, unless I am mistaken, has been sufficiently demonstrated in this work,
