units.tr: that the argument by which something is concluded to be true because the Fathers thought so is weak and unsound, since it presupposes what is plainly false, namely that the Fathers all had their opinions from the revelation of Christ. What kind of argument would be that of one who concluded from the Fathers' consensus that all souls are kept apart in some custody until the day of judgment, or that the Eucharist is necessary for infants, or other such things? In these cases no one fails to see the futility of such proofs. And yet this is exactly how the Roman Church reasons when it argues from the authority of the Fathers, in order to prove its own dogmas, which the Protestants reject. I likewise admit that the argument would be faulty and foolish of one who inferred from the fact that all the Fathers, taken together, were silent about some article of faith not necessary to salvation that the article is therefore false or null. For one who thus concludes presupposes what is manifestly false, namely that the Fathers clearly saw and acknowledged each and every thing that Christ revealed to us in his Word. The same judgment would be made in the school of the Franciscans of one who argued from the silence of the Fathers and contended that the Blessed Virgin was conceived without sin. Yet I acknowledge and profess that an argument drawn from the Fathers is valid whenever it is concluded that a dogma is not necessary to salvation because the ancient writers were all equally silent about it. For example, if someone were to prove that those secret means of salvation which Muhammad, or David Joris, or other impostors of the same stamp, delivered to their disciples as most certain and necessary, are therefore false and empty and contrary to the will of Christ, because the Fathers plainly and utterly did not know them and never said a single word about them anywhere, then, as I for one judge, his argument would be firm and invincible. And this is precisely the very reasoning by which Irenaeus disputes against the Valentinians and other Gnostics, who put forward the frantic dreams of their own brains, ...

units.la: Zz servos. Vix ulla est facies adeo venusta, quæ omni prorsus nævo & labe careat. Etiam laudatur, etiam amatur ea pulchritudo, quæ tamen suas sed leves habet mendas. Nostra hæc fors est, ut nihil apud nos sit ab omni parte beatum, ut nemo sine venia placeat. Præterea licet & alium insignem fructum ex Patribus percipere. Exurgunt nonnunquam homines carnis suæ sensu inflati, qui ex ingenio, non ex ullis veræ religionis principiis hausta dogmata procudunt. Ad horum hominum compescendam audaciam peropportunè potest Veterum auctoritas adhiberi. Videlicet si doceas, Patribus penitus ignota fuisse quæ isti obtrudunt dogmata. Quod si demonstrati potest pro certo statuendum est ejusmodi dogmata à Christo vel ab Apostolis generi humano nunquam fuisse tradita nulla enim veri specie fingi poteft, sanctos superiorum seculorum doctores, per quos ad nos manavit Christianismus, aliquid eorum latuisse quæ Dominus, quod esset alicujus momenti & ad salutem necessaria, nobis revelavit & commendavit. Equidem non negaverim Patres, fallaci aliqua ratiocinatione, aut speciosa auctoritate deceptos, ea nonnunquam docere quæ Christus nunquam revelavit, & quæ sunt liquidò falsa, nullóque idoneo fundamento nixa, ut allatis exemplis supra ostendimus. Non item inficias ierim ex iis, quæ nobis quidem Christus in Scriptura revelavit, sed quæ non sunt tamen absolutè ad salutarem fidem necessaria, quædam potuisse Patres fugere, vel quòd Scripturarum de talibus sensum, tempus & eventus rerum nondum aperuissent; vel quòd ipsi non satis attentionis ad ea expendenda attulerint; vel quòd aliquo studio affectúve præpediti ea non animadverterint, quæ jam tum elucebant. Sed fugisse ipsos omnes aliquid quod necessario ad fidem pertineret, fieri nequaquam potest. Id enim si ita esset, concedendum esset ipsos salute excidisse, à qua cogitatione plurimum abhorrent omnes boni. Fateor ergo, quod hoc, ni fallor, opere satis demonstratum est, argumentum quo aliquid verum esse ex eo concluditur quod Patres ita sensetint, fluxum & infirmum esse, cum id supponat, quod liquidò falsum est, Patres, scilicet, omnes suas opiniones à Christi revelatione habuisse. Qualis esset ejus argumentatio qui animas omnes, usque ad diem judicii, seorsum in custodia aliqua detineri, vel Eucharistiam infantibus esse necessariam, vel alia ejusmodi ex Patrum de iis consensu concluderet, in quibus nemo non videt probationum iltarum futilitatem. Atqui sic omnino disputat Ecclesia Romana, cum ab auctoritate Patrum argumentatur, ut sua, quæ à Protestantibus, repudiantur, dogmata probet. Fateor item vitiosam ineptámque fore ejus argumentationem qui ex eo quòd omnes in universum Patres de capite aliquo fidei ad salutem non necessario sensuerint, ipsum nullum vel falsum esse inferret: Id enim qui sic concludit, supponit quod manifestè falsum est; Patres nempè omnia & singula quæ Christus nobis in Verbo suo revelavit clarè vidisse & agnovisse. Idem in Franciscanorum schola judicium fieret deo qui à silentio Patrum argumentatur & contenderet B. Virginem sine peccato conceptam fuisse. Cæterum valere è Patribus ductam argumentationem agnosco atque profiteor, quoties dogma non esse ad salutem necessarium inde concluditur, quòd de eo Veteres Scriptores pariter omnes altum siluerint. Exempli gratia, si quis arcana illa ad salutem media quæ Mahumetes aut David Georgius, vel alii ejusdem farinæ scelerati impostores discipulis suis tanquam certissima & necessaria tradiderunt, inde falsa inaniáque esse, & cum voluntate Christi pugnare probaret, quòd ea Patres planè penitúsque nescierint, neque unum usquam de illis verbum fecerint: hujus, ut ego quidem judico, argumentatio firma invictaque esset. Atque hæc ipsissima ratio est qua Irenæus adversus Valentinianos, aliosque Gnosticos disputat, qui vesana cerebri sui somnia in medium proferebant, suigentes mundi Creatorem merum Angelum fuisse, qui superiores se haberet divinitates quasdam, quas Aeones, id est, secula vocabant, quarum alii plures, alii pauciores constituebant, quidam ad cccLxv. recensebat, & sexcenta alia portenta, nullo neque rationis, neque Scripturæ fundamento suffulta. Irenæus ergo ut propudiosam istam doctrinam non à Christi Spiritu, sed ex uno istorum ingenio natam esse doceat, omnium Ecclesiarum, quas vel plantaverant, vel rigaverant Apostoli, tabulas & sacra: diptycha excutit; Actorum commentarios, literas & monumenta scrutatur, in quibus cum nulli essent isti Aeones, Achamot & Barbelot Gnosticorum, nec usquam ulla eorum vestigia apparerent, inde concludit Apostolos, neque scripto neque viva voce, quicquam, ut fingebant isti sycophantæ, suis discipulis de Gnosticorū mysteriis tradidisse. Si quid enim hujusmodi Apostolorum discipulis ulla ratione traditum esset, fieri profecto non potuisset, ut id tam brevi ex omni hominum memoria interciderit. Eadem methodo usus est Tertullianus in confutandis illis ipsis hæreticis, aliisque ejusdem furfuris, ut videre est, De præscript. cap. 22. & alibi. Tantis præeuntibus viris validam & efficacem esse hanc methodum affirmare non dubito. Hinc apparet Patrum auctoritatem, veluti secundum quoddam post Scripturas esse repagulum, ad eorum impostorum comprimendam ac retundendam audaciam, qui novam fidem procudere, novaque, & inaudita mysteria fallo Christi nomine orbi obtrudere aliquando moliuntur. Certum est quidem Scripturam, si ei ab omnibus quæ debetur reverentia, verè exhiberetur, unam ad hoc sufficere posse. Sed ii qui ex suo sibi cerebro nova dogmata comminiscuntur S. Scripturas plerumque fastidiunt ac contemnunt, idque ipsis vetustissimis hæreticis quos confutat Irenæus solenne fuit. Cum enim (inquit) ex Scripturis arguuntur, in accusationem convertuntur ipsarum Scripturarum, quasi non recte habeant, neque sint ex auctoritate, & quia varie sint dicta, & quia non posset ex his inveniri veritas ab his, qui nesciant traditionem. Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed viva voce. Itaque adversus hoc Scripturarum fastidium, longè sunt hoc loco utilissima Patrum monumenta; quæ ad hunc præsertim usum & hoc maxime consilio inter tot tantasque rerum humanarum perturbationes ac confusiones sapientissima Dei optimi providentia tanto numero ad nos conservata fuisse videntur. Si quid ergo Protestantes ex suo ingenio procuderent, ac velut ad salutem absolutè necessarium urgerent, quod nusquam apud Veteres compareret, liceret eos, fateor, hac methodo refutare. Sed notissimum est nihil eorum fide, quod hujusmodi sit, contineri. Nihil illi ponunt, nihil affirmant aut statuunt quod vel diserte in Scriptura non habeatur, vel quod ex ea evidenter non sequatur, quod non si paucissima exceperis) antiqui Patres non solum in libris, sed etiam in Symbolis & Synodorum decretis suis expositurint ac definierint. Protestantes nullam sibi privatam revelationem arrogant; nullam arcanam traditionem jactant; nullum novum doctrinæ principium obtrudunt. Uno, cöq; antiquissimo & maximè authentico Christianismi instrumento Veteres scilicet & Novo Testamento nituntur. Non nego quædam eos, sed pauca, in locorum Scripturæ expositionibus afferre, quæ vix in Patrum Scriptis occurrant. Sed ea, quod non sint ad fidem necessaria, argumento à Patrum silentio ducto refelli validè non possunt. Multa enim tempus & experientia, multa ipsæ Patrum regulæ, imò etiam interdum hallucinationes, in divina revelatione aperuerunt, quæ olim obscuriora ac difficiliora erant. Quis nescit Pygmæum gigantis humeris impositum altius & longius quam gigantem ipsum prospicere? Ridiculus esset qui quæ prospicit pumilio in rerum natura exiitere ideo negaret, quod ea gigas non vidisset. Neque sanior esset si quis Pygmæum arrogantiæ accusaret, quòd ea sibi visa referret de quibus nihil gigas dixerat, qui, etsi ista ipse non vidit, effecit tamen ut ea Pygmæus videret; ita ut omnis hujus cognitio illi quoque accepta ferenda sit. Eadem est nostri ratio, inquiunt Protestantes. Stamus in humeris proceræ illius & celsæ Antiquitatis. Itaque quòd potiori ac celsiori quàm ea fuit, loco (quanquam & ipsius beneficio) sumus, eo fit ut in Scripturis quædam ultra quam ipsa vidit intueri atque animadvertere possimus. Neque verò est quòd nobis idcirco multùm placeamus, cùm si quid ultra Antiquitatem videamus, id, ut plurimum, ipsis Antiquitati debeamus. Ex quibus constat Protestantes quidem esse extra omnem hujus disputationis aleam, si ea spectentur quæ ipsi affirmativa, ac (ut loquimur) positiva in fidei suæ expositionibus habent. Ecclesiam verò Romanam, ob rationes supra à nobis expositas, nihil juvant Patrum monumenta ad ea probanda dogmata quæ ipsa, præter Protestantium fidem, ponit atque constituit, ita ut omnino de aliis argumentis cogitare eam necesse sit, si quid velit hanc causam promovere. Cæterum in ea sum sententias, ut Romæ, non quidem bono ac commodo, sed potiùs damno ac exitio antiquitatem utilissimè adhiberi posse putem; nempè si diligenter ac summo labore summaque attentione inquiramus, an quæ Roma, præter Protestantium fidem ponit ac decernit, ea quoque pariter posuerit ac decreverit Antiquitas. Nam si non potuisse deprehendatur, certum erit, nisi fallor, inde argumentum, ista qualiacunque de cætero sint, certè capita Christianissimi necessaria nequaquam esse. Fateor argumentum in iis non valere quæ Roma sic docet, ut ea tamen nondum censeat in capitibus ad fidem necessariis; nam quæ sunt hujus census ea, & à veteribus potuerunt, & etiamnum à nobis possunt, nullo periculo ignorari. Sed omni exceptione majus mihi videtur argumentum in iis capitibus quæ Roma ad fidem necessaria esse contendit, & in quibus salutis ipsius summam collocare non veretur qualia sunt, exempli gratia, summa Papæ Ecclesiæ quæ eum pro capite agnoscit auctoritas. Eucharistiæ sacramenti adoratio. Missæ sacrificium, Arcanæ confessionis necessitas, & alia ejus commatis. Ista, si ejus revera sunt, cujus esse dicuntur, momenti, nescivisse Patres nemo pius dixerit, scivisse autem ista eos, neque de iis tamen in tam multis quæ superstunt operibus verbum unum fecisse, nemo prudens vel asseruerit vel crediderit. Neque illud cuiquam cordato in mentem venire potest, scripsisse quidem de istis Patres aliqua, sed loca fuisse aliquorum fraude vel expuncta vel vitiata. Si quid enim hujusmodi factum esset, eorum ipsorum damno factum esset qui libros asservabant; quod non est verisimile ita factum esse. Justius, veriúsque est suspicari libros Ecclesiæ Romanæ bono, ac in fidei, quam illa docet, gratiam esse mutatos, quoties antecedtis seculis mutati sunt; quod fuisse, priore libro, ostendimus. Ergo si postquam tandiu in hoc desudavit Ecclesia Romana, experimentisque tam multis docuit se & cupere vehementer illa fidei suæ capita testimoniis Patrum confirmare, neque admodum ab eo abhorrere, ut Patrum monumentis quæ desunt ea de suo asuat vel inferat; si (inquam) post tot molimina ac tempora probari posset, Patrum tamen voluminibus nondum illa contineri, quis dubitaret ea toti Antiquitati fuisse incognita? nedum ut creditu ad salutem necessaria jam tum censerentur? Quæ vero credita necessaria non putarunt illorum temporum Patres, ea cur nunc necessaria facta esse existimemus, nulla plane ratio est. Ergo quæ Roma, præter Protestantium fidem, definit ac docet vera esse, non potest quidem ex Antiquitatis auctoritate demonstrari (etiamsi cum Roma de his consensisse probaretur) sed ista falsa esse & inania valide demonstrabitur, si probetur hæc, vel veteribus prorsus ignotafuisse, vel certe non eo quo nunc habentur loco ac numero fuisse. Hoc autem ego quidem, tanti esse judico, ut ad id consequendum Protestantes temporis ac labo-
units.tr: Hardly any face is so lovely that it is entirely free of blemish and stain. Even a beauty that has its own faults, though slight, is still praised and loved. Perhaps it is our lot that nothing among us is wholly blessed, so that no one pleases without indulgence. Besides, the Fathers also yield another notable benefit. Sometimes men arise who are puffed up with the sense of their own flesh and who forge doctrines drawn from their own wit, not from any principles of true religion. To check the boldness of such men, the authority of the ancients can be most opportunely brought to bear. Clearly, if you show that the doctrines they push were wholly unknown to the Fathers, then, if this can be demonstrated, it must be firmly held that such doctrines were never handed down to mankind by Christ or the Apostles. For no plausible pretence can be made that the holy teachers of earlier ages, through whom Christianity came down to us, were ignorant of anything that the Lord revealed and commended to us as being of some importance and necessary for salvation. I would not deny that the Fathers, deceived by some fallacious reasoning or by a specious authority, sometimes taught things that Christ never revealed and that are clearly false and rest on no sound foundation, as we have shown by the examples given above. Nor would I deny that some things which Christ did reveal to us in Scripture, but which are not absolutely necessary to saving faith, could have escaped the Fathers: either because Scripture had not yet disclosed the meaning, time and outcome of such matters; or because they did not bring enough attention to weighing them; or because, hindered by some zeal or passion, they did not notice what was already shining forth. But that all of them should have missed anything that pertained necessarily to faith is by no means possible. For if that were so, it would have to be conceded that they had fallen from salvation, a thought from which all good people shrink. I confess, therefore, that the argument, which this work, if I am not mistaken, has sufficiently demonstrated, is weak and unsound: the argument by which something is concluded to be true because the Fathers thought so, since it presupposes what is plainly false, namely that all the Fathers had their opinions from the revelation of Christ. What kind of argument would it be that concluded, from the agreement of the Fathers, that all souls are kept apart in some custody until the day of judgment, or that the Eucharist is necessary for infants, or other things of that sort? In these cases everyone sees the futility of such proofs. Yet this is exactly how the Roman Church argues when it appeals to the authority of the Fathers to prove its own doctrines, which the Protestants reject. I also admit that the argument would be faulty and foolish of someone who inferred from the fact that the Fathers in general did not think some article of faith necessary to salvation that the article is nothing, or false. For one who so concludes presupposes what is manifestly false, namely that the Fathers clearly saw and acknowledged each and every thing that Christ revealed to us in his Word. The same judgment would be made in the school of the Franciscans of one who argued from the silence of the Fathers and contended that the Blessed Virgin was conceived without sin. But I acknowledge and affirm that an argument drawn from the Fathers is valid whenever it is concluded that a doctrine is not necessary to salvation because all the ancient writers alike kept a deep silence about it. For example, if someone were to prove that those secret means of salvation which Muhammad, or David Georgius, or other wicked impostors of the same stamp handed down to their disciples as most certain and necessary, are false and empty and contrary to the will of Christ, because the Fathers knew nothing of them at all and never said a single word about them, then, in my judgment, such an argument would be firm and unanswerable. This is exactly the method by which Irenaeus argued against the Valentinians and the other Gnostics, who put forward the mad dreams of their own brains, sucking out of them that the Creator of the world was a mere angel, who had over him certain higher divinities, which they called Aeons, that is, ages; some set up more of them, some fewer, and one man counted three hundred and sixty-five, and countless other monsters, supported by no foundation of reason or Scripture. Irenaeus, therefore, to teach that this shameful doctrine was not born of the Spirit of Christ but from the wit of one of these men, examined the records and sacred diptychs of all the Churches that the Apostles had either planted or watered; he searched the commentaries, letters and monuments of the Apostles. In them, since there were no such Aeons, Achamoth and Barbelo of the Gnostics, and no trace of them appeared anywhere, he concluded that the Apostles, neither in writing nor by word of mouth, had handed on anything to their disciples about the mysteries of the Gnostics, as those sycophants pretended. For if anything of this sort had been handed down by any means to the disciples of the Apostles, it certainly could not have happened that it would have perished so quickly from the memory of all men. Tertullian used the same method in refuting those very heretics and others of the same chaff, as may be seen in De praescript. cap. 22, and elsewhere. I do not hesitate to affirm that this method is strong and effective, since such great men went before us in it. Hence it is clear that the authority of the Fathers serves as a kind of second barrier after the Scriptures, to check and blunt the boldness of those impostors who attempt at times to forge a new faith and to thrust new and unheard-of mysteries upon the world under the false name of Christ. It is certain that Scripture alone could suffice for this purpose, if it were truly given the reverence that is due to it by all. But those who invent new doctrines out of their own brains generally despise and scorn the holy Scriptures, and this was a common practice of the very oldest heretics whom Irenaeus refutes. For, as he says: When they are refuted from the Scriptures, they turn the accusation against the Scriptures themselves, as though they were not right nor authoritative, and because they are variously expressed, and because the truth cannot be found in them by those who do not know the tradition. For that tradition was delivered not by letters but by the living voice. Therefore, against this contempt for Scripture, the monuments of the Fathers are most useful in this matter; and it seems that they were preserved for us in such great number, amid so many and so great upheavals and confusions of human affairs, by the most wise providence of the best God, chiefly for this purpose and with this aim in view. So if the Protestants were to devise something of their own wit and press it as absolutely necessary to salvation, something that appears nowhere among the ancients, I grant that they could be refuted by this method. But it is well known that nothing of this kind is contained in their faith. They lay down nothing, affirm or establish nothing, that is not either plainly found in Scripture or clearly follows from it, and which the ancient Fathers, if you except a very few things, did not express and define not only in their books but also in their creeds and the decrees of their synods. The Protestants claim no private revelation; they boast of no secret tradition; they thrust on no new principle of doctrine. They rest upon one document of Christianity, the most ancient and most authentic, namely the New Testament, and upon the Old Testament as well. I do not deny that they bring forward some things, but few, in their expositions of passages of Scripture, which scarcely occur in the writings of the Fathers. But these things, because they are not necessary to faith, cannot be effectively refuted by an argument drawn from the silence of the Fathers. For time and experience have revealed many things in the divine revelation, many things that were once more obscure and difficult, and so have the very rules of the Fathers, and even, at times, their errors. Who does not know that a pygmy, placed on the shoulders of a giant, sees further and higher than the giant himself? It would be ridiculous to deny that the things a pygmy sees exist in nature simply because the giant did not see them. Nor would someone be any more sensible if he accused the pygmy of arrogance because he reported things that he had seen and about which the giant said nothing; for, although the giant did not see those things himself, he nevertheless made it possible for the pygmy to see them, so that all knowledge of them must be credited to the giant as well. The same is our position, the Protestants say. We stand on the shoulders of that tall and lofty Antiquity. So, because we are in a higher and loftier place than it was (though by its own benefit), it follows that we can see and notice in the Scriptures some things beyond what it saw. Nor should we be very pleased with ourselves on this account, since if we see anything beyond Antiquity, we owe it, for the most part, to Antiquity itself. From these things it is established that the Protestants are indeed beyond all risk of this dispute, if one considers what they hold in their expositions of faith as affirmative and, as we say, positive. But as for the Roman Church, for the reasons we have set out above, the monuments of the Fathers do nothing to help prove those doctrines which it itself, apart from the faith of the Protestants, lays down and establishes; so that it must of necessity think of other arguments altogether if it wishes to advance this cause. Moreover, I am of the opinion that antiquity could be most usefully brought to bear against Rome, not indeed for its good or benefit, but rather for its harm and ruin; namely, if we inquire diligently, with the greatest labour and the greatest attention, whether Antiquity also laid down and decreed the things which Rome, apart from the faith of the Protestants, lays down and decrees. For if it cannot be found that it did, it will be certain, unless I am mistaken, that from this there follows the argument that those doctrines, of whatever kind they may be, are certainly not necessary articles of the Christian faith. I grant that the argument does not hold in the case of those things which Rome teaches in such a way that it nevertheless does not count them among the articles necessary to faith; for whatever is of that kind could have been unknown to the ancients, and can still be unknown to us without any danger. But the argument seems to me to be of the greatest weight, beyond all exception, regarding those articles which Rome insists are necessary to faith, and on which it does not hesitate to place the sum of salvation itself; such as, for example, the supreme authority of the Pope, the Church which acknowledges him as its head; the adoration of the sacrament of the Eucharist; the sacrifice of the Mass; the necessity of secret confession; and others of that kind. If these are truly of the importance that they are said to be, no pious man would say that the Fathers were ignorant of them; yet no prudent man would assert or believe that they knew them, and yet made not a single word about them in so many works that survive. Nor can it come into the mind of any sensible person that the Fathers did indeed write something about these matters, but that the passages were struck out or corrupted by the fraud of some people. For if anything of this kind had been done, it would have been done to the loss of those very people who kept the books; and it is not likely that it was done in this way. It is more just and more true to suspect that the books have been altered for the benefit of the Roman Church, and to the favour of the faith that it teaches, as often as they have been altered in earlier centuries; which, as we showed in the previous book, has happened. Therefore, if, after the Roman Church has laboured so long at this, and has shown by so many attempts that it greatly wishes to confirm those articles of its faith by the testimonies of the Fathers, and is not at all averse to adding or inserting from its own resources what is lacking in the writings of the Fathers; if (I say) after so many efforts and so much time it could be proved that those articles are still not contained in the writings of the Fathers, who would doubt that they were wholly unknown to all Antiquity, much less that they were already then regarded as articles to be believed for salvation? But as for those things which the Fathers of those times did not think necessary to believe, there is absolutely no reason to suppose that they are now necessary. Therefore, what Rome defines and teaches as true, apart from the faith of the Protestants, cannot indeed be demonstrated from the authority of Antiquity (even if it were shown that Rome agreed with Antiquity on these matters); but that those things are false and empty will be powerfully demonstrated if it is shown that these were either wholly unknown to the ancients, or at least did not hold the place and number they now hold. Now I judge this to be of such importance that, in order to attain it, the Protestants ought to devote some part of their time and labour, beyond what they already give, to reading the Fathers.

Id unum tum ab his, tum etiam ab alterius partis hominibus postulo ac flagito, ut ad opus tantum omnibus rebus necessariis instructi accedant, ut linguarum & historiae & S.Scripturarum cognitione; tum ut in id cum cura & attentione sedula incumbant, accuratèque quicquid veterum scriptorum superest evolvant, ita ut nihil quod haberi possit negligant aut praetermittant, cum brevia interdum & exigui in speciem momenti loca plurimum lucis ad Veterum mente percipiendam afferant, neve putent (quod nonnullis scio contigisse) se omnem veterum de religione sententiam tenere, postquam quatuor aut quinque menses in ea inquirenda collocarint. Sed nihil in hoc instituto magis necessarium arbitror, quam ut eo animum afferas studiis & odiis, aliisque affectibus vacuum, ex quibus omnis fere illa obscuritas nascitur, quam in his scriptoribus experimur, dum utrique ad sensum singuli nostrum eorum verba inflectere contendimus, quos vero affirmare posse videor de controversiis hodie capitibus cum neutris plane penitusque conferre, sed in his aliquanto quidem quam Protestantes ulterius, multo vero quam Romanos citerius, ac parcius provectos esse. Neque in hoc instituto satis est testimonia, quae formaliter (ut loquuntur) & discerne id ipsum quod quaeritur vel negant vel affirmant, annotasse, (utcunque enim perspicua fuerint, vix erit ut sophistarum acumina ac praestigias effugiant, qui suis technis interdum efficiunt, ut etiam in claro meridie nox fit, quod ex hodiernis controversiarum libris intelligi poterit, in quibus utrique locorum e veteribus objectorum vim tanta arte eludunt, ut quid sequaris vix appareat.) Sed observandae etiam sunt unius cujusque dogmatis consequentiae necessariae. Fieri enim non potest ut quicquam, quod sit alicujus momenti, ponas, quin ex eo ita posito multa statim tum intra, tum extra Ecclesiam consequantur. Ut, exempli gratia, diligenter ad ea attendendum est, quæ panis Eucharistici Transubstantiationem, Purgatorium, auctoritatem Papæ Monarchicam consequuntur; & cùm ea probè animadverteris considerandum est, an Veteres legenti vel omnia, vel quædam certè occurrant. Nam si nulla apud eos extent, argumentum est invictum ea dogmata, ex quibus hæc nascuntur, nullo, tum temporis, loco fuisse. Sed non est nostri instituti fusiùs ista persequi. Alii non pauci abundè præstiterunt. Neque ex his quæ hactenus disputavimus difficile est intelligere, quo modo, quave methodo, vel quo fructu legenda sanctorum Patrum scripta putemus.
units.tr: [marginal mark in text, no printed note text legible] of their time and labour to reading the Fathers. This one thing I demand and insist upon, both from these men and from people of the other party: that they come to the work equipped with everything necessary, namely a knowledge of languages, of history and of the Holy Scriptures; and then that they apply themselves to it with care and diligent attention, and work carefully through whatever remains of the ancient writers, so that they neglect or pass over nothing that can be had. Brief and seemingly unimportant passages often throw much light on the mind of the ancients. Nor should they think (as I know has happened to some) that they hold the whole opinion of the ancients about religion after they have spent four or five months inquiring into it. But in this undertaking I judge nothing more necessary than that you bring to it a mind free from partisanship and hatreds and other passions, from which almost all that obscurity arises which we experience in these writers, while each of us strives to bend their words to his own sense. I seem able to affirm that on the controverted questions of today they have advanced not at all, or fully and entirely, toward either side. Rather, they have gone somewhat further than the Protestants, but far less far than the Romanists, and more sparingly. Nor, in this undertaking, is it enough to have noted the testimonies which (as they say) formally either deny or affirm the very point in question. However clear they may be, it will hardly be possible to escape the subtleties and tricks of the sophists, who by their arts sometimes make it night even in broad daylight. This can be understood from the modern books of controversy, in which each side so cleverly evades the force of the ancient passages cited against it that it is scarcely apparent what you are following. But the necessary consequences of each doctrine must also be observed. For it is impossible that you posit anything of any importance without many things at once following from that position, both inside and outside the Church. For example, one must attend carefully to the things which the transubstantiation of the eucharistic bread, Purgatory, and the monarchical authority of the Pope entail. When you have carefully noted these, you must consider whether the ancient writers present to the reader either all of them or at least some of them. For if none of them appear among the ancients, it is an unanswerable argument that the doctrines from which these arise had no place at that time. But it is not within my plan to pursue these matters at greater length. Not a few others have done this abundantly. And from what we have discussed so far, it is not difficult to understand how, by what method, or to what profit we think the writings of the holy Fathers should be read.
